believe that the use of EI development tools in the English language teaching (ELT)
classroom will improve the quality of training graduates and equip them with essential
21st century competences.
2
Analysis of Recent Research and Publications
The concept of EI was disclosed in a non-cognitive theory of EI offered by R. Bar-On
[1]; theories of emotional and intellectual abilities were formulated by J.D. Mayer and
R. Salovey [2]; a mixed theory of emotional competence was developed by D. Goleman
[3]. W. Zhang and O. Adegbola wrote about EI-based training for future public relations
leaders, and discussed an EI model used to develop professionalism in public relations
education [4]. The necessity and beneﬁts of the development of EI for the managerial
as well as research and teaching staff of education institutions was substantiated [5–8],
along with the beneﬁts of its development in the workplace and in the training process [9].
The question of using interactive technologies in the educational process was considered
by T. Bondarenko, O. Kupriyanov [10] et al.
Yu. Fedorova, K. Babenko, Ya. Malykhina, O. Yarmosh and V. Malykhina [11] claim
that under the pressure of the digital revolution a set of competences that a successful
modern person should possess is changing. The economic paradigm shift is focusing
on human capital and the use of human knowledge and intelligence to create added
value [12], leading to the introduction of lifelong learning and “just in time” educa-
tion, encouraging the development of soft skills, which ensure effective communication,
cooperationandrelationshipmanagement,and,therefore,enhancingEI.Emotionalintel-
ligence embraces some of the top 10 skills that will be in demand by 2025 according to
the list of the International Economic Forum [13], namely, leadership and social impact,
endurance, stress resistance and ﬂexibility. English proﬁciency is also recognized as a
basic 21st century life skill. In July 2019, at a meeting of the MES Board, the Min-
istry of Education and Science of Ukraine devised and approved the Concept of English
Language Development in Universities [14]. The document provides for the organiza-
tion of language courses and intensives, and requires students of all higher education
institutions in Ukraine to demonstrate that they possess the expected English language
proﬁciency level. Reforms in the ﬁeld of education have increased the interest of scien-
tists in researching the questions of human capital and students’ emotional perception of
the learning process. This automatically requires expanding the range of research topics,
and increases the demand for high quality teaching at higher education institutions in
free economic zones, as noted in the work of Yu. Fedorova [15]. However, despite a

Developing Students’ Emotional in the Speaking Club Format
43
considerable amount of foreign scientiﬁc papers dealing with issues of developing EI in
the ELT classroom, there are still a number of uncertain questions about EI development
tools within the system of higher education. We consider the development of emotional
intelligence in the teaching and learning processes in the ﬁeld of higher education to be
a very promising research area in Ukraine and abroad.
The aim of the present research is to design and test tools for the development of
emotional intelligence of students in the process of learning English in classes organized
in the speaking club format.
3
Results and Discussion
The study necessitated applying a combination of research methods aimed at assessing
the level of EI development during English language classes taught in the speaking club
format. The qualitative method was used to consider thoughts, ideas and achievements
of the participants in a subjective way. The quantitative method was chosen to collect
quantiﬁable data from students, analyze the ﬁgures, and conduct tests in an objective
way.
All in all, 62 students of Ukrainian Engineering Pedagogics Academy (UEPA) took
part in English classes held in the speaking club format. 158 students of Ukrainian
Engineering Pedagogics Academy and V.N. Karazin Kharkiv National University took
part in psychological testing. The participants were aged between 17 and 25.
The study included the following stages: 1) designing an instrumental model of
EI development; 2) conducting English classes in the speaking club format at UEPA
during the 2020/2021 academic year in such a way as to ensure the development of
each component of the model; 3) developing a questionnaire and implementing the ﬁrst
psychometric tests; 4) validating the EI test; 5) analyzing the obtained results.
The processing of the testing data was performed in MS Excel, SPSS, STATISTICA,
FACTOR, and R-Studio. At the ﬁrst stage, the discriminativity of the test was conﬁrmed,
and an exploratory and conﬁrmatory factor analysis was performed using the principal
components method with the polychoric correlation coefﬁcients, direct Oblimin rotation
and hierarchical factor solution (Schmid-Leiman solution) to check the correctness of the
test structure. At the second stage, two other tests for a similar psychological construct –
EI – authored by N. Hall and D. Lyusin were used to verify the validity (correctness,
reliability) of the new test, and Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was performed.
All the participants were informed verbally about the details of the research and a
signed written consent on being included in the experiment was received from each of
them.
The term “emotional intelligence” has existed for more than 30 years, but began to be
widely used and studied only in the last decade. R. Bar-On [1], an Israeli psychologist,
ﬁrst introduced the concept of emotional coefﬁcient. The most popular EI models were
proposed by R. Bar-On [1]), J.D. Mayer and R. Salovey [2], and D. Goleman [3].
According to J.D. Mayer and R. Salovey, who authored the original concept of EI,
emotional intelligence is a group of mental abilities that contribute to the awareness
and understanding of one’s own emotions and the emotions of others. The possibility
of developing these abilities throughout life necessitates the development of appropriate
tools and methodological bases in the learning environment.

44
Y. Fedorova et al.
Quite often, along with the term “emotional intelligence” the term “emotional com-
petence” (EC) is used. According to C. Saarni [16], emotional competence shapes the
ability to adapt and believe in one’s own abilities. To describe emotional competence,
C. Saarni uses the term “skill”, which distinguishes it from the concept of emotional
intelligence. Emotional competence is the knowledge and skills that a person can acquire
in order to be able to act appropriately in different situations. It depends on the ability to
“turn on” emotions, or rather, to manage them in such a way as to achieve certain goals.
Similarly, emotional competence is a prerequisite for an active social life. J.D. Mayer and
R. Salovey [2] also believe that emotional competence comprises an ability to process
the most complex information related to emotions and use that information as a guide
in the process of thinking and acting. D. Goleman [17] deﬁnes emotional competence
as an acquired property based on emotional intelligence. The author identiﬁes 25 emo-
tional competences, which are grouped by 5 components of EI, namely self-awareness,
self-regulation, motivation, empathy, and social skills.
Despite a considerable number of approaches to developing EI, so far no convenient
model of EI development has been proposed that could be easily employed in applied
business and education. Therefore, we simpliﬁed the structure of EI according to the
model devised by D. Goleman, and now offer a 4-component instrumental model of EI,
which is based on the following components: self-awareness, self-management, social
awareness, and relationship management (Table 1).
The proposed model contains four components of emotional intelligence, which
allows building a convenient graphical representation of the results as an EI diagram
consisting of four quadrants (Fig. 1). The horizontal axis shows the direction of EI
coverage (from left to right): from the individual level to the social group level, and the
vertical axis shows the degree of EI control (bottom up): from understanding to managing
one’s own emotions and the emotions of others. Quantitative characteristics of each of
the four indicators for the 4-component instrumental model of EI are displayed as a
side of the corresponding quadrant (Fig. 1). Within the training process, this approach
allows demonstrating the dynamics of each component of EI by increasing the area
of the corresponding quadrant. The side of the quadrant can range from 0 to 10. This
corresponds to the STEN (standard ten) score system. According to the STEN score
system, results ranging from 0 to 3 demonstrate a low level, results ranging from 4 to 7
show a medium level, and results ranging from 8 to 10 demonstrate a high level of the
development of the components of the 4-component instrumental model of EI. Figure 1
also shows how experiencing spontaneous emotions is transformed into EC.
For the ﬁrst time, the proposed 4-component instrumental model of EI was used
during English language classes of the speaking club format at Ukrainian Engineering
Pedagogics Academy (UEPA). Participation in the empirical study was voluntary.
Speaking club classes involved delivering speeches, watching and discussing audio
and video presentations, ﬁnding group solutions to business problems etc.
Group classes were carefully planned by the teacher, as reﬂected by H. Korniush
[18]. The students found classes particularly engaging and engrossing since they con-
tained elements of improvisation. Classroom activities of the speaking club format were
thoroughly and regularly analyzed.

The analysis of the main methods of diagnosing emotional competence suggested
by R.D. Roberts, Dzh. Metyuz, M. Zaydner and D.V. Lyusin [19], namely ECI (Emo-
tional Competence Inventory-360), EQ-i (Bar-On Emotional Quotient Inventory), SSRI
(Schutte et al. Self-Report Index), TEIQue (Trait Emotional Intelligence Question-
naire), MSCEIT (Mayer-Salovey-Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test), MEIS (Multi-
factor Emotional Intelligence Test), LEAS (Levels of Emotional Awareness), and EARS
(Emotional Accuracy Research Scale), revealed a large number of approaches and the
acceptability of a subjective approach to measuring EI, which is characterized by the
fact that it simpliﬁes the organization of testing, fosters cooperation and builds trust in
the testees.
Fig. 1. EI development diagram according to the 4-component instrumental EI model.
Taking into account the above methods and emotional competences of the compo-
nents of the 4-component instrumental model of EI given in Table 1, we developed a
test-questionnaire “Emotional Intelligence in Business”, which demonstrates the level
of EI and the degree of students’ readiness to perform professional activities.
158 people (120 women and 38 men) took part in the ﬁrst psychometric trial of the
new test, which is reﬂected in the work of O. Lutsenko, Yu. Fedorova and V. Tsokota
[20]. The testing was conducted on an online platform at https://testing-system-nure.her
okuapp.com/auth. Data processing was performed in MS Excel, SPSS, STATISTICA,
FACTOR, and R-Studio. First, the test contained 80 statements dealing with the business
area of using EI, with 20 statements assigned to each of the 4 scales (self-awareness, self-
management, social awareness, and relationship management). Further, as a result of the
psychometric checks, the test was shortened to 40 most effective statements (Table 2).
The discriminativity of all scales and the test as a whole is very high, with the
Ferguson coefﬁcient δ equaling 1.00. It means that the test is informative. It also means
that the test scores evenly distinguish people by EI level differences, and when a rather
big sample of people is surveyed, it is possible to identify individuals with very low,

low, middle, high, very high and everything in between levels. That is why the test can
differentiate people at as many levels of EI as there are scores in the test. The exploratory
factor analysis was conducted using the method of the principal components, polychoric
correlation coefﬁcients, direct Oblimin rotation and hierarchical factor solution (Schmid-
Leiman solution). It extracted one general factor and four subfactors, and showed that all
test items correlated with the relevant factors at the level of 0.30–0.83, i.e. at a sufﬁcient
level.
Relationship management and social awareness were found to be the most important
components for EI in Business as these factors explained the greater dispersion of the
EI construct. The internal reliability of the test and test scales turned out to be very high:
the Cronbach’s alpha coefﬁcient for the test of EI in Business in general equaled 0.932;
it reached 0.778 for the scale of self-awareness, 0.846 for the scale of self-management,
0.868 for the scale of social awareness, and 0.906 for the scale of relationship manage-
ment, with the minimum allowable being 0.600 (the higher, the more reliable the scale).
The reliability of the scales tested in the exploratory factor analysis was even higher:
0.927, 0.906, 0.866, and 0.865 respectively. This indicates the internal consistency of
the test and the low measurement error.
The social awareness component was discovered to have a signiﬁcantly higher level
among women in comparison to men (Mann-Whitney U Test: U = 1682, p = 0.014).
The self-awareness component increased proportionally along with the increase of the
year of study among higher education students: Kruskal-Wallis test: H = 12,618 p =
0,027. This was also conﬁrmed by correlating the level of self-awareness with the year
of study: ρ = 0.234, p = 0.003.
The convergent validity of the new EI test was conﬁrmed during the second stage of
the psychometric trials. To check the validity (correctness, reliability) of the new test,
two other tests were used for the same psychological construct – EI – designed by N.
Hall and D. Lyusin. Spearman’s rank correlation analysis and a sample of 26 people of
different ages and genders were used for testing. The results are demonstrated in Tables 3
and 4.
As evidenced by the data in Tables 3 and 4, the validity of the new test is proved by
high logical correlations between the scales and the general indicator in the test of EI
in Business and the scales of the already validated EI tests developed by D. Lyusin and
N. Hall. There is only one correlation missing between the scale of self-management

48
Y. Fedorova et al.
according to our test of EI in Business and the scale of emotional awareness in N. Hall’s
test. That is, self-management in the test of EI in Business is not equivalent to emotional
awareness embodied in N. Hall’s test. Indeed, if we compare the statements of these
test scales, the substantive validity of N. Hall’s test mostly involves awareness of the
value of one’s own emotions as a source of information about changing, improving and
managing one’s own life; for example, “For me, both negative and positive emotions are
a source of knowledge about how to act.” In contrast to the test designed by N. Hall,
in our test the substantive validity of the self-management scale refers to the control of
one’s own impulsive emotional reactions, in particular, reactionary criticism, conﬂicts,
stress, fatigue, change, anxiety and fears; for example, “I calmly respond to criticism
from employers.” One correlation was recorded at the level of a reliable connection
trend, which is between self-awareness according to the test of EI in Business and
emotional awareness according to the test developed by N. Hall: ρ = 0.374, p = 0.059.
An insufﬁcient level of reliability is likely to be sufﬁcient with an increase in the sample
of testees.
We calculated the norms for our test in “raw scores” according to the statistical
rule of “three sigma”, and translated them into the standard STEN score system. The
calculation of the norms showed that in our sample the least developed component of EI
is self-management: according to it, the largest numbers of people have low indicators
and the smallest numbers of people have high indicators.

Table 5 reveals the ways of building all the four components of the proposed model
when studying in the speaking club format. Such English classes develop students’ self-
awareness, self-management and social awareness as well as improve their relationship
management skills. The decisive advantage of boosting students’ emotional intelligence
through discussions is the development of their skills of self-reﬂection, self-control,
empathy and emotional inﬂuence under the greatest intellectual stress. The need to use
a foreign language intensiﬁes the process of developing new EI skills. The necessity to

52
Y. Fedorova et al.
leave the comfort zone constitutes the most effective condition to build soft skills, in
particular emotional competence.
Basic principles for conducting English classes include:
• Relevance (topics for discussion should be engaging and relevant);
• Spontaneity (as a rule, students do not know topics for discussion in advance);
• Openness (the teacher expresses their own opinion on each topic and listens to the
viewpoints of each student);
• Moderation (the teacher encourages students to take part in the discussion process,
regulates their talking time and equally gives each student a turn to speak);
• Interactivity, digitalization and edutainment features (modern games and interactive
methods for mastering the material through emotional perception should be used).
The introduction of the 4-component instrumental model of EI in English classes
held in the speaking club format allows students not only to gain relevant knowledge,
improve their vocabulary, grammar, speaking and listening skills, but also enhance the
most relevant 21st century soft skills, including EI, in a comfortable and engaging way.
4
Conclusions
The article has led through the process of developing the 4-component instrumental
model of EI, which helps to enhance students’ EI when studying English in group classes
organized in the speaking club format. The process of developing the key components of
EI(self-awareness,self-management,socialawareness,andrelationshipmanagement)in
foreign language classes organized in the speaking club format was described in detail.
The research showed that the need to speak a foreign language, i.e. to get out of the
comfort zone and to be able to think in a state of increased emotional stress, contributes
to a faster development of students’ emotional competence. In accordance with the
offered 4-component instrumental model of EI development, a reliable, discriminatory
andvalidtest“EmotionalIntelligenceinBusiness”wascreated,whichallowsmonitoring
the obtained outcomes. The use of this new tool provides an opportunity to improve
the quality of training and adaptation of graduates into the changing socio-economic
environment.
A further area of research is the development of information technology for diag-
nosing and enriching English classes with effective techniques for improving emotional
intelligence of students, monitoring the development of emotional intelligence of stu-
dents of different specialties during classes taught in the speaking club format, and
designing guidelines to conduct English classes for teaching staff similarly organized in
the format of a speaking club.

A Comprehensive Model for Augmented
Conﬁdence Based Learning (ACBL)
Rajeev Chatterjee1(B)
, Jyotsna Kumar Mandal2
, and Sadhu Prasad Kar2
1 National Institute of Technical Teachers’ Training and Research, Kolkata, India
chatterjee.rajeev@gmail.com
2 University of Kalyani, Kalyani, West Bengal, India
Abstract. Conﬁdence Based Learning (CBL) is a state-of-the art method of
Teaching and Learning System (TLS), where the customized content is deliv-
ered to a typical learner based on his lacunas in terms of knowledge level as
well as the level of conﬁdence in that knowledge. This system is of immense
importance in imparting training to the workforce where the performance of the
personnel is dependent to human live and properties and in case of deviation in the
performance it may lead to a catastrophic event. The CBL based system mainly
consists of three phases namely diagnose, prescribe and learning. The system prior
to delivery of any content identiﬁes the lacunas in terms of knowledge and level
of conﬁdence. Once the gaps in knowledge and conﬁdence level are identiﬁed, a
customized prescription of learning plan is provided to an individual learner. The
learner learns using the customized content and takes the assessment for obtaining
mastery. However, in context to this, there is a lack of an enhance and compre-
hensive framework for CBL based system, which will provide a blueprint for
development of applications related to this new TLS. The authors in this research
have identiﬁed the voids and propose a comprehensive framework which is com-
pared to the existing available solutions which shows considerable improvement
with respect to methodology and practical implications.
Keywords: e-learning · CBL · ACBL · ACBL framework
1
Introduction
The conventional Teaching and Learning System (TLS) plays a vital role in the Human
Resource Development (HRD) especially in the professional world, where knowledge
and skill set perform a crucial role in the performance in the world of work. Recent
development in the ﬁeld of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) has also
improvised the design development and dissemination of content and learning materials
that have eventually augmented the process of learning. In the professional world or at
jobsite it is needless to mention that certain domain requires knowledge as well as level
of conﬁdence in applying the knowledge for decision making failing which catastrophic
can happen and a loss of property and human life is inevitable. This includes domain of
work such as medical science, aviation, transportation and logistics, heavy industries,
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 55–66, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_6

56
R. Chatterjee et al.
and critical research areas. Inappropriate measures taken at any point of time can lead
to massacre and therefore appropriate decision making is required. Thus, Authentic
Learning (AL) can be applied in these domains. Further, it also requires building sound
knowledge and conﬁdence level in that knowledge so that appropriate decision and/or
measures can be taken at the nick of the moment. This open-up a new methodology in
TLS known as Conﬁdence Based Learning (CBL) [1]. Following Subsects. 1.1 and 1.2
discusses the concepts of AL and CBL.
1.1
Authentic Learning (AL)
AL plays a vital role in the TLS especially in the ﬁeld of professional programs. AL
maps the classroom knowledge and skill set to the real-world problems in the world of
work. This is particularly done by problem-based learning approaches [2]. This form of
learning plays a key role in carrying out knowledge to the ﬁeld work and hence enhances
the problem-solving skills of a typical learner.
1.2
Conﬁdence Based Learning (CBL)
CBL is a state-of-the-art methodology of TLS that not only assess the learner for its
knowledge level but also takes care of the level of conﬁdence in the domain knowledge
[3]. This enhances the decision-making capabilities of a learner, thus enabling him/her to
take appropriate decision in the nick of the moment. On the other hand, this enhancement
of a typical learner makes the system more reliable, efﬁcient and performance oriented.
A CBL based system consists of three phases namely diagnose, prescribe and learning.
In the diagnose phase, a learner is assessed for his/her knowledge gaps and lacunas
and the gaps in the level of conﬁdence in the knowledge in an appropriate domain.
The prescribe phase provide customized knowledge content to a typical learner. This
knowledge content is prescribed based on the identiﬁed lacunas of a learner, which were
identiﬁed in the diagnose phase. In the learning phase the learner learns to develop
knowledge level as well as to build the conﬁdence level in that knowledge. This prepares
him/her for further assessment. CBL based systems are iterative in nature and the learner
continues to traverse through the various phases described here until he/she attains
mastery level in a particular area or domain.
Initially, at a few medical schools Certainty Based Marking (CBM) were applied
for their students in diagnosing patients [4]. Thereafter, the researchers in the ﬁeld of
education came with the model of CBL. However, very few comprehensive models were
available for implementation of the CBL based system in real scenario. The authors of
this manuscript have proposed a comprehensive model of CBL based system and termed
as Augmented Conﬁdence Based Learning (ACBL) model.
This manuscript is organized as follows. Section 2 contains review of the related
work. The proposed model has been suggested in Sect. 3. Results and discussions are
given in Sect. 4. Section 5 provide a conclusion and future scope.
2
Review of the Existing Work
CBL based systems are predominantly used in the training and education in the profes-
sional world. This has primarily created a separate domain in the ﬁeld of education and

A Comprehensive Model
57
training where the system is not only concerned with the knowledge dissemination but
also banks on the 2-D assessment technique that will not only assess the knowledge level
of the learner but also the level of conﬁdence the learner has in the knowledge compo-
nent. This conﬁdence level will precisely help the learner at the jobsite to take decision
in ordinary and extraordinary situations. The authors in this research review the existing
work done by the peer level research towards the accomplishment of a comprehensive
model for CBL based system.
According to Benjamin S. Bloom in his book Taxonomy of Educational Objectives
the TLS has three distinct domains namely cognitive, adaptive, and psychomotor [5].
Cognitive domain deals with the knowledge component of a typical learner. This domain
primarily has 6 distinct levels popularly identiﬁed as knowledge, comprehensive, appli-
cation, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. The affective domain as well as psychomotor
domain also deals with 5 and 7 levels. However, in context to Blooms taxonomy little
evidence was established between knowledge and conﬁdence level of a typical learner.
Marton and Saljo in their article proposed the concept of deep vs surface learn-
ing approaches [6]. They experimentally established the role of these two learning
approaches. However, no study was done to establish that these approaches were used in
problem solving methods. Furthermore, none of these approaches were used to establish
the level of conﬁdence for the knowledge of a learner.
CBL based systems are designed to cater to personalized content that may augment
the knowledge level as well as level of conﬁdence in that knowledge. Aleahmad et al. in
their paper, highlighted the tasks of customizing learning chunk for a learner [7]. This
process demands varied learning content in any domain. The challenge is in creating
and maintaining of large amount of learning substance varied in content that can satisfy
various interest and abilities. The authors suggest and assess a web-based tool for open
authoring of learning resources that were given to professional and amateur instructors.
However, the authors failed to establish the relationship between the customized content
development process and the conﬁdence level in that customized content.
Jong et al. in their manuscript suggested a model for constructivist pedagogical
approach to game-based learning [8]. It incorporates the creation of a near real-life
online interactive world modelled upon a set of multidisciplinary domains, in which
each learner plays a role in this “virtual world” and shapes its development. However,
no evidence has been provided in establishing the knowledge level and conﬁdence in
the knowledge for a typical learner.
Churchill in his research article have highlighted the importance of LOs [9]. The
author conceptualized the learning objects as an interactive tool in representation of
knowledge components.
Northrup in her book Learning Objects for Instruction, clariﬁes how practical mod-
els of LOs should be designed and developed in the ﬁeld of education, management,
industry and military [10]. These LO have diverse application from theoretical concepts
to practical applications in the ﬁeld of work.
Ritzhaupt in his article explain the requirement of the LO in the era of ICT [11]. The
authors gave a theoretical framework of an LO and created a taxonomy for the LO.
Fernandez-Diego et al. in their research article introduced a concept of Aggregated
Quality Index for assessing the quality of LOs by using statistical method from the

58
R. Chatterjee et al.
resources [12]. Metadata standards for LOs are adopted as metrics for quality and
their appropriateness is determined by statistical methods. Metadata Quality Assess-
ment Certiﬁcation Process (MQACP) addresses the way in which metadata quality can
be improved in Learning Object Repositories (LORs).
However, in the above review work none of the authors have presented any
relationship with the knowledge component and conﬁdence level.
Stanley in his research provided several parameters to exhibit the conﬁdence includ-
ing a penalty mechanism in two level hierarchy [13]. First, the learner has to perform in
rationalmannerinaconﬁdenceweightagesituation,indicatinghighrelationshipbetween
possession of knowledge and willingness to express. Second, the methodology is not
biased against certain learners. The conﬁdence weight was presented on a three-point
scale namely guess, fairly conﬁdent and very conﬁdent.
Gardner-Medwin et al. their manuscript has introduced Conﬁdence-Based Assess-
ment (CBA), in which a student’s rating of his/her conﬁdence in an answer is considered
in the marking of the answer [14].
Nath & Chatterjee proposed a 2-D assessment method by implementing with
weighted level of conﬁdence factor [15]. The conﬁdence-based assessment was having
three level of conﬁdence factor say 1, 2, 3.
Kar et al. in their study on assessment elaborated about the limitation of objective
assessment items [16]. They presented the limitation of the objective type responses
when a learner is required to be evaluated for deep learning approaches.
However, in these research activities a comprehensive mechanism for establishing
relationship with knowledge and conﬁdence level could not be established.
Lombardi in her research contribution presented the concept of AL [2]. She stressed
on the importance of learning by solving real world complex and ill-deﬁned problems.
She reported that this methodology of learning cultivates and exhibit portable skills such
as judgement, patience, synthetic, ability, and ﬂexibility.
Wornyo et al. have proposed to have authentic learning in soft-skill domain, espe-
cially into domain of English language as a second language [17]. The learners were
involved in the tasks and activities of the Authentic Learning Process (ALP) including
Group Discussion (GD) and interview sessions.
However, none of the methods applied in the above two cases have been fruitful in
establishing relationship between AL and CBL.
Chatterjee et al. in their manuscript presented a macro level design of a LMS for
CBL [3]. The macro level design was presented using UML, where use case diagrams
were presented to establish relationship of various process.
Bhattacharya et al. in their research work proposed an intelligent recognizer of the
cognitive state of an e-learner as an integral part of Conﬁdence-Based e-Learning (CBeL)
system [18]. This addresses the problem of providing technology-driven pedagogical
support to an e-learner to achieve the desired cognitive state of mastery.
However, none of the research papers have provided a comprehensive design of an
LMS that will implement a CBL based system as a process.

A Comprehensive Model
59
2.1
Problem Domain and Research Gap
In CBL based system the knowledge as well as conﬁdence level of a typical learner is
required to be measured so that appropriate level of learning content may be prescribed
to the learner. This is very critical because the CBL based system identiﬁes a learner
knowledge and conﬁdence level in one of the four quadrants namely mastery, doubt,
ignorant and misconception. The knowledge component as well as conﬁdence level
together help in decision making in ordinary and critical situation. The LMS for CBL
based system thus require a comprehensive diagnosis mechanism as well as learning
content prescription methods to accomplish the requirement placed by the system. In
the existing solutions, that are available, a comprehensive architecture or framework for
the aforesaid TL mechanism is missing. Based on these shortcomings a comprehensive
methodology has been proposed.
3
Proposed Methodology
In the proposed model for ACBL, the authors analyze the requirement of a TLS that
works on the principle of CBL based system. The model has been proposed using the
tools and techniques of the software engineering. At an initial level, the actors of these
model have been identiﬁed. There are three major types of actors, namely:
• Learners: Learners are the major stakeholders of the CBL based system. They are the
important beneﬁciaries among all.
• Instructors: After learners, the instructors are the important actors in the CBL based
system. They are involved with the learning content development, design, and devel-
opment of the assessment items and last but not the least they are involved with
monitoring of the learning process.
• Administrators: Administrators are responsible for the proper administration of the
CBL based system. They supervise the overall performance and manages the three
phases of the system.
3.1
The Proposed Model
The proposed model has been designed based on software engineering methodology con-
sisting of two signiﬁcant components. These are ‘diagnose’ and ‘update’ components.
The schematic diagram of the proposed model is given in Fig. 1.
The ‘diagnose’ component is further classiﬁed into two subcomponents, namely
CBA and DD. Similarly, the ‘update’ component has two processes namely prescribe
andleaning.Thearchitectureproposedintheﬁgureisbasicallyaniterativeinnature.This
implies that unless or until a leaner obtains mastery, he/she will be traversing through
the ‘diagnose’ and ‘update’ components. The four different states of a learning using
the knowledge quadrant has been given in Fig. 2.
Learner with little knowledge and low conﬁdence will be in ‘Uninformed’ quadrant.
Learner with sufﬁcient level of knowledge with low conﬁdence level is placed in ‘Doubt’
quadrant. Learner with insufﬁcient knowledge and high conﬁdence level is placed in

‘Misinformed’ quadrant. These mental states of a learner require to pass through the
Update component of the architecture and again sit for the assessment. Only learners
who have high level of knowledge and conﬁdence level obtain ‘Mastery’. The signiﬁcant
components of the proposed architecture are given in Sect. 3.2.

• 2-Dimensional Assessment,

The brief discussion about each component is given in the subsequent section.
Structure of LO. It was observed during the research that content development in form
of conventional LOs has severe limitations in implementation of the CBL based system.
Therefore, a separate structure of LO was proposed that can handle the situation of
surface vs deep learning as well as superﬁcial vs detailed learning [19]. In the proposed
structure, the entire LO is classiﬁed into ﬁve subcomponents. They are given as follows:
• Concepts/terminologies/taxonomies
• Extra knowledge/references
• Examples/Illustrations
• Assessment/item banks
• Pre-requisite
2-Dimensional Assessment. In the existing assessment method for CBL MCQ were
used to assess the learners with Certainty Based Marking (CBM) or the learner who
is being assessed provide level of conﬁdence in the answer. If the response is correct,
higher the conﬁdence level more marks are awarded. On the other hand, if the response
is incorrect, higher the level of conﬁdence more the learner is penalized. In this situa-
tion, at times some of the learners used to provide responses based on guess work and

62
R. Chatterjee et al.
hence the existing assessment model was unsuitable. In the proposed model a modi-
ﬁed 2-dimentional assessment also known as Conﬁdence Based Assessment (CBA) was
proposed [20].
Learning Record Store (LRS). In the previous section 2-D assessment was discussed.
However, in due course of the research, it was found by the authors that mere 2-d
assessment is insufﬁcient to identify the lacunas of a learner in a CBL based learning
system. This is since CBL based system are applied in authentic learning and primarily
related to world of work. Hence it is proposed that assessment or evaluation based on the
performance at the world of world must be gauge to identify the lacunas. In this respect
the authors have proposed intelligent mining technique [21].
Dependency Structure Matrix (DSM). Once the diagnose phase has identiﬁed the
lacunas of a typical learner, the identiﬁed lacunas are passed on to the prescribe phase
where the content prescription is done for a particular iteration. The content is prescribed
based on the learning mode i.e., surface, and deep learning mode. Moreover, superﬁcial,
or detailed learning is prescribed based on the identiﬁed lacunas and placement of the
learner in one of the four quadrants of Knowledge Quadrant given in Fig. 2. To reduce
the repetition of the content, DSM is used. In the DSM, Atomic Competencies (ACs)
are mapped to reduce the repetition of the tasks as well as ACs [22].
Performance Monitoring of a Learner. It is signiﬁcant to measure the performance of
the learner during the multiple iteration a typical learner passes through it. It may happen
that despite providing the most relevant content based on the identiﬁed lacunas, it is being
observed that instead of incremental approach for a typical learner, the learner may be
in detrimental path. In order to measure a learner on the incremental path, Huffman Tree
and modiﬁed Huffman Tree are applied [23].
Inclusion of Authentic Learning (AL). In this section, mapping of activities with the
tasks of CBL is done. This requires intervention of the instructor at the preliminary
level to associate individual real-world problem to an outcome or IO. To achieve this the
problem must be subclustered into individual assignment/activity that will be connected
to tasks. Each individual assignment when solved by executing a task will in-turn have to
be executed with a set of ACs. As individual tasks are further classiﬁed into ACs. These
ACs are categorized into four different categories and respective ACs are assigned to
quadrants based on their level of dependencies. ACs with no dependency known as Non-
Dependent ACs (NDAC) and are placed in quadrant 1. AC that are directly dependent on
ACs which have no dependency are known as Direct Dependency ACs (DDAC), placed
in quadrant 2. ACs which are dependent on other AC which in turn are dependent on
NDAC are known as Transitively Related AC (TRAC). They are placed in quadrant 3.
Quadrant 4 consists of all ACs that are having a dependency on TRAC. They are known
as Fully Dependent ACs (FDAC). The details including quadrant relationships are given
in Table 1.

4
Results and Discussions
TheproposedmodelofACBLhavesigniﬁcantenhancementovertheexistingapproaches
that comprises of CBL based system. Authors identiﬁed the limitations of the existing
LOs and proposed a modiﬁed LO for the CBL based system. The proposed research is
compared with Bhattacharya et.al [18] and it was observed that the proposed system is
better with respects to the criteria including format of a structured LO, content based
on IO, decomposition of IO into tasks, analysis of dependency and interdependency of
tasks, and ﬁnally support for various learning approaches and learning modes.
A modiﬁed 2-D assessment system is proposed, and solution is compared to various
existing works. It was observed that the proposed 2-D assessment system is better com-
pared to the system proposed by Stanley [13], Conﬁdence-based assessment proposed
by Gardner-Medwin et al. [14], assessment on PBL given by Waters and McCracken
[24], and qualitative assessment method by Parker et al. [25].
In this model LRS is used to map the lacunas and deﬁciency from the world of work.
The authors compared their work with existing three research work. The comparison was
based on three main criteria namely assessment based on PBL [24], Data-mining tech-
niques [26] and CBe-L based recommender system [18]. The proposed system performs
better on these stated criteria.
In the prescription phase, the content modelling was proposed, and performance
of the system was judge based on two standards. They are namely optimization of the
content and involvement of human expert. This has proposed content optimization and
management at individual learner’s level which were missing in the existing techniques.
Similarly, regarding human involvement, the system has enhanced the optimization and
management of content using automated technique and remove human intervention to
a great extent.

A Comprehensive Model
65
Finally, two important measures were remarkable in this proposed model. First,
integration of AL with CBL. The proposed system has incorporated AL with CBL by
integrating real time problems into assignment and mapping them to tasks for CBL based
system. Secondly, truly randomization techniques are used for to make the system fair
and unbiased. This enhances the assessment by covering the entire range of knowledge
domain.
5
Conclusion and Future Scope
In this research work, a thorough and complete model of ACBL has been proposed
which has the following objectives to fulﬁll. These include proposal for a new structure
for LO, a novel and modiﬁed 2-D assessment mechanism, mapping of assessment to
real world work at jobsite using LRS, efﬁcient management of content by decomposing
tasks into ACs and efﬁciently managing them using DSM. Further to this incorporation
of true randomization techniques and implementing AL in conjunction with CBL has
enhanced the system and provided a comprehensive framework for LMS based on CBL.
However, it was not possible to solve every research problem and certain issues like
prescription of learning approaches and learning mode can be included in future scope
which was beyond the scope of the exiting research work.

Analysis of Classroom Interaction Using
Speaker Diarization and Discourse
Features from Audio Recordings
Oscar Canovas(B) and Felix J. Garcia
Department of Computer Engineering and Technology, University of Murcia,
Murcia 30100, Spain
{ocanovas,fgarcia}@um.es
Abstract. In this paper we present the rationale, and some initial
results, of an automated system for classroom analysis which is based
on speaker diarization techniques and non-verbal discourse features
extracted from audio recordings. We have employed several Machine
Learning algorithms and audio processing methods with classroom
recordings related to several undergraduate courses. After determining
the identity of the speaker in a recorded class, we can distinguish whether
the speaker is a teacher, a student, there are multiple speakers at the
same time, or silence. An important contribution of our work is that,
from that information, we derive several non-verbal features that can be
used to describe patterns. Our preliminary results show that it is possi-
ble to extract valuable information using data visualization. As we show,
diﬀerent teachers and teaching methods generate identiﬁable patterns,
that might be used to analyze, for example, which methodologies and
teaching styles provide higher levels of interaction or participation.
Keywords: Audio analysis · Teaching practices · Data visualization
1
Introduction and Motivation
Many educational research ﬁndings have shown that the successful student inter-
action in a classroom, that is, sharing ideas with the teacher or participating in
peer discussions, is correlated with high quality learning [7]. However, student-
teacher relationships and interactions are complex and there is not a one-size-
ﬁts-all approach. We believe that the quality of interactions between teachers
and students can be measured through standardized observation methods pro-
viding teachers with data about relevant features from classroom interactions. It
has been proven that by analyzing their own lessons teachers can improve their
student’s academic achievement [11].
The main purpose of this work in progress is to present the rationale, and
some initial results, of an automated system for analysis of classroom proﬁles
which is based on speaker diarization techniques and discourse features from
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 67–74, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_7

68
O. Canovas and F. J. Garcia
audio recordings. Identifying the identity of the speaker in a recorded class, we
can distinguish whether the speaker is a teacher, a student, there are multiple
speakers at the same time, or silence. An important contribution from our work
is that, from that information, we derive several discourse features that can be
used not only for classiﬁcation purposes, but they are also informative because
they describe patterns and measure levels of interaction. Therefore, our prelimi-
nary results show that it is possible to provide timely generation of a classroom
proﬁle based on data visualization to help teachers to analyze and improve their
classroom activities.
We have developed and integrated data analysis techniques based on machine
learning to diarize the audios, that is, to automate the annotation of when each
speaker (or type of speaker) is talking. This diarization information is then used
to extract features that describe speciﬁc aspects of the classroom activities,
providing data about the participation rate, turn taking, pauses, or multiple
speakers. These features will be used in future works to perform an automatic
classiﬁcation of the diﬀerent activities and teaching methods. At his moment,
they are used to create a classroom proﬁle, using data visualization techniques.
Fig. 1. Timelines of diﬀerent audio patterns for diﬀerent teaching methods
Our preliminary results are very promising about the suitability of the system
to provide timely feedback for the teachers. After analyzing audios from diﬀerent
classroom activities, such as lectures, problem solving, ﬂipped classrooms, or
the use of audience response systems, we have conﬁrmed that the results from

Analysis of Classroom Interaction from Audio Recordings
69
the diarization process show very diﬀerent patterns for each type of activity,
as Fig. 1 shows. We have also observed contrasting patterns for the diﬀerent
teachers performing the same type of activity. Finally, we have conﬁrmed with
the participating teachers that it is possible to grasp meaningful insights about
interaction and teaching styles from the information displayed by our system.
2
Related Work
In recent years, we can ﬁnd several works analyzing the classroom climate and
discourse. As it is our case, some of them employ audio recordings and machine
or deep learning techniques to analyze diﬀerent teaching practices and styles.
Those recordings can be analyzed using non-verbal features or natural language
processing techniques [10]. This latter option is out of the scope of our prelimi-
nary work, so we will focus on works based on non-verbal features.
Usually, the ﬁrst step is to label the audio recordings to identify “who spoke
when”. There are multiple approaches to address this task, from classical meth-
ods to advanced neural networks [9]. Some previous methods for classroom audio
analysis relied on participants to wear individual microphones [14] and the use
of Language ENvironment Analysis (LENA) to achieve automated unsuper-
vised classiﬁcation of class activities. However, James et al. [3], as it is our
case, adopted recent state-of-the-art speech processing technologies, and non-
intrusive set-ups, to detect speakers and to infer the climate in the classroom
from non-verbal speech cues.
Diﬀerent research works have used machine learning models to detect teach-
ing practices using spectral audio features, paying special attention to the role of
the teacher [2,12] or classifying active learning tasks [5,8,13]. In general, these
works are specially focused on the classiﬁcation accuracy of the employed tech-
niques and they do not provide discourse features that can be used as descriptive
and informational data.
Some of the discourse features in Sect. 5 were adapted from those presented
in [1,4] for group meeting analysis, since some of the turn-taking features, par-
ticipation rates, or silence ratios are also suitable for the teaching analysis.
3
Context
In this work we analyze the audios recorded from two courses (Computer Net-
works and Computing Foundations) of a bachelor’s degree in Computer Sci-
ence. In particular, four teachers from our university have weekly recorded their
classes. The recording setup was unobtrusive since it consisted of placing a hand-
held digital recorder (TASCAM DR-07X) located at least 1.5 m apart from the
teacher and the front row students. Consequently, we ended up with a dataset of
twelve recordings for each teacher, with lengths ranging from 90 to 125 min per
audio ﬁle, and registering up to four diﬀerent teaching methods (lecture, prob-
lem solving, audience response systems, and ﬂipped classrooms). The dataset was
completed with a weekly survey submitted by the teachers about the student

70
O. Canovas and F. J. Garcia
participation level per class and a ﬁnal survey from the students about teacher’s
instructional support. All the information was collected with the approval of the
teachers, students and the Institutional Review Board.
4
Audio Pipeline
This section provides details about the designed pipeline shown in Fig. 2. First,
an initial audio processing extracts low level features from the audio record-
ings. There is a thresholding method to separate silence from voiced segments,
and, using small audio frames, we compute Mel Frequency Cepstral Coeﬃcients
(MFCCs) [6], pitch and average energy for each voiced frame. These features are
widely used in the scientiﬁc literature as input for speaker diarization techniques.
Fig. 2. Pipeline of processing stages and data elements
The second stage is to determine “who spoke when”, that is, to label every
second of each recording with the corresponding speaker (or silence). In our
preliminary prototype, we do not distinguish which particular student is actually
speaking, and all the intervening students are labeled just as “Students”. We
also annotate if there is silence or multiple voices. This diarization process is
based on machine learning techniques making use of Support Vector Machines,
and it is a semi-supervised process as we have to train the system with some
audio fragments that are tagged as “Teacher”, “Students” or “The crowd”. This
method only requires 30 s of audio, for each category, to provide a classiﬁcation
accuracy around 91% with other test audios. Consequently, we obtain an time-
ordered sequence of labels that will be used in the next stage of the pipeline but
it can be also be visualized using timelines, as Fig. 1 showed.
The third step is the calculation of non-verbal discourse features from the
sequence of labels. As we detail in Sect. 5, we compute participant speaking rates,
average pause duration, turn taking counts, etc.
Finally, as we will show in Sect. 6 we provide several data visualization alter-
natives to display the computed features and also the results from the diarization

Analysis of Classroom Interaction from Audio Recordings
71
process. The main rationale behind those graphs is to provide straightforward
and valuable information to the teachers in order to analyze some classroom
activities, such as levels of interaction or teaching styles.
5
Features for Audio Analysis
As we mentioned previously, considering some previous works [1,4], we have
deﬁned several non-verbal features extracted from audio recordings that are
useful for the characterization of discourses. Speciﬁcally, we deﬁne two discourse
features per role (teacher, students, the crowd, or silence):
– Participant Speaking Ratio (PSR). It measures the ratio of participation
of each role during the classroom recording.
– Average Participant Speaking Utterance Duration (APSUD). Mea-
sured in seconds, it is the average duration of the utterances of each partici-
pant.
Additionally we have also deﬁned ﬁve global discourse features:
– Average Pause Duration (APD). It measures how long is the average
silence interval between utterances of the same participant.
– Participation equality (PEQ). It is an indicator of how balanced is the
participation of the diﬀerent roles and it is calculated as shown in [4]. Values
close to 1 denote equal participation.
– Turn taking count (TTC). It represents how many turn changes occurred
in the dialogue between students and teacher.
– Silence Ratio (SR). It measures the ratio of silence during the classroom
recording.
– Very Short Utterances Ratio (VSUR). It shows the ratio of very short
speech utterances (less than 2 s) over the total.
6
Insights from Data Visualization
One of the main goals of this work is to provide valuable visualization for the data
derived from the audio processing pipeline. Our prototype uses diﬀerent graphs,
such as timelines, bars, and distribution functions, to gain some knowledge about
the classroom activities.
After an initial analysis of the recordings obtained from the set-up described
in Sect. 3, we observed interesting patterns that show the diﬀerences related to
diﬀerent teaching methods. For example, when we apply the diarization process
to recordings related to diﬀerent methodologies (for the same teacher) we per-
ceive distinguishable patterns for each of them in the timelines, as Fig. 1 showed.
Lectures provide lower levels of interaction (the students’ participation is scarce),
ﬂipped classrooms tend to be more participatory and noisy (in the example the
class was solving problems in small groups) and the use of audio response systems
involves alternating periods of silence, explanations, and questions.

72
O. Canovas and F. J. Garcia
Fig. 3. Timelines of diﬀerent teachers but the same lecture contents
We have also analyzed whether the timeline representation allow us to detect
diﬀerent discourse patterns for diﬀerent teachers who are lecturing the same
contents in their respective classrooms. As Fig. 3 shows, we observe some clear
diﬀerences in relation to the amount of “NO VOICE” or silence patterns, that
is, the number of pauses made by each teacher.
However, these diﬀerences are more clearly visible when we compute the non-
verbal discourse features for each audio and we visualize the results, as Fig. 4
shows. Teachers can analyze the level of participation of the students (in this
case is less than 4% for all the classes), their participation rates or the average
utterance duration (with notorious diﬀerences between teachers), turn taking
counts, participation equality, etc.
Even if the teachers do not have access to the data related to other teachers,
they can ﬁnd valuable information about their own teaching style and levels of
interaction after each class. In fact, our prototype also visualizes data about the
statistical distribution and temporal evolution of each feature. Figure 5 shows,
for example, three diﬀerent graphs (cumulative distribution function, histogram
and time-ordered) for one feature, teacher participation rate, along the whole
course. In this case, the histogram shows that teacher participation tends to be
bimodal, depending on the teaching method (higher for lectures and lower for
ﬂipped classroom).

7
Conclusions and Future Work
In this work in progress, we have successfully developed a system for visualizing
diﬀerent features, extracted from audio recordings, that can be used to provide
a classroom proﬁle with information about the student participation, degree
of interactivity and teaching styles. The preliminary results show that the data
visualization is found very useful by the teachers and reveals meaningful insights
about the diﬀerent classroom activities.
As a statement of direction, we would like to build a bigger dataset with
additional audio recordings. Moreover, we are working on automatizing our audio
pipeline to generate data reports for each teacher, with customized information
for each teaching activity. We are also applying clustering techniques based on
machine learning to identify groups of teachers with similar discourse behaviors

74
O. Canovas and F. J. Garcia
in the classroom. Finally, for the reproducibility of our scientiﬁc research results,
another step would be the distribution of our dataset and source code in open
repositories.

How the Pandemic Helped and Hindered
Student-Centered Learning
Alexandra Posekany1,2(B), Dominik Dolezal2,3, and Gottfried Koppensteiner2
1 TU Vienna University of Technology, Vienna, Austria
2 TGM – Vienna Institute of Technology, Vienna, Austria
aposekany@tgm.ac.at
3 University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria
Abstract. The student-centered learning approach “learning oﬃce” has
been established in vocational school education under constant evalua-
tion through a team of education researchers. In the past two years, emer-
gency online teaching has aﬀected education world-wide with a severe
impact on teacher-centered as well as student-centered education.
Our goal is to evaluate teachers’ and students’ perspectives on emer-
gency and systematic online teaching and to get an impression of stu-
dents’ perceived competence in 21st century skills which the learning
oﬃce is speciﬁcally designed to foster. For this, we reconcile the change
in perspectives through comparisons of open text answers from a ques-
tionnaire after experiencing emergency online teaching and interviews
with students and teachers regarding their perceived change in the way
contents are taught.
We ﬁnd diverse aspects which are partially favourable for student-
centered learning in times of self-reliant education at home. However,
we also identiﬁed adversary eﬀects of studying alone at home for the
learning oﬃce due to its interactive nature. On the one hand, students
felt more self-reliant and able to work on materials on their own accord
without constant input or supervision of a teacher. On the other hand,
students missed the personal interaction with their peers, but even more
with their teachers in the online setting.
Based on our questionnaire and interviews, we ﬁnd that student-
centered learning indeed helped to develop the skills for self-reliant learn-
ing in students. However, the position of the educator as a coach and
guiding ﬁgure to the students is irreplaceable, especially in student-
centered learning.
Keywords: Student-centred learning · 21st century skills · Learning
oﬃce · Emergency online teaching
1
Introduction
The COVID-19 pandemic had a tremendous impact on people’s life. In the edu-
cational sector, many institutions of education were aﬀected by regional and
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 75–86, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_8

76
A. Posekany et al.
national lockdowns and were thus forced to implement online teaching with
hardly any prior notice [1]. Naturally, this posed severe challenges to both teach-
ers and students: Teachers who relied on giving lectures and direct instructions
were required to use digital technologies to deliver and assess the subject mat-
ter, while students had to use digital media to access content and submit their
work. The average usage time of digital media increased dramatically for both
stakeholders; in many cases, students and teachers had to sit in front of the
computer for the whole day, ﬁve days a week, without being required or allowed
to go outside, raising a variety of ergonomic and health concerns.
At the same time, digital competencies are considered to be an integral part
and valuable asset of the modern skills required in the 21st century (see, e.g.,
[2–6]), also known as “21st century skills”. This set of skills includes, but is not
limited to, creativity, innovation, digital literacy, communication, information
management, life skills, critical thinking, and problem solving. A method to
foster these kinds of skills proposed in the literature is student-centered learning
(see, .e.g., [7–10]), which is also the foundation of the learner-centered learning
oﬃce approach [1,11–14]. The learning oﬃce approach is based on the work of
Margret Rasfeld [15,16] and represents an own branch at the IT department of
the TGM,a European vocational upper secondary school.
Learning oﬃce students work independently on exercises and projects and
are able to take advantage of a ﬂexible course schedule, while teachers become
coaches helping students reach their learning goals [11–14]. Previous work
revealed several advantages of this learner-centered approach, including fewer
absent days of students [11], higher satisfaction with teachers’ support [12],
more cooperation among students [13], and an increase in self-perceived 21st
century skills [9] and ICT skills [10]. In recent research, we discovered that stu-
dents of both approaches, the learning oﬃce approach and traditional classrooms,
achieved equal learning outcomes in distance learning as in on-site teaching at
the grades 10–13, measured by the average grade [1].
This paper extends previous work by using a qualitative approach and analyz-
ing students’ and teachers’ opinion on online teaching, addressing the following
research questions:
– RQ1: What challenges did students encounter due to the sudden switch to
online teaching?
– RQ2: How did teachers respond to and experience online teaching?
– RQ3: Which lessons could be learned from online teaching that can be applied
in traditional on-site teaching?
2
Methodology
2.1
Survey
We conducted an online survey among students to collect and analyze their
experiences regarding distance learning. Parts of the survey have already been

How the Pandemic Helped and Hindered Student-Centered Learning
77
analyzed and published in previous work [1], quantitatively evaluating students’
answers to 12 statements regarding online teaching to be rated on a Likert scale.
In this paper, we focus on the qualitative feedback provided by students and
present their answers to the open question: “I want to provide the following
feedback on the switch to online teaching:”. Answering the anonymous survey
was voluntary. The survey was sent out to the 125 students majoring in media
technology at the 12th and 13th grade and has been answered by a total of 99
students, 53 of which provided written feedback on the mentioned open question.
To analyze emerging themes, a content analysis [17] has been performed by
two of the authors. The 53 units of analysis were split into 68 meaning units and
analyzed iteratively in two sessions to inductively identify recurring categories
and, consequently, abstract emerging themes.
2.2
Interviews
In order to complement and deepen our survey, we conducted interviews with
selected students and teachers alike. We interviewed 4 students and 4 teachers,
taking care to balance gender by interviewing two male and two female individ-
uals per group. In order to take care of the type of education in case of students,
we interviewed 1 male and 1 female student of the learning oﬃce and the tra-
ditional system respectively. For teachers, we wanted to capture the bias based
on the type of subject and interviewed 2 teachers of general subjects, such as
English, German, Mathematics, and 2 teachers of technical subjects, speciﬁc for
the vocational school focusing on IT education. Also, we only interviewed stu-
dents and teachers who had been in the school for at least 4 years to assure that
they were able to compare against pre-Covid times.
We designed the interview questions based on the survey questions and spe-
ciﬁc aspects which arose from analysing the open text answers. Table 1 shows the
interview questions and the interview partner groups the questions have been
used for.
3

World. Figure 1 visualizes the identiﬁed categories and abstracted themes; the

thoughts and worries related to working and performing in a pure online teach-

3.2
Interviews
Our interviews with students were meant to deepen our understanding of cir-
cumstances which aﬀected our students in the switch from full presence in school
to emergency online teaching, systematic distance learning and hybrid forms of
online and oﬄine learning.
Both students of the learning oﬃce agreed that they had no diﬃculties switch-
ing to remote learning and organising themselves from the ﬁrst day onward. One
pointed out the additional time he had per day without spending 2 h commut-
ing between his home and the school, the other appreciated having time for
hobbies and physical exercise than usual during the emergency online teaching
in summer term 2020, when schedules where no strictly covered and students
given much freedom, but also required a rather larger intrinsic motivation for
self-organisation. Both students from traditional classes reported struggling with
the period of emergency online teaching and especially feeling lost in the begin-
ning being left on their own terms. Yet, they also reported adapting to the system
well once the structure of class schedules was returned and, when teachers were
giving “online lectures”, where they could directly ask questions.
All students in both systems reported an increased stress on their time and
concentration, once the emergency online teaching with the freedom of reschedul-
ing classes to students’ and teachers’ needs changed to keeping the tight original
schedule of classes. Teachers and students agreed that the hybrid form of teach-
ing a part of the class online and a part of the class working on its own remotely
oﬄine was the worst way of teaching they had experienced. All students agreed
that this took away the structure and reliability they required of school putting
an additional strain on them rather than relaxing them. All teachers agreed
with that assessment, as they had even less possibility to actively involve stu-
dents compared to full online teaching and noted the students suﬀering due to
lack structure.
All students and teachers reported exhaustion due to the long hours in front
of the screen without actual long pauses which were required to be used for
having lunch and tending to other acute physical need rather than being used
for the much needed physical exercise. Teachers with familial responsibilities for
their own children being taught at home reported the double stress as extremely
hindering in their teaching and making pauses almost non-existing for them.
All students reported that aside from exhaustion and increasing lacking the
time for hobbies, they suﬀered the most from not seeing each other directly
during classes. A student from the traditional system reported that they had
solved this problem creatively by starting calls on communication platforms in
parallel to the teachers main calls and speaking their comments in these as they
would in class. Especially dedicated hard-working students reported feeling close
to burn-out due to the working conditions of being only at home working as hard
as possible on assignments and lacking the direct comparison with their peers
which they typically received in class.
While the interviewed students reported having a quiet working environment,
teachers with families typically had no quiet working place with their partner

82
A. Posekany et al.
and also their children having to be taken care of and no time for recovery
for themselves adding to the stress and exhaustion from teaching in front of the
screen for hours. Yet, even in quiet ”almost ideal” working environments, all stu-
dents pointed out that the lack of separation between work place, sleeping place
and place for their hobbies became increasingly distressful and they resented the
possible distractions of their home rooms.
When asked about whether their appreciation for teaching and learning in
school rather than at home, students and teacher alike agreed that interacting
face-to-face increased their motivation and was more productive in that sense.
The ﬁrst question for which students’ and teachers’ perspectives diverged
completely was focused on their future chances. All interviewed students reported
that they did not believe that their future chances had been reduced due to years
of emergency online teaching and reduction of taught contents. On the contrary,
they believes that their ability to adapt to a new way of learning and succeed
in a very stressful situation made up for what they lacked regarding some lost
contents.
Teachers pointed out that aside from content knowledge which could be
looked up online and learn on your own accord to a certain degree, that younger
students lacked the most in their social behaviour. Lack of respect for other
students and teachers and the ability to agree on compromises were the most
worrisome for them regarding the students’ future.
The second question with diverging perspective was asking about whether
students had learned responsibility and self-organisation. All students from both
systems agreed that they had learned this and responsibly felt able to handle
their daily school and future work life. Teachers on the other hand reported that
the ones already able to organise themselves before had improved their ability,
while the least adapt at this had completely been lost during emergency online
teaching and never were able to regain their footing, unless they were kept in
school permanently.
The third question with diverging views was the one about gaps in the stu-
dents’ knowledge due to online learning and whether this was felt by students or
teachers. While students did not perceive that they had gaps in their knowledge,
teachers were under the impression that these gaps were immense knowing what
was usually taught and what would be expected in centralised ﬁnal exams which
none of the students had experienced yet.
The last question only asked of teachers pointed out that they felt far less
able to connect with their students online and unable to help and supports
them with problems other than content-focused ones. In class, an unhappy face
or dejected body language became obvious for good pedagogues taking care
of their students, while online teaching without camera images, failing online
connections or students just disappearing from anyone’s radar made the humane
support much more diﬃcult.
Students’ answers were less consistent regarding their interaction with teach-
ers and their peers. While learning oﬃce students felt that they had more
teacher time and support online, when teachers were available and less students

How the Pandemic Helped and Hindered Student-Centered Learning
83
contacted them directly compared to class, students from the traditional system
reported struggling with the hesitation to asked questions online and not seeing
their teachers’ face to read the meaning of small statements such as jokes, but
also of explanations where they were not sure about the wording. The reported
missing to see their peers’ faces even more during complex explanations to reas-
sure that they were not the only ones not understanding what was taught.
3.3
Interpretation
In the following paragraphs, we want to link our survey ﬁndings with the inter-
view results. As the interpretation of students’ answers to our survey was biased
by the view of the teachers interpreting them, we wished to remove our per-
sonal bias by directly asking students and teachers alike. We are fully aware
that neither the amount of interview partners nor the selection of them is fully
representative of all views of students and teachers, but covered a certain variety.
While the workload was a big issue in the survey of summer term 2020 and all
students at that current time, in retrospective during the interviews in summer
term 2021 only a single student reported the workload as seriously aﬀecting her.
From the interview as well as personal conversations with students who gradu-
ated in those two years, the workload was aﬀecting the more hard-working and
intrinsically motivated students much more than the average students causing
psychological problems such as burn-out. For the others the workload apparently
was a momentary stress which they reported clearly but did not aﬀect them on
the long run.
Having a quiet working environment was the key to success in distance learn-
ing. All interviewed students reported such and linked this to successfully work-
ing at home on their own accord independent of whether they were learning
oﬃce or traditional students or high-performers or average students. We admit
that there is a clear bias in our choice of interview partners, as all students were
from 12-th grade and thus the ”sucessful” ones in the school system.
The clear emotional preference of being taught in school rather than at home
persisted for all teachers and students. Most interestingly, regarding future imple-
mentations of digitalisation in school was that the hybrid form of leaving some
students to work on their own accord at home, while others were taught in school
switching between the groups on daily or weekly basis was the least attractive
for students and teachers alike, as it destroyed any rhythm the students required
and wished to be given by school by far outweighing the partial gain of free time
for hobbies for every single one of them. Some students’ resentment for online
learning went as far as a student’s statement: “I want to never attend a single
online course in my life anymore.”
All students and teachers consented that the important human factor of being
supported and having skills fostered by a teacher was far better performed in
school rather than online. Also the between students’ human interaction was
much needed and craved for by all students. While some classes had been able
to create a good interaction through creative ideas such as parallel online calls,
other classes had their relation as a whole group completely destroyed by the

84
A. Posekany et al.
lack of interaction and the class splintering into small group with hardly any
interaction even after returning from distance learning.
Between our survey and the interviews, we found that the exhausting con-
ditions online were taking their toll on all students and teachers alike, espe-
cially when coupled with a rigid schedule which limited time for physical exer-
cise. Additionally, several students reported depression due to social isolation or
burn-out due to tackling a theoretical workload without peer comparison and a
regulation for throttling down from their teachers under online conditions.
With respect to 21st century skills we found that students agreed between
survey and interviews that they perceived themselves more able to organise
their schedules, acquire new knowledge on their own and deal with stressful
situations. While all interviewed students found that these skills outweighed any
lost contents, others worried in the survey that their future might be aﬀected.
They suspected that this might not be due to their own skills and making, but
rather due to prejudice of future employers against the ”lost generation” as they
perceive themselves titled by the media.
4
Conclusion
Summarising our survey and interviews, we found that emergency online teach-
ing and systematic distance learning provided a large impulse for digitalisation
in school, as it did in other ﬁelds of life. On the one hand establishing systematic
e-learning, increasing digital communication between students and teachers and
shifting their relationships towards online mentors brought positive aspects for
individualised student-centered learning.
On the other hand, the lack of inter-human communication with their peers
and teachers alike resulted in students drifting into loneliness, depression, but
also burn-out and over-working, as they had no-one stopping them before and
not as many hobbies consuming time as before. Teachers especially found that
pedagogical and psychological support, helping out with their students prob-
lems after noticing them become so much more diﬃcult, unless students directly
approached teachers online. This human element is also a key element of the
student-centered learning oﬃce approach. Losing it resulted in failure and sev-
eral troubles for many of the younger students not successful enough yet at
reaching the older ones’ level of self-organisation and maturity.
Therefore, the teachers’ more pessimistic view on the lost knowledge, con-
tents, behavioral role models and gaps is mostly focused on the ”lower end” of
success of students. Contrary to that, our interview partners where in the middle
in upper end of the success ladder and thus provided us with a diﬀerent per-
spective of the generation on themselves: a generation which the successful ones
learned to deal with constantly shifting learning scenarios in which they self-
dependently organised their schedules, their question time with teachers, their
relation with their peers and honed their own digital competences.
In spite of all this, the basic notion is that digital media are unable to provide
the human support students required for their success as much as content-driven

How the Pandemic Helped and Hindered Student-Centered Learning
85
individualisation which could be upheld to a certain degree in online learning
scenarios. Especially, the introduction to the meta-skills of self-organisation,
scheduling and responsibility have to happen in an oﬄine scenario in order to
make responsible online learning an option for individualisation of students’
schedules.
Acknowledgments. We want to thank all our colleagues and students who partici-
pated through the surveys and interviews, but also through discussions broadening our
view on the topic.
