Integrated and Virtual Learning as Element
of Coping with Multiple Transitions in Health
Care
Harald Kviecien(B)
KOHS, Vienna, Austria
hk@kohs.at
Abstract. The paper at hand describes a step further into the upcoming approach
of integrated pathways in health care and the increased demand of integrated
learning and knowledge (re-)production in health care organizations. The overall
concept and technological infrastructure developed in order to enable the imple-
mentation of this concept step by step in health care organizations includes fol-
lowing components: Two newly established and certiﬁed learning arrangements
in health care (learning modules), a learning platform tool, an online conferencing
tool, a tool for creating learning content, an approach for working on graph based
knowledge structures as well as an approach for “integrated working science”
[13], which aims at the enhancement of continuous learning in organizations by
regarding several meta levels. The virtual learning concept – as part of the app-
roach – has been applied by performing courses with groups of participants of
different profession in health care during the last two years. The concept offers
insights for people involved in management of education as well as organiza-
tional development in health care on how to implement approaches of integrated
learning.
Keywords: Virtual learning · Integrated learning · Health care · Knowledge
work
1
Context
The European social systems face several transitions causing a higher demand to cope
with them for health care organizations. This implies the demand to adapt the educa-
tional processes at several levels. An actual challenge for the society is to increase the
integration of processes in different health domains (health care and occupational health)
entailing increased demand of knowledge (re-)production.
The transitions take place in following areas:
1. The core processes of health care
2. “New” approaches of care (i.e. community health care, primary health care)
3. Occupational health management (from e.g. “early exit” prevention to facing a
higher complexity of organizations (addressed by the concept of “integrated working
science”))
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 87–98, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_9

88
H. Kviecien
4. The use of technology (or even the involvement in processes of agile development).
The paper at hand describes a step further into the upcoming approach of inte-
grated pathways in health care, particularly regarding questions of how to reduce the
complexities which are linked to this kind of higher integration.
Thefocusissetonthetechnologyofintegratedandvirtuallearningusedtoimplement
learning arrangements in the given context.
1.1
Objectives
The objectives of the approach and technology outlined here is to allow individuals to co-
work on health and enable health professionals to improve care processes by introducing
early problem detection and dynamic adaption of interventions (in the dimensions of
diagnosis, care and primary prevention). One of the transitions to be mentioned is a new
model of care introducing the health of health care worker as a relevant factor as well as
a patient oriented care. Though this model has been proposed at least back in the 1990s
[1] this “social innovation” could not be implemented so far in the mobile care [2]. To
converge to these objectives the integrated learning approach including collaborative
technology described here is supposed to be valuable.
1.2
Purpose
The purpose of this work is to outline the realization of learning modules in health
care education, learning activities in occupational health institutions and the concepts
this realization is based on. While technology and methodology for blended learning
the concept at hand is based on has been in practical use since about the year 2000 in
occupational health domain, learning activities in health care underlie an abrupt change
towards digital learning since March 2020 (Covid-19 impact). Thus the paper at hand
focuses on the recent output regarding the development of blended learning arrangements
in health care education as consequence of this change.
2
Approach
The overall concept and technological infrastructure developed in order to enable the
implementation of this concept step by step in health care organizations includes follow-
ing components: Two newly established learning arrangements in health care (learning
modules), a learning platform tool, an online conferencing tool, a tool for creating learn-
ing content, an approach for working on graph based “knowledge structures” as well as an
approach for “integrated working science”. The “integrated working science” approach
aims at the enhancement of continuous learning in organizations using elements such as
“distributed knowledge work” and involvement in “agile development” processes.
The two learning modules have been newly developed as learning arrangements
including synchronous and asynchronous elements as well as virtual and presence learn-
ing phases. The ﬁrst learning module is addressing the “base and middle management”

Integrated and Virtual Learning as Element
89
in care organization. The second learning module is addressing the “mentorship” as a rel-
evant part in the educational process in health care. Both modules are certiﬁed according
to §64 GuKG (Austrian law).
The learning platform and the online conferencing tool in use are both based on open
source technology, integrated into the overall technology.
Thetoolforcreatinglearningcontent(theVICO(VideoContentproduction)module)
has been used to create digital content for asynchronous learning. The VICO module is
a content creation tool for slide based content but also for multi-perspective content to
enable lecturers to demonstrate work ﬂows or the use of tools and supplies for work.
The approach for working on graph based “knowledge structures” allows structuring
information e.g. for case based learning, but also allows to visualize more complex
relations in order to enable “distributed knowledge work”.
The virtual learning concept – as part of the approach – has been applied by per-
forming courses with groups of participants of different profession in health care during
the last two years. An evaluation concept has been deﬁned.
2.1
Methodology
Learning concepts highly rely on practical experience and expert knowledge in health
care and educational science as well. The composition of learning courses need to focus
on the target groups and on simpliﬁcation. At the other hand the research and devel-
opment on the subject of integrated learning needs to regard more advanced concepts
of technology. The methodology thus includes the work on advanced concepts (partly
integrated into the development and performance of the learning courses). This happens
on three paces (see).
The concept for the evaluation of virtual learning (in the given approach) is based
on well balanced learning courses, which are curriculum based, performed for about
10 years (2010–2019; participants in total: n = ~2200). These learning courses get out-
come evaluated by examination (co-chaired by public authority) and by getting feedback
from participants employer (which is a health care organization) about long term aspects
of the education. Other aspects of evaluation of learning processes are considered as well
(e.g. feedback from participants).
2.2
Methods for Virtual Learning
As element of integrated learning with direct beneﬁt to the learning process the “case
based learning” has been applied. Three aspects of case based learning are relevant in
the given context: work on real cases (1). Participants have to identify actual situations
from their work which suit a given topic (e.g. dealing with conﬂicts); Provide elaborated
case studies (case study repository) (2) and the moderation of the learning unit by expert
lecturers (3) (here: expert in health care plus experience in leadership (regarding the
management education)). The work on case studies is being realized by combining
synchronous and asynchronous phases as well as group works.
Another element of integrated learning is the participative observation of real world
situations. This method can be applied using risk based methods or resource based

90
H. Kviecien
methods or even mixing these approaches. Further this element can get focused on
aspects of process quality or on occupational health. Again these approaches can get
mixed enabling to work on more complex learning subjects. This element is rather
dedicated for advanced learning courses, but can also get applied to basic learning
courses (when keeping the focus dimension small).
3
Actual Outcome
One of the actual outcomes is the deﬁnition of the two certiﬁed learning modules, which
include a practical approach to apply integrated learning activities. This contributes to
the aimed reduction of complexity as outlined (Fig. 1).
Fig. 1. The technical infrastructure used for the learning arrangements.
A further outcome is the description of the overall concept of “integrated learning as
element of coping with multiple transitions in health care” focusing on the technology
used for virtual and integrated learning (see Advanced concept).
3.1
Virtual Learning Concept
The development of the virtual learning concept precedes the development of the two
certiﬁed learning modules and has been performed on the learning module: “Support
with basic care” (“Unterstützung bei der Basisversorgung” (UBV), which is regulated
by law). The module comprises 140 h. Until March 2020 (ﬁrst Covid-19 lock-down in
Austria) the education of this course took place completely in face-to-face classes. At
this moment the education has to be switched to virtual learning immediately. Thus a
didactic concept for this subject developed in a multi-phase construction process. One
of the most relevant research questions has been: “Which digital media can be used to
teach basic nursing skills.” In the ﬁrst phase the technical and pedagogic infrastructure
has been built up. This includes the concept for production of digital content in the
context of health care [18], the visualizing of knowledge(-structures) [18, 19] as well as
concepts of virtual learning [9].
Following 3 technical components became relevant for the development and the
performance of the learning module:

Integrated and Virtual Learning as Element
91
1. elearn.dpgo: a learning platform (based on open source platform “moodle”)
2. meet.dpgo: a video conferencing tool (based on open source software “bigbluebut-
ton”
3. VICO: a video content production tool.
The learning platform (elearn.dpgo) is used for providing access to the actual learning
content of interest. The video conferencing tool (meet.dpgo) is used for synchronous
virtual teaching. This tool is targeted at didactic reduction, used features were mainly
slide based presentation, chat and breakout rooms. Additionally the tool allows hybrid
teaching sessions having some participants physically present and others connected
virtually.
The VICO tool has been used mainly to produce video content holding the slides,
which are presented usually (in presence or virtually) together with the lecturer (presenter
video and audio). The video content is placed on the learning platform so that participants
can recall all learning content on demand for self education (asynchronous learning). The
VICO tool provides a set of functionality (screen capture, mixing of different sources into
slide based content, mixing data into video). VICO is part of the H_ technology, which
is the successor of the HERIVIS environment [12, 14]. The H_ technology includes
elements at highest technology readiness level (TRL 9) [22] as well as elements, which
are still in research and development.
The virtual learning concept for the learning course mentioned here has been
performed with participants in total: n = ~500 (covering roughly the years 2020–2022).
The evaluation of the virtual learning concept is in progress. First results of the
evaluation suggests that video content created based on this concept is appropriate for
the target group. A publication of the evaluation is planned for the near future.
3.2
Learning Module: “Base and Middle Management”
The learning module “base and middle management” is structured itself into 6 modules.
The education takes place within 9 blocks (presence: 4 times a 3 day block and 1 times
a 2 day block; virtual: 3 times a 2 day block and 1 times a 1 day block; in total 21 days
(of 9 units per day). Additionally the participants have to self-study along their personal
learning portfolio.
This learning course is completed by a ﬁnal examination before a board (including
representatives of public authority). The development of this learning course is based
on the experiences with virtual learning (see) and the work on concepts of management
in health care [6]. Within this course mainly levels A and B of the 3x-meta model are
addressed (see Advanced concept).
An interesting feedback of participants acquired for evaluation ex ante: Participation
to such a learning course would not be possible without considerable portion of virtual
learning phases.
3.3
Learning Module: “Mentorship”
The learning module “mentorship” can be seen as link between theory and prac-
tice. The target group (graduate nurses) get qualiﬁed to plan, perform and evaluate

92
H. Kviecien
teaching/learning processes for apprentices on their practical education in health care
organizations.
This learning course is structured into 6 modules. The education takes 195 units of
theory (in presence, virtually and including self-study) as well as 40 units of practical
education. The learning course is completed by a ﬁnal examination before a board
(including representatives of public authority).
4
Advanced Concept
In this section the methodical and technological theory and development get described.
Some elements mature for quite a long time (e.g. PIMEX) while others had been added
in recent years (e.g. JCS).
The following ﬁgure tries to integrate the transitions in socials systems with the
meta-model of improvement, the observation as methodical element and considerations
of meta-prevention as well as the individual learning dimension with regard to health
knowledge (Fig. 2).
Fig. 2. “3x-meta” model (in progress) of facing transitions in health care organizations (Kviecien
2022)
The meta-model of improvement (A-B-C) is oriented on the schema described by
Spohrer & Engelbert [3]. The level A includes all the core activities within an organiza-
tion, the level B refers to all structures and processes to improve the core activities and
ﬁnally the level C refers to activities, which aim to improve the capabilities of level B.
The transitions are represented by two items: “ + cititzen” indicating that the primary
end-user of care is not only a client (or patient) any more, but a citizen who should
get included to “co-work on health”. Further the item “ + new models of care” is a
placeholder for emerging models such as “community care” but also for upcoming, yet

Integrated and Virtual Learning as Element
93
unknown models.The “3x-meta” model gives orientation for the strategic and operative
planning of learning activities and for integration of the organization in research and
development processes.
The development of the advanced concept and the technology happens at 3 paces:
I.
Bottom up: care intervention & base management (levels A, B)
II.
Top-down: new models of care, management of transition (including C level)
III. In-between: methods of monitoring, participation, observation & collaboration
(see: PIMEX based mixed-method approach for risk assessment and knowledge
generation).
4.1
Joint Cognitive System (JCS)
A further model used for orientation is the “Joint cognitive system” (JCS). The act-
ing individuals and the processes of care are regarded as elements of a joint cognitive
system (JCS) which is an extension to the working system theory in working sciences
where humans are using and interacting with technical artifacts (sensing and information
processing artiﬁcial things) (Fig. 3).
Fig. 3. Joint cognitive system approach (Kviecien 2020, oriented on Mühlbradt & Hartmann,
2019 [20])
According to Hollnagel [4] in the CSE (Cognitive System Engineering) terminology,
“it is more important to understand what a joint cognitive system (JCS) does and why it
does it, than to explain how it does it”. “The revised deﬁnition of a cognitive system is a

94
H. Kviecien
system that can modify its behavior on the basis of experience so as to achieve speciﬁc
antientropic ends.” [4]. Hollnagel [4] further explains that “most living organisms, and
certain kinds of machines or artifacts [and also] organizations are cognitive systems.”
JCS, by deﬁnition always include a human begin.
The JCS approach introduced here regards 2 levels: The “Intervention” representing
the inner complexities of care and the “Integrated innovation and implementation” rep-
resenting the outer complexities regarding the continuous design of an organization in
the health care domain.
Intervention. Severalprocessesinhealthcareshouldbemethodicallyseenas“interven-
tion”. Interventions in health care can get classiﬁed (e.g. health professional →client).
Also a learning action has to be seen as intervention (health care organization →health
professional). In order to be able to improve the quality of health several processes and
(particularly cross-process paths) in health care need to be better understood (demand
of capacity building in health care organizations).
Integrated Innovation and Implementation (I3). To
address
the
challenges
of
change in the health care systems a new research and implementation approach has
to be considered, which integrates the following main concepts: “integrated working
science”, “distributed knowledge work” and “agile development” [13]. The concept at
hand incorporates this approach at the “I3“ level and further integrates main strate-
gies proposed by researchers as well as political agendas (e.g. new primary health care
concepts, more complex design of organizational processes combined with integrated
networking [2] or better co-working on health of patients/clients).
From the perspective of the occupational health institution it has to be realized that
it is not sufﬁcient any more to provide information on regulations and good practice
and support via isolated services. To reach the European aim of being a prospective
society new ways of cooperation have to be established. A new research approach is
the “integrated working science” which may ideally get introduced into an extended
PHC (primary health care) model [13, 21]. Two main factors will be the key aspects of
introducing this approach:
1. The direct interactions between health care workers and the individual users, who
are not reduced to the role of being a patient as well as occupational health experts
and ergonomic experts.
2. To perform case studies within the PHC team, (ideally moderated by ergonomic
experts), to learn from experience and be able to reproduce the gained knowledge.
For both aspects a high demand of capacity building in health care organizations can
be assumed.
Following this approach the main goal at “I3” level is to design working systems
(considered as joint cognitive systems) in order to enable cognition enhancement of
health care professionals. A relevant dimension of control of a joint cognitive system is
the knowledge about cognitive load.
Integrated systems and interconnection communication are in line with tradi-
tional and modern ergonomic requirements, which are in constant static and dynamic
interaction [5].

Integrated and Virtual Learning as Element
95
4.2
PIMEX Based Mixed-Method Approach for Risk Assessment and Knowledge
Generation
PIMEX (PIcture-Mix-EXposure) is a method for visualizing health hazards at the work-
place [16]. A work sequence is recorded by video camera, and simultaneously exposures
and other information of relevance are aquired via sensors. By performing task analy-
sis in relation to the measured expositions and the physiological data, interrelations
between a certain work sequence and prevalent hazards as well as speciﬁc strains can
be recognized and measures of prevention can be derived [10, 17].
The approach enables the analysis of working processes and an assessment of risks,
resulting in a package of measures for the purpose of workplace improvement and risk
optimization. A priority objective is to increase employees’ awareness of health hazards
by imparting knowledge about interrelations between occupational strains, exposures
and their consequences on health [15]. Achieving an optimal design of a working system
constitutes the aim of any PIMEX intervention [7].
A key aspect for a health promoting design of work by means of an embracing
working system analysis with the PIMEX method is the involvement of at-risk person-
nel in the analysis process. Other factors are the visualization of relevant information
at the time of data acquisition, the representation and assessment of risks, the evalu-
ation of effectiveness and the provision of a meaningful documentation. Results from
PIMEX interventions turn out to be a starting point for establishing a knowledge base
for employee training and instruction as well as the development of individual learning
concepts [15, 19].
Based on the experiences with using the PIMEX method the concept of “HERIVIS
analysis and controlling instrument (HERIVIS-ACI)” has been introduced, which rep-
resent concrete instruments for measurement, assessment, studying and evaluation of
deﬁned risks. HERIVIS-ACI mean a mixed method approach combining individual and
organizational aspects of working systems. Some parts, such as the PIMEX method act
as key component, to serve a task based orientation for other parts of the method mix
[12, 14].
The effectiveness of the methodical use of PIMEX could be conﬁrmed from different
point of views [7, 10, 11].
The methodical use of PIMEX has to be seen as an intervention strategy [8] which
is also of importance for the generation of knowledge [13].
To achieve a distributed knowledge work in occupational health a suitable medium
is required. PIMEX visualizations link virtual learning environments with real world
working life [9]. The learning processes may be performed by means of case studies
[13]. From the perspective of knowledge generation the PIMEX intervention is used for
observing working systems as well as organizational structures. PIMEX media is used
for educational processes (see Fig. 4).
4.3
Visual Structure Interface (VSI)
Forperformingactionsof(distributed)knowledgeworkthegraphbased“Visualstructure
interface” (VSI) concept is used (technically implemented as H_Graph component). The

96
H. Kviecien
Fig. 4. The PIMEX Intervention is dedicated to observe working systems and processes (at A
level) with focus on occupational health and process quality as well as organizational structures (B
level). Additionally it is possible to reﬂect organizations and learning processes (C level) (Kviecien
2022)
VSI concept evolved from the demand to explain complex subjects in occupational health
and for organizing learning and knowledge spaces [19].
The purpose of visualizing information items as well as their interrelations is to
facilitate learning and is also intended for use in health care education [18].
“Visual structure interfaces are intended to support and improve on-the-job training
concerning safety and health at the workplace as well as teaching and learning in the edu-
cational system, including traditional didactic methods, blended learning and e-learning
approaches.” [19].
H_Graph is a newly developed component to realize the VSI approach and addi-
tionally enable to develop tools of collaborative working and learning. (H_Graph as
part of H_technology is at TRL 4). The basic functionalities of the H_Graph compo-
nent is to manage nodes and edges (the elements of the graph theory) and to provide
a user interface to let the user operate the nodes and edges. Further edges in H_Graph
can be operated with or without strict classiﬁcation, where strict classiﬁcation (edge
classiﬁer) is useful for operating functionality based on H_Graph (such as MStrategy
(to process measurement strategies) or Hm_Designer (to design and work with mixed
methods)). The H_Graph component has been used recently for planning and perform-
ing virtual workshops for experts in occupational health domain (mainly working with
the MStrategy application).
5
Conclusions and Discussion
In recent years a lot more willingness and interest to implement approaches of digital
learning emerged in the health care domain. But still a high knowledge gap exists regard-
ing the implementation of new care approaches at one hand and approaches of integrated
learning at the other hand. Additionally a high demand of technical competences in health
care will keep virulent the next decade.

Integrated and Virtual Learning as Element
97
The concept at hand offers insights for people involved in management of education
as well as organizational development in health care on how to implement approaches of
integrated learning. Of course the approaches outlined here still needs further explanation
as well in detail but also how to apply them in combination.
The experiences from applying the virtual learning concept in health care during the
last two years show that participants of different backgrounds are able to beneﬁt from
such learning approaches. These experiences in detail will get published in a separate
publication in the near future.
One of the next steps is to derive new learning approaches based on the advanced
concept described here, which even may demand new roles and enable new functions
within an organization (= research demand). Another step will be to derive new tools
for collaborative learning in health care.
The involvement of health care organizations in research and development of
advanced concepts is something what seems to become more realistic in these days.
But there is still a demand of change in health care organizations to be able to take part
on innovation processes. Further there are still conceptual and practical challenges. One
of them is to increase interdisciplinary knowledge work in order to learn to integrated
teach and learn.

Evaluating Online Engagement
and Narrative Feedback as Indicators
of Student Performance
Philip Winﬁeld1(B), Charmain Cilliers1, and Barend van Wyk2
1 Nelson Mandela University, Gqeberha, South Africa
philip.winfield@icloud.com, Charmain.Cilliers@mandela.ac.za
2 Tshwane University of Technology, Pretoria, South Africa
VanWykB@tut.ac.za
Abstract. Learning Management Systems for online learning in higher
education allow for the collection of data that can describe student
engagement and online behaviour. Student engagement refers to the
degree of participation and active involvement with content by students
and is often linked to academic achievement. Narrative feedback given
by students can be used by academic staﬀto review and improve learn-
ing and teaching. Feedback can also be used as an indicator of student
engagement and shown to correlate to student performance. Machine
learning algorithms that predict whether a student will pass or fail, are
trained by using student engagement features. Text mining techniques
that help extract variables from narrative feedback are shown to improve
these models for identifying at-risk students. The feature distribution of
engagement factors indicate that there are patterns amongst the vari-
ables between the students who fail and those that pass.
Keywords: Learning Analytics · Student engagement · Feedback ·
Text mining · Machine learning
1
Introduction
A beneﬁt of Learning Management Systems (LMS) for online learning in higher
education is that it allows for the collection of data that can describe student
engagement and online behaviour. Student engagement refers to the degree of
participation and active involvement with content by students in the learning
and teaching environment. The impact of student engagement is often linked
to academic achievement [9]. In higher education, academic achievement is the
extent of student performance and is typically regarded as the successful comple-
tion of a desired learning outcome. There are drawbacks and advantages to the
way students interact with lectures and peers within online learning. Though,
in person communication is limited, tools such as online forums, questionnaires,
and surveys providing for narrative feedback, allow for additional support and
opportunities for interaction with the lecturer and peers [12].
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 99–107, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_10

100
P. Winﬁeld et al.
Higher education learning and the teaching environment is characterised by
oﬀering a variety of courses in various diﬀerent mediums, by a diverse group
of facilitators. For any particular course, facilitators are expected to constantly
modify and improve course content [10]. Narrative feedback from students within
the learning and teaching environments is a signiﬁcant contributory factor to the
improvement of courses [6]. In addition, feedback can be used to gain an insight
into the learning behaviour, attitude and disposition of students as they engage
with and participate in a course [16].
Exploring data within the educational environment facilitates insight into
how to improve learning and teaching. The term Learning Analytics (LA) is
used to describe this process and can be deﬁned as “the measurement, collection,
analysis and reporting of data about learners and their contexts, for purposes of
understanding and optimizing learning and the environments in which it occurs”
[14]. Statistics and Machine Learning (ML) provide sophisticated tools for the
analysis of educational data which include predictive modelling [7].
2
Aim of the Study
The study aimed to use machine learning algorithms to predict students’ aca-
demic success based on course engagement factors and narrative feedback by
answering set questions. Academic success was represented as a binary variable
of either a pass or fail. It is known that engagement has a positive inﬂuence
on achievement [9]. Online activity is seen as an engagement factor that can be
used in predicting student performance [4]. This study aimed to show whether
variables extracted from narrative feedback could also indicate success or failure
and can thus be viewed as additional measures of engagement for the prediction
of success.
3
Experimental Design
The research followed an experimental approach meaning experiments were per-
formed and results extracted. Experimental methods were used to test theories
and explore ideas to obtain new knowledge [5].
In addition, at the Nelson Mandela University in South Africa, the online
LMS Moodle1 is used by the Faculty of Engineering for the Built Environment
and Technology. A standardised template for subject format is used across the
faculty to improve quality and user experience by systematically packaging the
content and activities. The template created provides a consistent user expe-
rience across subjects with a standardised layout for ease of navigation. The
structure of this template divides a subject into various learning units where
lecturers are able to customise the content and activities of the units relating
speciﬁcally to their course. The template periodically gathers narrative student
feedback throughout participation in a subject, that can be fed back to academic
staﬀfor operational purposes.
1 https://moodle.com.

Evaluating Student Engagement and Performance
101
The research study focused on analysing non-academic metrics recorded in
the Moodle template and their relationship to student performance. Speciﬁcally,
the system user log ﬁles and the addition of information gathered from feedback
as a measure of student interaction. The variables extracted from the logs and
feedback were used to represent student engagement. Machine Learning algo-
rithms then test the usefulness and accuracy of these variables that describe
student engagement as features in the predictive models. Particularly, if written
feedback can be used as an indicator of student engagement to measure success
and contribute to or improve the accuracy of predictive models.
3.1
Data Collection
Online behaviour and student feedback were collected using Moodle LMS for
four undergraduate engineering subjects during the 2021 academic year, with
an aggregated sample size of 1234 students. These subjects comprised a diverse
range of students in terms of age, gender, and language. The subjects took one
(half a year) or two semesters (a year) to complete. Table 1 provides a summary
of the data.
Table 1. Subject information

Every interaction was recorded when a student accessed and participated
in a subject’s content on the Moodle site. These interactions were stored in a
report as the site’s log ﬁles. Four variables were extracted from the log ﬁles:
total duration online, the number of sessions, a total of page views and number
of clicks. These variables have previously been shown to be useful indicators of
student performance [4]. Summarising the large set of log data into four variables
signiﬁcantly reduced the size of the log data and produced a more meaningful
representation of the original raw logs.
Feedback activities in Moodle were responsible for capturing the feedback
from students periodically during the course of a subject. Completing the feed-
back activity was compulsory and the next section of work would only become
available once the questions had been answered. Feedback consisted of three
questions that prompted free-form narrative responses based on the reﬂection
of a student’s participation, learning, and understanding [15]. Basic text min-
ing techniques were used to extract variables from the narrative feedback that
were suitable for exploring correlation to academic performance and could be
used in predictive models. The variables included general statistics such as: the
number of sentences, word count, average characters per word, function words,

102
P. Winﬁeld et al.
vocabulary and percentage of language errors. Other linguistic markers aimed
to extract the learning intent, attitude and disposition of the students. The use
of verbs indicated action and intent toward active participation in the subject
[16]. While the use of pronouns possible gave a glimpse into the cognition of the
student and their relation towards what they have written [3]. For instance, the
presence of ﬁrst personal pronouns may indicate self-awareness [16].
For each subject, student information, log ﬁles and feedback were extracted
from Moodle and then merged and anonymised with the student data recorded
on the university’s information technology system, which included the ﬁnal
grades.
3.2
Data Analysis
Data analysis aimed at using variables that represented student engagement,
extracted from the log ﬁles and feedback, paired with the students’ ﬁnal grades to
build predictive models. Machine learning (ML) prediction models were trained
using student engagement features for the binary classiﬁcation of either fail or
pass. The machine learning algorithms were chosen based on: the desired out-
come, classiﬁcation of identifying categories, data available, including the ﬁnal
outcome, and required accuracy over speed [2]. This led to the following ML
algorithms being considered: Decision Trees, Random Forest, Logistic Regres-
sion, and Support Vector Machines. Decision trees use a tree data structure to
guide classiﬁcation based on the information provided. Random forests create
a collection of decision trees and randomly assigns a subset of features for the
nodes. Each decision tree in the random forest predicts a class and the class
with the most predictions is the ﬁnal outcome [1]. Logistic regression uses prob-
ability to determine a discrete outcome by describing the non-linear relationship
between the combination of all the independent variables and the target vari-
able [13]. Support Vector Machines (SVM) utilise mathematical programming
and kernel functions which aim to identify a hyperplane in an N-dimensional
space that optimally separates data points into two categories [11].
All the algorithms used supervised learning which divided the data into a
training and test set. The training set helped optimise the parameters in the
model to make predictions. Then the accuracy of the algorithms was measured
using the test set in terms of precision, recall, and F-measure (combination of
precision and recall) [8].
Precision = no. of correct prediction for tag
no. of predictions for tag
(1)
Recall = no. of correct prediction for tag
no. of tags in category
(2)
From the variables describing student engagement, the algorithm would tag
each student as either in the category of failing or passing. This would be per-
formed for the entire test set, then the accuracy measures would be compared
for each category. The overall accuracy of the algorithms was measured using a
weighted average of identifying each category of students correctly.

4
Results and Discussion of Results
The initial experimentation viewed the data from each subject as a combined
data set. This attempted to address the problem of portability in predictive
models between subjects [4]. This displayed weak results with logistic regression
producing the highest overall accuracy with a score of 86%. While this may seem
promising, the fail set accounted for only about 20% of the data and had an f1-
score of 43%. Overall accuracy is weighted by the size of each category. As a
primary concern was to identify at risk students, and those who were less likely
to achieve minimum requirements to pass, precision, recall and f1-scores of the
fail category were more important to consider.
4.1
Accuracy of Prediction Across Subjects
Subsequently, each subject was analysed individually by training the ML algo-
rithms on diﬀerent data sets. The features used in training the algorithms ﬁrst
consisted only of the four log variables. They were then trained with the inclusion
of the feedback variables to compare if there was any improvement in accuracy.
Figure 1 displays the average performance of the ML algorithms across the four
subjects by comparing the overall accuracy, and the diﬀerent accuracy mea-
sures for the fail category. Logistic Regression and SVM consistently produced
more accurate results compared to Decision Trees and Random Forests. Slight
improvement in the various accuracy measures was evident by the inclusion of
features extracted from narrative feedback. The accuracy of predictive models
across the subjects is described.
Fig. 1. Average performance of algorithms across all subjects

Subject A: produced the most accurate results across all the accuracy measures
compared to the other subjects. Figure 2, displays the classiﬁcation report of the
Logistic Regression model that produce the highest level of accuracy for the set.
The ’0.0’ category represents the measures of accuracy in tagging students as
failed. The ’0.0’ precision indicates, that of the students that were tagged as
failing, 90% were correctly labelled. Then the recall indicates of the support, the
number of students in the fail category in the test set, 90% were tagged correctly.
The f1-score is a combination of precision and recall. The results were obtained
by only using the features from the log ﬁles, the addition of features from the
narrative feedback showed no improvement to the model.

Subject B: The predictive models produced fair results with the use of features
from just the log ﬁles. The inclusion of features extracted from narrative feedback
increased the ’0.0’ f1-score by 10%, producing a fail set f1 accuracy of 79% and
overall accuracy 96%. This was achieved by the SVM predictive model.
Subject C: Good results were achieved and the SVM and Logistic Regression
produced similar accuracy. The f1-scores were 80% and 95% for the fail and pass
sets respectively. This was combined to an overall accuracy of 93%.
Subject D: Produced fair results though weaker when compared to the other
subjects. There was no change in accuracy between the models using only log
ﬁle features and those that included features for the narrative feedback. The
f1-scores were 67% and 95% for the fail and pass sets respectively. This was
combined to an overall accuracy of 91%.

5
Conclusion and Future Work
Student engagement was categorised by online activity and the inclusion of nar-
rative feedback. Online activity and engagement has been shown to correlate to
student performance and the results produced further corroborate these ﬁnd-
ings. The exploration of narrative feedback showed it could be a viable factor
for representing engagement linking to student success. Variables extracted from
narrative feedback using text mining may improve the accuracy of predictive
models for identifying at risk students. This is shown by the feature distribution
with diﬀerences between students who failed and passed. Thus, indicating trends
in students engagement and patterns between variables extracted from both the
log ﬁles and student feedback to performance.

Emotional Intelligence in the Development
of Entrepreneurial Competence
Juraj Mikuš1
, Anna Pilková1
, Marian Holienka1
, and Yuliia Fedorova1,2(B)
1 Comenius University Bratislava, Bratislava, Slovakia
{juraj.mikus,anna.pilkova,marian.holienka,
yuliia.fedorova}@fm.uniba.sk
2 Ukrainian Engineering Pedagogics Academy, Kharkiv, Ukraine
fedorova_yv@uipa.edu.ua
Abstract. The article proposes an approach to teaching entrepreneurship using
the 4-component instrumental model of emotional intelligence (4EI model), which
can be easily used in teaching and applied in business to form entrepreneurial com-
petence. This approach differs from the existing approaches and contains a toolkit
(questionnaire), which allows exploring the level and dynamics of the develop-
ment of emotional intelligence through the construction of respondents’ emotional
intelligence proﬁles. The article studies the individual’s behavioural characteris-
tics based on advanced methods for classifying role terms and offers recommen-
dations for building an optimal project team, taking into account the synergy of
the members’ emotional proﬁles. This study aims to develop recommendations
for the formation of a project team of youth and seniors, considering their emo-
tional proﬁles. The study’s practical signiﬁcance is the ability to form effective
business teams based on self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and
relationship management of each team member. The possibility of building opti-
mal entrepreneurial and/or project teams with the participation of two population
groups with professional integration problems - seniors and youth - has been
proven. The research was conducted in two European countries: Ukraine and Slo-
vakia. The research encourages implementing effective techniques for developing
emotional intelligence in the educational process of entrepreneurial competence
formation.
Keywords: Emotional intelligence proﬁle · Optimal team design · Seniors and
youth
1
Problem Statement
In Industry 4.0, the soft skills of modern entrepreneurs play a unique role in providing
economic growth for countries. The ability to build effective communication, negotiate,
lead projects, inspire and lead a team is the task of emotional intelligence in entrepreneur-
ship. Thus, the development of emotional intelligence contributes to the formation of
entrepreneurial competence and leads to additional ﬁnancial income. Entrepreneurs with
a high level of EQ have a clear vision of the company’s future, easily get along with
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 108–118, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_11

Emotional Intelligence in the Development of Entrepreneurial
109
business partners, get ahead of competitors, and use the energy of emotions to achieve
positive results.
Today innovation-driven start-ups and companies in developed countries understand
that the effectiveness of the management process is increasingly determined not only by
the mental abilities of the leader but also by the ability to apply emotional intelligence
and leadership skills. Modern leadership theory in management is based on emotional
intelligence. The new generation manager is an emotional leader. Emotional intelligence
shapes entrepreneurial competence and leads to ﬁnancial results. That is why a question
arises about studying the emotional intelligence and emotional capital in the management
of start-ups and established enterprises.
2
Analysis of Recent Research and Publications
The role of soft skills in the business environment is increasing, as was noted at the
World Economic Forum [1]. EI provides several top 10 skills in demand by 2025, namely
leadership and social inﬂuence, resilience, stress tolerance and ﬂexibility.
Since J.D. Mayer and R. Salovey [2] founded the concept of EI, the number of
studies using the term has steadily increased. This trend is particularly characteristic in
organisational psychology, but it is increasingly common in business. The number of
scientiﬁc papers that indicate the dependence of the company’s ﬁnancial success on the
ability of employees to build effective relationships is increasing. Some results show
the relationship between Emotional Intelligence and the achievement of nurse leaders
in healthcare [3, 4]. 169 Chinese construction companies’ executives were surveyed
and it was found that managers with a high level of emotional intelligence increase
the innovative activity of employees and increase work efﬁciency [5]. EI is needed
for future public relations leaders and for an EI model of professionalism in public
relations education [6]. Transformational leadership’s effect on employee engagement
is completely mediated by the leader’s emotional intelligence at work [7]. P.N. Lopes
[8] discusses strategies to enhance the impact of EI and leadership training and to drive
results through well-integrated organizational development initiatives. The research [9]
revealed that spiritual leadership and emotional intelligence were related to spiritual
well-being and creative performance.
The positive impact of emotional intelligence and the well-being of employees on
the productivity of work in the hospitality industry and customer satisfaction is noted.
The authors [10] encourage hotel managers and HR managers to consider EI as
one of the main criteria for recruiting and selecting hotel frontline employees. Emo-
tional intelligence inﬂuence of decision-makers studied on output value, alongside the
conventional capital and labour inputs, in the Cobb-Douglas (C-D) Product Function,
found that the multiple correlations increase both Sales Turnover and Value Addition
after inclusion of EI factors [11]. EI has been shown to impact health, relationships, and
work/academic performance [12].
Researchers argue that there are hidden connections between emotional intelligence
and a company’s ﬁnancial performance, which requires a more complex, layered, and
in-depth examination.
Assessing EI remains challenging and requires further quantitative research. There-
fore, we have focused on developing guidelines for building a project team based on

110
J. Mikuš et al.
the emotional proﬁle of its members. We believe that using EI development tools in
building a project team, will lead entrepreneurs to succeed in the market economy, build
intellectual capital and increase company assets.
In research papers, team roles are considered in terms of the functions of team mem-
bers (managerial approach) or in terms of the individual’s behavioural characteristics
(psychological approach). At the same time, the research is mostly descriptive, and there
is a real problem in quantifying the dependence of the result of teamwork on the indi-
vidual roles of team members. The number of existing studies indicates the presence of
unresolved methodological problems and conﬁrms the high scientiﬁc and practical rel-
evance of the problem. This topic is particularly relevant in the context of the increasing
role of project management technologies in management.
Today there are no clear instructions on how to form an effective team because no
quantitative approaches to measuring the competencies of team members have been
developed. There is no common understanding of an effective team for implementing
project tasks. Moreover, it is not easy to quantify each participant’s contribution to the
collective result. However, in the entrepreneurship context, it may be helpful to develop
recommendations for creating an optimal team of potentially possible participants based
on their proﬁle of emotional intelligence.
This study aims to develop recommendations for the formation of a project team
of youth and seniors, considering their emotional proﬁles. The practical aspect of the
study is the possibility of forming an optimal team based on the proﬁles of candidates’
emotional intelligence. In this case, people of different ages can be in the team. For
example, this approach is applied to two population groups with professional integration
problems—seniors and youth - and their limitations for entrepreneurship, despite their
undoubted capabilities.
The study’s novelty is an attempt to apply the proﬁle of emotional intelligence in
business to build an effective project team while involving quantitative analysis of the
emotional proﬁles of participants in two European countries.
3
Statement of Basic Material and the Substantiation
of the Obtained Results
This approach considers advanced methods of role classiﬁcation by R.M. Belbin [13]
and D. Winsborough, T. Chamorro-Premuzic [14]. The study was conducted based on
the Department of Economics and Management of Ukrainian Engineering Pedagog-
ics Academy (UEPA) and Department of Strategy and Entrepreneurship, Faculty of
Management, Comenius University Bratislava. The study involved 40 Slovak and 40
Ukrainian students of management and economic specialties, and 40 Slovak and 14
Ukrainian senior respondents aged 55 years and older.
The formation of entrepreneurial competence involves using a 4-component instru-
mental model of emotional intelligence (4EI model). 4EI model is based on the model
of D. Goleman but contains four components and focuses on the business context. 4EI
model comprises 4 scales (self-awareness (SA), self-management (SM), social aware-
ness (SocA), and relationship management (RM)). According to this model, the tool for
diagnosing and building proﬁles is the “Emotional Intelligence in Business” [15] test.

Emotional Intelligence in the Development of Entrepreneurial
111
This test was created as a result of development procedures, tests and psychometric test-
ing. The test can be used to monitor the dynamics of emotional intelligence in training
courses and educational projects. The “Emotional Intelligence in Business” test is a reli-
able, discriminatory, and valid test method that measures the overall level of the construct
and its components: self-awareness, self-control, social awareness, and relationship
management, and can be used in the formation of entrepreneurial competence.
The proposed model contains four components of emotional intelligence, which
allows for building a convenient graphical representation of the results as an EI diagram
consistingoffourquadrants.ThehorizontalaxisshowsthedirectionofEIcoverage(from
left to right) from the individual level to the population group level. The vertical axis
shows the degree of EI control (bottom-up) from just understanding one’s own emotions
and the emotions of others to managing one’s own emotions and the emotions of others.
Quantitative characteristics of each of the four EI 4-component instrumental model
indicators are displayed at a side of the corresponding quadrant. Within the learning
process, this approach allows demonstrating the dynamics of each component of EI by
increasing the area of the corresponding quadrant. The side of the quadrant can range
from 0 to 10, corresponding to the STEN (standard ten) score system. According to the
STEN score system, results from 0 to 3 demonstrate a low level, results from 4 to 7 show
a medium level, and results from 8 to 10 demonstrate a high level of the development
of the components of the 4-component instrumental model EI. According to the 4EI
model, the emotional proﬁle of the respondent consists of four quadrants, Fig. 1.
Fig. 1. The example of the EI proﬁle of the 4EI model
In the sample proﬁle, the respondent’s Self-awareness (SA) is 7,3; self-management
(SM) is 5,3; social awareness (SocA) is 4,9; relationship management (RM) is 7,1.
In this case, the demonstration of the results indicates the need to further develop this
particular student’s self-management and social awareness. Figure 2 shows the fragment

The Table 1 presents the 4EI model competence description. Using the emotional
intelligence proﬁles, it is possible to make recommendations for building an optimal
team based on psychological roles.
By team, we mean a project team whose members come together temporarily to
solve certain tasks (target task model). In practice, there are different models of teams:
traditional, team spirit model, leading-edge model, target task model, and cyber-team.
A project team is most suitable for entrepreneurship in a constantly changing external
environment. The psychological roles of participants play a key role in constructing
of such teams. Taking into account the peculiarities of participants’ emotional intelli-
gence development allows predicting the optimal compatibility of participants. Team
composition is a key factor affecting team performance.
As shown by the analysis of the effectiveness of hundreds of teams, when selecting
the composition of the team, we should consider two roles that each person plays in the
workgroup: The functional role, based on his/her ofﬁcial position and technical prowess,
and the psychological role, based on his/her way of interacting with other people and
values. The lack of psychological synergy leads to the team’s failure. A role indicates a
broad set of tasks, activities, deliverables, and responsibilities that a person must perform
as part of a project. Each team member can simultaneously play several different roles
in the project.
We relied on the most popular team building models to develop our recommenda-
tions. One of the most authoritative theories about the inﬂuence of team composition and

4EI model. Also, in the team should be the roles of Innovator (high-level Self-awareness

With the help of a chatbot and Google forms, a survey was conducted of students from
Ukrainian and Slovak universities, and the adult population of Ukraine and Slovakia. 134
respondents took part in the voluntary survey. Participation in the empirical study was
voluntary. As a result of statistical processing, we obtained the following conclusions.
In cases where the respondent had a high level of two components, the role of the higher
value was selected.
The results of the analysis of the survey are presented in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4.
The diagram shows a large difference in the level of Social Understanding between
Slovak and Ukrainian students. Slovak youth are more empathetic and can build teams
faster.
The data analysis also shows that it is possible to make optimal co-teams of respon-
dents: students and seniors from the same region. The composition of the optimal project
team in Slovakia and Ukraine is presented in Table 3.
Based on the model, possible variants of project teams are formed further. Taking
into account the functions of team members according to modern methods of managerial
approach allows optimizing the team composition as much as possible.
Group training held at Comenius University in Bratislava and Ukrainian Engineering
Pedagogics Academy allows and will further increase the level of emotional intelligence
of each team member. The training program “Emotional Intelligence in Entrepreneur-
ship” works through each quadrant of the 4-component instrumental model of EI. Thus,
the algorithm of optimal team building based on emotional intelligence proﬁles has
several stages:
Step 1. The team’s basic requirements, composition, work objectives, evaluation
criteria, terms, and other characteristics are determined. A competency matrix with
boundary values is created.

Conclusions
The research paper describes a comprehensive approach to developing the emotional
intelligence of entrepreneurs. The developed recommendations consider the modern
methods of team-building based on role classiﬁcation. On the basis of the 4-component
instrumental model of EI and thanks to the “Emotional Intelligence in Business” test,
the algorithm of construction and model of the optimal project team was developed.
The team should include 5 Team Roles by the 4EI model: Leader, Innovator, Specialist,
Team Worker, and Investigator, each of the participants corresponds to a certain type of
emotional proﬁle in the business. A quantitative model for building an optimal project
team is described. Based on statistical data, our study proved the possibility of building
optimal intergenerational teams involving both youth and seniors from the same region
representing a good potential for involving these population categories that face cer-
tain inclusion difﬁculties in entrepreneurial teams. The synergistic effect of combining
the efforts of each participant will create additional opportunities in entrepreneurship.
Conducting training sessions at universities on the development of emotional intelli-
gence increases the study participants’ EI and motivates them to create their businesses.
Moreover, building their awareness about potential intergenerational synergies in rela-
tion to forming optimal entrepreneurial teams enhances their openness to cooperation
with older generations.
Further areas of research are: a) to increase the number of respondents and mea-
sure the level of emotional intelligence in entrepreneurship in different countries; b) to
study the effectiveness of optimal project teams built based on the emotional proﬁles of
respondents.

Teaching English in Universities for IT Students
Giniyatullina Diana1(B)

Abstract. Modern standards of higher education put forward new requirements
for the preparation of students: they must be communicative, have a high level
of professional competencies, be ready to use them in non-standard situations
and strive for constant self-development. Competitiveness in the labor market
determines the ability of a specialist to solve problems in foreign language com-
munication. The relevance of this study lies in the use of active and interactive
teaching methods and technologies by the teacher. These techniques help to solve
the problem of the impossibility of creating optimal conditions for the develop-
ment of the competence of oral foreign language communication. The number
of classroom hours devoted to language disciplines at the universities of non-
language areas is limited; therefore, the Teaching Approach is the methodological
basis for the development of such technologies, which explains the relevance of
this study. The object of the research is the process of teaching a foreign language
in a university of non-linguistic areas (IT). The subject of the research is a technol-
ogy developed on the basis of an educational approach for teaching oral foreign
language communication at the university of non-linguistic areas. The aim of the
study is to determine the speciﬁcs of the technology of communicative training in
teaching a foreign language and to identify components that could be used as a
basis for developing a system of training exercises for teaching foreign language
communication to students of non-linguistic areas. In this study, the following
methods were used: Theoretical: analysis of sources on the problem under study,
description, generalization. Empirical: 1) questioning; 2) a survey of practicing
teachers; 3) analysis of teaching aids in order to study the communicative tasks
offered in them, as well as analysis and their teaching potential; 4) observation
of the educational process. Upon achieving this goal, the following results were
obtained: 1) The main methods of formation of foreign language communicative
competence in the university of non-linguistic areas have been determined; 2) The
degree of knowledge of the problem of using the training technology as a way
of developing the foreign language competence of the university has been deter-
mined; 3) Studied the features of the technology of communication training from
the point of view of psychology, pedagogy and “linguodidactics” (teaching lin-
guistics) and determine its educational potential; 4) Developed and tested a set of
tasks for communicative training in English classes for students of non-linguistic
areas (IT). The conclusions of the study are that the process of teaching a foreign
language to students of IT areas can be more effective when the teacher uses the

1
Introduction
The process of formation of foreign language communicative competence among stu-
dents of non-linguistic areas has its own speciﬁcs and requires special forms and tech-
nologies of teaching. Teaching a foreign language for the purpose of developing oral
foreignlanguagecommunicationiscarriedoutusingthefollowingpedagogicaltechnolo-
gies: technology (skill) of communicative teaching; differentiated learning technology;
ICT, which is a system of methods and methods for collecting, storing, accumulating,
searching, transmitting, processing information by means of a computer [1]; testing
technology [2]; design technology; game technology; technology for the formation and
development of critical thinking [3].
The training is a direction in teaching various social and psychological skills, which
has become widespread and used in foreign and domestic psychology. It should be noted
that today there is no generally accepted deﬁnition of the concept of “training” as such.
We have chosen the deﬁnition of “training” E.V. Sidorenko: “Training - teaching the
technologies of action based on a certain concept of reality in an interactive form” [4].
The main task of the training, according to experts, is the development of a person’s
personality, increasing socio-psychological and communicative competence. Teaching
technology is a kind of systemic category that encompasses certain means and methods
of teaching, as well as thoughtful pedagogical actions that are used in the course of
the educational process and contribute to improving the effectiveness of teaching. In
our research, we took the deﬁnition of E.V. Tikhonova, who deﬁnes communication
trainingas“learning,traininginpracticalexercises,closetotherealconditionsofactivity,
which contribute to the improvement of competencies, abilities and skills, as well as the
personality as a whole” [5]. We rely on this deﬁnition as the best one.
The main assets of communication training are the activity of the participants, an
emphasis on the current moment, as well as the exchange of experience between students;
goal setting, educational impact, intensity.
2
Methodology
The process of teaching a foreign language to students of non-linguistic areas can be
more effective when the teacher uses the training technology of teaching, which assumes:
the interactive nature of teaching. Therefore, in our study, the following methods were
used.
Theoretical methods: analysis of sources on the problem under study, description,
generalization.

Empirical methods: questioning; a survey of practicing teachers; analysis of teaching
aids in order to study the communicative tasks offered in them, as well as analysis and
their teaching potential; observation of the educational process.

Results
Tochecktheeffectivenessoftheuseoftrainingtechnologyinteachingaforeignlanguage
to students of non-linguistic areas, pedagogical approbation was carried out, which
consisted of several stages.
The purpose of this paper is to outline the three-stage model of teaching English to IT
students. The description of the highlighted stages enables specialists to apply the results
for experimental purposes. The level of our students’ (IT students) English language
proﬁciency ranges from B1 (intermediate) to B2 (upper intermediate) according to the
Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (2002).
The ﬁrst stage was a survey of students in order to identify their motivation to learn
a foreign language. In total, 100 students of the 1st course of IT directions took part
in the survey. The level of English proﬁciency among students is B1. Using a survey
conducted in November-December 2021 among 1st year students (40 people) of Kazan
Federal University, (25 people) National Research University, (15 people) Kazan State
Agrarian University, (20 people) Kazan National Research Technological University
named after A.N. Tupolev, students in IT areas, we were able to identify the main goals
of their language learning. These are the goals:
1) Knowledge of a foreign language at a level that allows you to achieve success
in your career, namely, to be competitive in the labor market. This goal is set by the
majority of the surveyed students (65%); 2) Knowledge of a foreign language for self-
education and self-realization in the scientiﬁc environment, the opportunity to take part
in international conferences, in scientiﬁc projects, the opportunity to engage in research
work abroad - 12% of the surveyed students; 3) Knowledge of a foreign language for
living abroad - 20% of the student; 4) Proﬁciency in a foreign language as a means that
allows you to communicate easily during tourist trips abroad - 3% of students.
The results of the survey of students allowed us to conclude that their motivation
to learn a foreign language is quite high, despite the fact that a foreign language is not
a major subject. Students are aware of the need for proﬁciency in a foreign language,
although some of them do not plan to use a foreign language in their professional
activities.
The next step in the pedagogical approbation was the observation of the pedagogical
process. 40 teachers took part in the survey. Of the 40 classes attended, which were con-
ducted by various teachers at these universities, the use of active teaching methods, and
in particular the technology of communication training, was not observed. To the ques-
tion: “What do you mean by “training technology of teaching a foreign language”?” the
following answers were received from teachers in percentage terms: “an active method
of development to master any kind of activity” - 55%, “communication training” - 31%,
“interaction with society” - 14%.
The main reason why the interviewed teachers do not resort to active (or interactive)
forms of education, they named the limited number of classroom hours devoted to

122
G. Diana et al.
teaching a foreign language. This reason was chosen by 70% of teachers. The second
reason was the large volume of material required for mastering by the students according
to standard teaching aids (20%), the third reason was the difﬁcult process of designing
tasks (10%) (especially if we take into account the disciple “English for professional
use”, where the tasks are often just: read the text, summarize the text, learn the new
vocabulary).
In the course of the study, the following criteria were established to make commu-
nication training tasks more effective in the context of improving the communication
skills of students: the topics proposed for discussion should be interesting and important
for the future professional activities of students; maximum approximation to reality;
minimizing boring and uninteresting texts; asking students to ﬁnd the material.
At the second stage of the research, the development and implementation of commu-
nication training tasks in the learning process were carried out. Communication training
was carried out in groups of students from these universities, studying in the 3rd year.
The total number of participants was 100 people. In total, 20 lessons were held in 10
groups. Each group had 2 lessons with training technology and 2 lessons with usual
method of teaching. These results of the usual lesson plan remained the same; however,
these lessons with training technology improved the English language of the students.

a positive dynamics was also noted in the number of statements of students, which they

Task 1. Each student receives a card containing a list of statements. Opposite each

The analysis of errors in speech was carried out at the end of each communication
task in order to prevent their appearance in the future. We have identiﬁed the main types
of mistakes made by students [10]:
1. The use of the wrong part of speech (“important” instead of “importance”, “de-
veloping” instead of “development”); 2.Errors in the use of stable constructions (“from
the one hand… From the other hand”, “in the one hand” instead of “on the one hand…
on the other hand”, “in my point of view” instead of “from my point of view”, not to
mention “like to going” instead of “like to go” in some cases, etc.); 3. Grammatical
errors when using the 3rd person singular verbs in the grammatical tense Present Simple
(“it reduce”, “he recycle” and so on), as well as when using irregular verbs in the “Past
Simple Tense”(“He broughted”vs of“ he brought”) [11, 12].

The conversation with the teachers revealed what results, in their opinion, the
systematic use of the training technology of teaching in the educational process can
bring:
– Development of oral speech skills and motivation to use a foreign language in real
life;
– Removing the psychological barrier when communicating with representatives of a
foreign language culture;
– Ability to listen to the foreign language speech of the interlocutor;
– Effective memorization of stable expressions and constructions;
As the survey has shown, the students (IT) as a whole positively perceived this form
of education and see it as an educational potential. 18 people out of 20 respondents
considered communication training to be one of the technologies necessary for the
implementation of the educational process.
The relevance of introducing training technology into the learning process is
determined by the following factors:
1. A small number of hours devoted to foreign language classes, as well as insuf-
ﬁciently rational distribution of tasks on a communicative basis; 2.A small number of
groups (on average 10–15 people), which is a favorable condition for conducting active

forms of education; 3.Quite a low level of practice-oriented knowledge of the English
language; 4.The predominance of reproductive activities over productive ones (mem-
orizing educational topics, texts and grammatical rules by heart); 5.The predominant
focus of the learning process is not on the formation of practical skills and their use in
foreign language activities, but on the transfer of formal grammatical knowledge. 6. The
use of IT in EFL classroom.
With the replenishment of the lexical stock of words, the student also develops a
worldview to another culture, which leads to an improvement in cognitive linguistics
[14]. The use of various translation transformations is favored by the study of the dis-
course of the language itself [15]. Constant interaction with the new surrounding world
forms in a person a new understanding of reality.
4
Conclusion
When designing communication training tasks, we considered it appropriate to take into
account the following requirements. We highlight some methodological recommenda-
tions for conducting communication training, namely:
1. Tasks of communication training should be carried out systematically, throughout
the academic semester. Regular and methodical carrying out of communicative tasks
will to a greater extent contribute to the effective social adaptation of the training
participants.
2. Communication training is recommended at the beginning or the end of the lesson
for 20–25 min, taking the rest of the time to complete traditional tasks. A greater
amount of time spent on the implementation of communicative tasks in the format
of training technology, due to the active load on speech-thinking mechanisms, leads
to a decrease in the motivation for their implementation.
3. Carrying out the training requires the teacher to develop the necessary didactic means
for the implementation of the educational process, which, within the framework of
the presented technology, are special visual cards with tasks.
4. The organization of the training involves the division of participants into groups.
5. Training can take place in various forms: In the form of a dialogue, when participants
complement each other’s thoughts; in the form of a dispute, discussion, a round table
(of no more than 4 students per group).
The work was carried out as part of the implementation of the Strategic Aca-
demic Leadership Program of the Kazan (Volga Region) Federal University
(“PRIORITET-2030”)
