A Disinformation Training Course Using
the PROVENANCE Veriﬁcation
Indicator Tool
Alexander Nussbaumer1(B), Sylvia M. Ebner1, In`es Dinant2,
´Oscar Espiritusanto2, Eileen Culloty3, Kirsty Park3, and Christian G¨utl1
1 Graz University of Technology, Graz, Austria
{alexander.nussbaumer,sylvia.ebner,c.guetl}@tugraz.at
2 Fundaci´on Cibervoluntarios, Madrid, Spain
{ines.dinant,oscar.espiritusanto}@cibervoluntarios.org
3 Dublin City University, Dublin, Ireland
{eileen.culloty,kirsty.park}@dcu.ie
Abstract. This paper presents a training course that aims to develop
the competence to identify disinformation and fake news. Disinforma-
tion constitutes a huge problem in our world of digital media and digital
communication. In particular, people with little understanding of prob-
lematic online content tend to share and distribute false information. The
training course aims at educating these people, so that they stop sharing
disinformation. The training course has been evaluated in a study with
36 participants regarding its learning eﬀectiveness. In a pre- and post-test
it could be veriﬁed that the participants increased their disinformation
competence, especially those with initially low competence. Furthermore,
the training course was rated very positively by all participants.
Keywords: Disinformation · Information literacy · Media literacy ·
News literacy · Training course
1
Introduction
Presently, our society faces an overwhelming amount of fake news and disinfor-
mation spread over digital technologies and social media. This situation leads to
a general societal challenge that includes the news market, the digital platforms,
and social media, as well as the consumers and their online behaviour [5]. Online
news is often distributed via digital platforms and shared in social media. Beside
traditional news publishers, an enormous amount of new and often dubious pub-
lishers have emerged [11]. In this situation consumers tend to lose overview and
control over their media behaviour.
Several approaches have been proposed to address and combat this almost
ubiquitous problem [2]: Manual fact checking and content veriﬁcation by non-
proﬁt organisations aim at identifying false information on the Web and make
them public including the information that is true instead. Automatic detecting
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 127–138, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_13

128
A. Nussbaumer et al.
fake accounts and ampliﬁcation mechanisms of false information should mitigate
their spread. Legal initiatives aim at regulating the use of information publication
on national level including information on the publishers. Media literacy training
of the consumers seeks to educate the users to identify false information.
However, there is a broad discussion on the deﬁnitions of media, news, and
information literacy as well as on other related areas of competence [3,8,10].
Some years ago, an expert group deﬁned media literacy as “[...] the ability to
access the media, to understand and to critically evaluate diﬀerent aspects of
the media and media contents and to create communications in a variety of
contexts” [4]. Not only media literacy is necessary for participation in the digital
world, but also other literacy skills like information or news literacy [9]. However,
information literacy refers to the ability to understand, ﬁnd, evaluate, and use
information. News literacy refers to the ability to critically evaluate and analyse
print and online news [8]. Obviously, all these types of literacy are overlapping.
While information literacy refers to general information, news literacy refers to
information in the context of news, and media literacy focuses on the media
through which information is retrieved.
Based on these diﬀerent literacy deﬁnitions, it seems obvious that such com-
petencies need time for a good development and that they also need to be trained.
The literature shows that some sort of skills can be fostered. In a study it was
demonstrated that media and information literacy training improved the judge-
ment accuracy about the quality of information [1]. This positive eﬀect on con-
tent veriﬁcation and sharing behaviour was proven with an experimental group
that got media and information literacy training while the control group did not
get this training.
Following the result of the aforementioned study, this paper presents an app-
roach on how to design and develop a course that teaches media and information
literacy. The main aim of this course is to increase the competence of consumers
regarding the identiﬁcation of false information on the web. The course concept
consists of three elements, namely (a) the delivery of theoretical knowledge on
how to identify problematic content, (b) practical examples to identify problem-
atic content, and (c) a tool that supports users regarding the identiﬁcation of
problematic content. Thus this approach addresses the problem of disinforma-
tion on the web by integrating both competence development and a technology
that makes people aware of problematic content.
In order to validate the course concept, an online course has been developed
and veriﬁed in an experimental study. This course is implemented as a web
application and integrates the Veriﬁcation Indicator tool that makes users aware
of problematic content. Two research questions that have guided the course
development, as well as the study design and the analysis:
RQ1: How can the Veriﬁcation Indicator be used to create a training course?
RQ2: Has a disinformation training course with the Veriﬁcation Indicator inte-
grated a positive learning eﬀect?
The next section describes the design and development of the course including
the Veriﬁcation Indicator tool and Sect. 3 presents the study including its design,
analysis, and discussion related to the research questions.

Disinformation Training Course
129
2
Disinformation Training Course
This section describes the concept of the disinformation training course. The
key element of the course is the so-called Veriﬁcation Indicator tool that helps
identifying problematic content. The course embeds this tool in a setting of
theoretical explanations and practical exercises.
2.1
Veriﬁcation Indicator
The Veriﬁcation Indicator tool has been developed in the context of the PROVE-
NANCE research project with the aim to support users in judging online news
[12]. This tool is implemented as a web browser plugin that monitors the articles
a user opens and provides warnings in case of problematic content. The tool
analyses seven aspects that are relevant for judging online articles, namely (1)
the date of an article, (2) the location of the publisher, (3) the publisher of the
article, (4) the writing style, (5) the tone regarding emotional language, (6) same
content reported in (other) reliable news outlets, and (7) the authenticity of the
included images. Each of these aspects can result in a warning.
The user interface is organised as a three-warning-level approach (see Fig. 1).
Level 1 is represented by a single icon in the toolbar of the web browser. It shows
a red exclamation mark if one of the seven aspects has a warning, otherwise it
shows a green check mark. By clicking on the icon, the level 2 information ﬁeld
opens where the warnings for the particular aspects are displayed. By clicking
on an aspect (with or without warning), further information on the nature of
the warning and a related media tip for critical thinking are given in level 3.
From a technical point of view, complex analysis is being made in the back-
ground, which is not explained in detail in this paper. The analysis of the writing
style and tone is being made with machine learning algorithms that are trained
with respective problematic and non-problematic articles. The analysis of similar
content elsewhere is done through semantic analysis of large amounts of news
articles. Image analysis is carried out using image reverse search techniques as
well as comparison analysis when images have been manipulated. The ﬁrst three
information categories (date, location, and source) are retrieved by analysing
the content of the article’s webpage and metadata.
It is important to note that the calculations and warnings have to be critically
reﬂected, since the algorithms can fail in their judgement. This matter of fact
is exploited by presenting media literacy tips on level 3 that ask the user to
critically reﬂect the presented tool information.
2.2
Course Concept
A dedicated web application has been created that makes available the course
in English, Spanish, and German language. Each participant can log in with a
given user code, which is necessary because the course should be taken over a
time period of at least two weeks. Basically the course consists of four units and
three homework tasks. The course start page provides access to these course

130
A. Nussbaumer et al.
Fig. 1. This veriﬁcation indicator concept.
elements, informs which one has already been completed and what should be
done next. The units contain explanations of the particular aspects of the Ver-
iﬁcation Indicator (e.g. shown for the writing indicator in Fig. 3). Furthermore,
the units contain practical exercises where real online news articles have to be
approached and assessed using the Veriﬁcation Indicator tool. After each unit
the users have to complete homework tasks, which consists of identifying articles
from a predeﬁned set with particular problems in a certain aspect. For example,
articles that are problematic in terms of writing style need to be identiﬁed. An
overview of the structure is given in Fig. 2 and details are provided in the next
paragraphs.
Unit 1: At the beginning of the course a short introduction to disinforma-
tion and the PROVENANCE project is given to the participants. Then the
participants introduce themselves and reﬂect on their experiences with dis-
information on the web. In the next step an introduction to and examples of
the ﬁrst three aspects (date, location, source) are given. Thus the unit focuses
on the origin of news articles. Thereafter the users get two online articles as
practical examples to try out the Veriﬁcation Indicator by making a judge-
ment of each article with the help of the Veriﬁcation Indicator. To deepen
the knowledge, a homework assignment is given at the end of the unit. The
participants have to ﬁnd examples in a given selection of 20 articles where
date, location, or source is problematic.
Unit 2: In the ﬁrst step of Unit 2 the content of Unit 1 is reviewed. This is
followed by the introduction to and examples of two further aspects of the
Veriﬁcation Indicator, namely the writing style and the tone. Thus the unit
focuses on the content of news stories. In the following exercise, the partic-
ipants try out the tool with the new aspects by evaluating the two articles
regarding the content aspects. Another homework assignment is given that
includes the search for articles where writing style and tone is problematic.
Unit 3: At the beginning of Unit 3 the content of Unit 2 is reviewed. Then the
two remaining aspects are introduced, which are the reported elsewhere and
the image and video aspects. Thus the unit addresses the context of news

stories. Again practical examples are used for a short exercise with these two
aspects. Finally, in a homework assignment the users deepen their knowledge
on these two aspects.
Unit 4: At the beginning of the ﬁnal unit, the content of the previous unit is
reviewed. Then the homework and its results are presented to each partici-
pant. The selected article for each aspect is displayed with an indication if
this assignment is correct or not. Furthermore, the whole set of the 20 articles
of the homework are listed again, but this time with the information which
aspect of each article is problematic. So the participants can explore them
again. Finally a discussion among the participants targets their experiences
and open questions. In the self-guided version the discussion is substituted
by questions on disinformation that stimulate the reﬂection.
3
Evaluation
In order to answer the research questions RQ1 and RQ2, an empirical study was
conducted in which study participants were asked to attend the course for at
least two weeks. In addition, the participants were given a pretest and posttest
to measure any increase of their disinformation competence, and a questionnaire
was used to assess their satisfaction with the courses. This section ﬁrst describes
the study method and its elements, then presents the results, and ﬁnally discusses
the results in terms of the research questions.
3.1
Method
Participants. The study was conducted from March to April 2022 in Spain
and Austria. For the recruitment of the participants, the link to the pretest
questionnaire with information to the disinformation training was sent out to
possible participants questioning if they were interested in participating in this
course. Those who wanted to participate in the course voluntarily were then
given a link to the course website and a user code to log in.
Spanish Participants: The Spanish target group was intended to represent
middle-aged to elderly people who engage with digital media, but to a low extent.
A total of 23 people participated fully in the training course in Spain, 17 men
and 6 women. The age groups were divided as follows: 2 people between 18
and 35 years old, 11 between 36 and 55 years old, and 10 people over 55 years
old. The highest level of education completed of the participants was secondary
school (degree or equivalent) for 2 individuals, a professional qualiﬁcation for 3
individuals, a bachelor’s degree for 10 individuals, and a master’s degree for 8
individuals. Of the 23 individuals, 8 participated in a trainer-supported course,
while the other 15 completed the course independently and used only the course
platform.
Austrian Participants: In Austria, the target group consisted of younger people
who were shortly after graduating from high school. A total of 13 people par-
ticipated fully in the training course in Austria, 4 men and 9 women. All par-
ticipants were students mostly in the second semester at an Austrian university.

Disinformation Training Course
133
The highest level of education completed was therefore secondary school (leaving
certiﬁcate or equivalent) for all. The trainer-supported course was attended by
9 people, while the other 4 conducted the course independently using only the
course platform.
Material. The material used in this study consists of the Veriﬁcation Indicator
and the course on a website as described above. Both were available in Spanish
and German language. For testing the acceptance and learning eﬀects of the
course the following questionnaires and assessments have been applied.
Demographic and Media Use Data: The demographic questionnaire includes gen-
eral demographic data referring to gender, age, and education level. The media
use questionnaire asks for the frequency of internet and social media use on a
10-point scale (from never to all the time).
Disinformation Competence Assessment: In order to measure an increase of dis-
information competence trained in this course, an assessment procedure has been
designed that (a) consists of a combination of self-assessment questionnaires and
a media quiz, and (b) a score which is calculated from these questionnaires and
the quiz representing a general disinformation competence score. The individual
items can be divided into three main competence areas. First, 4 items were asked
about media literacy (adapted from [8]), 6 items about news literacy (adapted
from [3]) and 1 about information literacy [7]. The second area consists of a con-
ﬁdence assessment on the seven aspects of the Veriﬁcation Indicator [7]. Third,
a media quiz was created to test the participants’ ability to correctly judge (not)
problematic content (similarly done in a previous study [8]). The quiz consists
of three mock articles and 13 aspects that have to be judged as problematic or
not problematic. This results in 13 items that constitute a performance test. In
order to calculate a single competence score, each of the three competence areas
is summed up to a score on a range between 0 and 1. Then the three scores are
summed up, whereby the quiz score is double weighted. Thus self-rating parts
have equal weight as the performance test. The range of the disinformation com-
petence score is between 0 and 4 with lower values indicating higher diﬃculties
in detecting problematic content and therefore lower disinformation competence.
Course Evaluation: In order to evaluate the experience of the participants with
the course, a questionnaire with eight items is employed that assesses satisfac-
tion, utility, knowledge gain, and application to practise (adapted from [6]).
Design and Procedure. The competence assessment questionnaires and quiz
were given before and after the disinformation training course, in order to make
a comparison analysis possible. Thus a pre- and posttest is applied that measures
the learning eﬀect regarding competence development. The quiz items measuring
the performance are diﬀerent in the pre- and posttest (item set A and B) to avoid
a memory eﬀect. In order to ensure a correct statistical analysis, the participants
were randomly split in two groups, whereby group 1 was presented with item
set A in the pretest and item set B in the posttest. Group 2 on the other hand
was presented with item set B in the pretest and item set A in the posttest.

134
A. Nussbaumer et al.
Both Spanish and Austrian cohorts were split into two groups, a group that
was guided by a trainer (trainer-guided) and a group without human guidance
(self-guided). This split was made to evaluate the diﬀerences between these two
groups.
By starting the training, each person had already ﬁlled in the pre-
questionnaire and received the link to the course website and the user code to
log in. The trainer-guided group participated in the 4 sessions during 2 weeks.
Individuals who worked through the course without an instructor were free to
schedule the course sessions and completed the course within one to two weeks.
3.2
Results
General Information. In the ﬁrst questionnaire the participants were asked
about their internet and social media use. Most people of both cohorts responded
that they use the internet several times a day to several times an hour or all the
time. Only one person used the internet several times a week. The majority also
uses social media (Spanish cohort: 18 of 23, Austrian cohort: 9 of 13). The main
source to get news information were news websites or apps, which were used by
18 people (Spanish cohort) and 7 people (Austrian cohort) respectively. Other
media to retrieve new information include television, social networks, radio, and
podcasts.

seven information categories of the Veriﬁcation Indicator tool, whereby the seven
ratings are pooled to a single average value. The third category shows the results
regarding the quiz, where correct, wrong, and undecided answers are listed.

According to the descriptive statistics presented in Table 1 and in Table 2 only
slight changes could be observed between the pre- and the post-test. However,
no signiﬁcant diﬀerences were found in media literacy (Spanish group: t = 1.49,

both cohorts (Spanish group: t = −2.61, p < .05, Cohen’s d = 0.55; Austrian
group: t = −1.23, ns). In the third assessment category a slight increase of correct
answers could be observed in the Spanish group (t = −1.30, ns), but not in the
Austrian group (t = 0.06, ns).
In order to combine all competence questions of the survey into one value,
a competence value has been calculated as described in the previous section.
Comparisons between the pre- and post-survey were made separately for the
two groups. There was no signiﬁcant change in the competence score of the
Austrian cohort (t = −0.56, ns), but the Spanish people showed signiﬁcantly
better competence scores after the training course than before (t = −2.41, p <
.05, cohen’s d = 0.67). So, a positive eﬀect of the training course can be partially
reported here.
In further analyses, the two diﬀerent conditions of the course (trainer-guided
and self-guided) have been analysed, assuming that they would lead to diﬀer-
ences in their eﬀectiveness. The assumption was based on the fact that the course
taught by a trainer could be consolidated better, so that competence and per-
formance would be better afterwards than in the group working out the contents
independently. However, there were no signiﬁcant diﬀerences between the two
diﬀerent conditions. No diﬀerence in the acquisition of competences could be
demonstrated for media literacy (t = −1.02, ns), news literacy (t = −0.30, ns)
and information literacy (t = −1.05, ns). There were also no signiﬁcant diﬀer-
ences in the evaluation of the individual provenance indicators (t = −1.78, ns)
as well as for the quiz performance of the media quiz (t = −0.85, ns).
A further speciﬁc analysis divided the whole sample in two groups based on
the quiz performance. The participants were separated according to the number
of correct answers. Those with more than 50% (16 people) are assigned to the
high-performance group and those with less than 50% (20 people) where assigned
to the low-performance group. An analysis of the low-performance group shows

3.3
Discussion
The results presented above are discussed with reference to the two research
questions RQ1 and RQ2 formulated in Sect. 1. The ﬁrst research question (RQ1)
deals with the question if and how a training course can be created using the
Veriﬁcation Indicator. In Sect. 2 it is shown that and how a training course

Disinformation Training Course
137
is being created that uses the Veriﬁcation Indicator. Furthermore, the feedback
from all participants on the course was very positive in all four areas (satisfaction,
usefulness, knowledge, and applicability). Hence, the ﬁrst research question can
be positively answered.
The results presented above also suggest that the training course has only
a minimal (not statistically not signiﬁcant) positive eﬀect on the competence
development. However, when separating the participants in two groups based
on their initial performance in the quiz, it turned out that the course had a
signiﬁcant eﬀect on participants with low-performance in the pre-test, while it
had almost no eﬀect on participants with good initial performance in the pre-
test. This result also positively answers the second research question (RQ2) that
a course with the Veriﬁcation Indicator has a positive learning eﬀect.
An unexpected outcome of the research was the fact that the two conditional
settings did not lead to diﬀerent results. Both the separation in two cultural
groups (Spanish and Austrian cohorts with diﬀerent demographic characteris-
tics) and the separation in two operation modes (trainer-guided and self-guided)
resulted in similar eﬀects. In particular, the second one was surprising, but also
promising. It demonstrates that the course can be used in a self-guided manner
to achieve a learning eﬀect.
Possible limitations of the study are certainly the sample size and which then
also made group comparisons (for example trainer-guided vs. self-guided, low-
vs- high performing groups) diﬃcult. In addition, hardly any eﬀects on media
and news literacy could be detected. However, these areas are long-term variables
that change slowly and only over longer periods of time and are not expected to
increase on the basis of a single course.
4
Conclusion
This paper presents a disinformation training course that makes use of a new
technology called the Veriﬁcation Indicator. The Veriﬁcation Indicator is a tool
that helps users identify problematic aspects in online news, and thus helps iden-
tify disinformation and fake news. In order to develop respective skills instead
of depending on the Veriﬁcation Indicator, a course has been designed that aims
to train users respectively. In a study the usefulness, acceptances, and learning
eﬀect of this course could be veriﬁed.
Future work might include a ﬂexibilisation of the disinformation course
regarding the initial competence state of the users, their preferences, and the
length of the course. This should enable a longer duration and more intense
practice of people with lower performance at the beginning and at the end of
the course. Furthermore, a group work setting with discussions between the peers
should be enabled and recommended.
Acknowledgement. The work reported has been supported by the PROVENANCE
project which has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research
and innovation programme under grant agreement No 825227.

Abstract. Any software respectively information system can be per-
ceived from the perspective of the provided functionality. The function-
ality is based on the very speciﬁcation of requirements – the basis even for
the design of a system of knowledge, skills, and competencies - Bologna
based perspective. Requirements engineering works with requirements
also in the form of use cases. Use cases are part of the UML standard.
In terms of the hypothetical analogy between a system and a graduate,
the interpretation of the student’s knowledge, skills, and competencies
can be modeled by use cases. The curriculum can be represented as a
model as well. A series of views on the model can point out the essential
aspects of the graduate’s knowledge, skills, and competencies itself and
represent a kind of commitment to the preparation of graduates. Such a
graduate perception uniﬁes the approach of several educational content
developers and supports their cooperation.
Keywords: Use case · Curriculum · Modeling · Content engineering
1
Introduction
Non-trivial advances in technology motivate further development across seem-
ingly unrelated scientiﬁc disciplines. This synergy is already communicated by
David A. Wiley in his book – The instructional use of learning objects: “Tech-
nology is an agent of change, and major technological innovations can result in
entire paradigm shifts. The computer network known as the Internet is one such
innovation” [18]. Object-oriented modeling in software development – whose sig-
niﬁcance becomes more obvious with the complexity of the software being devel-
oped – is another such innovation since 1968. The changes are also evident in
the domain of education. School, for example, lost its exclusive privilege for con-
tent providing thanks to the ubiquitous media. A large part of the educational
content can be conveyed in a computer-aided environment nowadays, etc. Not
only changes in technology but also the impact of these changes in other sci-
entiﬁc disciplines or domains result in agents that support a multidisciplinary
shift. A tangible example of such synergy are design patterns used in software
c

https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_14

engineering. However, the adopted idea of design patterns comes from architec-
ture. The author of the idea is Christopher Alexander, who published it in his
book The Timeless Way of Building, 1979 and later in A Pattern Language.
The already mentioned complexity that software engineering has dealt with, is
still relevant for the curriculum. Any information even software system can be
perceived from the perspective of the provided functionality. The challenge is to
think about a graduate in exactly the same way. Just try to implement such a
substitution for several reasons. We consider any information system as a sys-
tem for collecting, processing, maintaining, and providing information. Similarly,
a man generally consciously or unconsciously, purposefully but also purposeless
collects information through his receptors. Therefore, a graduate of a course, like
any information system, can provide a speciﬁc “functionality”. The functionality
is usually expressed using an active verb in imperative. The functionality of a
system is often described by epics, user stories, but most appropriately by use
cases. Use cases clearly describe the sequence of steps that lead to a measurable
and valuable result of using the system from the user’s perspective. The aim of
educational activity at our faculty, but not exclusively, is to provide a certain
system of knowledge, skills, and competencies for students so that the students
can handle standard situations, even more, they are able to handle alternative
situations where the standard procedure would not be applicable. Based on such
a consideration, it is possible to look at the graduate in a simpliﬁed way as
an information system. In this way, the analogy between software engineering
and educational content engineering can be continued. There is a strong pre-
sumption that solutions and approaches from the software engineering domain
will be at least a strong inspiration to positively inﬂuence the content creation
paradigm in the education domain. The rest of the paper is structured as fol-
lows. Section 2 introduces the similarity of processes in software engineering and
curriculum design and points out the importance of modeling in the analysis and
design phase as well as the absence of modeling and computer-aided educational
content engineering tools. Section 3 looks at the model of educational content
from the perspective of events. Section 4 presents the use case driven approach
and the importance of measurable indicators. Section 5 depicts the curriculum
as an Active Conceptual Model. Section 5 compares the approach presented in
this paper to related work. Section 6 concludes the paper.
2
Software Speciﬁcation and Modeling
In the context of software development, we come across the term speciﬁcation
when deﬁning some list of requirements – a speciﬁcation of requirements for a
software product even information system. In essence, however, it is always a
process from general to special which is a kind of requirements concretization
even reﬁnement of the requirements. Finally, the software – program code – as
a resulting product of the process represents the most accurate speciﬁcation.
There are usually multiple requirements lists that specify diﬀerent aspects of
the software. Such aspect-driven views of the feasible model required properties

Use Case Driven Educational Content Engineering
141
can be cultivated. The code program itself is also a model, even an executable
one. Software modeling thus represents the process of chosen interpretation of
the requirements speciﬁcation. Within modeling, we diﬀerentiate between mod-
eling the structure and behavior of the system, also between the analytical and
design model as well as the logical or physical model [5]. The result of mod-
eling is the model itself, which can be of the nature of a detailed speciﬁcation
– an executable model – or – a simpliﬁed model – in the case of complex sys-
tems by abstracting insigniﬁcant details. The list of requirements (requirements
speciﬁcation) serves as a framework from the perspective of the domain expert
as opposed to an executable model, which is a framework from the developer’s
perspective. The executable model as well as the list of requirements are usually
of a text form. Graphic notations make it easier to grasp the model mentally.
Several diﬀerent notations have spurred the drive for uniﬁcation and standard-
ization. Currently, the most widely used standard is Uniﬁed Modeling Language
UML. The successful application of the principle of abstracting in software engi-
neering is observable historically in solving the problem which was pointed out
by Friedrich Ludwig Bauer at the ﬁrst NATO Software Engineering Conference
in 1968 [1] also subsequently by Edsger Wybe Dijkstra in its 1972 ACM Turing
Award lecture [11]. Software lagging behind hardware, diﬃcult even no possibility
of reusing the source code has resulted in a paradigm shift. The solution received
clear contours in the form of object-oriented language by the authors of Simula
67 Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard. Finally, the three authors James Rum-
baugh, Grady Booch, and Ivar Jacobson introduced the object-oriented approach
and the general need for model visualization and modeling as such in software
engineering. Thus, modeling in software engineering made it possible to deal
with the upper mentioned complexity. There are several similarities between the
curriculum, their performance standard, and software development, mainly due
to complexity issues.
Similarity of Problem Issues: The current situation in curriculum design reminds
the problem in software engineering mentioned above. The complexity only
increases the availability of an enormous amount of information, low adaptabil-
ity to new conditions, insuﬃcient scalability, reusability, etc. This is reﬂected
in several attempts at curricular reform from the recent past but also in the
present1. The need for a new solution is obvious for the reason, I quote: “...edu-
cational content largely focused on encyclopedic knowledge.”, also “The quality
of the pedagogical process very often continues to rely on frontal encyclopedic
teaching instead of developing critical thinking, collaboration and the ability to
work with information.” etc. The high degree of analogy between curriculum
design and software engineering problems creates a precondition for the eﬀec-
tive application of successfully applied procedures from the domain of software
engineering. Relatively complex curriculum design can then be simpliﬁed to or
at least perceived as a set of techniques within educational content engineering
where modeling plays an irreplaceable role.

Role of Models in Other Domains: Many scientiﬁc disciplines have the formal-
ism to express an intention before its usually not-so-cheap implementation. This
certainly includes electrical engineering, which uses models of circuits and con-
nections to express intent regardless of the mother tongue of the author. There
are software tools for their simulations also for validation purposes precisely to
avoid unnecessary costs associated with questionable implementation. The sit-
uation is similar in the ﬁeld of construction and architecture. Architects used
to formally express in the form of construction drawings, studies, or models of
actual buildings and the like. The modeling is used in engineering, too. Model-
ing is applied in the ﬁeld of management, which describes in detail the various
business processes. Such models are used to optimize the individual processes.
In the education and training of humans for events handling (the key compe-
tencies knowledge, skills, and competencies) we can identify the processes as
well and thus should model them. Existing modeling support tools in software
engineering – Computer-Aided Software Engineering (CASE) tools support the
creation of executable models, check critical moments in the design, especially
due to security, underline syntactic errors and typos, etc. We currently do not
have tools available to support curriculum design in this regard.
Models in Curriculum Design:
There are already many diﬀerent systems to
support educational content management in the form of Content Management
Systems (CMS) even extended by learning support features (LCMS) conformed
with standards and speciﬁcations for web-based electronic educational technology
and interchange; from the family of Shareable Content Object Reference Model
(SCORM) standards. Their main purpose is to make the curriculum available for
their users. Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) have been popular in this
regard. However, there is still a lack of some uniﬁed process that would lead to the
identiﬁcation of objectively relevant Learning Objects (LO) as deﬁned in IEEE
1484.12.12. In terms of the accepted analogy of the system and the graduate, it
is then possible to look at the interpretation of the student’s knowledge, skills,
and competencies, the curriculum itself through the events or complex events. The
handling of a speciﬁc event represents elementary functionality. The functional-
ity reﬂects the requirements speciﬁcation most often captured in the form of use
cases. The implementation of any use case presupposes the association of partic-
ipating concepts [15]. The process of an Active Conceptual Modeling ACM con-
sists of an identiﬁcation of domain concepts, their properties, and relations among
them. Learning Objects as an instructional technology concept is attributed to
Wayne Hodgins as the author and there are several deﬁnitions available. David A.
Wiley deﬁnes Learning Objects as “any digital resource that can be reused to support
learning” [18], the original deﬁnition of the Learning Technology Standards Com-
mittee (LTSC)3 of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) was
too broad. Learning Object Metadata is deﬁned for the construction of Learning
Objects, formalized as IEEE 1484.12.1-2020 - IEEE Standard for Learning Object

Metadata (See Footnote 2). The portability of Learning Objects is supported by

Curriculum as an Event Hierarchy Model
To help in explaining the notion behind the event we can use an example from
software engineering. An event is an object that occurred in time. It may be a
message object indicating that something has happened, such as a button click or
mouse movement over a certain GUI element, etc. In the most general sense, we
can consider asking a question or assigning a task as an event as well. Of course,
an immediate response to an event is important. In the language of a software
engineer, this is an event-handling procedure. Event handling is considered to
be a response to an event occurrence. This is what happens after you click a
button etc. Similarly, by the observed analogy between software engineering and
educational content engineering (curriculum design), we perceive an answer to
a question as a response – event even question handling. We recognize the same
principle regarding a solution – to be a response to a given task. So there are
pairs: event - response, question – answer, and task – solution. For this reason,
we consider the premise that a student handles events, in other words, that he
answers questions and solves assigned tasks to be correct. There is a software
development approach driven by events. It is a software architecture paradigm
- Event-Driven Architecture (EDA), which is strictly pragmatic in its philoso-
phy. The program code does not contain any redundant parts, but only those
that relate to those events (production, detection, consumption, or response)
that were explicitly speciﬁed. Similarly, by the observed analogy between soft-
ware engineering and educational content engineering (curriculum design), the
explicit deﬁnition of events that a student should be able to handle is crucial
in the case of creating the minimum necessary curriculum. For this reason, we
consider the approach suitable in order to avoid overburdening the curriculum.
This is a signiﬁcant premise resulting from the similarity of the problems in both
mentioned domains – software engineering and educational content engineering
(didactics). We can perceive events at diﬀerent levels of granularity. Within the
analysis of complex events, we can identify elementary events. We can perceive
such decomposition in its vertex interpretation as a certain hierarchy of related
events. Symmetrically within the synthesis of elementary events, we can identify
a complex one. For example, a Message delivered is a complex event. It is com-
posed of the event objects: Message sent, Message received, and Acknowledged.
Similarly, by the observed analogy between software engineering and educational
content engineering (curriculum design), the task for the solution of the linear
equation in one variable may be composed of several elementary tasks for exam-
ple: to add, divide, multiply, etc. The suitability of such thinking with respect
4 https://scorm.com.

to this performance will be related to the anticipated number of questions and
tasks, the identiﬁcation of duplications, and similarities for the formation of clus-

CEP [14]. A collaborative approach to creating educational content can asso-

of a non-trivial burden comes from actual and real knowledge. One of the main
problems in the current world of information technologies is the ever-increasing
amount of digital data and the complexity of problems that are being solved.
Moreover, the anticipated problem could be the processing of potentially large
volumes of incoming messages or events from various sources is also speciﬁc to
reactive computing. And it can be assumed that the number of resources and
their diversity will only grow. We veriﬁed the behavior of such a system on the
example of a functional model of the electronic toll collection system, based on
the system speciﬁcations for Slovak conditions [14]. The main objective was to
verify the impact and beneﬁts of Complex Event Processing for the design of dis-
tributed reactive systems. And the main monitored attributes were modiﬁability,
performance, and implementation.

Use Case Driven Educational Content Modeling
with UML
Considering an absence of formalization in educational content notation analysis
and design on the contrary of other ﬁelds, where modeling plays an irreplaceable
role we have performed certain experiments. We have abstracted certain equiv-
alence between a graduate proﬁle and an occupation proﬁle. Subsequently, we
have substituted these proﬁles as a system of knowledge, skills, and competen-
cies. Applied substitution between proﬁles and a system allows us to treat it in
analogy with the software engineering process - Uniﬁed Process which describes
how requirements are turned into educational content. Such an approach leads
to models with zero redundancy which is very important for educational content
even for computer-aided education or distance learning. Educational content and
related issues are being examined by didactics (Greek: didáskein, to teach; lore
of teaching)5. Didactics distinguishes between educational content and teaching
process. It distinguishes between two related questions: What to teach? and How
to teach? The goal of our research is to deal just with the question What. The
teaching process is a common activity of a teacher and pupil, which is aimed
at achieving the objectives [16]. Objectives are deﬁned by teachers themselves
according to performance and content standards deﬁned by certain authorities.
This fact evokes a series of questions e.g., How subjective is the objectives def-
inition? How real are the requirements represented by the standards? Do the
standards reﬂect the diversity of the labor market requirements?, etc. It wouldn’t
probably be suﬃcient to think that the standards which perhaps update from
5 http://www.merriam-webster.com/.

145
time to time will faithfully replace the need to specify requirements for a speciﬁc
implementation reﬂecting labor market needs. Given this, we can say that the
education objectives issues can’t be considered as completely clariﬁed. Didactics
hasn’t done the necessary steps required in deﬁning learning objectives precisely,
clearly, and systematically. Therefore, this area remains incomplete in the ﬁeld
of education [17].
Use Case Driven Approach in Requirements Analysis: As we see a certain anal-
ogy between software engineering and content engineering (educational content
engineering) we can state that one of the most common challenges the content
development teams are facing involves inaccurate, incomplete, inconsistent or
even missing requirements also in the ﬁeld of didactics. In didactics, they often
operate with the notion of goals. Teachers deﬁne objectives (objectives of a cer-
tain course, teaching unit goals, etc.). These are objectives that deﬁne the change
in the state of the pupil in terms of his knowledge, skills, competencies, etc. This
change in behavior, however, we can express in the form of requirements as well.
There is a certain relationship between requirements and even educational goals
[9]. Curriculum development regardless of the form of education (presence or
distant, etc.) must be based on well-deﬁned requirements (in other words objec-
tives). The same type of requirements problem was successfully solved exactly in
the software engineering domain. In available literature from this ﬁeld, we can
read that use case driven development oﬀers an excellent solution to this type of
challenge [12]. Therefore we try to apply successful practices from the domain
of software engineering to the domain of didactics, curriculum development the
content engineering. A use case captures a contract between the stakeholders
of a system about its behavior [9]. A use case describes a coherent functional-
ity, which gives a result valuable to users [2]. A use case models the behavior
of a system. A use case is a sequence of actions performed by a system, which
yields an observable result that is typically of value for one or more actors or
other stakeholders of the system [12]. These three deﬁnitions say that a use case
is a certain functionality that has deliverable for its users. It is represented by
description expressed by a list of steps, typically deﬁning interactions between a
role (in UML known as an actor) and a system, to achieve a meaningful goal for
the actor. The actor can be a human or an external system. This is how we try
to think even when creating educational content. If we want to apply this app-
roach we have to consider a system providing certain functionality and its users.
Use cases are not only about a system functionality that can be initiated by an
actor described from the actor’s point of view in a technology-neutral manner
but also are descriptions of how actors use the system in order to accomplish
their goals. For a better understanding of the analogy mentioned above let us
make a substitution. It is important to perceive the graduate as a system that
provides certain functionality to its surroundings or better say users see Fig. 1a.
However, during his studies, it is just his teacher. We see the teacher as the
actor who can start any of the available use cases. The graduate is the one who
is responsible for performing actions in order to satisfy actor’s needs e.g. to cal-
culate the monthly salary. Graduate preparation for a speciﬁc profession, e.g. the

146
J. Lang
accountant has to correlate the real profession. The only and essential diﬀerence
is that the graduate’s user as an accountant will no longer be just a teacher
but e.g. employer or any customer see Fig. 1b. We provide a certain use case for
the ﬁrst class of the primary school. An integrated system of working positions
is rather career/profession-oriented. This direction is more interesting in order
to support lifelong learning in the way of distance learning. For this option we
provide an example of an accountant see Fig. 1b.
Fig. 1. Correlation at the level of functionality between the graduate and a particular
profession
In the experiment, we tried to capture requirements for the profession of an
accountant by a detailed description of the selected use cases. There we found
some diﬀerent types of actors e.g. employer (who employees the accountant),
customer (who uses the services of the accountant), etc. As the use case diagram
is just an overview of the use cases and the use cases are primarily textual
descriptions here we provide a detailed description of one of them.
UC1: CalculateTheMonthlySalary
Description:
The system calculates the salary.
Preconditions:
The salary has not been calculated for the previous month yet.
Main flow/Main success scenario/happy day scenario:
1. Use case begins at the moment when the user (employer or customer)
applies for the calculation of the employee salary.
2. System offers a list of employees.
3. The user selects the employee from the list.
4. System offers a form to specify the number of working days, the number
of days of leave, the number of days of sick leave, etc.
5. The user enters and confirms the required.
6. System calculates and records the base salary.
Postconditions:
The employee’s salary is calculated and recorded.

the employer and the accountant.

we can aﬀord to paraphrase the original statement: “When the use cases record
behavioral requirements for a piece of software, the system under discussion is
the computer program” [9], so analogically we can say that: When the use cases
record behavioral requirements for a specialist, expert, technician the system
under discussion are his knowledge, skills, and competencies. Also: When the
use cases record behavioral requirements for a graduate, the system under dis-
cussion is his knowledge, skills, and competencies. The graduate proﬁle of certain

Related Work
Concerning the applied principle of analogy, we ﬁnd related works in two sci-
entiﬁc disciplines in software engineering and education, speciﬁcally in curricu-
lum development. In the domain of software engineering, the use case driven
approach and UML modeling are presented relatively extensively. So in book
publications [2,5,9,12] as well as in scientiﬁc works. Research in the ﬁeld of
use case driven approach deals mainly with information systems requirements
speciﬁcation [4,10,13], where the most important is the Use-Case 2.0 require-
ments speciﬁcation approach depiction as use-case-driven development—light,
agile, and lean—inspired by user stories and the agile approach, Scrum frame-
work, and Kanban method; modularization [3,6–8], where the organization of
a non-trivial number of use cases ﬁnds a link directly to the code in order to
improve comprehensibility and maintainability, etc. In the ﬁeld of education,
instructional design theory addresses this issue. The instructional technology in
connection with the Learning Objects is interestingly depicted in David Wiley’s
book The Instructional Use of Learning Objects [18] and developed to the stan-
dard. The need for an adaptive, generative, scalable learning architecture has
resulted in the deﬁnition of the Learning Object Metamodel. Also available at
IEEE standard 1484.12.1-2020 - IEEE Standard for Learning Object Metadata7.
Interpretation of educational content by objects is based on the object-oriented
paradigm. David A. Wiley deﬁnes a learning object as “any digital resource that
can be reused to support learning”. This construction is fully in line with our
agile and lean concept of the event even in a historical context. By event, you
mean a question or a task. I remember university publications such as a collec-
tion of mathematics and physics problems even publications such as “Questions
and Answers”. This view of the educational content determined by questions
and tasks is inﬂuenced by the approach of complex event processing (CEP) and
event-driven architecture (EDA). Naturally, solving complex problems is non-
trivial. Complex events can be decomposed into elementary ones. In principle,
it is easier to solve small problems.

6
Conclusions
This thesis presented my research in the area of education content engineering
from the perspective of software engineering principles. It builds on the premise
that any information system can be viewed from the perspective of the function-
ality provided. So, if we perceive a graduate as an information system the educa-
tional content engineering, curriculum design even speciﬁc Learning Objects will
result from the analysis and design of requirements for this information system.
This emphasizes the importance of speciﬁcation requirements which is the basis
for the design of his system of knowledge, skills, and competencies (his function-
ality). A special approach in this research is use cases to capture requirements,
another form of learning goals, which subsequently ﬁnd mapping in Learning
Objects. Use cases in detail do model how diﬀerent types of users interact with
the system. The result of the curriculum in the form of a model represents a
platform for discussion for stakeholders. The research covers the understanding
of an event, a complex event as well as a hierarchy based on its decomposition.
The important content of the education is seen in events handling procedures.
The relationships between events associate the elementary curriculum and thus
create natural structures of knowledge. Interpretation of these relationships is
appropriate by looking at the model in a formal way. UML has proven to be
a suitable language for this purpose. Events can be more or less complex, but
their decomposition can identify the elementary ones. The hierarchy on the side
of events perceived through the perspective of their service oﬀers a view of the
hierarchy of goals, where the user goal is the goal of the greatest interest. It is
a goal pursued by the primary actor that makes sense to use this system. Such
a view of the graduate’s knowledge, skills, and competencies uniﬁes the app-
roach of several educational content developers and supports their cooperation.
The result in the form of a graduate model is thus ultimately confrontable with
the model of the profession. Educational content modeling is a challenge in the
domain of educational content engineering and presupposes the development of
specialized support tools in the form of speciﬁcally used Integrated Development
Environments (IDE).
