“In Vivo” Science Learning - Academic
Teaching Through a Game-Based Process
Charilaos Tsihouridis1(B), Marianthi Batsila2, Dennis Vavougios2,
and Anastasios Tsichouridis3
1 University of Patras, Patras, Greece
hatsihour@upatras.gr
2 University of Thessaly, Volos, Greece
{marbatsila,dvavou}@uth.gr
3 European University, Nicosia, Cyprus
tsabtsih@gmail.com
Abstract. The present study explores the potential of improving the attractive-
ness and efﬁciency of academic lectures at university science courses with the
use of online game-based tools. The main purpose of the study was to investigate
the extent to which the use of Kahoot can increase learners’ attendance, interest
and active participation in the science lectures, and whether it can demonstrate
students’ better cognitive results in science learning. A number of 287 university
learners from pedagogical departments, aiming to be prospective primary educa-
tion level teachers participated in the research. Students’ semester ﬁnal examina-
tions results, note taking, personal interviews and a focus group discussion were
used as research tools. According to the ﬁndings, the integration of Kahoot in
the teaching lecturing process enhanced students’ enthusiasm, class anticipation,
attendance and active participation. Students displayed a higher percentage of
success in the ﬁnal exams, as opposed to previous years’ lower performance.
Keywords: Classroom response systems · Kahoot · Game-based learning ·
Academic teaching · Lectures
1
Introduction
As the years go by, higher education teachers face the challenge of organizing teaching
and learning in a way that meets the educational needs and experiences of their digital
expert students of today [1]. Due to emergent contemporary teaching methods, tradi-
tional lectures are gradually being perceived as a continuous monologue during which
professors tend to speak and students to merely listen [2]. This passive lecturing process
does not in the least help learners remain focused on the topic of the session. On the
contrary, their attention is distracted as they gradually become bored, they begin losing
interest in the lesson, consequently resulting into lack of understanding and ultimately
having a non-desirable performance in their ﬁnal semester exams [3]. Thus, according to
research, lectures are in question in relation to their effectiveness [4]. According to those
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 151–162, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_15

152
C. Tsihouridis et al.
who object to the use of lectures and are proponents of active teaching methods, a major
weakness of lectures is that they cause passive learning, and turn students to indifferent
recipients of information and knowledge, transmitted by the teacher [4]. Thus, lectures
lead students to depend on the teacher to tell them what they need to know and fail to
enable them to take the responsibility for their own learning.
For instance, research argues that the use of lectures as a teaching method led to
learners’ boredom, loss of enthusiasm and ineffective learning. The authors suggested
discussion methods to replace lecturing in social studies teaching as these help learners
familiarize themselves with the cognitive input and increase their knowledge on the
subject [5]. Research also claims that, still today, the use of lecturing as a teaching
method often dominates classes, due to teachers’ lack of IT mastering, and/or the easiness
it displays when addressing large audiences. However, teachers should consider carefully
how to enrich them in order to make them more interactive for learners [6]. According
to ﬁndings lecturing can be boring unless teachers can ﬁnd a way to stimulate learners’
critical thinking and reﬂection, thus, integrating a more student-centered approach in
their teaching practices [7]. Based on other discussions lecturing is not enough to transmit
knowledge.Instead,teachersshouldemploy‘dialogicalapproaches’tohelplearnershave
a better cognitive understanding [8]. In a study conducted with academic learners, it was
found that demonstration methods have better results than simple lecturing in class, in
relation to learners’ performance and cognitive improvement [9]. In general, research
reveals that when lecturing can be replaced by active teaching methods learning results
can improve. According to ﬁndings [10] lectures are an ineffective method to promote
learning in academic contexts [11]. Elsewhere [12], it is argued that lecturing is less
effective than other more active ways used for teaching. Other ﬁndings [13] claim that
although lectures are a usual way to teach in academic contexts, in-class conversations
between learners are those that can change them into more pleasant ways to transmit
knowledge.
In recent years, and in an effort to devise ways to replace passive lectures with more
engaging procedures, there has been a tendency to use interactive and innovative tools,
that place learners in the center of teachers’ attention. Technology seems to be of sig-
niﬁcant support in this endeavor, offering a large number of digital media to be used
in educational institutions [14]. This technological development has as a consequence
the evolution of the educational process [15]. Academic teaching has been inﬂuenced
and co-shaped by the rise of technology, bringing about radical changes in the so-called
traditional classroom, transforming it into an active learning environment, turning bor-
ing lectures into activities that motivate and activate interaction among the learners [6].
This is due to the fact that Communication and Information Technologies (ICT) are
considered a signiﬁcant ally of the educational practice offering a variety of tools and
applications to support the teaching practice. Research reveals that digital tools dis-
play many beneﬁts with positive learning outcomes. Among them we discern enhancing
students’ motives for learning, activating their participation in class, promoting inter-
action between students and between students and teachers and many more [16]. An
important advantage of ICT is their ability to serve as a bridge for communication and
cooperation between individuals, and between groups and/or communities of teachers
and non-teachers [3]. Within the ICT framework, Classroom Response Systems (CRS)

“In Vivo” Science Learning - Academic Teaching
153
are known as digital environments that enhance learning in a playful way. CRS have
been found to actively involve students in the educational process through a fun and
interactive way in the teaching and learning practice [17].
A well-known CRS application, among many, is ‘Kahoot’. Kahoot is a free online
tool that allows teachers to easily and quickly create playful quizzes to evaluate students
in real-time. According to research, Kahoot has been found to be a useful and easy-
to-use assessment tool and can be integrated in all disciplines, motivating students to
focus on the subject taught, thus, studying more so as to achieve a good score in a quiz.
[18] Kahoot can be used to enhance collaboration between students as teachers can have
groups of students per electronic device [19]. Teachers can use Kahoot as a tool for
revision, starting with easy questions and moving on to more difﬁcult ones that require
critical thinking and attention [20]. Kahoot can also be used to motivate and activate
the whole class as students have the opportunity to engage in a game/quiz shown in
the classroom [21]. It can also be used as homework since teachers can set a quiz for a
following lesson, thus, checking learners’ input understanding and improvement [3]. For
more effective quizzes teachers should take into consideration some important issues:
the purpose and learning goal of a Kahoot quiz, students’ learning background, students’
learning needs and lacks [22]. It is also important to ask the right questions and always
in relation to the goals set allowing learners to test their abilities and giving them a
sense of accomplishment [3]. Teachers can even become creative by attaching pictures
and/or videos in a quiz to arouse students’ interest. It is also important that questions
promote students’ critical thinking and the ability for all participants to have a feeling of
success, thus, avoiding discouragement or disappointment and therefore, loss of interest
and dropout [22].
2
Rationale for the Present Study
Learning contexts of today are becoming increasingly demanding. Technology has
altered the physiognomy of education to a great extent over the past years. Both education
and its stakeholders (students, teachers, educational material, syllabi, curricula) seem
to go through a major change, in an effort to center attention to the needs of students,
contrary to teacher-centered practices of the past. The plethora of digital skills allows
the emergence of more exciting and innovative teaching methods and tools as opposed
to traditional and indifferent or unattractive teaching methods and materials. However,
academic teaching today, often focuses on linear lectures, failing to maintain students’
interest and active participation. Most particularly, large audiences, of more than perhaps
150 students participating are often characterized by passive attendance, and students’
recording of teachers’ lectures notes. Within academic contexts, science teaching is
often perceived as a challenging task, due to the fact that, a considerable percentage of
students seem to have a rather low level of scientiﬁc knowledge, especially those who
attend social or humanistic studies courses. This results on the one hand to learners’ lack
of engagement, disappointment or drop outs and on the other hand to teachers’ persis-
tent effort to conjure ways to facilitate learning and enhance students’ presence in the
teaching process. What is more, all too often, academic lectures may extend more than
four or ﬁve hours in a day, turning sessions to boring meetings that cause fatigue, lack of

154
C. Tsihouridis et al.
enthusiasm and/or purpose in the learners. Another problem that lectures present is that
it is difﬁcult for teachers to receive immediate feedback on their students’ performance
when addressing large audiences. What is more, students’ presence is rather minimum
when lessons are not obligatory, as opposed to that in laboratories where absences are
not allowed to be more than three per semester. Based on the aforementioned, the authors
of this paper decided to integrate Kahoot as a tool in the teaching lecturing process for
university students who attend pedagogical departments and examine its effectiveness
on student participation, interest and science concepts cognitive improvement.
3
The Research
3.1
Purpose and Research Questions
The purpose of the research was to examine the extent to which Kahoot can be used
in the teaching process to increase learners’ attendance, interest and active participa-
tion in the science lectures. The study also aimed to detect whether the use of Kahoot
can demonstrate students’ better cognitive results in science learning. To this end, the
research questions are as follows: 1. What is learners’ opinion on academic lectures in
general? 2. To what extent can the use of Kahoot in science academic teaching contexts
increase learners’ attendance, interest and participation in the lectures? 3. To what extent
can the use of Kahoot improve learners’ cognitive results in academic science courses
learning? 4. What is learners’ overall impression on the use of Kahoot in their lectures?
3.2
Research Sample
The population we aimed at was University students from Greece. Our sample was 287
University learners who participated in the present research. The participant learners
attended science courses taught at pedagogical University departments the aim of which
is to train and educate them accordingly in order to become primary education level
teachers in the future. A hundred and ninety-four (194) learners were female and ninety-
three (93) were male. They were all from all semesters (ﬁrst to eighth) (two semesters
per academic year) and attended a variety of science courses offered to them by the
Universities throughout all the four years of their studies, like physics, astronomy, earth
sciences, chemistry, etc.
3.3
Research Method and Tools
The study was carried out using a mixed method approach (qualitative and quantitative).
In particular, semi-structured personal interviews with ten randomly selected learners
were conducted for the research issues. For triangulation purposes, reliability and valid-
ity of the research [23] a focus group discussion with 16 randomly selected learners
was conducted to detect the participants’ opinion on the process. Note-taking was also
employed throughout the two academic semesters to offer us a better insight to the
research issues. The effectiveness of the whole process was examined through students’
performance in the ﬁnal written academic examinations. The focus group discussion and

“In Vivo” Science Learning - Academic Teaching
155
personal interviews were conducted in order to provide us with possible answers to the
research questions. The semi-structured items and focus group discussion questions were
similar and were formed basically based on four areas: attendance to the sessions, inter-
est in the sessions, active participation in the sessions, cognitive performance, overall
impression of the use of Kahoot in the sessions. Of course, students’ answers expanded
further, providing us with valuable material and information for our research issues. For
the validity of the research tools, the interviews and focus group questions were piloted
before their actual use with three students (for the interview questions) and another
three (for the focus group questions). All respondents in the piloting of the tools were
not participants of the actual research. The piloting of the tools aimed to test the items
for wording, accuracy, coherence, understanding and in case of inaccuracies or vague
points to redesign them based on the respondents’ comments.
3.4
Ethical Concerns
Before the implementation of the main study interviews and focus group discussion, and
in order to ensure the validity and reliability of the research, the necessary clariﬁcations
and explanations were provided to all interviewees, so that the topics of discussion
would be fully understood [24]. All participants were reassured that the discussions
would be anonymous, and that the data would be used only for the purposes of this
research. It was also explained to the interviewees that they could withdraw any time
they felt uncomfortable or uneasy. The place and time of the interviews and focus group
conversation were arranged based on the participants’ decisions. All respondents gave
their voluntary consent for their participation in this research. Finally, for ethical reasons,
in the discussion of the results section, all participants are referred to as P1 (participant
1), P2 (participant 2) and so on.
3.5
Data Analysis
For the analysis of the interviews and focus group discussion the conventional type “con-
tent analysis” method was employed [25]. After the transcription, the repeated listening
and reading of the discussion statements content, the most signiﬁcant parts that linked
to the research questions were isolated and recorded and the data analysis units/key
words were determined. The key words were “attendance”, “active”, “interest”, “par-
ticipation”, “understanding”, “science”, “academic”, “lectures”, “learning”, “Kahoot”,
“performance”, “game-based” that were included in the participants’ answers, in relation
to the aims of the research and research questions.
3.6
Research Process
The study took place in the academic year 2021 to 2022. Pre-organized by the tutor,
Kahoot quizzes were integrated in the lectures and used whenever and however it was
considerednecessaryduringthesession,dependingontheteachingaims.Thequizzesdid
not last more than 15–20 min so as not to reduce the time needed for the introduction of
the new material. In particular, and regarding the time of its implementation, Kahoot was

156
C. Tsihouridis et al.
used either: 1). As a diagnostic tool, in the beginning of the sessions in an effort to arouse
learners’ interest, activate them in the lesson and/or detect their background knowledge;
2). As a formative assessment tool during the sessions to receive immediate and quick
feedback on learners’ comprehension and if needed, make any additions or changes in
the lectures to facilitate understanding; 3). As a ﬁnal assessment tool in the end of the
sessions or in the end of a unit’s material to assess learners’ knowledge and performance;
4). As a metacognitive tool for feedback and revision purposes so as to check how much
learners remembered and assimilated after some time. Kahoot was created in a number of
ways. For the process to have better results students’ active participation was considered
signiﬁcant. More speciﬁcally Kahoot was created: 1). With questions devised by the
students themselves while watching the lectures. During a particular time of a lecture,
students were asked to take notes of what was taught at that time and based on them,
create one or two questions (‘in vivo’ – at the time of the lecture), provide answers and
the reasoning behind them, and upload everything on an e-class ﬁle during the break;
2). With questions that were created by the students upon the end of each lecture. At
their own time and pace, students were asked to form one or two questions based on
the whole lecture material and upload them on e-class again; 3). With questions that
were created by the students based on the whole educational material of the semester,
mainly for revision purposes and feedback. All students’ questions were examined for
any inaccuracies or repetitions by the teacher before integrated in a Kahoot quiz. All
in all, the actual aim of engaging learners in the creation of the Kahoot quiz questions,
based on the lecture material, was to engage them in the learning process, motivate
them in the lesson, receive immediate and valuable feedback and check their level of
understanding. The effectiveness of the whole process was examined through students’
performance in the ﬁnal academic fall and spring semester written examinations while
note-taking, interviews and a focus-group discussion were also conducted.
4
Results
The ﬁndings in this study will be discussed herein in relation to each of the research
questions:
Research question one: What is learners’ opinion on academic lectures in general?
Based on the interviews and focus group discussion answers academic lectures of
theoretical content, unlike laboratory sessions, tend to be boring and their linear structure
and presentation cause a sense of monotony, uneasiness and discomfort: “it is the same
old story… I nearly fall asleep after about 20 min [of lecturing]!” P6, “We [students]
know what to expect every time … there is no sense of innovation or change in lectures”,
P4, “I am always uneasy when the teachers talk. It’s annoying having to hear them speak
all the time. We hardly ever take part during them [sessions].” P7. “I am usually there
[in class] when the lesson starts but I leave after the ﬁrst break, very often, I can’t stand
listening [to a teacher lecturing] for two or three hours in a row … and taking notes
usually” P11. When asked what exactly it is they dislike about lectures the majority
replied that it is mainly lack of interaction and participation. As they explained, teachers
almost never involve them when in an auditorium session, except when they are in a lab
working on an experiment: “I don’t like to sit on a bench for hours just watching. If I had

“In Vivo” Science Learning - Academic Teaching
157
to do something it would be much better then” P9, “Working in labs is interesting and
we get to do things, work together [with other learners], but in class I am like ‘I’ll send a
message to someone to chat’” P16, “I think the majority of the teachers act as if they are
alone in class. I am not sure they care if we follow what they say, they never ask!” P8. In
our question what they think could be done to change this, students explained: “We can’t
tell teachers what to do, but they’ve been where we are now and they should understand
it’s tiring to listen to someone for so long and not be able to say a word!” P14, “I
think lectures will always be boring. But when we do something in class… together…,
something interesting, that we like, it wakes us up and we ﬁnd meaning to what is being
done” P5.
Research question two: To what extent can the use of Kahoot in science academic
lecturing contexts increase learners’ attendance, interest and participation in the lectures?
According to the participants the integration of Kahoot in the lectures was seen as
a ‘wonderful change’, a ‘brilliant idea’, an ‘unexpected transformation’, an ‘attractive
intervention’, an ‘innovative thought’, a ‘necessary action’, an ‘interesting process’ and
more. Students explained that the use of Kahoot namely augmented their anticipation
for the lessons and their presence in the sessions: “I like it that you added [addressing
the researcher-teacher] the activities with Kahoot! I wanted to come every time…it’s so
much fun” P12, “The truth is that although I like science lessons it was kind of boring
before Kahoot. With Kahoot I looked forward to them [lectures]!” P20, “Lessons with
Kahoot were a nice change, it made me want to come to class really!” P3, “The activities
[with Kahoot] were very nice and I couldn’t wait for the games and the quizzes to start!”
P12, “It is the reason [Kahoot tasks] I stayed till the end of the lesson [laughing] to be
honest!!” P17. Students admitted that lectures became more interesting as they waited
anxiously for the games to start. They enjoyed the sense of ‘friendly’ competition, the
fuss and the energy in class, which made them feel comfortable, familiar, relaxed, happy
and motivated. As they explained, even the time they had to focus on the lecture to keep
notes, so as to create their own questions to be used by the teacher in a Kahoot quiz next
time, was something that excited them and did their best to devise as ‘smart’ items as
possible. According to them, this process was not only fun but it also helped them pay
attention to the lecture without ‘complaining’, ‘turning heads elsewhere’ ‘playing games
on mobile phones’ or ‘drawing grafﬁti on notebooks”. As they said, their concentration to
thelectures,resultedtoabetterunderstandingofthescienceconcepts,introducedbytheir
teacher within the sessions. They argued that they could realize the better assimilation
of the new material, when, while taking part in the Kahoot quizzes, they were able to
answer a lot of questions displayed, which were actually the questions prepared by their
classmatesorthemselves,basedonthematerialofthelectures.Thestudentsadmittedthat
this was a ‘pleasant realization’ an ‘interesting experience’ and an ‘odd’ but ‘useful’ and
‘imaginative technique’ they enjoyed a lot. Mainly, they were surprised how the Kahoot
integration in the lectures quite changed their attitude towards the ‘boring lectures’
turning it into anticipation and active participation until the end of every session: “I used
to come to classes to take notes and leave but in these classes [with Kahoot] I came to
have a good time too, I always stayed till the end of the lessons and I enjoyed them [the
lessons] very much” P18, “With …. [student’s name] and some others we bet who will
be the winner! I actually hit the ﬁrst record three times! That was awesome!” P 22, “I

158
C. Tsihouridis et al.
tried hard to think of good questions for the quiz, it’s like a challenge to do this. It’s not
easy, but I want to do it, to see if I do well, how good I am, to check my understanding”
P14, “All I can say is I was absorbed in the lectures, which is not like me!! I barely
texted, that is something strange for me! I think because I wanted to know what was said
to form the right questions, I am pleased with myself! I stayed to the very end!” P8, “I
used to take notes and go home to revise, I mainly copied what was said in class. Since
we started lessons with Kahoot I have a good knowledge of the material from class and
when I go home I only revise, which is less stressful and less time consuming for me”
P11, “I cannot say science is my thing. I always struggled to ‘like’ it and it often felt like
a burden. Now, things have changed a bit. I think because I am more concentrated in
the lesson now and have a better understanding of the lessons in class, I never miss a
Kahoot… even though it’s in the end [of the session]” P15, “I have less questions and
gaps in the material than I had before the Kahoot quizzes…and I like it they are like a
game too, I want to add good questions, I want to have a good result!” P22.
Research question three: To what extent can the use of Kahoot improve learners’
cognitive results in academic science courses learning?
It should be explained here that the intervention was carried out during the years
2021–22 but the particular subjects were taught also all the previous years. The results of
this year’s ﬁnal exams – where there was the intervention with Kahoot - were compared
to previous years students’ mean scores in the ﬁnal exams. The ﬁnal exams of the
research had the same format as those of the previous years. In particular, the items
were not exactly the same but their content was of the same philosophy and of the same
gravity. All items derived from a bank of questions that the tutors had created over
the years for their students’ assessment in the ﬁnal exams. The exams comprised open
ended questions, multiple choice, or problem-solving items. They were prepared by the
researchers themselves who were also the tutors and were assessed by them. Regarding
the students, their cognitive level is not differentiated over the years as they all come
with the same cognitive background when they enter the university. More speciﬁcally,
the characteristics of the participants of this intervention were the same as of those
learners of the previous years who had not been taught using Kahoot.
Thus, based on the results of the ﬁnal semesters exams it can be said that students’
performance improved. In particular, before the integration of Kahoot in the lectures over
the past years, the percentage of students attending classes was around 45% and from this
number of participants 60% were those who successfully usually passed their ﬁnal tests.
During the year 2021–2022, when the research took place and Kahoot was integrated in
the lectures, the percentage of participant students ranged from 60% to 70% and from
this number around 98% of the learners successfully passed their science courses. Thus,
students’ attendance in the lectures raised to 30% as opposed to previous years, whereas,
their performance improved by 38% after working with Kahoot in the lectures (Table 1).
We consider this difference quite interesting, especially when it comes to lessons where
attendance is not obligatory, like the courses where Kahoot was integrated.
Research question four: What is learners’ overall impression on the use of Kahoot
in their lectures?
Based on the note-taking data, the interviews and focus group discussion answers,
it can be said that Kahoot “made a difference” for students and changed their attitude

5
Discussion and Conclusions
The present research focused on investigating the extent to which the use of the C.R.S.
application of Kahoot can be used in academic lectures to increase learners’ attendance,
interest and active participation in the teaching of science concepts. The study also
focused on whether the use of Kahoot can improve students’ performance in science
learning. The ﬁndings of the personal interviews, the focus-group discussion, the note
taking and the semester exams results data revealed that the use of Kahoot had a positive
impact on the learning process and students’ participation in lectures. They described the
integration of Kahoot as useful, innovative, necessary and interesting. The ﬁndings agree
with other ﬁndings about the positive effect Kahoot presents in the learning process [3,
19, 21, 22].
Students stressed the fact that the use of Kahoot transformed in a way the boring
lectures, turning them into interesting procedures. As they argued, the integration of
Kahoot and its social features mainly made them decide to come to class and stay till
the end, thus, complying with Freeman [26] who, very wittily argues that “If you’re
going to get lectured at, you might as well be at home in bunny slippers!”. Based on
learners’ remarks, the whole process in a way served as an anti-stress intervention ‘taking
out the burden of tiring lectures’ facilitating science concepts understanding, offering
them joyful and creative moments. It is worth noting how students’ lively energy and
active participation throughout the Kahoot games, the clapping of hands, the laughter
and happy exclamations in ﬁnding the right answers made heads of passing by students
or teachers turn, often wishing to join our class themselves.
According to the results of this research it can be said that learners’ involvement
in the creation of the Kahoot quizzes during the lectures, based on the lectures input,
motivated them to want to attend classes, to remain until the end of the sessions, while it
helped them have a better understanding of the material introduced. It is also noteworthy
that students’ performance was higher with a considerable number of A marks in the ﬁnal
exams as opposed to previous years. Students expressed their wish this process to be used
in other courses as well. Considering the importance of the effectiveness of students’
achievement in academic teaching contexts it can be argued that, as Freeman [8] claims
“We need to stop ‘killing’ students’ performance and interest in science by constantly
lecturing, instead of helping them think like scientists”. After all, being tutors, we should
always remember that “Good teachers do not merely ‘deliver content’ to students, but
wake them up, throw them on their feet, and pull the chair away.” [27]. Only then,
education could perhaps display better results and it is through this way that we could
perhaps be proud to claim that we live in a democratic society, practicing democratic
education that not only has meaning and conveys knowledge but also turns learning into
a joyful experience for those who wish and make a hard effort to learn.
Finally, it should be mentioned that the authors of this paper are aware that something
may change once the novelty of using this device wears off and will no longer be a
novelty. It is also suggested that any prospective preparation or training of teachers on
integrating strategies is carried out that can be put in place to keep this novelty effect in a
constant loop, and prevent observed improvements in student attitude and performance
from reverting to their original performance.

Towards User2Machine Model for Higher
Education - Enforced by Covid19 Pandemic
Ferial Khaddage1(B)
, Christoph Lattemann2
, and Pia Gebbing2
1 Deakin University, Melbourne, VIC 3125, Australia
fayekhaddage@gmail.com
2 Jacobs University Bremen, Campus Ring 1, 28759 Bremen, Germany
Abstract. The Covid19 pandemic hit the higher education system hard. Suddenly,
universities around the world are obliged to offer online educational instructions to
students. Innovative technologies made this transition possible, and new technolo-
gies have opened prospects, connected societies, and created new ways of com-
munication based on the three models in which humans initially communicated:
user2user, user2society, and user2society2user. Now, fostered by the covid19 pan-
demic and with advancements in technological innovations, “User2Machine”-
interaction, as a model, has been introduced to online education. This model is
helping in creating different methods of communication channels regardless of the
time and location of the user. Eventually, this has resulted in forming new interac-
tion modes in the virtual social space. In this paper the User2Machine-interaction
model is proposed, focusing on technologies and functionalities affecting this
model and contributing to changes in the way users interact with systems. Tech-
nologies such as Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI), Virtual Reality (VR) and Chatbots
are described to see where do they ﬁt in the new innovative model, and how they
affected online education and the ecology of higher education during and post
covid19 pandemic.
Keywords: Covid19 pandemic · Higher education · Innovative technologies ·
Model · User2Machine · Artiﬁcial intelligence · AI · Chatbots · Virtual reality ·
VR
1
Introduction
1.1
Covid19 Pandemic and Higher Education
Two years ago, the world how it was known to everybody has changed. Covid19 pan-
demic began in March 2020. Since then human lives have changed globally, shifting to
remote online emergency teaching and learning. Covid-19 pandemic brought huge dis-
ruption to higher education everywhere. Students were forced to stay home and learning
is offered online and mobile. This unexpected shift to online learning was complicated,
since it was unplanned for and not all universities had the proper infrastructure to cater
for this type of learning [1, 2]. On the other hand, students as well as instructors were
not fully prepared for this type of student-to-system interaction. However, out of the
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 163–171, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_16

164
F. Khaddage et al.
sudden everything had to change, and for safety reasons, and in an attempt to stop the
spread of the virus, governments around the world decided to move services and activ-
ities to online, not only for education but to all sectors. Higher education in particular
was affected by the pandemic, some universities were forced to cancel all face-to-face
interaction amongst students and instructors, hence forcing instructors to use mobile
and online interaction methods to offer teaching and learning. Therefore, online learn-
ing pushed itself into universities and this has made student-to-system interaction or
User2Machine interaction to become the norm during the pandemic.
User2Machine interaction mainly base on three unique technologies, (VR, AI, and
Chatbots), even though these three technologies are not new in online and mobile edu-
cation, however combining them in one model (the user2Machine) model and merge
them to serve different purposes, and to present them on three different (Information
Technology) IT-layers is unique, new and innovative.
1.2
Unique Technologies in Online Education
Virtual Reality (VR). [3] describes VR as the learning aid of the 21st century, and it
has become the learning aid for learners trying to learn remotely. VR can be deﬁned
as “the sum of the hardware and software systems that seek to perfect an all-inclusive,
sensory illusion of being present in another environment” [4]. Immersive VR devices
can be categorized into mobile VR (e.g., Google Cardboard, Samsung Gear), high-end
HMDs (e.g., Oculus Rift, HTC Vive), and enhanced VR (e.g., a combination of HMDs
with data gloves or bodysuits) [5]. All these devices allow users to experience immersion
in non-physical world to different degrees. Immersion describes the perception of being
physically present in a non-physical world [6]. A typical non-virtual environment is for
example a virtual world [7], where users are surrounded by digital images, sound, or
other stimuli and can interact with them [8]. Hence, VR technologies enable users to
immerse, to feel present and to interact with in non-physical environments.
Immersive VR technologies can be used for different learning objectives, such as,
analytical and problem-solving, communication, collaboration, and soft skills, proce-
dural–practical knowledge, declarative knowledge, learning a language, and behavioral
impacts [5]. Further, [5] identiﬁed that the success of immersive VR-based learning
depends on the learning content, the VR design elements and the underlying learning
approaches.
Research show that learners who use immersive HMDs are more engaged, spent more
time on the learning tasks, and acquired better cognitive, psychomotor, and affective
skills [9]. Further, learners retain more information and can better apply what they had
learned after participating in VR exercises [10].
Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) Technology is applied usually when a digital device stimu-
lates human thinking that is associate with human intelligence such as speech, learning,
making decisions, and reasoning [11].
[11] deﬁnes AI as “an automated digital human like brain, that can think and act
to solve problems, make decisions and understand, to form judgments by the process
of logic, based on given data and speciﬁc algorithm”. AI has been used in a variety of
settings in higher education, such as AI mentors for learners, virtual online tutor, smart

Towards User2Machine Model for Higher Education
165
assistance, rubrics and assessment systems [11, 12]. More and more smart AI system are
emerging now. As a matter of fact, Gartner predicts that 70% of enterprises are expected
to implement and integrate AI over the next couple of years. Also, as the world is already
witnessing 20% of projects are now deploying AI to make decisions and provide real-
time instructions [13]. Georgia State University is a good example of how AI is used to
develop chatbots, to help deal with students’ enquiries [11].
Chatbot technology is based on AI. Chatbots or conversational agents rely on autom-
atized conversation style interactions. They are designed as smart software application
to engage user in a conversation, chatbots treat conversations in a simple method, (talk or
type then reply/answer). Conversations can be via text-to text or text-to-speech. It is pow-
ered by deep learning (AI) and this can help with improving scalability and performance
of the software application [14].
Chatbots has empowered the learning process by reinforcement of learning tasks and
activities, hence allowing repetition and error recovery, so that it is easier for learners
to adjust repeat and retrain. Chatbots can handle multiple users at the same time, and
can communicate seamlessly since they can access the API (Application Programming
Interface) of any system the user might be connected to. Chatbot can handle static
and dynamic communication between user and the machine. Static communication is
offered when the chatbot does not require to look up or connect to the backend of the
IT system to provide the answer, the answer would be already predeﬁned. While on the
other hand dynamic communication required a query to be send from the chatbot to the
backend/server side to collect the required information to provide an accurate answer.
These technologies have made an impact on the online systems in higher education,
and with more innovation being underway, they are in the process of changing the
ecology of education [15, 16]. The foreseeable beneﬁts of these technologies are far
reaching in higher education and this is leading to a User2Machine interagtion model
that is contributing to changes in behavioral patterns amongst learners in the way they
behave, act, communicate, response, and interact. This will continue to grow and evolve
further in the near future.
In the next section, the authors focus on the three unique technologies they identiﬁed
(VR, AI, and Chatbots) and describe the underlying basic concept for each of them, their
application in teaching and learning in higher education along with their application in
a pedagogical concept.
2
Architectural Tripod for User2Machine Interaction

ing by the day, and may soon become capable of altering every aspect of interaction
amongst humans. In education, they are already forming unique and innovative methods
in teaching and learning, and they have been undergoing testing in different educational
contexts [17]. So far, it seems that the possibilities are endless and merging these tech-
nologies together in education and preparing learners for an innovative-tech-powered
context are changing the way we teach, communicate and interact with each other and
with technologies. To improve the learning process it is not enough to bring the tech-
nologies along to the system, but also this has to be followed by corresponding inno-
vative pedagogies [1]. For example, learning activities that involve technologies such

as Chatbots, AI and VR require innovative pedagogies, which are fairly different from
the conventional teacher-centered, static and instruction-based pedagogies [18]. These
do not provide sustainable and sufﬁcient support in teaching and learning hence, new
pedagogies should match the new technologies. Table 1 illustrates the three identiﬁed
technologies with a focus on the underlying basic concept, their application in teaching
and learning and their application in pedagogical concepts. Learners as well as teachers
should be able to draw the experience to guide proper practices for the application of
innovative and new pedagogies so that they can effectively interact with the system.
Table 1 lists the three unique technologies along with their underlying concepts
and applications in teaching learning and pedagogy. These technologies seem to be
applicable at different layers in the IT architecture and learning environment in order
for them to offer effective interaction within the User2Machine model. The three layers
are illustrated in Fig. 1.
Fig. 1. Three layers and applicable technologies
Layer One (Data Layer): AI plays a crucial role here, as it receives data, analyses
data, and provide suggestions/predictions to the user. The link within the User2Machine
model is that the AI receives the data from the user via a certain interface, but there is
not much more interaction. However, through Natural Language Processing (NLP) the
technology may enrich the content with data and is able to analyze behavior. Per se there
is no interaction intended, but it the basis for pro-active interaction.
Layer Two (Technical Interface Layer): VR plays the pivotal role as it is the technical
interface to immerse the user into the digital environment. Interaction through VR is
usually uni-directional. VR allows the user to immerse in the digital environment. VR
involves the learner by visualizing the environment and by allowing interaction. The VR
device plays a passive role and is not proactively interacting with the user. However, the
VR device can - with other technologies such as AI - for example provide relevant data
on the display.

168
F. Khaddage et al.
Layer Three (Interaction Layer): Conversational agents (chatbots) interact with the
user intensely based on communication, conversation, recommendations. All this is very
much linked to AI, and may also be linked to VR in a virtual world. Chatbots are also
usefultechnologyforsimulatingtheinteractionwiththevirtualenvironment.Thechatbot
is adaptable to the environment and to users’ behavior and needs, which enable them to
support learners by increasing their knowledge-based understanding of the concept.
Based on the three layers, the authors deﬁned the User2Machine model, which is
proposed in the following section.
3
The Proposed User2Machine Interaction Model
The world is becoming technology-driven, automated, intelligent - systems are becoming
smarter and experts. This trend has increased during COVID19 pandemic, as the world
continues to interact online using various methods of communication channels. Higher
education institutions have gone online and continued to offer remote distance learning
via online and mobile systems. Some of these technologies and concepts are expected
to remain after the pandemic. This has led the authors to come up with a unique model,
which integrates the most up-to-date technologies, so that it can ﬁt seamlessly within the
majority of higher education settings. However, developing an effective User2Machine
model is a challenging task due to the dynamic variation in real-world scenarios and
different types of available data (structured and unstructured) that the world is currently
dealing with.
In the following, a sustainable User2Machine model for higher education is pre-
sented, that is based on the three identiﬁed layers, i.e. the Data Layer, the Technical
Interface Layer, and the Interaction Layer. This is because the beneﬁt of three-layers
architecture is there to support innovative technologies and their functionalities. Each
layer can run on a separate mode or level to best ﬁt its functional requirements and
provide effective interaction between the user and the machine. The interaction between
a machine and the user is moving from static view, where the user controls the machine
based on given set of instructions, to automated AI or VR environment where the user and
the machine bi-directionally interact. This rapid advancement of technological innova-
tion is now reaching a high level of intelligence and becoming experts. This has enabled
the executions of complex activities to become robust, fast and efﬁcient. Machines are
now helping users, and at the same time users are teaching machines to help users
in numerous ways including enhancing users’ mental awareness and strength during
the learning process, empowering physical capabilities and simplifying interaction with
users and systems. Hence, they are now interacting and communicating in more reliable
and supportive ways.
Therefore, the proposed User2Machine sustainable model may enhance interaction
mode with the interface, and make smart, expert and autonomous interactive system,
instead of being an information system. This model is illustrated in Fig. 2.

Towards User2Machine Model for Higher Education
169
Fig. 2. User2Machine interaction model
In the proposed “User2Machine” interaction model, users are communicating with
machines by the application of innovative technologies and digital devices. At the same
time expert machines are communicating with users synchronously via the interface,
as seen in Fig. 2. The authors focused on three technologies that are dominating in
the 21centry, to illustrate how the interaction occurs. These three technologies are AI,
VR, and Chatbots. The three technologies together provide a powerful tool for the
User2Machine model and interfacing is based on the identiﬁed three layers (Data Layer,
Technical Interface Layer, and Interaction Layer), as illustrated in Fig. 1. As seen in Fig. 2
users’ input take place via the system and by using innovative technologies and a variety
of digital devices. Users interact and input data to the system via the layered architecture.
LayerOneistheuserinteractionviaAIwiththecapabilityofextractinginsightsfromdata
to produce recommendations, prediction, reasoning, guessing, ﬁnding expert solutions
etc., thus contributing to data-driven decision-making process. Hence making the process
of learning faster and the method of accessing the content quicker. Layer Two, the
interaction layer, is represented by VR, an innovative technology too. However, instead
of giving recommendations, it takes actions, as user should immerse in the environment;
and be part of the settings and the virtual learning atmosphere. The interaction occurs in
a 3D virtual space as if the user is in another real second life environment based on avatar.
Layer Three is represented by the chatbots. This technology is interactive and typically
allows user and machine to automate a two-way conversation. Chatbots sometimes uses
AI, however it does cover textual analytics, and natural language processing (NLP)
through which education systems can enjoy text recognition, speech-to-text conversion,
translation, and sometimes content generation capabilities.

170
F. Khaddage et al.
This proposed User2Machine model that is based on innovative technologies and is
applicable in higher education during and post any pandemic, may ﬁt seamlessly in any
online mobile learning settings.
4
Conclusions and Future Research Direction
This paper presented a User2Machine model in higher education that has the potential
to guide the integration of innovative technologies in education and how users interact
with them, and can ﬁt seamlessly into the changing ecology of higher education. The
model can demonstrate the affordances of various technologies, how they are already
challenging what is taught (the content) and how it is taught, (the pedagogies) [18], as
well as how user interact with the system, hence changing the mode of interaction.
With the presentation of this User2Machine model the authors aim to open a com-
munication channel between practitioners (instructors, students, higher education insti-
tutions), policymakers, and researchers, so they all can work together to highlight the
crucial need of technology integration in education and to make a place for unique
innovative model.
The authors suggest that new technologies must merge with innovative pedagogies
and eventually this will evolve and enhance the teaching practices in higher education.
There is also debate over how well students retain knowledge learnt from an AI, Chatbot
or VR applications, and this is an ongoing research and this will be based on the trailing
and evaluating process of the new interaction model proposed. Future studies as well
will focus on students’ and teachers’ perception of such model, barriers and challenges
they faced etc. and these will be available in future publications. Moving forward the
authors will be looking at issues related to method of interactions, as sometimes spending
substantial amount of time interacting with a machine instead of a human may decrease
social learning and face-to-face collaboration, however the authors believe that, if the
proposed model is integrated properly as part of a blended learning settings, it should
not interfere with any other interaction models and may be applicable during and after
any kind of pandemic.

Adult Learners’ Impressions About Intelligent
Tutorial System: A Case Study of Adult Basic
Education and Training
Ntima Mabanza(B)
Department of Information Technology, Central University of Technology, Free State,
Bloemfontein, South Africa
nmabanza@cut.ac.za
Abstract. This study was to establish whether using an ITS prototype developed
for delivering a technology course in Sesotho can enhance the training experiences
for ABET Sesotho-speaking learners and assist them in better understanding the
content of the technology course. The “magic number ﬁve” rule was used in the
study to test the developed ITS Prototype. The population of the study consisted
of 5 Sesotho-speaking adult learners. User tasks and questionnaires were used to
collect data needed for the study. Collected data were analysed using Descriptive
statistics. The results from the data analysis showed that the highest impressions as
perceived by participants with regards to using the ITS offering technology course
in their mother tongue were their ability to quickly understand the content of the
technology course, their high level of conﬁdentiality when using ITS providing
instructions in their mother tongue and their ability to learn the technology course
much quicker. Based on these results, the current study has established that the use
of ITS delivering course in the mother tongue could address the language barriers
faced by many previously disadvantaged black adults willing to join the ABET
programme.
Keywords: ITS Prototype · ABET · Mother tongue · Language barrier · Black
adults · Training experience
1
Introduction
In South Africa (SA), blacks make up most of the population. However, the level of
illiteracy is too high amongst this population group. The high level of illiteracy amongst
the black communities is mainly attributed to the inequalities of the past, whereby blacks
had limited or no access to education opportunities. The new SA democratic govern-
ment elected in 1994 put in place a form of education intervention such as Adult Basic
Education and Training (ABET) to try to eliminate the historic educational inequalities
of the past faced by black communities.
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 172–181, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_17

Adult Learners’ Impressions About Intelligent Tutorial System
173
1.1
ABET
ABET is an instructional program designed to promote lifelong learning, knowledge,
and skills development for the previously disadvantaged, speciﬁcally black adults who
missed an opportunity of obtaining formal education [1]. A range of courses are offered
in ABET programme: Economic Management, Life Orientation, Human and Social
Sciences, Mathematical Sciences, Technology, and Arts and Culture [2]. It is assumed
that ABET can assist in helping previously disadvantaged black adults to uplift their
educational levels and quality of life and function adequately in society. Despite that,
there are still more previously disadvantaged black adults who are reluctant to join the
ABET programme, particularly those who are supposed to beneﬁt the most from it.
Pasensie [2] identiﬁes the language barrier, shortage of qualiﬁed teachers, and geo-
graphical challenges as a few examples of possible challenges preventing adults from
engaging in ABET. In the context of this study, the emphasis will be on the language
barrier. The language barrier refers to an individual or a group of individuals’ inability
to effectively communicate or understand a different language(s) that is not their mother
tongue. The ABET curriculum is in English [3]. English can represent a threat to the
previously disadvantaged black adults willing to join the ABET programme. Numerous
reasons can be linked to this. English is not the ﬁrst language (mother tongue) of the
vast majority of black adults willing to join the ABET programme [4]. Hence, they can
be uncertain about their ability to speak, write and understand English. Also, most of
these adults lack formal education at a young age, making them lack conﬁdence in their
ability to learn. In the attempt to address these challenges, it is crucial to ﬁnd innovative
ways to support this group of adults facing a language barrier, so they can also have an
opportunity to participate in ABET programme. Incorporating the Intelligent Tutoring
System (ITS) into ABET can be seen as one example of these innovative ways.
1.2
ITS
AnITSisacomputersystemthatmimicsahumanteacher’sbehaviourtoeasethelearning
process and provide customised instruction or feedback to learners [5, 6]. The primary
purpose of ITS consists of reducing and making the learning experience enjoyable. It can
provide a one-on-one curriculum, allow learners to learn at their own pace, and monitor
learners’ performance [7, 8]. All of these can be done with little or without requiring the
intervention of a human teacher. Al-Bastami and Naser [5] claimed that ITS can improve
the human traditional teaching method. Aldahdooh and Naser [9] further afﬁrmed that
ITS could decrease the knowledge-gaining time for the learners and give them the ability
to become experts in any subject area.
Existing literature revealed that ITS had been used in different ﬁelds of study such
as Engineering, Biology, Medicine, Science, Mathematics, Database, Programming,
English, Computer Theory, and Information Security [10]. Likewise, several studies
had investigated ITS’ abilities to support and enhance teaching and learning activities in
different ﬁelds. These previous studies can be grouped into three categories: ITS’ abilities
to facilitate a subject’s understanding, ITS’ abilities to improve learners’ performance
in a particular topic, and learners’ satisfaction level when using ITS to learn a subject.

174
N. Mabanza
With regards to ITS’ abilities to facilitate a subject’s understanding, the results of
the studies conducted by [5–7], and [9] revealed that learners who utilized ITS during
learning had a clearer and better understanding of the subject’s contents than those who
did not.
D’Mello, Olney, Williams and Hays [11], Aldahdooh and Naser [9], Elnajjar and
Naser [12], Sabo, Atkinson, Barrus, Joseph and Perez [13], Grivokostopoulou, Perikos
and Hatzilygeroudis [14], Zarandi, Khademian, Minaei-Bidgoli and Türk¸sen [6], Al-
murshidi and Naser [15], Hilles and Naser [16] investigated the abilities of ITS to
improving learners’ performance in a particular subject. Although these researches.
were done using different subjects, and their common ﬁnding was that ITS success-
fully increases learners’ performance, including their level of learning engagement and
motivation in the subject.
The different results of the previous studies, as discussed above, conﬁrmed that ITS
is a tool that has the potential to ease and enhance the teaching and learning process.
The results of studies by [11, 17–19], and [20] revealed that there was a high level of
satisfaction from the learners when using ITS to learn a particular subject. Nevertheless,
these studies mainly focused on the use of ITS in the context of formal education settings.
Also, in terms of the population, the emphasis was on primary, high school, and university
students. Very little is known about the use of ITS in adult learning setting such as an
ABET, leaving a gap in the literature that needs to be ﬁlled. Hence, the need for the
current study sought to investigate the potentiality of ITS to support and enrich teaching
and learning in the ABET environment.
As pointed out earlier, the language barrier is one of the possible challenges prevent-
ing the vast majority of previously disadvantaged black adults from joining the ABET
programme. Bearing this in mind, the current study is one of the ﬁrst to mainly focus
on using an ITS that delivers a technology course in a local South African language,
precisely Sesotho, in an ABET setting. Hence, the objective of this study is to establish
whether the use of ITS delivering technology course in Sesotho can enhance the train-
ing experiences for Sesotho-speaking adults and assist them in better understanding the
content of the technology course.
2
Methodology
2.1
Study Participants
Purposive sampling was deemed an appropriate sampling technique for deciding the
potential participants in this study. The following were why purposive sampling was
chosen over others:(i) the researcher knew the characteristics of the targeted study par-
ticipants, and (ii) also knew where to get them. Hence, the study participants comprised a
group of previously disadvantaged ABET Sesotho-speaking adults from the Mangaung,
Municipality, Bloemfontein, South Africa.
In this study, all necessary ethical processes were followed. The contents of the
consent form were read and clearly explained to the participants about their rights,
contributions to the study, and the protection of their privacy. Also, all individual study
participants were requested to complete and sign a consent form before participating in
this study.

Adult Learners’ Impressions About Intelligent Tutorial System
175
2.2
Data Collections Methods
Three data collection techniques were used to collect data needed for this study, namely
ITS Prototype, user tasks, and questionnaires.
ITS Prototype. ITS Prototype is a simulated desktop program developed to deliver a
technology course on computer hardware and software topics in Sesotho. Figures 1, 2,
and 3 illustrated some features of the ITS, including explanations about the various steps
participants, had to complete to interact with the ITS.
Login is the ﬁrst thing that a user has to do before using the ITS. At the login popup
window, a user has to type in their credentials (See Fig. 1).
Fig. 1. ITS login popup window
Referring to Fig. 1, a user needs to supply two types of information: Lebitso (i.e.
name) and Nomoro ya sephiri (i.e. password). After typing in the two pieces of infor-
mation, the user can press Kena! button to login into the ITS. After successfully logging
into the ITS, depending on a user’s need, they can opt to choose any of the two following
options available:
(i)
The ITS tutoring Popup Window (See Fig. 2), if they would like to learn about any
technology course topics available in the ITS or
(ii) The ITS Test Popup Window (See Fig. 3), in case they would like to take a self-test
to assess/her understanding of the learned topic.
Fig. 2. ITS Tutoring Popup Window

176
N. Mabanza
Screenshots images in Figs. 2 and 3 illuminate how a user interacts further with the
ITS after login (Fig. 1) and choose either (i) the ITS tutoring Popup Window (See Fig. 2)
or (ii) the ITS Test Popup Window (See Fig. 3) respectively.
At the ITS tutoring Popup window (See Fig. 2), a user would be presented with a
list of the available technology course topics, as displayed in the ﬁrst column of the grid
view. After ﬁnding any topic of interest they would like to learn about from the displayed
list, a user would have to double-click on that speciﬁc topic. After double-clicking on
the topic, all the textboxes will be populated with information about the selected topic.
Also, to view any image related to the chosen topic, a user has to click on the Bula button
(See Fig. 2). Lastly, a user can move from one lesson topic to another.
After a user has completed learning their topic of interest, they can opt to take a
self-test to assess/her level of understanding of the learned topic. As shown in Fig. 3, at
the ITS Test Popup Window, a user will be presented with questions related to the topic
of interest that they learned about in the ITS tutoring popup window (see Fig. 2).
Fig. 3. ITS test popup window
Referring to the ITS Test Popup Window shown in Fig. 3 above, a question has a
list of possible suggested answers (i.e. four) from which a user can choose. To select a
correct answer to the question, a user has to click on a radio button next to the suggested
answer. To move to the next question, a user has to click on the Potso e Latelang button
(see Fig. 3). When a user has done answering all questions (i.e. at the end of the self-test),
a popup window will appear to indicate to them that they have completed the self-test,
and after that their test score will appear on the screen.
User Tasks. As mentioned earlier, previously disadvantaged ABET Sesotho speaking
adult learners from Mangaung were the ITS targeted user groups for which the ITS
delivering technology course in Sesotho was developed. Therefore, it was essential to
test the developed ITS Prototype with a representative of its intended user groups. This
allowed assessing if the developed ITS could achieve its primary goal, enhance the
training experiences for Sesotho-speaking adults and assist them in better understanding
the technology course content.
Initially, all study participants were introduced to the ITS prototype and received
basic training on how the developed ITS prototype work. This allowed them to familiarise

Adult Learners’ Impressions About Intelligent Tutorial System
177
themselves with the ITS’s features and to understand how each of these features works.
Afterward, they were given tasks to perform by themselves as part of user task testing.
During the user tasks session, study participants performed various tasks using the
ITS Prototype. The following were a few examples of the user tasks performed by each
of the study participants: (i) Login to the ITS, (ii) choose a technology course topic that
they would like to learn about, and lastly, (iii) take a self-test to assess their level of
understanding of the learned topic.
After completing their user tasks, all study participants ﬁlled in a post-test question-
naire. The post-test questionnaire sought to collect data about participants’ impressions
of their study experience using an ITS Prototype offering a technology course in their
mother tongue.
Questionnaires. Pre-test and post-test questionnaires are the two types of question-
naires used in this study to collect the necessary data needed from the Sesotho-speaking
adults.
The pre-test questionnaire gathered information about the study participants’ pro-
ﬁles. Also, it assisted in checking that each study participant fulﬁlled the proﬁles of the
ITS’ targeted user groups.
The post-test questionnaire collected comments from study participants about their
impressions and perceived experiences of interacting with the ITS delivering technology
course in their mother tongue.
3
Data Analysis and Discussion
3.1
Proﬁle of Study Participants
The existing literature in the ﬁeld of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) revealed that
a signiﬁcant number of many HCI researchers are in favour of Nelson’s “magic number
ﬁve” rule [21]. “Magic number ﬁve” states that testing a system with just ﬁve users would
turn up 85% of the usability problems [22, 23]. Hence, in this study, the researcher
adopted the “magic number ﬁve” rule approach to test the developed ITS Prototype.
Therefore, the data analysis presented and discussed in this section was gathered from 5
adult learners who voluntarily agreed to participate in this study. This was done to afﬁrm
the rule of thumb, generally referred to as the “magic number ﬁve”.
3.2
Pre-test Questionnaire
There were 5 participants, of which 80.0% were males and 20.0% were females. All
participants (100%) were between 18–24 years of age. More than half of the participants
(60%) indicated that Southern Sotho is their home language, while others indicated
Tswana (20.0%) and Zulu (20.0%). Regarding their Southern Sotho reading abilities,
20% indicated they were excellent, 40% were good, and another 40.0% were poor. Eighty
percent (80.0%) stated that they understood Southern Sotho well. The remaining 20.0%
had an excellent understanding of the Southern Sotho. Regarding speaking the Southern
Sotho language, quite a few participants (20.0%) indicated that they were perfect in
Southern Sotho. Amongst the remaining 80.0%, half of them (40.0%) were good, and
the other half (40.0%) were average speakers of the Southern Sotho language.

178
N. Mabanza
In Summary: Study participants comprised of both genders (i.e. male and female) where
the vast majority of them being male. Their age group was 18 to 24, indicating that all
participants were adults. Despite Southern Sotho not being the home language for all
the participants, they all could understand, speak, and read Southern Sotho. Also, all
participants were black South African adults, which is the focus of this study.

that the ITS offering course in Sesotho signiﬁcantly assisted them in achieving the
following:
• Being able to use the ITS interface
• Quickly understand the content of the technology course,

Findings: As per the statements listed in Table 1, the highest impressions as perceived by
study participants with regards to using the ITS offering technology course in Sesotho
were the following: their ability to quickly understand the content of the technology
course, their high level of conﬁdentiality about using ITS providing instructions in their
mother tongue and their ability to learn the technology course much quicker when using
the ITS. Several factors may have contributed to these results, such as the participants’
abilities to understand, speak, and read Southern Sotho could have made it easier, sim-
pler, and quicker for them to understand the content of the technology course, increase
their conﬁdence and make them learn much faster. Therefore, these results indicate
that participants were interested, had enjoyable learning experiences, and had positive
impressions of the ITS delivering course in their mother tongue. Based on these results,
it may be said that the ITS delivering course in their mother tongue can address the lan-
guage barriers faced by many previously disadvantaged Sesotho-speaking black adults
willing to join the ABET programme. The ﬁndings of this study are in line with the
claims made by [5–7], and [9] that learners who use the ITS have a clearer and better
understanding of the subject’s contents. The ﬁndings also support the claims made by [6,
9, 11–15], and [16] that the use of ITS successfully increases learners’ level of learning
engagement, and motivation in the subject, as well as the claims made by [11, 17–19]
and [20] that there is a high level of satisfaction from the learners when using ITS to learn
a particular subject. This study provides evidence that ITS has the potential to enhance
the technology training experiences for Southern Sotho-speaking adults. Hence, the use
of ITS delivering course in a mother tongue can also be extended to reach more adults
facing a language barrier dilemma but lack an opportunity to participate in ABET due
to other reasons beyond their control. For example, disadvantaged black adults living in
remote places or rural areas lacking ABET facilities might be willing to upgrade their
educational level. Still, their situations make it difﬁcult for them to do so. The use of
ITS delivering course in their mother tongue can be a suitable method to train such a
group of adults because ITS can facilitate self-training. Likewise, for adults who can-
not participate in ABET programme due to family responsibilities, workloads, etc. This
category of adults can also use ITS delivering course in their mother tongue to learn at
their own pace.

180
N. Mabanza
4
Conclusion
The current study sought to ﬁnd innovative ways to support the previously disadvantaged
black adults facing a language barrier, so they can also have an opportunity to participate
in ABET programme. An ITS delivering technology course in Sesotho was developed
in this study to enhance the training experiences for ABET Sesotho speaking adults and
assist them in better understanding the content of the technology course. The developed
Prototype ITS was evaluated by a representative of its intended user group to check if
it achieved its purpose. The ITS evaluation result, as per the Sesotho-speaking adults’
impressions about ITS delivering technology course in their mother tongue revealed they
could easily understand the content of the technology course, their level of conﬁdentiality
was high, and they could learn the technology course much quicker when using the ITS
providing instructions in their mother tongue.
Hence, based on this study result, it is argued that the current study has established
that the use of ITS delivering technology course in Sesotho can enhance the training
experiences for Sesotho-speaking adults and assist them in better understanding the
content of the technology course.
Nonetheless, similar to any other study, the current study also had its limitations.
Hence some possible suggestions were formulated for future research based on the
limitations identiﬁed during this study:
• All study participants were between 18–24 years of age. The possibility of using
including other age groups could be explored.
• The ITS prototype exclusively included limited features. The possibility of adding
more features in the future could be considered.
• Participants performed a limited number of tasks using ITS. In the future, the
possibility of including more tasks could be explored.
