Contribution of Artiﬁcial Intelligence
in Counselling: Study Case on Self-control
of Adolescents Studying Drama
Alina-Mihaela Munteanu1(B)
, Teodor-Cristian R˘adoi2
,
Constantin B˘al˘aceanu-Stolnici1
, Cristiana Glavce1
, and Adriana Borosanu1
1 Institutul de Antropologie – Academia Român˘a, Str. Calea 13 Septembrie, Bucharest, Romania
edimemune.amber@yahoo.ro
2 Polytechnics University of Bucharest, Splaiul Independentei 313, Bucharest, Romania
Abstract. The article studies the effectiveness of an online program to educate
self-control in students studying drama at “Dinu Lipatti” Art College in Bucharest
. The research presents the stages of the study and the platform of techniques and
exercises that is managed by artiﬁcial intelligence networks. The target group was
formed by 90 students aged between 14 and 17, who attend drama courses as a
vocational training at the forementioned institution. The ﬁrst step was to identify
the possible differences between the level of self-control of teens studying drama
comparing to their peers who attend courses at the informatics proﬁle from two
high schools in Bucharest. In this regard the teenagers applied Barratt impulsivity
questionnaire. The results were statistically interpreted using the social statistics
program and eventually analysed from psychological perspective. Consequently,
the target group ran the tasks from the online platform for three months and at
the end of the program they applied the Barratt again. The scores were compared
statistically to the initial results and then interpreted. The outcomes validated the
high efﬁciency of the program assisted by artiﬁcial intelligence. This represents
an opportunity to diversify the themes existing on the platform, considering the
needs of teenagers who study at any proﬁle in Romania.
Keywords: Artiﬁcial intelligence networks · Self-control · Adolescence ·
Drama · Platform
1
Introduction
Self-control is the ability that regulates the human conduct in different social or envi-
ronmental contexts. The term is a psychological construct that has been deﬁned as an
effort to inhibit the impulses [8], a capacity to delay the immediate gratiﬁcation [17], or a
dual-systems mechanism that can inhibit the impulses from the ‘hot‘ system (emotions,
fears, passion impulses) when the ‘cold‘ rational system has been precedingly turned
on by attention and cognition [16]. These deﬁnitions emphasize two dimensions of self
control: effort and inhibition. In 2011 an initiatory element of self control is added to
the previous components [3] and this has opened up perspectives to study strategies
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 182–189, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_18

Contribution of Artiﬁcial Intelligence in Counselling
183
for improving self-control [9] until present. This is the starting point in adaptation of
human being and a premise in shaping the personal resilience as well. From the very
ﬁrst days of life, the child ensures his survival through the relationship of attachment
that he establishes with his mother and this becomes the ﬁrst context of testing the
regulation of conduct [4]. During the preschool years, the child detaches emotionally
from the parental niche and develops socializing skills with the elderly and other adults
(the educators) by learning the ﬁrst methods to inhibate the impulses under the pressure
of the feedback received from others [20]. At this moment, the human being becomes
aware of the relationship between his attitude and his acceptance by the group, on one
hand, and tests the effectiveness of the ﬁrst methods of self-control, on the other. The
access to school provides the ﬁrst normative that facilitates a more effective behavioral
regulation. During this period, there are some moments when some desynchronizations
in regulating the self-control emerge and favor the appearance of risk behaviors [10].
This happens because of both the pressure of social environment that is felt dispropor-
tionately regarding teens‘ ability to cope with it, and the biological conditions due to the
hormonal changes during adolescence. The article presents a research on the training of
self-control on adolescents by applying an online program set on a platform managed
by artiﬁcial intelligence networks. The most studies on the state of art in education aim
at the technologies used for helping learners to improve the knowledge and skills level
by following the basic principle according to which education is accesible anyway, any-
time, whenever it is needed [5]. This could be a brief description for all educational tools
on the internet. Moreover, despite the fact that cell phones have been used during the
educational activities since the mid of the 2000s [13], these devices have become popular
with school lessons during the pandemic [2]. So, nowadays, it is commonly accepted
that cell phones are at hand tools that help pupils access information or applications on
internet.
The study was conducted between September 10, 2021 and December 20, 2021 on
a target group of 90 adolescents aged between 14 and 17, from the ﬁrst college year,
who study drama at ‘Dinu Lipatti‘ Art College in Bucharest. The implementation of
the program was chosen to be on the internet due to the fact that between 2019 and
2022 the society has faced the Covid 19 pandemic. This situation has moved school
activities from classrooms to online platforms. On the other hand, the pandemic can
be considered a population-based experiment that maximizes the self-control effects in
teens‘ behaviour. Furthermore, teenagers are fascinated by internet applications as their
daily activity swings among the social media platforms Facebook, Instagram, Tiktok and
Telegram. Therefore, the best choice to implement the study into their familiar space
was a condition to attract and motivate them to actively participate into the research. The
ﬁrst part of the school year was the start moment for the research in order to observe the
effectiveness of the self-control education program at the end of the ﬁrst semester.This
category of students was selected as their activity requires a high self-control due to
the speciﬁcity of their vocational work. In addition, the second motivation considers
the biological and psychological peculiarities of puberty that state the prevalence of
maturation of subcortical structure compared to the cortical circuits [6] thus predisposing
adolescents to risky behaviors. On the other hand, most of the materials aimed at teens
studying drama approach the theme as a self development extra-curricular activity or

184
A.-M. Munteanu et al.
as therapeutic tools for teens in need [21]. There have not been any researches on self
control for pupils studying drama as a compulsory vocational training in public schools.
2
Materials and Methods
Prior to the study, the students from drama classes were presented the program, the
working plan and the beneﬁts for their personal and vocational development. After that
the informed consents were signed by their parents and they enrolled voluntarily in the
program. The target group consisted of 90 students (age: 3.3% – 14 years, 58.9% –
15 years, 35.5% – 16 years and 2.2% 17 years; environment: 96.7% urban and 3.3%
rural areas; type of family: 11.2% single parent families – mostly mother, 84.5% nuclear
families and 4.4% extended families; ratio 1:1). The same procedure was followed to
form the group from the informatics proﬁle for the ﬁrst phase of the study. It included
90 teens the same age as their peers from drama classes (5.5% 14 years, 61.1% 15 years,
32.2% – 16 years and 1.2% – 17 aged; 100% from urban areas; 13,3% single parent
families, 85.5% nuclear families and 1.1% extended family; ratio 1:1). The study begins
with the application of Barratt impulsivity questionnaire for both categories of teens.
This is an instrument created by psychologist E.S. Barratt [1] and his colleagues from
University of Texas in 1959 and has been periodically revised. Impulsivity is the predis-
position towards unplanned and rapid reactions to internal and external stimuli that does
not take into account the consequences that may result from them [18]. Barratt considers
impulsivity is not a one-dimensional construct, which is reﬂected in the construction
of the questionnaire consisting of 30 items structured on several factors organized on
two types of scales named according to the ordinal criterion in the analysis, the ﬁrst
and second orders [1], as follows: 1. The ﬁrst scale structured on six factors: attention,
motricity, self-control, cognitive complexity, perseverance and cognitive instability; 2.
The second scale of three factors: a. attentional impulsivity – deﬁned as a low ability to
orient and focus attention on a task [14], summing up the factors of the ﬁrst order atten-
tion and cognitive instability; b. motor impulsivity, comprising the motor factors and
perseverance, and c. non-cognitive impulsiveness, representing self-control and cogni-
tive complexity from the ﬁrst order. In 2001, the Italian psychologist Fossatti [7] worked
with Barratt on a version for teens questionnaire, in which several items were adapted to
the age-speciﬁc routine. The present research uses the ﬁrst time the Romanian version,
after its translation by an authorized translator. The procedure of application is alike
the adult version. Out of the 30 items, 11 are reversed (the scores are calculated grad-
ually considering their appropriate opposite). The interpretation of the results obtained
at the questionnaire depends on the selected factors. There are specialists who choose
to analyze the sum of the 30 items. Results that indicate a high impulsivity show stan-
dard variation above the total score of 74 [19], which, in 2003, was decreased to the
score of 72 [15]. The same research indicates the band of results between 52 and 71 as
suggesting normal levels of impulsivity, while scores below 52 show people who show
excessive self-control [12] or who have given dishonest answers [11]. Adolescence is a
period when impulsivity is mainly caused by age-speciﬁc hormonal and neurophysio-
logical transformations that present the adolescent highly energetic, without inhibitions
and direction [10] and vulnerable to risk behaviors. That is why the second order scale

Contribution of Artiﬁcial Intelligence in Counselling
185
was more suitable for the present research and consequently helped to build the inter-
vention tool on the platform dedicated to the education of self-control. Ph.D Matthew
Stanford of Baylor University in the United States of America was contacted to get the
allowance to use the questionnaire. Consequently, the platform was designed, and the
questionnaire was uploaded on it. In addition to this instrument, the Big Five personality
test was added, in the version calibrated on the Romanian population ABCD-M, that is
available at the company Test Central. Prior to this, the license for multiple application
points was achieved. Next, the practical games, inspired by the four speciﬁc types of
items for self-control: anti-sacade tasks, go-no go, exercises such as strings of distract-
ing items and stop-signal games, were conceived and uploaded to the platform. Then
artiﬁcial intelligence networks were made and uploaded to the platform. These would
pick up certain types of tasks due to the combination of the scores obtained at Barratt and
Big Five test after the training session. The neural network is a programming method
that belongs to the ﬁeld of machine learning/artiﬁcial intelligence and is used to help an
algorithm learn on its own based on input and output data. Within this research the neural
network connects the two tests: Barrat (impulsivity) and Big Five (personality). Using
the inputs from Barrat (3 factors: attentional, motor, and non-planning impulsivity) and
the 5 factors of the Big Five as output neurons (conscientiousness, openness, agreeabil-
ity, neuroticism, extraversion) [22]. The structure of the network consists of two layers
of neurons with the activation functions of linear regression and softmax. The type of
training is a supervised learning, with labeled data from pupils and students. During the
production stage, the network is made to predict the results of the Big Five test using
the input data of the Barratt questionnaire. The score predicted later is used to generate
program recommendations for each user. Thanks to the architecture of the network, the
model learns by itself using the results of the Big Five test to train the neural network in
the ﬁtness stage. They give information about the user’s personality, on the one hand, and
suggest programs to practice self-control by combining tasks on the platform according
to the factors used by the algorithm. The network is being trained by all the pupils who
access it from many high schools from Bucharest. Every participant made an account
on the platform and then applied Barratt and Big Five. The scores were saved on the
platform. Two graphs in python representing the network for all factors at the beginning
(Fig. 1) and at the end (Fig. 2) were made as follows:
Fig. 1. All factors network before the
program
Fig. 2. All factors network during the program
The adolescents were chosen a training program depending on their results by the
artiﬁcial intelligence networks. The platform suggests an access frequency of three times
a week in the individual calendar where each game has a recommended date to be done.
A progress graph is updated regularly as the teens work on their account. After ﬁnishing

A.-M. Munteanu et al.
the online training, the participants applied Barratt again. The results were statistically
compared to the values from the initial testing. The one sample t-test was selected for
testing the research hypotheses. Then the size effect d-Cohen coefﬁcient was calculated.
Eventually the outcomes were psychologically interpreted.
3
Results and Discussions
The ﬁrst part of the study aimed to deﬁne the target group and to identify the differ-
ences from other categories of adolescents from the real proﬁle. Thus, it started from
the alternative hypothesis H1: there are statistically relevant differences between the
way self-control is reﬂected in the Barratt score of adolescents who study drama and
those from the real proﬁle. Alternative hypothesis H0 states that there are no statisti-
cally relevant differences between the two groups of adolescents. In this regard a paired
sample-t test was applied to the Barratt scores obtained by both groups, considering the
data got from the second order factors – attentional impulsivity, motor impulsivity and
non-planning impulsivity. Hence, regarding the attentional impulsivity, the difference
between the means, Md = 19.33 and Mi = 16.10 (where Md is the mean of the Barratt
scores for the drama proﬁle, and MI is the mean for the informatics proﬁle) is posi-
tive, which indicates that the average obtained by adolescents from the artistic proﬁle is
higher, and the result of the t-test shows a signiﬁcance p <. 001 (t = 11.913, df = 89),
that rejects the null hypothesis and afﬁrms the existence of a high relevant signiﬁcance
between the level of attentional impulsivity in the two groups (Cohen‘s d = 1.77). The
positive value of the mean difference indicates an increased level of impulsivity for the
target group versus the other group. For the motor impulsivity the null hypothesis states
that there are not any relevant differences between the scores reﬂecting the motor impul-
sivity of teens from the drama classes compared to their peers from the informatics. A
paired t-test was run to compare the two means, Md = 30, Mi = 25.14, and a signiﬁcance
value p<.001 (t = 12.446, df = 89) was found, which rejects the null hypothesis. The
test shows a high relevant statistical difference between the values of the two groups
(Cohen‘s d = 2.02), with the regard of the drama teens who scored the highest. Con-
cerning the non-planning impulsiveness, the t-test applied on the means, Md = 25.12,
Mi = 27.68, and a signiﬁcance of the test is p< .001 (t = –7.844, df = 89) was found,
which rejects the null hypothesis that states there are no statistical differences between
the values of the two groups. In this case, the difference between the means is negative
(–2.556), indicating higher values of impulsivity for adolescents from the informatics.
The differences identiﬁed can be explained considering the dominant activities of ado-
lescents. Therefore, the values of motor and attentional impulsivity of the adolescents
from drama are higher, for the adolescents who study sciences, the values are relevant
lower. The speciﬁc activity for the artistic proﬁle combines eurythmics with diction, and
requires physical activities, encouraging adolescents to express themselves visibly. This
can explain the increased level of the ﬁrst two Barratt factors for students who study
drama and are accustomed to being energetic. Regarding the real proﬁle, perhaps the
dominance of activities that require individual tasks of problem solving, concentration
of attention and elaboration of reasoning – activities that involve working in the ofﬁce
for longer periods of time precede a better self-control of attention and motricity than

Contribution of Artiﬁcial Intelligence in Counselling
187
those of the artistic proﬁle. The situation is different for the non-planning impulsiveness
that focuses on how they adapt their conduct to social life contexts, where adolescents
from the real proﬁle have higher scores than the target group. This indicates a weaker
adaptation to the requirements of social life. The explanation may be in the individual
kind of the activity this proﬁle requires. Mostly the problems of these adolescents are
the low capacity of communication with the elderly and their low sociability, compared
to those who study drama for whom the daily artistic activity puts them in contact with
their colleagues. In conclusion, the choice of adolescents studying drama is justiﬁed for
the research as they present a different pattern of self-control, due to the speciﬁc of the
vocational activity they carry out. For the study, the initial Barratt scores were referential
values for the next study. The second part of the research aimed to identify the efﬁciency
of the online platform. For this purpose, the hypothesis were formulated according to
the three factors in Barratt’s second order: attentional impulsivity, motor impulsivity,
and non-planning impulsivity. Thus, the ﬁrst alternative hypothesis is: H1- the average
of the ﬁnal scores for the attentional impulsivity factor is statistically signiﬁcantly lower
than the average of the initial mean. The null hypothesis is: H0: there are no signiﬁcant
differences between the ﬁnal mean obtained for the attention impulsivity factor and the
initial mean. In this regard, a t-test one sample was run for the two means, M1 = 19.33
and M2 = 17.43 (where M1 is the initial mean and M2 is the ﬁnal) and a signiﬁcance
p< .01 ( t = 94.891, df = 90) was obtained and rejected the null hypothesis. The size
effect was calculated by the d-Cohen coefﬁcient and obtained d = 1.035, which indicates
that the ﬁnal average of the values obtained after the application of the program on the
platform is signiﬁcantly lower than the initial one. In conclusion, the application of the
program on the platform had a statistically signiﬁcant effect in decreasing attentional
impulsivity and validates its effectiveness for the target group. The second alternative
hypothesis of the research is: H1 – the ﬁnal average is statistically signiﬁcantly lower
that the initial mean. Null hypothesis: H0 – there are no signiﬁcant differences between
the ﬁnal average and the initial mean obtained for the motor impulsivity after the pro-
gram was run on the online platform. A t-test one sample was run on the means, M1
= 25.03 and M2 = 30, and a signiﬁcance of p< .01 (t = 98.321, df = 90) was found,
which rejects the null hypothesis. The effect size Cohen, d = 2.02, indicates a highly
signiﬁcant difference between the two means. In conclusion, at a signiﬁcance of 5%,
there is enough evidence to support that the average of the ﬁnal scores was signiﬁcantly
lower than 30. Therefore, the effectiveness of the program applied for the formation of
self-control of this type of impulsivity is conﬁrmed. The third alternative hypothesis is:
H1- the ﬁnal average for the non-planning impulsivity factor is statistically signiﬁcantly
lower than the initial average. The null hypothesis is: H0 – there are no signiﬁcant dif-
ferences between the ﬁnal average for the non-planning impulsivity factor at the initial
mean. A t-test one sample was applied on the means, M1 = 24.87 and M2 = 25.12,
and a signiﬁcance of p< .01 (t = 127.326, df = 90) was obtained and rejected the null
hypothesis. In conclusion, for the non-planning impulsivity factor there are low signiﬁ-
cant differences between the mean of the initial scores and the mean of the ﬁnal results
as Cohen‘s d = 0.127. This indicates that the efﬁciency of the program for this factor is
not signiﬁcant.

188
A.-M. Munteanu et al.
4
Conclusion and Future Work
The reason why this factor did not register visible changes is reﬂected by the type of tasks
that the platform inserted into personalized training programs that did not include items
aimed at the cognitive complexity. Thus, the games created were suitable for focusing
attention on a task, training the inhibitory control, and diminishing the speed reaction in
choosing the right item. For these categories of tasks corresponding to the ﬁrst two second
order factors, the program was signiﬁcantly effective, for the attentional impulsivity the
coefﬁcient of size effect is d = 1.035, and for motor impulsivity d = 2.02. Incidentally,
the d-Cohen coefﬁcient values suggest that the program is more effective for training
self-control of attention and motor skills. For the target group represented by teenagers
who are being formed in drama, managing their own body expressivity is one of the
challenges of life as an actor apprentice, and the relevance of the program is justiﬁed by
theneedtostrengthenthecontroloftheirownreactionsduringtheperformanceandgroup
games they work. Self-control can be educated through online platforms, that is familiar
to adolescents today, where they can beneﬁt from a self-education program customized
by artiﬁcial intelligence networks that correlate the data individually from the initial
tests and consequently predict a certain training formula according to them, providing
them a progress report regularly. In perspective, this type of approach to counselling is
essential in building applications or support programs to assist adolescents in solving
their different emotional problems or difﬁculties that they do not face on their own.

Project Based Learning

POSTER: Proposing a Microlearning Approach
to Enhance Digital Story Telling Skills with Rich
Media in the PBL-Based Engineering Education
Kazuya Takemata1(B), Sumio Nakamura2, Akiyuki Minamide1,
and Toshiyuki Yamamoto3
1 Kanazawa Institute of Technology, Ishikawa 921-8501, Japan
takemata@neptune.kanazawa-it.ac.jp
2 PRODUCT DESIGN Bohr, Ishikawa 921-8806, Japan
3 Kansai University of International Studies, Hyogo 661-0976, Japan
Abstract. In recent years, PBL (Project Based Learning), which is an educational
method that promotes students’ autonomy, has been actively adopted at Japanese
universities. PBL is one of the leading methods of active learning. This study
examines pre-university education programs to be offered to help pre-university
studentssmoothlyundertakefull-scalePBLclassesafterenteringuniversity.Inthis
paper, developing the ability to accurately convey what a student wants to convey to
others (communication skills) is mentioned as an example of what students should
acquire before taking PBL subjects in university. Thus, we developed a practical
course incorporating animation production and conducted it for three years. Based
on the results of the questionnaire survey conducted after the classes, about 75%
of the 106 students who took the course gave positive comments regarding this
educational program. However, it was interesting that among the students who
answered negatively to the questionnaire, there were the students who thought
they did not have communication skills even though the teachers believed they did
through their observation of the classes. This was maybe because the students’
evaluation criteria of their own animation works were strict, making them judge
their communication skills as still low. Thus, when implementing this educational
program in the future, it is necessary to explain this point to the students in the
ﬁrst week of the course.
Keywords: Digital storytelling · Engineering design · PBL
1
Introduction
In recent years, PBL (Project Based Learning), which is an educational method that pro-
motes students’ autonomy, has been actively adopted at Japanese universities. PBL is
one of the leading methods of active learning. After the Ministry of Education, Culture,
Sports, Science, and Technology released “Toward a qualitative shift in university edu-
cation to build new future universities that promote lifelong learning and autonomy” in
2012, PBL courses have become available at many universities. Furthermore, this trend
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 193–200, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_19

194
K. Takemata et al.
of qualitative change in higher education has spread to secondary education, such as
high school and junior high school, and primary education, such as elementary school.
Thus, active learning education programs tailored to each grade are being discussed.
This study aims to help high school students smoothly engage in more practical
PBL subjects after entering university. In standard PBL, a small number of students
form a team and proceed with a project according to the proposed framework. For
example, during the 15 weeks of an academic semester, the students proceed with their
projects with the following stages: 1) to encounter problems, 2) to discover problems
to be solved, 3) to survey requests, 4) to create ideas, and 5) to solve problems [1]. In
the project activities, students practice self-directed learning and group learning. The
strength of PBL is that the knowledge students gain through the learning is deepened
through discussions [2–4]. More importantly, students need to be able to explain their
thoughts to others in team activities logically [5, 6].
Therefore, in this paper, we have developed an educational program for students
who have not yet entered university to express their ideas with animation. In the ani-
mation production activity, the students will prepare storyboards to clarify what they
want to convey before production. In animation, having a storyline is important. Thus,
the students build a story through storyboards while seeking advice from teachers. This
training leads to the development of their ability to explain things logically.
2
Developed Educational Program
This educational program can be practiced in 100 min of class time per week during the
15 weeks of an academic semester. The program starts with a lecture on the mechanism
of animation. During the 15 weeks, the students produce the following three types of
animation.
2.1
Scanimation Production
During the period from the ﬁrst week to the third week of the 15 weeks, animation is
produced by using the principle of scanimation. This is also called “slit animation.”
The mechanism of this animation is as follows: 1) A transparent slit sheet (a sheet
with black and white stripes drawn) is layered on a single composite image created by
superimposing “several frames of images expressing movement.” 2) By sliding the slit
sheet, the composite image can be seen as a series of several frames through the slit. 3)
For the invisible part, the brain interpolates the image information creating the illusion
that you have seen the animation.
Students try to entertain viewers or convey some kind of message through their
work. At the end of the third week, students and teachers will view the works of all the
students together, and the teachers will comment and evaluate each student’s work. The
evaluation criteria are 1) how entertaining the theme is, 2) the smoothness of movement,
3) the difﬁculty in expressing the illustration, 4) the meticulousness of the drawing, and
5) coloring (color, gradation, etc.).

POSTER: Proposing a Microlearning Approach
195
2.2
Production of Flip-Through Animation
From the fourth to sixth week, the students produce ﬂipbooks. By drawing slightly
different pictures in a special sketchbook and quickly turning the pages, the pictures
appear to move due to the afterimage effect. In this exercise, the students will draw their
works in a special sketchbook for the ﬂipbook [7]. This sketchbook measures 60 mm in
length and 120 mm in width and contains 50 sheets.
The work drawn by the students is videotaped and submitted as video data. The
student’s work is an animation for about 10 s. The students who excel in creating a
work with a storyline (expressing what they want to convey) would be the ones to
stand out. At the end of the sixth week, students and teachers will view the work of
all the students together, as in the case of the scanimation production mentioned above.
Teachers comment and evaluate each student’s work. Each work is evaluated by checking
1) storylines, 2) the meticulousness of drawing, 3) the movement of objects and people,
4) changes in angles, and 5) the quality of the movie.
2.3
Production of Stop-Motion Animation
From the seventh to the ﬁfteenth weeks of an academic semester, the students will
produce stop-motion animation. Stop-motion animation is an animation where you shoot
a stationary object while moving it little by little for each frame and edit the still image
as a moving image. Students have experienced ﬂipbook production prior to this exercise
and are aware of the need to incorporate storylines into their work. In this activity, we
instruct the students to create a storyboard that organizes their thoughts and stories and
explain to the students the importance of logical thinking that can be understood by
others to deliver one’s thoughts.
In order to reduce the burden of time-lapse photography for students, Fujitsu’s non-
contact scanner “SV600” is used. The reason is that the time required to set up equipment
for time-lapse photography can be reduced, and students can easily take continuous still
images. Another advantage of using this scanner is that you can move the object to be
photographed with both hands. Students are instructed to take about four images per
second and produce an animation work of about 2 min. Therefore, completing about
500 time-lapse shots within the set time is necessary. Based on the storyboards drawn in
advance, the students take time-lapse pictures and ﬁnish the work. Another goal of this
activity is to have them acquire a background in project management here.
The captured image is edited as a video in the same way as the ﬂipbook animation.
Producing work with a more realistic feeling can be achieved by adding sound effects
to the video. An interim debrieﬁng session will be held around the tenth week, and
teachers provide advice on the work. After the interim debrieﬁng session, some students
are inspired by the animation works of other students and review and recreate their own
works. In the ﬁfteenth week, students and teachers watch the work of all the students
together, as in the case of the scanimation and ﬂipbook mentioned above. Teachers
comment and evaluate each student’s work. Each work is evaluated by checking 1)
storylines, 2) the meticulousness of drawing, 3) the movement of objects and people, 4)
changes in angles, and 5) whether the characteristics of stop motion are utilized.

196
K. Takemata et al.
3
Program Implementation and Questionnaire Survey
This educational program was implemented for the second-year students at the technical
college (the Polytechnique) attached to our university for three years from 2016 to 2018.
A technical college is an educational institution students enter after graduating from
junior high school, and it is a higher educational institution for the purpose of training
engineers. After enrollment, students take a well-balanced curriculum of general and
specialized subjects for ﬁve years to acquire a rich education and systematic specialized
knowledge necessary for engineers. The second-year students of technical college must
prepare for advanced active learning in the upper grades (for fourth and ﬁfth-year stu-
dents). Thus, it was suitable for the experiment for verifying the educational program in
this research.
Figure 1 shows the student’s scanimation work. By moving the slit sheet, it seems
that multiple small balls are moving. For example, this work can be developed into a
work that shows the movement of planets in the solar system. Figure 2 shows a student’s
ﬂipbook work. The image of a stork carrying a baby is included in the work, and it is
about the declining birthrate, which is one of the problems facing Japan. Figure 3 shows
a student’s stop-motion animation work. It expresses the importance of helping each
other while depicting an incident in public transportation.
Fig. 1. A student’s work produced in a scanimation production exercise class.
In addition, after completing the course, a questionnaire was conducted for the stu-
dents who submitted the three works mentioned in the previous section. Of the 109
students who took the course from 2016 to 2018, we received 106 valid responses
(Fig. 4). The following are the questions of the questionnaire.
Q1: Do you think you have learned to plan and work on something in a limited amount
of time after completing this exercise?
Q2: Do you think that after completing this exercise, you were able to acquire the ability
to learn from others and actively learn by yourself?
Q3: Do you think that you have learned to reassemble your thoughts (develop your
thoughts) many times while making something after completing this exercise?

Q4: Do you think that you have learned to draw and prototype your own ideas after

Q5: Do you think you have learned to communicate your thoughts in the proper order

Q6: Have your motivation for creating things (manufacturing) changed after completing

Q7: Do you think that the experience gained from this exercise will lead to the improve-

Q1 is a question about project management, and Q2 is a question about active classes.
Approximately 75% of students answered afﬁrmatively to these questions as “learned it
well” or “learned.” This is a reasonable result for a course aimed at introducing active
learning. Q3 to Q5 are related to the ability to accurately convey the information you
want to deliver to a third party (communication skills). Q3 and Q4 are about developing
one’s thoughts and expressing ideas. 80% of the students gave positive answers to both
questions. After Q3 and Q4, Q5 aimed to make the students evaluate their ability to
convey their thoughts to others. 26% of the students thought they “do not have it” or
“do not have it at all.” Some of them were not satisﬁed with their work, which seems
to affect the result of Q5. Even though the teachers believed that these students could
convey thoughts to others, the students’ self-evaluation of their work was stricter than
the teachers’. Regarding the results of Q6, which asked about whether the student was
motivated to create something, there were 60% positive answers such as “I was much
more motivated than before” and “I was more motivated than before.” Therefore, we can
say that it is a good idea to motivate students to make things by taking into account the
state of efforts during the exercise. However, as with the Q5 results, it seems that about
40% of students who were not satisﬁed with their animation work gave negative answers.
Q7 is a question about whether this course will lead to future active learning. 80% of the
students gave positive answers such as “I think so very much” and “I think.” Based on
these results, we can say that the students were motivated to learn by themselves, and
this practical course was highly evaluated.
Fig. 4. Questionnaire survey conducted targeting students (n = 106).
4
Conclusion
This study discussed the curriculum development of the academic writing program,
attractive to the learner’s interest and curiosity. In order to arouse the curiosity, the

POSTER: Proposing a Microlearning Approach
199
animation technique as a communication tool was employed to nurture the writing
skills at the initial stage of learning. Three animation tasks were developed for the
2nd year students at a technical college (a Polytechnique in Japan): (i) scanimation, (ii)
ﬂip-through animation, (iii) stop-motion animation. The students tackled with all three
tasks.
The results from the questionnaire conduced at the end of the experiment proved that
the curriculum did nurture the students’ skills to tackle with a project with a well-thought-
out plan and to acquire proactive learning attitude. Furthermore, it was interesting that
high caliber students tended to give themselves lower scores to their ﬁnal products. Such
high caliber students’ ﬁnal products, in fact, deserved better scores. They displayed
more humble attitudes toward their accomplishments. It follows that the self-assessment
measure for products must be clariﬁed prior to the learning activities.
In the learning activity of digital storyboarding, the students were ﬁrst instructed to
produce storyboards. And then, based on them, they practiced explaining the entire story
orally before production. And yet, the students’ skills to storyboard varied greatly and it
was difﬁcult to provide instructional supports at the individual level in class. It is learned
that there needed a series of short lessons to develop skills to draw images or ideas
without paying attention to the details. Such lessons are different from ones in LMS. In
other words, microlearning contents would be ideal for such needs [8, 9]. The goal of
learning would be to draw to communicate properly. The purpose of such drawing is
different from skillful drawing. We must change the mindset in the development of the
microlearning contents [10, 11]. It is hoped that the TBL (Team-based Learning)-based
PBL must be incorporated in such microlearning.
The storyboarding skill is a powerful writing tool to visualize opinions and ideas in
words. We will continue developing the pre-university education program, making use
of the digital story telling strategy.

How to Flip a Classroom? Project Based
and Collaborative Learning
with Learner-Centered Methods and Its Impact
on Technical Teacher Education
Ibolya Tomory(B)
Óbuda University, Budapest, Hungary
tomory.ibolya@tmpk.uni-obuda.hu
Abstract. Creating a collaborative learning environment is one of the most impor-
tant school tasks today. It is necessary both to shape the attitudes of prospective
teachers and to broaden their methodological knowledge, so that learning based
on student activity can be implemented at all levels of education, including in
vocational training.
This study presents the collaborative learning environment and methods and
tasks that are part of a didactic module developed within the framework of an
internationalprogram.Theprimarygoalistodevelopthemethodologicalapproach
of teachers teaching STEM subjects, and to get to know the characteristics of
planning, forms of work and different methods and the possibilities of using them
in lessons, not only in theory but also in practice through their own experiences.
Tocompletethemodule,engineeringteacherandtechnicalvocationalstudents
are organized into small groups and work on a project assignment over a semester
on the topic of student-centered methods. In parallel, they learn and work on other
collaborative methods and a variety of tasks on other topics (ﬂipped classroom,
cooperative methods, mind mapping, ﬁlm analysis, etc.) and thus move towards the
main theme of the project (learner-centered methods). The groups take full respon-
sibility for the implementation of their projects, which is documented. To track
effectiveness, the study identiﬁes pre- and post-trial methodological approaches
and knowledge through mixed-method research. The results of follow-up stud-
ies so far (qualitative data) show that the project, the ﬂipped classroom and the
collaborative learning process have a positive impact on students’teacher aware-
ness, innovation and planning skills. The ﬂipped classroom has attracted a lot of
attention and different opinions, so we look at the factors that inﬂuence students’
opinions and satisfaction.
The results of follow-up studies so far (qualitative data) show that the project,
the ﬂipped classroom and the collaborative learning process have a positive impact
on students’teacher awareness, innovation and planning skills.
Learning embedded in a similar activity is a good way to prepare teacher
students to acquire and support the soft skills expected in the labor market, such
as collaboration. We recommend that student-centered collaborative and other
supportive methods be incorporated into teacher training at the university as part
of a separate didactic subject.

1
Introduction
The requirements for a successful career in the 21st century have changed, different than
before. Technological advancement brings constant change, new problems and new labor
market expectations, the solution of which requires not only cognitive skills but also soft
skills. These new demands make learning based on student activity, even class reversal,
the focus of 21st century education.
In science, technology, engineering, mathematics (STEM), the cognitive side is gen-
erally emphasized, but experiential research suggests that the use of learning methods
that support independent student work, thought-provoking challenges, and the develop-
ment of social competence yields better results. [1] “In the real world, solving social and
environmental problems does not occur in isolated domains, but rather at the boundaries
of STEM ﬁelds.” [2] Several studies point out that the integration of science subjects
and methods that support student activity increases learning motivation and may lead to
greater interest. [3] The creation of a learning environment that supports cooperation, as
well as the conceptual and methodological preparation of future teachers, is necessary
for the implementation of student-centered methods at all levels of education, including
vocational training [4, 5].
There are far more learner-centered methods than there are on a regular basis. Past
and present research similarly shows that the most commonly used methods are aimed
at mere knowledge acquisition. According to Hungarian research, 53.5% of the lesson
methodsareteachers’explanationsandpresentations,79%ofthewordsintheclassrooms
belong to teachers and no increasing effectiveness can be detected, because most teachers
teach in the same way (frontally) in small groups, too. [6, 7] The use of new generation
methods, such as cooperative methods and project-based education, is less than 50%.
[8, 9] The literature therefore draws attention to the need for a fundamental change in
educational methodology and developmental focus.
Our approach is close to the constructivist approach in which learning is a unique,
subjective process, the structure of a teacher’s knowledge cannot be transferred one-on-
one to the minds of students but need to provide experiential learning [10, 11].
2
Methodology
The aim of this study is to present a student-centered model tested at university and to
summarize its impact through student feedback. The theme and content were created
within the framework of an international project (CiSTEM), with a shorter version of
the topics highlighted from the framework of the module developed from the subject of
Didactics.
The testing group is mixed: consist of students with engineering teachers and a
technical vocational teachers with a common subject in Didactics. A total of 28 people,
most of them correspondence students, 70.4% are men and 29.6% are women. Age is

How to Flip a Classroom? Project Based and Collaborative Learning
203
mixed: 39.3% of those aged 41–50, 21.4% of those aged 18–20 to 26–30, 14.3% of those
aged 31–40, and some are aged 61 or older. More than half of the students (53.6%) have
a BsC degree and a technical or high school degree, and all work in vocational-related
jobs.
Effectiveness was monitored in a mixed way before, during, and after the trial: with
a questionnaire, observation, and text analysis to gather student feedback during the
process, based on lesson video recordings and semester-closing snapshots. In addition,
we examined previous student lesson plans and newer ones made during the program.
3
The Development Process
3.1
Course Design
During curriculum design, we proposed a novel learning-teaching model for students
to develop the teaching profession. The model was built in a complex way as part of a
module designed for the semester, which deals with topics highlighted from the subject of
Didactics. Based on previous practice in other groups, I selected the forms and methods
of work. The curriculum is built around the design and methods of learning-teaching
itself, and access was provided through the university Moodle interface. Most of it had to
be processed independently in or out of class. A formative evaluation form was developed
to link the presentation of project products to a group work evaluation thematic unit.
3.2
The Implementation Process

the module was integrated into three topics Fig. 1. Summarizes the milestones and dates

Outcomes
4.1
Changes in Methodological Knowledge
Students were asked in parallel and at the end of the module what methods they know
and what they use in their lessons. The questions included the basic frontal and module-
deﬁning methods. The majority of respondents are more familiar with and use traditional
teacher-centered methods at the beginning of the semester. The best known method is
lecture and explanation, students are 100% familiar with it and at least half of it is most
often used. Moving towards learner-centered methods, the proportions are reversed, the
project method is less well known (16 yes answers), but only three use it often and two
have worked with it no more than once or twice, others rarely or not at all.
Cooperative methods have generally been heard in proportion, but the speciﬁc meth-
ods involved are almost unknown. One of the best-known cooperative methods, the
expert mosaic, is not known at all by 24, for example, only three are familiar with the
three at the board and window method, but no one uses it, and four have heard of the task
sending method but do not use it. The proportions change only slightly for the ﬂipped
classroom method, 7 are known but only one is used. Mindmap is known by several
people (14 people), but only two are used. Figure 2 shows these ratios in summary.
In the course of qualitative data collection, it also turns out that some methods are
not known, there is only an assumption behind them, it is difﬁcult to separate the truly
cooperative methods from the others. The answers were therefore worth nuancing with
the non-numerical data. Methodological knowledge repeatedly interviewed at the end
of the semester shows changes. It is clear that the methods listed are already known to
students,butwhatismoreimportanthere,thattheproportionoflearner-centeredmethods
is increasing. The methods designed and/or tested have a high degree of learner-centricity
(see Fig. 3).
38% now work mainly with learner-centered methods (lecture, explanation), mainly
with student-centered methods (project, group work, creative task, etc.) 62%, and
methods based on teacher-student collaboration are marked as 100% by students.

Summary and Suggestion
Summarizing the experience of testing the module, learner-centered methods have a
positive impact on learning effectiveness, teacher-role interpretations, methodological
development and soft skills (collaboration, recognition of others, etc.). A process of
renewal has begun and interactions between students have improved. This is indicated
by the unbroken student activity during the semester and the fact that the project groups
consider their products and their own work to be their own and important. In the light of
the student feedback, it is recommended to introduce a separate didactic methodology
subject in university education to supplement the theoretical framework of didactics and
to introduce it as a good practice for the preparation of the professional methodology.
The aim is to provide a general methodological basis that can be used in any ﬁeld, in
any subject/topic. (For example, Project and other innovative methods called Learner-
Centered Methods).

Project Based Learning Approach to Developing
Presentation Skills
Diana Giliazova
and Elvira Valeeva(B)
Kazan National Research Technological University, 68 Karl Marx Street, Kazan 420015,
Russian Federation
gdr687@mail.ru
Abstract. Project based learning is widely used for training students to solve a
problem for an extended period. This approach aims at developing both hard and
soft skills, the combination of which is of great importance for successful career
promotion of future engineers. This article presents the project-based approach
which was implemented in the Foreign Language Course for students majoring in
Chemical Engineering at Kazan National Research Technological University. This
approach was applied to students receiving their Bachelor’s degrees in Chemical
Engineering, and then to the same students who continued their study and got
Master’s degrees. To implement this approach to the educational process, we
developed the project task in such a way as to combine students’ training in
Bachelor’s and Master’s programs. The project task was carried out by students
withthesupportofprofessorsfromForeignLanguageDepartmentandengineering
departments of the University. At the end of the course students presented their
results in English both at Bachelor’s and Master’s levels of education. Thus, we
could connect logically two levels of the university education for fostering the
English language communication skills for students’ professional and academic
purposes.
Keywords: Project based learning · Foreign language course · Engineering
education
1
Introduction
The last decade has brought tremendous changes in Russian university education. These
changes resulted in three-level system of higher education and creating new university
programs [1]. The Foreign Language Course is a compulsory subject included in all
programs of the university education. According to new Russian educational standards,
the course is to focus on developing English communication skills for professional pur-
poses for Bachelor’s students and academic purposes for Master’s and doctoral students
[2]. There is also a need to logically connect all three levels of university education
for more intensive English-language training of future engineers and scientists. There-
fore, we need to develop new course content for all levels of the university programs
as well as implement the appropriate teaching methods to the educational process [3].
The project-based approach was chosen as a method for developing professional and
academic communication skills of students.

M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 209–215, 2023.

D. Giliazova and E. Valeeva
2
Approach
Teaching a foreign language to engineering students in Russia is a speciﬁc technique
demanding both general English and English for professional and academic purposes. It
meansthatastudentofatechnicaluniversityshouldknowEnglishwellenoughforfurther
obtaining and mastering it as the language for professional communication. Moreover,
intercultural and management competences have become of great importance for future
career opportunities [4–6]. Therefore, different teaching methods and techniques have
been developed and implemented in Kazan National Research Technological University
[7–9]. We would like to present you the way we do it at our English classes for Bachelor
and Master degree students.
We analyzed the existing Russian and international best practices in teaching English
in order to ﬁnd the appropriate teaching method to university students. According to the
analysis, the project based learning was chosen as the most appropriate one for students
majoring in Chemical Engineering [10, 11]. Let us consider what project based learning
is and why it has become so popular.
Project based learning is a pedagogic framework to learn and teach a subject through
a project. This method implies the individual or collaborative work and encourages
students to learn by doing. According to Buck Institute for Education (2018), Project
Based Learning is a teaching method in which students gain knowledge and skills by
working for an extended period of time to investigate and respond to an authentic,
engaging, and complex question, problem, or challenge [12].
According to Cocco [13], project-based learning is a student-centred form of instruc-
tion, which is based on three constructivist principles: learning is context-speciﬁc, learn-
ers are involved actively in the learning process and they achieve their goals through
social interactions and the sharing of knowledge and understanding.
We use this method for developing student presentation skills in English. This app-
roach is applied for students receiving their Bachelor’s degrees in Chemical Engineering,
and then to the same students who continued their study and got Master’s degrees. To
implement this approach to the educational process, we developed the project task in
such a way as to combine students’ training in Bachelor’s and Master’s programs. The
project task was carried out by students with the support of professors from Foreign
Language Department and engineering departments of the University. At the end of the
course students presented their results in English both at Bachelor’s and Master’s levels
of education.
Decided on the project-based learning as the best method for our engineering stu-
dents, we pay attention to developing presentation skills. As the world has become
digital, the young generation, actually, has no difﬁculties using technologies in their
lives or studies; sometimes they even can help their university professor with that. So,
presentations skill development has been chosen as a way to master or improve their
foreign language skills and abilities.
3
Developing Presentation Skills of Bachelor’s Degree Students
At the ﬁrst and second years of Bachelor’s degree programs at English classes we usu-
ally have the topics closely connected with country studies and everyday communication

211
skills or real-life situations. We acquaint our students with the English-speaking coun-
tries, their customs and traditions, educational system, holidays and pastime. In this case
our students make several presentations on the following themes:
• English-speaking countries. Students search for information about the country, speak
about its geographical position, history, economics, education, climate, ﬂora and
fauna, interesting facts and traditions and landmarks.
• Etiquette of a country. This task supposes presenting the information about the traits,
habits of country residents and behavior rules (so-called do’s and don’ts). Though
students have some ideas about the country, some of the things can sound really
shocking, thrilling or funny. After the project according to the rules of behavior, we
can role-play the situation in order to memorize them.
• Universities of the world. Studying the educational systems of the English speaking
countries, engineering students make analysis and compare them to own educational
systems, share their thoughts about implementing different principles to the process
of education, and speak about pros and cons of each educational method.
All these tasks can be done individually or on a group.
However, to train students to present these topics in a proper way, a step-by-step
project task was developed.
The English language course starts with the study of presentation structure including:
• Introduction.
• Main body.
• Conclusions.
This structure is generally accepted as it allows the audience to understand the
main ideas of the presentation. According to this structure, students receive homework
assignments to prepare their ﬁnal project. They may be divided into several steps:
Step 1. In the introduction, a student is to greet the audience and present the topic of
the report. The ﬁrst slide of the presentation usually contains the title of the report, the
name of the speaker and his afﬁliation. At this stage of the teaching process, it is very
important to teach students to indicate the name of the university and the department in
which they study, as well as to indicate their names in English correctly. Students must
prepare the ﬁrst slide and present it to groupmates. The correctness of ﬁlling out the slide
is discussed by all students. This allows students to reinforce, what they have learnt and
prepare a template of the ﬁrst presentation slide for each student. In addition, students
are trained to introduce themselves in English presenting their majors, university and
department. They study English phrases for the presentation introduction.
Step 2. Students are to prepare the second slide of the presentation which focuses on the
outline of the report. Here students are to presents the main points of the report. The start
of the presentation should be bright, memorable and planned in such a way as to attract
the audience to the presentation and help the presenter adapt to the audience, thereby
setting a successful tone for the presentation. As a rule, this part of the presentation is

212
D. Giliazova and E. Valeeva
prepared when all other parts are completed. However, we need to train students to plan
the main points of the report and present them to the audience.
Step 3. Students start working on the main body of the presentation according to the
topic. It is the most complicated task and it takes more time than other homework
assignments. In this part of the educational process an English teacher pays attention to
the rules of presenting text and pictures in the slides. Students are to prepare this part of
the presentation and the report. The oral presentation should be made in such a way that
it is logically linked to each presentation slide.
Step 4. Students are to prepare the last slides of the presentation containing conclu-
sions and recapping of the main points. In this part of their project, students choose the
inspiration quotes of the great people, which reﬂect the main idea of the report.
At the end of these four steps students complete their presentations and are ready
to present their reports to the audience. Typically, mini-conferences are organized with
the participation of Bachelor’s students and professors. Such teaching method develops
skills of public reports and enhances English speaking practice.
Thus, we prepare students for presenting reports in English throughout the whole
semester, reinforcing the studied material through step-by-step tasks, which lead to the
development of the project.
4
Developing Presentation Skills of Master’s Degree Students
The English language course for Master’s degree students majoring in Chemical Engi-
neering contains the teaching module aimed at developing presentation skills, which are
connected with the Course developed for Bachelor’s degree students. During the Course
students are trained to present their research which they pursue for a Master’s degree.
The teaching module is divided into the following stages:
• Planning a scientiﬁc presentation.
• Designing the main presentation parts.
• Studying professionally-oriented English.
• Presenting a report.
Let us consider each stage separately.
Planning a presentation is the ﬁrst and the most important step in making a successful
report. It is important to choose the presentation topic and reveal it fully and carefully
for a speciﬁc audience. Our Master’s degree students are to choose topics related to
their majors or Master’s degree theses. They select the topic of the presentation together
with their research supervisors in order to foster the professionally oriented component
of teaching a foreign language. In addition, such approach allows a student to use this
presentation for defending a Master’s thesis or for the future study as a doctoral student.
To develop the skills of planning a scientiﬁc presentation by Master’s students, a
special task was developed. The task consists of a number of exercises, by performing
which a student makes up a plan for a future scientiﬁc project in the form of the following
points:

Project Based Learning Approach to Developing Presentation Skills
213
• Research aim;
• Research problem;
• Research questions;
• Experiment design;
• Data collection and analysis;
• Data interpretation;
• Conclusions;
• Future prospects.
These presentation elements repeat the main parts of experimental scientiﬁc articles
and the structure of scientiﬁc abstracts. Academic writing is one of the main skills which
is required for presenting research results in international journals by Master’s students.
The special attention is paid to the title of the presentation. It should be short and
reﬂect the main idea of the project in order to be comprehensive to the audience and at
the same time to grab the attention from the ﬁrst slide. Sanger and Ziyatdinova proposed
the special algorithm for formulating a successful name for a scientiﬁc project, on the
basis of which a special task was invented in the classroom in English [14].
Having planned the presentation, a student starts designing slides and preparing an
oral report in English. The latter is one of the most challenging parts of the project,
because it relates to the description of a research project in the ﬁeld of chemical engi-
neering. It contains scientiﬁc and engineering terminology for describing laboratory
facilities, physical and chemical parameters, technological processes and equipment.
The speaker should formulate the scientiﬁc and technical materials in such a way that
it is coherent and the audience becomes hooked. This part of the presentation is being
prepared jointly with a research supervisor of a Master’s students. The English teacher
acts here as a proofreader of the English text.
In order to make a scientiﬁc presentation simpler, it is necessary to use visual tech-
niques: pictures, graphs, tables, diagrams and ﬂowsheets. The less text on the slides, the
more successful your oral presentation will be. To present graphical and tabular informa-
tion,chemicalcompoundsandreactions,physicalandchemicalrelations,processparam-
eters of experimental installations and technological equipment, students must know the
stylistic and grammatical rules of technical English. To develop professionally-oriented
English communication skills, the study guide “How to Present a Research Project”
was created and published at the Department of Foreign Languages. The study guide
allows students to learn some aspects of technical English individually and improve their
presentations focused on research in the ﬁeld of chemical engineering.
The ﬁnal presentation of a scientiﬁc project is held in a large audience including
professors from the Department of Foreign Languages and engineering departments of
KNRTU. The following assessment criteria are used [15]:
• Independence of work on the project;
• The relevance, signiﬁcance and completeness of the topic disclosure;
• Presentation structure and slide design;
• Grammar and style of the English language;
• Question management;
• Scientiﬁc and engineering terminology;

214
D. Giliazova and E. Valeeva
• Artistry and expressiveness of the performance, appearance;
• Use of visual aids, technical means.
5
Conclusions
The project-based approach aimed at developing English communication skills have
successfully been implemented to the Foreign Language Course for Bachelor’s and
Master’s degree students majoring in Chemical Engineering.
Life-long learning has become an essential part of every educational system. And
our University is not an exception. We try to use different approaches, methods and tech-
niques to get our engineering students involved and fascinated during the class, to inspire
them in their current and future research. As a result of our work, we managed to connect
logically two levels of the university education for fostering the English language com-
munication skills of students at professional and academic levels. The interdisciplinary
cooperation of professors from engineering departments and the Department of Foreign
Language allowed us to foster both hard (professional, research) and soft (communica-
tive, critical thinking, creative) skills in the Foreign Language Course. This approach
has led to strengthening English communication skills of students, which was proved
by their higher scores at the end of the course. Moreover, the project based learning has
increased the interest of students in learning professionally focused English language.
At the Bachelor’s degree level of university education students learn to design pre-
sentations and make reports in public according to the Foreign Language Course con-
tent. The content is focused on the study of speech patterns and word combinations,
phrases, grammar and stylistic rules, country study and everyday communication skills
and activities.
Master’s degree level suggests the study of English terminology, advanced grammar
constructions and stylistic rules required for professional and academic communication.
The proposed approach plays a key role in the connection of these two levels of
the university education. It allows us to develop presentation skills in the framework of
lifelong learning. Moreover, students’ attempts while making presentations result in the
development of such skills as:
• Delivering a speech (monologue) to the audience in English;
• Enhancing conversation speech and question management in English;
• Creativity;
• Critical thinking;
• Searching for information in English;
• Analyzing and processing information;
• Designing presentation slides;
• Greeting and contacting the audience.
To sum up, we can surely say that the basis for the advanced study of a foreign
language for future chemical engineers during their Master’ degree program is required.
Such basis may be developed during Bachelor’s degree programs with the following
improvement of the foreign language communication skills.
