Integrating Sustainable Aspects to Robotic
Application and Its Impact on Course Design
in Human-Machine Interaction
Andrea Dederichs-Koch1(B) and Ulrich Zwiers2
1 FOM University of Applied Sciences, Essen, Germany
andrea.dederichs-koch@fom.de
2 Bochum University of Applied Sciences, Bochum, Germany
Abstract. The design of a course on human-machine interaction is based on
interactive cyber-physical systems, such as humanoid robots, and focusses on
the application of complex knowledge combining different disciplines such as
mechanical and electrical engineering and technical computer science. Thus, the
concept must provide not only the basics of human-machine interaction, but also
fundamentals of modelling, measuring and controlling. The functionalities of the
chosen interactive cyber-physical system should be easily accessible by possess-
ing a user-friendly software. For hands-on experience, the construction must be
robust, and complex interaction should be supported by signal processing tools.
Initially the humanoid NAO robot is chosen as learning tool, which provides a great
variety of interactive features, is easy to program, and possesses a motivational
design. As the course focusses on human-machine interaction the basic features
and functionalities also should be compared with an alternative robotic platform,
here the Robotis OP2 might be an alternative. So, in this contribution the chal-
lenges and opportunities of using different humanoid robotic platforms and their
impact on course design human-machine interaction with respect to sustainable
constraints are discussed.
Keywords: Human-machine interaction · Humanoid robot · Cyber-physical
system
1
Basic Considerations
Due to actual and future challenges, such as climate crisis or pandemic situation, engi-
neering education has to face the demands of not only developing technical skills but
also using scientiﬁc methods and complex knowledge in a reﬂective manner. Here the
application of problem-solving skills should be trained, applying to new constraints,
reﬂecting future impacts, especially sustainable aspects, such as long-term or resource
efﬁcient use of technical products [1–4]. Reﬂecting the own responsibility for shaping
technical products inﬂuences future socio-ecological impact, thus, these criteria must
be integrated in technical study course design and competence development should be
assessed using a holistic approach [5, 6]. Technical skills can be trained in design-
ing applications in human-machine interaction using cyber-physical systems, such as
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 216–226, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_22

Integrating Sustainable Aspects to Robotic Application
217
humanoid robots, which depict an ideal tool not only learning the different functional-
ities of the realized system but also thinking about e. g. social impacts. This approach
is already implemented und tested in different application course designs showing the
motivating effect of the humanoid NAO robot [7, 8]. Integrating sustainable aspects will
have an essential impact on course design. So, in this contribution, a brief overview of
an existing course concept on “Human-machine interaction” is outlined, before different
humanoid robotic platforms are reviewed with respect to sustainable aspects and holistic
competence assessment. Finally, the impact on the new course design and the evaluation
of developed competences using a typical application scenario are discussed.
1.1
Course Design “Technology of Human-Machine Interaction”
The course design “Technology of Human-Machine interaction” integrates different sci-
entiﬁc disciplines, mainly based on mechatronics, mechanical and electrical engineering
and technical computer science. In a ﬁrst approach the humanoid NAO robot is imple-
mented, and its interactive features ﬁt all requirements for the course design. By using the
virtual robot, it is also possible to integrate digital spaces into the course design support-
ing ﬂexible learning processes, both in terms of time and space. This additional digital
version leads to a higher quality for use of complex knowledge in interaction applica-
tion design and supports the real laboratory work leading to more efﬁcient interaction
application design and intensive learning processes [9].
The course design consists of different perspectives of human-machine interaction,
integrating digital tools, modelling static and dynamic behaviour in order to measure
and control the interactive cyber-physical system. Each course topic is divided into
several sub-categories, including project management and design speciﬁcations. In the
interdisciplinary-oriented course concept, students of different engineering disciplines
can participate, mainly mechatronics and mechanical and electrical engineering, but it
is also suitable for students of technical computer science or industrial engineering.
As activating learning methods the project- and scenario-based learning are used [10–
13]. The overall aim is that students develop within a working group an interactive
application scenario. They are encouraged to choose the particular subject of their own.
The number of group participants can differ due to the chosen scenario, and – wherever
possible – students of different disciplines should work together.
Due to the pandemic situation, parts of the course are being transformed to digital
space, not only enabling asynchronous learning but also providing the possibility for
students with handicaps to participate. It has also the effect that knowledge is preserved
digitally serving as common basis for future participants. To this end, the learning man-
agement tool Moodle is used providing learning videos within a structured learning
environment. In this context, the digital beginning of the course with theoretical input,
ofﬂine programming and project planning proves to be an efﬁcient approach towards
the design challenge, leaving plenty of time to rethink the user’s needs of the interaction
application, such as requirements engineering. This also builds the basis for the integra-
tion of gender and diverse aspects into the technical course design of human-machine
interaction. As the choice of the project subject is mandatory depending on the interests
of the participating students, the students have to think about designing an application for
the user’s needs, which leads to thinking about different perspectives and how it can be

218
A. Dederichs-Koch and U. Zwiers
realized through the technological functions of the robot system. On the other hand, the
free choice is motivating for the participants, but also shows insight views and interests of
the participating students. This leads to a great variety of the implemented applications:
the humanoid robot is used as a personal or ﬁtness trainer, playing cards or “tic tac toe”,
bringing beverage bottles, but it is also used as an assistive tool for disabled persons,
such as helping blind persons to ﬁnd things or assisting persons with autism spectrum
disorder. A correlation of statistical signiﬁcance between the study discipline and the
choice of the subject cannot be found yet, due to the limited number of participants and
available robots. So far however, experiences show that students of the engineering ﬁeld
do not often use the speech recognition and speech modelling tools of the robot, but
restrain themselves mainly to some keywords in order to control the robot’s functions.
Some participants focus their work on the mechanical construction and the possibilities
of constructive application such as climbing stairs.
1.2
Holistic Approach Integrating Sustainable Aspects
Inaholisticapproachforredesigningtheactualexistingcourseconceptnotonlytechnical
skills and competences should play an important role but also gender, diversity, socio-
economic constraints, and last but not least, particularly sustainability. This should not
also be discussed in an abstract manner but gaining experience by assessing concrete
technical products and their impact on environment, focusing repairability and long-term
and resource-efﬁcient use. Regarding these aspects the functionality, technical design
and applicability for the desired task is inevitable, measuring the development of multiple
competence by a holistic approach, integrating different perspectives [14].
Although the holistic model for developing and measuring multiple competence [15]
is used in vocational didactics, it may be adapted to engineering education, focusing on
the hands-on approach for practical training of engineers [16]. This holistic approach for
evaluating professional task solving processes comprises eight criteria. As robotic plat-
forms in human-machine interaction are not yet robust enough for commercial assistive
use, the criteria are adapted as follows:
– Functionality
– Technical Design
– Efﬁciency
– Process Orientation
– Gender and Diversity Aspects
– Sustainable Aspects
– Technological Impact Assessment
– Creativity.
Functionality and technical design depict the main criteria for the development of
functionalcompetence,efﬁciency,processorientationandgenderanddiverseaspectscan
be used to develop processual competence [17–20], sustainable aspects, technological
impact assessment and creativity are the criteria for the development of a holistic shaping
competence. For the design of complex interaction applications, the structure of knowl-
edge basis is crucial. Here, the four knowledge dimensions according to Bloom’s revised

Integrating Sustainable Aspects to Robotic Application
219
taxonomy are integrated in the holistic multiple competence development approach, that
distinguishes between factual, conceptual, procedural and meta-cognitive knowledge
[21]. Through the realization of interaction applications the participants of the study
course show which level of knowledge they have reached and how they have developed
their individual competence by integrating the different criteria in the presented solution.
The qualitative rating ranges are determined between not fulﬁlled, not rather fulﬁlled,
rather fulﬁlled to completely fulﬁlled. In order to visualize the assessment, the rating is
numerically normed.
1.3
Choice of Robotic System Under Sustainability Aspects
Regarding the course design and measurement of multiple competences, the choice of the
employed robot platform is crucial. Besides the functional components, the design and
outer appearance play an important role in order to support and motivate the participants
to acquire the complex knowledge of human-machine interaction, such as for the design
of assistive functions of robot interaction application. The actually used humanoid NAO
robot possesses a motivational design, is able to recognize emotions of the interacting
user and expresses emotion, i. e. it can interact in a social and intuitive manner. The
outer appearance and the construction and technical features are illustrated in Fig. 1.
Fig. 1. The humanoid NAO Robot [22–24].
The humanoid NAO robot’s size is about 58 cm, it has 25 degrees of freedom (2 in the
head, 5 in each arm, 1 in each hand, 5 in each leg and 1 in the pelvis) for ﬂuent movements,
it consists of a 1,91 GHz Processor Atom, quad core, 4 GB DDR3 RAM, 32GB SSD,
4 omnidirectional microphones and 2 loudspeakers, two 5 megapixels camera systems,
sonar, eight force sensitive resistors in the feet, an inertial system consisting of gyroscope
and accelerator sensory system and connectivity through bluetooth, ethernet-wiﬁ. The
camera system enables face detection and object recognition, the robot also provides
interactive concepts like the basic channel, basic awareness, autonomous life, language
processing including speech recognition, supporting more than 20 languages. Some
artiﬁcial components are also implemented such as a semantic engine, whereby the
robot is able to make some simple assertion through the dialogue system.
The project work with the humanoid NAO robot in the context of the course design is
suitable but there are some disadvantages, especially under the sustainable aspects. The

220
A. Dederichs-Koch and U. Zwiers
robot is hand-made, therefore every exemplar is unique, the construction is extremely
complex and fragile and gearing may be damaged by using and motion modelling.
Damages cannot be repaired easily and are cost-intensive. Also the inside construction
cannot be seen, that would be very interesting for engineering students to not only learn
about programming and static and dynamic stability but also about motor control for
complex motion modelling. These considerations lead to the question whether the robot
platform should be replaced by a more robust one, with similar features. The choice
is made to the humanoid Robotis OP2 of similar construction and height. Despite of
the fact of constructional similarity, the Robotis OP2 has different functionalities and
experimental work is supported by a different operating system, so the impact of the
course design has to be regarded and analyzed, especially due to sustainable aspects. Its
construction and technical design is illustrated in Fig. 2.
Fig. 2. The humanoid Robotis OP2 [25–27].
The ROBOTIS OP2 consists of 20 actuators, its size is about 46 cm with 20 degrees
of freedom, six degrees of freedom per leg, three per arm and two head movement, the
motor system enables gait velocity of 24 cm/s. The robot has a 1,6 GHz Dual Core Intel
Atom N 2600 microprocessor with 4 GB RAM, a Webcam mounted in the head for
computer vision, an inertial sensor system of a 3-axes-gyroscope and accelerator sensor
for movement control, a microphone for speech processing and the Lithium-Polymer-
Accumulator (1,8 Ah) enables about 30 min movement and intensive work.
Here the focus not only lies on the possibility of easy repairability, but also on the
possibility of changing the design of the robot outward appearance. Through additive
manufacturing technologies the robot’s shape can be changed, leading to a new subject in
the actual course design. In addition, the Robotis platform design is available in different
scalable types, such as Robotis Mini, which provides a greater variety to application of

Integrating Sustainable Aspects to Robotic Application
221
humanoid robots for human-machine interaction. The smaller Robotis Mini platforms
cost less so the resources can be extended, and constructive creativity can be integrated
into the course design with a greater variety of experimental work [28].
2
Interaction Application and Learning Scenario
The basic considerations depending on course design, development of competences and
choice of robotic platform lead to various designs of interaction applications yielding
to best practice learning scenarios using complex knowledge modelling. In robotics a
typical application for assistive function is the “Pick-and-Place”-Task [29, 30], based on
constructive elements, kinematic and dynamic modelling, integrating complex robotic
models such as visual servoing [31–33].
2.1
Modelling of “Pick-and-Place”-Task
In order to solve the “Pick-and-Place”-Task, the kinematic modelling process should
estimate the distance between the robot and the desired object, approaching and grasping
the object. The distance estimation and kinematic modelling for object grasping can be
realized by using the integrated camera and mathematical concepts for path planning
depending on the robot’s arm and hand construction. The modeling of grasping objects
using the humanoid NAO robot is illustrated in Fig. 3.
Fig. 3. Modeling of grasping an object with the humanoid NAO robot.
Due to the behavior model implemented on the robot, additional functions may be
realized to search various objects, estimate the orientation or verifying the success-
ful grasping of an object. In assistive scenarios it is also necessary to integrate object
recognition techniques using computer vision functions, or face recognition in order to
personalize the robotic functions. The realized model can be varied in scenarios that
depict real-life application. Such a scenario shows Fig. 4.
The “Pick-and-Place”-Task is realized in an application scenario in a more realistic
way. As an assistive robot, the humanoid NAO robot should take beverages from a
refrigerator, being embedded in a complex context with possible variation of constraints
due to the requirements of the interacting user. In this scenario the course participants
have to consider different realization options, regarding interaction components, such as
designing dialogues and reacting to different behavior of a user. Here the development

222
A. Dederichs-Koch and U. Zwiers
Fig. 4. Application Scenario of grasping an object with the humanoid NAO robot.
of shaping competence includes, besides functionality and technical design, gender and
diversity aspects and motivates for creative solutions. Efﬁciency and process orientation
can be observed during the implementation and realization processes. Sustainability and
technological impact assessment can be discussed theoretical in addition.
2.2
Redesign of Course Concept
The application scenario, as introduced, focuses on the functional and technical design
of the humanoid robot. In the learning scenario also the efﬁciency and process orienta-
tion can be assessed by monitoring the implementation of the work of the participants.
The gender and diversity aspects may be evaluated by the outer appearance, which is
designed user-friendly for both robot designs. Whereas the humanoid NAO robot cannot
be controlled exactly, especially in the case of grasping objects, the humanoid Robotis
OP2 has a robust motor control design, which has more accuracy and therefore may have
a better acceptance from male students. If the Robotis robot should be used for grasping,
a behavior model with different use of robotic hands, has to be implemented or, gripper
has to be mounted additionally. Here individual design is also applicable, realizing the
gripping tool with additive manufacturing (see Fig. 5).
The motor enables a simple opening and closing of a two-component gripper, which
can be individually designed. Through the motor control, objects that are complicated to
be grasped, such as a ball, can be easily picked as shown in the implementation scenario.
This leads to a more realistic application broadening the course concept to engineering
subjects such as technical drawing and construction.
2.3

Considering the selected robotic platforms and the possibilities in realization interaction
scenarios determined by the technical constraints leads to different speciﬁcation for the
multiple competence development. Each criteria is assessed in relation to technical and
interaction context and show the potential for developing multiple competence using the
different humanoid robots (see Fig. 6).

gramming functionalities and therefore supports efﬁciency and process orientation by

Technical constraints, creativity, combined with high support for sustainability are
showing a better applicability of the Robotis OP2. Depending on the interactive design
the Robotis system supports functionality, creativity and last but not least sustainability.
The robust constructive design leads to long-term use, adapting to individual robot
design by using new subject for engineering education. Integrating the new subjects of
designing and construction elements may lead to prolonging the course or reducing other
activities or shifting the core concept from programming to constructive activities. Here
it is important, whether students of technical computer science have enough knowledge
to apply technical design. This has to be taken into account by interdisciplinary group
work, integrating and focusing on process orientation and leading to typical situation
in professional work. Also, sustainability will play a more and more important role

Summary and Acknowledgement
In this contribution the course concept of “technology of human-machine interaction”
based on the interactive cyber-physical system, using the humanoid NAO robot, is ana-
lyzed due to a change of the robotic platform, using the Robotis OP2. The scenario-based
and project-oriented course design may also be realized by the different robotic plat-
form, validated through an approach, based on multiple competence model of vocational
didactics, adapted to engineering education, focusing sustainable aspects in combina-
tion with functionality, technical impact assessment and creativity. Here the potential not
only lies on a more sustainable approach and long-term usability of the robotic platform,
but also allows a more deeper competence development in order to strengthen students
of engineering disciplines to face future challenges.
The basic correlations were elaborated in a study work project from these highly
motivated students: Georg Reich, Felix Bennor, Arthur Sittek, Andreas Koehler, Amine
Rahou, Lisa-Marie Häfner, thanks for the inspiring idea and motivation on experimental
work.

Backup Systems for Solar Energy

Abstract. Challenge based learning is an essential characteristic of the
new educational model at Tecnol´ogico de Monterrey. Courses and work-
shops are oriented towards the solution of worldwide challenges such as
mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions. The present study was performed
during a one-week workshop where students are fully immersed on the
solution of a particular challenge. This work is focused on the analysis
of thermal energy storage devices for solar energy harvesting. Students
were asked to analyze a backup system based on phase change materi-
als. The goal was to determine the eﬀects of energy density and heat
transfer rates on the costs and amortization times of the backup system.
Students were organized in teams consisting of 5 members. Each team
developed a backup system and oﬀered oral presentations at the end of
the workshop. Teams presented the estimated costs, amortization times
and conclusions regarding the economic viability of the project.
Keywords: Challenge based learning · Educational innovation ·
Higher education · Professional education
1
Introduction
The new educational model of Tecnol´ogico de Monterrey is focused on Challenge
Based Learning, and there has been an intensive eﬀort to redesign undergraduate
courses during the last six years. The main goal of the new educational model
is to address most of the learned topics covered in a particular course into the
solution of realistic situations. During the fall semester of 2015, this idea was
tested through pilot workshops of one week long, where freshmen students were
fully immersed for the purpose of ﬁnding solutions to real life problems. Three
pilot workshops were focused on the following problems during the fall semester
of 2015: Logistics and inventory models, the Goldberg machine and electric gen-
eration through wind turbine without ﬁns and using piezoelectric materials [1].
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 227–238, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_23

F. Yescas-Mart´ınez et al.
The educational strategy is known as innovation week and has been implemented
in Tecnol´ogico de Monterrey since 2015. In this work, we present the results of the
implementation of this idea on a group of 25 senior students who were involved
in a more advanced project during the fall semester of 2021. Students were pre-
sented with a nonlinear heat transfer problem that involves ﬁrst order phase
transitions, also known as the Stefan problem, to determine the heat storage
capacity of phase change materials (PCMs) applied to thermoelectric generation
in concentrating solar power (CSP) plants. The modeling of PCMs used in ther-
mal energy storage (TES), involves the usage of more advanced heat transfer
theory and numerical techniques than oﬀered through conventional courses for
senior students of Mechanical and Chemical engineering.
The goal of this work is twofold, on the one hand, enhance and deepen the
understanding of heat transport theory of senior students of Mechanical and
Chemical engineering through the solution of nonlinear problems with appeal-
ing applications. On the other hand, to create awareness on the technological
challenges currently faced by highly intermittent renewable energies. The major
diﬃculty encountered in thermoelectric generation through CSP, is related with
daily and seasonal variations of solar irradiance in a given location. Weather
variations decrease signiﬁcantly the capacity of clean energy usage, which in
solar plants can be as low as 20% [2]. Electric generation during periods of low
solar irradiance in some cases, is supported through hydrocarbon based backup
systems. Examples of this type of backups can be found in private electric gen-
erators in Mexico, where the percentage of daily clean energy generation is only
12.5% and backup systems based on natural gas and diesel provide the remaining
87.5% of the generation [3]. In this work, some of the research results on liquid-
solid phase transitions at constant pressure recently obtained by the authors,
were shared with a group of 25 students. The group was presented with the
challenge of applying these ﬁndings, into the analysis of TES for the design of
low carbon footprint backup systems.
2
Phase Change Model, Investment Costs and
Amortization Times
Students were presented with a mathematical model that is based on the Stefan
problem, which is involved with the dynamics of phase transitions in the con-
ductive regime. The application of thermal storage in this work, is focused on
backup systems based on phase change materials, for thermoelectric generation
during periods of low solar irradiance. The students used a heat balance integral
method (HBIM) to ﬁnd approximate solutions to the temperature ﬁeld in each
phase and to solve the equations of motion for the liquid-solid interface position
and volume of the PCM. The application is focused on CSP plants, where salts
are used as PCMs with high melting temperatures for generation of superheated
steam.

2.1
Phase Change Model
The system considered in this work consists of a PCM layer of thickness xs(t) and
cross section A, with a liquid-solid front at some position x(t). The simpliﬁed
model assumes that the temperature is uniformly distributed throughout the
inner and outer surface of the PCM layer. The problem becomes one-dimensional
and the phase transition takes place in the conductive regime. The assumptions
mentioned above were used by the students to apply a previously established
model by the authors of this work, and that takes into consideration the volume
changes of a PCM during the melting or solidiﬁcation process [4]. The equations
of motion for the interface position and layer thickness used by the students,
were obtained through a local energy balance at the interface and imposing
mass conservation. Students were able to follow Ref. [4] in order to demonstrate
that x(t) obeys the following equation of motion:

Heat Balance Integral Method. Students were asked to follow Ref. [4] for the
implementation of the HBIM in Matlab. Workshops were oﬀered to the students,
where the statement of the problem given by Eqs. (1)–(3), and the HBIM along
with its implementation in Matlab, was described in two sessions of two hours.
The HBIM used by the students in this work, consisted of assuming quadratic
temperature distributions in each phase, as follows:
Tℓ(x, t) = aℓ(t) (x −x(t)) + bℓ(t) (x −x(t))2 + Tm for 0 ≤x ≤x(t), and
Ts(x, t) = as(t) (x −x(t)) + bs(t) (x −x(t))2 + Tm for x(t) < x ≤xs(t), (4)

230
F. Yescas-Mart´ınez et al.
where Tm is the melting temperature of the PCM. The time dependent coef-
ﬁcients ai(t) can be expressed in terms of the coeﬃcients bi(t), through the
boundary conditions, and the coeﬃcients bi(t) are found through the solution
of the model shown by Eqs. (1)–(3). The dynamics of the phase change process,
was solved through the following isothermal boundary conditions:
Tℓ(0, t) = Tmax,
Tℓ(x(t), t) = Ts (x(t), t) = Tm, and
Ts (xs(t), t) = Tmin.
(5)
Here, the inner surface of the PCM (left boundary) is subjected to a maximum
temperature Tmax which for this simpliﬁed boundary condition, represents the
temperature of superheated steam when the PCM is in the melting process. The
lowest temperature is represented by Tmin, which corresponds to the tempera-
ture of the outer boundary at x = x(t) (right boundary) and is the interface
between the solid PCM and the surrounding air. The coeﬃcients aℓ(t) and as(t)
can be expressed in terms of bℓ(t) and bs(t), by substitution of the boundary
conditions given above, in Eq. (4). The temperature proﬁles given by Eq. (4)
satisfy by construction, the isothermal boundary condition at the position of
the liquid-solid interface x(t). The heart of the method consists on substitut-
ing the approximate temperature proﬁles given by Eq. (4) after applying the
boundary conditions, in the equation of motion for x(t) and the heat equation
in each phase. Finally, the heat equation is integrated over the domain of each
phase, and students were able to obtain a set of ordinary diﬀerential equations
(ODEs) in time for bℓ(t) and bs(t). The HBIM is able to reduce the system of
partial diﬀerential equations given by Eqs. (1)–(3) to a system of four ODEs
for the dynamical variables x(t) and xs(t), and the coeﬃcients bℓ(t) and bs(t).
The set of ODEs was solved numerically by the students through a fourth order
Runge-Kutta method.

2.2
Investment Costs and Amortization Time
One of the goals of this work was to create awareness on a group of senior
undergraduate students on the current challenges that can be faced by highly
intermittent renewable energies, such as the solar energy used in CSP plants. The
capacity factor of solar plants is limited to a maximum of 20% due to the high
intermittency of solar irradiance during a 24 h period [2]. The need of backup
systems free of greenhouse gas emissions constitutes a key element to improve
the performance of solar plants. Based on the mathematical model used in this
work, students were asked to estimate the investment costs of a PCM based
backup system and the amortization time of these costs. Investment costs of
backup systems were obtained by considering the surface of the heliostat ﬁeld
and PCM market prices needed to harvest the solar energy during the hours
of highest solar irradiance. The stored energy is then used for thermoelectric
generation during periods of low solar irradiance. Cost estimation is highly cor-
related with the demand of electrical energy, weather conditions and seasonal

232
F. Yescas-Mart´ınez et al.
variations of solar irradiance. Weather data during the month of August of 2021
and close to Avelardo Rodr´ıguez in Tijuana, Mexico, was obtained from the
National Weather Service of Mexico (NWS). A constant demand of 400 MW of
electrical energy was assumed, and is based on the average demand close to the
hydroelectric plant of Pe˜nitas in the state of Chiapas. The students did not take
into account the seasonal variations of solar irradiance since one week for data
curation and analysis was not enough. Nevertheless, the students were able to
obtain a maximum of solar energy harvesting, since the site chosen is one of the
locations in Mexico with the highest solar irradiance during the summer season.

available solar irradiance and a 24 h period. The total mass of PCM needed to
satisfy the daily demand is given by:
MPCM = No. of Units (ρℓx(ts) + ρs (xs(ts) −x(ts))) A,
(14)
where A = 1 m2 is the cross sectional surface of a PCM unit, x(ts) is the interface
position at time ts, and xs(ts) is the position of the outer boundary at t = ts.
The investment cost related to the backup system is obtained by using market
prices for the PCMs considered and the total mass estimated through the last
equation. In this work, the amortization time is deﬁned as the time period needed
to cover the investment cost in thermal storage units. This time period was
estimated by the students, through the cost of several fossil fuels such as: natural
gas, carbon, diesel, etc., needed to satisfy the daily demand by a conventional
thermoelectric plant and during the periods of low solar irradiance. The daily
costs of fossil fuel consumption were calculated using international market prices
and the amortization time was obtained as follows:
tamort =
UCPCM MPCM
UCfossil (1 −PC) T (Daily Demand in Watts) /η ,
(15)
where UCPCM is the cost of a unit mass of 1 kg of PCM in US Dollars and UCfossil
is the cost per unit of energy of hydrocarbon in US Dollars. The numerator of
Eq. (15) represents the total cost of the backup system and the denominator
is the daily cost of fossil fuel needed to satisfy the demand during the periods
of low solar irradiance. In this work, students assumed that the energy conver-
sion eﬃciency of the steam turbine used in a CSP plant and a conventional
thermoelectric plant is the same.
3
Results and Discussion
In this section, the results and conclusions of the students will be presented.
Students were organized in teams of ﬁve members and each team was required
to provide a set of solutions to the problem of TES and conclusions on its lim-
itations. The ﬁrst two days of the week, students were given an introductory
workshop on the assumptions, heat transport theory in the conductive regime,

234
F. Yescas-Mart´ınez et al.
the mathematical model for the Stefan problem in ﬁnite systems and the HBIM
used to ﬁnd an approximate set of solutions. The next two days of the week,
students were given brief lectures on ideas about estimating the investment costs
and amortization times, where these costs are correlated with the numerical solu-
tions to the mathematical model. The last day, students were able to make a
20 min presentation on their understanding of the heat transfer theory used in
this project, their results and conclusions. The model presented in the previous
section was used to estimate the thermal energy absorbed considering two types
of PCMs: an eutectic salt and Aluminum. Figure 1 shows the Matlab code imple-
mentation of the HBIM developed by some of the students and the numerical
solutions obtained for the time evolution of the thermal energy stored.
Fig. 1. Example of Matlab codes used by students with the implementation of the
HBIM and their results for the thermal energy absorbed.
Figure 2 is an illustration of the diﬀerence in thermal energy stored between
the eutectic salt and Aluminum. The students were able to observe that Alu-
minum has two major advantages. On the one hand, heat transfer rates are sig-
niﬁcantly improved due to the higher thermal conductivity of Aluminum and on
the other hand, latent heat storage capacity is enhanced since metals or metallic
alloys have a higher enthalpy of formation Lf than common salts. The rate of
energy transfer is signiﬁcantly improved by using metallic alloys, and students
were able to capture this behavior through their implementation of the mathe-
matical model as illustrated in Fig. 2. Students were given some references with
experimental values of the relevant thermodynamic properties [5,6]; but, they
were free to search for other salts or metals to perform their analysis. Students
were aware that metallic alloys, still constitute a major challenge in this type

Challenge Based Learning
235
of applications due to their high melting temperatures and corrosive properties
that bring diﬃculties into their conﬁnement for usage in ultra high temperature
applications [7].
Fig. 2. Solutions obtained by one team of students for the thermal energy absorbed
when a) Aluminum and b) the NaNO3/KNO3 salt, are used as the PCM.
Investment costs and amortization time estimations performed by students
are shown in Table 1. This table illustrates the diﬀerence between costs and
amortization times when the eutectic salt or Aluminum is selected as the PCM.
The advantage of using Aluminum as a PCM, is that heat transfer rates are
enhanced due to higher thermal conductivities and this has a major impact on
the investment costs. The higher thermal conductivity of Aluminum decreases
charging times, and the result found by some of the students is that a unit of
Aluminum is almost able to reach the steady state (fully charged) in a period of
6 h, whereas a unit of salt takes approximately 600 h to reach its steady state,
as illustrated in Fig. 2. Table 1 also shows the maximum and minimum cost
obtained by the students and for each PCM considered, according to the day
with lowest and highest solar irradiance in the location of study.
Finally, the last day of the week, students made presentations based on their
numerical results as illustrated in Fig. 3. Based on the concluding remarks made
by students and a survey that was performed at the end of the project, it was
found in this work, that some students improved their understanding of heat
transport theory applied to heat storage applications. Additionally, the project
had a partial eﬀect on the perception about the limitations of renewable energies

of intermittent nature. The survey shown in Fig. 4 depicts the students percep-
tion on the following aspects: improvement of heat transfer theory understanding
(Understanding), perspective change on the cost of clean intermittent energies
(Perspective Change), worldwide need to migrate from greenhouse gas emissions
to more clean energies in spite of investment costs (Migration), technology chal-

According to the survey results shown in Fig. 4, only 40% of the students
think that this project changed their overall perspective on the real costs of
intermittent clean energies; however, almost 85% of them were able to realize on
the limitations and challenges of this technology. Regardless of the technological
challenges that the world is facing on TES applications, which is acknowledged

Challenge Based Learning
237
by most of the students in this group, this study had a limited impact on the stu-
dents perspective on the real costs. Almost all of the students in this study group,
are convinced that migration to this type of technology is needed, regardless the
costs, future challenges and low energy densities. The result is in agreement with
the projections of the US Energy Information Administration [8] on the future
renewable energy generation. Finally, only half of the students believe that their
understanding on heat transport theory was improved through this project. The
last result could be explained since most students, had taken or were enrolled
at the time of this study, in the Heat Transfer course for Mechanical Engineers
oﬀered at Tecnol´ogico de Monterrey.
Fig. 4. Survey results related to the students perception on their change of perspective,
improvement of their understanding on the subject, worldwide need of migration to
more clean energies, technology challenges and low energy density storage.
4
Conclusions
In this work, almost 50% of students think that were able to improve their under-
standing of heat transport theory and apply this knowledge to the analysis of
current worldwide problems such as mitigation of greenhouse gases. Students
believe that the time invested in this workshop was not enough to gain under-
standing on the study of liquid-solid phase transitions applied to TES. Most
students had taken a conventional course of heat transfer, previous to this work-
shop; however, they had some diﬃculties into understanding how the equation
of motion for the interface position is related to mass conservation. Additionally,
they were not able to fully understand all the assumptions used in this project.
Students did not realize for example, that equations of motion are only valid
when the phase change is close to thermodynamic equilibrium, and how this
aﬀects the rate at which thermal energy is absorbed. Students; however, were

238
F. Yescas-Mart´ınez et al.
able to implement the HBIM and applied this semi-analytical method to make
their predictions. The HBIM is not covered in conventional courses of heat trans-
fer and although is more conceptual than ﬁnite diﬀerent methods, it is easier to
implement in software that uses symbolic mathematics. This project had a mod-
erate eﬀect on the students perception of highly intermittent energies; however,
students learned that a solar plant capacity is limited by daily and seasonal vari-
ations of solar irradiance, heat transfer rates and energy density of materials.
Most students believe that these limitations represent technological challenges in
the future of intermittent renewable energies, such as improving energy densities
of materials. Finally, and in spite of the evident disadvantages of this technology,
students believe that migration to more clean energies is needed, regardless of
the economical costs.

The Role of Group Project-Based Learning
in Engineering Training
Svetlana Karstina(B)
Karagandy University of the Name of Academician E.A. Buketov, 28, Universitetskaya Street,
Karaganda 100028, Kazakhstan
skarstina@mail.ru
Abstract. Reforming education, changing its role and priorities, stimulating sci-
entiﬁc research and innovation has led to the need to ﬁnd new models of engineer-
ing training. In these conditions group project-based learning for both students
and engineering teachers seems to be promising. With this in mind, the purpose
of this paper is to analyze the speciﬁcs of group project-based learning in engi-
neering training and to develop a toolkit for building a graduate proﬁle based
on assessments of various key stakeholders. The paper analyzes the opinion of
experts, the results of questionnaire survey and interviewing of teachers and stu-
dents of engineering specialties of universities and colleges in different regions
of Kazakhstan about the role of group project-based learning in the integration
of engineering educational programs with industry, the results of students’ self-
assessment of their competencies and skills formed in the process of learning.
The results of students’ self-assessment and expert assessment ranking allowed
to identify ﬁve main groups of competencies. Groups 1 and 2 contain interdis-
ciplinary competences, group 3 - organizational competences, self-reﬂection and
control competences, professional and didactic competences, group 4 includes
mainly communication and teamwork competences, group 5 - information and
analytical competences. The approach used in the work allows highlighting those
competences and skills which are underdeveloped within the educational pro-
gram. The good correlation between the results of students’ self-assessment of
their formed competences and skills in the process of group project-based learn-
ing and the results of expert assessment allows us to consider the method of group
project-based learning effective and reliable in maintaining educational goals and
achieving the best results in engineers’ training. The application of the organiza-
tional forms, methods, and tools of group project-based learning proposed in the
article allowed us to propose a model of graduate proﬁle creation adapted to the
constantly changing requirements for specialists’ qualiﬁcations and gradation of
their skills.
Keywords: Engineering education · Project-based learning · Skills and
competencies
The work was performed within the framework of the international project 598506-EPP-1-2018-
1-PT-EPPKA2-CBHE-JP ENTER “Engineering educators pedagogical training”, co-ﬁnanced by
Erasmus + program of the European Union.

1
Introduction
In the modern world many countries have taken a course to reform education, change
its role and mission, prioritize training of engineering and technical personnel, promote
scientiﬁc research and innovation, take systemic measures to create knowledge-intensive
economy. In this connection the higher education institutions are faced with the task of
choosing the model of engineering specialist training, which is adequate to the changes
taking place [1–4]. This model should provide participation of universities in network
communities, personalized and hybrid learning environment, active involvement of stu-
dents in the learning process, promote technological entrepreneurship and innovative
activity of teachers and students [5]. Group project-based learning can become an impor-
tant element of such a model. The implementation of group project-based learning in
university educational programs is focused on 1) solving innovative engineering prob-
lems, 2) developing students’ skills in engineering risk management, forecasting results,
applying engineering technologies in the context of the performed project, 3) integrating
knowledge from different ﬁelds of science, technology and engineering, 4) systematiz-
ing basic foundations of engineering activities, 5) developing conceptual, technical and
critical thinking, skills to assess market and social signiﬁcance of innovative projects,
etc. This approach will allow students to learn how to analyze project tasks in terms
of modern trends and engineering achievements, determine strategic goals, objectives,
applied signiﬁcance of the project, assess the prospects of using its results, see the inter-
disciplinary nature of the problem, ﬁnd and justify ways to solve it, apply methods of
creative solutions of complex, ambiguous, weakly structured problems.
In order to organize project-based learning in higher education institution a ﬂexi-
ble, varied, comfortable educational environment should be created, which will provide
students and teachers with access to external and internal educational resources, search,
analysis and synthesis of information, its processing and making innovative decisions,
working out students’ professional skills [6]. The learning process in group project-based
learning can combine blended learning, virtual interaction, project work, synchronous
counseling, additional training.
The principle of “challenge-competence” [7] can be put in the basis of the edu-
cational process organization, which allows complex development of skills and com-
petences necessary for future professional activity through interdisciplinary commu-
nication and transdisciplinary learning, system of internal and external evaluation of
educational programs’ content and training quality. At the same time, the efﬁciency
of project-based group learning implementation largely depends on teachers’ readiness
to apply not only modern educational technologies, pedagogical science achievements,
but also relevant scientiﬁc achievements and innovations in the ﬁeld they teach [8]. It
means that modern engineering pedagogues should be in the process of constant self-
development and learning, experience exchange, practical improvement and reﬂection.
The teacher should be ready to ensure sustainable relationship between educational and
future professional activity of a student, identify and eliminate barriers to effective inter-
action of all team members, create innovative learning scenarios, apply various learning
management strategies, use effective assessment tools. In accordance with this, the aim
of the work is to analyze the features of group project-based learning application in
engineering training and to develop a toolkit for graduate proﬁle formation based on the

The Role of Group Project-Based Learning in Engineering Training
241
assessments of various key stakeholders. The research objectives included 1) analysis
of experts’, trainees’ and teachers’ opinions on the role of group project-based learning
in integration of engineering educational programs with industry; 2) selection of effec-
tive and reliable tools that should allow supporting educational objectives and achieving
better results in engineers’ training.
2
Methods of Research
The analysis of experts’ opinions, results of questionnaire survey and interviewing of
teachers and engineering students in universities and colleges of different regions of
Kazakhstan, results of students’ self-assessment of their competences and skills formed
in the process of group project-based learning have been carried out in the paper. The
total number of students participating in the survey is 588 people, teachers, employees
of enterprises and experts - 49 people.
In addition, 45 university teachers of engineering disciplines were involved as experts
in the application of group project-based learning methods. Among them 63.2% were the
trainees of the module “Problem-oriented, practice-oriented, project-oriented learning”
developed within the international project ENTER, 15.8% were the trainees of other
professional development programs on similar topics. The qualitative composition of
the experts was as follows: 75.6% of the teachers had more than 10 years of experience
in scientiﬁc and pedagogical activity, 17.8% had 5 to 10 years of experience, and 67%
had less than 10 years of experience. At the time of the survey 28.9% of teachers regularly
used problem-oriented, practice-oriented, project-oriented learning, 66.7% - sometimes
used these methods within individual disciplines, training modules, courses, etc. The
teachers’ self-assessment of their readiness to apply group project-based learning in
professional and pedagogical activity is presented in Fig. 1.
1
2
3
4
5
Fig. 1. Teachers’ self-assessment of their readiness to use group project-based learning in pro-
fessional and pedagogical activity: 1 - completely ready, 2 - requires additional theoretical
and/or professional training (self-training), 3 - requires additional assessment of administrative,
organizational, resource capabilities, 4 - not ready, 5 - ready, but not planning to use.

S. Karstina
As we can see from Fig. 1 24,4% of teachers are completely ready for group project
learning application in their professional and pedagogical activity; 44,4% of teach-
ers consider additional theoretical or practical training (self-training) necessary; 26,7%
of teachers consider it necessary to evaluate additional administrative, organizational,
resource opportunities; 4,5% of teachers are either not ready for group project learning
application or do not plan its application in their professional activity. Thus, it can be
considered that the choice of the expert group to analyze the application of group project-
based learning in engineering training is justiﬁed. The categories of answers in the ques-
tionnaire were varied between rating scales, single and multiple choice, open-ended
answers. When analyzing the results of the questionnaire, the methods of qualitative
analysis, assessment of weighted average indicators and ranking of assessed indicators
described in detail in [9] were used. The conducted analysis of the expert group partici-
pants’ opinions on the readiness to use group project-based learning in professional and
pedagogical activities allows to plan some steps for further research that will allow to
revise the content of theoretical and/or professional training programs for engineering
teachers, to determine the criteria for assessing administrative, organizational, resource
capabilities of the university and partner enterprise for joint implementation of group
project-based learning.
3
Research Results
The method of group project-based learning should contribute to the development of
students’ intercultural competences, social skills, teamwork skills, self-management
and emotional self-management [10]. These competences are in high demand among
employers and provide the university graduate with quick social and professional adap-
tation. At the same time, the application of group project learning allows increasing
cognitive activity of a student, creating conditions for creativity and critical thinking.
The choice of problems analyzed in the group project work should be based on the iden-
tiﬁcation and consideration of students’ interests, prospects for their future professional
activity, professional interest, take into account the social and professional context. The
goal of the project should be formulated based on the student’s needs and vision. When
solving a project problem, a student needs to learn how to transform the theoretical
knowledge obtained into practical activities, the end result of which will be a speciﬁc
innovative product. To achieve this, the instructor should propose various innovative
learning scenarios, manage the learning process and analyze its results, choose appro-
priate evaluation and feedback methods, use modern educational and information and
communication technologies.
According to the analysis of experts’ opinions, in order to achieve the goals and
learning outcomes when using group project-based learning it is necessary to provide:
prevalence of practical classes over theoretical ones, continuous professional practice
of students at the basic enterprises, application of training equipment similar to the
real production, demand for the results of student projects, high motivation of students
to perform project work, high level of student’s independence, interdisciplinarity, on-
the-job training, project assignments at real production sites, additional professional
training modules to ﬁll in the missing knowledge, corporate culture, communication and

The Role of Group Project-Based Learning in Engineering Training
243
teamwork, orientation to the result (its applicability in future), getting initial professional
experience, adaptation to professional activity.
The basis for the implementation of group project-based learning should be real
professional tasks, the complexity of which increases from course to course, taking into
account the speciﬁcs of individual, group, collective professional activity, integration of
knowledge, methods from different areas of science and practice, search for solutions
of socially formulated practical problems from the sphere of professional activity.
Based on the analysis of experts’ opinions on the role of group project-based learn-
ing in the integration of engineering educational programs with industry, the following
conclusions can be made. Volunteer movement, professional practice and on-the-job
training of students, implementation of dual education and joint training programs, tar-
geted training of specialists by the employer’s order, joint social, scientiﬁc and educa-
tional projects of university and enterprise, establishment of basic departments at the
proﬁle enterprises, mentorship and tutorship development, participation of enterprises
in specialized training laboratories creation at universities, in the ﬁeld of engineering
education, and in the ﬁeld of engineering education are the key to successful integration
of engineering educational programs with the industry.
When evaluating the criteria for selecting the target audience for group project-based
learning, the experts identiﬁed the following: students focused on work at a particular
company or studying in dual education programs, with high academic performance and
theoretical base in the core disciplines, high motivation for project and research activities,
ready for teamwork, proactive, communicative.
At the same time, it was of interest to analyze the results of students’ self-assessment
of competencies and skills formed in the process of group project-based learning and
compare them with the requirements of experts. For this purpose, students were asked
to give a grade for each item in the list of 23 competencies on a ﬁve-point scale, where
1 corresponds to the lowest grade, 5 corresponds to the highest grade. After that, the
average grade for each competency and the range of grade indicator changes were calcu-
lated. The resulting range was divided into ﬁve equally sized groups. Then, the analyzed
competencies and skills were divided into groups. The ﬁrst group included competences
and skills with the lowest assessment of students, the ﬁfth group included competences
and skills with the highest assessment. Accordingly, between the ﬁrst and ﬁfth groups
were placed competencies and skills with intermediate scores. As a result of our ranking
we have included interdisciplinary competences (social, psychological, intercultural and
normative-ethical competences) into groups 1 and 2, organizational (management) com-
petences, self-reﬂection and control competences, professional-didactic competences
into group 3. Group 4 includes communication and teamwork competences. Group 5
includesinformationalandanalyticalcompetences.Thedistributionofcompetenciesand
skills obtained by students into groups is relatively homogeneous in content and allows
highlighting those which have not been sufﬁciently developed in the framework of the
educational program. A similar approach was used in ranking of expert assessments.
The results of the ranking are presented in Table 1.
As can be seen from Table 1, the opinion of students and experts in the third, fourth,
and ﬁfth groups coincide, and there are differences in assessing the importance of the
competents of the ﬁrst and second groups. In view of the obtained result, we can conclude

that group project-based learning in general allows providing training of engineering stu-

tant to pay more attention to the development of psychological and normative-ethical
competencies within the educational programs of engineering students’ training. At the
same time, the degree of deviation of students’ self-assessment results from the expert
assessment can be considered as an important indicator for updating the content of edu-

is original and can be used to create a graduate proﬁle taking into account constantly

competence ranking method in engineering training will allow universities and colleges
to ensure ﬂexibility of educational programs and eliminate the gap between acquired
competences of graduates and their readiness for professional activity and career.
4
Conclusions
Modern models of engineering training should provide regular monitoring of the quality
of specialists’ training, adjustment of educational programs based on expert assessments
of students’ competences formed in the process of training.
The application of organizational forms, methods and means of group project-based
learning proposed in the paper allowed us to propose a model of graduate proﬁle creation,
adaptive to constantly changing requirements to specialists’ qualiﬁcations and gradation
of their skills.
The method of ranking students’ competencies proposed in this paper can be used as a
tool to assess and compare the achievability of educational goals by different stakeholder
groups.
The good correlation between the results of students’ self-assessment of their formed
competences and skills in the process of group project-based learning and the results
of expert assessment allows us to consider the method of group project-based learning
effective and reliable in maintaining educational goals and achieving the best results in
engineers’ training.

The Role of Group Project-Based Learning in Engineering Training
245
The analysis of experts’ opinions on the readiness to apply group project-based learn-
ing in professional and pedagogical activity has revealed the problem of ﬁnding effective
tools to assess the content of theoretical and/or professional training programs for engi-
neering teachers and factors inﬂuencing their updating, administrative, organizational,
resource capabilities of the university and partner enterprise for joint implementation of
group project-based learning.

10. Tramontano, C., Grant, C., Clarke, C.: Development and validation of the e-Work Self-

Competence-Based Support for Project-Based
Learning in Virtual Settings
Nargiza Mikhridinova1,3(B)
, Bertha Joseph Ngereja2, Bassam Hussein2,
Wim Van Petegem3, Jose Ramon Otegi-Olaso4, and Carsten Wolff1
1 Fachhochschule Dortmund, Otto-Hahn-Str. 23, 44227 Dortmund, Germany
nargiza.mikhridinova@fh-dortmund.de
2 Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway
3 KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium
4 University of the Basque Country, Bilbao, Spain
Abstract. Project-based learning in higher education becomes more relevant and
job-ﬁeld-related if it is done in real, or at least realistic, project settings, e.g.
including speciﬁc team situations or case studies from companies. Such projects
are speciﬁcally valuable if they are conducted by internationally mixed student
teams, best case in interdisciplinary teams. Online participation can be both more
realistic and helpful in case physical mobility is not possible. Therefore, we are
conducting virtual projects with cross-border student teams. Selecting the right
projects and matching the right students with the relevant company cases is very
important for an effective and efﬁcient competence delivery. The project selection
based on the desired competence gain, the development of a meaningful sequence
of projects in order to implement an individual competence development path, the
estimation of the contribution of the projects to the desired competence proﬁle of
the student, and the implementation of the projects need to be supported by digital
tools and a virtual environment. This allows access to projects and company cases
from different countries and an international, cross-border learning experience –
best case in realistic interdisciplinary teams. This paper describes the concepts
and tools for this approach and their experimental analysis.
Keywords: Project-based learning · Virtual settings · Soft skills
1
Introduction
Conducting projects is an important element in higher education curricula – summarized
as project-based learning (PjBL, also called PBL which we do not use in order to avoid to
mix it up with problem-based learning). In engineering education, projects are expected
to deliver in addition to the technical competences also professional and global com-
petences which are particularly relevant in today’s working environments [1]. Projects
train such competences in a holistic, implicit way, delivering soft skills integrated into
typical engineering work. Project competence is important for engineering graduates.
Instead of teaching it in theoretical courses, such competences are delivered by doing
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 246–257, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_25

Competence-Based Support for Project-Based Learning
247
projects and creating relevant project situations [2]. Project situations and the selected
project cases for PjBL should be as close as possible to real world situations which can
be achieved either by doing the projects in real situations (work-integrated learning [3])
or by using real company cases in student’s projects [4].
In the research documented by this contribution we are investigating a speciﬁc area of
PjBL: cross-border projects which are conducted by internationally mixed student teams
in a fully virtual online setting, using the agile framework Scrum (see Sect. 5.1) which is
widely used in software industry for self-managed small teams of software developers.
The resulting learning settings are offering an interesting variety of project situations,
especially with respect to communication and collaboration [5]. These projects are very
relevant for the international Master’s programmes in project management, IT and engi-
neering which we are conducting within the “European Partnership for Project and
Innovation Management (EuroPIM)” [6]. While doing such projects [7] we found that
there is a lack of methodology for selecting project cases and forming the student teams
with respect to the intended learning outcomes, especially regarding the soft skills which
are trained by doing the projects. In this contribution we present the underlying concepts
for the forming of soft skills in projects based on a literature review. Furthermore, we
present our conceptual model for the selection of projects and team roles (supported
by personality tests) based on intended competence gains. This model was discussed
in a number of semi-structured interviews with experts and an experiment with virtual
cross-border student projects was conducted where students assess the methodology and
the learning experience, including a supporting digital tool.
2
State-of-the-Art
2.1
Competences, Soft Skills and Personality Traits
Considering the acquisition of soft skills through teamwork and learning experiences
connected with team collaboration and communication links the PjBL concept to the
professional world and future work situations of graduates which inherently leads to the
development of more complex competences [8]; by competence authors mean “knowl-
edge, know-how and knowledge to be”, which enables people to acquire and develop
skills at individual and professional level. In their conceptualization, [9] distinguish
between soft skills and competencies, where skills branching to soft and hard skills
belong to a higher construct as competencies. The authors highlight that development
of competencies and soft skills depends on interaction between individual traits like
personality and abilities as well as contextual factors.
Although various studies have deﬁned soft skills in different ways, there appears to
be consensus that individual personality play a major role in inﬂuencing soft skills. [10]
deﬁned soft skills as a combination of the abilities, attitudes, habits, and personality traits
that allow people to better perform in their workplace, complementing the technical skills
required to do their jobs and inﬂuencing the way they behave and interact with others.
Several factors can inﬂuence a person’s personality like individual attitudes, behavioral
habits, personality traits and their individual competences (abilities). The Big Five factor
model represents a broad set of traits that are a collection of many facets; these are (i)

248
N. Mikhridinova et al.
neuroticism, (ii) extraversion, (iii) agreeableness, (iv) openness to experience and (v)
consciousness [11].
2.2
Project Teams: Inﬂuence of Personality Traits and Team Roles
An individual’s attitude towards teamwork can inﬂuence the individual’s ability to work
in a team. Several studies have adopted the Big Five theory to investigate inﬂuence of
personality traits on teams [11–13]. [12] reported on correlations between personality
traits and team performance; similarly, [13] studied contribution of people factors to agile
software project success and concluded that societal culture and personal characteristics
of the team members can impact the overall capability of the team.
Team effectiveness is an important predictor of long-term, sustainable improvement
of team performance, and also reﬂects the level of effort and sustainability of teamwork
[14]. The author advocates the Belbin role theory to be considered in a combination with
personal characteristics to ensure effective teams are created. Another study [15] tested
the performance of student teams formed using Belbin’s model roles in comparison to
and self-selected teams, and found that Belbin teams performed signiﬁcantly better than
self-selected teams. In addition, members in the Belbin teams performed better in terms
of attendance, efﬁciency, higher interest for the subject at the end of the course, improved
interpersonal relationships and social skills. In our experiment, the assignment of team
roles is based on results of a Belbin test taken by the students (after forming the teams,
so the test is not used for assigning students to teams but only as a decision support for
assigning roles within the teams).
2.3
Developing Soft Skills in Practice: Project-Based Learning
People acquire soft skills by undergoing training or taking up courses related to a partic-
ular job or profession [16]; however, in higher education, providing students with project
assignments and proper supervision and guidance enables students to get necessary soft
skills; this is possible due to embedding of project tasks into real cases and actual envi-
ronment [17]. Therefore, such educational methodology as PjBL linking teaching with
professional environment is crucial for skills development [8]. Although PjBL differs
from problem-based learning (PBL), both learning approaches aim at improving stu-
dents’interdisciplinarycompetences[18].Engagementinproject-basedmodulesintends
changing a paradigm where students, by activating and developing their interpersonal
skills, become proactive problem solvers and critical thinkers [19].
3
Competence-Based Projects and Team Roles
3.1
Cross-Border Master’s Education in EuroPIM
The “European Partnership for Project and Innovation Management (EuroPIM)” [6]
is a consortium of 5 universities from the EU: Fachhochschule Dortmund, Germany,
University of the Basque Country (UPV/EHU), Bilbao, Spain, Norwegian University
of Science and Technology (NTNU), Trondheim, Norway, Kaunas University of Tech-
nology (KTU), Kaunas, Lithuania, and KU Leuven, Belgium (10 further universities

Competence-Based Support for Project-Based Learning
249
are associated). The consortium conducts Master’s programmes especially in IT, Project
Management and Engineering. One focus topic is the management of the digital transfor-
mation. The Master’s programmes are connected with a number of exchange and cooper-
ation formats, virtually and with physical mobility. Many formats use projects and PjBL
where one of the goals is the interdisciplinary, intercultural and international (3 × “i”)
mix of student teams. Cross-border projects are conducted using realistic cases and sce-
narios, also in cooperation with industry partners, which is also researched and evaluated
[7]. In the past years, the virtual, online collaboration and education gained signiﬁcant
relevance, so the cooperating Master’s programmes are called a “virtual cross-border
Master School”.
3.2
Conceptual Model for Project Selection
In order to support the implementation of realistic projects with industry in such a
virtual cross-border Master School, according to our research and experience, several
core methods and tools are required:
1. It is desirable that a student project with a company from one country can be done
by a virtual cross-border team with students and teachers from several countries by
using online collaboration and digital project tools and platforms. Such a learning
setting is very similar to many international projects in industry, using agile and
digital processes and tools. It trains inherently not only the technical competence but
also the professional and global competence of students. It requires an elaborated
cross-border IT infrastructure which was implemented and tested by EuroPIM in
the past, especially due to COVID. We call this cross-border digital learning and
teaching infrastructure a “Digital Education Ecosystems (DEE)” [20]. Apart from
cross-coupled learning management (Moodle, ILIAS) and collaboration (MS Teams,
Big Blue Button) systems with a cross-border identity and user management systems,
the DEE includes management apps (for students and teachers), ﬁle sharing and
collaboration tools, especially for conducting projects.
2. To ensure the desired learning outcomes, it is important to deﬁne the competence
proﬁle of the students before and after the project and their desired competence
proﬁle at the end of the educational programmes. Based on the type of the projects
and company cases and based on the learning setting and the composition of the
student team, a competence gain can be assumed which we try to determine.
3. In order to support students and teachers in selecting the right projects and in order
to map students to projects and company cases which are relevant for them, it is
important to provide a tool for planning the individual student journey based on a
sequence of projects with the desired competence delivery. For this purpose, the
student journey conﬁgurator (SJC) tool of EuroPIM [21] is adapted and tested as
another result of this research. It is used to build the right sequence of projects for
the desired overall competence gain.
For our conceptual model of soft skills development by doing selected projects
(see Fig. 1) we assume, that we have a pool of projects (A, B, C) which are linked to
company cases (A, B). They are forming a “Virtual Project Campus” where teachers

250
N. Mikhridinova et al.
and students can select projects which they want to do. During their studies, we assume
that students are conducting a sequence of student projects (see Fig. 1, project A, B,
C) and that the projects are categorized by project type (see Fig. 1, type 1, 5, 7), e.g.
as agile innovation projects, digital transformation projects, international team projects,
customer-centric projects. Based on this, typical sets of competences are deﬁned which
are trained while doing such projects (and by conducting related educational activities,
e.g. team trainings, intercultural trainings). The project types are connected with a certain
set of soft factors which are typical for such projects. These soft factors deﬁne the
soft skills which are needed and which are trained by the projects. The soft factors
are derived from anticipated project situations (e.g. communication settings, potential
conﬂicts) which are connected with the team roles and team situations which occur in
such types of projects. In connection with the relevant technical competences, this forms
the competence delivery (CP) achieved by using the projects in PjBL settings. The
accumulation of competences (see right part of Fig. 1) leads to the desired competence
proﬁle CP(tn) of the graduates of the participating educational programmes. Section 5
provides a concrete example (experiment in Fig. 1).
Fig. 1. Conceptual model of the competence-based selection of projects and team roles for PjBL.
Based on the conceptual model we formulate the following research hypotheses
(H1-3):
H1: Conducting student projects with industry participation online and cross-border
supports the delivery of relevant competences, especially soft skills and project-related
competences. It is an effective didactic tool.
H2: Projects can be selected based on project types and the respective competence
delivery. This leads to the desired competence gain. Competence development can be
facilitated in this way. The team roles and the team situations within the projects are
linking the project types with the competence gain.

Competence-Based Support for Project-Based Learning
251
H3: For students and teachers, it is useful to plan the competence development supported
by a digital app which offers a selection of projects and recommends which projects to
use or to join. This can be supported by self-assessment of competences and their possible
ﬁt to team roles.
The development of the conceptual model is based on a literature review and on
interviews with experts in project-based education and project management from the
EuroPIM consortium (academic and industry experts, see Sect. 4). It is developed in the
context of the EuroPIM Master’s programmes and integrated into their curricula. The
competencedeliveryistestedandvalidatedinexperiments(seeSect.5)withcross-border
student teams which are doing such projects and which are doing a self-assessment of
their competence proﬁles before and after the project (see Sect. 6).
4
Model Validation with Experts
4.1
Semi-structured Interviews
A ﬁrst discussion and validation of the conceptual model and the hypotheses was done
with experts in PjBL selected by the authors from the EuroPIM network. A 30-min
semi-structured interview was set up either face-to-face or online. Two interviewers
conducted the interviews, transcribed them separately and ﬁnally discussed the results
to increase reliability and reduce bias. A total of 7 interviews were conducted with
experts (teachers) who have experience of using PjBL in their Master’s courses (see
Table 1). The respondents were asked to provide their experience with PjBL and their
opinions on various aspects such as, (i) the use of self-assessments to identify soft skills
gap, (ii) the identiﬁcation of competence proﬁles.
