4.2
Discussion of Results
The interviews ﬁndings conﬁrm H1, as there was consensus among all 7 respondents that
online and cross-border participation would contribute to a positive learning experience

252
N. Mikhridinova et al.
due to exposure to a multicultural and interdisciplinary environment. This environment
facilitates training of communication and collaboration skills and competences which is
an added advantage. Recommendations to improve the learning experience in online and
cross-border teams included (i) ensuring a high-quality IT infrastructure, (ii) providing
students with speciﬁc roles to properly manage their progress throughout the process,
and (iii) selecting projects that work best in such settings like software development
projects. There was consensus among all 7 respondents that speciﬁc learning outcomes
can be derived from a project type and team setting which are training speciﬁc soft skills.
DespitePjBLbeingacommonlyusedapproachinteaching,inmostcasespre-evaluations
of soft skills are not done. 6 out of 7 respondents do not conduct pre-evaluations in their
courses. And although they conduct post-evaluations, it is conducted on the whole course
experience, not focused on soft skills.
The interview ﬁndings support H2, as there is unanimity among all respondents that
self-assessments of soft skills can help students and teachers to understand the soft skill
gap in order to select appropriate project to address the gap. 4 out of 7 respondents
utilize various forms of self-assessment to identify student personalities to assign them
to speciﬁc project team roles. Some combine several assessments for better results, i.e.,
Belbin with DISC [22] or Belbin with own self-assessment. Others use the MBTI test
[23] or standard project management tools. Findings showed that competence proﬁles
are confused with project or team roles. These are two different aspects: the identiﬁcation
of team roles which suit the personality of students is a form of assessment but it is not to
be confused with the competence gain of the student during the project. Students do not
“learn”theteamrolestheyareassignedtobutdevelopsoftskillsduetolearningsituations
which are caused by their team role in connection with the overall project setting. To
address this gap, we are working towards determining the competences which are added
to a participant’s competence proﬁle by participating in a project as one of the intended
outcomes of this research.
The interview ﬁndings support H3, as there is consensus among the respondents that
having students select projects from a pool of projects from the consortium would be
convenient. Respondents would appreciate to have an online selection and recommenda-
tion tool. They agree that students like fast, reliable, and easy to use tools incorporated
in their learning process. However, it was recommended that the teachers should be
facilitators to guide students throughout the process.
5
Conducting a Cross-Border Student’s Project
5.1
Concept and Execution of the Project
For the experiment, we conducted a virtual cross-border project using the Scrum method-
ology for agile project management, as we did it already before, e.g. in an educational
setting with students from Kazakhstan and Germany [24]. Scrum is a method for smaller
teams (4–8 people) for iterative software development, e.g. mobile apps. In our experi-
ment, mixed teams of 4–6 students from Spain and Germany had to develop a prototype
of a mobile app for waste reduction. Within Scrum, the teams develop the app in time-
boxed (e.g. 1 week long) so-called sprints. The developers work quite independently
and meet each other during so-called Scrum ceremonies (see Fig. 2): the sprint planning

Competence-Based Support for Project-Based Learning
253
meeting (2), the daily standups (3), the sprint review (4) and the sprint retrospective
(5). Meetings can be conducted online, have a deﬁned scope and use speciﬁc methods.
Scrum uses only 3 team roles, the Scrum Master, the Product Owner and the Scrum
Team. Scrum is widely used in industry and it serves as a methodological scaffold for
team which do not know each other previously. We conducted the project over 2 weeks
(2 sprints) with 46 students, 18 from Germany (mainly IT and engineering students) and
28 from Spain (mainly project management and industrial engineering students). The
students were assigned to 10 teams, each team mixed with students from Germany and
Spain. The following steps were conducted (see details in [24]):
1. Students got a brieﬁng session 4 weeks before the experiment. A (Moodle) eLearning
course was provided, including the course concept and the project case study.
2. The weekend before the sprints started, students got a 3 h introduction into Scrum,
followed by an online test (passed by all students with 92% on average).
3. Each student conducted a Belbin test [15] and the Belbin team roles were reviewed
with respect to the Scrum roles (Scrum Master, Product Owner, Team Mem-
ber/Developer). Students decided in the teams to whom to assign which Scrum role.
Teachers don’t see the test results and there is no pre-selection of team members.
4. Scrum Masters set up the IT infrastructure for online collaboration, using Microsoft
Teams, Atlassian Conﬂuence (wiki-based documentation) and Jira (management of
backlogs and Scrum/Kanban boards), and tools for app development.
5. The teams conducted a 2–3 h meeting to develop the concept for their app, describe
user stories, assign story points and ﬁll a ﬁrst product backlog.
6. All students ﬁlled a pre-experiment survey, mainly with their previous experience,
their expectations for the experiment and their Belbin results and Scrum roles.
7. All team conducted the ﬁrst sprint, starting with the sprint planning meeting, then
developing a ﬁrst version of the app, showing it at the end of the week to the teach-
ers (acting as customers), and discussing their learning experience and potential
improvements in a sprint retrospective.
8. After the second sprint, again a sprint review and a sprint retrospective were
conducted and documented in Jira and Conﬂuence.
9. The experiment was concluded with another online survey, the post-experiment
survey which links the experience with the expectations.
5.2
Student Journey Conﬁgurator (SJC) Evaluation
Students were introduced to a demonstration of the student journey conﬁgurator (SJC)
[21] with a focus on possibilities to include projects into the plans for the individual
student journey, based on the competence proﬁle which they build step-by-step with this
app. It was demonstrated how projects can be selected based on the anticipated team
situations and the respective training effect on soft skills. In a survey, students were
asked to assess the usability of the app and to judge the relevance and usefulness of the
student projects and the expected effect on their soft skills.

6
Evaluation of the Cross-Border Project
The pre-experiment survey on the virtual cross-border project was answered by 46
students (28 from Spain, 18 from Germany) which were essentially all participants
since 3 German students dropped out during the experiment (for the Spanish students,
the course was mandatory, for the Germans, it was an elective). The evaluation survey for
the SJC was answered by all 49 participants before the experiment. 42 students (25 from
Spain, 17 from Germany) answered the post-experiment survey. The surveys were tested
and improved in a previous experiment [24] and contained sets of questions concerning
the feedback on agile cross-border projects in general, on the applied methods (e.g.
scrum) and on the gained softs skills. These questions were all asked before and after
the experiment. The post-experiment survey asked in addition about the general learning
experience. Spanish and German answers were not analyzed separately (yet).
Fig. 3. Experience of the participants (students) about the main issues during the experiment.

255
It is quite interesting that the participants (see Fig. 3) did not have big problems with
the communication in English (which is not the native language for them) or intercultural
issues (they expected even less in the pre-survey) which corresponds with previous
ﬁndings with German and Kazakh students [24]. Instead, they had issues with the online
communication and keeping the team going. Regarding Scrum, 78.6% of the student
found it a largely or somehow good methodology for this kind of virtual cross-border
projects and 71.5% found is a (very or somehow) valuable scaffold for working in newly
founded teams. On average, more than 80% of the participants rated the effect on soft
skills as at least to some extent positive (see Fig. 4).
Fig. 4. Feedback of the participants about project-based learning and the competence gain.
The students assess the agile cross-border project as very beneﬁcial for their soft
skills and project competence (see Fig. 4 of the post-experiment survey). The beneﬁt of
assigningspeciﬁcteamrolesisseenaslessrelevant.TheBelbintest(analyzedseparately)
showed very high results for team work and coordination skills, maybe explaining why
the soft skills were already well developed and the team roles were not such a big issue.
In the SJC evaluation survey, the students assessed the conceptual model of using
(agile, virtual cross-border) projects for the development of soft skills (see Fig. 5). From
the results of the survey, it can be concluded that the participants conﬁrm all hypotheses
which were formulated in Sect. 3.2. There is almost no doubt about the usefulness of
student projects for soft skill development (H1) while for the speciﬁc team role and
project type the relevance is a bit less clear (H2). The usefulness of the SJC and also of
soft skill self-assessments is conﬁrmed (H3).

7
Conclusion and Outlook
In international learning settings like cross-border Master’s programmes, the access
to projects with industry relevance and relevant learning outcomes is a critical success
factor. Transferring this into a digital and virtual learning experience offers the chance for
a better accessibility and a better match to individual student journeys. The design of the
Scrum project conducted online by internationally mixed student teams is a successful
format in that sense, especially with respect to the soft skills. Selecting the projects and
assigning the team roles with the effect on soft skill development in mind is perceived
as useful by teachers and students in our surveys and interviews. Future research has to
detail and to prove the process outlined in our conceptual model.

Work-in-Progress: DIY Ventilator - A CoVID-19
Action
Walter Koch1(B)
, Gerda Koch1
, Ramiro Ortiz1
, and Dietmar Rafolt2
1 Angewandte Informationstechnik Forschungsgesellschaft mbH, Klosterwiesgasse 32/1,
8010 Graz, Austria
kochw@ait.co.at
2 Zentrum Für Medizinische Physik Und Biomedizinische Technik, Medizinische Universität
Wien, AKH Wien, Währinger Gürtel 18-20, 1090 Wien, Austria
Abstract. In the Covid-19 pandemic, ventilators became scarce, especially in
countries with lower medical standards. A special project has managed to develop
a complete ventilator as a kit using cheap parts and 3D printers. In the ﬁrst two
phases of the project a demonstrator has been developed which allows ﬁrst tests.
With hands-on experiments, one can already control the ventilator together with
an artiﬁcial lung and learn how the ventilator works and what types of pumps,
sensors, and electronic components are necessary for this.
Due to its multidisciplinary character this project provides an excellent
basis for the elaboration of educational and instructional material. Disciplines
addressed comprise among others: informatics, physics, mathematics, biochem-
istry, medicine, material science, and electronics. In addition, the use of tools
is demonstrated on a wide range covering 3D printing, IDEs for software
development, wiring and soldering, etc.
The knowledge gained through this project could be used for setting up a
startup enterprise or as reference when starting research in the Edge Computing
or IoT domain. The education and training will be carried out in small groups
(four persons ideally) using a system for blended learning. It is envisaged to use
the Mediathread Development [1] from the Columbia University which provides
an excellent framework for the ﬂipped classroom approach. Besides the academic
domain also industries are the target for using the educational material which will
be delivered by the project.
Keywords: COVID-19 · Ventilator · Flipped classroom
1
Introduction
In spring 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic reached Austria and the Austrian government
decided to support research activities in this ﬁeld, including the development of a venti-
lator [2]. The Medical University of Vienna and the private company AIT-Angewandte
Informationstechnik ForschungsGmbH, founded in 1979 in Graz, Austria, were awarded
a research project to help develop a fully functional ventilator. The two partners com-
plemented each other excellently, as at that time AIT had just completed the interna-
tional research project Rhinodiagnost (www.rhinodiagnost.eu) [3, 4] as coordinator and
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 258–265, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_26

Work-in-Progress: DIY Ventilator - A CoVID-19 Action
259
had developed a demonstrator that experimentally simulated airﬂow through the upper
airways. The Medical University of Vienna, with its Centre for Medical Physics and
Biomedical Engineering, has extensive experience in the development of biomedical
devices and created an initial concept (block diagram) showing the functioning of a pos-
sible ventilator. After some discussions and revisions, both partners decided to develop
a ﬁrst prototype using low-cost components available as COTS (Commercial off-the-
shelf). Within the ﬁrst year of the project, a basic version of a demonstrator with reduced
functionality was successfully implemented and it was decided to implement a fully
functional device – the “SPIRITUM–Ventilator” - to be used primarily by the research
community. However, it was not ruled out that the device could eventually become a
commercial product. In order to make transparent the system (“SPIRITUM-Ventilator”)
and the construction concept, it was also decided to develop the product in such a way
(DIY: Do It Yourself) that it could be built by an experienced engineer or researcher
himself or herself. Meanwhile, the plan now also includes developing teaching material
and offering it in a blended learning environment (ﬂipped classroom) [5].
The project is divided into the following ﬁve phases:
1. Proof of concept to validate the realization possibility of the engineering concept.
2. Development of a demonstrator to achieve the Technology Readiness Level 6 [6].
3. Creation of the necessary documentation and publication in the Public Domain.
4. Development of multidisciplinary teaching material and provision of lessons in the
ﬂipped classroom mode.
5. Analysis of potential markets besides the educational area.
This four-year project is currently at the end of the second year of the project,
completing the second phase, preparing for the third phase and already introducing
university lectures.
The materials and components needed to build the DIY Ventilator can be pur-
chased through internationally available purchasing platforms or a variety of technology
providers and cost around US $ 1.500 per developed unit. If a researcher wants to start
development from scratch, he or she can set up a small electronic laboratory and work-
shop, which requires a budget of US $ 2.000 to 3.000 which already includes a 3D Printer
and a laser cutter. For this reason, this project can ideally be carried out in developing
countries, but needs an academic environment to be successful. All information will be
stored on a public GitHub including design documents, ﬁles for cutting and printing
system components, software code, BOMs (Bill of Materials), installation and testing
instructions and so on.
2
The Project
The concept of the SPIRITUM-Ventilator (block diagram) is presented in Fig. 1 and was
the starting point of the project:
Blue parts in this diagram identify the pneumatic parts of the system, red ones
electronic components and the black lines connect sensors and actuators to the electronic
components.

260
W. Koch et al.
Fig. 1. SPIRITUM-block diagram
Fig. 2. SPIRITUM system architecture
Out of this block diagram the System Architecture has been derived (Fig. 2):
The system consists of ﬁve building blocks: Control Unit, Ventilator, Data Logger,
Active Lung, and Passive Lung. The Control Unit provides the Graphical User Inter-
face which enables an administrator, technician, or nurse to run the system and can be
connected to a hospital information system via the MQTT-protocol (Message Queuing
Telemetry Transport). It stores all data measured by the sensors and the system status in
a relational data base. The Ventilator controls the interaction with a patient and consists
of a blower, valves, sensors (pressure, air ﬂow, oxygen, temperature, humidity) and an
alarm system. The Data Logger is integrated into the Console and can be used to mea-
sure pressure and ﬂow within a patient’s respiration cycle. This information controls the

Work-in-Progress: DIY Ventilator - A CoVID-19 Action
261
operation of the Active Lung which acts as part of a virtual patient and simulates the
respiratory cycles of patient or classes of patients (e.g. people already infected with the
COVID-19 virus). The Passive Lung is used for determining the parameters of the ven-
tilator to tailor the system to the compliance (lung) of a patient. The different building
blocks are already developed and can be seen in the following pictures.
The components of the Ventilator (Fig. 3, left) are installed on three mounting plates
(Fig. 3, right) and ﬁt into a box which can be placed on an A4-sized area.
Fig. 3. The SPIRITUM demonstrator and mounting plates
One Plate is dedicated to the electronic part, the other two to the pneumatic parts
(inspiration and expiration) of the ventilator. The Console (Fig. 4, left) communicates
with the Ventilator via a wireless Wi-Fi or wired LAN connection. Both building blocks
are equipped with a Raspberry PI 4 Micro Processor. The upper part of the Console
includes the Data Logger which acts like a spirometer. The Console Software is written
in Python and can be installed on a standard PC and controls several ventilators in a
Client-Server Mode [7].
Fig. 4. SPIRITUM-console, data logger, and GUI (Graphical User Interface)

W. Koch et al.
The Graphical User Interface located at the Console provides the Nurse or an Admin-
istrator of the System with information like Air Pressure, Air Flow, Air Volume, etc.
(Fig. 4, right).
For testing purposes the whole system provides two artiﬁcial lungs which simulate
an intubated application of the ventilator (“passive lung”, Fig. 5, left) or the use of a
nasal mask when simulating spontaneous breathing (“active lung”, Fig. 5, right) [8].

3
The Instructional Strategy
The main objective of the project was to provide a fully functional ventilator for edu-
cational and training purposes, complementing the products already available on the
market. There are different ways of using either the whole set of components or selected
components as separate objects with which educational experiences can be gained. SPIR-
ITUM can be used as a model for training at undergraduate or academic level in edu-
cational institutions as well as - especially - in small industries. The form of blended
learning chosen was the ‘ﬂipped classroom’, where students are introduced to the content
at home and practice the work in the classroom, where both lecturers and students work
together [10]. In the process, the role of the teacher changes, who now acts more as a
coach and above all gives practical advice. A special feature of the Instructional Strategy
is that the components are built in a DIY (Do It Yourself) manner [11] which requires
also education and training in the use of different tools. How “Flipped Classroom” works
can be seen in the following Fig. 7.
Fig. 7. Flipped classroom workﬂow and SPIRITUM-actuator (valves)
A classroom course consists of one or more lessons which are divided into different
topics. The smallest element of the course can be considered as “educational cycle”
which consists of: 1) Preparation of a Topic and an Assignment (Coach), 2) Discussion
of Topics, Assignments, and Responses (Coach and Students), and 3) Learning of Topics
and Elaborations of Assignments, the “Responses” (Student or Team). As a special fea-
ture, students or teams can be provided with online support by the coach, provided that
an educational platform supports this mode. As example for a lesson the development of
an SPIRITUM actuator (e.g. “air valve”, Fig. 7, right) can be used. This special compo-
nent consists of a housing, a blender (oriﬁce, aperture), a stepper motor, a spiral spring,
screws and nuts. The housing can be printed using a low-cost 3D-printer, the ﬁlament
and all other parts are available at different online shopping platforms all together at the
cost of around US $ 10.
For example, this lesson could cover the following topics: deﬁnition of actuators and
their use in a ventilator, description of a stepper motor, design and 3D-printing, use of
a 3D printer, introduction to a CAD tool. The tools which should be provided to the
students comprise low-cost platforms (e.g. e-learning, remote/virtual labs, CAD) and
tools (3D printer, laser cutter, etc.) [12–14]. In order to assess the learning progress of a
student, the result of the self-constructed object (quality, functionality) should be used
in addition to the elaborated answers to the tasks [15].

264
W. Koch et al.
4
Outlook
Developing the SPIRITUM ventilator from scratch was only possible because experts
from different ﬁelds worked together. Another success factor was the availability of low-
cost electronic components that already allowed some integration of basic functions, e.g.
PCBs (Printed Circuit Board) hosting drivers for stepper motors. Since the target of the
project was the elaboration of a demonstrator at TRL (Technology Readiness Level)
6 an optimized and well-designed product for the commercial market was considered
less important than a functionally complete system. This made it possible to develop
different enclosures for all components by using a low-cost 3D printer and laser cutter.
Setting up a workshop from scratch is about US $ 2.000 – 3.000, while the material for
one ventilator system costs around US $ 1.500.
Due to its multidisciplinarity, the SPIRITUM project can already be used as a basis
for teaching various skills:
Learning skills for students of electrical engineering and electronics:
• Principles and application of sensors (pressure, ﬂow, O2, temperature), transducers
(ampliﬁer, ADC) and actuators (pumps, magnet valves, stepper motors including
driver electronics)
Learning skills for students of automation and control engineering:
• Implementation of control strategies (from simple PID-controller to complex super-
imposed control systems). Control systems are a fundamental strategy and applicable
in any ﬁeld, not only biomedicine. Control engineering problems occur in all disci-
plines (not just in technology). The basic task, the tracking of a variable corresponding
to the speciﬁcation of a set point and the correction of a system in the event of external
disturbances, can be found in a wide variety of tasks. Therefore, it is important that
students of all disciplines understand these basic principles. Based on our speciﬁc
task with quantities such as pressure and ﬂow, the knowledge acquired can be trans-
ferred to other problems. In order to establish a connection to the application, practical
details such as dynamics, limited manipulated variable, stability, etc. are also covered
in addition to the basics.
Learning skills for students of informatics and medical informatics:
• Implementation of above control strategies in real software, management of sensor
data including database; interface to a hospital information system and much more.
Learning skills for high school students:
• The systems developed can be used for the experimental treatment of various physical
laws such as Bernoulli’s equation, Hagen-Poisson’s law for ﬂow resistance, or even
more simple experiments at high school level.
Learning skills for medical students:
• In physiology, the interface to physics is particularly important. Technical skills should
also be learned for practice. For advanced medical students, the praxis of ventilation
is in the focus. Ventilators require practice and an understanding of the patient’s
individual situation and can be simulated with our devices. The development of the
educational material based on the SPIRITUM Ventilator is part of the next two project
years.

Akiyuki Minamide1(B), Kazuya Takemata1, and Satoshi Fujishima2
1 Kanazawa Institute of Technology, Nonoichi, Japan

Abstract. Kanazawa Technical College (KTC) has also introduced PBL-based
design projects, referring to the engineering design education at Kanazawa Insti-
tute of Technology (KIT). Since the curriculum of a college of technology differs
greatly from that of a university and time is quite limited, it was necessary to devise
a way to introduce PBL in the same way as at a university. Therefore, KTC’s design
project was implemented with an appropriate project theme provided by a local
printing company, and the quality of the student project deliverables was high and
effective.
Keywords: Design project · Project Based Learning · Engineering design
1
Introduction
InJapan,thereisoneschoolsystemofhighereducationcalledKosen(technicalcolleges).
This is a ﬁve-year school for junior high school graduates, which is two years shorter than
the typical high school-university program. In addition, students study not only general
education but also specialized subjects within the ﬁve years of a technical college, so
the density of classes is considerably higher than that of a university, and students are
very busy.
On the other hand, institutions of higher education have been actively introducing
Project-Based Learning (PBL) in recent years, and PBL involving team activities is
particularly important for the education of engineers. [1, 2] Some kind of contrivance
is needed to introduce PBL like that used at universities to technical colleges, where
there are many curriculum restrictions, and it is difﬁcult to devote time to extracurricular
activities.
Kanazawa Institute of Technology (KIT) was one of the ﬁrst universities in Japan
to introduce full-scale PBL. Kanazawa Technical College (KTC; The name has been
changed to “International College of Technology, Kanazawa”.) used KIT’s engineering
design education [3, 4] as a reference when introducing PBL to KTC. KIT’s engineering

design education has undergone several improvements and is now called Project Design
(PD) [5].
This paper summarizes the content and results of the design projects that have been
conducted based on KIT’s PD and arranged for KTC.
2
Project Design (PD) Programs at KIT
2.1
Comparison of KIT and KTC in the Japanese School System
First, the context of KTC within the Japanese educational system is explained. Figure 1
shows a diagram of the Japanese educational system. [5] Education is compulsory from
elementary school to junior high school. Many students who ﬁnish the compulsory
education go on to high school. KTC is a college of technology, which is a special kind
of school in Japan that is different from technical colleges in other parts of the world.
Literally translated from the Japanese, a college of technology is a ‘high specialty
school,’ and as such it offers a 5-year intensive study curriculum that integrates the gen-
eral education of a high school with the specialized technical training of a vocational
school. These schools are accredited as institutions of higher education by Japan’s Min-
istry of Education. However, not all students choose to enter the workforce immediately.
Thirty percent of our graduates transfer to a university in the 2nd or 3rd year depending
on their chosen ﬁeld of study.
Fig. 1. Comparison of KIT and KTC in Japanese educational system.

3
Implementation of KTC’S Design Project
3.1
KTC’S Design Project with Reference to PD Program
KTC spent the ﬁrst ﬁve weeks of the 15-week period learning about the minimum skills
needed to carry out the project, and the remaining 10 weeks implementing the actual
design project.
Due to the limited time available for the activities, (1) the process of ﬁnding a problem
was omitted, and a theme was given to the students by the company. Furthermore, the
themes were carefully selected to facilitate the creation of prototypes by (6) materializing
ideas.
This KTC design project ran from 2015–2020, and all of the project themes were
developed with the help of a local printing company. In order to prevent the students’
ideas from becoming unfeasible or empty theories, prototypes were always made. The
theme provided by the printing company had the advantage that the prototypes could be
made on paper, in a short time, and without the need for machine tools. The following
three themes are representative of the work we have done so far.
Theme A: Proposing new ways to use stone paper [7]
Theme B: Proposal of an original toy using stickers
Theme C: Proposals for new ways to use original sticky notes [8]
The following report describes an example of Theme B.
The local printing company, Wellco Holdings Co., provided students with a theme.
Therefore, the ﬁrst step, ﬁnding the problems in the design process, was done by the
company, and students started with the second step, clarifying the problems. The theme
provided by the company was “Proposed toys with stickers that children can stick or
peel off freely in casual restaurants.” This special sticker, called a magic sticker (MS)
[6], has the following features: It is printable on both sides of the sticker, is printable on
release paper, and has partial paste on the back of the sticker.
Many families with children visit casual restaurants in Japan. Gifts for children tend
to be simple toys, and children play with them while they wait for their food to arrive.
The company challenged students to propose a toy using MS that can be enjoyed by
children younger than primary school age.
The student project was carried out using the following procedures.
(1) Finding the problem (Providing the company’s theme to students)
At the beginning of the project, engineers from Wellco Holdings Co. came and
provided the company’s selected theme to students. They explained to students the
features of the MS, problems, examples of its present use, and so on.

270
A. Minamide et al.
(2) Clarify the problem
After listening to the explanations, students were divided into seven teams to
begin team activities. Each team consisted of three or four members. Students
extracted features of the MS and clariﬁed the problems of this project.
(3) Requirement speciﬁcation
The students investigated the characteristics of casual restaurant customers,
their length of stay, and the time it takes for food to be served, and clariﬁed the
requirement speciﬁcations for the toys.
(4) Creating ideas
The students worked in teams to generate many ideas according to the
requirement speciﬁcations using the brainstorming method.
(5) Idea evaluation and selection
In this process, each student team initially established ﬁve criteria for evaluating
ideas, a number of the ideas devised were scored in accordance with the criteria,
and the team selected their best ideas.
A prototype will be produced at the end of the project activity, but in order to
reﬁne its ideas, the team will organize its ideas into B1-sized posters and present
them to printing company engineers and other students. In this presentation, the
students were able to get advice from others outside the team, and the ideas were
improved. Figure 2 shows two posters created by students before planning their
ﬁnal idea.
Fig. 2. Posters explaining the ideas generated by the team.
(6) Materialization and veriﬁcation of ideas (Producing a prototype)
To conﬁrm their ideas, students made prototypes using simple materials such as
printing paper, glue, tape, and colored pencils.

Each team made presentations using slides and prototypes created by printing com-
pany engineers and ﬁelded various questions and opinions from the engineers. Figure 3
shows pictures of the ﬁnal presentation.
Students came up with ideas such as quizzes, board games, coloring books, paper
crafts, and shogi. Among the many ideas, not only printed stickers were used, but engi-
neers evaluated highly the idea of products that children could paint freely and use as

Questionnaire Survey After Project Completion
After the project was ﬁnished, we administered a questionnaire survey. The survey target
was 27 students who had taken the classes. Figure 5 shows the results of the survey.

For every question, 78% to 88% of students answered positively. Furthermore, the
engineers’ participation in the students’ projects signiﬁcantly raised the quality level of
students’ projects. Since students were able to come up with ideas that engineers would
not have thought of, we decided that KTC’s design project, which was redesigned based
on KIT’s PD, would be effective for engineering education.
4
Summary
This paper summarizes the content and results of the design project, which was based on
KIT’s PD program and adapted for KTC. KTC’s design project seems to have skillfully
incorporated the essence of the KIT’s PD program, as students were able to generate
ideas that led to commercialization of products, albeit for a short period of time. In
addition, the questionnaire results showed that many students had a positive opinion of
this project activity. However, because the project was short, students were not allowed
to experience the process of identifying problems, and this needs to be compensated for
in other subjects.

Work in Progress: Implementing and Evaluating
a Competency-Oriented Assessment
in an Innovative Application-Oriented Course
of Mechanical Engineering
Iris Groß(B), Alexandra Reher, Leona Brust, and Doerthe Vieten
Hochschule Bonn-Rhein-Sieg, University of Applied Sciences, 53757 Sankt Augustin, Germany
iris.gross@h-brs.de
Abstract. This contribution presents a competency orientated teaching course
and its applicated assessment approach for advanced students in mechanical engi-
neering. Focus lies on the course assessment to explain how the acquired compe-
tencies can be evaluated and grading conducted. Assessment of the course consists
of a written test and a group presentation of practical results. Grading is done by
weighted scoring after evaluating a set of requirements that reﬂect the intended
competencies. The course will be evaluated by Teaching Analysis Poll (TAP)
and a questionnaire; the aim is to evaluate how the assessment format affects the
acquisition of competencies. As work in progress one anticipated outcome is a
subjectively perceived adequate preparation for professional life due to the appli-
cated assessment format. Second, a successful grading method for learning objec-
tives. Based on theoretical background and former course evaluations, it is already
known that active discussions among students importantly inﬂuences the learn-
ing outcome. As conclusion we expect using competency-orientated assessment
methods resembling future working situations to increase grading and competence
level of students.
Keywords: Competency-oriented assessment · Constructive alignment · TAP
1
Introduction
Did you ever wonder whether your assessment format and grading method is supportive
to develop the competencies you want students to acquire in your course?
Competency-orientation in higher education shall help students to master their
future professional challenges and it is widely agreed that teaching shall concentrate
on competency-orientation [1, 2]. Many ideas for implementation are already presented
in literature [3]. The appropriate assessment is less often topic of discussions – although
in the sense of constructive alignment, the assessment has a major inﬂuence on the
learning process, since the students align their learning activities to the assessment’s
requirements. Quite often, competency-orientated learning, like project work, is not
graded at all or is not a mandatory part of the curriculum. Here we present a course in
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 274–282, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_28

Work in Progress: Implementing and Evaluating
275
which competency-oriented assessment is used. We want to use it to answer the research
question if the competence-oriented assessment is suitable to prepare students for their
professional life.
2
Theoretical Background
In the following we explain the terms and background of competency-orientation. In
contrast to classical forms of examinations, which are aimed at a more static repro-
duction of previously taught knowledge in the subject, competency-oriented forms
of examinations focus on understanding and the ability to use the learned content.
Competency-orientation is the core objective of the Bologna reform [4].
2.1
Deﬁnition of the Competency Concept Used in this Article
In literature, the concept of competency is not used uniformly [5]. With regard to higher
education, however, a common feature of the various deﬁnitions is that they consider
specialized knowledge to have an application-oriented perspective. The role of learning
content changes from a skill and knowledge base to action-guiding personality parts.
Competency is deﬁned as “the individual prerequisite for solving complex tasks” [6,
p.13]. These abilities are to be determined appropriately by means of competency-
oriented assessments. In order to use competency to successfully cope with environ-
mental demands, cognitive, motivational, volitional as well as social resources must be
acquired in a learning process [6]. On the one hand, this deﬁnition limits competency
on the action level of specialist knowledge and skills, on the other hand, it addresses a
possible review framework through successful management of real-world issues.
2.2
Dimensions of Competency
The Qualiﬁcation Framework for German University Degrees [7] describes a compe-
tency model in four dimensions: (1) knowledge and understanding, (2) use, application
and generation of knowledge, (3) communication and cooperation, (4) scientiﬁc self-
image, professionalism. The approach presented here consists to a large extent of tasks
that can be classiﬁed in the second and third dimension. We expect that the successful
completion of a practical task at this point in the course of studies can also contribute to
a change in self-perception from “student” to “professional”.
2.3
Assessment of Academic Competencies
Biggs and Tang [8] conceptualize teaching in the ﬁeld of tension between teaching
activities, learning objectives, and forms of assessment, emphasizing the need to align
all components of the teaching-learning process.
The resulting constructive alignment framework addresses a ﬁt between intended
competencesaslearningoutcomes,thelearningprocessesascontentdelivery,andassess-
ment [9]. In accordance with this model, we present in the following a two-stage exam-
ination process that features parts for knowledge veriﬁcation, but in a further step also

276
I. Groß et al.
Fig. 1. Constructive Alignment framework (adapted from [8]). Not only do teaching activities
and learning objectives determine suitable forms of assessment, but also choosing a certain style
of assessment necessitates suitable teaching activities to prepare students for given tasks.
considers how successfully competencies, working and thinking patterns of an engineer
have been achieved. According to Walzik [10], examining academic skills serves to
compare intended and achieved learning goals by assessing observable behavior, e.g.
giving legible answers to questions. The requirements for an examination are validity,
fairness of opportunity, reliability, and economy [11]. The approach presented here ful-
ﬁlls these conditions by its very nature. The task to be solved is a valid engineering task
(validity) that can be scaled to the students’ possibilities (reliability) and whose initial
situation is identical for each team (fairness). The testing economy is addressed by group
presentations.
3
Approach
In the following we describe the course concept and how we plan to evaluate the
competency-oriented assessment methods.
3.1
Description of the Course Concept
This competency-orientated teaching course imparts experiences as a test engineer,
addressing advanced students in a mechanical engineering study program. Its exam-
ination approach is design to contribute to competency-orientation. The course has a
weekly contact time of 5 h. Theory is presented in the ﬁrst part, while in the next hours
students work on the development of their project, putting the theory immediately into
practice. The practical task consists of developing a research question and conducting
tests with a self-built test rig based on strain gauge measurement. Theoretical input
comprises test methodology, strain gauge measurement theory, design of experiments,
statistics. It is important that students gain their own experience of the topics explained
in theory. The theory is thus closely accompanied by practical tasks to be solved.
Parallel to theoretical lessons, the students develop a research question and measure-
ment approach that can be solved by strain gauge measuring, e.g., opening forces on
canned drinks, friction underneath shoes for different conditions etc. The students work
in small groups to design a measurement device, e.g., a cantilever. They are subsequently
provided with strain gauges, measuring ampliﬁers, microcontroller and more to build a
measuring instrument based on the theoretical input. Students are expected to use it to
conduct investigations and evaluate them statistically (see Fig. 2).

Work in Progress: Implementing and Evaluating
277
Fig. 2. Set up of strain gauge ampliﬁer and Arduino microcontroller.
The aim of the practical application is to foster the learning result, so that the students
construct their own understanding or model of the physical world, aligning to the con-
structivist teaching approach [12]. Since emotional involvement ensures a much higher
learning outcome, positive group interaction is also desired.
This work in progress contribution focuses on the question, how the assessment of a
course contributes to the learning effect. We will explain how the acquired competencies
can be evaluated and grading can be conducted. The assessment of the course consists of
twoelements:awrittentest,counting30%andagrouppresentationoftheresultsfromthe
construction of the measuring devise, counting 70%. Grading is done by evaluating a set
of requirements that reﬂect the intended competencies, using a weighted score. Students
were informed about requirements and criterions in advance. In the last year, this course
was conducted by giving the students the material to take home and build their “Take
Home Lab”. As Gross and Gross [13] presented, the evaluation of the learning success
was already very promising and positive. When the students were asked to answer, which
points they liked in this course, they emphasized, for example, the opportunity to work
practically, to carry out experiments in a self-determined way in teams, the practical
relevance, and the very good preparation for their bachelor thesis [13]. They were also
asked to rate their ability to design a force measurement device before and after the
course. As the graphs below (Fig. 3) reveal, the ratings of the competency shifted from
low to high, indicating that the targeted competency acquisition was clearly achieved
and they saw the practical relevance of the course.
Fig. 3. Self-estimation of the ability to design a force measurement device before (left; ˜x = 1,
IQR = 2) and after the course (center; ˜x = 4, IQR = 1) as well as of practical relevance of the
topic (right; ˜x = 4, IQR = 2). [13]
Building on these ﬁrst results, this semester we want to evaluate the inﬂuence of the
assessment form on the competency gain with the help of suitable evaluation methods.

278
I. Groß et al.
3.2
Evaluation of the Competency-Oriented Assessment
We plan to evaluate the competency-oriented assessment by using a mixed-method
approach, combining qualitative and quantitative data to conﬁrm results across different
methods and to recognize pattern that would else remain hidden [14]. First, we use
the qualitative framework of TAP to evaluate how the described form of examination
affects the acquisition of competencies in the view of students. Second, we conduct two
quantitative questionnaires for the subjective assessment of competence progress.
TAP as an Innovative Feedback Method. TAP, a mid-term qualitative feedback
method, provides an effective way for lecturers to learn how students perceive the learn-
ingprocess intheir courses [15]. TAPis designedtohelpstudents reﬂect ontheir learning.
This can reveal aspects that promote or hinder learning. The students also make sug-
gestions on how the aspects that hinder learning can be rectiﬁed, so the teaching can be
adapted in the ongoing course. TAP is conducted by academic staff in higher education
didactics and includes consultations and trainings in didactics, which has been proved to
increase the effectiveness of evaluations to improve teaching [16]. TAP has been offered
at many American universities for several years and has only found its way into German
universities in the last few years [17].
Procedure of TAP. Participation in the TAP process is voluntary for lecturers and stu-
dents. At the agreed date of TAP, the lecturer ends the course about 30–45 min earlier,
hands over to the moderator of TAP and leaves the room to preserve the anonymity of the
students and their statements about the course. The moderator of TAP brieﬂy introduces
the method and asks students to discuss the following three questions in small groups:
• Which aspects of the course facilitate your learning?
• Which aspects of the course impede your learning?
• What suggestions do you have for improving the impeding points?
After a group work phase of 10 min, the sub-groups present their results to the plenum
and the moderator takes notes. Then the participants may give individual, anonymous
vote on the points that have been documented, via an online tool. Subsequently, the
moderator prepares a written report of the results, which is discussed in a personal
feedback meeting with the lecturer, preferably within a week or before the next course
date. The discussion of results can already be used to jointly develop initial ideas on
aspects of the course that can be changed, so that these processes can be implemented
during the current semester if possible. In the next session of the course, the lecturer
discusses the results with the students in order to jointly consider how to deal with the
results and, if necessary, who can contribute to potential changes and how.
Feedback Situations in the TAP Process. “Feedback represents one of the basic con-
stants of good teaching” [18, p. 157]. According to Ulrich [18], there are usually two
directions for feedback in the context of teaching: Frist, feedback from the lecturers to
the students to check the learning success, e.g., in the form of an assessment. Second,
feedback from students to lecturers in the context of teaching evaluation. Through the

Work in Progress: Implementing and Evaluating
279
TAP process, another feedback situation is added and connects the previously mentioned
directions. The moderator of TAP acts as the students’ voice by collecting their feedback
and passing it on to the lecturer in an anonymous form. The lecturer, in turn, gives the
students feedback on this. Only through this ﬁnal feedback can the overall process and
the student feedback be used effectively [16].
Adaptation of TAP for this Course. In principle, only the three described questions are
asked and dealt with in the TAP process. However, there is an opportunity for lecturers to
raise another special concern that will then be integrated during the process. This could
be, for example, a question about the effect of a new teaching concept. As a supplement
to the three standard questions, the special question offers lecturers the opportunity for
more detailed and speciﬁc feedback on their concerns. To better evaluate the effect of
the competency-oriented assessment on the students’ learning in this course, we plan to
conduct TAP at the end of the semester. We will ask the “normal” three TAP questions
and have the students work on them in groups. In particular, we would like to draw their
attention to their reﬂection of the learning process, considering the special assessment
formats. By doing so, we hope to gain deeper insights into student learning, which we
can then validate against the planned learning objectives. Because the students are not
asked questions about speciﬁc aspects in the TAP process, but rather freely describe their
views on the points that promote and hinder learning, this type of evaluation is very well
suited to obtain unbiased statements.
Questionnaire. In the quantitative part of the methodological section, we will use a
questionnaire study with a cross-sectional study design. The aim of the study is a subjec-
tive evaluation of the students regarding their competency progress in the corresponding
course as well as to what extend an application of the assessment helps the student to pre-
pare for their professional life’s. Therefore, the questionnaire will be given to the students
after both assessments. After the ﬁrst assessment, which is the written part, the three
parts application of the assessment, assessment as a predictor for professional life and
demographics will be answered by the students. After the second part of the assessment,
which is the presentation of group work, the parts mentioned above supplemented by
the parts personal motivation and achievement as well as learning objectives and com-
petencies will be ﬁlled in by the students. To be able to compare the students between
the two data sets a code will be conducted at the beginning of both questionnaires. All
results will refer to the summer semester 2022.
With personal motivation and achievement, we aim to evaluate to what extent the
students are interested in the course and how they value their personal outcome. Example
items are ‘The topics covered in this course interest me very much’ or ‘I am learning in
order to achieve the best possible degree’. Moreover, during this part we aim to evaluate
the mentioned positive involvement of the students with ‘I had fun doing the course’. The
second thematic part covers the learning objectives and competences. They represent the
course content. Items are for instance ‘I am able to set up a measurement experiment’,
‘I am able to set up a force measurement using strain gauges’ or ‘I am able to present
results appropriately’. The third part covers the topic application of the assessment to
evaluate how the students perceive it. Example items are ‘My knowledge has deepened
because I was able to apply it’ and ‘In the assessment, I was able to show how I can deal

280
I. Groß et al.
with certain problems instead of just showing what I know’. The following fourth part
covers assessment as a predictor for professional life to evaluate the student’s subjective
impression on how much the assessment prepares them for their later professional life’s.
Example items are ‘The assessment makes me feel well prepared for my professional
life’ or ‘The assessment encourages me to deal with the material in such a way that I
can use it in my professional life’. The following part contains open questions in order
to get more details and personal insights of the students concerning the advantages and
disadvantages of the course. The items are ‘What advantages do you see in the assessment
format comparedtoatraditional assessment?’ and‘What disadvantages doyouseeinthe
assessment format compared to a traditional assessment?’. The questionnaire concludes
with demographics (e.g., age and gender).
The items partly refer to the earlier mentioned four dimensions of the competency
model [7]. For instance, in order to evaluate communication and cooperation as dimen-
sion three we created the item ‘I am able to participate in group work in a goal-oriented
way’. With the item ‘I now perceive myself a bit more as an engineer than as a student’,
we evaluate dimension four, scientiﬁc self-image, professionalism. In the questionnaires,
free texts or a ﬁve-point Likert scale will be used to indicate how much the individual
statements apply. The answer anchors will range from strongly disagree (1) to strongly
agree (5). Overall this questionnaire allows us a speciﬁc feedback about the subjective
impression on the course content, the assessment and its application to evaluate to what
extent the assessment is a preparation for the professional life.
4
Anticipated Outcomes and Conclusion
Since both the qualitative and quantitative evaluations on the assessment format will
be conducted at the end of the lecture period, the results will be available in August.
These will be included in the presentation at the conference. In accordance with the
didactic design principles underlying the course as well as the theoretical preliminary
considerations, we expect higher values at the level of subjective self-assessment (ques-
tionnaire) on the various competence levels (see Sect. 2.2) in comparison to common
didactical designs and teaching styles. We furthermore expect a signiﬁcant increase on
the dimension of “scientiﬁc self-image and professionalism”, as the degree of freedom
given to the students is a main distinguishing criterion to common didactic designs.
Furthermore, with regard to the methodology we ﬁrst refer to the results from the
TAP. We expect that the students themselves will name the competencies that are fos-
tered by the practical examination format when asked what facilitates their learning.
In addition to that, the students will probably also mention the application for their
later professional life as positive. A comparison between the things perceived by the
students as helpful for learning and those asked for in the questionnaire can provide us
with additional insights into whether the examination format is appropriate for career
preparation. Additionally, we expect a positive correlation between the acquisition of
competencies through both forms of examination (written test and practical task) and
a subjectively perceived adequate preparation for profession-al life regarding the ques-
tionnaire. Moreover, we expect this correlation to be weaker for the classical form of

Work in Progress: Implementing and Evaluating
281
examination (written test) than for the more competency-oriented assessment (practical
task). In addition, by asking the second question in the TAP, we can uncover obstacles
that make it difﬁcult for students to learn. The student’s suggestions for improvements
shall lead to adaptions in the next semester, going along with further evaluations of
the improvements. The research approach as described can be used as a blue print for
evaluation of similar competency oriented courses, leading to further research activities.
In conclusion, we expect that the chosen competency-oriented assessment form will
have a signiﬁcant positive inﬂuence on the development of those competencies required
for a successful professional career.

Work-in-Progress: Building Up Employability
Skills and Social Responsibility in the University
of La Rioja Industrial Engineering Degrees
Alpha Pernia-Espinoza1(B)

Abstract. In this paper, we focus on the social value of the entrepreneurship
competence by describing the implementation of a service-learning project named
OSOR (Open-source and SOcial Responsibility). OSOR is aimed to provide assis-
tive products to people in a dependency situation. The needs to be solved are
proposed by patients from specialized institutions. The products are designed and
manufactured by 2nd-year engineering students. We describe the improvements
implemented along the current academic year: (i) the use of the EntreComp frame-
work; (ii) the delivery of focused seminars and visits to specialized centers; and
(iii) the promotion of student-patient interaction. We discuss the OSOR strengths
and weaknesses detected and the potential corrections and improvements for next
editions.
Keywords: STEM · Soft skills · Service-learning · EntreComp
1
Introduction
Higher education is intended to guarantee the acquisition of speciﬁc and general com-
petences of a profession, but equally important, it should promote the training on soft
skills to increase students’ opportunities for ﬁnding high-quality employment. EC stated
that “higher education institutions need to ensure that they equip graduates with relevant
and up-to-date skills” to “keeps pace with the fast-changing needs of our labour market
and society” [1]. A total of eight key competences were identiﬁed by the EC [2]. One of
them, entrepreneurship, refers to “the capacity to act upon opportunities and ideas, and
to transform them into values for others”. This competence is founded “upon creativ-
ity, critical thinking and problem solving, taking the initiative and perseverance and the
ability to work collaboratively in order to plan and manage projects that are of cultural,

social or ﬁnancial value”. In this regard, EC created a shared framework named Entre-
Comp [3] based on three competence areas: Ideas & Opportunities, Resources, and Into
Action; and each contains ﬁve essential competences. Several tools have been proposed
to assess entrepreneurship competence in recent years [4–6]. These authors agree on the
importance of subjective assessments of self-perceived competencies in developing an
entrepreneurial mindset.
Inthispaper,wefocusonthesocialvalueofentrepreneurshipcompetencebydescrib-
ing the implementation of a service-learning project named OSOR (Opensource and
SOcial Responsibility) [7]. During the last four consecutive academic years, the OSOR
has developed some of the entrepreneurship above competences. On the academic year
2021–22, we have reshaped OSOR to ﬁt into the standard EntreComp framework. A cus-
tomized survey (SoTK-SS) is developed to assess entrepreneurship competence. In addi-
tion, two peer evaluations were conducted to assess teamwork performance. Finally, we
discuss the OSOR strengths and weaknesses detected along the academic year 2021–22
and the potential corrections and improvements for the next editions.
2
The OSOR Project
The OSOR [7] is a service-learning project aimed at providing assistive products to
people in a dependency situation. The project started in 2018 and has signiﬁcantly
evolved when compared to the present day [8]. In this work-in-progress, we want to
describe the last modiﬁcations introduced in the present academic year (2021–22): (1) the
use of the EntreComp framework; (2) focused seminars and visits to specialized centers;
and (3) the promotion of student-patient empathy and interaction. OSOR represents 30%
of the subject’s ﬁnal score.
2.1
Stakeholders
The main stakeholders were identiﬁed relatively early due to the previous experiences
with the OSOR project. We summarize them as follows:
1. Teacher and students of the Manufacturing Technology (MT) subject. In this
academic year, two lecturers and a total of 47 enrolled students (6.4% female).
Students work in three-people teams (15 working teams in total). MT is a 16 weeks
course with 6 ECTS credits (with 60 h of in-person classes and 90 h of student’s
autonomous work) of the 2nd-year, common to the three industrial engineering
degrees offered by the University of La Rioja (UR).
2. Experts from three institution working with dependent people. In this case,
occupational therapist (OT) from ‘Fundación Hospital Calahorra’ (Calahorra Hos-
pital Foundation or FHC), ‘Asociación Riojana de Esclerosis Múltiple’ (Multiple
Sclerosis Association of La Rioja or ARDEM) and ‘Centro de Recuperación de
Personas con Discapacidad Física de Lardero’ (Recovery Center for the Physically
Handicapped of Lardero or CRMF-Lardero).
3. Thepatientsfromtheinstitutions:16patientsproposeddifferentneedsfor30cases.
The working groups selected 15 different cases that involved nine (9) patients.

Work-in-Progress: Building Up Employability Skills
285
4. The UR that ﬁnances the project and its dissemination through competitive grants
for teaching innovation projects.
Other complementary stakeholders were also involved in the project. For instance, M.
Espinar (@RedGuadalinfo), an external collaborator who, altruistically, gave a seminar
on Design Thinking oriented to the OSOR Project; people in dependent situation who
could replicate the products from public website; or the UR Communication Ofﬁce, in
charge of contacting local media. Other ones include the local media, who disseminate
the news about the project, and companies collaborating with the materials.
2.2
Project Development
Lecturers involved in the project carried out other necessary activities simultaneously
with the OSOR. Among those, lectures providing students with the essential knowledge,
fundamental descriptions of real-world cases, and practical sessions according to the
program of the subject were the most common. The OSOR was mainly divided into four
stages (Fig. 1): (1) Creativity, (2) Preliminary Project, (3) Progress Report, and (4) Final
Presentation. Some additional and complementary activities were included, such as peer
evaluation or prototype testing with the patient.
Fig. 1. Main schedule for planning and developing the OSOR project
3
The OSOR Under the EntreComp Framework
Brieﬂy, we will only mention (without description) the competences and average levels
established in the OSOR. Further information will be provided under request.
3.1
Key Entrepreneurial Competences Involved in OSOR
The OSOR gradually develops the following competences of the EntreComp conceptual
model:
1. Ideas & Opportunities: spotting opportunities; creativity; vision; valuing ideas;
ethical & sustainable thinking.
2. Resources: self-awareness & self-efﬁcacy; motivation & perseverance; mobilizing
others; ﬁnancial & economic literacy.
3. Into action: taking the initiative; planning & management; coping with uncertainty,
ambiguity & risk; working with others; learning through experience.

Activity 1, “Inform and raise awareness”, is planned to make students aware of
the importance of helping people in dependency situations and teach them how to use
what they learned in the MT subject. Several seminars are presented: “Design Thinking
tools for the OSOR”, “What is Occupational Therapy”. Students are also invited to tour
the specialized area in the CRMF-Lardero to see commercial and homemade products
oriented to assist dependent people. Activity 2 is “Gathering information from real

Work-in-Progress: Building Up Employability Skills
287
patients to prepare the cases” with experts and patients initially elaborating a list
of potential cases; and then, lecturers will choose the ones with complexity according
to students’ skills and available resources. We propose Activity 3 called “Students
propose several possible solutions” (Creativity Stage in Fig. 1). Student must use
creativity tools included in the Design Thinking, while lecturers should guide them to
the most reliable solution. The Activity 4 “Selecting the most plausible solution”
(Preliminary Project stage, in Fig. 1), involves student teams presenting their solutions,
and giving details of their potential implementation. The information includes tasks
required to manufacture the prototypes, assignment of roles and task according to the
strengths of the members, materials needed, manufacturing technologies to be used, and
an estimated budget. In Activity 5, “Implementation of the solution”, the teams work
on prototyping their proposals and are encouraged to present their best proposals to
patients, and receive some feedback. In this sense, the design-test-redesign process can
be carried out with greater guarantees of success. Every two weeks, the working groups
present their progress (Progress Report stage, in Fig. 1). By the end of the semester,
the last activity, Activity 6, is “Presenting the solution” (Final Presentation stage, in
Fig. 1) in which students show their products in public. Media, experts in the ﬁelds, UR
authorities, family, friends, and the general public are invited to this presentation.
4
Main Assessment Tools of the OSOR
Following university standards, the MT subject was evaluated, and several outcomes
were registered: (1) Attendance rate, (2) Student participation, (3) Final subject score and
success rate, and (4) Survey on essential Technical Knowledge and Soft-Skills (SoTK-
SS). The SoTK-SS is an ad hoc survey conducted at the beginning and the end of the
semester, using the same questions: students are asked about technical knowledge and
their self-perception of soft skills. The technical knowledge questions involve general
concepts on the use of CAD software and well-known machines such as 3D printers,
lathe, etc. The speciﬁc questions are focus on basic knowledge of welding, 3D printing,
machining, injection molding, etc. Self-assessment on entrepreneurship competences
are also registered with questions on oral communication, problem solving, leadership,
ﬁnancial literacy, etc. The complete list of questions is listed on [9].
The OSOR is speciﬁcally monitored along the semester, and the main three outcomes
are: (1) Scores from the four main stages (presentations and reports) (Fig. 1), (2) Two peer
evaluations, and self-evaluation regarding the teamwork performance, and (3) Number
and quality of functional products.
5
Results and Discussion
To this day (June 5th, 2022), we have not conducted the end-of-the-semester SoTK-SS
yet. Also, the ﬁnal subject score and success rate are not available. Regarding OSOR,
the Final Presentation took place on May 27th, 2022.
The attendance rate and student participation results were steady and not too low
compared to other subjects of the same semester (where attendance rates lower than
15% were reported). MT registered an average of 82% throughout the semester as well

288
A. Pernia-Espinoza et al.
as in the last months. Written exams, practical demonstrations, and OSOR deliverables
registered near 100% of attendance. OSOR Final Presentation registered an attendance of
100%. Student–lecturer interactions during sessions (as in previous semesters) were not
as active as desired, leaving much room for improvement. The greatest interaction was
registered during the practical sessions or near any written exam or OSOR deliverable
date.
The OSOR scores from the ﬁrst two main stages (Creativity and Preliminary Project)
were high, with an average of 9.4 (of 10). The Progress Reports evidenced two main
problems: the slow development of the prototypes and the consequent lack of student-
patient interaction. Most of the working groups prototyped with delay, and most of the
group never contacted the OT or the patient. Only one working group stablished an
active interaction with the patient, and it was later evidenced in the high quality of the
product delivered. The OSOR Final Presentation report has not been assessed yet but we
can anticipate that the presentation attracted around ﬁfty attendees between experts, and
general public. There was also excellent media coverage in the local newspapers, TV,
and radio [10–12]. All working groups (15 in total) delivered the planned products (18
products).Ingeneral,alltheproductswerefunctional,andbetterqualityandperformance
were evidenced in groups where high interaction between working group and patient
was established.
Regarding peer evaluations and self-evaluation during OSOR, the average scores
were 7.6 (out of 10). Only two working groups performed with low rates. Most of the
time, the members of these two working teams did not attend the sessions or take any
written exams. They only showed up during the OSOR Final Presentation with functional
products but were not suited for the target patient.
The EntreComp, although a renowned standard, could be challenging to implement
to its full extent due to its 15 entrepreneurship competences (classiﬁed into three main
areas), which could be broken down into 60 threads, each of which could be measured
using 8 progression levels [13]. Even though the EntreComp intrinsic methodology
establishes that not all the entrepreneurship competences, threads, and levels should be
addressed, the initial information to handle is overwhelming. Joensuu-Salo et. al [14]
claimed a simpliﬁcation, arguing that although the framework proposes three distinct
areas, entrepreneurship competence is unidimensional. Abdulwahed, et. al [15] proposes
EU OECD/HEInnovate framework as a better approach for engineering school projects.
For further works, the authors will explore these alternative approaches.
The lecturers reported that, although the beneﬁts of the project are evident, tasks
required for setting up the project, assessing the outcomes, keeping in touch with the
stakeholders, providing timely feedback, etc., required substantial time and effort. Also,
theavailabletimetoachievethetasksduringlecturingwasscarce.Apotentialsolutionfor
the next year could be the ﬂipped classroom, given the good results shown on engineering
degrees [16].
6
Conclusion and Future Works
In this work, we have presented the social value of entrepreneurship competence through
a service-learning project named OSOR. In OSOR, students are divided in teams to

Work-in-Progress: Building Up Employability Skills
289
design and manufacture assistive products for people in dependency situation. We
described the process of structuring OSOR’s activities using the EntreComp frame-
work. In addition, we tried to promote student-patient interaction, without much success
for the current academic year. Through one of the working groups, we were able to
verify that the empathetic bond created between the student and the patient, and the
progressive improvement of the product after the prototype tests, made the students give
their best and produce the ‘perfect’ product for the patient. To promote student-patient
interaction for the next edition, we will introduce an evaluation criterion to be veriﬁed
using a collaborative platform where students report the outcomes of the prototyping
tests, and the OT to validate these actions. In addition, implementing a ﬂipped classroom
methodology seems to be the right way to efﬁciently manage the short time available
for the subject in general, and OSOR in particular.

program ‘Proyectos de Innovación Docente 2021/22’. We are also thankful to the students, patients,
OT, and managers of the collaborative institutions involved in the project.

How Interdisciplinary Hackathons Foster
the Linking of Teaching and Practice
Daniel Beigel(B), Isabella Blaurock, and Victoria Sauter
MESH e.V., Großbottwar 71723, Germany
{daniel,isabella,victoria}@mesh-stuttgart.de
http://www.mesh-stuttgart.de
Abstract. As a result of a student initiative, an annual interdisciplinary
hackathon was established at the Cooperative State University Stuttgart
(DHBW Stuttgart). This has shown how this new innovative format can
be used to develop solutions to problems related to the UN’s 17 Sustain-
able Development Goals (SDGs). By bringing together students from a
wide range of disciplines, digital solutions are created in a short period of
time that deliver added value for all stakeholders. In addition, the trans-
fer of theory and practice is combined, so that students can apply what
they have learned to practical, real and relevant problems from a wide
range of areas. Furthermore they get the opportunity to follow up on
the ideas with the partners. Comprehensive evaluation criteria that take
into account the interdisciplinary background of the students ensures
comparability and promote the exchange of students among themselves
and the ﬁelds of study, is promoted. A hackathon can therefore make a
teaching-integrated contribution to innovation and curriculum on many
levels.
Keywords: Hackathon · Interdisciplinary · Innovation
1
Context
Due to the rapid development of new digital technologies, the format of a
hackathon, is becoming increasingly popular [1]. A hackathon is an event that is
usually organized by a company or an institution, to gather new ideas and poten-
tial solutions for their current problems. The word is a portmanteau derived from
“hack” and “marathon”, which already shows the general meaning. A hackathon
usually takes place within a short time, e.g. over a weekend, and has the goal of
solving a problem through technical developments such as apps or websites [5].
In 2021, students at the corporate state university Stuttgart (DHBW Stuttgart)
organized the ﬁrst interdisciplinary hackathon. The hackathon aimed to bring
together all of the university’s locations and all the faculties centrally and thus
create a space for innovation. In addition, the transfer between teaching and
practice is created, as students from all areas can directly implement practi-
cally what they have learned in theory. This is particularly evident in the design
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 291–297, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_30

292

of apps and applications, but also in the creation of a business model for the
use case. In summer 2021, the students joined forces in the association MESH
e.V. and organized the second hackathon in close cooperation with the DHBW
Stuttgart as well as the corporate partners. The hackathons each took up several
of the UN’s 17 SDGs to ensure a sustainable environment through digital inno-
vation. Due to the Covid-19 pandemic during the two hackathon periods, these
were held in an online format. Based on feedback, it was determined that an
online format also worked and produced valuable results, supported by a survey
conducted by Yong with 940 participants [13].
2
Potential of a Hackathon in the Context of University
Teaching
A hackathon can be assigned to an experimental learning development, according
to Kolb [4]. With this approach new knowledge is learned by actively applying
existing knowledge and by solving a concrete problem, which in turn allows new
knowledge to be acquired practically. Therefore a hackathon, in the broadest
sense, can also be understood as a case study according to Yin [12]. A hackathon
is suitable as a supplement to university teaching not only because of its prac-
tically oriented approach but also because of its technical reference, which is
becoming increasingly important in today’s society as well as in research [3].
Depending on the design of the hackathon, diﬀerentiated points from the teach-
ing can be deepened or diﬀerent aspects from the curriculum can be taken up
and applied as broadly as possible. The hackathon format is not only suitable for
linking teaching and practice, but also for solving current problems by applying
digital technologies. Therefore, it oﬀers added value for universities to ensure
the quality of teaching for students to combine and expand knowledge but also
for companies or institutions that participate in the hackathon by presenting a
problem.
The Challenge is an essential part of the hackathon as it paves the way for
teaching and transfers into practice. In order to enable real added value for the
company and society, the UN’s SDGs, for example, can be used. Using MESH as
an example, extensive work was done with partners, companies and universities
to identify challenges. A challenge is a problem that students try to solve using
digital technologies.
A hackathon does not have to be technically oriented towards computer sci-
entists only, but can have diﬀerent designs depending on the requirements and
problems. Besides a classic hackathon, other forms such as an ideathon are also
conceivable [1]. Due to the increasing complexity and interconnectedness of a
wide variety of disciplines, students can be brought together and prepared for
their future careers. According to a survey of participants in various hackathons,
the majority of participants take part because of the learning characteristics of a
hackathon, as shown in Fig. 1. This demonstrates the beneﬁts of the innovative
integrated and interdisciplinary hackathon also for the context of teaching.
