knowledge and skills that can be applied in everyday school practice.
5
Possibilities for Methodological Improvement
In our engineering teacher training, we strive to apply a variety of teaching methods, to
introduce to and test them on students. The applied methods help develop the soft skills
of our students and also acquaint them with the methodological possibilities that they
can in turn successfully apply in their own teaching.
In our classes, the tasks that are solved in group-work play an important role. Intra-
group discussion provides an excellent opportunity for students to express their thoughts,
to explain their own views, to argue and to pay attention to the other party. Dispute, a
game from the Anglo-Saxon language area that develops a culture of debate, can be
very effective in developing discussion techniques [11]. It aims to teach students the
techniques that will help them thrive as a critical, active citizen in an open, democratic
society. Dispute enriches the students’ cultural knowledge in a playful and entertaining
way.
In engineering teacher training classes, collaborative methods come to the fore.
Collaborative learning is an active and interactive process designed to give students
an active learning experience. In collaborative learning, the result of co-learning is the
successful achievement of a common goal. This is achieved through joint activities, in
which students also develop their cooperation skills indirectly [5]. One of the problems
with online teaching introduced because of the pandemic was that students felt isolated
and lonely while learning. Collaborative learning can be a solution to this problem, as
peer learning can also be used in an online environment.
The use of cooperative methods is also proving effective in technical teacher educa-
tion because these methods are also based on student collaboration. The four principles
of cooperative learning [12] – constructive interdependence, individual responsibility,
equal participation and parallel interaction – promote the development of soft skills.
Cooperative methods favour experiential learning based on student activity. Research
suggests that the use of cooperative learning techniques and courses to develop social
skills have had a positive effect on collaboration at work and on personal relationships
[13].
The project method also plays a key role in the training of engineering teacher
students, the application of which is based on students’ interest and the joint activities
of teachers and students. It is suitable for developing cooperation, empathy, conﬂict
management and communication. The focus of the project is mostly a practical problem,
so it provides an excellent opportunity to develop students’ problem-solving skills. When

Preparing Engineering Teacher Students for the Challenges
335
this method is applied, the traditional teacher-student relationship also changes. This is
also important because proper cooperation between students and faculty is an essential
condition for both academic and social integration. A study by Berglund and Heintz
[14] reported that project-based learning implemented in a real workplace environment
develops skills that facilitate students’ employment, such as teamwork, communication,
problem solving, and conﬂict management.
Our students also try the Problem Based Learning (PBL) method. This method
provides students with practical problems, thus preparing them for creative, critical
and analytical thinking and for ﬁnding sources of learning. In class, students solve
complex problems in group-work using peer and self-assessment [15]. The development
of the ability to self-assess helps to develop the ability for peer assessment, which in
turn makes self-assessment increasingly realistic, so the interaction of the two abilities
developing in parallel can be observed. Students working in groups not only develop
their problem-solving skills, but also their communication, cooperation, and leadership
skills.
In Inquiry-Based Learning (IBL), students collaborate on experiments, research, and
modelling. The method assumes the active involvement of students in the learning pro-
cess, in the construction of their own knowledge. Research-based learning contributes
to students’ understanding of the nature of science and the research methods of the nat-
ural sciences. They acquire general research skills (for example: formulating research
questions, setting up hypotheses, planning and managing research, analysing and pub-
lishing results) as well as speciﬁc research skills (methods for speciﬁc research studies).
Research activities can help students understand scientiﬁc content and apply scientiﬁc
knowledge. Students can experience scientiﬁc discoveries and the research process,
which can help develop their interest in science, research attitudes and positive attitudes
to school subjects [16].
Gamiﬁcation refers to the application of games and game elements to non-game
areas of life. Its purpose is to make the processes taking place there more interesting and
productive. This method can also be used successfully in engineering teacher education,
as it arouses students’ curiosity and provides them with pleasant experiences. Using this
method, the participants in the game feel good and are happy to complete the tasks. They
are driven by the desire to overcome the challenges and solve the problems posed by the
game. Gamiﬁcation is also used in our training for motivation and skills development
[17]. Students become familiar with a web application based on gamiﬁcation aspects, an
online application that helps the teacher’s work and provides a ready-made framework
to guide a class or group through a given training process [9].
Trainee teachers will also be introduced to innovations such as the use of teaching
robots in education. Robots can be used as teaching assistants and pedagogical assistants
in almost any ﬁeld of science, but they can also play a role speciﬁcally in the teaching of
computer programming [18]. They help to master the basics of programming in a playful
way, as well as developing logical thinking, spatial and temporal orientation, observation,
attention, social skills, creativity and digital competence. The use of teaching robots
can contribute to the development of students’ problem-solving skills and algorithmic
thinking. Educational robots play a role in motivating students and arousing their interest.

336
I. Holik
They provide opportunities for experimental learning and a wide range of tasks based
on experiential learning activities.
In engineering teacher training, we place a strong emphasis on school practices, as
this is when students can try out in the ﬁeld of vocational training what they have learned
at university.
We consider it very important that the higher education institution work closely
togetherwiththeinstitutionsinwhichthestudentscompletetheirteachingpractice.Thus,
not only theory prevails in the training, but students are also immersed in the practice of
vocational training. It is also important that qualiﬁed mentor teachers supervise trainee
teachers in the schools, providing them with pedagogical and methodological support.
Our students have a school practice period in each semester of their training where, in
addition to their university mentor, the school mentor also helps them with their work
[19].
Throughout the training, we place emphasis on preparing engineering students for the
real problems and educational situations of vocational training. This goal is manifested
in both their content and methodological preparation.
6
Summary
The technological, economic and labour market changes of recent decades have also
necessitated the renewal of vocational training. In Hungary, the system-wide renewal
andfurtherdevelopmentofvocationaltrainingandadulteducationisdeﬁnedbytheVoca-
tional Training 4.0 strategy. This renewal poses a major challenge for teachers working in
vocational training. Vocational teacher education, including engineering teacher educa-
tion, also faces these challenges while preparing students for teaching in secondary-level
vocational education.
My paper presented the impact of Industry 4.0 on vocational training in Hungary
and how vocational teachers can prepare for the changes. It dealt with current issues in
engineering teacher training. Based on the results of a questionnaire survey conducted
among engineering teacher students, it drew attention to the need for methodological
renewal and presented the possibilities of content and methodological development of
engineering teacher training through examples.

Teaching and Learning Transferable Skills
in Engineering Education via Service Learning:
Case Study of a University of Technology
in South Africa
Elisha Didam Markus1(B) and Nereshnee Govender2
1 Central University of Technology, Bloemfontein, Free State, South Africa
emarkus@cut.ac.za
2 Durban University of Technology, Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
NereshneeG@dut.ac.za
Abstract. Transferable skills are a vital requirement of engineering education
especially in South Africa. This is more so because statistics show that a high
number of engineering graduates are unable to ﬁnd work because of little or no
transferable skills. With the rising unemployment in the country, it has become
critical to introduce these skills into the curriculum. This paper discusses one way
of teaching these skills via service learning. A sample of undergraduate students
were asked about these skills and if they believe these skills are important. Results
show a staggering small number of students knew these skills existed and fewer
indicated they did not understand the relevance of these skills to their learning. The
study concludes with recommendations on how to teach these skills via service-
learning modules that are already being proposed at the various faculties of the
university.
Keywords: Transferable skills · Teaching and learning · Service learning ·
Engineering education
1
Introduction
Transferable skills (TS) also referred to as ‘soft skills’ are skills that are critical and
valuable in the workplace (Rogers, 2016). These skills could be learnt from every-
day life and interactions including voluntary work, service, or paid work. They are not
necessarily taught in school, hence could be lacking in graduates seeking work. This
is more so in South Africa as students go through university mostly on bursaries and
scholarships. Hence, they may not see the need to volunteer for ‘free’ to gain these skills.
TS are important and crucial in the workplace, and they could include teamwork, doing
extra, paying attention to details, leadership, communication, problem solving and civic
mindedness. Engineering students go through rigorous engineering pedagogy that may
include problem solving and group work, however, certain soft skills may still be lost
unless there is a deliberate effort to inculcate these into the curriculum.

M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 338–348, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_35

Teaching and Learning Transferable Skills in Engineering Education
339
As teaching and learning are at the centre of education in South Africa, the pursuit of
transformation in higher education institutions has necessitated that students be provided
with quality education that does not enslave them but empowers them towards a paradigm
forsocialandeconomicchange.TheCentralUniversityofTechnology,FreeState(CUT),
as a university of technology (UoT), currently has a plan and vision to achieve its teaching
and learning goals in line with the national development plan of South Africa.
The impact of this plan is being critiqued against the social transformation agenda of
South Africa. The student diversity and different learning theories and concepts they have
imbibed are constantly scrutinised and compared to national and international contexts.
The authors intend to expound on learning pedagogies that ensure epistemological access
and therefore TS for all students.
Recent statistics show that unemployment numbers have soared in South Africa,
with 33% of citizens unemployed (Stats SA, 2021). This means one out of every three
South Africans do not have a job. This has resulted in social and government structures
being on the edge to ﬁnd urgent solutions. Hence attention is again cast on the teaching
and learning agenda at universities to seek possible solutions as part of the aims of
higher education. This means that new ways to provide epistemological access with a
view to create an entrepreneurship spirit among students need to be found. How do we
produce graduates that would be able to access jobs? It is important to examine existing
learning theories and pedagogies with a view of ﬁnding more transformational ones that
would address present realities in higher education. This paper attempts to answer these
questions and more.
Service learning is introduced as a critical approach in the teaching and learning
agenda that could play a pivotal role in addressing some of the challenges faced by CUT
and other institutions alike. Emphasis is placed on service learning because of its close
nexus between learning and community service. This paper argues that service learning
correctly applied to the teaching and learning agenda of universities would sensitise
academics, practitioners, and students to the needs prevalent in the community. This
would motivate agencies to strive towards meeting these needs via education. Hence,
students could develop transferable skills that could address community needs within
national and global contexts.
Considering the problem of massiﬁcation, socio-economic challenges and back-
grounds of student cohorts in South Africa, there is need to revise strategies to deal with
prior learning experiences and the articulation gap of ﬁrst-year cohort enrolments. There
is a need for a structured framework to identify individual student’s schema and zone
of proximal development (Vygotsky, 1978) to support them, not just for ontological but
epistemological success throughout their higher education experience.
One of the learning theories that CUT bases its teaching and learning on is Carl
Rogers’ humanist theory (Rogers, 1985). His theory purports that humans possess a
natural innate capacity and inclination for learning. He suggests that signiﬁcant learning
could only occur if both intellect and emotions of learners are considered. He presents
intrinsic motivation to learning as opposed to extrinsic motivation.
Looking through social realist lenses, there are many issues with this assertion:
emotion could be subjective and not objective, hence a learner who does not attach any
emotion to failing an examination would not necessarily strain him/herself to achieve in

340
E. D. Markus and N. Govender
the examinations, or to learn in the ﬁrst place. Allowing learning to take place reﬂexively
with the justiﬁcation that we are human, could lead to a lack of commitment on the part
of the primary agents. This lack of commitment could, in turn, affect the transformation
that academic developers desire in their students.
2
Learning Pedagogies for Epistemological Access
Many learning pedagogies have been theorised (Stewart, 2012) however, a few will be
discussed in the context of a university of technology. Some of these theories include
behaviourist tendencies in learning, cognitivist, constructivism, situated learning and
humanist perspectives. Many scholars in teaching and learning dwell on the concept
of social and cognitive constructivist theories for epistemological access. Touching on
social constructivism (Vygotsky, 1978), which suggests that learning leads to develop-
ment, it can be argued that in the context of development, Vygotsky’s theory of social
constructivism is insufﬁcient in itself, keeping in mind that students need to acquire the
necessary schema in their backpacks to enable them to learn by interacting intersub-
jectively in order to lead them to development. Development should lead to learning
(Piaget, 1967). This is because, in the South African context, education is considered for
transformation purposes, and therefore Piaget’s version of constructivism is preferred.
This leads to the hypothesis of service learning as a transformative strategy for learning,
which will be discussed at a later stage.
Haggis (2006) raises the issue of retention and attrition rates in universities. The
author argued that concentrating on only the learner’s needs is problematic due to the
mix of diversiﬁed and contextualised learners. With high attrition and drop-outs in the
South African context, there is a need to move away from the individualised focus on
students’ needs, to planning for pedagogical cultures, referred to by Haggis as “activities,
patterns of interaction and communication failures” (Haggis, 2006:521). This will create
anenablingenvironmentforlearningandteaching.Thisthinkingisechoedandsupported
by many authors in the ﬁeld of higher education (Mckenna, 2013; Boughey, 2012,
Ashwin, 2015, Biggs, 2012; Markus, 2021).
Ashwin (2015) for instance, refers to reﬂective learning and how students’ prior
experiences and perceptions are important in the process of planning activities that
lead to learning. He advocates the engagement of students in curriculum design in the
form of problem-based learning, enquiry-based learning, and students as cocreators of
knowledge. Therefore, partnership between students and academics who are reﬂective
teachers is encouraged. On the other hand, even though Biggs (2012) focuses on what
the student does, he presents his argument in the context of creating an ecosystem for
the student to learn. He refers to constructive alignment using constructivist theories,
stating that we need to stipulate teaching and learning outcomes and assessment criteria
at the beginning, so that the student can drive the process from his schema. He noted
that students also learn differently, and often attention is placed on students’ deﬁcits
and not on teachers’ failures. This needs to change. Those in the academic project must
make this shift in teaching and engaging with students. Furthermore, reﬂexivity must
be practised before and after class sessions. This means constantly evolving in one’s
teaching practices by always challenging one’s views and the perceptions of students.

Teaching and Learning Transferable Skills in Engineering Education
341
Luckett and Luckett (2009) presented ﬁndings on an evaluation of a mentorship
support programme run by the Maskh’iSizwe Centre of Excellence for recipients of its
bursaries. Using Archer’s social realist theory (Archer, 2013), they reiterated the powers
of learners as primary agents, suggesting that learning should emphasise ontology and
practice, as well as epistemology. They concluded that “undergraduate ﬁnancially dis-
advantaged learners” (Luckett and Luckett, 2009:472) needed some form of support
to ensure that they ﬁrst develop a sense of personal identity and social agency as a
prerequisite for succeeding academically and developing a professional identity. We
concur that developing a sense of personal identity is critical to developing personal
emergent properties (PEPs) that are required for transformation in education. This is the
kind of thought that informs service learning (Bringle, 1996).
“Service learning is needed to develop effective citizenship among students, to ad-
dress complex needs in their communities through the application of knowledge, and to
form creative partnerships between the university and the community. Service learning
provides one means through which students, faculty, and administrators can strive toward
these aspirations” (Bringle, 1996:236).
Fusing community needs into teaching and learning practices will not only create a
deep sense of responsibility among students but will enhance decoloniality and promote
a sense of personal identity. This is critical for reﬂexive learning and makes the process
of knowing more practical rather than theoretical. It will take into cognizance the con-
textualised and diversiﬁed learner. Rosenberger (2014), Kezar (2001), Butin (2003) and
Hayes (1996) provided detailed descriptions of service learning in pedagogical structures
as a vital tool for effective teaching and learning.
As a university of technology, CUT is positioned to provide quality social and
technological innovations for socio-economic developments and technological advance-
ment. Service learning is a learning theory that will enhance that. Service learning helps
students to understand their own culture in new ways, appreciate cultural differences,
become more critically aware of social inequities and power relations, and to envision
a more democratic society (Hayes, 1996). Hence, there is a strong link between service
learning and acquiring transferrable skills (Huff et al., 2016).
3
Service Learning as a Pedagogic Strategy
Service learning could be deﬁned as a type of learning that actively engages learners in
various learning activities within a community in such a way that both academic and
communitystructuresoftenbeneﬁt.Itallowslearnerstopracticewhattheyhavetheorised
in the classroom. This enables them to critically reﬂect on real-world challenges as they
seek to make sense of their learning. Service learning allows for the praxis of learning.
Figure 1 summarises the core aspects of service learning.
Based on engagements and learnings from a Post Graduate Higher Education Studies
course within the South African context, the authors explain that a service-learning
cycle has been compiled showing the important components that affect student learning.
SL is considered constructivist in nature, as students who visit communities are often
allowed to construct their own knowledge based on their own experiences in the ﬁeld.
It is contextualised because students would see their learning through the lens of the

E. D. Markus and N. Govender

Fig. 1. Understanding service-learning components.
communities. It is also transformational, as the end-users of the knowledge created
during SL are the communities themselves. This creates access, improves equity, and
brings inclusivity among students and the communities alike. This pedagogic approach
can be considered as symbiotic as communities, students and faculties beneﬁt from the
SL experience. Furthermore, SL encourages critical reﬂection among staff and students
during debrieﬁng, reporting and other activities. Praxis is also a vital component of SL,
as students tend to view their learning not just as theoretical, but as practice, and practice
within the community. This reinforces the view of education for public, and not only
private good.
With unemployment statistics on a steep rise in South Africa, students need to app-
roach learning with a sense of responsibility. According to CHE Vital Stats (CHE, 2018),
1 036 984 people enrolled into universities in South Africa during 2017. In the same
year, only a total of 210 931 graduates were head counted. Compared to the previous
year (2016), 975 837 were enrolled, and only 203 076 graduates were recorded. This
data indicates an increase in enrolment of 6.3%, and an increase of graduates of only
3.9% respectively. The percentage of enrolments compared to graduates is almost dou-
ble. High attrition and dropout rates are affecting the universities and threatening the
higher education sector in South Africa. Another important question to ask is how many
of these graduates are employable? The country must begin to engage critically with
learning theories that will not only provide access to education for the contextualised
learner but will also prepare them to be power players and game-changers in society.
We need graduates who are not only employable, but who can create jobs. The current
teaching and learning strategies need to be revamped in the light of our current realities
in higher education.
To address these present challenges in South Africa, there is a need to ﬁnd more trans-
formational approaches to learning. Service learning is one strategy that may provide
a start to this discourse. SL has been practiced by many higher education practitioners
(Kezar, 2001; McNally, 2004; Butin, 2003; Swords, 2010; Carrington & Selva, 2010;
Abes, Jackson & Jones, 2002; Mooney & Edwards, 2001; Hart, 2006; Hullender et al.,
2015).

Teaching and Learning Transferable Skills in Engineering Education
343
Furthermore, the complex nature of South Africa’s economy and its prevailing cul-
ture of poverty requires that students’ learning needs to be innovative. South Africa is
often tagged the most unequal society in the world. Hence, as students fuse learning
in the classroom with community integration, they can constantly reﬂect on the ‘why’
of knowing, and not just the ‘what’. SL will help create an emotional attachment to
learning, as initially proposed by Rogers (1985). However, this kind of emotion is not
subjective, but rather reﬂexive, as it keeps the knowers in the presence of the communi-
ties’ realities. This will affect every strata of Archer’s sociological world (Archer, 2013).
First, the structure will be revised; these include, but are not limited to the curriculum,
policies, frameworks, departmental roles, research approaches, and so on. In terms of
the university culture, the entire value system of the university will focus on the commu-
nity’s problems, as opposed to just holding ideologies that promote educational access.
The primary and corporate agencies would emerge to drive this process. This strategy to
learning can be further unpacked to expatiate on the social realism paradigm. However,
this is not the emphasis here.
4
The Challenge of Gaining Transferrable Skills
A selected set of 200 students from the Faculty of Engineering at the university were
asked to complete a questionnaire asking them various questions about their under-
standing of transferrable skills. Hence, quantitative analysis was used to process the
data received. A total of 78% were between the ages of 21–30 years. The age group is
expected to be in the category that would understand what transferable skills are. How-
ever, when asked “Do you know what transferable skills are? Only 40.5% answered
‘yes’, 46% “did not know” and another 13.5% indicated “I did not know these skills
existed” (Fig. 2).
Fig. 2. Do you know what TS are?
Those that answered ‘yes’ were asked to mention some transferable skills they know.
Some of their responses included “communication, leadership problem-solving, team-
work and dependability”. Some clearly indicated “I don’t know.”
Other responses included:
“Having the position as a leader, it is required to lead a group of individuals as a
team.”

344
E. D. Markus and N. Govender
“I think is the ability to lead a group of people and guide them”.
“Problem Solving, teamwork, Time management, creativity, leadership, commu-
nication, critical thinking and multi-tasking”.
Some students mentioned “Cooking and Singing”; “teamwork, adaptability,
writing reports”; Communication, team playing as transferable skills.
Even though 52.6% of the students agreed that transferable skills were relevant to
their learning/education, 36.8% did not agree that transferable skills were relevant to
their learning or education. A further 10.5% were not sure.
When asked if they needed skills for the workplace, not just academic knowledge,
about 90% answered in the afﬁrmative. They understood that they required workplace
skills as classroom knowledge was not sufﬁcient in the long term (Fig. 3).

(b)
Fig. 3. (a) I know what interdisciplinary knowledge is (b) TS are relevant to my studies
Most of the students (58%) understood what interdisciplinary knowledge was but
they did not know how it could be achieved. Data revealed that 24% of the students did
not know what this meant and 18% were not sure.
5
Service Learning and Transferable Skills
Many authors have linked service learning with transferrable skills especially in engi-
neering. For example, Huff’s (2016) study demonstrated a strong link between partic-
ipating in service-learning activities and navigating the complexity of the work-place.
The study investigated how alumni perceived the impact of a service-learning program,
the Engineering Projects in Community Service (EPICS), in preparing them for the
workplace. It was realised from the study that the EPICS program helped to connect
education theory and practice. The integrated service-learning program also provided a
means for gaining workplace experience and developed a variety of professional skills
for the participants.
In another study by Barth et al. (2014), the integration of the concept of transdis-
ciplinary attitudes into service learning was discussed to support rich and meaningful
learning settings for students. The merging of separate ﬁelds with service learning by
using project-based seminars emerged to be a sustainable way of education. A recent
study by Winberg et al. (2020) also highlighted different curricular and pedagogical

Teaching and Learning Transferable Skills in Engineering Education
345
arrangements that promote engineering students’ employability. Engineering knowledge
and professional skills were prioritised. The review drew on a theoretical framework
that differentiated between engineering knowledge and professional skills to explain
how employability could be included in engineering programmes. Results found an
interdependent relationship between engineering knowledge and professional skills that
enabled engineering graduates to attain employability. However, as engineering students
focus on real-world problems, they tend to work together with others across different
divides. This skill of unravelling complex problems in an interdisciplinary environment
is a much-desired transferable skill.
There is also need to begin to see service learning as a tool that can disrupt the tradi-
tional in-class learning approach. Carnicelli et al. (2017) presented a counter normative
pedagogical approach to learning by linking service learning and transformative edu-
cation with the aim to co-engage educators with students for the purpose of promoting
social justice within the communities. This approach created a framework to enhance
reﬂections and promote ontological reasoning for social justice.
A qualitative assessment of transferable-skill development and attitudinal change of
alumni was studied by Stolley et al. (2017). The study showed that a unique engaged
learning experience can be achieved based on the broad experiences of service learning.
This results in changed stereotypes and broader worldviews, as well as the devel-
opment of transferable skills, including interpersonal and communication skills, leader-
ship, and teamwork. A further study into service-learning assessment was undertaken
by Humphreys et al. (2001). The study encouraged students to take a more proactive
role in assessing their performance via self- and peer-assessment. The development of
group-work, presentation and self- and peer-assessment was investigated for an indus-
trial engineering undergraduate course. The potential for enhancing student learning
through this means could enhance skill development. Students also found groupwork an
enjoyable learning experience.
A case study that showed that skills development is best taught in engineering cur-
ricula through integrated teaching approaches was presented in a study by Chadha
and Nicholls (2006). Their ﬁndings suggested that embedded and bolt-on teaching
approaches are helpful in building and augmenting student awareness in the development
of transferable skills. On the other hand, Krassadaki et al. (2014) showed that skills of
writing, speaking and teamwork could be enhanced by participation in volunteering ser-
vices. A great potential for improvement exists for transferrable skills with service-based
learning especially when coupled with project-based engineering education. Another
study highlighted this initiative and analyses the contribution of the workshops to skills
development. This study indicated that the knowledge and skills gained by the students
are at least on par with gains from traditional project-based learning (Bielefeldt et al.,
2010).
In another study by Marcus et al. (2019), during the Covid-19 lockdown, service
learning was used to improve the students’ generic skills in an online environment. These
skills were sharpened by students’ reﬂections. Their results showed that the design of
the learning environment was effective in promoting the development of generic skills
such as global citizen, scholarship, adaptability and teamwork. This can be promoted

346
E. D. Markus and N. Govender
through the hybrid strategy of service learning that combine both face-to-face and online
delivery.
In summary, most of these studies have shown that service learning could be inher-
ently linked to skills needed for the workplace. Including service learning in the cur-
riculum would not only beneﬁt the community but also the student. In order to create
graduates who are civic minded and transformative, there is need to push for a strong
transformative pedagogy that will not only provide epistemic access but will result in
lifelong learning and a change in the learners’ thinking (Mezirow, 2009, 229). This
means that after leaving the university, learning continues and becomes sustainable. It
is not a means to an end but a lifelong process (Torrance, 2012). SL as a transformative
pedagogy may help achieve this. Engaging with others helps us to transform our deeper
mental habits which has an overarching effect on our frames of reference (Mezirow,
2009, 230).
6
Conclusion
This paper discussed teaching and learning transferable skills in engineering education
via service learning. A case of the faculty of engineering at a university of technology in
South Africa was considered. A survey of selected students showed a poor understanding
of transferable skills. Students realised that they needed to equip themselves with skills
for the workplace, but they did not know how. The unemployment situation in South
Africa has put pressure on students to learn these skills. The importance of service
learning and its link to these skills were espoused. This study has outlined the beneﬁts
of service learning for bridging the gap towards the much-needed transferable skills
critically lacking in the teaching and learning experience of most universities. Including
service learning in the curriculum will not only produce civic minded graduates but
will also prepare them for the workplace. Future research can include conducting a
qualitative analysis on the effect of service-learning inclusion in the curriculum and its
role and inﬂuence in both epistemic and ontological access relating to the much-desired
transferrable skills.

New Forms of Pedagogical Assessment
in Engineering Teacher Education
István Dániel Sanda(B)
Óbuda University, Budapest, Hungary
sanda.daniel@tmpk.uni-obuda.hu
Abstract. Due to the accelerating changes in the (national) economy, the labour
market and in technology, the renewal of technical vocational training is becoming
more and more important. Following the fourth industrial revolution, the Hungar-
ian education government developed and implemented the Vocational Training
4.0 strategy, which deﬁnes the system-wide renewal and further development of
vocational training and adult education. Innovation poses a huge challenge for
teachers working in vocational training. Technical teacher education, including
engineering teacher education, also faces these challenges, as new pedagogical
methods have emerged in addition to traditional forms of education: cooperative
techniques and project-based vocational training. These methods, new to Hungar-
ian vocational education, require an assessment methodology that differs from the
previous student assessment practices and features a more differentiated pedagog-
ical toolbox. The study describes the methodology of developmental assessment
and its implementation into daily teaching. Based on the results of case studies (n
= 96) and of six focus group interviews with former and current teaching students,
it draws attention to the need for the widespread introduction of developmental
assessment. It presents the forms and techniques that can be used in vocational
training through examples.
Keywords: Engineering teacher education · Project-based vocational training ·
Developmental assessment
1
Introduction
Since the change of political regimes (1990), secondary-level vocational training in
Hungary has grappled with numerous problems, which have necessitated the structural
and content renewal of its system.
In Hungary, fewer students participate in vocational training than the European aver-
age. In addition, the dropout rate is high (12%). The number of students leaving the
vocational training without acquiring a diploma has risen year by year, as well as the
number of students who opt out from vocational training after the matriculation exami-
nation, without one or two additional years leading to a technician qualiﬁcation (46%).
Furthermore, a signiﬁcant number of students wish to work in a trade different from
what they learnt in vocational training.

I. D. Sanda
To make matters worse, an ever-growing number of students (almost 30%) arrive
from primary education with a lack of competencies so serious that it makes them unable
to acquire competitive knowledge. There is also a signiﬁcant difference in students’
performance depending on their socio-cultural backgrounds [1].
2
Changes in the System of Vocational Training
The structural and content transformation of vocational training was ﬁrst introduced in
Sept. 2020. The new structure seeks to make secondary-level vocational training more
attractive through ﬁnancial support and career paths. The process of renewal, however,
poses a number of challenges for the teachers in vocational training.
With the introduction of the List of Professions, new professions have emerged
and the content of the Training and Output Requirements and the Curricula have been
renewed, but the preparation of teachers for these rapid changes is lagging behind.
The two school types of the new, school-based vocational training system are the
3-year vocational school and the 5-year secondary modern school, which provides a high
school diploma as well as a technical qualiﬁcation. Dual training is key to both school
types. However, the personal and material conditions of secondary vocational education
vary greatly from one vocational training institution to another. Raising the standard of
vocational training is still a key goal.
In addition to structural changes, online teaching, introduced during the pandemic,
[2]hasalsobeenamajorchallengeforteachers.Theimplementationofeffectiveteaching
requiredopenness, ﬂexibilityandthedevelopment of ICTskills ontheir part. [3] Thehigh
average age and the shortage of teachers, especially new graduates, are also problems
in vocational training.
3
Challenges in Secondary-Level Vocational Training
Students in full-time vocational education belong to Generation Z (born between 1995
and2010).Themajorityoftheirteachers,ontheotherhand,aremembersofGenerationX
(born between 1960 and 1980), with few exceptions. These (sometimes opposing) differ-
ences in values and mentality, resulting from the two-generation age gap, pose challenges
to both teachers and students. (Grandparent-aged teachers teach grandchildren-aged
students.)
The reliability, control, in-depth professionalism, high motivation, cooperation and
precisioncharacterisinggenerationX,referredtoas“digitalimmigrants”intheliterature,
are in contrast with the following main characteristics of the global NET generation Z:
they are born in the smallest families to the oldest mothers; they comprise a generation
smallest in number, they are the most educated, have the longest life expectancy and a
highly developed critical sense.
However, the majority of this multi-media, Internet-connected, “wired” generation
face the following difﬁculties: alienation from the environment, almost exclusively mem-
bers of virtual communities, difﬁcult compliance, failures, lack of companionship, lack
of perspective, rush, lack of conﬂict management skills, temper-management difﬁcul-
ties, aggression. These traits have a tendency to accumulate and may result in a greater
risk of loneliness, anxiety and depression in generation Z populations than ever before.

The Need for Methodological Renewal
“qui male distinquit male docent”.
Our daily teaching experience shows that the above characteristics also have a nega-
tive impact on the school learning motivation and learning performance of this age group.
One of the keys to teacher work and student success is the selection and application of
the most appropriate pedagogical methods from a rich methodological repertoire. On the
one hand, it is essential not only to acquire digital teaching methods, but also to introduce
the practice of collaborative learning [4], cooperative learning [5], problem-based learn-
ing, research-based learning and project teaching into the work of engineering teachers.
On the other hand, it is also our main task to enrich the assessment culture of the future
teachers by introducing the methodology of developmental assessment and putting it
into their daily teaching practice. [6].
In the following, we discuss the methodological possibilities of the assessment and
testing of students, adapted to the needs formulated on the basis of the above-mentioned
characteristics of secondary school age students.
Measuring and Assessing Students Performance
The following aspects provide guidance for student performance assessment within the
school framework.
There are a number of criticisms in the literature related to the assessment of school
performance. The three “goodness indicators” as criteria that each test manual should
provide information on for each speciﬁc test are almost always overlooked when eval-
uating performance within the institutional framework. In our experience, the three test
criteria apply to student performance assessment to such a small extent that assessment
ought not to be risked at all. [7] These indicators are objectivity, reliability and validity,
explained in the following.
Objectivity: the degree of congruence between different assessors in judging the same
student performance,
Reliability:thedegreeofcongruencebetweenrepeatedassessmentsbythesameassessor,
Validity: the degree of “validity” of the assessment criterion which we aim to ﬁnd out
on the basis of assessing school performance.
Criticisms of institutional student performance assessment can be read, among oth-
ers, in the work of Karlheinz Ingenkampf. At the same time, in addition to the legitimate
criticism, we can also ﬁnd suggestions in the literature for improving the practice in the
school. Following a number of individual studies on the subject of grading, Jürgens and
Sacher made recommendations for avoiding more serious errors in the assessment of
student performance and for reducing or eliminating systematic assessment errors. [8].
Moving towards the humanization of assessment, our attention is drawn to an
alternative mode of assessment.
When we talk about the fact that assessment expressed in grades seems problematic
in many respects, and that forms of institutional student assessment should be aimed at
making it more “humane”, it often provokes resentment and sometimes misunderstand-
ing. This approach is defamed (i.e., its good name tarnished or is given a bad name)

352
I. D. Sanda
even before we get to know it. The intent to make school performance assessment more
humane is often defamed to the extent that it seems we want to abolish it altogether.
However, for the optimal progress of the learning process, it is imperative that students
receive feedback on the teacher’s acknowledgement of their learning activity. A more
humane approach to student performance assessment does not mean an intention to use
a less rigorous assessment scale or to “sugar-coat” mistakes made during the learning
process so that students should not even notice that they have made a mistake, let alone
forgoing feedback about the mistake.
Our preferred framework for humane assessment means that in the event of poor or
unsatisfactory student performance, the teacher seeks to understand why it is insufﬁcient
and show how the student could achieve better academic performance.
In Hungarian public educational institutions, students today are still given a less
active role in the assessment process than would be possible. At most, they are only
the recipients of feedback. In many cases, they are left to their own devices as to how
to evaluate their results, how to integrate them into their own learning process or what
further learning strategies to apply in the light of these results. Regarding the practical
application of developmental assessment, a proposition surfaced in British educational
affairs in the late’90s that was both valuable and forward-looking. It deﬁned the goals
- the opportunity for development and progress - in terms of exploring the learning
experience and expanding the forms of assessment, building on student activity.
An important starting point for the application of supportive assessment is the knowl-
edge of the students’ individual characteristics, abilities and circumstances, as these form
the basis for the creation of new knowledge, which is continuously assessed by both the
student and the teacher and is the basis for moving forward.
Supportive assessment is a speciﬁc psychological situation:
a. It can reassure students that what they are doing is right and will lead to results;
b. Or the error must be corrected and the shortcoming remedied.
Achieving the goals of this process, which are seemingly easy, can be halted if
teachers do not know enough about the learning needs, habits and characteristics of their
students,
• Therefore, they prefer to quantify (i.e. give grades) by way of assessment rather than
provide feedback to the student on the quality of their learning;
• They give grades more often to students considered to perform inadequately instead
of supporting their development with learning advice;
• They compare their students to each other too often, which can turn students against
each other and consequently demoralize them, thereby reducing their motivation and
ultimately, their academic success.
Implementing supportive assessment can be facilitated by the teacher’s prior agree-
ment with students at the beginning of the work on the rules for testing the learning
performance.
The following aspects must be included in the agreement:

New Forms of Pedagogical Assessment
353
• The speciﬁc form of testing, e.g. oral, written, workbook/project,
• The rules of announcing the test, e. g. one week prior at the latest,
• The teacher’s duty regarding the correction, e.g. one week after the test at the latest,
• The criteria for assessment, scoring and grading,
• The possibilities for making up for and retaking a test; e.g. a test missed due to illness
must automatically be taken at the ﬁrst lesson after the student’s return to the school,
or each student has one opportunity to retake a test in order to improve their grades,
• Whether (or to what extent) individually undertaken tasks, such as optional or extra
homework, will count towards the ﬁnal grade [9].
It seems commonplace, but it is an inevitable truth that the method of assessment
used by a teacher is crucial in determining the students’ method of learning.
Organising Learning on the Basis of Student Activity
If the learning process is to be built upon the mutual and continuous consensus of the
teacher and the students, only the kind of assessment can be supportive where:
• Students actively take part in the planning and implementation of the assessment
process;
• Assessment continuously follows and supports the learning process, thus making it
possible to plan the next step in accordance with the student;
• Testing serves not only to make student reproduce knowledge but also provides an
opportunity to identify the components of the competencies to be developed, because
the aim is to create knowledge as opposed to reproduce it;
• Assessment should, as far as possible, concern life-like situations; that is, ones that
point to real-life, out-of-school problems.
Supportive assessment not only seeks to make statements about a student’s learning
performance, but also to interpret development in order for the teacher and student to
make decisions together about how to move forward.
In addition, evaluation can also be “developmental”.
5
Developmental Assessment
Developmental assessment is the assessment of improvement and understanding through
frequent, interactive methods, which allow the teacher to apply personalized teaching
methods that better meet the recognized needs of learners!
Developmental assessment, however, is only viable if the goals of teaching are in
some way understood and embraced by the students themselves. Involving students in
the learning process is essential. “We start from here and want to get here. You are here
now, and this is what we need to do to move forward.” This is the motto of developmental
evaluation [10].
Thus, developmental assessment is always individual-oriented evaluation. Con-
versely, individual-oriented evaluation can be considered identical to developmental
assessment if its application is continuous in the teaching-learning process.

354
I. D. Sanda
Today’sinterpretationofdevelopmentalassessmentgoesbeyondtheconsciousappli-
cation of exploring the situation, diagnosis, and the role of facilitating the learning pro-
cess. The use of learning organization procedures built around developmental assess-
ment differs from situational assessment in that it is primarily a preventive approach,
while diagnostic assessment is a pedagogical practice that seeks out the most common
shortcomings and deﬁciencies and focuses on remedying them.
Developmental assessment differs from summative, qualifying assessment in that the
information gathered during the developing process is not intended to provide a summary
of students’ learning performance, but is instead used to plan their development.
At the same time, we must also see that the focus is not on acquiring knowledge, as
in today’s rapidly changing world, much of the knowledge content is rapidly becoming
obsolete. It is more important to develop the students’ learning ability, which allows
them to continue learning later. This includes teaching students to evaluate their own
knowledge and learning process.
The Practice of Developmental Assessment
Developmental assessment came about in the late 1990s by further extending forma-
tive assessment, based on the wok of Black and William. The two researchers aimed
to improve student performance in British schools through the promotion of formative
assessment. Their research was justiﬁed by the fact that input (curriculum) and output
(exams) regulations had already received sufﬁcient attention among the elements of the
education system, but the learning process had not; in fact, it was called a black box
of education. Subsequently, in 2002, the OECD’s Centre for Educational Research and
Innovation began studying the development approach in lower secondary schools in eight
countries. The results of the research were published in Hungary by the National Insti-
tute of Public Education in 2005 by the title “Developmental Assessment – Classroom
Methods for Improving Learning in Secondary Education”.
The OECD Deﬁnition of Developmental Assessment
Developmental assessment is the frequent, interactive assessment of students’ develop-
ment and knowledge, with the aim of deﬁning learning goals and adapting teaching to
them. Thus, developmental assessment is not the same as formative assessment because
it focuses on the process of development and does not primarily focus on achieving
external goals [11].
Based on the above, it is already clear that, contrary to previous practice, the new,
systematic approach also requires teachers to consider assessment as an integral part of
the learning-teaching process.
The essence of the change in attitudes is that the teacher has to deﬁne the requirements
for the learning performance at the beginning of the learning-teaching process instead
of at the end. Only after the deﬁnition of the assessment strategies should teachers begin
to consider what teaching methods, strategies, materials, tools and tasks are the most
appropriate to achieve the desired learning outcomes.

New Forms of Pedagogical Assessment
355
6
Survey on the Methodological Culture of Teacher Assessment
and Testing
The aim of our research conducted between 2018 and 2021 was to explore the method-
ological culture of teachers, with particular reference to the application of developmental
assessment. Our research questions were the following:
• What assessment methods are the surveyed teachers familiar with?
• Which evaluation methods do they use on a monthly, weekly or daily basis?
• What examples of using developmental assessment in their own teaching do they list?
• How often do they use the examples mentioned in the case studies?
In our study, we evaluated the results of 96 case studies and 6 focus group interviews.
Participating teachers have been in the teaching profession for an average of 20.5 years,
so they have extensive experience.
Theyknowthetraditionalassessmentmethods-diagnostic,formativeandsummative
assessment - well and apply them in their own school teaching in accordance with legal
requirements.
The typical uses of diagnostic assessment are testing students at the beginning of
each academic year and the placement tests given to them prior to dividing the class into
learning groups.
Due to its nature and the characteristics of the Hungarian public education system,
summative assessment is the most important form of assessment. The surveyed teachers
give their students ﬁnal tests on a particular topic once a month on average. In addi-
tion, summative assessment is used when a project or a major unit of the curriculum is
completed, as well as at the end of terms, academic years and on the occasion of the
matriculation (school-leaving) and various professional examinations.
Formative assessment is the practice of everyday life that interweaves nearly all
teaching processes. Its typical forms are oral presentations, quizzes and ﬁnal tests, the
common features of which is that the teacher discusses the correct and incorrect answers
with the student or group of students and makes suggestions on how to correct mistakes
and avoid them in the future. Most of the surveyed teachers use this form of assessment
on a daily basis.
The focus of the case studies was the presentation of forms of developmental
assessment as “good practices”. Within the framework of this paper, we only have
the opportunity to present a few examples in the following subsection.
The Practice of Developmental Assessment Among Teachers Participating
in the Study
As it has already become clear from the above, the school evaluation system of Hungar-
ian public education is not prepared for the system-wide application of developmental
evaluation. This is why it is of particular importance how our former and current stu-
dents apply and further develop in their own everyday teaching the modern assessment
techniques they have acquired during their university education.

and peer assessment competencies. Teachers ﬁnd that developing both the abilities of

b) Relating to the above example, I quote the following thoughts from a case study
for the developmental assessment of group work:

New Forms of Pedagogical Assessment
357
“One can also prefer group work because it is not the individual performance
that is assessed, and just as success and merit are shared among the members,
so is the experience of failure. Group competitions generally favour students with
lesser abilities, so it is advisable to try to create heterogeneous groups in terms of
abilities and to give a sensitive assessment of the common product.”
Hollenbeck and Klein describe the impact that a community can have on individual
motivation due to the fact that the individual’s commitment to greater challenges is
adapted to the level of commitment of those around them. For the less able student, this
form of assessment is motivating because if an individual feels that he or she is following
the norms accepted by others and has to adapt to accepted standards, he or she seeks to
adjust the level of his or her own performance to that of the collective performance [12].
The rules of assessment, also to be followed after oral “tests”, presentations,
completed tasks and reports:
• Avoid using labels
• Express our feelings
• Avoid saying offensive or hurtful words
• Do not over-value
• Explain why it was helpful for us to listen to the report, presentation, oral test, or view
the completed work.
• Justify our opinion on the content and presentation.

c) Many teachers use gamiﬁcation in a wide variety of subjects. One of our surveyed
teachers made his students interested in performance assessment with an application-
supported programme based on computer character-development games, which can be
used on both a computer and a telephone application. The programme, developed by
English teachers, works automatically and includes all the elements of gamiﬁcation
systems. Its name, Caerusia, is derived from the Greek word ‘search’ (choice), referring

358
I. D. Sanda
to the students’ ability to choose individual learning paths in the game. The application is
present in every lesson, as it can best be used in the classroom setting, but all the related
administration is completed online. Reward points for students’ classroom activity, good
behaviour, preparedness and individual or group performance are registered in the app
[13].
The motivating features of the gamiﬁed assessment and feedback system were
emphasised by the teacher. The purpose of the teaching-learning process in a gamiﬁed
context is to facilitate engagement by activating both intrinsic and extrinsic motivating
factors. One of these is rewards, which are classic elements of gamiﬁcation in order to
achieve levels, collect reward points, compete and be ranked. Points are key indicators of
performance, feedback tools and quantiﬁed markers of win-states. Following the main
components of reward systems, we can talk about the Points, Badges, Leaderboards
(PBL) model, based on the typical reward system of computer games [14].
d) Students are pleased and inspired by taking on the role of teacher. Using the
following method, students have a chance to practice the material three times, almost
unnoticed. Students are given the task of compiling a test of the given material, consisting
of various task types, instructions, scores and grading criteria. They have to write down
the correct answers in their notebooks. Thus, they have revised the material once. Then,
they swap the prepared tests and complete one designed by a classmate, using any source
or help they want. This is followed by the correction of the tests: everyone corrects the
one they had created. This is the third time the material is revised. The students score
and grade the tests and then return them for review to the student who had completed
it. They discuss any issues that may arise. Although not ofﬁcially recorded, the grades
received from each other are still important to students.
Students’ motivation is increased by being allowed to have a say in the process of
learning and testing.
e) For the evaluation of a lesson by students, the Wheel of Fortune, available on
wordwall.net, can be used. Students selected at random or by a draw can go to the
teacher’s laptop at the end of the lesson and spin the virtual wheel of fortune. Their task
is to complete the sentence by which they rate that particular lesson. For example, Today
I learned that ……; It would have been better if ……; I would have liked to…….; I
could have helped more with the task which……; In today’s lesson, what I least liked
was…… and similar sentences are provided by the Wheel of Fortune to be completed
by students.
f) A well-known technique for developmental assessment is the trafﬁc light method.
With this, students can use a simple sign to indicate how much they have understood a
particular material. Before moving on, the teacher can check the students’ understanding.
Students hold up the green sign when they understood everything, the yellow sign when
they understand but are not sure of their knowledge yet, and the red sign when they do
not understand. When a large number of yellow or red signs are shown, the teacher will
go over the given material again with the whole class and later put in extra time with the
students who still show a red sign afterwards.
A version of this method, which can be applied across all age-groups, was recorded
in a case study.

New Forms of Pedagogical Assessment
359
For example, we could start a source analysis by underlining the words in it with
one of three colours. Students use a green pencil to underline the words they already
know, a yellow pencil for the words they have heard but not sure of their meaning, and a
red pencil for unknown words and phrases. We then collect the words underlined in red
and discuss their meanings together. It is not as time consuming a task as it is useful in
exploring unfamiliar words. The only preparation it takes on the students’ part is to bring
the three colours of pencils, and for the teacher to photocopy the appropriate number of
texts to be distributed.
g) A learning diary is a document of the learning process, kept by the student, serv-
ing as written communication between teacher and student. This “record” may contain
various notes and the form and frequency of its use are best established by the teacher
in conjunction with the student. The teacher looks into it and reﬂects on it, but does not
grade it. Keeping a learning diary reinforces students’ sense of responsibility for their
own learning, of the role of conscious planning and analysis, and also provides a sense
of success.
Extending teacher reﬂections can be a joint analysis of a student’s learning process. A
personal relationship based on trust can help students ﬁnd successful learning strategies;
that is, it helps them learn to learn and become a more successful student [15].
7
Summary
Our research conducted between 2018 and 2021 among our engineering teacher students
drew attention to the need for a methodological renewal of pedagogical assessment. The
aim of the survey was to map the evaluation culture of engineering teachers. Based on the
analysis of 96 case studies, we can conclude that the teachers participating in the survey
prefer the traditional, frontal teaching methods that they had once seen and learned from
their own teachers. Also, with a few exceptions, they assess their students using the same
methods and procedures as had been used by their teachers in secondary school.
Focus group interviews with our students showed that prospective engineering teach-
ers are open to new assessment and testing methods. They expressed positive opinions
about cooperative and collaborative teaching methods, research- and problem-based
learning and the project method. However, the practical application of these divided
opinions: some students were happy to try them in practice, but a small proportion
of students feared that non-traditional, unconventional methods such as self- and peer
evaluation would upset the order in the classroom, perhaps distort the evaluation of a
student’s performance or even reduce the effectiveness of teaching.
In engineering teacher education, we can help enrich the methodological culture of
assessment and testing by offering proven assessment methods for speciﬁc pedagogi-
cal situations in addition to theoretical knowledge, i.e. by providing our students with
knowledge that can be applied in everyday classroom and workshop practice.

Students’ Behaviour in Stressful Situations
in Diverse Cultures
Judit Módné Takács
, Monika Pogátsnik
, and István Simonics(B)
Óbuda University, Bécsi út 96/B, 1034 Budapest, Hungary
{modne.t.judit,pogatsnik.monika}@amk.uni-obuda.hu,
simonics.istvan@tmpk.uni-obuda.hu
Abstract. Students experience signiﬁcant stress during their training. At the same
time, good stress management skills are also extremely important soft skills at
their future workplace. Educational institutions have recognized the importance
of developing stress management programs for students. In our study, we review
the most common stressful situations in students’ life and how the school can help
students deal with stress.
In our research, we aimed to examine the causes of stress in students’ life in
three different countries, the Netherlands, Hungary, and Uzbekistan. We assessed
the tools used in stress management and the coping strategies used by students in
speciﬁc cases. During the 2020–2021 school year, the survey was conducted over
two semesters in a mixed educational environment (normal, hybrid, online).
Students from the examined countries most often highlighted reading, music,
and other hobbies as their solutions to stress. Positive thoughts and awareness
also appeared in large numbers among students. We tried to group the problems
listed and observe how similar difﬁculties students encountered. The answers were
mostly related to school life, such as difﬁculties arising from the exam situation
or difﬁculties related to school tasks. In addition, problems in private life and at
work were also explained.
Keywords: Stress management · Higher education · Engineering student
1
Introduction
The university period can be a stressful experience for many students, social and aca-
demic pressures can be major challenges for them. Stress is not just a harmful effect, but it
also helps to adapt to the environment, and cope with the challenges. Problems arise when
stress becomes chronic. Important levels of school stress can have consequences in stu-
dents’ lives [1], such as various psychosomatic and somatic or even school burnout symp-
toms. Knowledge of the factors that are a source of stress for students can enhance stu-
dents’ well-being and stress management skills. During their training, university students
face concerns such as adapting to a new environment, expectations about academic per-
formance, overwork, concerns about future employment opportunities [2, 3], and other
social and ﬁnancial concerns [4]. These factors are often considered to be stressful by
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 361–371, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_37

362
J. Módné Takács et al.
students and can cause signiﬁcant damage to their performance as well as their health [4,
5].
Promoting students’ ability to cope with everyday learning challenges and pressures
can signiﬁcantly reduce school stress experiences [6]. If students think they have enough
resources to overcome failures and control their workload, they can perceive challenging
situations as more positive and less stressful. Teachers can also help their students how
to deal with stress and cope with difﬁculties [7].
Educational institutions have recognized the importance of developing stress man-
agement programs for students [8–10]. At the same time, good stress management skills
are also extremely important soft skills [11, 12] at their future workplace.
Students can use different coping strategies [13, 14], such as problem-focused and
emotion-focused coping, or maladaptive coping which might work in the short run, but
is detrimental to their well-being in the longer run. Resilience is the ability to bounce
back from adversities and grow from them. Everyone can be resilient; we frequently
refer to resiliency as an individual trait, it also involves learnable skills, knowledge, and
techniques.
Stress leads to a variety of mental and emotional problems, such as anxiety, depres-
sion, and overwhelm. Anxiety is one of the most common forms of mental illness. Social
anxiety is used to describe feelings of anxiety and fear that occurs in response to social
situations, which is a common phenomenon among students [15, 16].
2
Stress Management with Different Cultural Backgrounds
In our research about stressful situations in students’ lives, and the stress management
tools students use, we had the opportunity to ask questions from students studying
technology in diverse cultures. We asked Uzbek students studying in Central Asia,
Hungarian and Dutch students from Europe the same questions. Before presenting the
results of our research, we should ﬁrst take a little look at the three countries, the cultural
background of our research, the training system, and when students meet work ﬁrst.
The current students are members of Generation Z, the so-called millennials, who
were born around the turn of the millennium. They are the so-called digital natives, for
them it is almost impossible to exist without the use of the internet, mobile phones, and
laptops.
In Hungary, most full-time university students are in the 19–25 age group. Some of
them started university after having completed 8 years of primary school and 4 years of
high school, while others are beyond 2 years of technical training and a profession. A
different school background means different experiences in the world of work. Anyone
who has obtained a technical qualiﬁcation has already gained practical, on-the-job expe-
rience. A sizeable proportion of full-time students work in addition to studying. There is
a remarkable number of students in dual training in technical higher education. In con-
trast to traditional training, they are dual trainees of an industrial company in addition
to university. This means working one day a week during the university period (autumn
semester 13 weeks, spring semester 13 weeks) and ﬁve days a week for the rest of the
year. In addition to their full-time studies, many of the students in traditional education
have already been working partly in a professional environment of their study ﬁeld and

Students’ Behaviour in Stressful Situations in Diverse Cultures
363
partly in other student work, often through a student cooperative. Thus, full-time students
are typically part of the world of work in addition to the required 6–8-week internship.
Therefore, in terms of sources of stress, both university-related and employment-related
as well as personal factors are worth examining in their case.
In the Netherlands, students who opt for a technical education go through the fol-
lowing trajectory: Children go to primary school from the age of four. There they go
through eight grades. Around the age of 12, the children must make the ﬁrst choice. The
technology students mainly come from VMBO (pre-vocational secondary education).
In addition to this choice, you can also choose between HAVO (higher general educa-
tion) and VWO (pre-university education). There are also various levels within VMBO,
but students of the highest level are admitted to secondary vocational education (MBO,
level 4). At the age of about 16, students enter secondary technical vocational education.
There are the levels 2, 3 and 4. The full-time level 4 courses last for 4 years, in which
almost all years are pieces of practical vocational training. In addition to these full-time
courses, there are also part-time courses, where students work for 3 days for a company
and come to school for 2 days for general education. At the age of about 20, students
can complete a level 4 education. In addition to secondary vocational education (MBO),
there are also technical courses at higher vocational education (HBO) and universities.
In Uzbekistan, the majority of full-time bachelor students in a Higher Education
Institution are between 19–23 years old, and master students are in the 24–26 age group.
Most of them came to the institution after having completed 11 years of school (includ-
ing 4 years in primary and 7 years in high school), while others are beyond 3 years
of vocational/ professional colleges (they are awarded with profession diplomas) and
academic lyceums (provide exact knowledge for entering HEIs). A different education
in the school background means different experiences in the world of work. Those who
have obtained a technical qualiﬁcation could gain good practice on job experience. Apart
from studying at a university, a particular proportion of full-time students work in dif-
ferent places in order to earn some money for paying their tuition fee or just to increase
the income no matter if they get monthly stipend/scholarship or not. There is a remark-
able number of students in dual training in technical higher education. In contrast to
traditional training, they are dual trainees of an industrial company in addition to uni-
versity. This means working two days a week during the university period and four days
a week for the rest of the year. Moreover, to their full-time studies, most of the students
in traditional education have already been working partly in a professional environment
of their study ﬁeld and partly in other student work, often through a student coopera-
tive. Thus, full-time students are typically part of the world of work in addition to the
required 6–8-week internship. In terms of sources of stress, both university-related and
employment-related as well as personal factors are worth examining in their case.
3
Participants, Methods, and Instruments
The research primarily focused on students’ stress management skills. The study aims to
identify the most common causes of stress in education in students’ daily lives. Tools and
coping strategies used to manage stress were assessed. Stress management is a critical
need for workers in the rapidly changing world of the 21st century. Along with stress

364
J. Módné Takács et al.
management, the study examines the learners’ environments to compare and highlight
cultural characteristics. The conclusion is inductive. This research is based on an online
questionnaire survey using a targeted sampling technique. A total of 202 students partic-
ipated in the survey, with details of N = 102 Hungarian students, N = 63 Dutch students
and N = 37 Uzbek students.
The research questions focus on the signiﬁcant stress triggers, students’ tools used
to cope with stress, coping strategies, the impact of external stressors on academic
performance and the available help-seeking options used by students. The survey is
composed of explicit, open-ended questions. This methodology combines the advantages
of a personal interview and the quantitative questionnaire method. The use of an online
format facilitates collecting more conﬁdential responses to questions, and anonymity
helps participants to respond more honestly.
4
Results
The survey results provided by the questionnaire were examined through basic statistical
analysis, exploring the average scores and the patterns of data distribution. The sample
demographic representation overall is 73% male (N = 148) and 27% female (N = 54),
showing that women are signiﬁcantly underrepresented in our sample. Regarding the
ﬁeld of study, 86% of respondents are studying STEM (science, technology, engineering,
mathematics) ﬁelds, such as engineering, geoinformatics, computer science, and labora-
tory technology. The method of sampling used indicates that the results of the research
are not generalizable and further sampling would be necessary. In all three countries
combined, more than 80% of respondents are aged between 18 and 22.
4.1
Analysis of Stressors and Stress Factors
The survey started by looking at the stressors and sources of stress most experienced
by students in higher education. The results are presented in Table 1. The aggregated
results show that 40% of respondents highlighted school and exam-related stressors. As
a large part of their lives is linked to education, it is natural that education appears as a
prominent source of stress.
Examining the results for each country has a different pattern of stressors. A quarter
of Uzbek students highlighted relationships and family, while this area was less promi-
nent among Dutch and Hungarian students. School and exams were identiﬁed as less
signiﬁcant sources of stress by Hungarian students, while work and ﬁnancial problems
and the feeling of pressure to conform were highlighted by Hungarian students compared
to students from the other two countries. For Dutch students, school and exams are the
most difﬁcult things to cope with and the most stressful.

4.2
Exploration of the Stress Management Tools/Methods Applied
The methods and tools used to manage stress can be described overall as positive thoughts
and mindfulness, as well as various hobbies, listening to music and reading activities,
which are the most prevalent among respondents, but not uniformly the most prominent
in terms of their distribution across countries. These techniques are used by 35% of
Hungarian respondents, 42% of Dutch respondents and 66% of Uzbek respondents in
stressful situations. Figure 1 illustrates the regional variation by country in the tools and
methods that students prefer to use when dealing with stress.
Students in Hungary prefer to play sports and relieve stress more than students in
Uzbekistan,witha12%differencebetweenthetwocountries.Incontrast,Uzbekstudents
opt for mental stress management rather than the use of physical therapy, as can be seen
from the graph in Fig. 1, showing the difference in this response compared to Hungarian
and Dutch students.
4.3
Analysis of Stress Management Presented Through a Concrete Situation
Survey respondents were asked to give a real-life example of a problem they had success-
fully or unsuccessfully solved. N = 133 speciﬁc situations were explained by respon-
dents, while N = 69 students did not answer this question. It is possible that this was
a too personal question for them, and they did not want to share a concrete example.
When asked how they have coped with the stressful situation presented, the unanimous
response, 80%, was awareness and avoidance, two completely contradictory ways of
coping. Uzbek students were 47% aware, 40% preferred distraction, Hungarian students
were slightly more aware at 53% and avoidance was only 26%, but the most aware were
