4.4
Exploring External Signs of Stress Among Students
The responses of the students surveyed do not differ between countries in terms of how
noticeable they are to others if they are stressed. There is a 30:70 ratio between not
noticeable and visible to the outside observer. 70% of the students have difﬁculties in
controlling and managing stressful situations, they do not have the routine and practice to
handle these situations easily. The most common symptoms are illustrated and presented
in Fig. 4, with distributions by country.
The results show that students’ stress management skills need to be greatly improved.
Many students ﬁnd it difﬁcult to control their emotions, some even report aggression
in stressful moments. Mood changes are also a common symptom, and concerning the
answers to the previous questions, this can often lead to the use of drugs/alcohol to alter
attitudes, or it affects their ability to manage relationships. The results show that Uzbek
students are more likely to exhibit psychological coping strategies (67% of respondents)
such as mood swings, introversion, and isolation, while physical symptoms such as
facial ﬂushing, and shaking are less common. In Hungarian students, on the contrary,

psychological coping (only 16% of student responses) is less common, with physical
symptoms being more prevalent.
4.5
Identifying the Use and Direction of Requesting Help in a Stressful Situation
In a stressful situation, asking for help is a tough process. The previous results of the
survey show that students can recognize difﬁcult situations and indicate clearly that most
of them cannot cope with them. In many cases, it is difﬁcult for people who need help
to ask for it, and there are also situations where they ask the wrong person for help. The
aim was to ﬁnd out if the survey participants dare to ask for help in a situation of need
and, preferably, to whom they would go.
In Fig. 5, the percentage of responding students who use external help is shown
by country, while Table 2 highlights the type and nature of external help. Hungarian
and Dutch students gave almost similar answers to the question concerning the use of
external help in stressful situations. Half of the respondents use it and the other half try
to solve the problem on their own, suppress their feelings, and psychological problems
or even hide their physical symptoms from the outside world.
Examining the types of external help sought, one of the main results is that Uzbek
students mentioned only parents as the only people they seek advice from in various
stressful situations, but Fig. 5 shows that this is the case for the one-ﬁfth of respondents.
Hungarian and Dutch students identiﬁed family, relatives, and friends as the overwhelm-
ing majority. None of these choices indicates professionals, so the direction for seeking
help previously explained is not always the appropriate one and it may not always be the
right one to get help from these sources. This mainly occurs when students choose from
their own age group, from the same environment where the same problems are present,
often hidden from the environment as we have seen from the answers.
50% of students in all countries know that there is a professional in their educational
institution to whom they can turn for help at any time. However, the answers show that

they do not turn to them for help. Many students mention introversion as a barrier, but
others simply do not trust this form of help, do not know how to open up to a stranger

4.6
Examining Correlations in the Light of Successful Coping Outcomes
The correlation coefﬁcients can be examined in terms of the methods, tools and help
used in stressful situations, and the magnitude of the correlation indicates its strength.
A correlation of r = 0.573 indicates a strong positive correlation between successful
coping in stressful situations and the methods used in stressful situations when examining
mindfulness. By awareness, we mean all skills that help to cope with stress, such as time
management skills, self-conﬁdence development and self-control.
Parallel to these results, there is a positive correlation of r = 0.461 between unsuc-
cessful coping with stressful situations and coping strategies such as ignoring and letting

370
J. Módné Takács et al.
go. So, those who prefer not to deal with problems, despite recognizing them, not try-
ing to deal with known stressful situations, not conducting self-examination in these
situations and not improving their skills, are more likely to have unsuccessful coping
attempts.
5
Discussion and Conclusion
Our research on the topic of stress management was especially interesting because we
also examined the attitudes of students of similar ages studying in a similar ﬁeld in three
different cultures, in the Netherlands, in Hungary and in Uzbekistan. The purpose of the
research was to map the stressors and the stress management experience of the students,
so that we could plan an appropriate English-language curriculum that students in each
country could use.
We examined the similarities and the differences of the students. The biggest source
of stress in their current life is school, but it appears to a slightly lesser extent among
Hungarian students. In the case of Uzbek students, in addition to school, family and
relationship problems were also signiﬁcant sources of stress, which was common to a
lesser extent for European students.
Different methods have been used in stress management. Uzbek students prefer to
read and listen to music above the average, while Hungarian students choose sports
activities. In the case of the coping strategies applied in speciﬁc cases, the awareness of
the students of each country was higher than the avoidance, but in a different proportion.
The biggest difference was in the assessment of the stress management situation, with
Dutchstudents evaluatingtheir results several times morepositivelythanUzbekstudents.
Students in all three countries have reported different physical and mental symp-
toms caused by stressful situations, which is why it is so important to develop stress
management techniques and prepare the students for their conscious use.
Uzbek students are the least willing to turn for outside help and almost exclusively
turn to their parents in stressful situations. Hungarian students are happy to turn to their
friends in addition to their parents, while Dutch students mostly turn to their friends for
support. Uzbek students do not ask for professional help at all, whereas Hungarians, and
Dutch do so to a small extent.
Based on our research, we can conclude that the development of a stress manage-
ment curriculum would be particularly useful for students in all three countries. It is
an important skill not only in dealing with their current school problems, but also in
resistance and resilience in the world of work.

Why is It so Difﬁcult to Apply Student-Centered
Approach?
Silviano Rafael(B)
and Júlia Justino
ESTSetúbal and CINEA, Polytechnic Institute of Setúbal, Campus do IPS, Estefanilha,
2914-508 Setúbal, Portugal
silviano.rafael@estsetubal.ips.pt
Abstract. It is common to think about generational differences. However, it is rare
for the teaching-learning process to adapt to the characteristics of new generation
students that currently attend courses in higher education. Despite the Bologna
directives proposing student-centered approach for the new generation curricu-
lums, this implementation process is still far from complete. This paper presents
the pedagogical methodologies most applied in a Portuguese higher educational
institution of engineering and the difﬁculties in implementing the student-centered
approach from the institutional point of view and from the teacher’s point of view.
Also, possible solutions are proposed for the different points of view, giving the
reasoning for the application of the student-centered approach.
Keywords: Student-centered approach · Research in engineering pedagogy ·
Engineering pedagogy education · Generation Z
1
Introduction
Generational changes enforce different student proﬁles with their own characteristics.
Generation Z that currently access engineering courses at Portuguese higher educational
institutions meets a training system that is still not very ﬂexible.
Generation Z is characterized by young people born in a digital environment, used to
getting answers and information very quickly, hyperconnected, communicative, critical,
with a strong social and environmental responsibility, pragmatic and undeﬁned in gender,
class or age [1]. However, they have difﬁculty in dealing with the work routine and
frustration, preferring an immediate lifestyle which makes them more vulnerable to
emotional disorders [2, 3]. In formative terms, the teacher-centered approach is not
in line with the focus instability of these students. Also, this restlessness that brings
a new way of being and learning, supported by the still not fully integrated Bologna
declaration into the courses’ curriculum, despite having passed about 23 years since it
was signed [4], mainly based on student-centered approach, is a new challenge that needs
to be considered in the training offer of this generation. In fact, without clear, concise
and duly supported ministerial guidance on adapting higher educational programmes to
Bologna’s objectives, the task of implementing the pedagogy referred to in the treaty,
so necessary to generation Z’s training, is left to the discretion of higher educational

M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 372–379, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_38

373
institutions. Within the European framework, efforts are being made to “add cooperation
in innovative learning and teaching practices as another hallmark of the EHEA” [5],
contributing with several teaching-learning recommendations: the ﬁrst being to make
student-centered learning a reality by 2030, the second fostering future teaching and
the third strengthening higher educational institutions’ and systems’ capacity to support
learning and teaching.
2
Institutional Challenge
Within the Portuguese framework, there is a national regulatory vacuum in terms of
effective support. So, higher educational institutions do not feel the urgent need to
adapt their teaching-learning process to student-centered approach, in addition to the
lack of ﬁnancial availability, due to budgetary constraints, which make them impossible
to afford the teachers’ investment in new pedagogical skills to foster the changeover
from the traditional teacher-centered approach to the student-centered approach. Over
and above these, it is necessary to coexist an institutional culture of openness for the
application of adapted and innovative pedagogical techniques, promoting support for
the application of different learning styles according to the needs and training interest
of each course or curricular unit. In this context, higher educational institutions face a
framework of challenges and difﬁculties whose resolution depends a lot on the objectives
and management methods of the institutional leaders, the priorities they establish and
the beliefs and convictions they have about pedagogical methodologies.
Regarding the European recommendations, Portuguese higher educational institu-
tions are ineffective because there produce unclear indications concerning the imple-
mentation of the student-centered approach or, if any, few of them offer a coherent path
for the development and implementation of measures leading to the application of the
student-centered approach in a generalized way. This means that, in the absence of clear
and concrete directives with institutional backing and follow-up, the change of peda-
gogical methodology in a Portuguese higher educational institution is very much up
to the goodwill of the teacher in the domain of his action to apply it or not. Although
there are occasional trainings on active learning techniques, or more general pedagogical
training, these are usually insufﬁcient and of little consequence for a true change in the
pedagogical paradigm.
3
Pedagogical Methodologies Applied
Taking into account the particular case of Setúbal School of Technology of the Poly-
technic Institute of Setúbal, which has more than 25 higher educational programmes of
technology and engineering degrees involving more than 250 teachers in more than 500
course units, it is possible to take a broad view of the pedagogical methodologies applied
in theoretical or theoretical-practical classes of technology or engineering degrees in a
Portuguese higher educational institution, which can be divided into four groups.
The ﬁrst group is identiﬁed by the pedagogical approach mostly applied in course
units of cross-cutting scientiﬁc areas, the content-centered approach (CC), characterized

374
S. Rafael and J. Justino
by the strict follow-up of the course unit’s syllabus. Students assume a passive attitude
in learning a classic document, which requires great focus and concentration.
The second group is established by the vast majority of the faculty staff which applies
the teacher-centered approach (TC), characterized by the passivity of students in class-
room while the teacher exposes the content’s course unit as he pleases. In this context,
the teacher is the agent that deﬁnes and disseminates the subjects and its knowledge and
the only responsible for students’ learning.
Although the student-centered approach (SC) is often mentioned and praised in
several pedagogical research works, its practical implementation is complex, it has the
special feature of being gradual and it is characterized by active participation of students
in their learning, relating the course unit’s contents to the students’ basic knowledge.
This means that student-centered approach may vary between where the learning context
is directed to the limit of full freedom of choice of the contents students want to learn [6].
So, there is a high degree of freedom that requires a balance between understanding the
learningneedsofstudentswhoareattendingthecourseandthestructureoftheknowledge
to be learned in the context of the course unit. This balance depends on the proﬁle of
the students, the subjects involved and the learning objectives to be achieved, requiring
detailed and speciﬁc planning. This pedagogical approach, unlike the previous two,
allows the application of a wide range of active teaching-learning techniques depending
on the aforementioned balance. This makes the student-centered approach very rich in
terms of pedagogical resources but difﬁcult to apply due to the variety of active learning
techniques when one does not have the knowledge nor the necessary experience for its
implementation. For a successful implementation of the student-centered approach, it is
crucial to develop the entire pedagogical structure of the course unit, properly aligned
with the learning outcomes, the contents, the resources, the active techniques to apply, the
means of formative and summative assessment to be carried out and the feedback given
to the student related to each learning objective [7]. Due to this complexity, monitoring
and ensuring effective pedagogical support is essential for teachers who are new to this
pedagogical methodology.
The last group is characterized by a combination of the previous approaches (Mix),
normally performed by teachers who are in a pedagogical methodology transition phase
or experiencing the application of some good pedagogical practices or stand-alone active
learning techniques. It is a normal consequence of the search for adaptation of the
teaching methods to the characteristics of new students, however, in most cases, without
a good pedagogical support structure.
A perception of the approximate distribution of the pedagogical approaches afore-
mentioned applied in theoretical or theoretical-practical classes of technology or engi-
neering degrees in a Portuguese higher educational institution is presented in Fig. 1,
based on the information system platform data of the institution combined with the
assessment maps of the course units. It can be noted that 68% of the theoretical and
theoretical-practical classes apply traditional pedagogical methodologies (CC and TC),
which represents a large majority of this universe of course units, while the remaining
32% course units apply a pedagogical method closer to student-centered approach.
For any higher educational institution that highlights the contribution of innovative
pedagogical methodologies to enhance the quality and excellence of its students’ training

and training weaknesses of generation Z, a real challenge to be discussed and overcome.
From the student’s point of view, which is the main target of the teaching-learning
process, the student-centered approach stands as a landmark of pedagogical method-
ologies due to the greater proximity and communication of the teacher, as well as the
transparency in teaching-learning activities and in the course unit’s learning objectives.
Also, the typical pedagogical alignment of the student-centered approach, under a certain
degree of freedom of choice in the learning environment, is recognized as more moti-
vating, providing the acquisition of transversal skills which contributes to the success of
the student academic performance [8].
4
Teaching Challenges
The pressure by higher educational institutions on academic staff to develop more
research work is well known, which leads teachers to develop a lot of technical and
scientiﬁc research work in their areas of knowledge to have a higher ranking in their
careers. Hence, the pedagogical research work carried out by teachers of technology
or engineering areas is often undervalued and many times not even considered in their
evaluation performance, with the argument that pedagogy is not their scientiﬁc area.
However, one of the difﬁculties that is reﬂected in the course units’ available data and
in the teachers’ interviews is the lack of practical knowledge on the student-centered
approach, its techniques, good practices and implementation rules which makes the
pedagogical transition process complex and difﬁcult to apply without adequate training
and support. In fact, this pedagogical methodology requires from the teacher a signiﬁcant
knowledge of pedagogical concepts and techniques and also an initial effort on planning
a new pedagogical structure which has to be designed to interconnect the technical and
scientiﬁc learning outcomes of the course unit with the attitudes and skills of the students,
along with suitable didactic resources, providing a fruitful learning environment which
facilitates the student’s learning [9]. The teacher must be open-minded and prepared to
leave his comfort zone of traditional classes, with the ability to promote and apply more
creative, integrative and rewarding solutions in case of different situations in the domain
of the student-centered approach.
According to Dweck [10] most individuals in society have a ﬁxed mindset and teach-
ers, unfortunately, are not the exception. This kind of mindset is characterized by teachers

376
S. Rafael and J. Justino
with difﬁculty in getting out of their comfort zone when facing the challenges that the
implementation of other pedagogical methodologies imposes, exacerbating a range of
arguments to discredit or oppose failed or poorly tested previous implementations.
A common mistake is to believe that by applying an active technique in the context of
one class or another, such as collaborative working group, the student-centered approach
is already being applied in the course unit. Applying an occasional active technique is
not the application of the methodology itself. Moreover, deception may come from a
bad experience when applying an active learning technique whose results were negative,
which can undermine the student-centered approach and deprived it of any credit.
The student-centered approach allows the exercise of transversal competences while
working on the contents’ course unit. These competences contribute to the student’s
academic and professional success. However, most of higher educational programmes in
engineering do not mention them nor the level of development it should be implemented
during term time in each course unit. This is something worthwhile, very important to
consciously implement in the courses’ curriculum, but still has an evolutionary path
ahead. This gap poses a difﬁculty for the teacher since there is no proper articulation
of the exercise of transversal competences with the other course units. Therefore, it
is utopian and inconsequential to merely have guidelines of purpose in the institution
regulations to apply the student-centered approach.
Last but not least, another important aspect that makes it hard to implement the
student-centered approach is to consider, as a principle in the academic recruitment
phase, that in the selection of a candidate teacher for a higher educational institution it
is not necessary to have pedagogical training.
5
Course Challenges
To verify the efﬁciency of the learning-teaching process applied in ten short-cycle higher
educational programmes of technology (2 years – 180 ECTS), called CTeSP, at the
Polytechnic Institute of Setúbal in Portugal, a follow-up of the accumulated results
obtained regarding the number of students that completed, attended or dropped out each
course was carried out over three straight academic years since 2017/18. Those results
are presented in Fig. 2 where it can be shown that the lack of pedagogical guidelines
towards student-centered approach translates into a rate of no more than 30% of the
enrolled students that were able to complete any of the ten courses, referred by letters
A to J.
It is increasingly important that academic courses, in addition to technical skills,
indicate which transversal skills are intentionally exercised or provided throughout its
academic path. The development of soft skills contributes to improving the students’
academic performance and their attitudes and behavior in professional activity, leading
to their professional skills’ enhancement. In fact, these transversal skills are highly
appreciated in the workplace, allowing to enhance the operationalization and ﬂexibility
of any workforce.
Despite the discussion, at theoretical level, about the dilemma of directing teaching
more in the acquisition of technical knowledge than developing transversal competences,
the experimental reality demonstrates the possibility of combining the two in different

measures, depending on the course objectives and the necessary professional proﬁle.
The idea that is necessary to exist a particular course unit, as portfolio or project, to
develop the students’ soft skills is reductive. The speciﬁc transversal competences of the
professional area in which the course is inserted can and must be intentionally combined
throughout all the stages of the course, with the appropriate reinforcement and level of
depth workable in the course. In fact, all course units can allow students to consciously
exercise transversal competences as long as the teacher takes them into account in the
planning of the pedagogical structure, as well as in the learning activities applied using
appropriate technologies, simultaneously integrating them with the technical-scientiﬁc
knowledge. However, this should not be carried out by the teacher’s own initiative, but
as a result of the design of the course, with the set of basic and speciﬁc soft skills duly
deﬁned by semester and curricular year, so that all course units, together, contribute to
its development in pedagogical practice considering the proﬁle of generation Z students.
This requires coordination and articulation of the pedagogical methodology supported by
active learning techniques and the application of emerging technologies among different
course units, which is not yet culturally applied within the organization of Portuguese
higher educational institutions and presents a real challenge in the design of new or
standard academic programmes. Moreover, diversifying active learning techniques in the
classroom and working platforms in the context of the course unit, properly coordinated
throughout the semester, is motivating from the student’s point of view, by progressively
increasing the student’s adaptability.
6
Solutions
The ﬁrst step to implement student-centered approach must be part of the institution’s
governmental action plan, the intention of truly convergence to this pedagogical method-
ology adapted to generation Z with the desired quality. The institution’s guidelines must
be clear and unequivocal regarding the greater appreciation of teaching work in the
pedagogical context, encouraging pedagogical research work with the same concern as
technical-scientiﬁc research work. Clear pedagogical guidelines regarding the progres-
sive implementation by semester/course, integrating them into the institution’s strategic

378
S. Rafael and J. Justino
planning, must be produced which are operationalized through a set of actions such as:
creation of basic institutional conditions for implementation; course design preparation;
preparation of teachers in terms of pedagogical-scientiﬁc performance and preparation
of students who attend the course.
Regarding institutional terms, it is important to review the creation of operating
conditions for the course and for supporting students and teachers in laboratory activities,
seminars, classrooms and study visits, to implement blocks of 4 h schedules for the
teacher’s management of theoretical-practical and laboratory work components of the
course unit and also to produce speciﬁc regulatory support and professional development
for teachers who embrace this pedagogical approach.
Regarding the course monitoring committee, the review and discussion of the initial
educational project of the course, by including soft skills and deﬁning for each course
unit the contribution of technical-scientiﬁc and transversal competences concerning the
professional needs and the proﬁle of generation Z students, should be carried out.
Regarding the set of teachers of the ﬁrst semester of the ﬁrst curricular year of each
course, their pedagogical preparation and training within the depth degree of application
of the student-centered approach should be carried out, developing the entire pedagogical
structure, learning activities, active learning techniques, didactic resources and evalu-
ation method by course unit. A good example of the application of this pedagogical
strategy can be found in [11], where the application of collaborative working group
aggregated students, reduced the dropouts and an 80% success rate was achieved, which
contrasts with the results presented in Fig. 2.
Regarding the course students, a motivational lecture, explaining the way the course
works, the inherent culture, the pedagogical approach, the technical-scientiﬁc skills and
the soft skills concerning the teaching activities should be carried out at the beginning
of each semester, preparing students for what is expected in terms of their participation,
monitoring of the course management and support of the teachers during term time,
being mentally prepared to overcome the various stages of their training.
7
Conclusions
The implementation of student-centered approach is not easy to integrate into teaching
activities without training and continuous support of an experienced work team in this
pedagogical approach. In a less elaborate way, through trial and error, the pedagogical
transition process becomes slower and the natural obstacles of implementation, such as
the passive resistance of students or the feeling of loss of mastery/importance of the
teacher in the context of class, can discourage the most conservative minds.
Successfully implementing the student-centered approach reinforces the sense of
professional satisfaction, conﬁdence in the active learning techniques applied and greater
mastery and security in the pedagogical activity due to the increase of capacity and
creativity to generate alternatives in the teaching-learning process according to the needs.
However, at the same time, there is a feeling of dismay for not having the constructive
contribution in terms of soft skills of the remaining course units where the traditional
methodology is used. This imbalance between course units makes it difﬁcult to apply the
student-centered approach in a ﬁrst phase, which usually leads rookie teachers to give

Why is It so Difﬁcult to Apply Student-Centered Approach?
379
up. A different outcome can be achieved when most course units, simultaneously and
complementary, develop soft skills that contribute to the academic success of students
due to the continued execution of the necessary soft kills. Thus, it becomes important that
courses are designed in terms of technical-scientiﬁc competences as well as transversal
competences, highlighting the emphasis of decision-makers being aware of this reality
to create suitable conditions.
Finally, all variables exposed in the setting of a pedagogical structure must be
reassessed and reﬂected in each study cycle, ensuring continuous improvement by adapt-
ing to the characteristics of the generations that will come throughout our teaching
activity.

Which Pathway Towards Mathematics’
Assessment in Engineering Education?
Júlia Justino(B)
and Silviano Rafael
ESTSetúbal and CINEA, Polytechnic Institute of Setúbal, Campus do IPS, Estefanilha,
2914-508 Setúbal, Portugal
julia.justino@estsetubal.ips.pt
Abstract. In Portuguese engineering education it is frequent to come across
teachers expressing that the student-centered approach doesn’t work out after
changing their assessment method to include more evaluation elements in one
academic year in which the success rate remains the same. This paper intends
to show how the implementation of a suitable assessment method, constructively
aligned with the learning outcomes and the learning activities of the course unit,
represents a step to foster the change from the teacher-centered approach to
the student-centered approach, improving the students’ academic performance.
This changeover is particularly relevant for teachers of cross-cutting scientiﬁc
areas of technology or engineering degrees like mathematics who present passive
resistance to this change.
Keywords: Student-centered approach · Continuous assessment · Research in
engineering pedagogy
1
Introduction
It is now more than two decades since the Bologna process entered into Portuguese higher
education, aiming to reform the whole teaching-learning process in academia to better
prepare students for the constant changing needs of employers and society. However,
the teacher-centered approach is still widely applied in course units of cross-cutting
scientiﬁc areas of engineering degrees like mathematics. In fact, assessment little appears
tohavechangedoverthepast40yearsinmathematicsteachinginPortugueseengineering
education, mostly based on two summative tests. Pedagogical studies standing up for
teacher-centered approach [1, 2] reinforce the teachers’ passive resistance to student-
centered approach.
Also, in mathematics’ course units of engineering courses the contents taught have
been discovered over a century ago. This fact seems to be correlated to ﬁxed mindset
teachers, asserting that no pedagogical change is needed to teach these classical contents.
Many of these teachers also enjoy having a quiet classroom where they retain full control
of all activities, ensuring that no important topic is missed by students.
Moreover, ongoing failure rates in course units of cross-cutting scientiﬁc areas,
as mathematics, are seen as a “natural problem” and no amendment in the teaching

approach is requested or recommended by the course coordinator or by the coordinator
of the scientiﬁc area. This can be frustrating for the academic community concerning
the ensuing institution’s bad performance [3].
In addition, in Portuguese engineering education it is frequent to come across teach-
ers expressing that the student-centered approach doesn’t work out after changing their
assessment method to include more evaluation elements in one academic year in which
the success rate remains the same. This fact is often related to the maintenance of the
learning activities’ focus on contents instead of learning outcomes, although more eval-
uation elements are included in the course unit’s assessment. And with no improvement
on the students’ academic performance, the increase of the teacher’s work effort during
term time does not pay.
2
Assessment Schedule
At the beginning of term time the teacher must establish which assessment method, in
addition to the teaching activities, will be implemented in its course unit. This means
setting the types of assessment to be applied and also the number of evaluation elements
to be carried out during term time.
Regarding the types of assessment, there is a wide range of them: academic, adap-
tive, analytic scoring, aptitude, benchmarking, blended, competence based, diagnos-
tic, differentiated, external, formative, holistic, informal, integrated, ipsative, linear,
modular, norm referencing, predictive, proﬁciency, proﬁling, psychometric, qualitative,
quantitative, subjective, summative, synoptic and triangulation, among others [4].
Regarding the number of evaluation elements, it can be from one (the traditional
ﬁnal exam) to the total number of classes, which matches the concept of pure continuous
assessment. If the number of evaluation elements is too low students will have a lot of
topics to cover in each assessment, fostering rote learning. On the other hand, if the
number of evaluation elements is too high the amount of work could be overwhelming,
both for teacher and students, mainly addressing declarative knowledge [5]. In fact, each
evaluation element carried out in a course unit is directly associated with a moment of
pressure and a considerable amount of work, both for teacher and students. Hence, more
evaluation elements in a course unit implies a linear increase of the teacher’s work effort
during term time. This can be as shown in Fig. 1.
Fig. 1. Evaluation elements versus work effort.

382
J. Justino and S. Rafael
It should be noted the difference between periodic assessment, distributed assessment
and continuous assessment. In periodic assessment the evaluation elements are sched-
uled according to the academic timetable, having the same time period between them,
regardless of the course unit’s learning objectives. This situation is often accomplished
by two traditional summative tests. In distributed assessment the evaluation elements
are scheduled according to the course unit’s learning objectives, being carried out by the
end of the teaching activities upon one or two learning outcomes. In continuous assess-
ment evaluation elements are carried out in almost every class. So, the big question is:
what is the suitable number of evaluation elements to enhance the students’ academic
performance in a course unit?
3
Context of Application
First-year mathematics’ course units of technology or engineering degrees in Portugal
usually have a large number of enrolled students which supports the ongoing use, over
the last decades, of a ﬁnal written exam and, at most, also a mid-semester summative
test to mitigate the pressure at the end of the semester. This practice is wrongly taken as
continuous assessment [6]. The result of this assessment schedule is a success rate that
almost always stays well below 50%. In fact, most of the students that does not reach
a positive grade at the mid-semester evaluation just withdraw from the mathematics’
course unit, many times only trying to pass it again when the course is almost concluded.
This paper intends to show how distributed assessment can contribute to improve the
success rate of mathematics’ course units.
4
Implementation
Sincetheacademicyear2018/19severalassessmentmethodswereimplementedinmath-
ematics’ course units of different engineering degrees and short-cycle higher educational
programmes of technology (2 years – 180 ECTS), called CTeSP, at the Polytechnic Insti-
tute of Setúbal in Portugal. This was carried out over three straight academic years to
the same course units in order to verify the impact of more or less evaluation elements
during term time on the students’ academic performance. The follow-up of the results
obtained was carried out using the available data on the information system platform of
the institution.
Until academic year 2018/19 the teacher-centered approach was the pedagogical
methodology applied in all this mathematics’ course units, in which lectures were given
at regular classes, focused on contents with no speciﬁc learning outcomes established,
and assessment was simply based on two traditional summative tests.

successive amendments of assessment inﬂuenced its success rate. These CTeSP, with a

4.3
Computer Engineering Degree
From the academic year 2018/19 to 2020/21 the teacher-centered approach was the
pedagogical method applied in a ﬁrst-year mathematics’ course unit of the degree in
Computer Engineering (CE). This course has one of the highest entry average rates
of the institution and its students, in general, have a fair mathematical background.
In the academic year 2018/19 the evaluation elements were aligned with the learning
outcomes of the course unit, although the teaching activities were focused on contents.
In the two following academic years, the teacher was shifted, along with all the didactic
resources and learning activities. Also, contents were taught in a different manner and the
quantity of evaluation elements were severely increased, keeping the teaching activities
very focused on contents and with no formative assessment provided to students. The
evaluation elements implemented were summative tests (ST) and assignments (A) during
a term time of ﬁfteen weeks. The following Table 3 presents the students’ academic
performance during these academic years.

5
Outcomes
The evaluation methods implemented at CTeSP show that distributed assessment
enhances the student’s academic performance when compared with periodic assess-
ment, as long as the evaluation elements are aligned with the course unit’s learning
outcomes, even if student-centered approach is not fully applied.
The evaluation methods implemented at TIM degree show that continuous assess-
ment is no better than distributed assessment, as long as student-centered approach is
fully applied.
The evaluation methods implemented at CE degree show that distributed assessment
can be no better than periodic assessment if teacher-centered approach is applied, even
when students have a fair mathematical background.
In short, assessment only based on two traditional summative tests in general does not
foster the students’ learning and engagement in a mathematics’ course unit, contributing
to the mitigation of its success rate. However, if the assessment method is not aligned
with the learning outcomes and the learning activities of the course unit, more evaluation
elements does not mean better results.
6
Conclusions
Mathematics is a cross-cutting scientiﬁc area whose contents in Portuguese higher edu-
cational institutions are often taught focused on the course unit’s syllabus instead of its
learning outcomes. Thus, even if more evaluation elements are included in the assessment
of a mathematics’ course unit, no improvement on the students’ academic performance
may be achieved.
If the course unit’s planning is developed within the teacher-centered approach, the
teacher’s reﬂection, preparation and assessment is focused on the organization of the
topics or contents to be learned by students. In this context, the students’ characteristics
and the teaching techniques to be applied during term time are not taking into account.

Which Pathway Towards Mathematics’ Assessment
387
It is essential to implement the student-centered approach, with formative assessment
being provided to students during term time, and to establish the pedagogical alignment
in the entire pedagogical structure of a mathematics’ course unit. This changeover of
the pedagogical approach is not an easy task since it requires a cultural change inciting
learning more than teaching, giving more importance to the students’ learning conditions
and resources rather than to the amount of contents lectured.
The adoption of a suitable assessment method, constructively aligned with the learn-
ing outcomes and the learning activities of a course unit, can foster the change from the
teacher-centered approach to the student-centered approach. Also, the balance between
periodic assessment (two summative tests during term time) and continuous assessment
(evaluation data in almost every class) must be found in order to optimize the teacher’s
effort and the success rate of a mathematics’ course unit.

Abstract. This paper presents the evaluation results of an online training course
in Online Engineering Education and Pedagogy (OEP). The course consisted of
a series of modules implemented on a mix of online communication synchrony
strategy of synchronous activities carried out on the Zoom platform, together with
work on a Moodle-based LMS platform. Based on the IGIP Curriculum offered
for the TU Dresden and the demands for effective online education, a training
course for the academic staff of an Engineering Faculty at a Chilean University
was implemented for a second time. The course was called “Introduction to the
online teaching and learning in engineering” and was offered in e-learning modal-
ity in 2021 with the participation of a group of more than 50 academics. The main
goal of the study was to identify the perception of the participants of the training
course (academic staff) about their experiences and valuation of the competencies
developed during the course. The research question that guided the research pro-
cess was how the participants evaluate: (1) the course in general, (2) the didactic
designofthecourse,(3)theusefulnessoftheacquiredknowledgefortheirteaching
practice, (4) the teaching competencies, and (5) a self-evaluation about their par-
ticipation and their learning process. The participants correspond to the careers of
Mechanical Engineering, Electrical Engineering, Industrial Engineering, Mining
Engineering, and Computer Engineering.

Online engineering education and pedagogy

1.1
Engineering Pedagogy in the Chilean Context
MelezinekdeﬁnesEPasadisciplineorientedtotheengineeringeducationprocess,which
connects the engineering sciences and techniques with pedagogy and the educational
system [6]. The author describes various component elements for EP such as (i) engineer-
ing ﬁelds (sciences) themselves, (ii) natural sciences, (iii) psychological and sociological
approaches, (iv) educational sciences, (v) communication sciences, (vi) information and

communication technologies (ICT), and (vii) ethics, among others [6]. Although Engi-
neering Pedagogy (EP) has a long tradition in German-speaking areas (particularly in
Dresden, with a tradition of more than 60 years) [1–3], the concept of “EP” is relatively
recent in Spanish-speaking countries. In the speciﬁc case of Chile, the application of

Chilean Universities 2014–2018” (PEDING Project) and “Strengthening engineering
training at Chilean universities through practice partner-ships” (STING Project) [4, 5].
Different authors recognize several aspects and factors that condition the engineering
education and pedagogy and the training of the teaching staff in engineering careers [6–
11, 17–21], but the societies of the 21st century evidence diverse demands derived, for
example, from different actors of the society and the scientiﬁc engineering ﬁelds, among
others. Gormaz-Lobos et al. [10] shows multiple factors that condition and inﬂuence the
EP: (i) the production and service structures of each country (needs determined by the
labour market), (ii) the society and culture (the needs for the development of technology
and technique is also determined by cultural and social aspects), (iii) the engineering
sciences (needs determined by matters of research, methods, and technologies at the
engineering subjects), (iv) the academic staff or university teachers (with speciﬁc com-
petencies at engineering ﬁelds but also of with pedagogical competencies), and (v) the
learners (students) or individuals studying engineering (with age-speciﬁc psychologi-
cal characteristics, individual needs, characteristics of the personality, values, attitudes
among others).
1.2
The Digital Competence (DC) Framework
The OECD [27] established a deﬁnition of “key competencies” that citizens would
require for a successful life and a correct functioning in society in the context of the
21st century, considering the growing demands of society, globalization, changes in the
world of work and the constant incorporation of technologies in people’s lives. These key
competencies are organized into three major dimensions: (1) Competencies for interac-
tion with the environment (use of language, mastery of information and communication
technologies, etc.), (2) Competencies for interaction in heterogeneous groups (abilities
related to tolerance, respect, and interculturality among others.), and (3) Autonomy and
responsibility (personal responsibility for their own development and in relation to the
social context) [27]. OECD will later point out in its “Programme for the International
Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC), that adults should have the necessary skills
and competencies to solve problems and perform complex tasks in “technology-rich”
environments”. This would mean that not only basic competencies should be considered,
but also higher-order skills needed to use information, evaluate information critically,
and use it to solve problems [29].
A key concept in the present proposal is related to Digital Competence (hereafter
DC). Ferrari et al. deﬁne DC as the [30]:
set of knowledge, skills, attitudes, abilities, strategies, and awareness that is
required when using ICT and digital media to perform tasks; solve problems;

390
C. Galarce-Miranda et al.
communicate; manage information; behave in an ethical and responsible way; col-
laborate; create and share content and knowledge for work, leisure, participation,
learning, socializing, empowerment and consumerism.
The ETS Report of the International ICT Literacy Panel (International ICT Liter-
acy Panel 2002) and the IEA International Computer and Information Literacy Study
(ICILS) from Fraillon et al. [32] offer one such deﬁnition. This proposal is based on
the very detailed approach outlined in the DIGCOMP framework, which deﬁnes digital
competencies as the “conﬁdent, critical and creative use of ICT to achieve goals related
to work, employability, learning, leisure, inclusion and/or participation in society” [32].
The DIGCOMP framework integrates the following ﬁve competencies in the context
of digitization: (1) information and data literacy (2) communication and collaboration,
(3) digital content-creation, (4) safety, and (5) problem solving [5]. The ﬁve dimen-
sions of competence encompass the following deﬁnitions [29–33]: information and data
literacy is the ability to identify, locate, retrieve, store, organize and analyze digital
information. Individuals with this competence have the ability to judge the relevance
and purpose of information and data. Communication and collaboration are the abil-
ities to share resources through online tools and to use digital tools to link with and
collaborate with other people in a digital environment. This competency involves inter-
acting with and participating in communities and networks and requires cross-cultural
awareness. Digital content-creation is the creation and editing of new content (from word
processing to images and video). Content creation focuses on creative expression, media
output, and programming. Dealing with and applying intellectual property rights—for
example, working with licenses—is an important aspect of this competence. Safety is of
great importance due to its connection with personal, data, and digital identity protec-
tion issues, security measures, and the need for safe and sustainable digital technology
usage. Finally, problem-solving is the ability to identify digital needs and resources.
Informed decisions on the most appropriate digital tools should be made in accordance
with the purpose or need. Conceptual and technical problems can be solved through
digital means. As a result, creative use of technologies and keep own and others’ com-
petencies updated are important skills in this dimension [29–32]. As can be seen from
the above, the breadth of the scope dimensions of the exercise of DC is not only related
to the “simple use” of ICTs, but also to interactions (communication skills), information
management and selection, as well as ethical and safety aspects, among others. It is also
observed that the spaces for the development of CD are not exclusively related to formal
learning spaces (such as schools, universities, PIs, and CFTs), but also to other social
spaces (real or virtual), where informal learning also plays an important role [31, 34].
1.3
A Proposal for Teacher Training in Online Engineering Pedagogy (OEP)
Based on the IGIP Curriculum developed by the TU Dresden (Germany) [2] and the
demands for effective online education [12, 26–39] a training course for the teaching
staff of the Engineering Faculty at a Chilean university was developed and executed
for a second time. This course was previously implemented and evaluated in 2020 with
the participation of 32 academics. The course was called “Introduction to the online
teaching and learning in engineering” and was offered for a second time in e-learning

Improving the Digital and Pedagogical Competence
391
modality during June and August 2021 with the participation of a group of 53 university
teachers. The participants are part of the careers of Industrial Engineering, Mechanical
Engineering, Electrical Engineering, Mining Engineering, and Computer Engineering
(Fig. 1).
Fig. 1. Overview of the main page of the pilot course in OEP in moodle.
The course required a minimum work of 1,5 Credit Points (also 45 h of training
according to the SCT-Chile system). The course consists of four modules according to
the objectives and contents of the IGIP Curriculum from TU Dresden [2] and deepens
into the main aspects of the effective online training of university students. The choice
of content considered the areas in which teachers needed support to transform and
effectively adapt their traditional classroom methods to be applied in online education,
such as structuring teaching and learning processes, designing and using educational
technologies, structuring communicative processes, and assessing student learning in
online learning environments. An overview of the modules and units is presented in
Table 1. The design was based on a mix of online communication strategy of synchronous
activities carried out on the Zoom platform (20 h), together with asynchronous work on
a Moodle-based LMS platform for asynchronous independently and collaborative work
(25 h approximately). The pedagogical design was conformed by expository, practice,
and collaborative teaching-learning strategies.
The student (participant) role contemplated listening and reading texts activities and
solve problems as individual activities or in collaboration with peers.
The course evaluation was formative and based on the independent work materials at
LMS. At the end of the course, each participant presented a ﬁnal product to demonstrate
the developed competencies along the course (planning of online teaching activities,
development of online learning, and evaluation material, among others).
At the last stage of the training course implementation, the research group imple-
mented an evaluation survey with the goal to obtain the participants’ evaluation about
their experiences at the course.

Evaluation Results of the Teacher Training Course in OEP
2.1
Materials and Methods
The main goal of the study was to identify the perception of the participants of the train-
ing course (academic staff) about their experiences and valuation of the competencies
developed during the course. The research question that guided the research process
was: how the participants evaluate (1) the course in general, (2) the didactic design of
the course, (3) the teaching competencies, (4) the usefulness of the acquired knowledge
for their teaching practice, and (5) a self-evaluation about their participation and their
learning process.
Based on [12–15, 21, 39–42] and their previous experience in engineering pedagogy
research projects in Germany and Chile [2, 5, 16], the authors developed a categories
system with indicators for the instrument design. The instrument consists of a question-
naire with closed and open-ended questions organized into ﬁve main categories with
their respective items (see Table 2). Due to the location of the participants (Chile), the
questionnaire was developed in Spanish and consisted of 34 items on a Likert-type scale
(5 levels) grouped into ﬁve categories. The internal consistency of the full scale and

Improving the Digital and Pedagogical Competence
393
sub-scales was analyzed using Cronbach’s alpha. All statistical analyses [14, 43, 44]

2.2
Characterization of the Sample
In total, 42 academics answered fully the questionnaire: 23,8% are women (10) and
76,2% men (32). Regarding the age ranges of the respondents, 69% (29) of the partici-
pants are between 30–39 years old, 19% (8) are between 40–49 years old and 12% (5) of
the participants are older than 50 years. Related to the distribution of the involved partic-
ipants by engineering school, most of them work in industrial engineering (45.2%; 19)
and mechanical engineering (35,7%; 15). Therefore 11,9% of the participants work in the
ﬁeld of computer sciences (5) and only 7.1% work in electrical engineering (3). Concern-
ing the years of teaching practice experience, 76,2% have between 0–5 years (32), 21,4%
have between 6–10 years (9), and 2,4% (1) of the participants have more than 10 years of
teaching practice experience. Of the total number of respondents, approximately 95,2%
(40) have already participated in some teaching training courses previously.

“Self-assessment of the own learning process” (under 80%), and was: "Commitment
and motivation with the course”. The item “Dissatisfaction with the participation in
the course” was valuated as very low or low with 100% of the preferences. Another
important aspect is the perception of the participants about the relevance of the different
items/questions by gender. For the female participants of the teacher training course,
most of the items were low valued, except the items “Satisfaction with the duration of
the course” and “Utility of the acquired learning for professional development”.
By grouping the participants by engineering ﬁelds (Fig. 2), the participants from
Computer sciences gave the high average of preferences in the valuation of all items
(94,56%), and the participants from Mechanical engineering the lowest average with
87,69%. (Industrial engineering with 90,26% and Electrical engineering with 91,59%).

Regarding the differences between the relevance of the items for the participants by

most of the “indicators” were low valued (average of 90,8% in all items).
3
Discussion and Conclusions
The main goal of the study was to identify the perception of the participants of the train-
ing course (academic staff) about their experiences and valuation of the competencies
developed during the course. The research question was: how the participants evaluate
(1) the course in general, (2) the didactic design of the course, (3) the teaching compe-
tencies, (4) the usefulness of the acquired knowledge for their teaching practice, and (5)
a self-evaluation about their participation and their learning process. Concerning the cat-
egories “Evaluation of the course development (in general)”, “Evaluation of the didactic
design of the course”, “Evaluation of the teaching competencies”, and “Evaluation of
the teaching competencies” - in line with other studies [16, 27, 29] - all aspects related
were as high valuated. These results coincide with the comments of the participants
during the teaching-learning activities. The ﬁndings conﬁrm the relation-ship between
the average of the evaluations with the years of teaching experience of the participants
[16, 22–27]. Participants with up to 5 years of experience evaluated the course better,
and participants with over 10 years of teaching experience tend to evaluate the course
lower; something that had already been demonstrated in the literature [16]. The item with
the lowest relevance (“Commitment and motivation with the course”) is related to the
category “Self-assessment of the own learning process”. That can be explained because
most of the participants had a high amount of teaching time and said that they wanted to
dedicate more hours to the program but could not because of their other responsibilities.

Improving the Digital and Pedagogical Competence
397
The survey’s results of the open-ended questions were analyzed using qualitative
methods [14, 15], but due to the size of the content analysis, they are part of a second
publication that shows the triangulation and concordance with the results of the quan-
titative analysis from the present study. The evaluation results of the training course
and its online implementation showed a high valuation of the course by the participants.
However, due to the “pilot nature” of this project and the small sample of academics who
participated (42 participants), some questions remain open about the impact and valua-
tion that this type of training course can have on other engineering faculties throughout
Chile. Due to the size of the sample, the authors consider that the results of the research
cannot be generalized. However, they serve as a case study about teachers’ experience
with a training course, speciﬁcally oriented towards OEP.

The Impact of the Computational Pedagogy
STEAM Model on Prospective Teachers’
Computational Thinking Practices
and Computational Experiment Capacities.
A Case Study in a Training Program
Sarantos Psycharis1(B), Paraskevi Iatrou2,3, Konstantinos Kalovrektis4,
and Apostolos Xenakis4
1 School of Pedagogical and Technological Education-ASPETE, Marousi, Greece
spsycharis@gmail.com
2 Hellenic Education Society of STEM, Athens, Greece
3 Socialinnov, Athens, Greece
4 University of Thessaly, Volos, Greece
http://www.e3stem.edu.gr, https://www.so-cialinnov.gr/
Abstract. This article presents -as a case study- a training program where the
computational interdisciplinary STEAM pedagogy model is applied to prospec-
tive teachers. Didactic scenarios related to everyday phenomena were applied,
following the STEAM content epistemology. Research aimed to examine the
impact of teaching and learning sequences on: 1) students’ engagement in the
practices of scientists and engineers through the Computational Pedagogy model
2) students’ engagement in the STEAM epistemology when physical computing
activities were implemented when crosscutting concepts were included, and 3) stu-
dents’ engagement in the practices of Computational Thinking (CT). We present
ﬁndings of a teaching course implemented virtually and students had to submit
a didactic scenario-as their ﬁnal assessment essay-based in the interdisciplinary
STEAM approach combined with the cross-cutting concepts, boundary objects
and computational models.
Keywords: Engineering education · Computational pedagogy · STEM ·
Computational thinking · Cross-cutting concepts
1
Introduction
The problems that science and society face lead to the need for a holistic approach
that cannot be meet by “isolated” disciplines or by stereotype methodologies based on
traditional cognitive areas (National Academy of Engineering 2016; Bryan and Guzey
2020). There is also a general consensus that the objectives of education should not
focus on teaching separate disciplines, but the focus should be on to “develop a reliable
compass and the navigation tools to ﬁnd their own way in a world that is increasingly
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 400–411, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_41

The Impact of the Computational Pedagogy STEAM Model
401
complex, volatile and uncertain.” (Schleicher 2019, The OECD Learning Compass 20
https://www.oecd.org/education/2030-project/teaching-and-learning/learning/30).
There is a variety of different-sometimes conﬂicting-interpretations and suggestions
of “STEAM education and STEAM integration” and these suggestions span a spectrum
ranging from disciplinary to transdisciplinary approaches (e.g., English 2016). This leads
to the necessity for “discovering” a concise and compact “deﬁnition” of STEAM educa-
tion/STEAM integration. This “deﬁnition” should be in alignment and correspondence
with new instructional strategies with appropriate STEAM tasks, and new evaluation
approaches and new learning outcomes, based on-mainly-interdisciplinary and/or trans-
disciplinary epistemological approaches. For example, what are the proper indicators
to assess students when interdisciplinary approach is implemented based on a unique
activity that includes the so-called transversal concepts, and how students could make
computational experiments that provide real data using the computer (through the so-
called physical computing). This leads to the inclusion of the Computational Science as
part of the STEAM pedagogy enhancing students’ capacity to develop models and make
experiment-equivalent to the physical experiments.
There is an extensive research work for ﬁnding a conceptual framework for “in-
tegrated STEAM education”. (e.g., Sanders 2012; Guzey et al. 2017; Psycharis 2018;
Mayes 2019; Tytler et al. 2019; Psycharis et al. 2017, 2018, 2018, 2020; Psycharis and
Kalovrektis 2021), indicating the need to clarify the “integrative STEM education.” In
order to conceptualize the “STEAM integration” we have to discuss the concepts of:
Computational Thinking, Computational Science, boundary objects that cross the dis-
ciplines, the cross-cutting concepts/big ideas and the epistemologies of the disciplined
included in the acronym of STEAM.
1.1
The Computational Thinking
A lot of discussion for the connection of STEAM integration with the Computational
thinking (CT) practices/dimensions has been reported.
“Computational Thinking involves solving problems, designing systems, and under-
standing human behavior, by drawing on the concepts fundamental to computer science
while is also considered as a universal skill and attitude that complements thinking
in mathematics and engineering with a focus on designing systems that help to solve
complex problems humans face” (Wing 2008).
This deﬁnition is concise and compact, but for a more operational function we need
some more feasible elements. Weintrop et al. (2015) proposed a deﬁnition of computa-
tional thinking for mathematics and science in the form of a taxonomy consisting of four
main categories, namely: data practices, modeling and simulation practices, computa-
tional problem-solving practices, and systems thinking practices. There are fundamental
research questions related to (CT) inclusion in STEAM, like:
what are the pedagogical aspects of computational thinking, how computational
thinking is linked to existing subjects, what a computational thinking progression might
look like, how to train teachers in computational thinking practices, and how best to
assess computational thinking (NRC, 2011a, 2011b). All these questions lead to consider
that (CT) can take the form of “conductors” between the different SETAM disciplines
through the “cross-cutting” concepts (see below the Computational Pedagogy Model).

402
S. Psycharis et al.
While computational thinking draws upon concepts that are fundamental to comput-
ing and computer science (Denning 2007), it also includes practices such as problem
representation, abstraction, pattern recognition (machine learning) decomposition, sim-
ulation, veriﬁcation, and prediction (Sengupta et al. 2013; Bower et al. 2017; Psycharis
2018). These practices are related to the developments of models (as representations
of the physical world) and the scientiﬁc reasoning which will serve as an indicator for
assessment in interdisciplinary STEAM.
1.2
The Computational Science (C.S.)
There are already suggestions to include Computational Science in STEAM (e.g., Yasar
et al. 2016; Psycharis et al. 2021). Computational Science is a cognitive area distinct from
Computer Science (e.g., Taub 2013, 2015) where research suggests that Computational
Science (C.S.) is related to Computational Thinking (as a problem-solving process) For
example, Weintrop et al. (2015) consider that Science and Mathematics are becoming
computational endeavours and “computational learning” is related to Computational
Thinking.
The essential characteristic of Computational Science is the development of a model
through the abstraction process, while abstraction is a practice of Computational Think-
ing. Computational Science applies methodologies that integrate computer science,
numerical analysis and the speciﬁc scientiﬁc area where we implement the model
(Psycharis 2016).
The essential feature of Computational Science Computational Pedagogy model
combines Computational Thinking, Computational Science and STEM content episte-
mology as a holistic transdisciplinary approach to the curriculum for Primary, Secondary
and Higher education. Computational Science is considered as a renaissance in exper-
imental approaches, since implementing its epistemology we can have real data in the
computer. Research refers that (e.g., Ya¸sar 2013; Yasar and Landau 2003) Computational
Science (C.S.) overlaps with many other knowledge areas, so an educational program
in Computational Science, naturally draws strength from all of them.
Nevertheless, in addition to over-lapping with computer science, math, and science
and engineering application areas, Computational Science has its own core knowledge
area. Juszczak (2015) states that Computational Science, in both natural and social
sciences, is different than the usage of computers to analyze complex systems and data
sets. Computational Science is a non-empirical science where data are gathered through
simulations and virtual experiments and attempts to use data about the real world in
order to conduct real experiments in a virtual universe.

The Impact of the Computational Pedagogy STEAM Model
403
1.3
The Boundary Objects and Cross-Cutting Concepts
Consideration of STEAM as interdisciplinary or transdisciplinary approach inevitably
leads to the inclusion of boundary objects that serve as agents for ‘STEAM integration
through the integration of the methodologies included in the acronym of STEAM (e.g.,
Star 2010; Polman and Hope 2014).
Boundary objects are inevitable as: “Disciplines do not have cores or essences, but
rather histories of inscription practices and procedures within cultural contexts for pure
and applied ends” (Tytler et al. 2019) and their origin comes from the difﬁculty to con-
ceptualize STEM integration when attempting to cross between isolated disciplinary
disciplines. Boundary objects serve as pedagogical content knowledge boundaries we
need to pass when interdisciplinarity is applied (Leung 2020). To conceptualize the
Computational Pedagogy-STEM content interdisciplinary model, we propose the cross-
cutting concepts and CT practices to act as boundary objects. The crosscutting concepts
are (NGSS 2013): 1. Patterns 2. Cause and effect: Mechanism and explanation 3. Scale,
proportion, and quantity 4. Systems and system models 5. Energy and matter: Flows,
cycles, and conservation 6. Structure and function 7. Stability and change.
1.4
The Computational STEAM Pedagogy Model-Didactic Strategies
and Assessment in Computational Pedagogy Model
Our approach for STEAM integration has the same essentials with that of (Boon Ng
2019).The fundamental characteristic of this approach is to consider that interdisciplinar-
ity is implemented by using as a “nucleus” concept, one of the transverse/crosscutting
concepts and making connections with core disciplinary concepts in different disciplines
in the framework of a unique curricular activity in alignment with the STEM content
approach. The “STEM content approach” is clearly described in (Moore 2008; Bryan
et al. 2015).
Our approach is based on interdisciplinarity as: “a fusion of the four disciplines of
Science, Technology, Mathematics and Engineering, where the focus of learning is not
the individual discipline in itself, but on solving real-world problem”s (Boon Ng 2019).
The Computational Pedagogy model articulates the above fundamental character-
istics, and it differs from other approaches for “STEM integration” as it applies the
methodology of Computational Science in order learners collect real data instead of
virtual ones. This model uses standard platforms for physical computing, like Arduino,
Microbit etc.
2
Methodology
The objectives of this research were to examine the impact of the Computational STEM
Pedagogy model –and engagement in Computational Thing practices implemented
through physical computing activities (mainly through the Arduino and micro:bit plat-
forms) when computational pedagogy integrated STEM interdisciplinary epistemology
is applied through didactic scenario.

404
S. Psycharis et al.
Data were collected and analyzed through the Jamovi software (https://www.jam
ovi.org/) with descriptive and induction statistics. A validated questionnaire for Compu-
tational Pedagogy (Yasar et al. 2016)-modiﬁed by the authors-was adapted in order to
connect the questions with the scenario based on physical computing and implemented in
acoursewhichcontainedissuesrelatedtotheinterdisciplinaryapproachandthepractices
followed by scientists and engineers. Scenarios were based on cross-cutting concepts
and boundary objects that operate as agents for the interdisciplinary approach while the
inquiry teaching and learning approach and the engineering design instructional strat-
egy were applied. For the Computational Thinking practices a validated questionnaire
by (Weese et al. 2016) was applied before and after the instruction.
Graduated students-from different disciplines were enrolled in a course related to
STEAM concepts through a training program implemented for the last three years.
The theoretical part pf the course includes the general concepts related to the STEAM
epistemology and how students could develop STEAM interdisciplinary scenario using
platforms like Arduino and Tinkercad. Scenario were related to real – life problems, con-
cerning phenomena that students had met. During the course the Inquiry based teaching
and learning approach was integrated with the engineering design process, providing the
affordances to students to be engaged in real data collection, in analysis of data in order
to ﬁnd patterns and suggest optimal solutions. In order to examine the effectiveness of
the program two validated questionnaires were provide before and after the course.
One questionnaire refers to the practices of Computational Thinking and the other
one refers to the practices included in the Computational pedagogy, and reports were
registered. During the learning and teaching sequences students constructed artifacts,
related to the core and cross – cutting ideas included in the design of the phenomena and
availabledatawerecollectedandanalysedthroughthestandardpracticeswithdescriptive
and induction statistics.
For Computational Thinking concepts the questionnaire of (Weese et al. 2016) was
used while for the “Computational Pedagogy Model” the questionnaire of (Yasar et al.
2016) was employed and adjusted by the authors in order to include the cross-cutting
concepts and boundary objects. Examples of questions for the “Computational Pedagogy
Model” follow:
1. I am committed to developing program skills to integrate technology into teaching
cross cutting concepts
2. I want to continue developing programming skills to teach cross cutting concepts.
3. Technology can be used to motivate learning of science and math concepts
4. I would enjoy designing instruction by combining math and science concepts with
technology.
5. I want to pursue computational modeling as a means to teach STEM content.
The different questions (23) included in the questionnaire of (Weese et al. 2016) are:
• Four (4) for algorithmic thinking (ALG)
• Three (3) for abstraction (ABS)
• Two (2) questions for problem decomposition (DEC)
• Two (2) questions for data (DAT)

• Three (3) questions for parallelization
• Five (5) questions for control ﬂow (CON)
• Two (2) questions for incremental and iterative (IAI)
• One (1) question for testing and debugging (TAD)
• One (1) question for questioning (QUE).
Examples of questions are as follows:
1. Does math operations like addition and subtraction, which covers concept of CT
(Algorithms).
2. Look how information can be collected, stored, and analyzed to help solve the

3. Break the problem into smaller parts”, which covers concept of CT (Problem
Decomposition).
4. When creating a computer program I…break my program into multiple parts to carry
out different actions”, which covers concept of CT (Problem Decomposition).
We describe some of the activities implemented during the training program. Edu-
cation activities were designed in alignment with the “Computational Pedagogy model”
and learners were engaged in the Inquiry based teaching and learning approach combine
with the engineering design process (Plageras et al. 2020). The problems learners had to
solve were “open/ill-deﬁned”, so students had to develop a model (Inquiry process) and
ﬁnd optimized solutions (Engineering design). Training program was divided in three
sessions:
At session one (lasted for 10 weeks) the focus was on the familiarization of learners
with software for design 3d artifacts, use of sensors, actuators, electronic platforms
(Arduino, microbit (Kalovrektis et al. 2017; Chatzopoulos et al. 2019) (see Fig. 1).
Fig. 1. 3D artifact of an activity using Tinkercad & Arduino block programming
At session 2 (10 weeks) activities focused on combining the issues form section
one (hardware and software) followed by the development of applications in order to
measure the temperature, the solar radiation, to control the revolutions of a fan etc.). At
session 3(8 weeks) activities were focused on the development of activities for solving
real open /ill-deﬁned problems according to the Engineering Design Process. Learners.
For example, one open problem was to design, construct and operate a smart greenhouse
(Fig. 2) taking into account the constraints (i.e., materials used, cost etc.) while they had

Results for Computational Thinking (CT)

to exam the Factor loading for conﬁrmation statement. The factors include:
• Algorithmic
• Control of path
• Decomposition
• Abstraction
• Parallelism
• Collection and analysis
According to the result of CFA, the most factors are statistically signiﬁcant (value p
< 0.05) (except for item A2). From the results we concluded that the CFA is conﬁrmed.
A part of this, from the result of the “χ2 test” we have statistically signiﬁcant, p value
< 0.05, and the χ2/ df = 1.99 (the acceptance value must be χ2/ df < 3.00). From the
results we accept the test for the sphericity of Latencies variables. In addition, the results
by the criterion of the normality test (Shapiro-Wilk), showed statistically signiﬁcant p
value < 0.05 (except for Factor Problem Decomposition). Because our sample is more
than 56 persons we accept that the distribution is normal. We also accept that the CFA
is conﬁrmed. As Fig. 3 shows the path diagram of factors from CT questionnaire.
The result of Paired Samples T-Test shows statistically signiﬁcant (p < 0.05) for all
factors except for the factor Control Flow (p = 0.353, p > 0.05). The range of the mean
values varies between 0.157 to 0.424. Using a pair T-test for the mean values for the
Pre-test and the post-test, we found a positive affect for the CT practices (statistic =
2.374, p < 0.005) (Table 1) (Fig. 4).

4
Conclusions and Recommendations
In this paper we have discussed and analyzed the impact of the Computational Pedagogy
STEAM model on prospective teachers’ Computational Thinking Practices and Com-
putational Experiment capacities using a case study in a training program. Initially from
the results we observed a positive affect (statistic = 2.374, p < 0.005) that the Compu-
tational Thinking Practices after the activities using the epistemology of STEAM in a
period of 9 months. Secondly according to the factors created from the Conﬁrmatory fac-
tor analysis (CFA) and exploratory factor analysis (EFA) we conclude that, the activities
using the epistemology of STEAM and followed the Computational Pedagogical Model
because did not create adaption errors in the factors of models. Finally, the results are
encouraging since they strongly support the inclusion of interdisciplinary Computational
STEAM Pedagogy model when cross-cutting ideas are included. Further considerations
should be included, relative to the inclusions of more examples, larger scale researches
and extended examination of the engagement in the cross-cutting concepts.
