Modeling the Learning Activities of Future IT
Specialists with Using of Fuzzy Logic
Tatjana Yaschun1
, Tetiana Bondarenko1(B)
, Oleksandr Kupriyanov1
,
Sevinc Gulsecen2
, and Iryna Khotchenko1
1 Ukrainian Engineering Pedagogics Academy, Kharkiv, Ukraine
{yashun_tv,bondarenko_tc,a_kupriyanov}@uipa.edu.ua
2 Istanbul University, Istanbul, Turkey
gulsecen@istanbul.edu.tr
Abstract. This article describes various approaches to the fuzzy set theory in
different areas of science, as well as deﬁnes the necessary mathematical framework
and the concept of its application within the study. It has been revealed that the
learning activity for future IT specialists is highly speciﬁc, as it is inseparably
connected with the shaping of algorithmic thinking and skills of formalizing ill-
posed problems. These factors strongly inﬂuence the set of input parameters of the
model and the selection of terms for their fuzzy measurement. The authors propose
a software model of learning activities for future IT scientists based on the fuzzy
set theory. The proposed approach allows generating the appropriate model based
on the verbal fuzzy estimates of input parameters, using a large array of input
parameters, and correctly accounting for hard-to-formalize factors. The results
of the work bring the process of predictive assessment of students closer to the
intuitive way of communication, which was successfully related to mathematics
by LotﬁZadeh, the founder of fuzzy logic.
Keywords: Modeling · Learning activities · Fuzzy logic
1
Problem Statement
Modern communication trends, based on maximum approximation with natural com-
munication, contribute to the increased share of “fuzzy logic” and “fuzzy sets” in all
areas of science. Building “approximated” models of various human activities and their
implementation by computer devices is one of the promising areas of modern research
today. This trend applies to the pedagogical sciences as well, keeping up with the times.
Educators, of all people, have to make the right decisions in an environment lacking
clear and complete information! Watching a student from the earliest days of school and
having an intuitive or “fuzzy” idea of his or her abilities and efforts, an educator can
predict learning outcomes and the overall success of that individual in the vocational
arena. These days, instead of subjective thinking, we are used to shifting all decisions
to IT and software facilities. Consequently, computer modeling of students’ learning
activities based on some indicators with “fuzzy” measurements may allow both the edu-
cator and each student to perceive their results for years to come, adjust them, and try
to improve.

2
Analysis of Recent Research and Publications
Fuzzy logic is a fairly recent branch of mathematical science. It was proposed by Lotﬁ
Zadeh, an American mathematician and logician, in 1964 to link mathematics with an
intuitive way of communication [1]. Since then, this area has become widespread. Japan
is a leader in using fuzzy logic, with over 5,000 “fuzzy” patents. The most striking
areas of fuzzy logic applications are the control of robots, TV cameras, car engines,
household appliances, optimization of industrial control systems, bus schedule planning,
healthcare diagnostics, recognition of handwritten characters, objects, voice, motion,
images, subway management, improvement of the safety of nuclear reactors.
Fuzzy logic, unlike classical logic, employs such a term as “degree of truth” instead of
“true” and “false”, accepting values from an inﬁnite set from 0 to 1 inclusive. Thus, Lotﬁ
Zadeh offered an alternative to the rigid “black and white” parameters of traditional logic
and set more “fuzzy” boundaries that emulate the way people see the world. Possibilities
of fuzzy logic relevant to the purposes of this study include:
• Knowledge modeling through words instead of explicit meanings, which does not
need exact rules and allows making decisions in most of our routine actions [2];
• Building models of a variety of technological predictions using multiple membership
functions [3].
Fuzzy logic is widely used in medicine. Fuzzy expert systems, fuzzy processing of
medical images, fuzzy applications for information retrieval in medical databases, and
fuzzy analysis of medical data are the most well-known areas of these applications [4].
The achievements in such a successful area could not remain unnoticed by modern
researchers in pedagogical science. The following learning areas of modeling based on
fuzzy logic can be distinguished:
• Preparation of instructional content. Researchers from Azerbaijan are designing
and building an automated architecture of the educational complex through a model
based on fuzzy logic, which improves the quality of training programs, agendas, and
other instructional resources [5]. Foreign educators suggest fuzzy models to imple-
ment the instructional project, which allow us to consider both quantitative and qual-
itative characteristics, as well as provide fuzzy descriptions through fuzzy sets and
linguistic variables [6].
• Game-based learning. Researchers from Mohammadia School of Engineers
(Morocco) are developing educational games based on fuzzy logic. They suggest a
method for modeling personalized and adaptive instructional games as learning tools.
This method employs gameplay data and expert rules to predict students’ preferred
learning styles and games [7].
• Creating an instructional knowledge database. The Azerbaijan Technical Univer-
sity offers a mathematical model of the educational environment based on linguistic
variables to develop an instructional knowledge database. During the modeling, a
knowledge assessment membership function and fuzzy knowledge architecture, based
on a set of two types of fuzzy rules, covering all possible situations in the educational
process were created [8].

414
T. Yaschun et al.
• Quality assessment of educational services. The Turkish University suggests assess-
ing the learning outcomes through a comprehensive evaluation of students’ mastery
of competencies, estimated by fuzzy logic [9]. The choice of an assessment scale for
competence components that are used as input parameters of the model was explained.
The calculations are based on the mathematical framework of fuzzy set theory by the
Mamdani algorithm [10] using the application called Fuzzy Logic Toolbox in the
MATHLAB software environment [11]. A complex assessment is deﬁned through
modeling. Indian researchers build the information and analytical system for moni-
toring the quality of educational services on the fuzzy logic model [12]. As part of
fuzzy modeling, a hierarchical tree of the educational process with the determination
of linguistic variables whose values are calculated using membership functions fol-
lowing the generalization principle of L. Zadeh is created. The knowledge database is
shaped by the experts in the subject area. Both quantitative (the level of scientiﬁc and
scientiﬁc-pedagogical staff, the results of educational and scientiﬁc activities, etc.)
and qualitative characteristics (satisfaction with the quality of educational services,
etc.) appear as input parameters. The ﬁnished model allows us to conclude achieving
the goal of the learning activity.
The analysis of the current development of fuzzy logic theory by L. Zadeh conﬁrms
the advancement, relevance, and widespread evolution of this branch of science. The
results of the analysis may involve a conclusion about the minor percentage of studies
of the learning process by methods of fuzzy logic. There are no studies devoted to
improving the efﬁciency of learning activities through the results of modeling based on
the parameters of learning activities. Consequently, this scientiﬁc space is free and open
to the modeling techniques described above.
This study aims at developing the technology of fuzzy modeling of learning activ-
ities for future IT specialists based on the fuzzy set theory, as well as designing the
corresponding copyright software product as a modeling tool.
3
Statement of Basic Material and the Substantiation
of the Obtained Results

Considering the results of the publications [6–9, 12] and the above scheme, the task
of the LA modeling based on fuzzy logic is divided into stages:
1. Identifying the model’s input parameters.
2. Generating a fuzzy statistical database – knowledge matrix.
3. Building the membership functions.
4. Linking input and output variables using Zadeh’s compositional rule of inference
[1].

particular student.

number of parameters of students’ learning activities, considering the speciﬁcs of com-
puter specialties, measuring their informativeness level based on Shannon information
statistics [15], and screening out irrelevant factors.

One of the major steps in modeling based on fuzzy logic is the selection of the
type and construction of membership functions µT(x). . These functions take values in
the interval [0, 1] and describe the subjective level of the expert’s conﬁdence that the
precise value of x corresponds to the fuzzy term T. Triangular, trapezoidal, and bell-
shaped membership functions are the most widespread. During the LA modeling, we
used piecewise linear functions for estimating the LA parameters (Fig. 3) and triangular
functions for estimating the LA outcomes, which are easy to use and yield fairly accurate
prediction outcomes.

To interpret the fuzzy set d* found for a particular student by the formula (4), the

algorithm based on the minimization of the generalized Hamming distance [16].
The study suggests a model of learning activity based on a predicate-logical form,
describing fuzzy logical inference of the LA score. That model made it possible to
consider the LA parameters, admitting only qualitative measurement, and to carry out
a quantitative assessment of the LA results based on fuzzy, verbal statements. Software
implementation of the proposed model was performed by the authors in Visual Basic
for Application for MS Word processor.
4
Conclusions
The authors suggest a creative approach to modeling the learning activities for future
IT-industry professionals through the principles of fuzzy logic. Fuzzy logic is widely
used in various areas of science due to its ability to make correct decisions with uncertain
input data. This feature is relevant for pedagogical research. The model is built through
multiple steps with a clear mathematical expression: Building the knowledge matrix,
creating a hierarchical inference tree, determining the linguistic variables and mem-
bership functions, obtaining the results of a particular student’s LA based on Zadeh’s
compositional rule of inference, and interpreting them. The developed modeling tech-
nology expressed in the author’s software product has undergone complex approbation,
conﬁrming the high degree of reliability of the obtained LA results. The application
of predictive assessments based on the modeling results can be effective in ofﬂine and
online learning.

The Use of Computerized Laboratory
and Training Complexes in Engineering
and Pedagogical Education
Olena Kovalenko1
, Tetiana Bondarenko1(B)

Luís Cardoso2
, and Hennadii Zelenin1
1 Ukrainian Engineering Pedagogics Academy, Kharkiv, Ukraine

2 Polytechnic Institute of Portalegre, Portalegre, Portugal

Abstract. The article gives insight into the problem of reforming the practical
professional training of engineer-teachers on the basis of integrated use of modern
information and computer technologies. To solve this problem, it is proposed to
improve and develop new technologies of practical training, considering mod-
ern development of information, computer and production technologies as well
as modernization and reorganization of existing infrastructure and material and
technical support of practical training of workers as well as engineering and peda-
gogical personnel. This article shows that the use of modern teaching technologies,
especially information and computer technology, makes changes in the structure
of teaching environments, which in turn result in additional elements in the form of
teaching environment management tools, information and communication tools.
It describes an innovative approach to the organization of a teaching environment
based on the use of computerized laboratory and training complexes, the com-
position and functions of these complexes, means for managing components of
a teaching environment, and means for information and multimedia communi-
cation of students with the teacher on the basis of demonstration and projection
equipment as well as networks with an educational content server.
Keywords: Engineering and pedagogical education · Learning environment ·
Computer learning technologies · Training complexes
1
Problem Statement
Practical training is an important part of becoming a professional, especially if you are
involved in production. The organization of the use of acquired knowledge and skills
in real production processes is the main condition for the formation of professional
competencies of the specialist. Practical training becomes even more important when
mastering working professions. Modern production requires a competent specialist who
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 420–427, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_43

The Use of Computerized Laboratory and Training Complexes
421
owns modern equipment and is able to master the updated equipment or production
technology in a working team within a short time.
It is impossible to acquire such skills directly without using the appropriate equip-
ment, tools, means, technologies and cooperation with a team. Therefore, the profes-
sional education system should consider this fact when adjusting curricula, updating the
material base, and establishing links with relevant companies. Thus, an important task of
engineering and pedagogical education is to reform practical training that should focus
on the latest technologies and equipment, promising organizational forms of produc-
tion, interaction with devices and tools, the relationship of information, computer, and
production technologies. This will affect not only the content of practical training, but
also its material and technical support, which requires the modernization of production
workshops, not only in terms of technical reequipment.
2
Analysis of Recent Research and Publications
One of the main challenges in the training of engineer-teachers in Higher Education
today is the adequacy between theory and practice, without forgetting an appropriate
pedagogical framework and a strong connection to the world of work that allows the
inclusion of companies’ information in universities curricula, corresponding to the labor
market desires and speciﬁc technical needs.
The twenty-ﬁrst century brings us great challenges regarding engineering education
[1], authors highlight, shouldering their analysis on UK Engineering Council (1994);
engineers and teachers Australia, (1996); Fortenberry [2] and Journal of Engineering
Education [3], but all the changes have been identiﬁed a decade ago, and this is the
origin of a new paradigm that includes an outcomes-based approach to accreditation.
Nevertheless, the major challenge still is the preparation of future engineers and the
need to adapt the engineering and pedagogical education [4]. Moreover, skilled human
resources are vital when we consider competitiveness and productivity, as Mayasari and
Samsudi [5] well noted. The researchers also underline the importance of improving
the education sector due to its relevance in current employment procedures, based on
the pertinence of computer learning strategies, which is supported by many authors like
Altbach, Reisberg, and Rumbley [6], Amirault [7] and Ghavifekr and Rosdy [8].
Lowe, Goldﬁnch, Kadi, Willey, and Wilkinson [9] add that a successful beginning
of graduates in the labor market is connected to the development of technical skills
and professional competencies. But the authors emphasize the urgency of learning these
aspects in practice, which means the real context where all will be used.
One of the ways for deeper integration of the practice in the current curricula of
engineering courses is the use of technologies, namely computer-based technologies.
Nowadays, technologies are common in educational systems, not just as tools for teach-
ing but mainly because they are essential in Higher Education Institutions as part of the
pedagogical structure that allows teaching to be more efﬁcient and gives each student
the opportunity of contributing to his learning process, as Geladze [10] wrote.
Liscouski [11] identiﬁes the potential of the use of the laboratory that integrates
technologies and establishes several lines of application of this system, always empha-
sizing its main aspect: the ability to incorporate practice in the training of students and

422
O. Kovalenko et al.
expand their contact with the real situations they will face in enterprises and daily work-
ing requirements: “The laboratory is a challenging environment to work in or support.
Its work grew out of experimental sciences and attracted technologies from a variety of
sources to improve its scientiﬁc ability to perform research, measurement and testing
services. Those working in laboratories learned to use information technologies to make
that work more efﬁcient, and faster, and at the same time improve their ability to manage
workﬂows, and the results of their research and experiments”.
Isosaki [12], like Osborne [13], advocates the need to give more attention to lab-
oratory work, reminding us that it has been integrating science education for decades.
The author demonstrates the role of the laboratory in science teaching, for example,
and argues that practical work has to be considered a needful pedagogical strategy for
teachers, who must be always supported because “Without enthusiastic and knowledge-
able teachers, the beneﬁts of quality facilities and an established system cannot be fully
realized. Thus, in conducting practical work, emphasis ought to be placed on its purpose
and what students can learn from the experience - not on merely the actions they perform
in conducting such work”. Kolarov [14] states that a computer laboratory has a lot of
advantages including technical and methodological, the possibility of registration and
observation, and can eliminate several educational problems.
Razali and Trevelyan [15] noticed the growing levels of approaches to engineer-
ing and pedagogical education due to the rise of new technologies. The authors argue
that students need to gain practical knowledge in engineering laboratories to perform
with adequacy and responsibility in the labor market. For this, students develop practi-
cal intelligence in laboratories, a very important skill, incorporated through experience,
in laboratory classes, where they can contact with real equipment, and obtain practical
skills. Computerized laboratory and training complexes are considered vital in engineer-
ing degrees by many authors, who support the idea of exposing students to experimental
work.
3
Statement of Basic Material and the Substantiation
of the Obtained Results
Reforming practical training faces several speciﬁc research challenges that should form
the basis for further improving the instrument package of engineer-teachers. The ﬁrst
problem is the development of an ergonomic tool package for a worker’s activity. The
second problem is the relationship between information, computer, and production tech-
nologies, as a factor in changing the nature and direction of professional tasks. The third
problem is the development of information and computer technologies for theoretical
and practical training. The ﬁrst two problems relate solely to branch sciences since
they should consider speciﬁc technologies, norms, and conditions of production speciﬁc
to each profession. The third problem is pedagogical and relates to the latest didactic,
methodological, and psychological ideas in the formation of information computer train-
ing technologies for training workers. For a comprehensive solution for these issues, it
is proposed to create an innovative training environment based on a computerized labo-
ratory and training complex, as the quality of the educational environment is one of the
main factors inﬂuencing the effectiveness of training [16].

ences that are possible in a conventional or specially modiﬁed environment. At the same

simulators, such as functionality, accuracy and scale.
The functionality of computerized simulators depends on the set of instructor func-
tions and training functions (training model). Accuracy depends on the training model
relevance to the set of technological process operations. The scale is related to the
completeness and accuracy of implementation at the level of operations of the entire
production cycle (certain degree of simpliﬁcation is allowed).

The Use of Computerized Laboratory and Training Complexes
425
The standard functionality of the computerized simulator implies the implementation
of the functions of the trained engineering teachers and instructor of industrial training.
The implementation of the functions of the trained engineer-teachers should provide
the ability to perform the necessary set of production operations with a high degree
of similarity to real production processes. Instructor should provide all the opportuni-
ties for training management (initialization of the workﬂow from the typical initial and
specially created intermediate states of production process, shutdown and restarting the
workﬂow, setting the speed of demonstration of work operations, monitoring and evalua-
tion of training tasks). To analyze the results and accumulate the methodological base of
professional training, the monitoring results are recorded in a specially created database
[19]. Figure 3 shows samples of training and laboratory complexes of radioelectronic,
electrical as well as electromechanical purpose.
Fig. 3. Samples of training and laboratory complexes of radioelectronic, energy, electrical as well
as electromechanical purpose
Let’s consider a laboratory training complex for the training of specialists in energy,
electrical and electromechanical proﬁle. This complex is designed for practical work and
laboratory tests. It can be used in the training practice of vocational technical school,
electrical workshops and technological laboratories to study the principles of operation
of various devices, as well as gives real practice in setting up and repairing technical
electrical equipment of enterprises. Training tables are designed for use by both students
and experienced electricians.
The training stand is an industrial assembly table ﬁtted with an equipment mount-
ing board. The board may include a set of electrical equipment, including connectors,
controls and terminals. The use of such computerized laboratory and training complexes
increases the efﬁciency of students’ mastering of the procedure of installation operations.
The developed laboratory and training complexes are used in the practical training of
students of engineering and pedagogical specialties. The use of these stands conﬁrmed
the effectiveness of the incorporated design solutions. The advantage of this approach
is that the professional training process becomes manageable in terms of a number of
parameters (quality, speed, error-free performance of work operations). In addition, the
use of laboratory training stands allows to bring the performance of work operations
to automatism, which means the transformation of professional knowledge into profes-
sional skills. Further research and improvement of computerized laboratory and training

426
O. Kovalenko et al.
systems for the training of engineer-teachers is associated with the use of virtualiza-
tion and visualization of work processes. Considering the fact that the ﬁnancial costs
of hardware implementation of laboratory and training complexes are quite high, and
their further modernization is not always possible, it is necessary to develop specialized
software that supports the necessary technologies for virtualization and visualization of
work processes. Such approach saves ﬁnancial and other resources for the development
of new software technologies compared to hardware implementation, and further mod-
ernization of computerized laboratory and training complexes is limited to the correct
choice of the initial project architecture.
4
Conclusions
The main advantage of this approach is to increase the level of information, communi-
cation, and control of practical activities of students, which improves the quality of their
training, especially in team teaching. The use of many means of visual control, auto-
mated learning, and cognitive visual aids, combined with the accumulation and analysis
of statistics of practical activities of each participant signiﬁcantly simpliﬁes the “routine”
moments of training and intensiﬁes it. In this case, the teacher or foreman can focus on
more systemic issues, placing the level of reproductive activity on automated learning
and simulators, and focusing on control and correction. On the other hand, several spe-
cialists can be easily involved in the training process, who, using the available means
of communication and training, will jointly participate in the management of practi-
cal training, sharing functions and areas of educational and methodological inﬂuence
depending on their qualiﬁcations and specialization.
The described methods of building remote practical training can reduce the cost of
moving highly qualiﬁed employees to places of practical training, and in some cases to
provide these employees with the necessary working conditions. In the future, it is pos-
sible to implement remote individual or group forms of practical training in occupations
using individual equipped workplaces directly in production areas or in regional training
and retraining centers. All transformations are a consequence of the development and
increasing availability of modern information and communication technologies.
This article was prepared as part of a study in Ukrainian Engineering Pedagogics
Academy during implementation of the Erasmus + project PAGOSTE «New Mech-
anisms of Partnership-based Governance and Standardization of Vocational Teacher
Education in Ukraine» (609536-EPP-1-2019-1-DE-EPPKA2-CBHE-SP).

Potential of the Learning Project’s Task
Gesine Haseloff(B) and Tiana Christin Weiß
University of Siegen, 57068 Siegen, Germany
Haseloff.tvd@uni-siegen.de
Abstract. The article refers to a learning project of the research focus “Cooper-
ation of learning locations in vocational education and training” (LOBB) of the
Chair of Technical Vocational Didactics at the University of Siegen. It was under-
taken by teachers and students in grades 9 to 12 at general education schools in
Olpe (North Rhine Westphalia, Germany). A shaping-oriented task “Development
of a smartphone holder” was central to the project. The task was devised together
with teachers and includes ecological, economic and social conditions.
The authors submit the thesis that reference to sustainability can be established
in shaping-oriented projects. Nevertheless, this requires a suitable task. To test
their thesis, the authors deal with the shaping of the LOBB project - commencing
with the project task. In addition to literature research, they use the COMET
competence measurement procedure and the participatory development method
for their research.
The COMET competence measurement procedure shows whether the project
participants were able to acquire further competence for sustainable shaping. Par-
ticipatory development accompanies the process of solution development. This
method is indicated because the authors themselves are involved in the project
and their own role as learning facilitators cannot be ignored.
Keywords: Project orientation · Sustainability · Competence measurement
1
The Basis for the Development of the Project
1.1
Initial Situation
At the outset of the project there is the question of how learners can familiarise them-
selves with technical work processes while concurrently acquiring the competence of
sustainable shaping. The aim of the project is not to treat the questions of sustainable
shaping in isolation but to integrate them into the student’s activities, as recommended
by Vollmer (2010) and Lehberger and Rauner (2017).
It is also planned to test the COMET competence measurement procedure in general
education for the ﬁrst time. It has already been used successfully internationally in
vocational education and training (Rauner 2017).
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 428–439, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_44

Potential of the Learning Project’s Task
429
1.2
Research Question
According to Vollmer (2010), the authors put forward the thesis that learners in technical
professions can best acquire a reference to sustainability in shaping-oriented projects.
This is justiﬁed because learners experience in projects how they can independently
inﬂuence and change (technical and other) work processes through their active shap-
ing. In this way, they experience the development or the changeability of technology
(Kuhlmeier and Vollmer 2017, p. 138) and learn to reﬂect by asking “why is that?” and
“Why so?” (Adolph 2001, p. 186). This means that they can understand that sustain-
ability can be brought into these processes by themselves. According to Vollmer (ibid.),
learners acquire the competence to shape sustainably in this way. The increase in com-
petence is to be assessed in the project using the COMET competence measurement
procedure according to Rauner (2018).
1.3
Methodology
The authors use the method of participatory development (Clement 2006). The term
is understood to mean a process in which new structures, procedures or processes are
developed and at the same time “... Researchers actively carry out this development
work through their expertise together with actors from the research ﬁeld” (Clement
2006, p. 664).
Competence development is measured using the internationally tried and proven
COMET method (Rauner and Zhao 2009). It is chosen because it provides reliable
and objective insights into the holistic acquisition of skills on the basis of scientiﬁc
evaluations, especially in practical application. At the beginning and at the end of the
project, the development of competencies (in the sense of sustainable shaping) of the
students is empirically recorded.
Basic position in the philosophy of science
In project work, an interdisciplinary approach to vocational science is chosen. This
is based on a vocational understanding “... That is not only directed at the vocational
subject area, but also at the job-related work and the associated work processes” (Pahl
2006, p. 30). In this context, “...the focus is on [...] the learning individual, who is to be
enabled to (co-)shape work and society” (Bohne et al. 2017, p. 30).
Educational processes should focus on this. In this context, product-related, techni-
cal, social, economic and ecological circumstances that are related to work, “... Life-
world consequences that can be caused by certain actions” (Fischer 2006, p. 312), and
lastly personality and identity-shaping mechanisms that promote a development into
“... Mature citizens who can responsibly, self-critically and constructively shape their
professional and private lives and participate in political and social life” (KMK 2004,
p. 6) should be taken into account.
1.4
What Does “Shaping” Mean?
Shaping can be understood as an overarching construct that has methodological and
practical signiﬁcance. It follows Richter and Meyer, who see shaping as a work activ-
ity in which one succeeds in “... Purposefully inﬂuencing and changing the personal,

430
G. Haseloff and T. C. Weiß
professional and social environment by one’s own actions. To do this, it is necessary to
look for alternatives, to assess the consequences of one’s own actions and to decide on a
course of action on the basis of a well-founded evaluation” (2004, p. 23). Especially in
the (German) discussion on competence orientation in vocational education and training,
shaping in this way has become a paradigm (Arnold 2012, p. 45ff.).
With reference to the considerations of Leontjew (1973) and subsequently of
Holzkamp (1979) and Wulf (1978), shaping is associated with individually shaped cre-
ation or effect (action), which has or triggers effects on economic and/or social conditions
and developments in the community (activity). This contains a reference to a reﬂective,
independent and active approach that cannot simply be copied but can be learned. The
effects mentioned are intended to and can contain offers or indications of change or
themselves represent and/or trigger practical change. Because they aim to change real-
ity, they touch on ethical aspects that extend into social and economic realities. Thus, a
possible orientation of shaping towards “common good orientation” and sustainability
(Münkler and Fischer 2002, p. 15) is addressed.
In any case, however, shaping expresses important conditions of given social devel-
opments that open up possibilities for action or, better, for shaping (Holzkamp 1983,
p. 234). The creators are not dominated by the surrounding environment or society, but
“... Continually re-establish the relationship to the world through their own activity”
(Holzkamp 1996, p. 81). The prerequisite for this is that a trigger for the need to shape
is present and identiﬁable (Holzkamp 1983, p. 348).
In vocational education and training, problems or tasks in the real working and
living environment are the most important source of a need to shape (Gerds 2006,
p. 368f.). Through the impulse from outside (work and business circumstances, social
conditions, educational mandate) and/or the “own concern”, the self-intentioned “own
educational path” (Gerds 2006, p. 368), the shaper is presented with a task that is set
out and justiﬁed. Shaping the solution to the task happens (like acting) in the process,
where it is important to “... Individually tailor developmentally beneﬁcial learning tasks,
learning environments and teaching/learning arrangements” (Gerds 2006, p. 369).
For the identiﬁcation of tasks and their successful solution (in shaping), it must be
possible to understand and reﬂect on one’s own actions. A “contextual understanding”
(Laur-Ernst 1990, p. 14) is necessary about the operational processes, the speciﬁc charac-
teristics of the materials, systems and equipment used in the company, about the internal
characteristics - which lie in the character of the mechanical, chemical or other processes
themselves - as well as about the life-world consequences that result from these actions
(ibid.). This goes hand in hand with the educational process, the development of one’s
own personality (Gerds 2006, p. 369).
2
The LOBB Project Smartphone Holder
Project Participants
The Technical Vocational Didactics (TVD) department at the University of Siegen, teach-
ers from the Gymnasium Olpe (in Olpe, North Rhine Westphalia, Germany) and pupils
from grades 9 to 12 were involved in the project. The two authors belong to the TVD team

at the University of Siegen (North Rhine Westphalia, Germany). The different project
phases took place at the Gymnasium or at the university. At the university, a workshop
with a 3-D printer was used.
Project Idea
The smartphone holder project was initiated by the University of Siegen and the Gym-
nasium Olpe with the intention of arousing greater interest in the sustainable solution of
technically dominated problems among students and teachers. The project participants
agreed that more important than a successful product at the end of the project was the
acquisition of the competence to shape technical processes in a sustainable way. The
learning project should be about a project that has to do with the living environment of the
young people, involves several subjects and can be implemented at the same time with
modern production processes or technology. The assignment to develop a smartphone
holder combined all of these requirements.
Project Implementation
Various project phases were implemented in class at the Olpe grammar school and at
the University of Siegen. Some dates planned as face-to-face events had to be made
available online due to the Corona pandemic (Table 1).

3
The Task is the Linchpin
3.1
Requirements for the Task
The assignment of tasks is crucial for the competence acquisition of learners. According
to Franke and Kleinschmitt (1987, 47ff.) it should contain certain criteria for this.
The project task must originate from a serious situation and address a real problem. It
must be characterised by appropriate complexity and problem content and must neither
over nor under-challenge the learners. Learners must be able to recognise and use room
for manoeuvre in solving the task. The task must be open enough to allow learners
to take alternative approaches and to respond to changes in the situation and context.
The task must allow for a holistic approach to work in contrast to Taylorism. This is
about understanding a job in its larger context of framework conditions. The task must
offer learners the opportunity to act independently in all solution phases. There should
be incentives to network with other learners (and others involved in the task) and to
work in a team. Space for reﬂection and for asking for support as well as for help and
feedback must be made available. Finally, the task must provide room for the learner’s
development - something new should be able to be learned and done.
3.2
Learning Task: Design a Smartphone Holder
Situation Description. As part of an internship at the company SmartMobile, your
supervisor will involve you in the innovation process of a new product. SmartMobile
wants to launch a product on the market that makes smartphones easy to use and visible.
Especially because of your experience in the ﬁeld of home-schooling, he sees you as
important experts for the customer needs and requirements for such a product.
Work Order. Develop justiﬁed proposals for solutions and variants of solutions for
your planning and development of the product. Following the planning, you must be
able to present and explain your innovative proposals to the foreman responsible for the
technical implementation.
Working and Auxiliary Tools. The ofﬁce and workshop equipment of SmartMobile is
at your complete disposal for planning and development.
3.3
Justiﬁcation of the Task
As Franke and Kleinschmitt (1987, 47ff.) explain, the shaping-oriented task “Developing
a smartphone holder”, which was developed together with teachers, has a degree of
complexity that is appropriate to the learning level of the students. For this purpose, the
subjects of physics, chemistry, German and microteaching at the university are included
in the project. The topic “Developing a smartphone holder” relates to content in demand
from the everyday life of the students. The students develop their solutions independently
in the group. They deal with a variety of new topics and situations. They can solve their
task at different networked learning locations and use the different potential of school,
university and the workshop.

Potential of the Learning Project’s Task
433
The assignment is holistic in nature. This means that the students follow their project
from the identiﬁcation of the task and the planning through to the implementation and
evaluation of the solution. The task is chosen in such a way that it offers enough room
for manoeuvre - also for the investigation of any alternative solutions. It encourages the
team to look for a common solution, to make decisions and to present the solution.
Students are encouraged to use digital media to develop their ideas. They learn to
shape and share these media for their learning.
The solution of the task is associated with a gain in shaping competence, as Rauner
(2007) presents it in his competence model. At the beginning and at the end of the
project, this development is measured with the COMET procedure. It then becomes
apparent to what extent the learners meet the criteria of shaping competence with their
task solution. This means that the functionality, clarity, sustainability, utility value ori-
entation, economic efﬁciency, business and work process orientation, creativity, as well
as environmental and social compatibility of the task solution are assessed.
This is a holistic, vocational approach as recommended by Franke and Kleinschmitt
(1987), Gerds (2005) and Rauner (2018). The focus is not on imparting knowledge from
speciﬁc subject areas, but on ﬁnding a comprehensive solution to a problem with direct
relevance to the students’ lives.
4
Independence and Competence Acquisition in Learners
4.1
Micro Teaching
Since competence can only be acquired through one’s own actions (Gerds 2005), care
was taken in all phases of the project to ensure that the students largely solve their project
tasks independently.
In addition to the school lessons accompanying the project, which are shaped inter-
disciplinary and holistically by the teachers in close consultation with the team, the
students receive suggestions as part of micro teaching to reﬂect on the context of the
task. The microteaching on technological progress, manufacturing processes, manufac-
turing methods and economic aspects is designed in such a way that problems relating
to sustainability can be thought through.
By using the learning environment in the authentic 3D printing laboratory at the
University of Siegen, the students experience that a project can be developed, planned
and implemented at various networked learning locations (school, university, workshop).
With regard to the feasibility and shaping at the various learning locations, they take up
different conceptual thoughts and incentives and can develop them further in consultation
and with the support of the supervisors. This is of great relevance for the reﬂection of
one’s own solution. In this way, holistic, varied thinking is promoted and required.
4.2
Excursion day
During an excursion day, the students can actively work on the individual solution of
their technical problem through the project task in an authentic learning environment.

434
G. Haseloff and T. C. Weiß
In addition to micro teaching units, there is the opportunity to develop ideas and
approaches in groups. The input on sustainability with regard to social, economic and
ecological factors triggers reﬂection processes beyond the narrow context of the task. In
the protected setting of the workshop, the students experiment with ideas for solutions.
Experienced skilled workers are there to support them. The authenticity of the university
as a place of learning with its laboratory and workshop environment can lead to a
detachment from school-based, subject-speciﬁc activities. It can be observed that in the
university workshop, the students ﬁnd their way into the role of the skilled worker and
develop professional solutions.
4.3
Group Work with Digital Media
It is important for the project leaders to encourage group work. The students should try
out negotiation and decision-making processes. The project task is worked on by the
students after the individual entrance test (ﬁgure) in group work within the framework
of the school lessons, at the university and in the workshop.
Especially through digital media - such as the shared Padlet - the students have a
constantly available possibility to collaborate. They can save all ideas and proposed
solutions for all participants and continue to work on the “common cause” (Adolph
2001) in the group or individually at any time.
This also takes into account the aspect of authenticity and openness to shaping
through the possibility of free student decision-making between work-sharing and joint
processing of the solution in each step of the group work (Locke and Latham 2002).
At the same time, the teachers have the opportunity to monitor the current status of
the individual groups and to provide targeted advice and support (Fig. 1).
Fig. 1. First sketch made in group work by students

Potential of the Learning Project’s Task
435
5
Teacher: In-Service Training
5.1
Joint Planning and Rater Training
The task development for the learning project takes place in joint workshops. Teachers
from the Gymnasium Olpe and the team from the University of Siegen take part. The
project group follows the guidelines of Rauner and Lehberger (2022).
The aim is to develop a task for the students that allows them to acquire shaping
competence, in particular the competence to shaped in a sustainable way. This acquisition
of competence is to be measured with the COMET method.
5.2
Rater Training
The project group tests the development of test items in rater training sessions. Under the
guidance of an experienced rater, the items of a competence-promoting task are analysed
on the basis of the problem “Designing a smartphone holder” (ﬁgure).
Here, the problem is systematically designed with the help of the item catalogue
according to Rauner and Lehberger (2022, p. 216 f.) in such a way that it represents an
authentic life situation that enables a holistic valid solution.
Finally, the task solution is tested by the trainees. It is evaluated by others (by different
raters) and put up for discussion. In this way, a solution space is developed. This is the
starting point for a concept for the shaping of the following teaching process with regard
to thematic input, support and learning supervision.
In addition to the tasks, rater training plays a very central role in COMET competence
measurement. Only with successful rater training can the quality criteria of objectivity,
validity and reliability be met.
Due to the quick and easy-to-learn procedure, it is possible within a short time to
sensitise the participants to the items and to deﬁne a common solution space.
In this way, the teachers arrive at almost identical assessment criteria independently
of each other, which is a seemingly large hurdle, especially in the case of open-ended
tasks. The Finn value, which is a measuring instrument for the agreement of the raters’
evaluations, means an agreement of 100 % for a value of 1, and no agreement for a value
of 0. The Finn value of inter-rater reliability, for example, is in a very good range at the
end of a rater training: <0.7 up to 0.85, as empirical studies in international projects
show (Rauner 2018, p. 105 f.).
6
Competence Measurement with COMET
6.1
The COMET Procedure
According to the KMK’s guiding principle of “enabling people to help shape the world
of work and society in a socially, ecologically and economically responsible manner”
(KMK 1996), the COMET process is based, according to Rauner (2017), on the need to
model task solutions holistically with reference to the eight overarching criteria of vivid-
ness/presentation, sustainability/use value orientation, economy/efﬁciency, business and

436
G. Haseloff and T. C. Weiß
work process orientation, and social and environmental compatibility and creativity
(Rauner 2018, p.21 f.).
According to Martens and Rost (2009), the COMET measurement procedure accord-
ing to Rauner is a way of assessing the abilities of students to solve open, authentic
(vocational) tasks. These must be both challenging and qualifying. Due to the open
tasks, the students must be able to understand their solution as well as be able to take
responsibility for it in a reﬂective manner (Rauner 2017).
In order to enable a holistic task solution taking into account aspects of economic
efﬁciency, environmental compatibility and utility value orientation, the task must be
carefullyselectedaccordingtothequalitycriteriaofagoodtaskandlegitimisedbymeans
of an item catalogue according to Rauner and Lehberger (2022). Through individual and
group evaluation, a high degree of guess reliability is achieved with regard to the solution
of an objective evaluation of an open task. The task designed within the framework of
the project aims at a high degree of shaping competence through the holistic solution
of all requirements, in particular through the situational embedding in the professional
everyday life of the students as experts for digital work.
6.2
The First COMET Test
Within the framework of the ﬁrst COMET test, which also serves as an introduction to
the project work, the students have 60 m to work individually on the task, without the
special criteria and requirements of the possible solution space having been addressed
in advance in the school context.
The description of the situation serves, in particular, to help the students ﬁnd their way
into their function as experts or specialists for digital work in the area of home-schooling.
At the same time, this accentuates the level of the expected solution.
Since these are students at a general education school who rarely have the opportunity
for cross-curricular project teaching due to subject-based teaching, the COMET test is
a challenge. It is necessary to link separate subject knowledge and already acquired
action competence to a problem-oriented task solution in the context of a new innovative
question.
6.3
The Second COMET Test
The second COMET test at the end of the project term serves to check the competence
gain and the simultaneous evaluation of the project.
Here, the students will have to solve and justify a second COMET task, which is
similar to the ﬁrst one, so that the individual competence gain of the students becomes
graphically visible.
Here one expects a more holistic solution space than in the ﬁrst test, since the students
have become acquainted with the necessity of a holistic view of a problem in different
facets in addition to the criterion of functionality within the framework of the project
and have embedded this in their actions and procedures within the framework of the
participatory observation of the project leaders.
At the same time, the second Comet test and the resulting competence measurement
enables an evaluation of the project, as an overlap of the characteristics is expected,

Potential of the Learning Project’s Task
437
which makes the course of the project, the need for support through input, specialists
and learning support clear, as well as an optimisation and weighting for the following
students possible.
7
Summary
Without the second COMET test being completed, a gain in competence can be observed
throughparticipatorydevelopment. Thelearners concretisethetaskfor themselves. From
the assignment, they identify a task for themselves or their group. They show that they
have looked at different variants of the smartphone holder - they look for alternatives and
experiment with solutions. After discussing advantages and disadvantages, they decide
in the group to implement one of their plans.
They have previously considered technical, economic and ecological conditions and
included and emphasised sustainability aspects. They can use and shape the digital media
(Padlets) they use in such a way that it helps their task solving and teamwork.
The students present their solutions, they justify and discuss them in front of their
classmates. They show a good ability to reﬂect. Lastly, learners demonstrate the practical
feasibility of their solutions.
The students cooperate with each other and with the other project participants
throughout the project. They actively ask for supervision and support. The independent-
active action - with the help of the teachers and supervisors - became clear in every phase
of the project.
8
Conclusion
At the end of the article, the authors once again address the thesis that precedes this
article. It can be conﬁrmed that the learners have acquired competence for sustainable
shaping in a shaping-oriented project.
The students establish a relationship to a real problem through their own activities
and gradually try out an action with sustainable alternatives to solve it. To do this, they
use the potentials of the different learning locations of school, university, workshop
and the online medium. They work on the joint project at each of these learning sites -
even if they are active individually. In this way, they use the advantages of networked
working. This is an important step in the direction of a “self-directed educational path”
(Gerds, 2005, p. 368). For the goal must be that the students independently tend towards
alternative sustainable work processes in the future.
The developmentally supportive task - this has also been demonstrated - was essen-
tial for this. As a “creative source” (Gerds 2005, p. 368), it provides impetus for the
students’ activities and reﬂections. In addition, it has sufﬁcient potential to evoke an
“understanding of coherence” (Laur-Ernst 1990, p. 14) in the students for processes of
an economic, ecological and social nature. The students are thus enabled to deal with
these processes themselves and can consider the consequences in alternatives and try
them out in their own actions. This initiates an educational process in the direction of
alternative sustainable shaping.

Teaching Interchange – An Interactive Online
Event for Peer Learning Among Educators
Linda Bücking(B), Stefanie Hürkamp, and Paula Carstens
Institute of Mechanics and Computational Mechanics, Leibniz Universität Hannover,
Appelstraße 9a, 30167 Hannover, Germany
linda.buecking@ibnm.uni-hannover.de
Abstract. The COVID-19 pandemic has fundamentally challenged the educa-
tional approaches in Higher Education. Educators have adapted to the highly
uncertain situation by developing emergency remote teaching scenarios. Real-
time knowledge exchange between educators is crucial for transitioning these
improvised teaching practices to professional online or blended learning scenar-
ios. Thus, the online event “Teaching Interchange” was developed as a catalyst for
peer learning among practitioners in the ﬁeld of engineering education. It is a cus-
tomized event considering the current needs and interests of the participants and
consists of interactive online sessions. The two editions described in this paper
successfully connected educators from various universities and equipped them
with tangible ideas for their next steps.
Keywords: Teacher training · Peer learning · Emergency remote teaching
1
Introduction
The COVID-19 pandemic has demanded a sudden change in teaching methods in Higher
Education (HE) institutions. Educators needed to adapt their course formats, teaching
styles andcorrespondingmethodologywithinashort periodof time. Althoughthis abrupt
change has posed a challenge to teachers and students alike, it also offers great potential
for innovation, such as the introduction of novel learning scenarios. However, in order for
this development to be sustainable, the teachers need to make the shift from emergency
remote teaching [1] to actual online or blended learning. To fully implement online
learningformatsandmethods,itisthereforecrucialtofosteracultureofexperimentation:
A continuous, yet thorough reﬂection of the new experiences is needed, in order to
identify promising practices, learn from mistakes and make adaptations in real time.
This way, lecturers can improve their teaching methods and are better prepared for
possible future emergency situations [2]. Additionally, they learn to adapt their teaching
methods to an increasingly digitalized world and the corresponding demands of the labor
market.
A practical yet impactful way to reﬂect remote emergency teaching is by exchang-
ing experiences with fellow educators facing similar challenges. Traditionally, these
exchanges among peers occur either in an informal way or during structured conference
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 440–446, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_45

Teaching Interchange – An Interactive Online Event
441
sessions. However, both of these exchange formats were poorly suited for the circum-
stances characterizing the COVID-19 pandemic: As interactions have mainly occurred
via virtual platforms, it has been difﬁcult to simulate an informal environment for peer
exchange. In addition to informal settings, a more structured environment is helpful to
foster a deeper reﬂection process. On the other hand, attending conferences requires a
certain level of expertise in educational sciences which does not encourage educational
practitioners to share their struggles. Besides, online conferences often do not provide
sufﬁcient space for interaction so that the attendees merely consume knowledge rather
than engage with the content presented.
Hence, this workshop report describes the design and implementation of the two
editions of the Teaching Interchange - an online event for peer learning among educators.
Interactive elements, easy accessibility and an adaptive, needs-based agenda design
characterize this online event format. The ﬁrst edition of the Teaching Interchange took
place in March 2021 after one year of emergency remote teaching; the second edition
followed in September 2021. Addressing attendees from the ﬁeld of civil engineering,
the event directly responded to the current challenges in engineering education due to
the COVID-19 pandemic.
2
Objective and Approach
The Teaching Interchange is an interactive event for best practice sharing and for gath-
ering input among colleagues. The event aims at improving engineering education by
means of peer learning. As it connects educators who experience similar challenges,
the event provides a platform for jointly exploring current issues and approaches in
engineering education.
As opposed to conferences targeted at experts in the ﬁeld of engineering education,
the Teaching Interchange has a low threshold for participation. Its target group are prac-
titioners, i.e. teachers and other contributors to educational activities in higher education.
As Wenger [3] highlights, such informal “communities of practice” make learning and
development processes of social participation.
The agenda design of the Teaching Interchange follows a bottom-up approach, as
the topics are entirely based on the participants’ current needs, interests and challenges.
Further, the event aims to provide an international perspective, in order to inspire the
participants by means of hands-on examples from other educational systems. Due to
the interactive methodology, the educators take on the role of active practitioners. This
empowersthemtolearnfromeachotheranddoesnotrequireabackgroundineducational
sciences.
In absence of a textbook solution to the implementation of online learning during a
global pandemic, the event is designed around the principle of learning from experience.
According to the experiential learning approach, “Learning Is an Holistic Process of
Adaptation to the World” [4, p. 31]. Kolb states that reﬂecting individual experiences is
a crucial factor for learning and a prerequisite for acting based on the acquired insights
[4]. In this context, the Teaching Interchange offers the practitioners an opportunity to
reﬂect amid the current crisis. Next to valuable insights presented by their colleagues,
the educators engage in various reﬂective practices in a group setting. This enables the

442
L. Bücking et al.
participants to review their own online teaching methods and become inspired by the
presented approaches. Based on their ﬁndings, they can draw conclusions and improve
their teaching methods accordingly.
3
Assessment of Individual Needs
As the Teaching Interchange is an event tailored to the interests and current challenges
of the individual participants, the attendees ﬁlled in a needs assessment form upon
registration. In this form, the attendees speciﬁed their current role and topics of interest
as well as their expectations towards the event. Further, they could optionally register
for giving a best-practice presentation of ﬁve, ten or ﬁfteen minutes. The evaluation of
these forms provided the basis for designing the agenda of the event.
The two events gathered approximately ten educators each. The participants inhibited
awiderangeofroles,includingprofessors,scientiﬁcstaffandexpertsofmediapedagogy.
They originated from seven universities in four different countries. Figure 1 shows
the participants’ expectations for the event: The educators mainly hoped to acquire
knowledge and new ideas on different aspects of online teaching.
Fig. 1. Expectations of the participants.
4
Content and Implementation
The online event lasted three hours and took place on the platform Webex which allowed
the participants to interact in a main session and various breakout rooms. The virtual
board Mural was used for the poster gallery and the collection of the event’s takeaways.

Teaching Interchange – An Interactive Online Event
443
The board was easily accessible through a link and did not require additional registration.
To enable effective learning, it is crucial that the participants learn using the respective
virtual platforms and tools before engaging with the actual content of the event [5].
This was achieved by hosting the icebreaker activities in breakout rooms. The breakout
rooms would later be employed for the Open Space session in a more complex, self-
directed format. Further, the interactive coffee break offered incentives for exploring the
functions of the virtual conference tool and the virtual board.
The event started with a short introductory presentation which was centered around
the participants: Besides brief information on the agenda and logistics of the sessions, the
presentation included an overview of the participants’ backgrounds and expectations.
Next, the participants were split up in pairs to become acquainted with each other.
In separate breakout rooms, each pair discussed the questions about their strengths,
struggles, learningstyles andcurrent experiences. This offeredtheopportunitytoconnect
with fellow educators on a personal level and to reﬂect on the current status quo of one’s
own teaching activities and approaches.
During the second part of the event the participants presented their best practices to
each other. The agenda of this part consisted of presentation topics related to blended,
onlineanddigitallearning,onlineassessment,conceptsforactivelearningandpeerlearn-
ing. All of the topics presented were highly relevant to the educators’ current situations,
as they showed successful examples of adaptation to the crisis situation.
The following discussion session was structured according to the Open Space tech-
nology [6], a dynamic method to foster exchange and idea synthesis. The topics discussed
during the Open Space session were based on the needs assessment form. After a short
introduction to the principles of the Open Space [7] - adapted to the online setting -
the participants self-responsibly moved between four different breakout rooms. Each of
those rooms represented one topic, based on the results of the needs assessment. Moving
between the virtual rooms, participants discussed the topics of interest with the attendees
present in the respective room.
After the Open Space session, the participants conceptualized their individual learn-
ing outcomes of the Teaching Interchange. They reﬂected on the question “Which
insights do you take home from the Teaching Interchange?”. Further, they planned
their next steps by answering the question “How can you use the methods and tools
you experienced today in your courses?” (ﬁrst edition) or “What is your intention/plan
for the next semester?” (second edition), and provided feedback to the organizers. The
participants answered the questions on a virtual board and the results were sent to all
attendees after the event.
During designated time slots, the participants could access a gallery of the partici-
pants’ departments’ posters on an online board. These posters had been designed by a
participant of each attending department prior to the event. Figure 2 shows an exam-
ple of a department’s poster. Despite the virtual format, this enabled the participants to
learn more about the other educators present at the event and about their respective con-
texts. Additionally, the posters gave a good overview over the knowledge and experience
present in the room which was useful regarding the upcoming Open Space session. Using
the functions of the virtual board, the participants could attach questions to the posters
which were then answered by the creator of the poster. Alternatively, they could interact

444
L. Bücking et al.
via the private chat or in a breakout room, which offered them various communication
channels.
Fig. 2. Example of a department’s poster.
5
Outcomes and Conclusion
The individual takeaways identiﬁed by the participants are shown in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 and
can be clustered according to three common themes. Firstly, the participants accumulated
new ideas for teaching methods and approaches, such as peer review, formative feedback
or how to integrate self-directed learning elements. Secondly, they concluded the event
with insights on how to enhance their teaching with technology. Lastly, the participants
increased their self-awareness and identiﬁed strategies and approaches to improve their
self- and project management. The participants left the event with speciﬁc ideas for their
next steps, as shown in Fig. 5.
TheparticipantshighlightedthattheTeachingInterchangesupportedtheminexpand-
ing their network of fellow teachers and possible future collaborators. Especially in
times of physical distancing, the participants appreciated the opportunities to discuss

Teaching Interchange – An Interactive Online Event
445
Fig. 3. Outcomes of the ﬁrst edition of the Teaching Interchange.
Fig. 4. Outcomes of the second edition of the Teaching Interchange.
challenges and receive feedback on their projects. Establishing a sense of community
was a positive outcome of the events.
In conclusion, the Teaching Interchange is an informal, yet structured conference
format for educators. Its major strength is the needs-based peer learning approach. The
participants can develop themselves and their teaching methods. The event’s adaptive
design and low threshold of participation are especially valuable in unprecedented sit-
uations like the current COVID-19 pandemic. The employed peer learning approach is
a promising tool to use in crisis situations characterized by rapid change. Its interactive

446
L. Bücking et al.
Fig. 5. Future plans of the participants of the second edition of the Teaching Interchange.
methodology is adaptable to any group size. In addition, the event provided the opportu-
nity to reﬂect and learn from one’s own experiences which empowered the participants
to adapt their actions in face of high uncertainty.
The format of the event could be further extended by including design thinking
processes to initiate collaborations on speciﬁc projects. Further, experts could be invited
based on the needs and background of the participants. To further lower the threshold of
participation, the poster preparation could be omitted and substituted by an interactive
introduction of the participants. The format of the Teaching Interchange can empower
people in any ﬁeld to adapt in situations of high uncertainty. It is therefore equally
promising in other ﬁelds facing developments of rapid change.
