Training Engineering University Students
to Participate in Academic Mobility Programs
Natalia V. Kraysman(B)
, Farida T. Shageeva
, Julia Ziyatdinova
,
and Andrei B. Pichugin
Kazan National Research Technological University, Kazan, Russia
n_kraysman@mail.ru
Abstract. Today, Europe pays much attention to mutual recognition of academic
degrees and international cooperation in science and education, which is very
important for Russian universities. The paper is relevant due to the importance of
academic mobility in integrating foreign students into the educational environment
of European universities. The paper is to show that there are special educational
programs that prepare students to study in Europe. The paper demonstrates the
Professional Success Psychology program implemented at KNRTU. In order to
properly prepare students for academic mobility, the program includes the follow-
ing topics: interpersonal communication, psychology of success, cross-cultural
communication, ethics in business communication, general principles for build-
ing a successful professional career, leadership, image, academic mobility – to
name just a few. The paper also shows the French for Academic Mobility pro-
gram implemented. This educational program include cultural, methodological,
and linguistic aspects necessary for preparing students to study in France. The
paper shows that in order to draw up and implement a program for preparing stu-
dents for academic mobility, a survey was conducted on the reasons why students
attend classes in preparation for studies at French universities. The analysis of the
reasons listed allowed the teacher to properly draw up a plan and a program of
classes in order to use more effective methods, techniques and means of training.
The paper also presents the content of the developed program prepared according
to the requirements of students.
Keywords: Students’ academic mobility · International educational space ·
Language training program · Professional Success Psychology program
1
Context
Currently, academic mobility is developing rapidly throughout the world and European
universities are admitting more and more students from different countries, including
Russia. Foreign students who study at European universities major in a variety of spe-
cialties, but most often they choose technical and legal areas. Known for their quality
of education, European universities offer the opportunity to continue their studies, open
to the international environment [1–4]. It should be noted that Europe pays much atten-
tion to mutual recognition of academic degrees and international cooperation in science
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 447–454, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_46

448
N. V. Kraysman et al.
and education, which is very important for Russian universities. In integration of Rus-
sian universities into the international educational space, a signiﬁcant role is given to
the academic mobility of students, which is conducive to improving education quality,
developing mutual understanding between cultures and peoples of different countries
[5–8].
2
Purpose
The purpose of this paper is to analyze the existing practice of organizing the aca-
demic mobility for engineering university students, analyze the Professional Success
Psychology program, and develop a language training program to facilitate the students’
academic mobility.
3
Approach
The development of students’ academic mobility in modern environment is a strate-
gic goal not only at the university level, but also nationwide. For a Russian student,
participation in mobility programs provides motivation for learning foreign languages,
replenishing cultural and professional experience. The important thing is that once gain-
ing this experience, students return back to their native university. On the one hand,
it stimulates the process of international integration in higher education. On the other
hand, it promotes popularization of our native values among students abroad [9–12].
Moreover, in modern conditions, universities are in ﬁerce competition with each
other. Indicators directly related to students’ academic mobility, such as the number of
foreign students, the number of participants in exchange programs or mobility programs,
partnership agreements with foreign universities, not only allow the university to claim
a worthy place in the world educational rankings, but also promote the image of the
university globally [13–16]. Academic mobility represents the following key character-
istics of an academically mobile person: mobility of motivation and ﬂexibility of goals;
ability to self-education and the need for self-improvement; readiness for change, com-
munication, and cooperation; language skills at a level that allows effective interaction
in a socio-cultural and professional environment; readiness to master new knowledge
and techniques; mental ﬂexibility and ability to assess one’s own activities and critically
analyze incoming information [17–20].
Since2006,theRepublicofTatarstanhasbeenimplementingAlgaryshgrantprogram
of the Government of the Republic of Tatarstan for training, retraining and internship of
citizens in Russian and foreign educational and scientiﬁc organizations. This is the ﬁrst
regional program of its kind in Russia. It solves two important socio-economic problems
at a time: training and support of the intellectual elite of the Republic of Tatarstan and
meeting the needs of the republic’s economy in high-end professionals.
One of the important areas of international activities at Kazan National Research
Technological University (KNRTU) is providing the students’ academic mobility. To
this end, an educational program was created to prepare students for academic mobility.
Thisprogramallowsstudentstoacquirelinguistic,interdisciplinary,methodological,and

Training Engineering University Students to Participate
449
didactic knowledge for their successful studies, as well as for the fastest possible adap-
tation to both university and non-university activities. This program has been running
since 2014. Besides, in order to prepare students for academic mobility in November-
December 2021, KNRTU implemented the Professional Success Psychology program.
In order to properly prepare students for academic mobility, the program includes the
following topics: interpersonal communication, psychology of success, cross-cultural
communication, ethics in business communication, the basics of goal setting and time
management, general principles for building a successful professional career, leader-
ship, image, academic mobility – to name just a few. This program has been success-
fully completed by 39 KNRTU students. In classes, students took active part in work,
learned new things and considered interesting subjects. All participants felt at ease in a
friendly environment, were always in high spirits, were open to share their knowledge
and opinions.
The Psychology of Professional Success program aims at professional and psycho-
logical training of students, increasing the level of preparedness for academic mobility,
for effective professional activity, formation of a holistic view of behavior psychology in
various situations, development of professional and psychological orientation of an indi-
vidual, that shows itself in constant attention, aspiration, habit to identify and account
for psychological aspects when performing any professional actions. To achieve this
goal, the following issues were addressed in course of the program: revealing theoreti-
cal foundations of modern psychology, patterns of development and functioning of the
psyche and personality, features of interaction between people, effective functioning in
various situations of professional activity; formation of students’ psychological knowl-
edge, skills and qualities necessary for effective professional activity; gaining hands-on
experience in the development of communicative and other soft skills that contribute to
achieving success in professional activity, revealing the opportunities for self-realization.
As has been shown, the Psychology of Professional Success program contributes to
the formation and deepening of methodological and theoretical knowledge in general
psychology, occupational psychology, mastering the psychological analysis methods to
effectively solve various applied problems related to professional activity, formation of
readiness for academic mobility. Upon completion of the program, the students will
be expected to know: the psychological aspects of professional development; the main
factors determining professional choice; the essence and social signiﬁcance of future
profession; ways to develop self-conﬁdence; strategies for setting goals; ways to resolve
conﬂict situations; psychological patterns of socialization; psychological speciﬁcs of the
individual-society interaction.
In addition, mastering the program will enable students to: analyze the social devel-
opment situation characterized by a system of personal relationships with others; react
correctly to the behavior of other people; analyze professional communication situa-
tions; adequately perceive themselves and others; activate their professional psycholog-
ical potential; analyze the relationship between personal characteristics and professional
performance, and carry out their activities based on the ﬁndings of this analysis; apply
emotional and volitional self-regulation techniques; form the need for achievement and
self-afﬁrmation; perform a professional self-evaluation; design the trajectory of their

450
N. V. Kraysman et al.
professional self-development; predict, prevent and resolve business and interpersonal
conﬂicts [21–24].
The following competences are developed as a result of completing the program:
preparedness for acting in non-standard situations, bearing social and ethical responsi-
bility for decisions made; readiness for self-development, self-realization, use of creative
potential; readiness for communication in oral and written forms in Russian and foreign
languages to address professional issues; tolerance to social, ethnic, confessional, and
cultural differences; ability to search for, analyze, synthesize, and generalize scientiﬁc
information, to set research goals and choose optimal methods and techniques to achieve
them, etc.
Upon completion, we developed questionnaires to be ﬁlled out by all participants.
The following questions were asked in the questionnaire: 1) What prompted you to take
part in the Psychology of Professional Success program? 2) Why do you think you might
need foreign language skills in your professional activity? 3) Do you intend to study or
do internship at a foreign university? 4) What do you like about the foreign education
system? 5) Is it vital for a modern specialist to be ﬂuent in foreign languages, in your
opinion? 6) Do you intend to work abroad after graduation? 7) Which countries would
you choose to study or work? 8) Do you have any friends among foreign students?
For question “What prompted you to take part in the Psychology of Professional
Success program?” three answers were offered and the students could choose one or
more options, if desired. Almost all students chose more than one option. According to
the survey results, 33.3% of students took up the Psychology of Professional Success
program to improve their professional competence, 90.5% because of the need for self-
improvement and learning new things, and 81% because of interest in psychology and
foreign languages.
To the question “Why do you think you might need foreign language skills in your
professional activity?” 10 answer options were suggested, the students could choose one
or more, as well as add their own answer. According to the survey results, 66.7% of stu-
dents answered that second-language skills may be needed to participate in professional
activities in international companies; 61.9% - to participate in international conferences,
seminars, forums, and other scientiﬁc events; 47.6% - to study and work abroad, for pro-
fessional retraining/advanced training abroad; 42.9% - to establish partnerships; 33.3%
- to develop international programs and projects and provide expert and consulting ser-
vices in professional activities abroad; 19% - to study the experience of international
companies; 4.8% - for travel. To the question: “Do you intend to study or do internship
at a foreign university?” 70% of students answered positively, while the rest said they’d
like to but weren’t sure if they’d be able to. To the question “What do you like about the
foreign education system?” the students answered the following: more opportunities;
quality of education; the opportunity to fulﬁll their potential; new experience, relations
and acquaintances, the opportunity to get a job abroad; a new environment with foreign
friends; professionalism of teachers, new equipment, constant updating of information;
high level of education; a practice-oriented approach to learning; an atmosphere where
you can fully immerse yourself in a foreign language, to name just a few.
To the question: “Is it vital for a modern specialist to be ﬂuent in foreign languages,
in your opinion?” all students answered that this is critical and that learning new things

Training Engineering University Students to Participate
451
is always necessary. According to the students, in today’s context, when everything is
changing rapidly, students need to have a better command of foreign languages to grasp
knowledge and take advantage of opportunities. To the question “Do you intend to work
abroad after graduation?” four people answered that they were not planning to work
abroad, the rest gave a positive answer. To the question"Which countries would you
choose to study or work?” three people answered that they would like to study or work
in the USA, 5 people in France, one in each of Australia, Ecuador, China, and Korea, the
rest preferred European countries. To the question “Do you have friends among foreign
students?” a slim majority of the students answered that they do, while the rest said they
haven’t made friends yet but would like to.
In general, the study showed that the Psychology of Professional Success program is
important and interesting for students and that more attention should be paid to teaching
foreign languages and various aspects of psychology. It’s also important to focus on
training students for academic mobility so that they’re more prepared for university and
non-university life in other countries. When asked if they were satisﬁed with the program
and whether it was effective and fascinating, nearly all students said they were entirely
satisﬁed and that the program was effective for them; two people answered that they
were partially satisﬁed.
KNRTU also provides the academic mobility to French universities. To this end,
an educational program was created to prepare students for academic mobility, called
French for Academic Mobility. The program continues for one academic year, classes are
held twice a week, each lesson lasts for 3 h, the program is divided into two parts: the ﬁrst
part is French for Everyday Life and Preparation for DELF (levels B1, B2), the second
part is French for University. Classes in preparation for academic mobility of students are
conducted according to specially developed programs and plans to motivate students to
enter the master’s program in France. This program allows students to acquire linguistic,
interdisciplinary, methodological, and didactic knowledge for their successful studies at
French universities, as well as for the fastest possible adaptation to both university and
non-university activities. The program helps them optimally integrate into the various
components of French universities, namely, understand lectures and practical classes
by ear, keep notes during classes, read specialized books, understand documents in
all the disciplines studied, write term papers and master’s theses, pass exams, address
administrative issues at the university, and much more.
To improve the effectiveness of the classes, we have conducted a survey among the
students who are preparing for academic mobility, to reveal why the students need to pre-
pare in advance for studying at French universities. The students identiﬁed the following
reasons: know basic information about theoretical and practical classes at French univer-
sities, about the structure of studies, the tasks given during classes; know the professional
vocabulary in French; understand and know cultural and linguistic skills and abilities;
be able to make lecture notes in French in order to use them in seminars and exams;
learn to reproduce oral and written speech at exams; be able to word their problems
when communicating with the university staff (at the dean’s ofﬁce, in the department of
international affairs, etc.); be able to translate texts within their major, render them, make
presentations, write summaries, make presentations, know how practical and theoreti-
cal classes are conducted at French universities; be familiar with the higher education

452
N. V. Kraysman et al.
system in France; be able to communicate with French students (choose the right lan-
guage for emails, when communicating at student forums, be able to verbally introduce
themselves, tell about their studies, etc.).
The analysis of the above reasons why students attend classes in preparation for
academic mobility allows the teacher to make a correct plan and program of classes in
order to use more efﬁcient methods, techniques and teaching tools. This program aims
at preparing students for studies at French universities, that is, at improving their French
to meet special requirements and introducing them to the higher education system in
France. Also, French teachers of KNRTU stimulate interest of students to pass the inter-
national examination DELF/DALF and to obtain international certiﬁcates on French.
Students of KNRTU successfully pass these examinations and receive B1, B2 levels.
The program includes the following topics: admission of foreign students to French
universities, organization of lectures and practical classes, organization of industrial,
educational and scientiﬁc internships in French companies, writing motivation letters,
CVs, working with the websites of French universities, socialization in France, regional
traditions and much more. During the academic mobility preparation classes, students
are taught to: express their thoughts in French and understand the French language in the
university administrative environment (in deaneries, departments, international activi-
ties departments, etc.); carry on ofﬁcial business correspondence in French, which is
necessary for admission to the university; know international etiquette; know the rules
of conduct in various situations of university and non-university communication; be
able to use vocabulary related to the main topics in business, cultural, socio-economic,
university and professional communication; master monological and dialogical speech,
so that students can participate in practical classes, colloquiums, prepare reports, speak
to the teacher and students and much more.
4
Actual Outcomes
After the students have completed educational programs for preparing to academic
mobility, they successfully undertake Master’s programs at European universities, study
there, and get Master’s degrees. After studying at European universities, the students
return to Russia and work in companies using their knowledge, experience, and skills
acquired in Europe. For example, over the past six years, 14 KNRTU students have won
the Henri Poincaré grant co-funded by the French Embassy in Russia and the government
of Tatarstan to study for a master’s degree in France.
5
Conclusions
KNRTU has provided all necessary conditions for organizing the academic mobility for
engineering university students to European universities: the French Language Resource
Center is in place, academic mobility preparation programs are being implemented, stu-
dents participate in grants for studies at European universities and linguistic internships,
to name just a few. All these academic mobility preparation activities arouse great inter-
est among students. Preparing for academic mobility motivates students to enroll in
European universities and helps them adapt more quickly to their studies and everyday

Training Engineering University Students to Participate
453
life abroad. Thanks to such training, technological university students win grants and
study at foreign universities, then return to Russia and ﬁnd jobs in the specialty mastered
in other countries, applying their knowledge, skills, and experience.

Student Associations as a Way of Improving
Professional Competencies and Soft Skills
Julia Lopukhova1
, Elena Makeeva1,2(B)
, Ekaterina Gorlova1
,
and Tatyana Rudneva3
1 Samara State Technical University, Samara, Russian Federation
helenmckey2205@gmail.com
2 Samara State University of Social Sciences and Education, Samara, Russian Federation
3 Samara University, Samara, Russian Federation
Abstract. Nowadays higher education institutions, technical universities, and
large corporations all over the world support student associations in the belief
that they aid student learning in many important ways. Engagement in associa-
tions gives students an opportunity to learn in the ways that simulate necessary
professional competencies and soft skills. They also engage students in social
learning and provide links to the relevant communities of practice. Thus, mem-
bership and involvement in university and professional associations is a signiﬁcant
factor in students’ professional and personal development. The present research
emphasises the importance of student associations in a technical university ecosys-
tem. The authors start with a brief insight into associations history and review
existing associations such as Research Center of Expertise (RCE), and Interna-
tionale Gesellschaft für Ingenieurpädagogik (IGIP) as according to the survey
these two associations are the most well-known among students and serve as a
source of motivational ideas for students’ initiatives and projects. The research
proves that university authorities should pay a special attention to this important
matter as there is a shortage of associations aimed at developing professional com-
petencies. Also, students’ involvement in such associations increases the students’
cooperation with professors in different dimensions and enhances the individuals’
motives.

IGIP

Introduction
Nowadays higher education institutions, technical universities, and large corporations
all over the world support student associations in the belief that they aid student learning
in many important ways. Engagement in associations gives students an opportunity to
learn in the ways that simulate necessary professional competencies and soft skills. They
also engage students in social learning and provide links to the relevant communities of
practice. Thus, membership and involvement in university and professional associations
is a signiﬁcant factor in students’ professional and personal development. Student affairs

Student associations, clubs, and organizations help students create connections, build
relationships, and expand their skills beyond the classroom. Student associations are
great for improving their university experience, skills and professional connections. The
role of student associations is critical, especially now during the time of the COVID-19

organizations were also scrambling to ﬁgure out what comes next. Students were sent
home, and that broke up many of the connections forged between students when they

important as ever, despite all difﬁculties created by the pandemic.

Research Background
Though the present research emphasises the importance of student associations in a tech-
nical university ecosystem, it’s important to start with a brief insight into associations
history and review existing associations such as Research Center of Expertise (RCE), and
Internationale Gesellschaft für Ingenieurpädagogik (IGIP) as a leading global engineer-
ing association which has 50 years of tradition in contributing to engineering pedagogy
and consolidates individuals and institutions as well as local branches represented by aca-
demics in the ﬁeld of Engineering Pedagogy. This choice is not a random one. According
to our survey (over 1000 students covered), these two associations are the most well-
known among technical students at Samara State Technical University (SSTU) and serve
as a source of motivational ideas for students’ initiatives and projects.
An important role in promoting education for sustainable development (ESD) among
students in many countries is played by Regional centres of expertise (RCE) established
under the auspices of the UN University [3, 4]. Initially, RCEs were conceived as inter-
mediaries between local authorities and educational organizations. The RCE network
bringstogethermulti-sectoralandinterdisciplinarymemberswhomightnotusuallywork
together: formal education institutions, informal educators, local authorities. According
to RCE Mission, “RCEs help prepare local leaders of tomorrow with the tools and infor-
mation they need to make smart and sustainable choices for the future. RCE efforts
encourage innovation and new approaches to sustainable development. They translate
existing knowledge into concrete actions and empower individuals to make sustainable
choices for themselves and their communities” [5].
Their ﬁve priority areas of action are: “advancing policy by mainstreaming ESD,
transforming learning and training environments using the whole-institution approach,
building capacities of educators and trainers, empowering and mobilizing youth, and
ﬁnally accelerating sustainable solutions at the local level” [5]. At all levels of soci-
ety, RCEs play a crucial role in implementing these goals using their local knowledge

and global network. Local knowledge, expertise, and best practices are shared globally
through the network and can be adapted and applied successfully in other regions. RCEs
also play a central role in the transfer of global technologies, knowledge, and experiences
at the local level through their programmes and activities.
RCESamara was approved in 2007. It was the ﬁrst center in Russia and one of the ﬁrst
centers in Europe along with the centers in Munich, Graz and Skane. The key partner and
the hosting organization of RCE Samara is Samara State Technical University. After the
merger of two regional universities (Samara State Technical University and Samara State

them (SGASU) requires brand new start. Samara State Technical University (SSTU)
today is the largest Technopolis of the Volga region, which in 2014 celebrated its 100th
anniversary. The whole era of the formation and development of engineering education
and science of the Samara region and neighboring regions is connected precisely with
this university.

Systems on the Biosphere, the Institute of Social and Human Sciences and Technologies,

focuses on students carrying out participatory action research enabled by collaboration
with regional stakeholders on ESD.
After the merger of two regional universities (Samara State Technical University

celebrated its 100th anniversary. The whole era of the formation and development of

3
Project Description
3.1
Purpose of Study
In the present research, the authors investigate the role of student associations in students’
education and their professional and personal development and the inﬂuence of RCE
and IGIP in developing student associations. The object of the research is the level
of professional competences and soft skills used by students to effectively study and
then ﬁll their job positions. The following soft skills are examined: communication,
collaboration, creativity and critical thinking. Professional competences, in their turn,
aredeﬁnedincloseconnectionwithrelevantprofessions.Theauthorsparticularlyspecify

460
J. Lopukhova et al.
professional competences necessary to successfully perform job positions in engineering
education and open up the opportunities student associations offer for improving both
professional competencies and soft skills.
3.2
Research Basis
Student life is a complex and multifaceted process including academic, scientiﬁc, per-
sonal and creative and leisure aspects. In SSTU, in order to develop a student and prepare
a professional specialist, much attention is paid to extracurricular life. Extra-educational
students’ activities departments are an integrated part of the university process which
create students’ learning support through programmes and services that promote leader-
ship and development. They are typically led by vice rectors and deans. The main goal
of these departments is to work in every way with students to support their personal
and professional advancement. Objectives of these departments include the following:
commitment to extraordinary learning by students, staff and community members, both
within and outside the universities; support for enterprising students and engagement
with the world; current and future trends affecting students and campus life to meet
students’ needs; support of students’ self-governance and initiatives; ensuring social
protection of students; ﬁnancial aid information assistance; pre-admission and post-
admission orientation; and alumni affairs. Students’ extracurricular life is commonly
carried out through student associations which are created with the aim of solving var-
ious issues to improve the quality of student life and activities [14]. Thus, the student
association can become a platform for the development of professional and soft skills.
Depending on the ﬁeld of activity, the researchers distinguish the following types of
student associations:
• Social associations (trade union committee, council of student initiatives)
• Research associations (scientiﬁc communities)
• Creative associations (student creative center, vocal studio)
• Sports (student sports clubs and associations)
• Volunteer (association of volunteers)
• Media (student television, student newspaper)
• Patriotic (memory club)
• Intercultural (international cooperation club), etc.
• Professional (student teams, student recruitment agency).
Student associations can also be divided by the following levels:
• Group level
• Faculty level (any student association that includes students from several faculties)
• University level (including students from several faculties).
• Interuniversity level (there are many student associations that include students from
different universities; in fact, this association can be considered interuniversity, but
ofﬁcially it belongs to one of the universities).
Absolutely every student can become a member of one of these student associations
or of several student associations of different levels that are close to him or her interests.

Student Associations as a Way of Improving Professional
461
Student associations and initiatives enable students to interact around common aspi-
rations and share their areas of interest with an academic community. They provide a
means of living their citizenship to the full; they contribute to developing the culture of
debate and intellectual curiosity encouraged by universities; they constitute an invaluable
experience in project management and teamwork.
4
Discussion
Samara State Technical University has recently assumed the duty of organizing profes-
sional associations. Thus, several student associations aimed at developing professional
competencies are now open for technical students (Young Architects Association, Chem-
istry Engineers Project Group, Association of Would-be Mechanicians and others). At
the moment, students upon their own initiative are creating an international association
named Study Buddies. This association currently unites students of all majors from
Technical University. The student initiative of creating this association was born while
students took part in the educational programme “The School of Leaders” for the 1st
and 2nd year bachelors which aims to develop and implement social-educational project
to help schoolchildren and adult to master digital technologies and to provide better
employability. Study Buddies is aimed at increasing the prestige of the teaching profes-
sion among schoolchildren of the Samara region and other countries. This is the moment,
when the collaboration of Study Buddies and RCE can be mutually beneﬁcial in terms
of outcomes for both partners.
The task of RCE is to facilitate the collaboration between pre-existing local and
regional stakeholders, creating a global learning space [15–17]. Establishing connections
between authorities, employers and HEIs is a stimulus for implementing ESD into the
whole Samara region. The RCE Samara as it was started from a university base has
the potential to provide knowledge hubs, as well as to link learning with action. The
ESD programme at the university is valuable not only because it helps develop ESD
practitioners and leaders, but also because with the help of RCE it activates the ESD
activities in the community. The collaboration between citizen groups and university
students and staff will strengthen the partnership and is expected to lead to empowerment
of citizens in the regional community. It will provide feedback for the development of
the RCE and for raising awareness of ESD in the region. Although the main focus of
interest among staff members who are working on the ESD programme and the RCE
Samara has been higher education, adult education, and informal learning in civil society,
supporting ESD activities in primary and secondary education in the region is also an
important mission of the RCE.
Study Buddies develops its project based on ESD mission in three directions. Firstly,
they have created two interconnected courses that complement each other. The ﬁrst
courseisaninteractiveQuizletcourseinRussian“100greatteachers”.Thiscourseallows
students to memorize a large amount of information about teachers and psychologists in
a playful way, starting with Plato and Aristotle and up to the present day in the shortest
possible time. The second course “Over a cup of tea with a famous teacher: a conversation
through the prism of times and cultures” is an interdisciplinary English language course
based on subject-language integrated learning (CLIL). This is a reasonable combination

462
J. Lopukhova et al.
of Russian and English languages, pedagogy, psychology and methodology. In this
course, students study the traditions and peculiarities of education in various countries
through the biography and scientiﬁc works of famous teachers. The course includes 40
online lessons, which are planning to place on the Edvibe platform.
Secondly, they are creating an entertaining podcast “Information over Saturation”,
the target audience of which are high school students and students who reﬂect on the role
of a teacher in the modern world and how to make education modern and comfortable.
Thispodcastisanadditiontotheexistingone,inwhichmodernteachersrevealinteresting
pedagogical topics. It’s like two sides of the same coin. On the one hand, teachers talk
about what they think about education, on the other hand, schoolchildren present their
views on education.
The third direction is an intercountry online camp “Russian Express: 5 days with
friends”, which is based on the rich experience of the Russian leadership movement
and pedagogical teams. The Covid-19 crisis provided a clear picture of how important
cross-culturalinteractionfordevelopingcommunicationindifferentﬁeldsis.Limitations
of academic mobility inspire to seek for new ways of communication and to work
out creative solutions for improving it. Students are trying to create an ecosystem of
temporary children’s groups through an online event system based on the experience
of organizing a children’s camp life. The attributes and team-building events are the
foundation for understanding and mutual respect between schoolchildren of different
cultures and nationalities.
Study Buddies is an example a professional student association (PSA) which repre-
sents the institutionalization of a continuous improvement in staff involvement in dif-
ferent professional associations (in our case, RCE and IGIP) as well as student learning
upon instructional practices.
5
Conclusion
The results indicate that student associations have a signiﬁcant effect on engineering
students. Students’ involvement in university associations increase their academic expe-
riences and is followed with higher scientiﬁc achievements. The authors are sure that
institutions should encourage students to join associations of their choice or even create
their own associations from the very beginning of their tenure at the institution. Student
associations should be an integral component of not only particular educational pro-
grammes but of a technical university ecosystem in general since student associations
enhance such forms of learning that are difﬁcult to integrate with traditional courses and,
therefore, supplement formal programmes of study in important ways.
The example of Study Buddies proves that PSAs enable teachers and students to
continually learn from one another via shared visioning and planning.
Long-standing staff-wide beliefs and behaviours that support successful PASs
include:
• Failure, mistakes and uncertainty in work are openly shared and discussed;
• Colleagues agree on broad educational values, but accept disagreements that foster
new dialogue;

Student Associations as a Way of Improving Professional
463
• Teachers receive respect and consideration as people;
• Administrators support “dispersed leadership,” where teachers develop the conﬁdence
to select and adapt strategies that drive improvement.
Further, in successful PASs, high expectations of teachers and students emerge within
a set of priorities that beneﬁts the whole school as well as teachers’ personal ambitions.
Finally, effective PSAs address the interpersonal skills of trust, collaboration and
communication.
Thus, the research proves that student associations aim at increasing and promoting
students’ level and help them to ﬁrstly become a part of a university ecosystem and
then a member of a community of practice. Involvement in associations is effective
on the student life of individuals, and results in the increase of students’ research and
academic experience. Also, students’ involvement in such associations increases the stu-
dents’ cooperation with professors in different dimensions and enhances the individuals’
motives. University authorities should pay a special attention to this important matter as
there is a shortage of associations aimed at developing professional competencies.

Work-in-Progress: Interrelation Between Types
of Social and Psychological Adaptation
and Personal Identity in the Age of Digitalization
Elena Yu Dvoinikova1
, Natalia A. Gridneva1
, Ksenia S. Oparina1
,
Elena Makeeva2(B)
, and Ludmila Kurilenko3
1 Samara State Technical University, Samara, Russian Federation
2 Samara State University of Social Sciences and Education, Samara, Russian Federation
helenmckey2205@gmail.com
3 Samara University, Samara, Russian Federation
Abstract. The paper examines the interrelation between the type of social and
psychological adaptation and personal identity of ﬁrst-year students in a technical
university. The results of an ongoing study are described with a particular focus
on changes of psychic content of social and psychological adaptation and its
constructive and destructive types which were observed. During the experiment
the personal identity characteristic of students and its evolution over a period of
12 years were studied. The paper presents preliminary results which show a decline
in the constructive type of social and psychological adaptation and an increase in
the number of students with diffuse personal identity. Further studies on this topic
are considered.
Keywords: Types of social and psychological adaptation · Personal identity ·
Digitalization
1
Introduction
The digital era has given mankind a new quality of life. Digital technologies accompany
almost all branches of modern human activity. In comparison with previous phases,
these technologies have brought an enormous number of changes in the world in recent
decades. Mode of human life has become completely different, the proportion of physical
activity has diminished, communication has increased, and inﬁnity of self-realization has
arisen. At the same time, human does not acquire exceptional abilities, but replaces them
with digital resources often identifying these resources with his / her own. This effect
impacts on human emotional and psychological health. In general, it can be explained
by an active technological development, which reduces time for mastering new compe-
tences, but simultaneously increases the ﬂexibility of tasks and complicates operational
conditions. It leads to the necessity of an active and immediate adapting to the rapidly
changing social space. That is why the issue of social and psychological adaptation is
becoming particularly topical.
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 465–471, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_48

466
E. Yu Dvoinikova et al.
Social and psychological adaptation is presented by its constructive and destructive
types. In conjunction with content components of adaptation, the characteristic of emo-
tional background accompanying vitality of a person is taking shape. A person with the
constructive type of social and psychological adaptation aims to cope with a problem
when it occurs and chooses from a variety of strategies the wright one. This is achieved
due to potential provided by his / her emotional and psychological state [1]. Because of
high anxiety, a person with the destructive type of adaptation is skeptical about success
of her / his activity and uses known strategies, even if they are not appropriate for this
situation, and a high constriction does not allow expanding the diversity of strategies for
addressing the problem [2].
Personal identity is of great importance for the emotional and psychological resis-
tance of a person in the process of reciprocal social interaction alongside with social
and psychological adaptation. While digitalization of social space, personal identities of
representatives of different generations have various characteristics. Youth is the most
important stage in a personal identity development [3, 4]. So, E.H. Erikson [5, 6] argued,
that the main task of adolescence is the development of a “satisfying identity.” The sci-
entist acknowledged, that “identity development is a lifelong process that individuals
revisit periodically as they engage in subsequent developmental tasks such as intimacy,
generativity, and wisdom” [6, 7]. However, adolescence is the ﬁrst and most important
stage in the further identity development.
For today’s adolescents and emerging adults, a personal identity development is
inextricably linked to the usage of social networking sites. It is becoming increasingly
difﬁcult to separate the “digital life” of adolescents and emerging adults from their real
life environment. Besides in recent years, the COVID-19 virus pandemic has contributed
to the increase of time, which adolescents have spent on social networking sites [8].
It is obvious that virtual space provides expansive opportunities for adolescents to
construct and express their identity using various self-presentation practices. It can be
put down to the fact that in social networking sites social exposition and validation is
extended to a wider audience and therefore provides wider feedback [9, 10].
An extensive analysis of research papers has shown that, basically foreign researchers
of the digital identity of youth and adolescents focus on the following issues:
1. Technical opportunities for digital identity construction. Internet resources offer ado-
lescents such identity development opportunities as “editable affordances to perfect a
user’s identity proﬁle” [11], “tactics to exploit likeability” [12] or “the self-promotion
of only the positive aspects of user identity” [13].
Thebestpresentationservestoachieveanothermainpurposeofself-presentation,
“image control” [14] or “management of the impression caused” [15]. Image control
in a digital space contributes to the fact that projections of real or fake identity of a
social networking sites user can be ampliﬁed. This control is realized through a vari-
ety of means: presenting several similar or different identities on various social net-
working sites or through different proﬁles on the same Internet resource; opportunity
to select the audience that can see these proﬁles, etc.
2. Interrelation of youth identity with self-presentation in social networking sites and
applications. Are these social media and apps a facilitating or hindering factor for

Work-in-Progress: Interrelation Between Types of Social
467
youth identity development? The theory of personal identity has been long formu-
lated, but the Internet has fundamentally changed its understanding. However, it
is crucially important, that Internet communication itself has undergone signiﬁcant
changes throughout its existence. Internet technologies can be asynchronous, round-
the-clock and public. Besides, researchers remark that internet communication has
been losing its anonymity in recent years. This leads to a close interweaving of real
virtual life. As a consequence, youth strengthen relationships with family, relatives,
friends and colleagues. On the other hand, the problem of managing developing iden-
tities arises. Adolescents are increasingly using social networking sites for image
control [7, 16].
3. “Feedback from the community”, based on feeling of group membership and social
capital [16, 17]. Puberty is characterised by a shift in priorities. During this period,
it is important for many adolescents to have prestige not by a primary caregiver,
but by their friends and peers. This is why international researchers remark, that
“… adolescents must walk a ﬁne line between authenticity and enhancing the self
to create a good impression” [18]. Feeling of group membership is inextricably
linked to the concept of a social capital. Personal identity development of youth in
social networking sites allows to increase a social capital: «This kind of effect is
related to personal strategies of self-disclosure and strategies of feedback from the
community. Concerning the former, Knop et al. … link feelings of group membership
tosharingpersonalinformationandself-disclosure,whichareimportantmechanisms
for building and maintaining relationships and for increasing trust between members
of a social group and strengthening group identity» [19, 20].
The authors of this paper believe that the foregoing represents in general the main
trends in the study of a digital identity of adolescents and emerging adults in a foreign
scholarly literature.
These processes also refer to youth and student environment. Over the recent 12 years
of observation of students’ behaviour during social interaction, when searching for learn-
ing tasks solutions, the researchers observed a decrease in interaction activity with each
other and a more frequent usage of Internet sources. The authors also studied personal
identity particularities in the age of changing norms and values of social space inﬂuenced
by the inﬁnite possibilities of information sharing in a digital environment, which create
a criterion of personal potential with no limits. Qualitative changes in the indicators of
students’ personal identity have been observed for 12 years.
2
Project Description
2.1
Purpose of the Study
Purpose of the study is to determine how the type of social and psychological adaptation
and the personal identity interrelate in the context of digitalization.

468
E. Yu Dvoinikova et al.
2.2
Research Materials
The social and psychological adaptation of personality is a phenomenon of ontogenetic
development of personality characterized by speciﬁcs of psychic content, orientation of
activity, perception and interpretation of social phenomena [2].
The ability to social and psychological adaptation develops from a very young age,
in the process of socialization. Adaptation provides an individual with emotional safety
and normal mental state in the dynamics of social change, as well as personal activity
and transforming activity in regard to environmental conditions.
Personal identity plays a great role in making a success of human activities. As a
personal position, it deﬁnes adequacy of realization of social roles and ego-states. An
individual, developing under natural conditions of social interaction, in the process of
socialization masters strategies of own behavior and increases diversity of communi-
cations and so gains experience in meeting the challenges of social environment and
adequacy of expression of emotions in the process of social interaction. The experience
of understanding own feelings is another protective factor in regard to development of
behavioral deviations.
As an artiﬁcial condition of personal socialization and activity, digital environment
decreases the reference level of adaptation tasks, opens up speciﬁc opportunities and
is not taken as a problem, but provides comfortable conditions for prompt access to
information and self-realization and eases playing a role in communication. On this
basis, an individual is not properly impressed by his / her activity and so does not gain
experience of meeting the challenges of social relations to the full extent.
Demand for social interaction causes communication activity of an individual. The
quality of this process is largely determined by the type of social and psychological adap-
tation. Monitoring the changes of social conditions and adaptation of technical students
during 12 years shows the evolution of content of social and psychological adaptation
among different generations of ﬁrst-year students. The study shows a decline in self-
acceptance and emotional comfort against the background of increased escapism, change
of locus of control for the external one, increased submissiveness. All these changes of
content components don’t show disadaptation but conﬁrm decrease in adaptation. In
parallel, the reserchers ﬁxed some anxiety, frustration and constriction indicators, as
well as a steady tendency to their increase.
Monitoring the changes of orientation of empathy has relevance, too. The experiment
with stimulus material shows the change of orientation of sympathy towards characters
of anime and movies to the disadvantage of real people in difﬁcult situations. Students
representing the earlier generation (2009), which did not use digital gadgets on a daily
basis, did not have pronounced reaction for stimuli used and demonstrated more empathy
for feelings of real persons. Methodology applied to measure the level of empathy
conﬁrmed the results of monitoring.

Work-in-Progress: Interrelation Between Types of Social
469
2.3
Research Participants and Means
In the study, the ﬁrst-year students of different generations (generation 2009 – 112
persons and generation 2021 – 120 persons) took part.
2.4
Research Methods
The diagnostic of social and psychological adaptation of personality was run using the
Test of personal adjustment by Rogers-Diamond [21].
At the same time, the study of personal identity of students was carried out using the
diagnostic technique for personal identity research [22], which has led to determination
of evolution of interconnectedness between the degree of digitalization, the level and
the type of social and psychological adaptation.
3
Research Description
The behaviour of the ﬁrst-year students of Samara State Technical University was
researched. This was group work for situation problem solving in accordance with the
course of psychology studied.
The reserahcers monitored the behavior of participants while searching for a solution,
which could be found in consequence of a direct personal collective discussion as well
as through seeking relevant information on the Internet.
4
Discussion
The 12-years-monitoring shows a steady increase in using the Internet by students for
solving the same tasks.

among students in the number of 112 persons in 2009 and 120 persons in 2021.
Figure 1 shows a qualitative decrease in the number of students with the constructive
type of social and psychological adaptation in 2021 in comparison with the number of
such students in 2009.

5
Conclusion
1. Thus, this study has shown a link between the type of social and psychological adap-
tation and the characteristics of personal identity in a digital environment. Comparing
the results for years 2009 and 2021, one can see a considerable increase in the num-
ber of students with diffusive identity accompanied with the growth of students with
the destructive type of social and psychological adaptation.
2. Now it is difﬁcult to make any deﬁnitive predictions about consequences of changes
in psychic content of human life manifested in adaptation and identity under condi-
tions of digitalization. It can only be assumed that while further substitution of human
resources for digital ones the number of neurotic disorders resulting in destruction of
components of social and psychological adaptation and in degradation of qualitative
characteristics of personal identity will keep increasing.

Abstract. Learning programming can be challenging for some students. As Com-
putational Thinking (CT) is one of programming’s basic foundations, this paper
aims to assess the impact of introducing CT prior to learning programming. We
compare two groups of informatics students, one with a CT course and another
without it. Our quasi-experiments show that students with the CT course have bet-
ter theoretical and laboratory exam results; they also have higher retention. From
a questionnaire survey, students from both groups agree that CT can assist them to
learn programming logic, syntax, and runtime. We conclude that introducing CT to
informatics students can help them to learn introductory programming, especially
in increasing student retention.
Keywords: Computational thinking · Informatics education · Programming ·
Student performance · Student retention
1
Introduction
To assist students in introductory programming, some educational tools or methods
have been explored. PlayVisualizerC [1] is a program visualization tool that provides
capability, installability, and usability for novices in C programming. Python Tutor as a
program visualization tool has assisted students to learn programming quite effectively
[2]. Ramirez presented technology-enhanced learning tools to improve the learning expe-
rience in introductory programming [3]. The evaluation of a teaching plan approach that
used multiple active methodologies in an algorithms subject compared to the traditional
teaching method showed signiﬁcant results [4].

Work-in-Progress: The Impact of Computational Thinking
473
Computational thinking (CT) has been known as thinking processes engaged in a
problem formulation so that solutions can be shown as computational stages and algo-
rithms [5]. Shute mentioned six components of CT to solve problems efﬁciently: abstrac-
tion, decomposition, algorithm design, debugging, iteration, and generalization [6]. Den-
ning [7] stated that CT supports programming with ﬁve basic elements for computation
(modularity, data structures, encapsulation, control structures, and recursion).
Agbo reviews the use of CT in supporting students to learn programming [8]. Kaz-
imoglu has explained a study that incorporated CT to learn introductory programming
constructs through digital games [9]. The results indicate that the approach could expand
the problem-solving ability to learn introductory programming. Philip has developed an
approach to using CT for novices in learning programming based on group activity [10].
The results supported the students to differentiate between the problem analysis, design,
and implementation levels. Shyamala has studied a CT course with many students before
they learn introductory programming in the next semester [11].
To the best of our knowledge, no studies have addressed the impact of introducing CT
as a one-semester course before introductory programming in helping IT students learn
programming. Shyamala’s study is focused on Engineering students where a number
of them are not enrolled in IT and do not expect to take future careers in that ﬁeld
[11]. Further, the analysis and the discussion about the improvement are quite limited.
Our study has three research questions (RQ); the ﬁrst two are addressed via a quasi-
experiment while the remaining is addressed via a questionnaire survey. RQ1: Does CT
course help informatics students have higher proﬁciency in programming? RQ2: Does
CT course increase informatics student retention in programming? RQ3: Do IT students
think the CT course helps them to learn programming?
2
Method
RQ1 is addressed by comparing two batches of introductory programming stu-dents:
one with a CT course before learning introductory programming and another without
such a course. CT course helps students to learn programming if students with CT course
have higher marks than the counterpart. Six marks are considered in this study: average
assessments mark, mid-test mark (theory), mid-test mark (lab), ﬁnal test mark (theory),
ﬁnal test mark (lab), and ﬁnal mark. Statistical signiﬁcance is measured via two-tailed
independent t-test with 95% conﬁdence rate.
The CT course is conducted in the semester I, right before introductory program-
ming (semester II). The CT course materials can be seen in Table 1. The course ma-
terials cover the basic concepts of CT and an introduction to higher-order thinking skills
(HOTS). Students need to understand the basic concept ﬁrst and then continue with
visual programming. We are using Blockly Games, Scratch, Blockly, and also Code
Combat to help students understand more about programming concepts in a fun way.
Students are also introduced to modeling and simulation and data analysis so students
can get a big picture of informatics. The course was performed in two hours lecture
sessions weekly.
The introductory programming materials consist of an introduction to algorithms,
data types, variables, sequences, conditional statements, loops, nested loops, func-tions,

474
M. Ayub et al.
arrays, matrices, searching, and sorting. The course was performed in two hours for
lectures and four hours for laboratory sessions weekly.
Both batches of introductory programming students have comparable lecture materi-
als, assessment designs (one lab and one homework assessment per week), and marking
schemes. In total, there are 61 students enrolled in 2019 offering (without CT) and 43
students enrolled one year later (with CT).

We are aware that 2020 offering was conducted during the pandemic. Although
transitioning to online learning might negatively affect students, it does not really affect
student performance [12]. Students might be more tempted to cheat during online learn-
ing, but it is compensated with the introduction of an assessment sub-mission system
that educates the student about academic integrity [13].
RQ2 is addressed similarly to RQ1 except that we consider participation in tests
instead of the marks. Four tests are considered: mid-test (theory), mid-test (lab), ﬁnal
test (theory), and ﬁnal test (lab). It is worth noting that theory and lab tests are conducted
on different days, and it is possible some students just participate in ei-ther of them. No
statistical signiﬁcance tests are performed as the proportion of participation is a single
unit.
RQ3 is addressed via a voluntary survey given to students involved in RQ1. Students
with CT course provide their perspective based on experience while students without
CT provide their perspective based on expectation. The responses are then summarised

3
Result and Discussion
RQ1 is about whether students with CT course have higher proﬁciency in pro-gramming.
Table 3 shows that it is not the case. Although students with CT course seems to have
higher marks, most of the differences are not statistically signiﬁcant. The ﬁnal test
(lab) is the only test where students with CT experience statistically signiﬁcant mark
improvement. CT might have a positive impact, but it is considera-bly small to affect
student performance in general.
RQ2 is about whether students with CT course have higher retention in program-
ming. Table 4 somehow supports the statement with three-fourths of the tests expe-
riencing a substantial increase. Students with CT might have higher conﬁdence to com-
plete the tests and the course given that some programming concepts are related to
CT.
RQ3 is about whether students think CT course helps them to learn programming.
The survey was responded to by 31 students with CT (2020 offering) and 22 students

the counterpart as no statistical differences are found in those questions. Hence, it can
be stated that the expectation of CT aligns with the real experience.

4
Conclusion
This study measures the impact of introducing CT as a one-semester course be-fore
introductory programming in helping IT students learn programming. Even though stu-
dents with the CT course appear to have higher marks, most of the differences are not
statistically signiﬁcant, except for the laboratory ﬁnal test. Students with CT might have
higher conﬁdence to complete the programming tests because the course gave some
programming concepts related to CT. Students from both groups agree that CT assists
them to learn programming logic, syntax, and runtime. Students with CT gave opinions
that CT is arguably beneﬁcial to learn programming.
For future work, we plan to replicate the study and check whether the ﬁndings are
similar. We also plan to improve the design of our CT course and test its effectiveness.
Acknowledgment. This research is ﬁnancially supported by the Maranatha Christian University
Re-search Committee, by means of the Maranatha Christian University Grant.

Improving Secondary School Engineering
Education Access in Rural Ohio
R. F. A. Hamilton(B), Colin Doolittle, Kelly Cichy, and Marianna Doolittle
Northwest State Community College, Archbold, OH 43502, USA
{rhamilton,cdoolittle,mdoolittle,kcichy}@northweststate.edu
Abstract. The US system of education often ignores engineering instruction in
secondary schools. While inroads have been made to include engineering prac-
tice and thought in curriculum, secondary teachers often receive no training in
engineering concepts. The mismatch results in few engineering principles being
taught and students leaving secondary school with little idea of what it means to
study engineering at the university level. This creates a self-perpetuating cycle of
inequality and homogeneity in the population of US secondary schools who study
engineering at the university level. This is particularly acute in rural areas. North-
west State Community College serves rural Northwest Ohio, an area of over 5000
square kilometers. In this region there are no other public institutions of higher
education. In order to facilitate a better understanding of engineering principles
among high school teachers in rural Northwest Ohio, Northwest State Community
College has launched a summer program for high school teachers. In an all-day
two-week format, teachers are taught the basics of engineering design and prac-
tice. The course is a modiﬁed version of the introduction to engineering course
entering students complete. Teachers learn the basic principles, but also receive
instruction in engineering pedagogy and best practice. This course is taught as
project based course to both students and secondary teachers.. At the end of the
two weeks, secondary teachers receive an endorsement from Northwest State to
teach Introduction to Engineering. After the course is completed secondary teach-
ers are able to stay in contact with and receive mentoring from the faculty at
Northwest State. This paper describes the initial cohort of teachers and outcomes.
It also describes changes being made to prepare for the second cohort.
Keywords: Secondary education · Teacher training
1
Background
1.1
US Engineering Education
In the US, engineering education is not typically included in secondary education. For
most students formal engineering courses do not occur until they enter university. Quite
often engineering courses at university are only open to students that have declared a
program of study in engineering. This prohibition on non-engineering students enrolling
in engineering courses further compounds the problem of lack of exposure to engineer-
ing in secondary education. Lack of exposure in secondary education leads to fewer
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 479–488, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_50

480
R. F. A. Hamilton et al.
students understanding what engineering is and selecting it as a program of study in
post-secondary education. A result of this, is that engineering students at university
level are predominantly from urban and suburban areas [1].
The dearth of engineering education in secondary education can be traced back
to teacher education programs. Most teachers in the US, even science teachers, com-
plete university level teacher education programs before entering into practice. Very few
teacher education programs at the bachelor’s level include any instruction in engineer-
ing. Each state selects and adopts its own curricular standards for secondary education.
Forty-Four states have adopted curricular standards based on Next Generation Science
Standards (NGSS) [2]. These learning standards include learning outcomes based on
engineering [3]. Rural secondary schools in particular face greater challenges ﬁnding
qualiﬁed teachers and promoting access to such courses [4].
While the inclusion of engineering learning outcomes is laudable, there remains an
unaddressed issue of how to train teachers in the ﬁeld of engineering. The development
of accessible training programs for in-service teachers in engineering is of critical impor-
tance to the success of NGSS and diversifying the bachelor’s level engineering student
population.
1.2
Northwest State Community College
Northwest State Community College (NSCC) is a rural community college with a six
county service area in Ohio. Five of the six counties are classiﬁed as rural and the sixth
is classiﬁed as suburban. The six counties together encompass an area of 6475 square
km (2500 square miles). The population of these counties is roughly 1.9 million. Within
this area NSCC is the only community college and the only public institution for post-
secondary education. The only other option for post-secondary education in the service
area is a small private liberal arts college. As a community college, NSCC is open access
and provides the ﬁrst two years of higher education. In engineering, programs are offered
leading to associate of applied science degree that students can use to either enter the
workforce or transfer to a bachelor’s degree program at a university. During the 2021–
2022 academic year there were 29 secondary schools in the NSCC service area enrolling
8389 secondary students.
2
The Program
2.1
The Concept
In order to facilitate an increase in qualiﬁed teachers in the local service area, NSCC
began a special class for in-service teachers. The course was MET 299 Intro to Engineer-
ing Technology for Teachers. The course was initially run in the summer of 2021. The
course took the same information and learning outcomes as taught in our MET 100 Intro
to Engineering Technology course and infused it with pedagogical teaching content to
help teachers teach an introduction to engineering course for high school students. The
course was offered in compressed format. Students met with instructors for several hours
a day Monday through Thursday for two weeks. The course had ﬁve learning outcomes
related to engineering:

Improving Secondary School Engineering Education Access in Rural Ohio
481
1. Recognize the difference between different disciplines in the engineering ﬁeld,
2. Be able to maneuver basic mathematic structures,
3. Be able to perform dimensional analysis,
4. Demonstrate proﬁciency in utilizing computer skills for a successful venture through
programs in the engineering technologies department and career, and
5. Demonstrate the ability to think creatively and critically about problems and
solutions.
Pedagogically students were to learn how to create 5E lesson plans. 5E lesson plans
are inquiry based and work to create lessons which are engaging and dynamic for stu-
dents. The ﬁve E’s in the 5E lesson plan are: engage, explore, explain, elaborate, and
evaluate [5]. The 5E lesson plan model has also been demonstrated to pair very well as
a tool to successfully implement the NGSS [6].
2.2
Teaching the Program
Throughout the course there were two main faculty, who attended the sessions and were
responsible for grading and assessment. One of these faculty members was an engi-
neering technology faculty member who had a background in mechanical engineering
technology. The other faculty member has a background in pedagogy and has taught
numerous education courses across multiple levels of education and who has worked in
secondary curriculum development and as a secondary school teacher. The pedagogical
faculty holds a PhD in Anthropology and is well versed in STEM. Three other faculty
members from various engineering and technology programs were also faculty on the
course. These faculty members introduced the various areas of engineering that are their
specialty to the students. In total students were introduced to the ﬁelds of Electrical
Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Biomedical Engineering, Quality Control, and
Computer Science.
After each session on each area students wrote a brief reﬂection about what they
learned and what they found interesting. The different areas were also used to introduce
students to overarching themes within engineering. One of these themes was the use of
logic to solve problems. Another was the importance of ethics in engineering. Students
also worked throughout the two weeks on a project where they could work their way
through the engineering design cycle. Students built and tested “water rockets.” These
were powered by the compression of air and the release of the air and water inside in
the rocket. Students were provided minimal instruction and were allowed to proceed in
a manner of their choosing thus mirroring the pedagogy of a 5E lesson plan.
2.3
Motivation for Enrolling
Secondary school teachers in the US are required to obtain continuing education. How-
ever, there are easier and cheaper ways to obtain continuing education credit than enroll-
ment in a community college courses. In an effort to increase enrollment, NSCC offered
in-service teachers who enrolled the opportunity to become credentialed as a dual enroll-
ment instructor for Introduction to Engineering Technology. Dual enrollment programs

482
R. F. A. Hamilton et al.
in the US are used to award university credit to students while they are still in high
school.
In Ohio, the dual enrollment program is known as College Credit Plus (CCP). Stu-
dents can either directly enroll and attend course on a college campus as part of CCP or
they may take a course at their secondary school taught by a credentialed instructor to
also earn university credit through CCP [7]. Cost associated with CCP courses for stu-
dents are covered by the state. This includes tuition and fees. Courses taught at the high
school by credentialed instructors are often easiest for students in our service area, as
geographical distance often results in signiﬁcant travel time. The two secondary schools
that teachers in the ﬁrst cohort attended from are a 20 min drive and a 30 min drive from
the NSCC campus. Both schools operate on schedules where students would be unable
to take a class before or after the period of the course at NSCC campus. Students taking
a course at the end of the day would be deterred by the possibility of missing extracurric-
ular activities after the normal school day. Additionally, there is no public transportation
to the NSCC campus. Students must rely on personal cars or ride sharing apps to get
to and from the campus. Secondary schools also have the option of allowing students
who are not seeking college credit to enroll in CCP courses taught in their building. The
faculty at NSCC see this as advantageous as it will widen the scope of students in our
rural area that gain exposure to engineering.
Teachers who are able to teach CCP courses are at an advantage. They can often
negotiate for better working conditions with their district. This may include extra pay
or a more favorable teaching schedule or larger classroom to teach in. Quite often they
receive increased funds to buy more teaching equipment to supplement what schools
already have.
3
Results
3.1
Proﬁles of Teachers Enrolling
There were three in-service teachers who enrolled in the ﬁrst cohort. In following insti-
tutional protocol they will be identiﬁed with pseudonyms. The three teachers are Mark,
Daniel, and Sean. Mark and Sean teach at a rural comprehensive secondary school
in Williams County that enrolls approximately 840 students. Daniel works at a rural
comprehensive secondary school in Deﬁance County that enrolls approximately 325
students.
Mark holds a Bachelor’s of Science degree in Secondary Education with a special-
ization in Life and Earth Science. He has completed graduate course work to add an
Integrated Science endorsement to his teaching license. The integrated science endorse-
ment allows him to teach any secondary school natural science course. He had ﬁnished
12 years of teaching prior to the program. Mark has and continues to teach a range of
Natural Science courses.
Daniel holds a Bachelor’s of Science degree in Biology and a Master’s of Education
degree in Technology. He had completed eight years of teaching prior to the program.
Additionally, he had worked for 18 years in information technology both in industry and
in K-12 school districts. Daniel has taught and continues to teach courses in Information
Technology, Robotics, and Video Editing.

Sean holds a Bachelor’s of Science in Adult/ Young Adolescent Education with a

responses from each teacher about the course is included below.
3.2
Collection of Results
Results were collected from reﬂection papers teachers completed throughout the course.
The reﬂections were short write ups after a module. Students were asked to write about
what they thought of the topic that was presented, what they learned, and how they might
incorporate it into teaching an engineering course at their secondary school.
Engineering Technology and Engineering Module.
Sean
For the Engineering Technology session, [the instructor] mostly focused on what engi-
neering technology is, and how engineering technology differs from pure engineering
programs. As I understand it, engineering is more of your classic program, with a focus
on concepts and design. Engineering technology focuses more on the application of
engineering concepts to a speciﬁc problem, and teaching tangible skills. [The Instructor]
made sure to point out that there’s a huge demand for engineering technology and related
job ﬁelds. Starting salary and what sort of credentials and aptitudes were discussed.
I think that this information is vitally important to share with the students, as many
students may not be aware of the different positions that are open in an engineering
ﬁeld, and how much those positions can differ. I would view being an engineering tech
as being much more attainable than an engineer (from a math perspective and overall).
Mark
I believe this section is referring to the ethics of technology and engineering. The material
presented here is a simple drag and drop chunk that will be necessary for the students
to be informed on and take part in meaningful class discussions ethics in engineering.
It is interesting to consider some of the major accomplishments in technology and the
failures that have occurred along the way which motivated scientists and researchers
to come up with a solution to a problem. Sometimes the development of the solution
includes a discovery or advancement in technology and understanding.
Daniel
The discussion of ethics and engineering was a good one. In many cases there are forced
(sic) of good and evil so to speak. Students need to have an understanding that there
are many aspects to design that need to be considered. They also need to know that just
because something failed does not mean they are a failure. It just means that they must
learn something from it. My robotics class thrives from its failures. Redesign is part of
the process.
The ethics discussion has a place in the classroom for sure. Was it worth the high
cost to send a man to the moon? What about atomic energy and weapons? Will artiﬁcial
intelligence wreak havoc someday as in the terminator? Will we be able to engineer our
way out of climate change? Will we one day populate other planets?

Electrical Engineering
Sean
[The instructor] introduced us to basic electrical concepts, and how those concepts can

electrical circuits and electrical concepts, and almost everything we learned with [the

In the planning session for the bottle rockets, we brain-stormed the design of our rockets
