3.3
Analysis of Results
All the reﬂections used positive language and showed the teachers had a favorable view
of the modules. The most interesting result was that without prompting the teachers
mentioned connections between the engineering content and content from other areas
they had previous experience teaching and discussed how they could leverage that to
improve student learning in their future engineering courses. This backs up the 5E lesson
plan pedagogy. As the teachers relate the new material to previous material, they are more
likely to build lessons in the 5E lesson pedagogy for their students. Previous research
[9] has shown that the use of 5E lesson plans has a positive effect on the self-efﬁcacy of
pre-service elementary school instructors. These results indicate the same may be true
for in-service secondary school instructors. The use of such practices in the classroom
for students are highly effective [10].
4
Conclusion
Three teachers from two different secondary schools enrolled in the program. The three
were credentialed through CCP and their schools began to offer engineering courses for
the ﬁrst time. During the following academic year approximately 60 students enrolled in
engineering courses at the two secondary schools. Observation of the courses revealed
engaged and motived secondary students. The program was successful in allowing more
secondary schools to offer engineering courses. NSCC faculty would prefer to see higher
enrollments in the courses and more secondary students at more secondary schools be
given exposure to engineering.
The ﬁrst offering of this course was in late summer of 2021. Feedback from the
teachers involved indicated that early summer, likely in early June, would be better and
drive increases in enrollment. A second cohort was planned for June 2022. However,
there was no enrollment and this course was cancelled. Feedback will be taken from
a wider pool of teachers in regards to offering another cohort in the summer of 2023.
Various scheduling options will be considered. This includes shorter time over more
days, fewer days per week over longer weeks, and possible synchronous hybrid courses.
Another alternative that will be explored is offering the program as non-credit. Offering
as non-credit would eliminate the need for teachers to go through the NSCC admissions
process and possibly reduce the cost. It would also allow for the course to be offered
outside the normal academic terms.

Research in Engineering Pedagogy

Undergraduate Students’ Attitudes Toward
an Engineering Course that Integrates Several
Levels of Abstraction
Aharon Gero(B), Mohammed Ali Hadish, and Shahar Kvatinsky
Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa, Israel
gero@technion.ac.il, hadish16@campus.technion.ac.il,
shahar@ee.technion.ac.il
Abstract. Abstract thinking is considered higher-order that allows one to solve
problems while switching between levels of abstraction, i.e., moving between mul-
tiple levels of complexity. The Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering
(Technion – Israel Institute of Technology) combined two undergraduate courses,
focusing on different levels of abstraction, into a single course “Digital Systems
and Computer Structure” integrating multiple levels of abstraction, i.e., logical,
micro-architecture and architecture levels. The present study aimed to character-
ize students’ attitudes toward the course. This mixed-method study involved 103
undergraduate students. According to the ﬁndings, students hold positive attitudes
toward a course that combines multiple levels of abstraction. Students claim that
the course is interesting, provides a complete picture of computer systems, imparts
higher-order thinking skills, but at the same time imposes a heavy load.
Keywords: Abstract thinking · Students’ attitudes · Digital systems · Computer
structure
1
Introduction
One type of thinking relevant to engineering is abstract thinking, namely, focusing on
meaningful information for the current phase and temporarily ignoring the unnecessary
details [1, 2]. Abstract thinking is considered higher-order thinking that allows one to
solve problems while switching between levels of abstraction, i.e., moving between
multiple levels of complexity [3].
In view of the above, the Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering (Tech-
nion – Israel Institute of Technology) combined two undergraduate courses, dealing
with different levels of abstraction, into a single course “Digital Systems and Computer
Structure” integrating multiple levels of abstraction. This unique course is mandatory for
beginning electrical and computer engineering (hereinafter: ECE) students and computer
science (hereinafter: CS) students. The present study aimed to characterize students’
attitudes toward the course.

2
Abstract Thinking
Abstract thinking, as an important element of computational thinking [4, 5], is relevant
in many ﬁelds, and currently holds a major role in engineering [6]. This is due to the
increased complexity of engineering systems [7] and the Industry 4.0 concept, based,
inter alia, on big data [8]. Therefore, compared to the past, engineers must deal with
growing intricacy, especially in the hardware and software industry [9].
As mentioned earlier, a key concept in abstract thinking is a level of abstraction. It
is possible to characterize an arbitrary number of levels, ranging from the highest level,
where the problem is observed from a general point of view, to the lowest level at which
close attention to detail is needed [10].
For instance, the architecture level is the boundary between software and hardware.
At this level of abstraction, a set of software instructions that the computer can support is
deﬁned. Below this level is the micro-architecture level, focusing on the highest level of
implementation of the features deﬁned at the previous level. The next level, logic gates,
deals with the logical properties of the components deﬁned at the micro-architecture
level. Lower levels address the electronic devices that construct the logic gates and their
physical structure [11].
It is widely agreed that the major cognitive skills of the so-called abstract thinker are
recognizing the level of abstraction appropriate for a particular phase and maneuvering
between levels of abstraction [12, 13].
3
“Digital Systems and Computer Structure” Course
As noted earlier, the Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering (Technion – Israel
Institute of Technology) combined the course “Digital Systems”, which dealt with
Boolean algebra and the analysis and design of combinational and sequential systems,
and the course “Logic Design and Introduction to Computers”, focusing on advanced
logic design and computer structure, into a single undergraduate-level course entitled
“Digital Systems and Computer Structure”. The latter covers three levels of abstrac-
tion, i.e., logical, micro-architecture and architecture levels, switches between them,
and therefore provides a more complete picture of the computer.
The course “Digital Systems and Computer Structure” is compulsory for ECE (sec-
ond semester) and CS (third semester) students. The aim of the course is to provide
students with analysis and design skills at the three levels of abstraction mentioned
above. A prerequisite for the course is the course “Introduction to Computer Science”,
which deals with the algorithmic approach to problem solving and programming in C
language.

Undergraduate Students’ Attitudes Toward an Engineering Course
493
The course (frontal instruction) lasts 13 weeks, and consists of four hours of lectures
and two hours of tutorials every week. The teaching staff is comprised of lecturers (PhD
in ECE) and assistants (senior ECE students and graduate students). The contents of the
course overlap approximately with the contents of the preceding courses, and include:
Boolean algebra, the digital model, combinational systems, sequential systems, state
machines, von Neumann machine, hardware description language, addressing modes,
branches, stack, routines, traps, pipelined processor, control and data hazards [14].
The assessment is based on computer exercises (simulations in VERILOG), a mid-
semester test and a ﬁnal examination.
4
Research Goal and Methodology
4.1
Goal
The aim of the study was to characterize students’ attitudes toward the course “Digital
Systems and Computer Structure”.
4.2
Participants
One hundred and three undergraduate students (53 ECE students; 50 CS students), who
took the course “Digital Systems and Computer Structure”, participated in the study.
The students have not previously been exposed to learning that combines multiple levels
of abstraction.
4.3
Methodology
At the end of the course, students ﬁlled out two anonymous questionnaires, a closed-
ended and an open-ended. In addition, nine semi-structured interviews were conducted.
All instruments were aimed to characterize students’ attitudes toward the course.
The quantitative data were analyzed by statistical means, and a possible difference
between ECE and CS students was examined. The qualitative data underwent a directed
content analysis based on the tri-component attitude model.
4.4
Tools
The closed-ended questionnaire was a ﬁve-level Likert-like scale, extending from
“strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”. The scale was based on an instrument developed
in [15]. This self-reporting questionnaire consisted of 17 statements expressing attitudes
toward an engineering course that combines multiple levels of abstraction. Some of the
statements represented positive attitudes and others – negative ones. The statements were
validated by two engineering education experts. Cronbach’s alpha (α = 0.78) pointed
to acceptable internal consistency. Some statements are given in Table 1.
In the open-ended questionnaires and interviews, students were asked, among other
things, about their position toward the course and their preference, i.e., courses that
incorporate multiple levels of abstraction or courses that focus on a few levels.

several levels of abstraction.

5.2
Attitude Components
Content analysis of the open-ended questionnaires and interviews reveals various aspects
in respondents’ attitudes toward the course. Since there is no signiﬁcant difference
between ECE and CS students’ attitudes (Sect. 5.1), there is no distinction between
the two groups below.
Cognitive Domain. Cognitively, the vast majority of respondents (90%) argue that the
course provides a complete picture of computer systems:
Educationally, it [the course] is well built. You start from the simplest thing… start
from Boolean variables… then Boolean expressions, logic gates, combinational
components… you progress until you build a complete processor! (interview)
About one-third of the respondents (35%) claim that the course is appropriate for
beginning students:
The level [of learning] was appropriate… I felt it wasn’t something I couldn’t
handle. (interview)

Undergraduate Students’ Attitudes Toward an Engineering Course
495
But it is accompanied by a heavy cognitive load, stemming from the broad scope of
content (32%):
The load was too high… there were lots and lots of content. (questionnaire)
According to about a quarter of the respondents (24%), the course imparts higher-
order thinking skills, due to the combination of several levels of abstraction:
It [the course] has given me directions of thinking that I haven’t had until today…
I think it [combination of several levels of abstraction] develops ways of thinking.
(interview)
Affective Domain. In the affective domain, 28% of the respondents think that the course
is interesting because it maneuvers between several levels of abstraction:
Very interesting… I liked the progress from a very internal level of the processor
to an external one. (interview)
Behavioral Domain. Finally, from the behavioral perspective, the vast majority of
respondents (83%) prefer courses that incorporate multiple levels of abstraction over
courses that focus on a few levels:
I prefer to study the current [new] course over the two separate [preceding]
courses. (questionnaire)
6
Discussion and Conclusions
According to the results, students hold positive attitudes toward an engineering course
that combines multiple levels of abstraction, with no signiﬁcant difference between ECE
and CS students. This lack of difference may be due to the fact that the respondents are
beginning students. Thus, the speciﬁc program (ECE vs. CS) has not yet affected, if at
all, students’ attitudes.
Students argue that the course imparts higher-order thinking skills, due to the com-
bination of several levels of abstraction. This claim is in line with research ﬁndings
suggesting that representation that combines multiple levels of abstraction promotes
learning, especially when dealing with complex systems, such as physical [16] or bio-
chemical systems [17]. Moreover, incorporating multiple levels of abstraction allows
learners to maneuver between levels of abstraction and thus contributes to their cognitive
development [16].
Students claim that the load characterizing a course that incorporates multiple levels
of abstraction is very high. Indeed, as described in Sect. 3, course instruction is much
more extensive than is common in university courses.
Affectively, students ﬁnd interest in combining digital systems with computer struc-
ture. The behavioral aspect in their attitude is congruent with the cognitive and affective
components described above. According to it, the vast majority of students prefer courses
that incorporate multiple levels of abstraction over courses that focus on a few levels.

496
A. Gero et al.
The study faced a limitation: the number of students who took part in the research
was relatively small. To diminish the impact of this limitation, both quantitative and
qualitative tools were used.
The study’s main contribution lies in the ﬁrst analysis (to the best of our knowledge)
of students’ attitudes toward an engineering course that integrates multiple levels of
abstraction. This contribution is important in view of the inadequate abstract thinking
skills of beginning engineering students [18]. The authors recommend developing such
courses. However, they should be scheduled in a semester characterized by a relatively
moderate load and assigned with highly-qualiﬁed faculty.

Interdisciplinarity as a Means of Promoting
Learning in Electrical and Computer
Engineering
Aharon Gero(B) and Beto Catz
Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa, Israel
gero@technion.ac.il, betoc@campus.technion.ac.il
Abstract. Analog and digital electronics are traditionally taught separately in
higher education. However, the relevance of chips containing both analog and
digital circuits has increased signiﬁcantly. Thus, the Faculty of Electrical and Com-
puter Engineering (Technion – Israel Institute of Technology) decided to combine
two undergraduate courses, the ﬁrst dealing with analog electronics and the second
with digital electronics, into a single course “Electronic Circuits” integrating both
areas. The study presented here aimed to examine whether this interdisciplinary
approach promoted learning compared to the traditional one. The study, which
applied quantitative and qualitative instruments, involved 156 electrical and com-
puter engineering students. According to the results, the achievements of students
who studied electronic circuits in the interdisciplinary approach were signiﬁcantly
higher than those of their peers taught via the traditional way. Students claim that
interdisciplinary learning is interesting, constitutes a natural approach, improves
understanding, but also places a heavy cognitive load.
Keywords: Interdisciplinary education · Higher education · Electronic circuits
1
Introduction
Analog and digital electronics are considered as the main branches of electronics, and are
traditionally taught separately in higher education [1]. However, the relevance of chips
containing both analog and digital circuits has increased signiﬁcantly [2]. Thus, it might
be better to teach electronic circuits in an interdisciplinary approach that integrates the
two ﬁelds and underscores their interrelations [3].
In light of the above, the Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering (Technion –
Israel Institute of Technology) decided to combine two undergraduate courses, the ﬁrst
dealing with analog electronics and the second with digital electronics, into a unique
course “Electronic Circuits” integrating both areas. The study presented here aimed to
examine whether this interdisciplinary approach promoted learning compared to the
traditional one.
The article begins with a concise review of interdisciplinary education. Next, the
course “Electronic Circuits” is described. Then, the research goal is formulated and the
methodology is presented. Finally, the main ﬁndings are discussed.

2
Interdisciplinary Education
Most researchers agree that the degree of integration between two or more areas of
knowledge ranges from multidisciplinarity (negligible interaction), through interdisci-
plinarity (substantial interaction), to transdisciplinarity (intense interaction) [4]. As for
the distance between the disciplines involved, it is common to distinguish between nar-
row and wide interdisciplinarity. In the ﬁrst case, the ﬁelds of knowledge are close,
namely, share similar epistemologies and methodologies. In the latter case, such com-
patibility does not exist [5]. Here, the integration between analog electronics and digital
electronics refers to narrow interdisciplinarity.
Studies that characterized interdisciplinary programs identiﬁed strengths and weak-
nesses related to interdisciplinary education [6]. From the cognitive viewpoint, interdis-
ciplinary programs often promote students’ comprehension [7] and analytical skills [8,
9]. In the affective domain, interdisciplinary learning usually enhances intrinsic moti-
vation [10, 11]. At the same time, interdisciplinary education generally places a heavy
cognitive load [12, 13] and may be perceived by students as superﬁcial [14].
3
“Electronic Circuits” Course
As described in Sect. 1, the Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering (Tech-
nion – Israel Institute of Technology), decided to combine the course “Linear Electronic
Circuits”, dealing with analog electronics, and the course “Electronic Switching Cir-
cuits”, focusing on digital electronics, into a single interdisciplinary course “Electronic
Circuits”.
This unique course puts an emphasis on analyzing an electronic circuit from both
the analog and digital perspectives. Moreover, it demonstrates the interrelations between
these two viewpoints.
Similar tothetwoprecedingcourses, thenewcourseis mandatoryfor junior electrical
and computer engineering students, and lasts 13 weeks. Prerequisites for the course are
introductory courses in digital systems, electrical circuit theory, signals and systems and
semiconductor devices.
At the end of the course “Electronic Circuits”, the student should be able to analyze
electronic circuits while taking into account system considerations. The above learning
goal is identical to those formulated in the separate courses (for analog or digital circuits).
The curriculum of the new course includes most of the topics taught in the preceding
courses and at a similar level.
The course (frontal instruction) is comprised of four hours of lectures and two hours
of tutorials per week. Course faculty consists of a lecturer (PhD in electrical and com-
puter engineering) and teaching assistants (graduate students in electrical and computer
engineering). The assessment is based on home exercises and a ﬁnal examination. For
comparison, each of the preceding courses (frontal instruction) was comprised of three
hours of lectures and one hour of tutorial every week, and the assessment was similar to
that of the new course.

500
A. Gero and B. Catz
4
Research Goal and Methodology
4.1
Goal
The study aimed to examine whether an interdisciplinary teaching approach of electronic
circuits (i.e., combining analog and digital electronics) promoted learning compared to
the traditional one (i.e., teaching analog electronics and digital electronics separately).
4.2
Participants
The study involved 156 junior electrical and computer engineering students, who have
not previously been exposed to interdisciplinary learning.
4.3
Methodology
The study used quantitative and qualitative instruments in order to increase the ﬁndings’
trustworthiness.
One hundred and fourteen students attended the course “Electronic Circuits” (experi-
mental group), and the rest 42 students took the two courses “Linear Electronic Circuits”
and “Electronic Switching Circuits” in the same semester (reference group). According
to a t-test (equal variances), at the beginning of the study no signiﬁcant difference (p >
0.05) was found between the cohorts of the two groups in terms of GPA (Mexp = 84.10,
SDexp = 6.18; Mref = 84.54, SDref = 6.92), where 0 ≤M ≤100. The teachers of all
three courses were considered good instructors and had substantial teaching experience.
At the end of each of the three courses, students took an achievement test. Students
were tested on the type of circuits (analog and/or digital) learned in the course. The score
of a member of the experimental group was the score obtained in the achievement test
of the new course, and the score of a member of the reference group was the mean of
the scores obtained in the achievement tests of the separate courses.
In addition, students from the experimental group ﬁlled out an anonymous open-
ended questionnaire, designed to characterize respondents’ attitudes toward the inter-
disciplinary approach.
The quantitative data were statistically analyzed, and the qualitative data underwent
a content analysis. Due to ethical considerations (access to the individual student’s GPA
was not allowed), ANCOVA was not performed.
4.4
Tools
Eachofthethreeone-hour-longachievementtestsdealtwithanalogand/ordigitalcircuits
analysis learned in the relevant course, and were similar in their level of difﬁculty. The
use of a formula sheet and a calculator was allowed. Each test was written by course
faculty and validated by two experts in engineering education. The tests were graded by
two independent reviewers using a rubric. A sample of the achievement test questions
is given in Table 1.
In the open-ended questionnaires, respondents were asked, inter alia, about their
opinion on interdisciplinary learning of electronic circuits and their preference, i.e., the
interdisciplinary approach or the traditional one.

5.2
Attitudes
Content analysis identiﬁes various aspects in students’ attitudes toward interdisciplinary
learning of electronic circuits.

502
A. Gero and B. Catz
Cognitive Domain. From the cognitive viewpoint, students argue that interdisciplinary
learning includes strengths alongside weaknesses. Regarding the advantages, about a
quarter of respondents (24%) claim that interdisciplinary learning constitutes a natural
approach to electronic circuits analysis:
It [the combination of analog and digital electronics] feels natural and ﬂows well.
About one-ﬁfth of respondents (19%) argue that interdisciplinary learning is relevant
to electrical and computer engineering students:
It [the combination of analog and digital electronics] is very important for the
things I will study later in the program.
According to 10% of the respondents, interdisciplinary learning promotes under-
standing:
The combination [of analog and digital perspectives] provides a deeper under-
standing.
Alongside these strengths, students also identify weaknesses that characterize inter-
disciplinary learning. Most respondents (81%) claim that interdisciplinary learning
places a high cognitive load resulting from the very wide scope of content, i.e., analog
and digital electronics:
The main problem [of interdisciplinary learning] is the unreasonable amount of
material.
About a third of them (30%) think that interdisciplinary learning is superﬁcial
because the time allotted to it does not allow for sufﬁcient in-depth study:
Separate courses [in analog and digital electronics] are better... so that there is
time to study [in a more in-depth way].
Affective Domain. Affectively, about half of the respondents (45%) indicate that
interdisciplinary learning is interesting:
Interesting material.
Behavioral Domain. From the behavioral aspect, about one-third of respondents (38%)
prefer to learn electronic circuits in an interdisciplinary approach rather than the
traditional one.
6
Discussion and Conclusions
According to the ﬁndings, the achievements of students taught via the interdisciplinary
approach were signiﬁcantly higher than those of their peers taught via the traditional
way. The gap was characterized by a medium effect size. This result is in line with

Interdisciplinarity as a Means of Promoting Learning
503
ﬁndings indicating that interdisciplinary learning often promotes academic achievement
[15].
The improvement achieved in the present research is consistent with the claim of
study participants who were exposed to the interdisciplinary approach. According to
them, comprehension is advanced thanks to the combination that makes it possible to
analyze an electronic circuit from both the analog and digital perspectives. The result
is also congruent with reporting regarding high-school [16] and university [17] students
who experienced interdisciplinary learning and noted that their understanding improved.
These ﬁndings can be explained by the claim that compared to disciplinary learning,
interdisciplinary learning further develops students’ cognitive skills [7]. This is because
the latter provides more opportunities to link new knowledge acquired to knowledge that
already exists [8].
Students argue that interdisciplinary learning is interesting, constitutes a natural app-
roach, but also places a heavy cognitive load and tends to be superﬁcial. These ﬁndings
are in line with the results of other studies that have characterized interdisciplinary
learning [14, 15, 18].
The study had one major limitation: the number of participants in the reference group
was relatively small. The limitation was due to the low number of students who attended
the two separate courses simultaneously in the semester in which the study took place.
To reduce the effect of this limitation and increase the ﬁndings’ trustworthiness, both
qualitative and quantitative instruments were used.
The main theoretical contribution of the study is in the ﬁrst characterization (to the
best of the authors’ knowledge) of an interdisciplinary approach to teaching electronic
circuits in academia. This contribution is particularly important in light of the few studies
examining interdisciplinarity in engineering education [19]. The authors recommend
adopting the approach. However, the latter should be applied in a semester where the
load is moderate. It is also advisable to reduce the number of topics taught and allocate
sufﬁcient time for in-depth study.

Research Perspectives and Innovative
Applications for Sustainable Engineering
Education
Brit-Maren Block(B)
and Marie Gillian Guerne
Leuphana University, Universitätsallee 1, 21335 Lüneburg, Germany
block@uni.leuphana.de
Abstract. Sustainability and responsible use of the resources at our disposal are
among the most important goals of our time. Employees are looking for next-
generation employees with ever more skills. To ideally foster these in engineering
and prepare them for future challenges, the integration of education for sustain-
able development (ESD) with a linkage of technical and sustainability-oriented
issues in the curriculum is essential. This paper takes up two points: (1) An anal-
ysis of the research landscape in Engineering Education Research (EER) on the
topic of “sustainability” is undertaken. For this purpose, more than 3500 con-
ference papers of EDUCON and FIE of the years 2014 to 2018 as well as 2021
(EDUCON only) are evaluated. The methodology of the analysis as well as the
set of main and sub categories (among them “sustainability”) will be presented
at ICL 2022. The results of the analysis of the research landscape (1) show that
the topic of sustainability has so far played a negligible role in the conference
contributions. In (2), the focus is on the implementation process and the linking
of technical and sustainability-oriented issues. The study programme concept of
the Leuphana University offers two options for sustainable technical education by
combining major and minor study programmes. The interdisciplinary combina-
tions are presented and explained using module examples. The paper proves in a
research-based manner that the topic of sustainability has so far been underrepre-
sented in the engineering sciences, which is why evidence-based interdisciplinary
implementation procedures such as those presented in (2) are highly relevant.
Keywords: Sustainable engineering education · Sustainability in Engineering
Education Research (EER) · Sustainability competencies
1
Context and Goals
In 1992, at the United Nations Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, participating nations
agreed to work together towards the goal of sustainable development. Thirty years later,
progress has been made, but there are still many challenges that require the knowledge,
skills and commitment of engineers to overcome in order to ensure a sustainable future.
There is a need to increase the inclusion of sustainability (environmental, social and
economic) aspects in the core curricula of engineering courses, but this presents many
challenges.
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 505–515, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_53

506
B.-M. Block and M. G. Guerne
Studies worldwide show that the topic of sustainability is insufﬁciently addressed in
engineering curricula [1–5]. For example, the study by [1] assesses the Nigerian engi-
neering curriculum and shows that the dimensions of sustainability are insufﬁciently
addressed, with environmental concepts mentioned most frequently and social issues
least frequently. An analysis of the presence of sustainability issues in 16 Spanish higher
education curricula in education and engineering shows that they are more homoge-
neously represented in education curricula than in engineering curricula [2]. A survey
of students in the Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) programme at the Geor-
gia Institute of Technology investigated students’ interest, knowledge and experience in
sustainability. The results show that students are interested in sustainable development,
but that there is still potential to improve sustainability education [3]. An investigation
of the integration of social sustainability into engineering education at the Royal Insti-
tute of Technology (KTH) in Sweden is based on interviews and shows that curriculum
managers and teachers at KTH have difﬁculties understanding the concept of social sus-
tainability [4]. Finally, the article by [5], which examines the sustainability concepts of
newly enrolled engineering students in Denmark, shows that sustainability is a dilemma
for engineering students, as they are caught in a tension between their fascination with
technology and the blame they attribute to technical progress. Other studies show positive
developments in terms of sustainability [6, 7]. An analysis of the current state of Aus-
tralian universities shows that a large proportion of them have successfully introduced
sustainable engineering education, while the rest are currently focusing on integrating
it into their curricula [6]. In addition, [7] describe the progress made in incorporating
sustainability and green engineering content into chemical engineering curricula over
the past 25 years. The above analyses and studies show that there are some universities
that have met the challenges and are well on their way to implementing education for
sustainable development in engineering. However, a majority of the studies show that
sustainability aspects are strongly neglected in engineering education, especially social
sustainability aspects.
This is where this paper intervenes. An analysis is made of the research landscape
in engineering education research (EER) on the topic of “sustainability”. For this pur-
pose, 3570 conference papers from EDUCON and FIE from 2014 to 2018 and 2021
(EDUCON only) are analysed. The methodology of the analysis is described in the
following section. Section 3 presents the evaluation with a focus on the topic of sustain-
ability. Furthermore, the focus is on the implementation process and the linking of tech-
nical and sustainability-oriented issues. Therefore, the last section presents a successful
implementation of a sustainable engineering education. Through the study programme
concept of the Leuphana University with the combination of major and minor study
programmes, two options for a sustainable technical education are presented.
2
Methodological Approach
2.1
Systematisation of the EER Landscape in General
The research objectives in this paper stand for both theoretical understanding and edu-
cational practice. In order to design and to study within the same research process, see
[8], the systematisation of the EER landscape is carried out as design-based research

Research Perspectives and Innovative Applications
507
work, e.g. [8, 9], which contributes to theory building by providing a categorisation of
the international research ﬁeld, but also leads to the structuring and bundling of research
ﬁndings in practical application. Furthermore, this methodology has been used because
the main stages of the research interact with the educational practice. In this way the
research objective by dual outputs of innovative approaches and theoretical ﬁndings was
achieved.
For the purpose of gaining knowledge at the interface of engineering and sustainabil-
ity, two leading IEEE conferences of the international EER research landscape, the FIE
and EDUCON, were selected as the basis for the systematisation, whose publications
appear annually in a two-stage blind review process. With the aim of an international
and up-to-date analysis, contributions to EDUCON and FIE from the years 2014 to
2018 and 2021 (EDUCON only) were systematically analysed and categorised using a
catalogue of categories developed in advance. In doing so, EDUCON, like ICL Annual
conferences, focuses more on the European research landscape, while FIE expands the
research work to include a more international (especially American) view. This app-
roach addresses the critiques of [10, 11] and [12] who point to existing disciplinary and
geographical divisions in the research landscape. Although the research presented does
not provide a complete overview, basic statements and research trends on sustainable
engineering education can be derived. The number of articles from the respective years
that were used to categorise the scientiﬁc articles is presented in Table 1.

In the content-structured procedure according to [13], the categories for the system-
atisation of the EER research ﬁeld were developed inductively from contributions of
the EDUCON and the FIE of the years 2014 to 2018. The methodological design of
the systematisation and selected partial ﬁndings were put up for discussion within the
research community [14, 15]. The result is a research-guided category system consisting
of ten main categories and 78 subcategories, which encompasses the main aspects of the
research ﬁeld, their speciﬁcation and the relations and delimitations of the individual
categories to each other (exempliﬁed with a focus on sustainability in Sect. 2.2). To

508
B.-M. Block and M. G. Guerne
increase the quality of the research process and to minimise the subjectivity of the anal-
ysis, intersubjective validation was used consistently from the beginning of the research
process. In order to check the uniform understanding, several papers were randomly
selected from the total amount of contributions, individually categorised by at least two
people and the categorisation subsequently discussed in the team. The discourse about
the individual perspectives and the achievement of a consensus in the categorisation
led to a secure handling of the category system and consequently to a reliability of
the categorisation within the research team. Subsequently, 3570 contributions were sys-
tematically analysed and categorised using the category catalogue developed and are
available as an Excel list.
The category system developed consists of ten main categories with up to 12 subcat-
egories each, extracts of which are shown in Table 2. In addition to the categories, there
are coding rules that describe the assignment criteria for the respective category and
add concrete anchor examples or demarcation notes to other categories. For example,
the publications sorted into the main category “Teaching and Learning” focus on the
teaching-learning process and its design. The category “Topics related to Engineering”
categorises publications that place the thematic focus on topics that are not subject-
speciﬁc but are related to engineering content. One of the subcategories belonging to this
main category is “Sustainability” (see Table 3). Each contribution was assigned to at least
one and at most two main categories. The selection of two main categories ensures that
interdisciplinary contributions and contributions that form a transfer between individual
topics can also be considered in two different categories. One suitable sub-category can
be selected for each main category.

3
Outcomes from the Research Perspective
3.1
General Statements
The total of 3570 FIE and EDUCON conference articles from 2014–18 and 2021
(EDUCON only) were each assigned a minimum of one and a maximum of two main
and sub-categories. A total of 6627 categories were assigned. What is noticeable in the
overview of the results of the category allocation is the lower number of allocations in
the contributions to EDUCON, which can be attributed to the different absolute number
of contributions to the respective conference (see Table 1). In both conferences, topics in
the context of teaching and learning processes (main category “Teaching and Learning”)
were addressed most frequently by far. Articles dealing with project and problem-based
learning were particularly prominent. Many of the contributions at both conferences also
focus on issues and topics of a speciﬁc engineering discipline (main category “Discipline
Speciﬁc Issues”) or deal with the development, expansion or re-design of modules or
entire curricula (main category “Curriculum Design”) in the ﬁeld of engineering. For
limited reasons, a more comprehensive overall evaluation is not included in this paper,
as the focus is on the evaluation of the topic area of sustainability.
3.2
Results with Focus on the Subcategory Sustainability
As already pointed out in the introduction, many educational institutions lack references
to the topic of sustainability and thus to education for sustainable development. In the
following, the number of contributions dealing with the topic of “sustainability” is being
examined.

510
B.-M. Block and M. G. Guerne
Figure 1 gives an overview of the categorisations of the articles of the FIE and
EDUCON to the sub-category “Sustainability” in comparison to the sub-category
“Project- and Problem-based Learning”. Out of a total of 6627 categorisations, 48
(0.72%) were made in the sub-category “Sustainability” while 498 (7.51%) were made
in the sub-category “Project- and Problem-based Learning”. By way of explanation, it
should be added that a category is only awarded if the majority of the contribution deals
with the theme. Most articles to the topic of sustainability were published in 2017. In
general, the proportion of articles that address the topic of sustainability is extremely
low at 0.72%, which illustrates and supports the situation described in the introduction.
Contrary to expectations, there is no trend to be noted in the results.
Fig. 1. Categorisation of FIE & EDUCON articles in 2014–18 and 2021 (EDUCON only) into
the sub-categories “Sustainability” and “Project- and Problem-based Learning”, own data.
In order to ﬁnd out whether the topic of sustainability nevertheless plays a role in the
categorised articles, a “COUNT IF” query was carried out in Excel. It was analysed how
often the word “sustainability” was written in the title (9 times), in the keywords (20
times) and in the abstract (39 times). In addition, the words “sustainable” and “climate
change” were ﬁltered. The word “sustainable” appeared in a total of 18 out of 3570
titles, in 17 keywords and 55 abstracts. “Climate Change”, on the other hand, was only
mentioned once in the title and keywords and 3 times in the abstract. The occurrence
of the word “sustainable” should be interpreted with caution, as it refers not only to
sustainability aspects, but also, for example, to long-lasting projects that do not directly
include sustainability issues. With a total of only 5 mentions, the occurrence of the
word “climate change” can be neglected. Figure 2 shows the frequency of the word
“sustainability” in the title, abstract and keywords depending on the year.
The latter analysis conﬁrms the results of the categorisation, as the frequency of the
keywords is in similar dimensions to the allocation of the articles. Basically, however,
it becomes apparent that very little relevance is attributed to the topic of sustainability

511
Fig. 2. Analysis of the occurrence of the word “sustainability” in the title, abstract or keywords
of FIE & EDUCON articles in 2014–2018 and 2021 (EDUCON only), own data.
in engineering education research and practice, which urgently needs to be changed.
An approach for integrating sustainability aspects in engineering education is therefore
presented in Sect. 4.
3.3
Clustering of Articles Assigned to the Sub-category “Sustainability”
A more detailed examination of the articles allows the 48 articles that were assigned
to the category of sustainability to be clustered into ﬁve different areas. For this pur-
pose, all articles were ﬁrst screened and then categories were formed to sort the articles
thematically.
Most of the articles deal with the introduction of new study programmes or the
redesign of learning plans [15]. One example is the paper by [16] in which the intro-
duction of the joint master’s programme JAMILA (Joint mAster of Mediterranean Ini-
tiatives on renewable and sustainable energy) is presented. The programme was con-
ceived in cooperation with the European Tempus project and aims to establish a Master’s
programme on renewable and sustainable energy. In addition, distance learning study
programmes [17] or the establishment of MOOCs [18] are presented.
13 articles address methods for creating and measuring environmental awareness,
motivation and behaviour. It is important to involve students at an early stage in order to
raise their environmental awareness. For example, there are various approaches that use
educational games to increase awareness of electricity consumption [19] or waste man-
agement [20]. A “Sustainable Manufacturing” course measured students’ understanding
of sustainability concepts and its impact on innovativeness and creativity.
About 23% of the articles describe the implementation of speciﬁc projects, which
in turn are intended to solve environmental problems. This is of great importance as it
allows students to complement the knowledge acquired in their studies with a practical
application related to professions and companies in order to learn how to deal with
the responsibilities and challenges of the working world. Exemplary projects were, for
example, the design of a self-sufﬁcient house [21], the development of lighting projects
[22] or the construction of a solar settlement [23].

512
B.-M. Block and M. G. Guerne
Five other articles deal with very speciﬁc and future-oriented topics such as pho-
tovoltaic generators, variable power generation in the future, electric vehicles or green
telecommunications. Two articles could not be assigned to any of the above categories.

Outcomes for Innovative Applications for Sustainable
Engineering Education
4.1
Interdisciplinary BA Study Programme
The results of the analysis of the research landscape in Sect. 3 show that the topic
of sustainability has so far played a negligible role in the conference contributions.
The contents of the publications with reference to the design of innovative teaching
programmes with regard to the topic of sustainability are comprehensively presented.
The requirements derived from the research data lead to a consideration of change
in teaching practice. The focus is on the implementation process and the linking of
subject-speciﬁc and sustainability-oriented issues.
The interdisciplinary study model of Leuphana University provides a successful
framework for the curricular connection between technology and sustainability. The
individual study programme is created from major, minor and complementary studies.
Students even have the opportunity to customize their study focus and to freely combine
their major and minor subjects. For the realisation of a sustainable engineering education,
there are two possible combinations with different weighting of the technology and
sustainability components, see Fig. 3. The interdisciplinary combinations are presented
below and explained using minor and module examples.
The Major Engineering provides a sound engineering and scientiﬁc knowledge as
well as a deeper understanding of the controlling, optimising and controlling processes
in digitised production and prepares students for the complex challenges of industry 4.0.
Students of the Major Global environmental and sustainability studies acquire skills
which will enable them to actively contribute sustainable development on a global level
withaninternationalperspective.TheMinorSustainabilitySciencefocusesonissuesper-
taining to the future of sustainable development. Students pursuing this minor will anal-
yse the consequences of global change and develop sustainable solutions to real social
problems that arise from unsustainable practices. The Minor Engineering Fundamen-
tals provides an overview of the most important technologies and technology-oriented
processes in the manufacturing industry.

This paper makes a contribution to the research discourse adressed by ICL2022 - Learn-

the topic of sustainability has so far been underrepresented in the engineering sciences
and EER, which is why evidence-based interdisciplinary implementation procedures

education and research.

Impact of Students’ Initial Abstract
Thinking Competence on Successfully
Studying Computer Science
Axel B¨ottcher1(B), Veronika Thurner1, Daniela Zehetmeier2,
and Tanja H¨afner1
1 HM Hochschule M¨unchen University of Applied Sciences, M¨unchen, Germany
{axel.boettcher,veronika.thurner,tanja.haefner}@hm.edu
2 Lufthansa Aviation Training GmbH, S¨udallee 15, 85356 M¨unchen-Flughafen,
Germany
daniela.zehetmeier@lat.de
Abstract. Many ﬁrst-year students of Computer Science struggle when
attempting to learn software development. If as teachers, we want to
eﬀectively help our students to overcome this hurdle, we need to better
understand the main causes for these diﬃculties. To gain a systematic
insight, we merge data we gathered from a test instrument that assesses
the competence of abstract thinking, with the students’ performance data
as documented within our student administration system. On this basis,
we apply methods from data analysis to detect correlations between the
skill level in abstract thinking and the overall study success in our degree
program on Computer Science.
Keywords: Abstract thinking · Assessment · Evaluation
1
Motivation
First-year students of Computer Science often struggle when attempting to learn
the fundamentals of the domain, especially software development. Based on our
everyday observations as lecturers that teach in close contact with our students,
we suspect that one major reason for this phenomenon is a lack of several relevant
cognitive competences in our ﬁrst-year students. Most prominently, our ﬁrst-year
students seem to be ill-equipped with the competencies of abstract thinking and
logical thinking.
The ability to think in an abstract manner (in addition to logical and ana-
lytical thinking) is considered an essential prerequisite for learning computer
science [6,12]. To better understand the situation, identify the problem causes
and thus be able to eﬀectively help our students to overcome their initial dif-
ﬁculties, we investigated in detail the competence of abstract thinking and its
signiﬁcance for learning software development and computer science in general.
We started this endeavor several years ago. As major parts of this work, we
developed a comprehensive deﬁnition of the competence of abstract thinking.
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 516–527, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_54

Students’ Abstract Thinking Competence
517
Furthermore, we developed an assessment instrument that measures this com-
petence in our students – the Abstract thinking assessment (ATA). The ﬁrst
cohort enrolled in our degree program on Computer Science was assessed using
this test instrument in 2017 [14]. By now, virtually all students of this cohort
have ﬁnished this course of studies – either successfully as graduates, or by
dropping out. Therefore, even under the very strict European data protection
regulations, we are now able to include this cohort in our project for analyzing
our students’ performance data [1,2].
To better understand the relevance of the competence of abstract thinking for
successfully studying computer science, we merged the data from both projects
and thus are now able to correlate the results from the ATA with the data
of our oﬃcial student administration system, which documents our students’
performance along their course of study.
2
Related Work
Data analytics is nowadays well established and widely used for prediction of
study success or dropout [9,13]. Typically, prediction is based on sociodemo-
graphic characteristics, school grades and the students’ early performance in
the respective degree program. However, sometimes other performance data are
available, which can be included in the data analysis process, such as aptitude
tests, speciﬁcally designed self assessments or diagnostic assessments, to name a
few.
In our country’s educational system, university attendance is basically free or
charge. However, for reasons of limited teaching capacity, access to those degree
programs that are very sought-after among the students-to-be is limited via
access restrictions. Traditionally, these access restrictions were mainly based on
the grade point average of the grades earned at school, as documented in the sec-
ondary schools’ graduation certiﬁcates that serve as university admission certiﬁ-
cate in our country. However, as this grade point average (as all averages) rather
obscures individual strengths and weaknesses, many institutions – or even whole
domains (such as the area of medical degree programs [5,7,10,11]) – use specif-
ically developed aptitude tests to assess the aspirants’ incoming qualiﬁcations,
to help to ensure that admitted students will properly meet the requirements of
the study process they aspire to, and thus to reduce drop-out.
In addition, several institutions use speciﬁcally designed aptitude tests as
instruments for their students’ self assessment, for diagnostic purposes that e. g.
uncover the need for counseling, and for predicting the students’ academic per-
formance [2,4,11,16].
At our institution, we employed data analysis to gain some insights into which
factors are decisive for the students’ success or drop-out in the degree program
of their choice [1]. As well, we developed a test instrument for measuring the
competence of abstract thinking [14]. In this work, we now integrate the data
gathered from both approaches.

518
A. B¨ottcher et al.
3
Goals
In our Bachelor-degree programs on Computer Science and on Scientiﬁc Com-
puting, the cohorts that commenced their studies in the winter term of 2017
were the ﬁrst whose initial abstract thinking competence we assessed right at
the beginning of their studies, by means of the test instrument we developed [14].
By now, almost all students of this cohort have ﬁnished the degree program –
either by dropping out, or by successfully graduating from it with a Bachelor’s
degree. Therefore, we are now able to thoroughly analyze in its entirety the inte-
grated data from the assessment of our students’ abstract thinking competence
on the one hand, and on the other hand the data that our student administration
system provides on the students’ study progress and the ﬁnal outcome of their
studies (i. e., successful graduation or drop-out).
Our goal is to validate or falsify the following hypotheses on the relation
between the students’ abstract thinking competence on the one hand, and the
students’ performance throughout their study process on the other hand:
1. Our abstract thinking assessment provides a basis for measuring both the
existence and the skill level of the abstract thinking competence in our stu-
dents.
2. Abstract thinking is a necessary prerequisite for developing skills in software
development.
3. The competence of abstract thinking that ﬁrst-year students initially possess
at the beginning of their studies correlates with – and thus is somewhat
predictive for – their overall study success in the Bachelor-degree programs
on Computer Science and on Scientiﬁc Computing.
4
Abstract Thinking Assessment
As a ﬁrst step towards creating an assessment instrument, we conceptualized
the competence of abstract thinking and developed a competence model that
reﬂects various deﬁnitions gathered from literature [15], which describe typical
thought processes that occur when thinking abstractly. This conceptualization
results from a cluster analysis, by which we identiﬁed the three components of the
competence as described in the following. Note that the verbs used within these
descriptions denote the essential activities that characterize abstract thinking.
1. Commonalities and Diﬀerences: Identify similarities to summarize them and
determine diﬀerences to normalize them (e. g. through parameterization).
2. Hide and Keep: Decide which information is essential for a speciﬁc purpose
and which is not.
3. Expand: Establish theoretical relationships between objects or processes.
Based on the identiﬁed clusters, we developed an assessment instrument to
measure the competence of abstract thinking. As we intend to use the assessment
instrument with our ﬁrst-year students right at the beginning of their studies, it

Students’ Abstract Thinking Competence
519
deliberately does not require any CS expertise. Rather, it reﬂects typical ideas,
principles, and concepts that are crucial for software development and which
require abstract thinking.
To give an idea of the assessment instrument, we provide as example the task
called “Password security status”, which belongs to the component of “Common-
alities and Diﬀerences”. Table 1 visualizes the introductory text of this task.

To ensure that the students’ textual answers are evaluated as objectively and
uniformly as possible, we created a coding manual for the open (short answer)
questions of the assessment. Within this document, each answer is evaluated
with respect to two dimensions, i. e., in the dimension correctness and in the
dimension level of abstraction. The correctness dimension distinguishes between

520
A. B¨ottcher et al.
“correct” and “wrong”. For the dimension level of abstraction, we identiﬁed the
classiﬁcations “concrete”, “speciﬁc” and “generic”. In addition, for each dimen-
sion codes are provided that indicate whether the answer is empty, or whether
the provided answer is in no recognizable way connected to and related with the
question. Furthermore, for each task of the ATA, the coding manual speciﬁes
criteria for mapping a given answer to a speciﬁc gradation level of each of the
two dimensions under consideration, i. e., correctness and level of abstraction.
In order to facilitate the correct coding of the students’ answers, the cod-
ing manual lists quotations from student answers as examples. For the task
“Password security status” as speciﬁed above, the coding manual provides the
following speciﬁcation and examples for grading in the dimension correctness.
1. The grading “concrete” is assigned if the student’s answer provides a “descrip-
tion of the words, but no rule”. Typical examples are:
– “... used more than seven characters ...”
– “... switched between capital and lower case letters ...”
– “... special characters as replacement for digits ...”
– “... long enough, but no special characters present ...”
2. The grading “speciﬁc” is assigned if in the student’s answer, “additional rules
are introduced to describe the given examples more speciﬁcally”. Typical
examples are:
– “... more than seven characters, irregular case ...”
– “... seven characters or more, but no digit and/or capital letter ...”
3. The grading “generic” is assigned if the student’s answer provides a “rule
description that classiﬁes all given examples without describing additional
speciﬁc restrictions”. Typical quotes are:
– “... at least seven characters and two of the four components are used...”
– “... more than six characters, but only characters from up to two diﬀerent
character groups ...”
All in all, our abstract thinking assessment comprises a total of 61 tasks. 37
of these tasks are closed questions, with a strictly limited range of possible solu-
tions, and thus automatically gradable. For example, students are requested to
order given items according to their degree of abstraction, from “most concrete”
to “most abstract”. In another category of closed questions, example pairs of
(message, code) are provided, and students are requested to specify the match-
ing code for a given message, which of course was not part of the example set.
In addition to these 37 closed questions, the assessment instrument includes
24 open questions, where students are requested to create themselves an abstrac-
tion, or to specify the rule underlying a given set of examples (as in the example
task provided above). Students’ answers reﬂect diﬀerent levels of abstraction,
thus making it possible to draw conclusions on the skill level or degree of abstract
thinking that a student possesses. The coding manual speciﬁes how to evaluate
the student’s answers to these open questions, thus ensuring an objective and
uniform interpretation of the results, and a reproducible grading. Each short
answer question whose answer is graded as “correct” in the dimension correct-
ness, and either “speciﬁc” or “generic” in the dimension level of abstraction, is

Students’ Abstract Thinking Competence
521
awarded a point. Therefore, when every one of these tasks is answered on a suf-
ﬁcient level of abstraction, a maximum score of 24 can be achieved on the open
questions.
Summing up, the evaluation of the abstract thinking assessment shows that
this instrument is very well suited to measure both the existence and the
skill level of the abstract thinking competence in our students, thus conﬁrm-
ing hypothesis 1.
5
Hypothesis 1: Evaluation of the Assessment Instrument
At the beginning of the winter term in 2017, the assessment instrument was
completed by 134 students as part of a compulsory ﬁrst-semester course in the
Bachelor’s degree programs on Computer Science and on Scientiﬁc Computing.
Of these 134 students that participated in the assessment, ﬁve students were
from a higher semester, but had to repeat some ﬁrst-semester exams due to a
previous fail. Thus, the assessment was taken by a total of 129 “real” ﬁrst-year
students.
Based on theses students’ test results, as a ﬁrst step we evaluated the qual-
ity of our assessment instrument by examining the aspects validity, reliability,
objectivity and psychometric diﬃculty.
Validity addresses the correspondence of the assessment instrument with
the underlying model, which is achieved by explicitly designing the assessment
instrument along a well-researched competence model.
Reliability denotes the accuracy of the measurement that is achieved by the
assessment instrument. We measure it as internal consistency, by determining
the reliability coeﬃcient Cronbach’s Alpha, which represents the revised average
correlation between items [3]. The Cronbach’s Alpha coeﬃcient evaluates to 0.80
for the scale of dimension correctness and to 0.82 for the scale of dimension level
of abstraction, thus indicating a good reliability of our assessment instrument.
To check the objectivity of the measurement, 10% of the tests were randomly
selected and evaluated by a second, independent person. This person received a
so-called rater training beforehand. The agreement of the ratings can be deter-
mined using Cohen’s Kappa, which represents how far the agreement of two
diﬀerent raters exceeds coincidences that would be expected by mere chance [8].
Averaged over all items of the respective scale, Cohen’s Kappa evaluates to 0.87
for the correctness scale and 0.92 for the scale level of abstraction, thus indicating
an almost perfect objectivity of the assessment instrument.
Finally, the psychometric diﬃculty evaluates whether the assessment instru-
ment is able to detect a variety of levels of proﬁciency and thus to properly assess
the entire spectrum of performance that students deliver.
An analysis of the results achieved in the dimension correctness across all
participating students indicates that the assessment instrument comprises 29.5%
easy (19 items), 59% medium (35 items) and 11.5% diﬃcult tasks (7 items). Here,
items that are solved correctly by almost every participant (80% or more) are
considered to be easy, items that are solved correctly by more than 20% and less

522
A. B¨ottcher et al.
than 80% of the participating students are deemed to be of medium diﬃculty,
and those items that are solved correctly by 20% or less of the participants
are labeled as being diﬃcult. Summing up across all tasks and all participating
students, 61.6% of all given answers were correct. Furthermore, an analysis of
the individual performance of the students reveals an individual items’ solution
rate that ranges from 9.7% up to 99.25% of correct answers.
In the dimension level of abstraction that is determined from the 24 open
questions, 18% of the answers were either missing or inappropriate (i. e. in no
recognizable way connected to and related with the question). 24% of the answers
were on skill level “concrete”, 11% on level “speciﬁc” and 47% on level “generic”.
The example task “Password security status” described in Table 2, where
students were asked to extract from a set of given examples the underlying rules
for password classiﬁcation, students achieved the following results. For the rule
for weak passwords, 57.5% of the given answers were on a “generic” level of
abstraction, as opposed to only 40.3% of the rules given for strong passwords. In
the dimension correctness, 55.2% of the answers were correct for weak passwords,
in contrast to a mere 25.4% correct rules for strong passwords. Therefore, both
items classify as being of medium psychometric diﬃculty.
By positively evaluating our instrument for assessing the competence of
abstract thinking, we can conﬁrm our hypothesis 1 that the instrument is well
suited for measuring both the existence and the skill level of the abstract thinking
competence in our students.
6
Correlating Abstract Thinking Skills and Study Success
Having thus validated the appropriate quality of our assessment instrument, as
a next step we correlate the data of the assessments with the data gathered from
our students’ individual study process. To achieve this, we need to integrate the
students’ assessment results for the short answer questions with the data from
our student administrative system. Furthermore, we purge our data set from
faulty data items and data records that represent inactive students.
The latter aspect requires some explanation. In a previous study on causes
for drop-out for which we analyzed the data from our student administrative
system, we identiﬁed that a signiﬁcant percentage of enrolled students does not
study actively, and thus does not seem to seriously strive for earning a degree
in Computer Science [1]. To deal with situation, we classiﬁed students into the
following categories:
– Ghost students are enrolled for one to ﬁve semesters, without taking any
exams at all during this time, thus never earning any ECTS points. (Note
that in our country, university education is not only free of charge, but also
oﬀers several ﬁnancial beneﬁts to enrolled students – even inactive ones.)
– Parking students denote students that want to study in a degree program
with restricted admission, but do not yet fulﬁll the requirements. Therefore,
they enroll in some other program for only one semester, before moving on to
their destined degree program. During this parking time, they participate in

Students’ Abstract Thinking Competence
523
up to three exams, usually in modules that will be recognized in their desired
course of studies.
– Poor performers invest some eﬀort into studying actively, as indicated by
exams taken and ECTS points earned. However, they eventually drop out
due to bad grades.
– As other dropouts we denote students that quit studying within their selected
degree program, in spite of an adequate academic performance.
– Finally, graduates are those students that eventually pass all requirements
and thus are awarded their degree.
As neither ghost students nor parking students show any serious attempts
for studying actively, we purge them from our data set, focusing our analysis
on those students that display an intention of pursuing their studies seriously.
Having thus created the data set to work on, as a next step we analyze the data
with respect to our hypotheses 2 and 3.
6.1
Hypothesis 2: Abstract Thinking and Software Development

that they had not fulﬁlled the necessary requirements in the ﬁrst place. These

These exam grades are plotted against the score that students achieved in
the abstract thinking assessment, which they underwent at the beginning of
their studies during the ﬁrst days of their 1st semester. Abstraction test scores
range from none = 0 to full marks = 24, where the score indicates the number of
answers to open questions that were graded on level “speciﬁc” or “generic” for
the dimension level of abstraction. In the ﬁgure, the size of the circles reﬂects
the number of students at that point of the data grid.
As visualized by the blue triangle in the bottom left area, no student with
a low score in the assessment of their abstract thinking competence was able to
achieve a good grade in the formative exam of the module on Software Devel-
opment. This observation strongly indicates the validity of hypothesis 2, that
the ability of abstract thinking is a necessary, but not suﬃcient, prerequisite for
developing appropriate skills in software development.
Further results suggest that the level of our students’ abstract thinking com-
petence depends on the type of secondary school education they underwent. For
a closer look into this issue, Fig. 2 provides box plots of the distribution of the
abstraction test score diﬀerentiated relative to the students’ educational history.
As before, the abstraction test score indicates the number of answers to open
questions that were graded on level “speciﬁc” or “generic” for the dimension
level of abstraction, thus creating an ordinal scaled representation of this dimen-
sion. The box plots visualize all values of the so-called ﬁve-point summary, i.e.
the median, the two quartiles and the two extreme values of each category, thus
visualizing the localization and distribution of the data.
Furthermore, Fig. 2 indicates that the vast majority of students that grad-
uated from high school are rather well equipped with abstraction skills, closely
followed by graduates from the technology branch of vocational school and from
professional school. In contrast to this, students from prep colleges for students
from abroad, graduates from the social branch of vocational school, as well as
graduates from vocational high school seem to be less skilled in abstract thinking.
Note, however, the rather small number of data points in these data sets. The
majority of graduates from the economic branch of vocational school possesses
intermediate abstraction skills.
As another result, the data analysis depicted in Fig. 2 does not show any
indicators for gender-speciﬁc diﬀerences. Quite to the contrary, in the majority
of the educational history categories under consideration, the lowest scores in
abstract thinking correspond to male students. This observation strongly sup-
ports our conviction that the reasons for the rather low rate of female students
of Computer Science is not due to cognitive reasons.

7
Conclusions
In our work, we related the results that our students achieved in the assessment of
their abstract thinking competence right at the beginning of their studies, to the
data on their study process and ﬁnal outcome of their studies (either graduation
or drop-out), as documented in our student administrative system. The results
strongly emphasize the relevance of the competence of abstract thinking for
successfully studying Computer Science.
However, we could show as well that even with a low initial skill level, every
student still has a chance of graduating successfully.

E-Portfolio as a Component of the Information
and Analytical System of Scientiﬁc Staff
Training
Marina Rostoka1,2
, Gennadii Cherevychnyi3(B)
, and Olha Kuzmenko4
1 V.O. Sukhomlynskyi State Scientiﬁc and Pedagogical Library of Ukraine, National Academy
of Educational Sciences of Ukraine, 9/of.31 M. Berlynskoho Street, Kyiv 04060, Ukraine
2 National Aviation University, 1, Liubomyra Huzara Ave., Kyiv 03058, Ukraine
3 Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv, 60 Volodymyrska Street, Kyiv 01601, Ukraine
gscherevichnyj@gmail.com
4 Flight Academy of the National Aviation University, 1 Dobrovolskogo Street,
Kropyvnytskyi 25005, Ukraine
Abstract. In the conditions of extremely dangerous human life (COVID-19 pan-
demic, martial law, etc.) the urgent tasks of science and education are the preserva-
tion of values, the creation of E-communications for adaptive and comprehensive
support of scientists.
The goal of the research is to intensify the problems of information analytics
in the system of scientiﬁc staff training (SST) and to develop a methodology for
building an information-analytical system (IAS), which will ensure the integrity
of the process of intellectual potential formation. This is aimed at the rationality
of the IAS, in particular, its component – E-Portfolio. This will make it possible
to convert the accumulated information into electronic form and facilitate the
transition to the creation of fundamentally new types of information resources.
They can be combined into digital collections, which in the projection of the
educational space become a system complex of digital scientiﬁc and educational
resources – part of the IAS.
When force-majeure makes radical changes in the education system and
causes a certain failure in all spheres of scientiﬁc activity, the E-Portfolio itself
becomes a reasonable and well-reasoned decision. Its development as an open
component of the IAS for SST is using methods of adequate deﬁnition of structure
based on of systematic, competency, transdisciplinary and diagnostic approaches.
The components of the structure are combined into meaningful blocks based – on
conceptual, organizational, socio-psychological, and diagnostic. This allows for
establishing transdisciplinary relationships between researchers in different ﬁelds
of science.
Thus E-Portfolio is an effective IAS-tool for distance SST and also helps with
the adaptive performance of scientiﬁc tasks.
