E-Portfolio as a Component of the Information and Analytical System
529
1
Problem Statement
The ﬁeld of scientiﬁc activity is quite diverse. Research is carried out in almost all
sectors of the economy countries and is provided by the systematic work of scientiﬁc
units of higher education institutions (HEI) and research institutions (RI). In addition,
great attention is paid to scientiﬁc education, i.e. improving the efﬁciency of the scientiﬁc
and educational process of the SST.
In situations of extreme danger to human life, caused by the introduction in 2020
of quarantine restrictions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, force majeure, as well
as those that led to martial law in Ukraine in 2022 and shook almost all concerned
world public space, topical issues and the main tasks of science and education is the
preservation of values acquired by mankind during its existence.
Adaptive provision of quality activities of scientists and educators, creating effective
conditions for remote communication with of applicants of scientiﬁc education and per-
formers of scientiﬁc research using asynchronous and online technologies using modern
software and mobile applications has become increasingly important.
Today, more than ever, the task is to intensify the technology of information ana-
lytics in the system of SST and ensure the dynamic improvement and development of
methodology for building information systems in this vector. This will ensure a high
level of integrity in the process of forming and maintaining the intellectual potential of
the state in extreme conditions.
In addition, modern information technologies make it possible to transform the
accumulated information into electronic form to create fundamentally new types of
information resources. Such resources will be combined into so-called digital collec-
tions (repositories, databases, knowledge bases, libraries, etc.), which in the projection
of the educational space become systems of electronic/digital educational resources
(EER/EDR). One of them is a dynamic component of the ECO-environment of IAS for
SST – E-Portfolio.
The rationality of providing the SST using the ECO-environment of IAS, in particular
its functional component E-Portfolio, will become more effective in the conditions of
remote work. Transdisciplinary relationships of the process of its development in the
context of research in various ﬁelds become the basis of a holistic view of scientists,
HEI and RI where they study or work, as well as the development of certain scientiﬁc
areas in the context of individual and team research, in the relevant scientiﬁc school. In
this way, the results of scientiﬁc activity are generalized and systematized according to
certain criteria for transdisciplinary, scientometric and personal indicators of scientists,
which characterize the integrity of their research activities.
2
Analysis of Recent Research and Publications
Considering that force majeure, caused by both quarantine measures from the COVID-
19 pandemic and the imposition of martial law in Ukraine, slows down the real course of
the scientiﬁc and educational process (even at a distance). After all, the need for scientiﬁc
support for the country’s economy, and the formation of intellectual potential is obvious
and requires adaptive information and analytical support by all possible means, given

530
M. Rostoka et al.
the challenges of today – the development of global world science and transformational
changes in scientiﬁc and educational space.
Content analysis of various sources, retrospective experience and results of studying
the practical aspects of today’s scientiﬁc and educational space indicate that the active
introduction of various EER/EDR in the SST has certain advantages.
The problem of creating and functional support for the content of the E-Portfolio has
been an active interest of researchers for many decades. Attention is paid following: the
semantics of the concept of “E-Portfolio”, the structure and content, tools for building
an E-Resource portfolio, the use of appropriate software and more.
Thus, O. Berezhna and T. Andriushchenko deﬁne the E-Portfolio as a collection
of reliable and diverse data that demonstrates the achievements of an individual or
organization for a certain period (of revealing the possibility of using an electronic
portfolio of the department as a tool to improve the learning process at the university)
[1].
In turn, researchers M. Swell, M. Markzak and M. Horn believe that the E-Portfolio
is a tool for evaluating professional programs, which reﬂects the progressive process of
the author or author’s team [2].
There is also an interpretation of the E-Portfolio as a web-based information
management system that uses electronic media and services.
In turn, S. Kuku conducts some research and gives examples of existing E-folio
systems such as: eFolio Minnesota (high-quality learning-based E-Portfolio system),
ModernEfolio(photo-basedsystem), TheNASAExplorer Schools Project (NES: eFolio-
system is the result of NASA’s collaboration with teams from various US educational
institutions) and others. The researcher argues that when developing an E-Portfolio
system, the goals of its further use should be clearly stated and attention should be paid
to the universality of the created system in terms of its use both for educational purposes
and for individuals (creative or working) [3].
In turn, researchers N. Morze and L. Varchenko-Trotsenko believe that the “mod-
ern electronic university learning environment should provide an open decentralizing
component that would contain a webpage with every educational process participant’s
qualitative and quantitative indicators of educational activity – an E-Portfolio”. They
believe that “indicators of a portfolio should include those of a priority for university
development at a certain time and be taken into account on different ratings, including
international and Ukrainian” [4].
Researchers study the problem, determine the main vectors in this way, systematize
andsummarizetheresults,andshareguidelinesandtechnicalandtechnologicalsolutions
for the formation and development of E-Portfolio [1–7]. It should be noted that the E-
Portfolio is already one of the effective tools of E-Learning, including in open science
education.
Thus, in developing a methodology for building an information-analytical system
taking into account the component of the E-Portfolio as a team-personal data bank in
the SST, in our opinion, rationalizes a single electronic document management database
HEI/RI, which provides quality information and analytical support for each of applicants
of scientiﬁc education (undergraduates, graduate researchers, doctoral researchers, etc.).

E-Portfolio as a Component of the Information and Analytical System
531
Thus, it is in the E-Portfolio as a Component of the IAS for SST that the storage,
processing, analysis (synthesis) and provision of information necessary for research
activities are carried out in a convenient form for the subjects of SST.
3
Statement of Basic Material and the Substantiation
of the Obtained Results
It should be noted that competent scientiﬁc training is carried out in the HEI and RI in the
vector of modernization of the scientiﬁc and educational process. And during the quar-
antine activities of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020, it was temporarily transferred
to remote mode. Then there was an urgent need to use modern online tools (conference
platforms, mobile applications and other Internet services) for educational communica-
tions, such as: Zoom, Google Meet, Jitsi Meet, Skype and others [6]. However, the issue
of control, evaluation and various measures for the certiﬁcation of subjects of scientiﬁc
training (undergraduates, graduate researchers, doctoral researchers, etc.) was resolved
in the mode of feedback using these electronic resources and communication via e-mail.
Only when martial law has brought radical changes in the education system, including
scientiﬁc, and caused some failure in all areas of scientiﬁc and educational activities
has, E-Portfolio become a reasonable and reasoned solution that allows for generaliza-
tion, systematization and control and assessment of acquired scientiﬁc knowledge in the
speciﬁcs of the ﬁeld of knowledge and relevant competencies.
TheE-PortfoliotechnologyisbecominganeffectiveIAS-toolforremoteSST,includ-
ing in martial law because E-Portfolio helps to improve the quality of rational and adap-
tive performance of scientiﬁc tasks set by research rules and in the future will provide
a methodological basis for construction and functional support of IAS for SST [8]. For
the effectiveness of the development of an open E-Portfolio as a component of the IAS
for the SST, certain methods have been used to determine its components based on
systematic, competency-based and diagnostic approaches.
Ensuring its dynamic basis, which will change over time and depending on the
acquired knowledge and experience of predecessors, will take into account the method-
ology of transdisciplinary (including adaptive and ontological resources of this app-
roach). For example, these components can be combined according to the content
blocks based on technological approach – conceptual, personal, socio-psychological,
professionally-oriented, practical, speciﬁc to the scientiﬁc profession, and so on.
It is projected that the general structure of the transdisciplinary IAS will include
several main blocks (see Fig. 1) – information content, analytical content, open E-
Portfolio of scientiﬁc training and interrelated individual E-Portfolio of applicants for
scientiﬁc education (undergraduates, graduate researchers, doctoral researchers, etc.),
as well as other subjects of scientiﬁc training.
The transdisciplinary relationships [9] that take place in the IAS for SST are also
reﬂected in the content of the open E-Portfolio of scientiﬁc training. The developed
structural and logical model of such an E-Portfolio, which operates in the transdisci-
plinary ECO-environment of IAS for SST [8] allows for clarifying its main components
(see Fig. 2).

M. Rostoka et al.

Note that it is logical to carry out scientiﬁc training taking into account the experience
of scientiﬁc schools operating in HEI/RI, which have a close relationship with the open
E-Portfolio of SST through close transdisciplinary links between the main blocks:
– the conceptual block is based on the implementation of the ideas of the scientiﬁc
school, the strategy of research in this vector, etc.

– the organizational and activity block is aimed at providing adaptive principles of man-
agementandmonitoringofSST,aswellastheself-managementandself-monitoringof
applicants for scientiﬁc education and other subjects of activity in the SST, their mobil-
ity in the world academic space and the publishing activity (scientometric indicators),
etc.
– socio-psychological block is related to personalized content and the main thing in
providing the content of personal content in Individual E-Portfolios of applicants
for scientiﬁc education and other subjects of activity in the SST (see Fig. 2: 1, 2,
3, 4 … n) – summaries, achievements, author’s ideas and publications, network of
socially organizing scientiﬁc communications, etc.
– the diagnostic unit reveals the rating indicators of applicants for scientiﬁc education
and other subjects of activity in the SST – evaluation and self-evaluation, control and
self-control,respectively–monitoringandself-monitoring.Thiscomponentcombines
research and educational activities of applicants for scientiﬁc education, educators’
other subjects of activity in the SST, using technical and technological tools, helps to
ﬁll both individual E-Portfolios (see Fig. 2: 1, 2, 3, 4 … n) and thus an open E-Portfolio
as a component of IAS for SST.
It should be noted that all these blocks are transdisciplinary connected and are in
some interdependence and have some interinﬂuence.
For example, the rating component of the applicants for scientiﬁc education, in the
structure of the diagnostic unit of the individual E-Portfolio (and collectively in the open
E-Portfolio of SST) includes not only a qualitative assessment of research activities but
will reﬂect individual and team rankings – organizational and activity aspects (event-
analysis of participation in scientiﬁc-practical events, content-analysis of publishing
activity, scientometric indicators, etc.). At the same time, the conceptual aspects that
position a certain scientiﬁc school will reﬂect the scientiﬁc position in the E-Portfolio
of IAS for SST, both the scientiﬁc team of researchers and each of them individually,
and others.
4
Conclusions
Thus, the analysis of scientiﬁc and practical experience on the problem of the method-
ology of building IAS, in particular, regarding the formation of E-Portfolio in the SST,
allowed us to state that:
1. SST in the conditions of modern educational transformations takes place in a mixed
form, in particular by remote means, the qualitative experience of application of
which is active gained during the introduction of quarantine from the pandemic
COVID-19. In this context, it is important to preserve the integrity of the research
system and ﬁnd rational approaches to self-organization and self-development of
applicants for scientiﬁc education (undergraduates, graduate researchers, doctoral
researchers, etc.).
2. Traditionally, the SST is carried out in HEI or RI and in-branch academies, and in-
state RI. Of course, the main departments in this sense are postgraduate and doctoral

534
M. Rostoka et al.
studies, admission to which is regulated by current legislation. The process of SST
is the development of speciﬁc knowledge of the applicants for scientiﬁc education
in relevant ﬁelds, the basis of which is based on the classiﬁcation of sciences, which
is integral to the formation of new scientiﬁc knowledge, determined by a particular
specialityandspecialization. However, specialities as scientiﬁcareas arecomponents
of natural sciences, humanities and technical sciences.
3. Analytical conclusions based on the results of the research once again conﬁrm that
in the system of SST it is important to provide each applicant for scientiﬁc education
with scientiﬁc education and adaptive conditions for acquiring the appropriate level
of theoretical knowledge and practical competencies in the research implementation
of and their product quality organization.
4. Given that the current state of systemic educational transformations encourages the
scientiﬁc and educational staff of the HEI and RI to organize effective information
and analytical support for research activities of applicants for scientiﬁc education,
updating scientiﬁc and methodological support for training in the digitalization of
modernization and reform the educational ﬁeld is considered relevant and timely.
An important role in this context is played by the E-Portfolio as a component of the
IAS for SST.
Thus, the above conclusions are generalized current results of scientiﬁc research,
obtained in the process of the ﬁnal phase of the ascertaining stage of the doctoral research.
In the future, their experimental veriﬁcation is planned. This, in turn, will allow us to
begin the next stage of research – analytical-synthetic – their mathematical justiﬁcation
for a certain engineering and technological interpretation.

Students’ Feedback on Teaching and Learning
English for Speciﬁc Purposes Before, During,
and After the Covid-19 Pandemic
Ludmila Faltynkova, Ivana Simonova(B)
, and Katerina Kostolanyova
University of Ostrava, Dvorakova 7, 709 03 Ostrava, Czech Republic
faltynkova@epol.cz, {ivana.simonova,
katerina.kostolanyova}@osu.cz
Abstract. Due to the covid-19 pandemic, great changes appeared in education
in general and digital technologies played a substantial role in the process. The
main objective of this research is to consider students’ feedback and opinions
on teaching and learning English for Speciﬁc Purposes (ESP) in (a) the present
form before schools were closed due to the pandemic, (b) the online distance form
of instruction during the pandemic, and (c) the present form of instruction after
the pandemic. Research questions focused on three areas: (1) what form(s) of
instruction students preferred, (2) whether/how digital technologies contributed
to the process of instruction, and (3) in which form of instruction they learned
more. The ex-post-facto approach and mixed methodology were applied. Data
were collected by questionnaire. It was available online for students of the upper
secondary school for medical staff (N = 153) and advanced school for higher
medical staff (N = 183). We expect that (1) the present form of instruction after
the covid-19 pandemic will be appreciated; however, there will also be some
supporters of online distance instruction; (2) it will be the present form that will
allow students to learn more compared to online distance instruction; (3) both
teachers and students will improve their digital skills during the pandemic so that
technologies can be exploited to a wider extent in the present form of instruction
after the pandemic.
Keywords: Covid-19 · English for Speciﬁc Purposes · ESP · Students’ feedback
1
Introduction
Either we belong to supporters or rejectors of online distance instruction (ODI), we
should admit that there were not too many other solutions on how to continue lessons
when the covid-19 pandemic started and schools were closed immediately. In the Czech
Republic, this period began in the middle of March and continued until the end of June
2020. Then, during the summer holidays (July–August 2020), several acts, e.g., [1],
and directions, e.g., [2] were issued to provide educational institutions of all levels with
didactic support with online distance instruction in the next school (academic) year.
Based on these documents, for example, attendance to online distance instruction was
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023

https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_56

Students’ Feedback on Teaching and Learning English
537
compulsory, schools were ﬁnancially supported from various sources, bought hardware
and software and provided it to needed learners, etc. From September 2020, online dis-
tance instruction continued by May 2021, with several (local) short interruptions. During
this period, continuous but not centrally managed research activities were carried out,
mainly administered by regional universities. In addition, large surveys were conducted
within an international context, e.g., [3].
In English for Speciﬁc Purposes (ESP), numerous research activities have been car-
ried out, the results of which provide valuable insight into students’ satisfaction with
online learning, and pose practical questions for its implementation. Students’ satisfac-
tion with online courses was examined, for example, by Avsenjuk et al. [4]. The study
focused on the effectiveness of online ESP learning, the availability of learning material
used by ESP teachers, and students’ difﬁculties with ESP distance learning. It was clearly
visible that students were pleased with ESP courses taught online and were able to meet
expected learning objectives. The main problems that made an impact on online ESP
teaching and learning during the covid-19 pandemic were the lack of technical support
and communication discomfort. Finding the problems and making changes in online dis-
tance English language teaching and learning led to examining classroom engagement
of another group of university students during the covid-19 pandemic. Anxiety while
learning, the perception of the online learning, the level of involvement and enjoyment,
the online class environment and dynamics of online class activities, comparison of the
face-to-face and online experience were the main features under focus. As expected, pos-
itive features, that is, enjoyment and engagement, resulted in a less stressful environment
[5].
From the ESP teachers’ perspective, it is important to know how conﬁdent teachers
are in teaching online distance and whether/how their feelings are impacted by their
previour experience. In the study conducted by Gavranovic and Prodanovic [6], the
respondents’ answers revealed a high level of self-conﬁdence in language teachers about
teaching online, and their ability to solve potential problems during online classes. On
the other hand, teachers were not sure about their active involvement in the use of social
networks and lack experience in teaching exclusively in an online environment. Contrary
to the self-conﬁdence mentioned above, they were rather critical of themselves. Most of
the respondents believed that online instruction allows learning outcomes to be achieved
to a high degree through online distance learning. However, regardless of this opinion,
respondents still preferred face-to-face instruction, and what they missed most in online
distance instruction was face-to-face interaction. From the point of view of language
skills, most respondents ﬁnd teaching three of them online distance more demanding
(speaking, writing, listening).
Reﬂecting the above mentioned, this research will focus on students’ feedback on
teaching and learning ESP before, during, and after the covid-19 pandemic, when edu-
cational institutions of all levels were closed due to pandemic restrictions. The main
contribution of the research is to monitor and compare the students’ opinions, and try to
explain the ﬁndings.

538
L. Faltynkova et al.
2
Methodology
2.1
Research Problem and Objective
Teaching and learning ESP has a long tradition within engineering education. However,
the during the covid-19 pandemic, most of the activities of medical staff (for example,
nurses) and higher medical staff (for example laboratory workers) concentrated on han-
dling the healthcare and ESP was not the topic of the day. When the pandemic started
to fade away, students began to attend online distance lessons. Apart from a few post-
poned deadlines and exams, they were expected to meet all requirements deﬁned by
the syllabus. Therefore, they expected the lessons to be efﬁcient. However, the one size
ﬁts all approach of Felder [7] does not work in online distance instruction. Therefore,
the main objective of the research was to collect students’ feedback on teaching and
learning ESP before, during, and after the covid-19 pandemic. Students’ responses were
compared and considered in the context they relate to.
2.2
Research Questions and Statements
Research questions focused on three areas: (1) What form(s) of instruction do students
prefer? (2) Did digital technologies contribute to the process of instruction? (3) In what
form of instruction did they learn more?
In the ﬁrst area, students expressed their preferences in the form of instruction in
four statements: (1) I prefer face-to face lessons before the pandemic to online distance
instruction during the pandemic; (2) I prefer face-to-face lessons before the pandemic
to face-to-face instruction after the pandemic; (3) I learned more face-to-face before
the pandemic; (4) Face-to-face instruction after the pandemic differs from face-to-face
lessons before the pandemic.
In the second area, six statements were set that focus on digital competences of
teachers and students: (5) Teachers use digital technologies more frequently after the
pandemic than before; (6) Students use digital technologies more frequently after the
pandemicthanbefore;(7)Teachersaremorecompetentinusingdigitaltechnologiesafter
the pandemic than before; (8) Students are more competent in using digital technologies
after the pandemic than before; (9) There is still much to improve in teachers; (10) There
is still much to improve in students.
In the third area, two statements dealing with online distance instruction are included:
(11) I learned more during online distance instruction than in face-to-face lessons before
the pandemic; (12) I learned more during online distance instruction than in face-to-face
lessons after the pandemic.
2.3
Expectations
Based on the research questions, we expect that (1) the present form of instruction after
the covid-19 pandemic will be appreciated; however, there will also be some supporters
of online distance instruction; (2) it will be the present form that will allow students
to learn more compared to online distance instruction; (3) both teachers and students
improved their digital skills during the pandemic so technologies can be exploited to a
wider extent in the present form of instruction after the pandemic.

Students’ Feedback on Teaching and Learning English
539
2.4
Methods, Tools, Sample
The ex-post-facto method was applied. Data were collected by an online question-
naire. It included multiple-choice items, that were evaluated on a four-level Likert scale
(Fully agree, Rather agree, Rather disagree, Fully disagree), and open-answer questions
that provided additional information. The frequency of occurrence was calculated in
multiple-choice items; the qualitative reﬂection was based on open-answer items. In
total, 336 respondents participated in the research. They were students of the upper
secondary school for medical staff (N = 153) and advanced school for higher medical
staff (N = 183) enrolled in the course of ESP – English medical students. This was a
convenient sample – all the students were taught by two authors of this paper.
3
Results and Discussion
3.1
Statements 1–4
In the ﬁrst area, students expressed their preferences for a form of instruction: face-to-
face before the pandemic, online distance during the pandemic, and face-to-face after
the pandemic. Almost 90% of the respondents expressed the preference for face-to-face
instructionbeforethepandemiccomparedtoonlinedistanceinstruction;however,almost
60% of the respondents did not agree with the preference of face-to-face lessons before
the pandemic for face-to-face instruction after the pandemic. More than two thirds of
them stated that they learned more before the pandemic, but almost 40% did not agree.
So, we can see that students’ reﬂection is not clear enough to give preference for one of
the periods. The results are displayed in Fig. 1.

were 60% of rejectors of this opinion. The reason may be that learners were tired of

not only negative, but they discovered a wide scale of emotions regardless of the age of

3.2
Statements 5–10
In the second area, six statements were set that focus on digital technologies in teachers
and students. The score is rather indecisive in the question whether teachers and students
usedigitaltechnologiesmorefrequentlyafterthepandemic(53%ofrespondentsagree,in
students, 40% agree). After such long experience in using digital technologies, we expect
that both teachers and students have appropriate skills that let them use technologies
freely, without constraints. However, there might be another reason why they do not
do so, and these are psychological constraints. They feel a distaste for any technology
and are demotivated when expected to work with them. They long for personal contacts
and are eager to work face-to-face. In addition, more than half of the teachers (60%)
and almost half of the students (47%) do not think they are more competent in using
digital technologies. In other words, 90% of teachers and 70% of teachers mean that
there is much to improve regarding their work with digital technologies for educational
purposes. As there are more teachers (47%) than students (20%) who fully agree that
improvement is needed, we can deduce that teachers are less conﬁdent about their skills.

[9]. In online distance instruction, particularly in ESP, the amount of qualiﬁed supporters

two reasons: ﬁrst, there are numerous sources available that can be exploited for the

and other devices, the price and size of which enable the users to take them (and learn)

the online distance form was compared to face-to-face instruction before and after the
pandemic from the view of learning content acquired by learners. In both ﬁgures, we
can see that respondents declared that they learned more in both periods of face-to-
face instruction, that is, before and after the pandemic, compared to the online distance
instruction. Although disagreement is increasing steadily with respect to the period
before the pandemic (33% and 43%), there is a jump in the post-pandemic period (57%,

This sharp decrease could arise from general frustration in students with a long-term

supporters of this form. The study by Holzer et al. [11] aims to identify psychological
characteristics that relate to the well-being in terms of positive emotion and intrinsic
learning motivation, which are the key features of their learning behavior in involuntary
and unplanned distance education. More than 25,000 students from eight countries in
Europe, Asia, and North America responded to the online questionnaire. The collected
data proved that deeper competence in learning autonomy strengthens positive emotions,

L. Faltynkova et al.
intrinsic learning motivation, and active learning behavior in terms of engagement and
persistence.
3.4
Limits of Research
The results are limited by the research sample. It consists of respondents from two
institutions, both of them dealing with medical staff preparation. The learning content
of English for Speciﬁc Purposes develops reading, writing, speaking, and listening;
however, it concentrates on related topics only.
4
Conclusions
Digital technologies have been supporting instruction for more than two decades. They
played a crucial role in online distance teaching and learning during the covid-19 pan-
demic. They are expected to do so in the future; either the lessons will be carried online
distance, or in the present face-to-face form. Feedback collected from students and
teachers should contribute to attaining higher quality of instruction, and the latest tech-
nologies are expected to enhance the development of new blended learning models. The
comments provided by the teachers in the survey of Gavranovic and Prodanovic [6]
correspond to a high degree with the comments given by the students in a study that
examined students’ satisfaction with online teaching organized in a similar context by
Prodanovic and Gavranovic [12]. Identically, data from teachers’ and students’ views
were collected by Faltynkova et al. [13] and Simonova et al. [14]. To carry the lessons
efﬁciently, their results suggest pre-service and in-service teachers should be trained in
online distance didactics immediately. To contribute to the training is an objective of the
papers.
Negative opinions do not relate to online distance instruction only, they indicate
frustration in the whole society. To avoid or prevent them in education, thorough didactic
preparation of teachers and students is necessary. Once online distance instruction is
understood as a common way of teaching and learning, it will not cause negative feelings.
If hardware and software is available to teachers and students, as well as technical support
and a quiet place to study from anywhere, the process will work as planned and expected.
To reach this objective is feasible under current technical, technological, and didactic
conditions.

The Relationships Between Career Image
and Teaching Intention Among First-Year
Engineering Teacher Training Students
Zsóﬁa-Irén Horváth(B)
, Erzsébet Szentes
, and Katalin Harangus
Faculty of Technical and Human Sciences, Sapientia Hungarian University of Transylvania,
O.p. 9, C.p. 4, 540485 Târgu-Mure¸s, Romania
{horvathzsofia,eszentes,katalin}@ms.sapientia.ro
Abstract. In our study we present our survey conducted among ﬁrst-year teacher
candidates of Sapientia Hungarian University of Transylvania, which we com-
pleted in the 2020–21 and 2021–22 academic years. The goal of our study was
to assess the extent to which it is important for undergraduate engineering stu-
dents, who enroll in teacher training education at the beginning of their higher
education, to pursue a teaching profession after completing their studies, and how
attractive the teaching profession is to them. We examined whether there is a corre-
lation between the teaching career image, the students’ own pedagogical potential
(teacher self-image) and the teaching intention, as well as what the qualities of a
good teacher are according to the students. We hypothesized that the image of a
teaching career is related to the intent to teach, i.e., if a teaching career is attractive
to students, they would prefer to teach after graduation. Similarly, we hypothe-
sized that if a student’s teacher self-image was positive, they would prefer to teach
after completing their studies.
Keywords: Teaching intention · Career image · Engineer - teacher training
1
Introduction and Theory
Sapientia Hungarian University of Transylvania Teacher Training Institute undertakes
the psycho-pedagogical training of Hungarian language students who want to acquire
the skills and didactic competencies needed for teaching, besides obtaining a qualiﬁ-
cation corresponding to their university degree. A signiﬁcant number of engineering
undergraduate students study at the institute, who would be in great demand in public
education. In addition to their undergraduate degree, teacher training students complete
a ﬁrst-level pedagogy module. This will give them the opportunity to work as teach-
ers in the compulsory stage of public education: four grades of primary school (grades
5–8); lower secondary education (grades 9–10). The Ministry of Education publishes a
summary of the subjects that can be taught with this degree, and changes are announced
annually.
In minority education, besides the knowledge transfer and educational function, its
identity-forming function is also of paramount importance, which can prevail if young
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 544–552, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_57

The Relationships Between Career Image and Teaching Intention
545
people participate in Hungarian-language education [1]. For the community, the key
to preserve identity lies in mother tongue education, transmission of national culture
values and the foundation of mother tongue literacy [2]. According to the Romanian
Law of National Education, people belonging to national minorities have the right to
learn in their mother tongue and to be taught in their mother tongue, they have the right
to establish independent institutions. The task of Hungarian-language teacher training
institutes is to contribute to the quality teacher training in Hungarian by providing a
professional, scientiﬁc background and organizational framework, and thus serve the
quality development of Hungarian-language education in Romania [3]. It is well known
that young people who participate in higher education successfully graduated from high
school, i.e. met previous school requirements, and most likely continue their studies by
their own choice. Participating in teacher training is another decision for them, which
involves additional tasks compared to the basic training [4]. In terms of staying in the
profession and career socialization, the starting quality of a career will be crucial for
them [5].
Sapientia Hungarian University of Transylvania Teacher Training Institute provides
teacher training for undergraduate specializations in three ﬁelds of education (technol-
ogy, language and communication, humanities and society). Competence-based educa-
tion is provided in teacher training, and it is of great importance for teachers to help
teacher candidates achieve professional well-being. Teachers in public education play
an important role in the process of socialization and education, therefore, in addition to
the adequate professional and methodological training needed for an effective pedagog-
ical work, assertive behavior, effective communication, problem-solving and decision-
making skills are also required. These competencies make it possible to establish and
maintain good cooperation, to create discipline and a good work atmosphere, and to
build a trusting teacher-student relationship with all age groups [6].
In Romania, the teaching profession “does not have sufﬁcient social prestige, it is
not one of the well-paid professions; the social judgment and appreciation of teachers
does not reﬂect the essential role they play in the life of the community” [3]. According
to Marin - Macri [7], the prestige of the teaching profession declined in recent years.
This is also reﬂected in our survey results, as students believe that teachers’ work is only
moderately paid and they have little free time during the school year. A signiﬁcant part
of them perceive teaching as an emotionally stressful profession that requires a lot of
work, outstanding communication skills and a high level of professional knowledge [8].
The situation of teaching careers is more unfavorable in terms of income, career and
social prestige, compared to other professions requiring a university degree (e.g. lawyer,
mechanical engineer, economist). The beneﬁts of the teaching career are compatibility
with the family, a source of joy related to the profession, and job security [9].
It is important to analyze the career motivation of teacher candidates, and regarding
those who are interested in a teaching career to examine what resources they have, what
kind of career-image they have upon starting the teacher training, what they consider the
qualities of a good teacher, and what they think about their own pedagogical potential.

546
Z.-I. Horváth et al.
2
Presentation of Survey
In the 2020/2021 academic year a total of 147 (95%), while in the 2021/2022 aca-
demic year 142 (92%) ﬁrst-year teacher training students of Sapientia Hungarian Uni-
versityofTransylvaniarespondedtothequestionnaire.Thecomponentsoftheself-edited
questionnaire were: socio-demographic questions, characteristics of the teaching career,
characteristics of a good teacher, a scale to assess the importance of teaching, and a
list of metaphors. The list of metaphors contains 19 elements that name professions
and life roles. The task of the survey subjects is to select the three elements they con-
sider the most similar to teaching and justify their choice. Deeper correlations appear in
metaphors, when comparing the teaching profession to the professions that are presented
as metaphors [10]. Data processing and analysis was performed using SPSS 22.0 soft-
ware. The presented study is part of our multi-year research among teacher candidates.
The measurements were carried out with the intention of applying our ﬁndings in the
teacher training education.
3
Results
3.1
General Characteristics of the Sample
The gender distribution of the surveyed students is almost the same: in the 2020/2021
academic year 53.1% girls, 46.9% boys, and in the 2021/2022 academic year 54.2% girls,
45.8% boys. The distribution by specialization is as follows: in the 2020/2021 academic
year 49.7% human sciences, 22.4% agriculture, 26.5% technology, in the 2021/2022
academic year 53.2% human sciences, 4.3% agriculture, 35.5% technology and 7.1%
economics. The distribution by professional domain is as follows: in the 2020/2021
academic year 49.3% engineering students, 50.7% not engineering students, and in the
2021/2022 academic year 39.4% engineering students, 60.6% not engineering students.
3.2
Teaching Intention
We used closed-ended questions to examine students’ intention to teach, i.e. how do
they feel about a teaching career at the beginning of their studies. From the following
ﬁve answers they had to choose the one that suits them the best: very important to me, I
deﬁnitely want to teach; important to me, if I would have the opportunity, I would want
to teach; it is a good opportunity, but it is not my main career aspiration; not important, it
is only a backup plan; not at all important, I would only teach if I could not ﬁnd another
job.
Regarding the proportion of teaching intention, we found no signiﬁcant difference
between the study groups of the two different academic years. There are signiﬁcant
differences in the answers of students from different specializations. According to spe-
cializations, a higher proportion of students studying human sciences consider a teaching
career to be important, while engineering students see it as an opportunity.
We were curious to learn, if the teaching career is more attractive to students who have
a teacher in their family. 46.7% of the surveyed students have a teacher in their family,

The Relationships Between Career Image and Teaching Intention
547
while 53.3% of them don’t. Surprisingly, the results show that there is no signiﬁcant
difference in this respect, since students who don’t have a teacher in their family want
to teach to the same extent as their peers. More than 90% (93.4%) of students answered
that they had at least one inspiring teacher during their high school studies. We found
no correlation between the intention to teach and the presence or absence of inspiring
teachers.
3.3
Career Image
Students’ opinion on the teaching career was examined with 13 statements (Table 1),
using a 5-point Likert scale (1 - not at all true, 5 - completely true). Students’ responses
from both classes show, that the highest values were given to professional aspects, such
as outstanding communication skills (rank 1) and high-quality professional knowledge
(rank 3). The statement that educators serve society (rank 2) was similarly highly ranked,
meaning that vocational calling is the central element of their career image. Regarding
the work of a teacher, they are aware that it involves a lot of work (rank 4) and it leaves
little free time (rank 13), also it is an emotionally stressful (rank 5) activity and teachers
do not earn well / are not well paid (rank 12).

3.4
Self-reﬂection: Resources for the Teaching Profession
In terms of teaching intent and teaching career image, we considered it important to
examine how students think about themselves in terms of their abilities, characteristics
and desires. Eight statements (Table 3) were rated on a Likert scale from 1 to 5 (1
strongly disagree, 5 strongly agree). For teacher skills, characteristics and attraction to
the profession, we used the collective name of teacher potential, since we think that
the internal resources, a person’s inner reserves, and knowledge about them are the
fundamental criteria for someone to be a good and effective teacher.
Regarding the statements, when we compared the means of the two study groups we
found no signiﬁcant difference. The comparison by professional domain indicates that
both, engineering students and not engineering students, think they have the qualities

550
Z.-I. Horváth et al.
and possess the abilities necessary for teaching. At the same time, it is signiﬁcantly more
characteristic to girls that they want to teach and educate, they are interested in teaching
and want to work with young people, children. The environment also tends to encourage
and motivate girls to pursue this career. In both classes students want a future job where
they can learn and develop.
We found no correlation between the self-reﬂexive view of a teaching career and
a teacher family member, i.e. regardless of whether there is or not a teacher in the
family, they think similarly about their teacher potential. The results show an interesting
correlation between inspiring teacher and teacher potential: engineering students, who
in their previous study years had one or more inspiring teachers, are more likely to think
they have the qualities and skills to teach, they think others also see them as potentially
good educators and they would prefer to work with children and young people.
3.5
Correlations Between Teaching Intention and Teaching Potential
of Engineering Students
The research results show a strong correlation between teaching intention and teacher
potential: engineering students, who consider it important to teach, believe to a signiﬁ-
cantly greater extent that they possess the qualities and abilities of a good teacher, they
ﬁnd this career highly attractive, and others also encourage them to become educators
(Table 3).
Contrary to our assumption, the image of the teaching career does not show a cor-
relation with the teaching intention. On the other hand, the intention to teach depends
to a great extent on students’ perception of their own pedagogical potential (teacher
self-image, personality traits, abilities, interests, engaging with children, etc.).

The Relationships Between Career Image and Teaching Intention
551
4
Summary
Characteristics of ﬁrst-year students’ teaching career image: pedagogical work requires
outstanding communication skills, it beneﬁts society and requires a lot of work, it is
unpredictable, not well paid, and very little free time comes with it. Half of the surveyed
students (51%) would like to teach, while 42% consider teacher training to be just
an option. According to the results, students consider professional factors to be the
most important in judging the teaching career and the criteria of a good teacher. At the
beginning of their studies, engineering students consider the teaching profession less
important, than students from human sciences.
It emerges from our research that the presence of an inspiring teacher, i.e. at a young
age students meeting educators who become their role models, has a positive effect
on the perception of their own qualities and abilities, and deepens their interest in a
teaching career, working with children and young people. Students’ intention to teach is
less inﬂuenced by their career image, therefore, their self-belief is what’s decisive and
not the fact that teachers are not respected by society and teaching is not a well-paid
profession.
Undergraduate engineering students see participation in teacher training education as
an opportunity for development. Higher engineering training is a very intensive stage of
professional development in the career formation of students, therefore, in addition to the
acquisition of psycho-pedagogical knowledge, formation of attitudes, skill development
and didactic competencies should also be pursued in teacher training. Our long-term
goal is to examine the correlations between graduate students’ teaching career image,
their teacher self-image and the intention to teach.

New Generation of Engineering Students: Do
We Know How to Teach Them?
Tatiana Polyakova(B)
Moscow Automobile and Road Construction State Technical University (MADI),
64, Leningradskiy Pr., 125319 Moscow, Russia
kafedra101@mail.ru
Abstract. Rapid changes in the activities of engineers under the inﬂuence of
the Fourth Industrial Revolution make engineering pedagogy to deﬁne up-to-
date teaching aims, content, environment, aids and methods. At present university
teachers use modern methods, technologies and educational aids to make educa-
tional process more effective. Nevertheless, the university teachers are not always
quite satisﬁed with the outcomes of the educational process, with the achieve-
ments of their students, and sometimes we come to the conclusion that we do
not know how to teach our students. The hypothesis is that one of the reasons for
educational failure of engineering students may be connected with the fact that the
methods and technologies we use in the classroom are not always adequate to the
new generation of students. Based on the analysis of works in pedagogy of higher
school including engineering pedagogy, the results of the research undertaken
by the author and other specialists, the paper describes the main characteristics
of the new generation of engineering students that may inﬂuence the choice of
teaching methods and technologies. Many representatives of this generation are
characterized by pragmatism, narcissism, stratiﬁcation, clip mentality, high speed
of searching for information, time limit of attention, good operational memory,
problems with long-term memory, cause-effect relationship, analysis, and com-
munication. These characteristics should be taken into consideration by university
teachers when choosing teaching methods and technologies.
Keywords: Engineering students · New generation · Characteristics · Teaching
methods and technologies
1
Context and Goal
Rapid changes in the activities of engineers under the inﬂuence of the Fourth Industrial
Revolution make engineering pedagogy to deﬁne up-to-date teaching aims, content,
environment, aids, and methods. At present university teachers use modern methods,
technologies and educational aids to make educational process more effective. At our
disposal we have electronic whiteboards, desktops and laptops, projectors, we use infor-
mation and communication technologies, various simulations, e-learning, virtual and
remote laboratories, etc. Nevertheless, nowadays the university teachers are not always
quite satisﬁed with the outcomes of the educational process, with the achievements of
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 553–560, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_58

554
T. Polyakova
their students, and sometimes we come to the conclusion that we do not know how to
teach our students.
Currently, higher education is moving towards student-centered learning, which is
a further development of the personal and individual approaches traditionally used in
engineering education. The personality of the student, who becomes a real subject of
the educational process, largely determines its ﬁnal results. In this regard, the general-
ization of the characteristics of the current generation of students, identiﬁed by various
specialists, and the determination of the possibilities of taking them into account while
choosing most appropriate methods and technologies in engineering education is of
particular relevance.
The hypothesis is that one of the reasons for educational failure of engineering
students may be connected with the fact that the methods and technologies we use in
the classroom are not always adequate to the new generation of students.
The goal of the paper is to determine the main characteristics of the new generation of
engineeringstudentsthatmayinﬂuencethechoiceofteachingmethodsandtechnologies.
2
Approach
Considering the features of the modern generation of students it is necessary to turn to
the theory of generations that was developed at the end of the 20th century. The theory is
connected with the names of two American scientists, Neil Howe and William Strauss,
who published a book in 1991 under the title “Generations: The History of America’s
Future, 1584 to 2069” [1]. Based on the data of economics, demography, history and
other sciences, the theory proves that the period of time in which a person was born
affects his worldview. According to this theory, a generation is a group of people born in
a certain time period, who have been inﬂuenced by the same events and upbringing, and,
as a result, have similar values [1]. It is the values and their similarities that determine
our behavior, including our attitude towards education. Nowadays generation theory is
widely used as the basis for sociological analysis.
Describing the situation since the beginning of the 20th century Neil Howe and
William Strauss distinguished several generations that depended on the period of their
birth and formation. These are the following groups: The Greatest Generation (1900–
1923), Silent Generation (1923–1943), Baby Boomer Generation (1943–1963), Gen-
eration X (1963–1983), Generation Y (1983–2000) and Generation Z (2000 +). Now
specialists are speaking about Generation Alpha (Gen Alpha) to denote the children
who were born after 2010. The term “Generation Alpha” was introduced by Australian
researcher M. McCrindle who used the ﬁrst letter of the Greek alphabet to name it. The
current generation of engineering students with some perspective can be attributed to
Generations Y and Z.
Generation Y, also known as the “Network Generation”, “Millennium”, “Next”,
“Millennials”, “Echo Boomers”, “Zero”, “Digital Immigrants”, was formed in the 80s
of the 20th century. It was the period of the end of the cold war and of rapid changes in
science and technologies. Information, digital and communication technologies, mobile
telephony and the Internet rapidly burst into their lives and made serious changes to it.
The next generation, Generation Z, was born under conditions of relative social
and political stability, which provided its representatives with a so-called “problem-free

New Generation of Engineering Students
555
childhood”. With regard to information technology, this generation, unlike the previous
one, did not know the world without access to the Internet, social networks, computer
games and virtual communication. That is why the representatives of this generation
are no longer “Digital immigrants”, but those who were “Born in the digital world”
(Digital natives). For the same reason, along with the names “Generation MeMeMe”
and “Homebodies”, which reﬂect the value orientations of this group, most of the names
reﬂect the characteristics of the world in which they were born and formed: “Digital
Generation”, “Generation XD”, “Digital children of generation X”.
At the moment the characteristic features of these two generations are at the stage
of reﬂection, their boundaries are blurred to some extent, they have a lot in common,
and on this basis, when considering the characteristics of modern engineering students,
it seems that the characteristics of both Generation Y and Generation Z should be taken
into account.
These common characteristics of Generations X and Z inﬂuence greatly the rela-
tions between teachers and learners and make the traditional generation gap between
them unique. Throughout the history of mankind, the older generation had the indis-
putable authority of knowledge that was passed on to the younger ones. For the ﬁrst
time, in contrast to the previous centuries, the younger generation, which does not yet
have sufﬁcient life experience, is better able to use the achievements of civilization and
surpasses the older generation in this respect. As a result, parents and teachers are losing
their traditional authority. The communicative distance between parents and children,
teachers and learners is increasing, and there is a danger of breaking the chain of social
inheritance.
This situation places new demands on the teachers of engineering universities. First
of all, this situation requires high erudition of the teacher, their willingness to cooperate
with learners and their ability to use adequate modern educational technologies. In other
words, it is necessary to reconsider how to teach them.
Determination of the main characteristics of the new generation of engineering stu-
dents that may inﬂuence the choice of teaching methods and technologies is based on
the analysis of works in pedagogy of higher school including engineering pedagogy, the
results of the research undertaken by the author and other specialists.
3
Actual Outcomes
The personality of a human being is based on the motives, claims, values and goals of
a person. Many authors note that generations Y and Z are pragmatic and practical. This
statement is conﬁrmed by the results of various surveys. According to the survey of
graduate students [2] the main motives to take a master study program are the possibility
of promotion (41,1%) and the increase of salary (13,5%), but not motivation to acquire
new knowledge and competences. The research undertaken by Moscow State Institute
of Tourism Industry in 2016 [3] also showed that the leading position among the sig-
niﬁcant motives for obtaining higher education among students is the desire to secure
their own material well-being in future (95% of both ﬁrst year and ﬁnal year students).
These data are also conﬁrmed by the results of a survey of Moscow Automobile and
Road Construction State Technical University (MADI) students [4], which showed that

556
T. Polyakova
students’ motivation to study a foreign language at a technical university is based on the
pragmatism that is the need to use a foreign language in their future profession (98%).
The pragmatism of engineering students requires practical orientation of teaching.
This requirement may concern not only the whole courses but all the segments of the
teaching process including separate tasks. It is necessary for teachers to demonstrate the
practical value of what students are doing for their future profession.
The current generation of students is also characterized by certain narcissism [5].
It is for that reason that the name “Generation MeMeMe” is used as an alternative
for Generation Y. Narcissism is characterized by an overestimation of oneself and
a high level of self-acceptance. A person is usually “satisﬁed with himself”. How-
ever, high self-assessment is combined with the lack of methods and skills for solving
problems [6].
When studying a foreign language, narcissism manifests itself in an overestimated
self-assessment of the level of knowledge of a foreign language. The results of a survey of
ﬁrst year MADI bachelor students in the specialties of the Faculty of Road Construction,
which was conducted in February 2017, showed that 72% of the respondents assessed
their knowledge of a foreign language as preintermediate, intermediate or advanced
[4]. However, unfortunately, the results of these learners’ objective assessment did not
conﬁrm these data.
In this regard, the organization of regular objective assessment of knowledge, skills
and abilities of students is of particular relevance to show students the real situation with
their progress though only 30% of the surveyed MADI students ﬁnd it necessity [4]. But
at the same time all the achievements of the students should be notices, encouraged and
praised.
Sociologists record the intellectual and cultural stratiﬁcation of young people [7].
Some young people are interested in acquiring knowledge, they study intensively, and for
them knowledge is of high value. The other part includes teenagers, for whom the value
of culture, education, knowledge are devalued is low. In their opinion, one can get a good
job and a high salary without having any special knowledge, skills and competences [7].
In the university classrooms we see the representatives of the both groups in front of
us. Those who are making efforts towards excellence are interested in improving their
level of knowledge in various disciplines, in developing professional and soft skills,
they become participants of various competitions so popular now. At the same the rep-
resentatives of the second group experience great difﬁculties in the process of studying
humanitarian and technical subjects. For example, studying English they have problems
connected with reading comprehension. Translating the word combination “Westmin-
ster Abbey” some of them interpret it in their native language as “Western Minister
Abbey”. The analysis of such cases registered by the Department of Foreign Languages
of MADI shows that the students have a well-developed linguistic guess, but the unsuc-
cessful results of its application indicate that the students do not have a general outlook,
knowledge of global cultural values and achievements.
Apparently, teachers should be aware of this stratiﬁcation phenomenon and apply the
differentiated approach while training representatives of these two groups of the current
generation of students, requires the use of in teaching a foreign language.

New Generation of Engineering Students
557
We live in the information society and the redundancy of information is one of the
main factors requiring the adaptation of the psychological characteristics of a person.
The educational process is closely connected with the transfer of information from the
teacher or any other source to the learner no matter it is aimed at acquiring knowledge or
developing habits, skills or competences. Information turns into knowledge only in case
valuable and useful information a particular person gains thanks to intellect, feelings
and experience [8].
Weshalltrytoconsiderthepeculiaritiesofmoderngenerationofengineeringstudents
taking into consideration information transfer. As it is known, in the process of meeting
the information need, we can distinguish the stages of information search, its perception,
processing, storage and transmission.
The modern generation of students copes most successfully with the information
search stage. Given the availability of information and the high speed of its receipt,
modern students easily navigate the world’s information resources and quickly ﬁnd the
information they need. At school, they were not taught to take notes and read textbooks,
but to search for information on the Internet and complete test tasks. As a result, students
always know where to look for it. It is natural for them to be constantly involved in
search activities, they know how to use a variety of information resources, and the
search they perform is carried out at a high speed. They manage to quickly ﬁnd sources
of information, that contain relevant information, as well as illustrative material in the
form of diagrams, graphs, drawings, and photographs. According to the survey of master
students [2] the majority of them (71%) possess the ability to work with data. In foreign
language classes, students demonstrate a quick search for a translation of unfamiliar
words.
In connection with this ability of students, a wider application of tasks requiring
information search is necessary. This may be the preparation of reports at the confer-
ences, referencing selected sources of information, implementation of “Flipped class-
room method”, in accordance with which the teacher sets a certain cognitive task, stu-
dents independently search for information to solve it in literature, and in the classroom
they organize joint discussion of the solutions.
For the implementation of the next stage of meeting the information need, namely the
perception of information, attention is extremely important. According to recent research
[9], Generation Z has reduced attention span to eight seconds. Foreign language teachers
often observe how difﬁcult it is for students to focus on learning material for relatively
long periods of time. However, experts believe that it is more correct to speak of “eight-
second ﬁlters”, which are the result of the younger generation’s adaptation to the need
to quickly perceive and evaluate huge amounts of information in the conditions of time
pressure. As a result, their attention is characterized by a high degree of switching and
tracking many virtual objects. However, unfortunately, in general this leads to a decrease
in the ability to concentrate. The process of perception is dominated by reliance on visual
images.
Undertheseconditions,theintroductionofneweducationalmaterialinsmallportions
by dividing it into blocks using visual images in the form of tables, graphs, and ﬁgures
becomes an urgent task. In this case, each portion of the new material should immediately

558
T. Polyakova
be followed by its primary ﬁxation. Exercises should not be too large and different in
form.
The most important step in meeting the information need is processing of informa-
tion. The processing of information is closely related to the peculiarities of the processes
of thinking. The excess of information that accompanies the younger generation from
the ﬁrst years of life affects the peculiarities of students’ thinking, for which the term
“clip mentality” is used [10].
Clip mentality is characterized by an inability to assimilate large amounts of infor-
mation, a quick but shallow comprehension of information, that is, a superﬁcial fragmen-
tary approach to the analysis of information, reﬂection of reality objects without taking
into account the connections between them, illogicality, fragmentation, mosaicism, mis-
understanding of complex material, inability to systematize information, build logical
connections, structuring knowledge, the ability to focus on several information objects,
combined with a decrease in the productivity of each of the tasks being solved [10].
These conclusions are conﬁrmed by the results of the analysis of typical mistakes
of National Examinations participants in mathematics [11]. The analysis showed that
the mistakes were made because the basic logical culture had not been formed, some of
them were caused by the inability to analyze the conditions of the problem and search
for ways to solve it, the inability to apply standard algorithms in changed situations, the
failure to ﬁnd and correct errors in their own reasoning and calculations.
Thus, the successful fast search for information made by many modern students very
often ends with enormous difﬁculties associated with its comprehension. One of the
possible ways to overcome these difﬁculties can be scrupulous work on the information
processinganddevelopmentofcriticalthinking.Wecansuggestthatfurtherdevelopment
of reading techniques both in a native and foreign language can really improve the
situation, since it is reading that provides a lot of opportunities for the development of
analysis and synthesis of information. However, it is important to realize that this work
is complicated by the fact that the ability to isolate the main information, to separate
it from the secondary, to systematize it, is often not sufﬁciently formed when reading
in the native language. In accordance with the results of a survey of students of the St.
Petersburg State Medical University, 56% of the students surveyed read books in their
native language rarely [6].
After processing information, the stage of its storage begins, which is associated, in
particular, with the possibilities of short-term and long-term memory of a person. Since
the virtual environment requires operational interaction, this leads to the development
of short-term, operational, memory of modern students [12]. At the same time, the
availability of the Internet and the latest communication devices eliminate the need
to memorize information, which leads to a lack of memory training. In addition, the
information received is quickly erased, since memorization is built only on the basis of
analysis and the establishment of logical connections, which, as mentioned above, is a
serious problem for young people. As a result, the possibilities of long-term memory
deteriorate [12], which often leads to very detrimental consequences, since the increase
in the complexity of the studied material in the absence of reliance on already mastered
material often leads to its absolute misunderstanding and, ultimately, to a loss of interest
in the subject being studied.

New Generation of Engineering Students
559
Studying a foreign language requiring memorizing a lot of new words and gram-
mar structure may stimulate the development of long-term memory mechanisms. For
successful memorization at the stage of introduction and consolidation of new words,
apparently, it is necessary to use more actively all organs of perception - hearing, sight,
touch. It is desirable to have a constant representation of the sound and graphic form of
words, the image of the meaning of the word in drawings, and so on. At the same time,
it is very important to create an associative series, “embedding” a new word or phrase
in existing language systems, for example, synonymic series.
The transfer of information can take place both orally and in writing. As for oral
communication, it should be noted that the spread of virtual communication in social
networks leads to a reduction in face-to-face communication [13]. It is often easier for
students to share their experiences with a thousand virtual interlocutors than in person
with friends or parents. The psychological features of the current generation of students
include insufﬁcient development of communication skills, the inability to clearly and
distinctly express their thoughts in the process of oral and written communication [6].
In this regard, the tasks connected with the expression of students’ thoughts either
orallyorinwritingarebecomingmoreandmoresigniﬁcant.Takingintoconsiderationthe
difﬁcultiesthatstudentsexperiencewiththeexpressionofcause-and-effectrelationships,
teaching the expression of thoughts should begin with fairly short fragments of speech.
This is conﬁrmed by the data of the Institute of Philosophy and Law of the Ural Branch
of the Russian Academy of Sciences, in which, at the third level of higher education,
many graduate students note the need for additional courses in writing at the level of
sentences and paragraphs [14].
The analysis of meeting information needs and peculiarities of the new generation of
engineering students involved in this process should be taken into account for choosing
adequate educational methods and technologies.
4
Conclusions
The new generation of engineering students may be referred to Generation Y and Gen-
eration Z. Common values, psychological and intellectual peculiarities of the new gen-
eration of students determine their behavior including their attitude towards education.
The communicative distance between teachers and learners is increasing, we are having
unprecedented generation gap and quite often the teachers think that they do not how to
teach them.
Many representatives of the new generation of engineering students are characterized
by pragmatism, narcissism, stratiﬁcation, clip mentality, high speed of searching for
information, time limit of attention, good operational memory, problems with long-term
memory, cause-effect relationship, analysis, and communication.
Today’s learners are different from those we used to have in the past, and the uni-
versity teachers should be aware of these differences. The new generation of students is
not good or bad, they are just different and their peculiarities should be taken into con-
sideration by university teachers when designing new courses, presenting new teaching
material, choosing methods and technologies to help students acquire knowledge and
develop necessary skills and competences.

Computer Aided Technologies in Learning
Foreign Languages for Engineering Students
R. S. Valeeva1
, E. I. Murtazina2
, G. N. Fakhretdinova1(B)
, L. P. Dulalaeva1
,
and Diana Giliazova1
1 Kazan National Research Technological University, Kazan, Russia
gulnaz_khamidull@mail.ru
2 Kazan Federal University, Kazan, Russia
Abstract. Currently, the teaching methods are constantly evolving in terms of
education digitalization. There is a strong need for a qualitative transfer of the
educational environment, its methods and tools into smart education. In the con-
text of foreign language studies, this transition can be accomplished through the
development and use of all opportunities of various language tools and digital
technologies. In our study, we focus on the Web-based application Quizlet, a ﬂash-
card program considered a tool for mastering vocabulary in various ﬁelds of study.
However, it offers various options for sharpening skills and they are not limited
only to vocabulary skills development. Thus, this study aims to reveal the efﬁ-
ciency and feasibility of Quizlet for foreign language purposes of the engineering
students.
Keywords: Quizlet · Feasibility · Engineering majors · Foreign language (FL)
1
Introduction
The current development of society requires constant transformation and evolution of
teaching approaches and methods, a growing trend in higher education [1–8]. Above all,
using digital tools and technologies has become imperative in the learning and teaching
process [9]. Currently, the number of virtual learning tools is increasing at a rapid pace,
and educators face several challenges on how to justify the feasibility, effectiveness
and limitations of these communication technologies [10, 11]. In fact, they have deeply
inﬂuenced the educational environment, making a real breakthrough in the process of
acquiring knowledge, skills and abilities. Among these are online programs for mastering
various language skills [10].
One such program is Quizlet. Instructors gravitate toward Quizlet over other digital
tools for its vocabulary ﬂash-cards and view it as the most convenient tool for language
acquisition [12]. This Web-based application is mostly used for learning vocabulary,
though it offers several options for sharpening various skills not only limited to vocab-
ulary skills development. The primary purpose of the article is to reveal the efﬁciency
and feasibility of Quizlet for the foreign language purposes of engineering students.
