2
Methodology
In our study, we evaluated Quizlet using the BRIDGE checklist. It is a useful resource
created by Arizona State University to review the online educational tool’s characteris-
tics. The checklist helps to understand the potential and efﬁciency of the interactive tools
from an educational perspective. Each letter of the title BRIDGE refers to: B – build
language, R – research, I – innovate, D – develop critical thinking, G – get together,
E – expand technology skills. During one academic term, students getting their Master’s
degrees in Dairy Science and Technologies were assessed based on Quizlet. The total
number of students was 70. This online tool was used as a formative assessment to see
students’ progress.
3
The Bridge Checklist
3.1
Build Language
The ﬁrst item on the Checklist called Build Language comprises developing language
skills. It should answer the following questions: Does the online tool help students to
better understand and use the language they learn?
Vocabulary. Learning vocabulary is a key part of foreign language training for science
majors. At our university, engineering students study general, scientiﬁc, technical and
professional terminology. The general scientiﬁc part includes the study of vocabulary in
such areas as chemistry, mathematics, physics, physical and chemical methods of analy-
sis, processes and devices of chemical technology, promising areas of chemical technol-
ogy development, etc. The professional module covers the study of professional topics
[13, 14], depending on the training program. In an FL class at Kazan National Research
Technological University graduate students majoring in Dairy Science and Technolo-
gies study the basic issues of processing technologies for milk and milk products. This
course covers topics on dairy product production: pasteurization and ultra-high tempera-
ture processing; fermented dairy products; cheese making technology; butter production
technology, etc. It takes a lot of time and effort to memorize it. Learning vocabulary using
various modules of Quizlet is quite an effective method of ESL instruction and versatile
in terms of the learning topics. It promotes the development of pronunciation, spelling,
and we use its various memorizing options in virtual classes [13]. For Food Science
majors we make ﬂashcards with various tasks. Below is an example of a ﬂashcard with
the task “Fill the gaps”, a screenshot from Quizlet page (Fig. 1).
Translating. At engineering universities, it takes considerable time to study profes-
sional texts. The main task of an instructor is to teach engineering students how to trans-
late simple and complex terms related to some professional ﬁelds and annotate technical
texts. Regarding it, the skill of translating professional terms, phrases and sentences is
consolidated and trained. When translating vocabulary and texts, we lay great emphasis
on the words with several meanings, word collocations and attribute constructions and
train them through Quizlet [15].

Computer Aided Technologies in Learning Foreign Languages
563
Fig. 1. Flashcards with tasks aimed at building vocabulary
Grammar. Grammar is an important language component for increasing proﬁciency
in a foreign language. Apart from vocabulary acquisition, we use Quizlet for the study,
consolidation and revision of simple and complex grammar structures. Quizlet helps
students learn any grammar units (verb forms, degrees of comparison of adjectives, etc.);
various grammar features and structures (uncountable nouns, prepositions, participles,
word combinations and collocations, phrasal verbs, etc.).
The ﬁelds do not have to be represented by a word or phrase; you can use short
sentences containing grammar units being studied, such as the tenses and structure of
the question or the article. To practice and revise grammar using Quizlet, we prepared
sets of grammar ﬂashcards with different tasks such as completing the gaps, choosing the
correct option, the sentence transformation, an explanation of various grammar rules,
etc. Examples of the tasks assessing the use of voice and tag questions are shown in
Fig. 2.
Fig. 2. Flashcards with tasks aimed at building grammar skills
Language Assessment. Quizlet provides opportunities to evaluate the students’
progress through mode “Test” and has two forms of assessment: self-evaluation and
direct assessment by an instructor. To do this, Quizlet provides an interactive test. The
test can contain various types of assignments, including multiple-choice questions, “true-
false” and matching statements. The types of assignments and the number of questions
in the test can be altered depending on the purpose of the assessment and the module
content. As a result, the app generates an individual test for each student. If students
want to retake a test, the programme will create a new test based on the module they have
already studied. At the stage of consolidation and self-control, we consider it appropriate
to encourage students to complete tasks until a one-hundred-percent result is achieved.
Learners stop worrying about the tasks as soon as they realize that they can complete
tests several times and ﬁnally get a positive assessment.

564
R. S. Valeeva et al.
However, online Quizlet tests are not appropriate for intermediate and ﬁnal testing
since students have access to the learning content and can take the test several times
[16]. If the educator wants to conduct an achievement test, he/she can choose available
modules or create a new one with questions and answers, and make printable copies
for students to ﬁll out. Instructors can also print the keys to facilitate the veriﬁcation
process. The platform offers several versions of the test. Instructors can use this option
for students’ assessment during mid-term or end-of-term exams [16]. This option has
proved to be very useful to assess distant-learning students.
Gaming. To help students understand the use of words, we refer to the games. The app
offers several games, which contribute to the faster and more effective acquisition of
learning content. There are three types of games in Quizlet. The ﬁrst one is Selection
where the students should choose the right word pairs or deﬁnitions against the clock.
The next one is Gravity; students must enter the answers as quickly as possible to avoid
being hit by an asteroid. One of the most fascinating team-building games is Quizlet
Live.
3.2
Research
The second section of the checklist deals with the research and responds to the following
question: Can students use Quizlet to collect, evaluate, and use new information?
In connection with rapid technological advancements, research skills are required
for experts in every area of the economy, including engineering. Universities should
prepare their students to handle any serious emergency promptly. Future engineers must
be willing to use all sources of information, deal with various professional, social and
intercultural issues [3, 4, 17–23]. In this regard, one of the main goals of engineering
education is to develop students’ research skills and professional qualities.
Research is an important part of the educational process for graduate students major-
ing in Food engineering. As a ﬁnal project of their English language course, they must
present a research project. Developing research skills has several stages. The ﬁrst stage is
translating the article based on their major. Even at this stage, they pick up such research
skills as the independent search for reliable data on the research topic, the analysis of
a considerable number of various information sources. As part of their research, the
students compile their own vocabularies. To do this, they used Quizlet and made their
individual ﬂashcard sets. The next stage covers presenting research ﬁndings. To help stu-
dents present their results, we offered them a set of ﬂashcards with questions concerning
their research with true and false responses in Quizlet. They had to evaluate the answers
and select the right one. Quizlet helps students enhance logical thinking, searching and
analysis skills.
3.3
Innovate
The third point on the Checklist is called Innovate, and it reviews if students can create
new products with Quizlet.

Computer Aided Technologies in Learning Foreign Languages
565
This section is closely connected to creativity. It has become a real and urgent need
for engineering development practice [24]. To pursue this goal, it is necessary to provide
a creative learning environment for developing creative attitudes among engineering
students toward their future occupation. Well-structured foreign language classes make
it possible to develop and stimulate creativity through various methods and techniques
[24]. Quizlet can promote creativity in students and prepare them for innovative life in
the future. Students created their own ﬂashcards and tasks via this tool. Besides, using
these ﬂashcards students made their own dialogues, created situation tasks, and stories.
Figure 3 shows ﬂashcards made by Master’s Degree students.
Fig. 3. Flashcards with tasks aimed at developing creativity
3.4
Develop Critical Thinking
Currently, critical thinking skill is considered a fundamental aim of education. Critical
thinking implies the analysis and evaluation of a vast amount of information, knowl-
edge representation and reasoning, logical conclusions, raising problems and rational
decision-making strategies. Engineers should think critically and this is one of the
most essential engineering skills. Making important judgments, choosing the best deci-
sion from various options, understanding the responsibility for its implementation, and
long-term projection of results are all characteristics of engineering work. Problem-
based learning facilitates critical thinking skills in a foreign language class. The goal
of problem-based learning is to encourage students to solve problems independently,
express their own perspectives, and try to come to reasonable conclusions [25, 26].
Flashcards with diverse tasks can help students build critical thinking skills. Engi-
neering discourse questions with multiple choice responses and “confused logical
chains” are examples of these tasks. These types of assignments help students think
more clearly, rationally, and logically. Figure 4 shows an example of a ﬂashcard with a
“confusedlogicalchain,”wherestudentsareaskedtocreateachainoflogicalconnections
from the stated expressions about sour cream processing.

566
R. S. Valeeva et al.
Fig. 4. Flashcards with tasks aimed at developing critical thinking
3.5
Get Together
The ﬁfth section of the Checklist examines how Quizlet fosters communication in a
classroom and encourages ‘working together’ environment.
We use various Quizlet games to develop interaction and communication skills.
They contribute to the closer cooperation of students with each other. Quizlet Live
is the most exciting virtual team-building game that encourages students to cope with
group tasks and promotes strong collaboration between all team members. The instructor
selects a module, and then the students are randomly divided into teams and join their
team members. All students in the team are asked the same question, but only one
team member gets the correct answer [16]. It is the most popular among engineering
students. The games Selection and Gravity, as well as Quizlet Live can be used to develop
interaction skills. We adapt them for pair work.
3.6
Expand Technology Skills
This point should reply to the following questions: Does the tool teach students new
technology skills to make their learning easier?
Digital technology skills are becoming an increasingly important professional tool
for engineering graduates [21]. Students learn how to practice vocabulary on their phones
or computers using Quizlet. Instead of merely consuming, they use various tools to create
their own online content.
4
Conclusion
In this paper, we have provided insights into the feasible options of Quizlet for foreign
language purposes of engineering majors that meet the requirements of smart education.
The use of these options extends the variability scope of Quizlet, enhances greatly
and diversiﬁes teaching and learning methods and increases the degree of students’
engagement in learning foreign languages. Thus, the results of the BRIDGE Checklist
have conﬁrmed the efﬁciency of Quizlet for engineering students since it possesses

Computer Aided Technologies in Learning Foreign Languages
567
all the characteristics indispensable for teaching FL of engineering students because
it covers such key constituents of the engineering profession as research, innovation,
critical thinking, and technological skills. BRIDGE proved to be a very convenient and
versatile strategy. Quizlet deserves the attention of the foreign language instructors at
engineering universities as it greatly facilitates and enhances the teaching process. We
hope that the study of Quizlet feasibility will be helpful for FL instructors in reaching
their various educational objectives.
Future studies on the current topic are therefore required to extend the tasks in Quizlet
on research, innovation, and critical thinking for engineering students.

A Study About the Effects of Educational
Robotics Activities on Students’ Self-efﬁcacy
Regarding STEM Career Decisions
Georg Jäggle1(B), Wilfried Lepuschitz2, Peter Wachter3, Richard Balogh4,
Tanja Tomitsch2, and Markus Vincze1
1 ACIN Institute of Automation and Control, Vienna University of Technology, Vienna, Austria
{jaeggle,vincze}@acin.tuwien.ac.at
2 PRIA Practical Robotics Institute Austria, Vienna, Austria
{lepuschitz,tomitsch}@pria.at
3 CVTI Slovak Centre of Scientiﬁc and Technical Information, Bratislava, Slovakia
peter.wachter@cvtisr.sk
4 STU Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology, Slovak University
of Technology in Bratislava, Bratislava, Slovakia
Abstract. This study represents an important step to bring innovative teach-
ing practices to schools. The study underlines the effects on increasing the stu-
dents’ interest in STEM, self-efﬁcacy and STEM career decisions with educational
robotics activities. The implementation of robotics equipment in activities is not
the only factor that inﬂuences the students’ STEM career decisions. Other fac-
tors are the didactical design in various settings or the use of different robotics
equipment. The study evaluated data from app. 1500 students with questionnaires
before and after the activities and identiﬁed the different effects on students’ STEM
interest and their self-efﬁcacy. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, which prevented
the implementation of on-site activities in schools for a longer period, also online
workshops using simulations were carried out and evaluated. Besides, a speciﬁc
case study was analyzed that applied an innovative hybrid setting with 23 students
at a business school in Vienna, Austria.
Keywords: STEM career · Educational robotics activities · Robotics
self-efﬁcacy
1
Introduction
Austria, like many other EU countries, lacks students interested in pursuing degrees
in STEM ﬁelds. Educational robotics is a proven tool for practical learning in STEM
topics, but also an effective tool to inﬂuence the students’ interest to pursue a STEM
career. Further relevant factors to inﬂuence the interest in STEM are the effects of
role models, hands-on activities and the increase of self-efﬁcacy. Interventions tackling
the ﬁrst factor about role models are to establish a relationship between tutors with
STEM background and students. These role models show that success in STEM is part
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 570–579, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_60

of their personal interest and not just based on natural skills. Fostering the interest in
STEM is also achieved through “learning by doing” with hands-on activities. The last
factor is to increase the students’ self-efﬁcacy through practical tasks and inﬂuence.
Self-efﬁcacy is what an individual believes they can accomplish using their skills under
certain circumstances. The results of several studies point out that self-efﬁcacy along
with a knowledge of STEM careers are essential factors in whether young people will
pursue a STEM career or not. In this context, educational robotics is a useful tool to
foster the interest in STEM by young people. This study shows the effects by using the
relevant factors in educational robotics to foster the interest in STEM ﬁelds and STEM
career decisions. For this purpose, the next section explains the frame and standards
of design for the educational robotics activities. The third section explains the research
design with the research methodology and the research questions. Section 4 shows the
results regarding the effect on the students’ robotics self-efﬁcacy during the educational
robotics activities. Section 5 reports the results about students’ STEM career decisions
and Sect. 6 informs about the new innovative hybrid design with the title ‘Educational
robotics workshop with hands-on and programming in a hybrid session’ showing results
with a case study. The ﬁnal section discusses the results and presents a conclusion as
well as further steps.
2
Educational Robotics Activities
Educational robotics activities are an effective tool to foster the interest of young people
inSTEMandhasproventobeusefulwhentheydecidetopursuefurtherSTEMeducation,
even sometimes against the will of their parents [1]. Previous studies have shown that
educational robotics activities positively inﬂuence the students’ motivation [2] and their
interest in math and science careers [3]. The goals of educational robotics activities in this
study are to inﬂuence the students’ interest in STEM, their self-efﬁcacy in the context of
robots and their STEM career decisions positively. The design of all educational robotics
activities in this study are based on the C4STEM framework [4] with the AVIVA model
and include pedagogical interventions to reach these goals. Relevant factors for the
interventions are role models [5], hands-on activities [6] and the increase of self-efﬁcacy
[7]. Tutors introduce their positive background in STEM and represent role models for
the students. They give them the feeling that success in STEM is a result of their interest
and not of their natural skills. Fostering the interest in STEM is also achieved through
“learning by doing” with hands-on activities. The last factor is to increase the students’
self-efﬁcacy through practical tasks and inﬂuence. Self-efﬁcacy is what an individual
believes they can accomplish using their skills under certain circumstances. The results
of several studies point out that self-efﬁcacy along with a knowledge of STEM careers
is an essential factor whether young people will pursue a STEM career or not.
The AVIVA Model is a didactical design with ﬁve phases (see Table 1) for the
educational robotics activities and includes both a constructionism-oriented approach
and an instructionism-oriented approach [4].
One important purpose of the constructionism approach is to increase the self-
efﬁcacy of solving problems in the robotic ﬁeld. In this context, this study shall identify
the impact of the educational robotics activities with different robotics equipment on the

research design for the evaluation process to identify the effects of different educational
robotics activities.
3
Research Design
The goal of the research design is to identify the effects of different educational robotic
activities and it is based on the approach of mixed methods that include the evaluation of
quantitativeandqualitativedata.Thequantitativedatawerecollectedwithquestionnaires
before and after the educational robotics activities. Each questionnaire provides data
about the gender, age, native language, experience with robots and programming before
the workshops, interest in STEM, as well as self-efﬁcacy in the context of robotics and
STEM career decisions. These data from 1562 students with 34.3% girls and 63.7% boys
being 10 to 23 years old help to identify the different effects of the educational robotics
activity designs and were analysed with the statistics software SPSS 27. The qualitative
data are presented as case study and present more details about the effects of a hybrid
workshop. The case study also involved photos from the activities and tutor reﬂections.
The research questions are as follows:
• RQ1: What are the effects of on-site and online designs regarding STEM career
decisions?
• RQ2: What are the effects of using different robotics equipment regarding STEM
career decisions?
• RQ3: What are the effects of different settings regarding gender and different age
groups pursuing STEM careers?
• RQ4: Which design does support schools by implementing educational robotics
activities at the school in a pandemic?

A Study About the Effects of Educational Robotics Activities
573
• RQ5: How can out-of-school-institutions offer in-school activities during a pandemic
with physical equipment?
4
The Positive Effect in Robotics Self-efﬁcacy
The concept of self-efﬁcacy is an important factor regarding STEM career decisions
[9]. It is the belief of a person in their own ability to successfully perform a particular
task based on the perception of their own capabilities and the likelihood of successfully
achieving the task. Self-efﬁcacy beliefs are an essential aspect of human motivation and
behaviour leading to actions that can affect one’s life [7]. The principle of self-efﬁcacy
theory is that people are more likely to engage in activities in which they have a high level
of self-efﬁcacy, and less likely to engage in those where they do not [10]. For a better
understanding about the effect of educational robotics activities a robotics self-efﬁcacy
scale was developed. It is a standard test which measures the conﬁdence and resilience
of students when solving problems with robots [11]. The goal is to increase the students’
self-efﬁcacy during the educational robotics activities in order to encourage students
towards a more active interest in STEM ﬁelds. The robotics self-efﬁcacy scale offers to
compare the effect by different groups. This study compared the effect of educational
robotics activities on different age and gender groups.
The ﬁrst result compares the effect on the robotics self-efﬁcacy of two different
age groups. Students from 10 to 23 years participated in different educational robotics
activities and this comparison is meant to show the different effects on two age groups
for answering research question RQ3. The ﬁrst group A represents students with an
age of 10 to 14 years. The second group B represents students aged 15 to 23 years. A
one-way between-subjects ANOVA (analysis of variance) was run with these two age
groups and the value about the difference of students’ robotics self-efﬁcacy before and
after the educational robotics activities. The results of the ANOVA showed a signiﬁcant
difference between the age groups; F(1,460) = 15.660, p < .001. The result shows that
group A (n = 358, M = 13.2, SD = 24.9) had a signiﬁcant higher increase of the robotics
self-efﬁcacy during the educational robotics activities in comparison to group B (n =
104, M = 3.9, SD = 12.0). This result underlines further studies that the students’ interest
and self-efﬁcacy in STEM ﬁelds often decline throughout the childhood [12]. Therefore,
it can be deduced that it is more difﬁcult to increase self-efﬁcacy in older students than
in younger students. The results show that the educational robotics activities have a
positive effect on students’ robotics self-efﬁcacy in both age groups. They underline
that educational robotics activities with a common didactical design (AVIVA) and the
relevant pedagogical interventions increase students’ self-efﬁcacy and therefore their
interest in STEM.
The second result compares the effect on the robotics self-efﬁcacy by gender. The
idea of this comparison is to show the different effect on gender groups and answers
also research question RQ3. A one-way between-subjects ANOVA was run with the
two gender groups and the value about the difference of students’ robotics self-efﬁcacy
before and after the educational robotics activities. Results of the ANOVA showed a
signiﬁcant difference between the age groups; F(1,468) = 14.554, p < .001. The result
shows that girls (n = 177, M = 16.07, SD = 27.04) had a signiﬁcant higher increase of

574
G. Jäggle et al.
the robotics self-efﬁcacy during the educational robotics activities in comparison to the
boys (n = 293, M = 7.87, SD = 19.36). These results offer a new perspective because
previous studies reported that boys are more conﬁdent in STEM ﬁeld than girls [13].
Hence, these results show that educational robotics activities can increase the robotics
self-efﬁcacy signiﬁcantly more on girls than on boys with the accordingly appropriate
design.
5
STEM Career Decision
Relevant key factors to inﬂuence the STEM career decision from students positively are
thefamily,teachersasrolemodel,schoolcurriculaaswellasout-of-schoolactivities[14].
Besides, several studies point out that self-efﬁcacy along with a knowledge of STEM
careers are an essential factor in whether or not young people will pursue a STEM career
[15]. This section answers the research questions RQ1, RQ2 and RQ5. The educational
activities took place in different settings with different robotics equipment. The different
settings were on-site with robotic kits or online using a simulation. The robotic kits used
on-site were Thymio, Hedgehog, Lego Mindstorm or Kitronik: move. The simulations
used online were the Hedgehog IDE and the Thymio Suite. The ﬁrst online simulations
can use for free on a webpage, the other can be downloaded as free version (Fig. 1).
Fig. 1. Robotic kits (Hedgehog, Kitronik: move, Thymio, Lego Mindstorm)
At the on-site workshops with the robot Thymio 36 students (34%) responded that
they are now more interested in studying science, 54 students (47.4%) that they are now
more interest in studying technology and 42 students (38.2%) that they are now more
interested in studying informatics. At the on-site workshops with the robot Hedgehog
102 students (28.9%) responded that they are now more interested in studying science,
140 students (39.2%) that they are now more interest in studying technology and 137
students (38.9%) that they are now more interested in studying informatics. At the
workshops on-site with the robot Kitronik:move 122 students (44.4%) responded that
they are now more interested in studying science, 231 students (76.7%) that they are
now more interest in studying technology and 226 students (75.1%) that they are now
more interested in studying informatics. At the on-site workshops with the robot Lego
Mind storm no students (0%) responded that they are now more interested in studying
science, 6 students (60%) that they are now more interest in studying technology and 4
students (40%) that they are now more interested in studying informatics (see Fig. 2).
At the online workshops with the robot simulation Hedgehog IDE 155 students
(49.7%) responded that they are now more interested in studying technology and one

6
Case Study with a New Innovative Hybrid Design
This section describes the educational robotics activity with the title ‘Educational
robotics workshop with hands-on and programming in a hybrid session’ and answers
research question RQ4. Recently, the COVID-19 pandemic prevented educational
robotics activities face to face in schools for a longer period. Consequently, activities
came up with online simulations in a virtual world [4]. However, a further developed
solution is a design with a hybrid setting that involves a combination of activities in the
school with virtual support. The activity took 240 min with two breaks of 10 min.
6.1
Innovative Hybrid Design
The new innovative hybrid design is based on the C4STEM framework [4] and offers a
barrier-free access for robots into schools. The educational robotics equipment in this
case was the already mentioned robot Thymio. It is a small gender-neutral robot with
series of LEDs and sound effects. Coding is done using a visual programming language
(VPL). The activity took place in a classroom from a business high school and was
supported by two teachers in the room and two tutors of the Automation and Control
Institute of the Vienna University of Technology being remotely connected through the
video conference software Zoom. The activity started with a presentation by the tutors
about robots’ diversity and opportunities. The presentation was streamed to the class
via a projector and the students could ask questions. After the presentation the students
got an introduction about the function of the robot Thymio and started with the ﬁrst
hands-on exercise in groups, named explore a robot. The students learned to control
the robot with by pushing the buttons and by VPL coding with learning-by-doing and
trial and error. Every group had one laptop and one robot while being online during the
workshop. Hence, the tutors saw the students’ activities with one webcam in front of
the classroom as well as with the other webcams of the students’ laptops. The students
were able to ask for support from their teachers or the tutors in Zoom. The teachers got a
teacher training before the activity online about the session with the different exercises,
working sheets and information sheets (Fig. 4).
Fig. 4. Students’ activity in the new innovative hybrid session.

A Study About the Effects of Educational Robotics Activities
577
6.2
Results of the Case Study
In the workshop 25 students (16 girls and 9 boys) from a business high school participated
being in grade 9. Regarding previous experience, six of them already had built a robot
and 12 of them had programmed already before the workshop.
The online survey before and after the workshop was ﬁlled out by all 25 students. The
result shows a signiﬁcant positive correlation between the robotics self-efﬁcacy (RSE)
value before and after the workshop (r = .675; p = .002). However, the effect is a little
bit different by gender. The boys had a higher RSE-Score (M = 29.71, SD = 10.97)
than the girls (M = 28.08, SD = 9.3) after the workshop, but girls RSE-Score increased
more than of the boys. This difference is not signiﬁcant (F(1,16) = .368, p = .553). The
STEM interest is not signiﬁcant increased by boys (see Table 2).

Regarding the STEM career decision six students (24%) responded that they are
now more interested in studying technology than before and two students (8%) that they
are now more interested in studying informatics. Ten students (40%) responded that the
tutors were a role-model for them and eleven (44%) responded that the tutors motivated
them to have more interest in technology.
The tutor reﬂection reported that the communication between the different student
groups was successful via Zoom. The tutors supported the teachers with the exercises
for the students and had the overview about the time plan and duration of activities. The
teachers reported that the hybrid design engaged more students to work with robots than
the pure online simulation. It is a good option for learning-by-doing for the implementa-
tion of educational robotics activities in the school lessons. Teachers could discuss their
problems with activities or exercises during the workshop with the tutors. Consequently,
through the hands-on activities also the teachers learnt to use robots with their students
in the school. The students increased their problem-solving skills with robots and their
self-efﬁcacy during the hybrid educational robotics activity with the valuable support
from both the teachers and tutors.
7
Discussion and Conclusion
Educational robotics activities are proven as effective tool to foster the interest in STEM,
which is conﬁrmed by this study. It motivates young students to solve problems with
robots, to increase students’ self-efﬁcacy in the context of robotics and increase the

578
G. Jäggle et al.
interest to study in the STEM ﬁelds. These factors together increase students’ decisions
for a STEM career. The implemented educational robotics designs follow a common
didactical design using the C4STEM framework with the AVIVA model. This allows to
compare the different effects of different designs like on-site or online workshops and
the use of different robotics equipment.
Research questions RQ1 (What are the effects of on-site and online designs regard-
ing STEM career decisions?) and RQ2 (What are the effects of using different robotics
equipment regarding STEM career decisions?) were answered in Sect. 5 with the app-
roach to increase the interest to study in the STEM ﬁelds and shows that the answer is
not clear. The activities with Hedgehog had more effect in the online format than the
on-site workshops with actual robotics equipment. On the contrary, the effect of on-
site workshops with Thymio was higher than in the online workshops. These different
results conclude that further analyses should evaluate which workshop worked ﬁne for
which age group or gender group. Such information could help teachers to choose the
right robotics equipment or workshop format for their students. Research question RQ3
(What are the effects of different settings regarding gender and different age groups
pursuing STEM careers?) was answered in Sect. 4 with the approach on self-efﬁcacy.
The results show a signiﬁcant positive effect on all students and particularly with girls
and students with an age of 10 to 14 years. The results underline previous studies and
the subsequent use of educational robotics activities. Research questions RQ4 (Which
design does support schools by implementing educational robotics activities at the school
in a pandemic?) and RQ5 (How can out-of-school-institutions offer in-school activities
during a pandemic with physical equipment?) were answered in Sect. 6. The innova-
tive hybrid design offers the option to carry out educational robotics activities during a
pandemic. This hybrid design helps teachers to implement a new technology like robots
in their school lessons and helps out-of-school institutions like a university to offer
activities during a pandemic for schools.
As next step a further analysis will evaluate the suitability of different workshop
designs in regard to various age or gender groups. This should reveal especially how
the interest of girls towards STEM ﬁelds can be increased with educational robotics
activities.

Abstract. The main objective of the research is to monitor online distance instruc-
tion at the higher education level and to discover whether there were any changes
in the process within the period of 18-month period, when schools were closed
due to the covid-19 pandemic.
The ex-post-facto method was applied in the research. Data were collected
by questionnaire. In total, almost 300 (resp. 642) respondents from three institu-
tions participated in the research. Four statements were under focus: (1) Teachers
invested much effort in online distance teaching; (2) Students invested much effort
in online distance learning; (3) I appreciate online distance instruction; (4) I did
not learn much through online distance instruction. Respondents’ dis/agreement
with statements was considered on a four-level Likert. A quantitative approach
was used to calculate the frequency of occurrence of responses in single state-
ments. We anticipated that there will be both supporters and rejectors of online
distance instruction. Particular expectations are reﬂected in the responses to the
statements. However, the results are limited by the convenience of the sample and
also/mainly by the ability and willingness of the students to consider their learning
objectively, to confess whether they are able to learn autonomously, in particular,
whether they have sufﬁcient level of inner motivation to learn.
Keywords: Online distance instruction · Emergency remote teaching ·
Covid-19 · Higher education · Questionnaire · Students’ reﬂection
1
Introduction
In the Czech Republic, online distance instruction was the only way how to conduct
lessons during the covid-19 pandemic. Higher education (HE) institutions were the ﬁrst
that were closed and the last that were re-opened. In total, the closure lasted 18 months
(from March 2020 to August 2021); the ﬁrst restrictions were partially cancelled in
May 2021. At the beginning of online distance instruction, a lack of skills in how to
exploit the latest technologies for educational purposes was detected with both teachers
and students [1]. However, their digital competence and the ability to teach and learn
in the online distance environment changed step by step during the 18 months, mainly

through brief training held during summer holidays (July–August 2020) and through
gaining and sharing practical experience in online distance instruction among teachers
and among students. In addition, the process was supported by several acts, directions,
and recommendations issued by the Czech government [2, 3], the Ministry of Education
[4, 5], the Czech School Inspectorate [6, 7], and considered within the international
context [8].
This development was the focus of the research, the results of which are presented
in this paper.
2
Theoretical Background
2.1
Online Distance Instruction and Emergency Remote Teaching
The process we call online distance instruction, in reality, does not meet the deﬁnition.
For example, Britannica [9] deﬁnes distance education (using terms distance learning,
e-learning, online learning, and others as synonyms) as a form of education in which
teachers and students are physically separated during instruction and various technolo-
gies are exploited to conduct lessons student-teacher and student-student communica-
tion. Usually, students who (from any reason) are unable to attend face-to-face lessons
enroll in distance education.
Compared to Britannica, Merriam Webster Dictionary [10] deﬁnes distance learning
as a method of study. Teachers and students meet in a classroom on the Internet and
use various tools to have classes. In other words, students learn remotely, without direct
contact with teachers and peers.
In Cambridge Dictionary [11], distance learning is deﬁned as a way of studying in
which learners do not attend a school, college, or university, but study from where they
live, usually being taught and given work to do over the Internet.
In contrast, emergency remote teaching (ERT) is meant to be a temporary change
from the ‘normal’ modes of teaching. ‘Normal’ conditions disappear if a crisis occurs that
requires schools to shut down. Then, emergency remote teaching and learning appears
on the scene. ERT can be conducted using various tools, for example, lessons on radio,
television, or the Internet [12]. If we follow the above-mentioned deﬁnition, from the
view of covid-19 pandemic, emergency remote teaching should be applied. However,
in this text, the term online distance will be used as it prevails in the Central European
context [12].
2.2
Study Materials for Online Distance Instruction
In the Czech educational environment, the term distance education was deﬁned by Zla-
malova [13]. She emphasizes that distance education is mostly based on autonomous
study, when learners use study materials of special structure that support the autonomy
and help simulate face-to-face learning environment. The text should be presented in
one column having subheadings on the left and another column on the right for making
notes. Before the student starts learning, they should acquire the manual on how to study
online, that is, they should know how to work in the online environment. On the ﬁrst

582
K. Kostolanyova et al.
page of the course, the syllabus of the course and the content of the study material should
be available. At the beginning of each chapter, learning objectives should be established,
as well as skills that the student is going to acquire after learning the chapter (topic).
Each chapter should be structured into shorter paragraphs that introduce one idea in each
paragraph. Several paragraphs could be grouped into a section. In sections, open-answer
questions could be used to give learners feedback whether what they learn is correct
and provide them with further topics to think about. The ﬁnal questions that summarize
and apply new knowledge should be asked at the end of each chapter. Furthermore,
teachers can ask more personal questions to the student, and/or make comment, share
their experience, that can show the students that study materials and teachers are there
to help them and that even the teachers went through similar problems like they did.
In our opinion, no learning management system or platform can replace this structure
and a distance teacher approach. Therefore, the structure of the study material should
be followed. If it is not possible for any reason, then, the process of instruction should
not be called online distance but emergency remote teaching.
We understand that most schools were closed unexpectedly and that there was neither
time to prepare such study materials, nor to train in-service teachers and learners in using
them. We should not forget now, when the pandemic seems to be fading away, that no
one knew before spring 2020 that there would be such a need for skills in online distance
instruction and how long the instruction would be held.
2.3
Teacher Training
As mentioned above, the level of teacher and student competence in online distance
instruction was low. During the ﬁrst summer holidays within the pandemic time (July –
August 2020), Czech teachers had time to improve their skills. However, there still were
two pandemic restrictions. The courses were held in the form of international webinars;
that is, participants were expected to have a certain level of English language and dig-
ital skills. In most cases, the teachers did not meet one or both of these preconditions.
Therefore, at the end of August, when most of pandemic restrictions were cancelled,
local authorities (or colleagues in schools, which was the case in this research) organized
face-to-face courses. The course content focused on improving digital skills and imple-
mentation of didactic principles in online distance instruction. The course lasted ﬁve
days and included 20 h of work with the computer with the trainer and practical exer-
cises for homework. Every day, the participants discussed and shared their experience
face-to-face. This activity continued throughout the whole pandemic period, although
it was conducted online in MS Teams when face-to-face lessons were cancelled again.
From a didactic point of view, teachers considered these discussions to be the greatest
contribution of the training. Based on their knowledge and skills, teachers trained stu-
dents at the beginning of September 2020, when face-to-face lessons were cancelled
again and the second period of online distance instruction began.

3
Research Methodology
3.1
Research Problem, Questions, Objective
Duetotheunexpectedappearanceofthecovid-19pandemicandtheimmediateclosureof
all educational institutions in the Czech Republic, the move to online distance instruction
was interwoven with technical, technological, and didactic problems and incompetences.
Lacks in several ﬁelds were detected, for example, in hardware (HW) and software (SW)
equipment in schools and families [14], in technical and technological support to the
users so that HW and SW could be exploited to the maximum extent [15], in teachers’ and
students’ digital skills to use HW and SW for educational purposes [16], etc. Altogether,
these and other features create cornerstones of online distance instruction which is under
the focus of this research. In particular, attention was paid to teacher and student effort
devoted to online distance teaching and learning, how much students appreciated online
distance learning, and how much they learned. The main objective of the research was
to monitor how students perceive online distance instruction in higher education and to
discover whether there are any changes in the process.
3.2
Research Methods and Tools
The ex-post-facto method was applied in the research. The period of 18 months of online
distance instruction was divided into three parts as follows:
Period 1: from March 2020 to June 2020 (summer holidays in July and August 2020);
Period 2: from September 2020 to January 2021(end of the semester);
Period 3: from February 2021 to May/June 2021 according to the pandemic situation
and the teacher decision; end of semester; summer holidays in July and August 2021).
Data were collected by questionnaire. The students provided feedback on four
statements:
(1) Teachers invested much effort in online distance teaching;
(2) Students invested much effort in online distance learning;
(3) I appreciate online distance instruction;
(4) I did not learn much through online distance instruction.
Respondents expressed their agreement/disagreement with statements on a four-level
Likertscalechoosingoneoftheoptions(Fullyagree,Ratheragree,Ratherdisagree,Fully
disagree). A quantitative approach was used to calculate the frequency of occurrence of
responses in single statements.

584
K. Kostolanyova et al.
3.3
Research Sample
In total, we collected data from 642 respondents: 228 students provided feedback on
the ﬁrst period, 272 expressed their opinions on the second period, and 142 respondents
reﬂected on the third period of online distance instruction. Almost 300 respondents par-
ticipated in all periods of the investigation. They attended three higher education insti-
tutions: University of Ostrava, Faculty of Education, Department of English Language,
and Department of Information Technologies, and Advanced studies for higher medical
staff, Olomouc, Czech Republic. The sample was convenient – the authors worked as
teachers at the institutions and trainers in courses of online distance instruction there.
4
Research Results and Discussion
The research results are presented in four subchapters, each devoted to one statement.
The frequency of occurrence in each period is described and compared to other periods.
Results are displayed in Fig. 1.
4.1
Statement 1
In statement 1 Teachers invested much effort in online distance teaching, approximately
one third of respondents Fully agree and Rather agree with the statement in the ﬁrst and
second periods. In the third period, the occurrence is even higher. This result indicates
that since the very beginning of online distance instruction, students were aware that
teachers work hard despite the fact they fail in some activities and need additional
training. In other surveys, for example, Klimova et al. [17], Simonova et al. [15], students
expressed understanding of teachers’ weaknesses. In the ﬁrst and second periods, the
most appreciated advantages of online distance learning were the convenience of the
home environment for learning that lowered the stress from learning, enabled individual
pace for learning, provided students with time ﬂexibility, eliminated the need (time and
ﬁnancial expenses) for commuting, etc. At that time, the students did not feel the lack
of social contacts. They were more motivated by a new way of instruction in the ﬁrst
period. During the time, students’ appreciation of teachers’ work even increased, as we
can see in the third period.
4.2
Statement 2
In statement 2 Students invested much effort in online distance learning, the occurrence
of Rather agree in the ﬁrst period is the highest in the whole research (50%). This means
students highly appreciated their engagement in online distance instruction. Their effort
slightly decreased in the next periods (to 46% in the second period and to 41% in the
third period). However, it still remained high. In general, it should be honestly recognized
that if a student aspires to succeed in online distance instruction, their engagement (and
otherfeatures,e.g.,motivation,tenacity,etc.)mustbestrong.Theseresultswerecollected
under Rather degree, so we can speculate that there was a small group of those who did
not devote fully to online distance learning (they could be also included under Fully

Online Distance Instruction in Higher Education
585
disagree group in all periods). The question is why some students did not invest much
(enough) effort in learning. As Klimova et al. [18] mentions students’ ability to perform
self-regulated learning could be the reason. Klimova et al. focused on Czech and Slovak
students and investigated whether they are capable of achieving their learning objectives.
Their survey was conducted at the same time as the second period of our research (in
February and March 2021) and the methodology was also based on a questionnaire. Their
ﬁndings discovered a need to improve the role of teacher as facilitator who monitors the
process of learning, provides students with feedback, reviews their progress, and offers
the ways how to improve. From the view of students’ skills, Krelova et al. [19] focused on
the level of digital competence and consequent exploitation of technical aids in the times
of covid-19 pandemic. Furthermore, for example, Dvorakova et al. [20] also addressed
students’ learning experience, skills, and stress during online distance lessons. Exposure
to technologies and the impact on learning behaviour was examined by Lukavska et al.
[21]. They deﬁned prevention measures to lower the risks. On the other hand, students are
satisﬁed with online distance instruction if the teacher is adaptable to the new conditions,
has good digital skills, time management, and creativity to keep students engaged [22].
Thus, the results of several surveys create a picture of what students are expected to
know contrary to what knowledge and skills they actually have. On the basis of this
reﬂection, further student training can be designed.
Statements 1 and 2 are closely connected. Changes in one statement are reﬂected
in the other. Similar relations can be found between statements 3 and 4. Good results
(knowledge and skills) gained in online distance instruction are conditioned by appre-
ciation of the process. Of course, exceptions may appear, caused by individual learning
styles, as mentioned below.
4.3
Statement 3
In statement 3 I appreciate online distance instruction, rather similar results, that is,
positive and negative approaches to this statement were detected in the ﬁrst and second
periods. Contrary to this result, an increase in Rather disagree was found in the third
period (41%). This increase could have been caused by the length of the total time
that the online distance instruction was conducted. Students were tired of what they
had appreciated a year earlier, they were stressed by many factors, mainly by missing
social contacts, communication within the lessons, as a result that felt a lack of theoretical
knowledge and lack of practical skills, lower motivation, unability to learn autonomously
for a long period, uncertainty of how long the state can last, etc. The ﬁnding shows that
attention should be paid mainly to the home environment, teachers’ competence in online
distance teaching, and the technical support to the process [15]. Then, online distance
lessons go smoothly from the didactic point of view and students can reach learning
objectives as in the face-to face learning.
4.4
Statement 4
In statement 4 I did not learn much through online distance instruction, the results are
very similar in all periods. Frequencies of occurrence oscillate around 40% in Rather
agree and Rather disagree, and they are much lower (but similar) in other options. In

586
K. Kostolanyova et al.
other words, there is almost half of the students who learned enough through online
distance learning, and identical amount of those who did not. We can speculate about
the reasons, but, for example, lack of autonomy in learning, or lack of motivation are
frequently mentioned. Most students are aware of the need for autonomous learning,
but they are not able to learn that without the help of the teacher. Thus, they may resign
to develop this skill, and consequently, they cannot succeed in online distance learning.
They are mainly those who invest a lot of effort without any positive result [23].
Furthermore, improper learning styles could also be the reason that limited or
supported how much students learned in online distance instruction.
In Rochester Community and Technical College (n.d.) [24], they identiﬁed six
types of learners: independent, collaborative, dependent, competitive, participant, and
avoidant. They mention them in the context of online distance instruction, but they are
also applicable for face-to-face learning. Independent learners prefer to work alone, at
their own pace. They study what is important to them, not to the teacher. They like to
develop their own ideas about how lessons should be conducted. Due to their autonomy
and self-motivation, they do well in online learning. However, the teacher should check
from time to time whether they follow lesson (course) plans. Collaborative learners pre-
fer to work in groups, to discuss, they like class sessions and are willing to help others.
Similarly to independent learners, they also do well in online distance learning. They
prefer online interaction activities (mainly discussions, chats) compared to face-to-face.
Dependent learners wait for teacher’s decision on course (test) requirements, then follow
them precisely. If there is a lack of directions, they are frustrated. Competitive learners
compete with other students for teachers’ attention, they aim to get a good grade (and are
able to ﬁght for it), they target to be the best student, or solve problems before others. So
that not to embarrass the others, it is preferred competitive learners should compete with
themselves. Participant learners do not avoid personal responsibility, they ﬁnd online
learning interesting and worth attending. They complete tasks before deadlines and also
do extra work willingly. Contrary to them, avoidant learners do not like to attend online
lessons because they ﬁnd them boring, useless, and time consuming. To succeed, they
need to have a serious success strategy that makes them concentrated on learning. For
both participant and avoidant learners, GPS LifePlan may help (GPS: Goal + Plan =
Success).
4.5
Limits of the Research
The research results are mainly limited by the sample that was convenient for the research
team. Furthermore, in the third period, the sample was half-sized compared to the ﬁrst
and second ones. As the participation in the research was voluntary, this feature may
indicate lower willingness of the students to work with digital materials, in this case, to
ﬁll in the questionnaire. A similar approach could be observed in relation to everything
‘computer-mediate’, that is, students were sick of activities led through technologies and
longed for face-to-face contacts, not only in education.

5
Conclusion
As expected, there were supporters and rejectors of online distance instruction. As proved
in our research, advocates for both sides are in equilibrium. However, due to the fact
that covid-19 (or another) pandemic may appear repeatedly, we consider it beneﬁcial
for teachers and learners of all school levels to acquire didactic principles of online
distance instruction. If there is no reason for future school closure, some features can be
implemented in blended learning strategies and used for learning in the ‘normal’, non-
pandemic era. This approach should be applied in all ﬁelds of engineering pedagogy so
that experience gained with so many difﬁculties is not wasted.

Work-in-Progress: Exploring
Psychological and Behavioural Diﬀerences
Between University IT Student Segments
Formed Based on Dropout Time
and Academic Performance
Eerik Sven Puudist1(B), Ago Luberg1, and Kati Aus2
1 Tallinn University of Technology, Tallinn, Estonia
eerik.sven@gmail.com, ago.luberg@taltech.ee
2 Tallinn University, Tallinn, Estonia
katiaus@tlu.ee
Abstract. This research project investigates the role of self-regulated
learning competencies and other psychological factors in the dropout
times and academic performance of students on their ﬁrst semester at
university in a programming course. The students were broken into seven
segments based on their dropout times and study outcomes. The psy-
chological and behavioural diﬀerences between the segments were inves-
tigated. It was found that students who leave at the beginning of the
course, who leave after a negative test result, and who fail the ﬁnal exam
have diﬀerent psychological proﬁles and require diﬀerent kinds of sup-
port. Based on that, suggestions were given for decreasing dropout rates
and increasing academic performance.
Keywords: Learning analysis · University dropout · Self-regulated
learning · Machine learning · Segmentation
1
Introduction
The high university dropout rate, particularly in the ﬁeld of information technol-
ogy, is a pressing problem in higher education. In Estonia up to 32% of students
quit their studies already at their ﬁrst year [1, p 3].
A common reason for resigning in programming related courses is the accu-
mulation of small gaps in apprehending the subject which makes it hard for the
student to keep up with the pace of the studies. How well the student is able to
handle such a backlog depends depends largely on their self-regulated learning
competencies [2] e.g., their adaptive beliefs, motivation, and study strategies.
The problems leading to the student quitting their studies thus begins long
before they become apparent to the teacher and once the problems have already
developed that far, the right timeframe for supporting the student might already
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 590–596, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_62

591
be over. This issue is especially topical with bigger group sizes where the teacher
does not have the opportunity to personally monitor each student. Especially
during a pandemic situation when study in the classrooms is not possible, it
might take several weeks before the teacher recognises that a student is not
participating anymore.
It is therefore essential that the students in the risk group could be identiﬁed
in advance so that they could receive special mentoring and support throughout
the course. That mentoring could help the student to obtain the necessary under-
standings and study strategies to be successful on the course. If the complexity
level of the course exceeds the student’s capacity or if the student recognises that
this subject is too far from their real ﬁeld of interest, the mentoring program
could help them to ﬁnd a curriculum which aligns better with their interests and
abilities so that failure in the given curriculum would not cause the student to
give up their academic pursuits.
Fruitful research for implementing a binary classiﬁer for identifying the stu-
dents with higher dropout risk for similar courses has already been conduced,
such as [3]. However, this project aims to identify more nuanced student seg-
ments, since both the risk group and the better performing group are very het-
erogeneous with diﬀerent segments needing very diﬀerent approaches from the
teacher.
This research is part of a joint project of Tallinn University of Technology and
Tallinn University for developing a more personalised approach to programming
courses, where psychological diﬀerences and various backgrounds of the students
could be taken into consideration to help each student to derive most value from
the course.
2
Methods
The research is based on the data regarding the “ITI0102 Introduction to Pro-
gramming” course (hereinafter referred to as “the course”) taught in Tallinn
University of Technology at the fall of 2021. The aim of the course is to give an
overview of programming in Python language assuming no prior experience. For
the majority of the students the course is taught on the ﬁrst semester of their
studies.
2.1
Measured Features
The following sets of features were measured:
– Information about the student: age, gender;
– Information about the studies: curriculum, form of study (daily vs session),
whether the given course is compulsory;
– Study
motivation
based
on
achievement
goals
theory
[4]
and
self-
determination theory [5];
– Beliefs and mindsets based on implicit beliefs theory [6,7];
– social and emotional aspects related to studying [8,9];
– study strategies [10–14].

592
E. S. Puudist et al.
2.2
Data Sources
The data was collected from a variety of sources:
– General information regarding the student and their studies from the study
information system ˜OIS;
– Psychological factors survey (hereinafter referred to as “the survey”);
– Homework submission logs;
– Course chat messages;
– Data from plagiarism detection service.
The survey consisted of 87 questions regarding self-regulated learning compe-
tencies, prior programming experience, and problem-solving abilities. The survey
will be published as a separate paper.
The students took the survey on the ﬁrst week of the semester, thus it reﬂects
primarily their general tendencies and predispositions, not their experiences with
the speciﬁc course. Taking the survey was not compulsory. From the 376 students
who declared the course 264 took the survey and gave the permission for using
the data for research.
The majority of the exercises on the course where programming tasks with
automated tests. While the student was solving the exercise, they could submit it
to the test system as many times as they wanted and use the automatic feedback
to enhance their solution. The homework submission logs can thus be used to
estimate when and for how long the student was solving each exercise.
The course had a dedicated Discord server where the students could ask for
help for solving the exercises. There were also separate channels for extracurric-
ular communication such as sharing programming-related jokes.
2.3
Software and Algorithms
The scientiﬁc Python stack, most notably pandas [15], was used for the analysis.
Scikit-learn [16] was used for calculating feature importance. The hierarchical
clustering module1 from SciPy [17] was used for drawing dendrograms. The plots
were created with Matplotlib [18].
3
Results
Based on the dropout time and study outcome students where divided into seven
segments:
– above avg dropout – students who resigned although their study results
were close to or above the course average;
– early dropout – students who dropped out before the bigger test on the
10th study week;

– post test dropout – students who dropped out directly after the test, usu-
ally after receiving a negative grade;
– late dropout – students who dropped out later, but still before the exam;
– failed exam – those who did not pass the exam;
– mediocre results those who ﬁnished with mediocre results (grades 1–3);
– excellent results – those who ﬁnished with excellent results

That the students who leave despite their good study results are very similar
to the students who ﬁnish with excellent results: both are very active in the
Discord chat and put time into solving the harder exercises. However, the leavers
group contains more members for whom the course is not compulsory and who
do not have prior programming experience and their average age is higher.
The early dropout group consists primarily of people without prior program-
ming experience. Moreover, they have very little interest in the subject, high
burnout, and very low perceived autonomy support.
Students who leave after receiving a negative test result have problems with
task avoidance and procrastination. However, their math exam results and prior
programming experience are both above average and higher than for any other
group who did not pass the course. Thus, it seems that they would have potential

Psychological and Behavioural Diﬀerences Between IT Student Segment
595
to complete the course if they would receive support for ﬁxing the issues with
task avoidance and procrastination.
Most people who fail the exam are starting without prior programming expe-
rience. They seem to be very diligent people as they start early with the exercises
and have participated on olympiades during school time, but they have a lot of
ineﬃcient strategies and low intrinsic regulation.
The group with mediocre results already has some prior programming expe-
rience, but they do not develop as far as they could as they are bounded by a
relatively ﬁxed mindset. The group with excellent results could possibly perform
even better if they had learned eﬃcient study strategies and developed a more
growth-oriented mindset.
4
Discussion
Although the course is designed for people without any prior programming expe-
rience, even a little prior experience turned out to greatly increase the probability
of passing the course. It can be speculated that there is so much novelty for the
student on their ﬁrst semester at the university that it is hard to keep up with a
course with such high pace. Since simplifying the course is not an option for the
knowledge is required for subsequent programming courses, it might be useful to
suggest the students to go through some online introductory materials regarding
programming in Python in their own pace before the course starts.
The study showed that psychological factors have a strong inﬂuence on the
students’ dropout rates and study outcomes and that students with ﬁxed mindset
and tendencies for task avoidance and procrastination are likely to quit the course
even though their mathematical abilities are suﬃcient.
The students are already receiving some psychological coaching in terms of
self-regulated learning on their ﬁrst semester, but that does not seem to be
suﬃcient. Further research is required to explore that deﬁciency in detail, but
it can be assumed that the students do not develop the ability to apply what
has been taught in real life. Such training should therefore be integrated into
the programming course itself. That would be especially necessary after students
have received a negative test result and when they are most likely to resign.
The most capable students would also need more psychological training as
they could achieve even more if they were introduced to eﬃcient study strategies
and if they could become more conscious of their beliefs and motivations.

Alena Hašková1(B), Dominik Zatkalík1,2, and Martin Zatkalík2

Abstract. The ever-increasing pace of innovation and technological change in the
automotive industry has a signiﬁcant impact on car sales and after-sales services.
Ability to respond quickly to the relevant changes and innovations becomes an
imperativeinbothsalesandafter-salesservices.Relatedtothisistheneedtoensure
adequate training of employees for the given sector. In this context, the authors
of the article analyze possibilities of innovation and development strategies for
the study branches Transport and Automotive Service and Repair in focus on a
selected Upper Secondary Vocational School located in Bratislava, which is one
of the important providers of vocational education and training of labor forces
for transport and transport services in Slovakia. Main results of their analyses are
summarized in SWOT and STEPE tables.
Keywords: Secondary vocational schools · Vocational education and training ·
Study branches Transport and Automotive Service and Repair · Innovation and
development factors
1
Introduction
Phenomenon of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, so-called Industry 4.0, represents for
the national economies one of the most signiﬁcant challenges for creating development
strategies for the next time-periods. The platform for innovative solutions to this phe-
nomenon is development and use of advanced technologies with a strong emphasis on
the digitization of all areas and processes of the national economy but also the social life.
According to experts, technological development within the framework of the Fourth
Industrial Revolution differs qualitatively in three respects compared to the previous
development [1, 2]:
• exponentiality of progress in the development of information and communication
technologies (increasing operating speeds, cost and energy efﬁciency),
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 597–606, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_63

598
A. Hašková et al.
• expanding digitization (digitization of all spheres of economic and social life, creation
and subsequent use of digital data),
• recombinability of innovation (innovation in materials, biological and digital tech-
nologies).
It is logical that the Fourth Industrial Revolution will have a signiﬁcant impact on the
labor market. The most important barriers to the implementation of the Fourth Industrial
Revolution are the capital intensity of the technological background, the transition to
fully automated production, the creation of IoT (Internet of Things) network, and security
of data exchange between suppliers and customers, including competitors, within IoT.
Another major problem often highlighted is labor shortages. The determining factor that
will enable active participation in the processes of the Fourth Industrial Revolution will
be an educated workforce in ﬁelds such as information and communication technologies,
manufacturing, engineering, automation, digitization of services [3, 4]. The upcoming
demands of the labor market should be reﬂected in the environment of education, not
only in the environment of higher education institutions like universities but also in lower
levels of education, especially in the environment of secondary vocational schools and
vocational education and training, as training of professionals for work in Industry 4.0
begins at primary schools and then continues at secondary schools.
Even though Europe today has one of its most highly qualiﬁed cohorts of young
graduates entering the labor market, high skill mismatches undermine economic com-
petitiveness and growth, sustain unemployment and high social insurance costs and affect
social inclusion [5, 6]. Skills hold the key to higher productivity growth for Europe and
are crucial for overcoming declining living standards due to the shrinking future work-
force [7]. EU countries characterized by higher levels of competitiveness and dynamic
labor markets generally do not only invest in education and training (both initial and
continuing), but also in skills maintenance in the workplace [6]. Cedefop’s research [8,
9] has paid much attention to the education, training and development strategies that can
help mitigate skill mismatch for both individuals (employees) and enterprises (employ-
ers). At the same time the research showed that despite Europe has highly qualiﬁed
graduates entering the labor market, even 31% of the survey respondents whose current
job was their ﬁrst (and 27% of those who were in education or training before they
started their current job) declared that their skills were lower than required when they
started. This is signiﬁcantly higher than the average incidence of underskilling at job
entry for the whole sample (22%) and conﬁrms that a signiﬁcant share of people making
the transition from school to the labor market do not possess the level of maturity in
their skills required by their jobs.
The main industry in Slovakia is the automotive, engineering and electrical engi-
neering industries. As far as the automotive industry is concerned, in the context of
the Industry 4.0 phenomenon there are expected signiﬁcant changes due to the intro-
duction of alternative forms of propulsion (electromobility, hydrogen-powered engines)
and the development of autonomous driving. Today, the largest automotive companies
already have a signiﬁcant proportion of electric cars or hybrid vehicles in their prod-
uct portfolios. As many as 90 of all innovations in the automotive industry today come
from the electrical engineering industry, which generates 35% to 40% of vehicle value
[10]. Today, megatrends in automotive production are described by several experts and

Vocational Education and Training in Context of Industry 4.0
599
by the automotive companies themselves as a transformation to the ACES model (A -
autonomous management, C - connectivity, E - electromobility, S - shared mobility ser-
vices). These megatrends inﬂuencing the further development of the concerned industry
name the basic assumptions of the development, when up to 8 of the 10 largest vehicle
producers are going to develop autonomous vehicles. According to McKinsey surveys
[11], the number of customers willing to change the car brand in the near future for better
connectivity has doubled. A major technological change will be autonomous vehicles,
which can potentially be more efﬁcient and safer than conventional vehicles, reducing
congestion, emissions and changing existing transport and logistics models [12, 13]. As
early as 2012, Nevada was the ﬁrst state in the United States to pass a law allowing
(autonomous) driving without a driver [14].
2
Background of the Case Study
The ever-increasing pace of innovation and technological changes in the automotive
industry has a signiﬁcant impact on car sales and after-sales service. The imperative in
both sales and after-sales service is the ability to respond quickly to relevant changes
and innovations. The pace of innovation in the technical ﬁeld brings with it the need to
know how to respond quickly to these changes. We are already seeing several trends in
the area of vehicle sales and service, which will be marked by signiﬁcant changes in the
next decade:
• decline of traditional service procedures - fewer service interventions for electric cars,
• autonomous driving - poorly set assistance systems will directly endanger the safety
of the crew after the vehicle has been repaired,
• remote access to vehicle repair by the manufacturer - fewer service visits, more repairs
and settings of the vehicle by the manufacturer or the manufacturer’s representative
can do it remotely by software,
• repairs of vehicles after accidents - the need to use the manufacturer’s techni-
cal procedures - multimaterial bodies - AHSS, UHSS and PHSS steels, composite
materials,
• block exemption valid until 2023 - withdrawal of factory representations of manufac-
turers and gradual transition to the model of direct sale of vehicles online,
• shared mobility - the demand for a cheap, accessible and practical form of transport.
Content and focus of vocational education and training (VET) at secondary voca-
tional schools for the sales and after-sales services segment must correspond to the
current state of innovation and technology. Formal education at secondary schools is
deﬁned by school curriculum state education programs, which schools transform into
school curriculum of education programs in the context of regional needs. School cur-
riculum contains educational areas and speciﬁc subjects of theoretical general education
and professional character and practical subjects.
The purpose of a quality VET system is to eliminate or reduce the differences that
exist between the current and the required state in the performance of work activities.
The most common issues identiﬁed are [15–18]:

600
A. Hašková et al.
• the quality of the work performance of the employee or group of employees, (use of
equipment and technology),
• speciﬁc gaps in knowledge (knowledge of current theories),
• imperfections of the current level of theoretical qualiﬁcation training (interest in
supplementing education and certiﬁcation).
One of the providers of vocational education and training of labor forces for trans-
port and transport services is Upper Secondary Vocational School for Transport in
Bratislava. The school prepares graduates directly for practice [19, 20], while a part
of them continues in their studies at universities, mainly those with technical and trafﬁc
orientation.

The school and its staff take up the challenges of arming its students with relevant
