3
Methodology of the Case Study and Its Results
The processed case study was to be focused on the possibilities of developing the study
programs Transport and Automotive Service and Repair in the context of Industry 4.0.
Focus of the case study was at SWOT analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of
the possibility of school development in the context of Industry 4.0. Elaboration of the
SWOT analysis was based on the assessment of the content of education provided within
the given study programs, personnel and material provision of the provided education,
and vocational training carried out within the given two study programs.
In terms of the content of education, the school adapts curricula to the needs of stu-
dents by increasing efﬁciency between subject relationships, linking theory with practice
and preparing students for real life conditions. The content of education of the particular
study and programs is thoroughly prepared in accordance with the State Educational Pro-
grams. The school supports professional development of teachers and students through
training, conferences, seminars and other educational activities. Work of teachers is
coordinated through the subject committee of general education subjects and the subject
committee of vocational subjects and practical training. Further education of the school’s

602
A. Hašková et al.
pedagogical staff takes place in the form of adaptive, continuous, innovative and func-
tional education. As to the students, they acquire theoretical knowledge, but above all
practical skills. The school puts great emphasis on students‘ personality development,
on formation of their personal and professional qualities, attitudes and value orienta-
tion. During their studies, students spend signiﬁcantly more time on practical vocational
training either in school workshops, or directly in companies, where they are preparing
for the tasks they will be face in practice. In practical teaching, students acquire skills
and work habits, become acquainted with the organization of work in the workplace.
Vocational training is carried out either in school workshops or in contract or dual work-
places throughout the territory of Bratislava and in catchment areas on productive works,
which are rewarded with a ﬁnancial reward.
Regarding the stafﬁng of vocational education and training, the professional ped-
agogical and lecturer stafﬁng is 22% with 3rd degree of higher education, 11% with
international IGIP certiﬁcation, 61% with 2nd degree of higher education and 100%
of vocational masters trained in the relevant ﬁelds. The school cooperates with external
lecturers ZAP SR, CPA SR and importers of motor vehicles, repair and diagnostic equip-
ment. The school uses textbooks and teaching materials approved and recommended by
the Ministry of Education, Science, Research and Sport of the Slovak Republic and pub-
lishes its own textbooks, worksheets and methodological manuals. Accommodation of
students is provided within the accommodation capacities of Bratislava self-governing
region.
The school closely cooperates with unions, professional and vocational organiza-
tions. It is an active member of Automotive Industry Association of the Slovak Repub-
lic, Association of Logistics and Forwarding of the Slovak Republic, Union of Trans-
port, Posts and Telecommunications of the Slovak Republic, Association of Employers’
Unions and Associations of the Slovak Republic, Association of Secondary Vocational
Schools of Slovakia, Dealers and Car Repair Guilds of the Slovak Republic, Slovak
Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
Cooperation with strategic employers within the private sector is carried out with 32
major employers in system of dual education and 89 employers in the system of contract
workplaces, with emphasis on current labor market requirements.
Material and technical equipment of the Upper Secondary Vocational School of
Transport in Bratislava for the given study branches is according to the mandatory
norms of the Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports of the Slovak Republic. The
school is equipped with compulsory and recommended spatial, material and technical
equipment. The equipment has been gradually innovated since 2017 with modern car
repair technologies and ICT technologies.
As the SWOT analysis assesses in external factors only opportunities and threats, in
additiontotheSWOTanalysis,therewasusedalsotheSTEPEanalysisofexternalfactors
which provides a more accurate view on the given issue at the level of social, technolog-
ical, economical, political and environmental factors with assignment of development
forecasts (trends) and expected impact.

4
Conclusion
In order to ensure that there are enough experts for Industry 4.0, a number of important
changes need to be made in education. It is important to emphasize not only the educa-
tional process, but also the motivation of teachers and students, as well as the integration
of students into the industrial environment and increasing their interest in the professions
needed for Industry 4.0. In this context, we perceive the connection between schools and
industrial practice in dual education very positively.

Teachers’ Digital Literacy as a Prerequisite
for Technology-Enhanced Teaching
Ján Záhorec1(B), Alena Hašková2, and Ján Gunˇcaga1
1 Faculty of Education, Comenius University in Bratislava, Bratislava, Slovak Republic
{zahorec,guncaga}@fedu.uniba.sk
2 Faculty of Education, Constantine the Philosopher University in Nitra, Nitra, Slovak Republic
ahaskova@ukf.sk
Abstract. Teachers’ digital literacy is an essential prerequisite for them to be able
to use technology-enhanced teaching effectively in their pedagogical practice. In
2018, the National Institute of Certiﬁed Educational Measurements of the Slo-
vak Republic launched the PIAAC – Programme for the International Assessment
of Adult Competencies project, which includes research on key cognitive and
non-cognitive competences, reading, mathematical and digital literacy of teach-
ers working at the ISCED 2 level of education – PIAAC online. Teachers’ digital
literacy is deﬁned as a set of problem-solving skills using information and com-
munication technologies that teachers need for their full-ﬂedged employment in
modern society. The authors present in this article a preview of the main results of
the PIAAC-online project focusing speciﬁcally on teachers’ digital literacy. The
presented ﬁndings of the project conﬁrm a strong correlation between the teachers’
level of ICT usage in their personal and professional life.
Keywords: Digital literacy · Technology-enhanced teaching · Teacher
competences · PIAAC online
1
Introduction
According to the OECD’s Future of Education and Skills 2030, skills generally refer to
people’s abilities and their capacity to perform certain processes. They are essentially
the ability to use acquired knowledge to achieve a goal, which is done. As part of a
holistic concept of competences, they involve the linking of knowledge, attitudes and
values and enable people to cope with the more complex demands of society. Cognitive
skills refer to reading literacy, mathematics literacy, and the ability to solve problems
in a technologically advanced environment using information and communication tech-
nologies. These cognitive skills are key information processing competences that are
relevant for adults in many social contexts and work situations. They are essential for
full integration and participation in the labour market, in education and training, and in
full participation in social and civic life [1].
According to Blömeke and Delaney [2], the level of teachers’ cognitive skills is
one of the essential elements of teachers’ appropriate pedagogical competence. The
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 607–616, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_64

608
J. Záhorec et al.
OECD [3], in its publication on adult skills, states that the level of cognitive skills is
also shaped and developed depending on how often people use these skills in everyday
life. It is generally assumed that, if the people more often do at work or in their private
live mathematical tasks and calculations, read or analyse different texts or use digital
technologies (i.e., solve different tasks using software applications), then their level of
cognitive skills is higher. A research study by Hanushek, Piopiunik and Wiederhold [4]
conﬁrms that teachers’ cognitive skills are an important factor in explaining students’
academic performance and are directly related to each other. The authors point to the
fact that pupils of those teachers who achieved high levels of cognitive skills scored
higher on international measures (PISA) of reading, science, and mathematics literacy.
The fact that higher reading and mathematics literacy of teachers was related to better
student performance in reading and mathematics is conﬁrmed in their studies by Meroni,
Vera-Toscano and Costa [5].
The results of the OECD’s large-scale research project Innovative Teaching for Effec-
tive Learning (ITEL), which (among other research strands) has been devoted to a
broad-based investigation of the pedagogical knowledge of student teachers and prac-
tising teachers, have highlighted the research respondents’ reserves in this area. In the
intentions of the project implementation, general pedagogical knowledge and skills were
perceived as professional competencies enhancing teachers’ professional status and pro-
fessionalism [6]. The project output publication states that in the pilot testing, Slovak
teachers and student teachers scored low in all tested dimensions of pedagogical knowl-
edge. Based on these facts, the National Institute of Certiﬁed Educational Measurements
of the Slovak Republic (hereinafter referred to as NUCEM) started in 2018 to implement
the national project Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competen-
cies (hereinafter referred to as PIAAC), which includes research on key cognitive and
non-cognitive competencies of pedagogical and professional staff of regional education
in Slovakia PIAAC online.
2
Assessing of Teachers’ Digital Literacy in the Context of Their
Cognitive Competences
2.1
Methodology of the Project PIAAC Online
The project Education and Skills online (PIAAC Online) focuses on the reading, mathe-
matics and digital literacy of teachers working at ISCED 2 level of education. Teachers’
digital literacy is deﬁned as a set of problem-solving skills using information and com-
munication technologies that teachers need for their full participation in modern society.
In contrast to the international PIAAC adult survey, the research sample of the PIAAC
online project is not representative, but only available, and it is focused exclusively on
teaching and professional staff in schools. The project is implemented in order to obtain
objective feedback on the level of cognitive skills of teachers of lower secondary educa-
tion (ISCED 2), which in Slovakia is the second level of the so-called primary schools
and the ﬁrst four years of grammar schools with an eight-year educational programme.
The aim of the research was to assess the competency proﬁles of primary school
teachers (lower secondary level, hereafter referred to as primary school teachers) aged

Teachers’ Digital Literacy as a Prerequisite
609
up to 65 years. A total of 958 teachers at primary schools and the corresponding grades
of grammar schools with an eight-year education programme (OGY) were involved in
the research in two successive phases. In November 2018, the ﬁrst phase of respondent
testing was conducted, in which over 2 000 lower secondary teachers were contacted (all
primary schools and OGYs from TALIS and PISA projects were contacted), of which
666 expressed interests in participating, while later in May 2019, in order to increase
the number of participating teachers, a further wave of data collection was conducted, in
which 292 teachers expressed interest in participating in the online testing. The research
sample covered the whole territory of Slovakia, but is not representative (composition
of the research sample: 958 respondents, including teachers of primary schools and the
relevant grades of grammar schools with an eight-year education programme (79%),
teaching assistants (8%), professional staff (6%) and principals (8%); of the 958 respon-
dents, 16% were male and 84% were female; average age of males was 40, average age
of females was 42).
To provide an objective picture of teachers’ use of the mentioned cognitive skills both
in their professional practice and in their private life, the answers to partial questions of
research investigations of the following type were to be provided:
• how often teachers read or analyse different texts,
• how often teachers perform various mathematical operations and calculations,
• how often teachers search for and evaluate relevant information using ICT, and how
often they use software applications or tools when they work with information.
The partial issues mentioned above correspond to reading, mathematical and digital
literacy, as a basis for the development of more complex skills and competences, which
are necessary for solving various tasks in working or private life. The items in each of the
three domains (literacy, mathematics, and digital literacy) of the PIAAC online survey
are based on the items of the ﬁrst cycle of PIAAC 2012 testing.
A questionnaire entitled People’s Use of Skills at Home and Work, compiled by
experts in psychometrics and test design, was used to collect the research data. Respon-
dents answered each questionnaire item through responses scaled from very infrequent
to everyday usage. The range of points (scores) that respondents could obtain in rating
the respective individual cognitive skills was 0–500 points. Within that range, the levels
of each cognitive knowledge and skill (the knowledge and skills required to complete
the tasks within that level, each level being deﬁned to include more complex tasks as
the level increases) were determined.
2.2
Research Results of the PIAAC Online Project and Their Discussion
Based on the results of descriptive statistics measuring the level of cognitive skills, the
sample of teachers participating in the PIAAC online project research can be described as
cognitively superior. Most teachers scored favourably in the cognitive domains studied,
which were not statistically different between males and females.
It canbeseenfromTable 1, that inreadingliteracyalmost 53%of theteachers reached
the third – average – level and just over 24% reached the fourth and ﬁfth skill levels.
In comparison, 17% of the Slovak higher education population reached the fourth and

J. Záhorec et al.
ﬁfth – highest – skill levels in the ﬁrst cycle of PIAAC testing in 2012 [7]. In mathematical
literacy, almost 44% of teachers reached the third skill level and up to 48% of teachers
reached the highest, i.e., the fourth and ﬁfth skill levels. A sample of 30.2% of the
higher-educated population in Slovakia reached the fourth and ﬁfth – the highest – skill
levels in the ﬁrst cycle of PIAAC testing in 2012 [7]. Almost 58% of teachers ranked
in the ability to solve problems using ICT (on a scale of levels up to 3) at the second
level and less than 9% of teachers reached the highest third level of digital skills. In the
1st cycle of the PIAAC Adult Competency Testing 2012, 8.6% of the higher education
population in Slovakia ranked at the highest, third level of digital skills [7].

The ﬁndings of a positive correlation of mathematical and reading literacy with the
ability to solve problems using ICT for the whole research sample of teachers, i.e., with-
out their differentiation into groups due to the segmentation factor of age and gender,
are important, as reading, and mathematical literacy form the basis for the development
of more complex cognitive skills (analytical thinking, processing information from dif-
ferent contexts, problem solving, etc.). The data presented in Table 2 show that a high
correlation is identiﬁed between the literacy domains studied, with correlation coefﬁ-
cient values ranging from 0.5 to 0.69. The results from the PIAAC online measurement
correspond with the results obtained at the international level of the PIAAC 2012 mea-
surement, when it was shown in both measurements carried out that the level of reading
and mathematical literacy is directly related to the ability to solve problems using ICT
[3]. The higher the respondents’ scores in reading and mathematical literacy brings the
higher their scores in ICT problem-solving ability. Developing problem-solving skills
using ICT can have a positive impact on reading and mathematical literacy levels and
vice versa. In developing teachers’ cognitive skills, it is important to consider com-
prehensive development so that the transfer of information and knowledge to pupils is
also more effective and so that teachers could apply progressive pedagogical trends and
methods (see Table 2).

The authors of the ﬁnal report of the PIAAC online measurements state [8] that
the results of the respondents – teachers involved in the PIAAC online study in reading
literacy were comparable to the university-educated population in Slovakia from the ﬁrst
cycle of the PIAAC 2012 study, but the results in mathematical literacy and problem-
solving skills with the use of ICT of the involved teachers (T) were signiﬁcantly better
than the university-educated (UE) respondents in Slovakia from the ﬁrst cycle of the
PIAAC 2012 study, in all age categories (Table 3). It is important according to the
authors of the above ﬁnal report by interpreting the data, to consider that more than half
of the participating teachers (51%) taught one of the subjects of mathematics, computer
science, science, so they have a stronger inclination towards digital online tools, are more
likely to meet electronic tests and thus have a better chance of solving test questions and
tasks more effectively.
This may have inﬂuenced their better performance in mathematical literacy and
ICT problem-solving skills compared to the college-educated population from PIAAC
2012 Cycle 1. In terms of the relevance of the comparative analysis, it will be more
interesting to compare the data with future data from PIAAC Cycle 2, PIAAC 2023,
with a representative sample of teachers created with random selection.
The assumption regarding age differences, that teachers in the younger age group
(25–34 years) would exhibit the highest level of cognitive skills, as manifested in the
analyses of adults in the representative sample of PIAAC 2012 Cycle 1, was not con-
ﬁrmed.Conversely,olderteachersaged45–54yearsappearedtohavesigniﬁcantlyhigher
mathematical literacy scores than teachers of age under 35 years (Table 3). The scores
achieved in reading and mathematical literacy by teachers of older ages did not show
a decreasing trend; thus, the measurements did not conﬁrm a negative effect of age-
ing on these cognitive skills. The authors of the ﬁnal report conclude that this may be
inﬂuenced by several years of practice and experience, continuous teacher education, as
well as intensive usage of teachers’ skills both in private and professional life [8]. The
fact that younger teachers (25–34 years old) did not reach higher levels in reading and
mathematical literacy than their older colleagues (45–54 years old) indicate a low level
of intergenerational acceleration.
It can be a result from the poor efﬁciency of the education system, which for Slovakia
raises the need to improve the quality of pre-service training and teacher motivation,
which is closely linked to the social and ﬁnancial evaluation of teachers. A tabulation

of test scores in the literacy domains under study (Table 3) shows that teachers in the
youngest age category (25–34 years) scored signiﬁcantly better than older teachers (44–
54 years) in the cognitive skills measurement only in the ICT problem-solving skills,
which corresponds with the results of the PIAAC 2012 measurement reported by the
OECD in its publication on adult skills [3]. It is possible to argue that the use of digital
means in solving various problems is a phenomenon dominant for the younger popu-
lation, which is conﬁrmed by the results in the PIAAC 2012 Cycle 1 testing, in which
people aged 55 and over showed a low level of experience in using ICT.
Another of the partial objectives of the PIAAC online research was to ask teachers
to what extent they use digital didactic tools (ICT) in their teaching and to approach the
factors that determine or inﬂuence the usage of these technologies by teachers in their
teaching practice. The Supplementary Attitudinal Questionnaire was used for inquiry in
this area, which was based in content and structure on the 2018 OECD TALIS interna-
tional teacher survey [9] and included questions such as: Has the use of ICT in teaching
been part of your formal education? To what extent did you feel prepared to use ICT
in teaching? To what extent do you feel the need for further training in ICT skills?
How often do you have pupils use ICT for projects or classroom work? Have ICT skills
in teaching been a part of any further training you have attended? The sample of 958
teachers were surveyed. 76% of these teachers had formal training as part of their under-
graduate professional training in the use of digital didactic technologies in teaching or
had practical experience, with 58% rating themselves as adequately prepared to use skills
with digital didactic tools in their teaching activities [8]. Despite the fact, that in-service
training activities in which the teachers involved in the research had recently participated
included topics such as the application of skills in the use of ICT in the classroom, 65%
of these teachers expressed a relatively high level of need for further training in the appli-
cation of digital didactic tools in the classroom. Participating teachers who scored lower
on the measurement in reading, mathematical and digital literacy expressed a higher
need for further training in the application of skills with digital didactic tools in their
teaching activities. Teachers, who had completed in-service training activities on the use

Teachers’ Digital Literacy as a Prerequisite
613
of ICT skills in teaching, said that the activities provided them with opportunities to
put new ideas and knowledge into practice (85%), to learn actively (78%) and to apply
innovations in teaching their disciplines (83%). It corresponds with the ﬁndings reported
in the OECD TALIS study [9] that teacher education has a positive impact on the quality
of teaching as well as higher levels of teacher job satisfaction.
Teaching strategies practiced by teachers in their pedagogical activities have been
the central interest of several researches dealing with the issue of innovative trends in
the didactics of teaching subjects, since effective teaching practices are an important
prerequisite for achieving better learning outcomes for students [10–12]. Among teach-
ing methods aimed at activating cognitive processes, i.e., processes that require students
to evaluate, integrate and apply knowledge in a problem-solving context, the highest
proportion of teachers involved in the PIAC online project (65%) assign students critical
thinking tasks. A third of teachers (37%) reported that they use a variety of teaching
strategies, methods, or other resources to stimulate students’ cognitive processes. Of
the teaching methods that allow pupils to work independently during the lesson, e.g.,
solving problems using ICT skills or working on long-term projects, a large majority of
teachers (59%) let pupils use ICT during the lesson and only a ﬁfth (21%) of teachers
assign pupils to long-term projects.
The measuring the level of development of cognitive skills of primary school teachers
was not only the one goal of the project PIAAC online. This project also measured
the extent to which teachers use the cognitive skills surveyed in their personal and
professional lives. The usage of skills in private and work life includes 8 activities
namely reading at home, reading at work; writing at home, writing at work; calculations
at home, calculations at work and ﬁnally use of ICT at home and use of ICT at work.
The extent of implementation of the above activities was assessed through a response
scale of low extent, medium extent, and high extent. According to the results of the
PIAAC online measurement, the activities implemented by teachers are most associated
with reading at work and writing at home [8]. This result corresponds with the nature
and nature of the teaching profession and is partly in line with the results of the PIAAC
2012 international measurement [3], which also showed that on average people use
writing and reading most often at work, while performing calculations and using ICT
are less frequent activities. When looking at the statistical signiﬁcance of differences in
the frequency of writing, reading, computing and ICT use in problem solving between
private and work life, it was found that teachers are more likely to write at home than at
work, statistically signiﬁcantly more likely to use ICT in private life than at work, and
also signiﬁcantly more likely to do computations at home than at work. Only reading
is done statistically signiﬁcantly more often at work than at home. Of all the activities
observed, teachers do calculations at work least often.
In terms of intersex differences, men’s and women’s responses to questions on the
usage of the above cognitive skills in private and work life differed statistically signiﬁ-
cantly only in the use of ICT for problem solving. Based on the results of the responses,
male teachers are more likely to solve problems using ICT at home and at work than
female teachers. Other activities are carried out by male and female teachers with com-
parable frequency. On the other hand, depending on the age of the teachers, statistically
signiﬁcant differences in the frequency of using ICT for problem solving in work and

614
J. Záhorec et al.
private life were not conﬁrmed. As shown in Table 4, signiﬁcant correlations were
demonstrated between the frequency of use of the studied cognitive skills in work and
private life. The implementation of activities at work was directly related to how often
teachers performed each activity at home. Based on statistical analyses, there was a
directly proportional high correlation (correlation coefﬁcient value ranging from 0.50 to
0.69) between how often teachers performed the skills at home and at work, namely for
reading (r = 0.53) and a medium correlation (correlation coefﬁcient value ranging from
0.30 to 0.49) for using ICT (r = 0.45), calculations (r = 0.43) and writing (r = 0.30).

Statistical analysis of the data obtained from the measurement showed that the fre-
quency of teachers’ usage of ICT skills in their personal and professional lives was
related to how often teachers let students use ICT to solve problems during class time.
The results of the analysis showed a direct relationship between these aspects. If the
teachers used ICT skills in their private and professional life more often, then they used
digital didactic tools in the classroom or let pupils use, i.e., the more often ICT in the
classroom to solve problems.
3
Conclusions
It is becoming almost essential for people in the context of the needs of today’s society,
as well as in the sense of a successful entry into the labour market, to have not only
good cognitive skills, but also to be able to solve problems effectively using ICT. This
need is even more pressing as the society is currently facing a global pandemic caused
by the COVID-19 disease, because of which teachers are being asked to effectively

Teachers’ Digital Literacy as a Prerequisite
615
apply skills in the usage of various online technologies in both face-to-face and distance
learning. Teachers’ digital literacy is an essential prerequisite for them to be able to
use technology-enhanced teaching effectively in their teaching practice [13–15]. At the
same time, as the presented ﬁndings of the PIAAC online project show, there is a strong
correlation between teachers’ level of ICT use in their personal and professional lives.
It can be argued in this way that teachers’ level of “general” digital literacy has an
impact on the application and active use of their digital competences in their teaching
activities (i.e., it strengthens the conscious application of this component of the teacher’s
competence proﬁle in the exercise of their profession, see also [16, 17]).

Teaching Best Practices

Simulation-Based Learning in Higher
Education: 5 Reasons Why Gamiﬁcation
Completes Online Teaching
Max Monauni1(B) and Sascha Götte2
1 School of Business, Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts, Rotkreuz, Switzerland
max.monauni@hslu.ch
2 School of Engineering and Architecture, Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts,
Horw, Switzerland
Abstract. Online and blended learning offer a strong upside potential to enrich
university learning. On the one hand, long before the Covid-19 pandemic, the
optiontoaccessvirtualclassroomsettingswasontherise,butthepandemiccleared
the path regarding legal and organizational limitations. On the other hand, virtual
learning comes with additional concept-speciﬁc requirements and challenges, e.g.,
a strong demand for students’ self-organization and intrinsic motivation.
The conjunction of online teaching with simulation-based tools introduces
new options to address these challenges. Online- and simulation-based teach-
ing concepts’ ﬂaws are not system-inherent but can be overcome by combin-
ing simulations and online learning within a holistic setting. By applying differ-
ent gamiﬁcation elements from simulations and the adaptability of cloud-based
online tools, an online- and simulation-based intensive block week module is
designed and conducted for students from different countries. Based on this mod-
ule’s structure, learning outcomes and students’ feedback the advantageousness
of an online-simulation-setting will be illustrated.
The results lead to a combined Strengths-Weaknesses-Analysis from joined
online teaching and simulation-based elements. First, the requirements and cir-
cumstances are investigated and described under which the delicate require-
ments of simulation-based learning can be minimized by online teaching. Sec-
ond, challenges from online teaching are researched to be addressed through
simulation-based learning.
Keywords: Strategic and technology management · Simulation · Online learning
1
Introduction
1.1
Research Object and Research Question
Due to the restrictions following the Covid-19 pandemic, governments required uni-
versities to replace on-site lectures by online alternatives using various communication
tools. The Covid-19 restrictions introduced would have negatively affected the university
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 619–628, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_65

620
M. Monauni and S. Götte
exchange activities if there is no platform in which (international) students could enroll
and participate online. As a consequence of the Covid-19 restrictions, a variety of new
instruments for virtual collaborations have been brought to market, existing tools have
been improved and the new pandemic-inﬂuenced requirements enhanced the legally
limited boundaries of learning, teaching and testing in higher education drastically. As a
result, students and lecturers are becoming more open for and familiar to tools for online
learning.
However, online learning still holds certain challenges for students and lecturers
in terms of motivation, interaction, and structure, especially because the lecturer as an
anker to the virtual learning environment is either limited in his/her options (synchronous
learning) or not even directly present (asynchronous learning) [1]. On students’ side, this
increasestherequirementforself-motivationandself-organizationtokeepupacontinues
learning engagement [2]. On lecturers’ side, the time- and task-structure must be more
self-explanatory and clearer and a virtual platform for speciﬁc and continues feedback
needs to be provided.
Independent from online-learning tendencies, the usage of simulation-based learn-
ing has become a more present phenomena in higher education within the last years.
Learning simulations as educational tool are existent since more than ﬁfty years at
universities. These simulations aim to transfer theoretical knowledge into application-
oriented competencies. By modelling an artiﬁcial, but realistic environment participants
can experience complex and dynamic cause-effect relationships in terms of a multi-step
learning process “experiential learning” [3]. Charles Crawford stated: „…simulation is
not a mechanical exercise nor is it a means of bottling truth inside a computer – it is a
way to bounce our ideas and values against reality and see how they bounce back.” [4].
Due to a stronger focus on interactive, more case study-oriented and holistic learning
approaches simulations become very present in higher education [5, 6].
The application of simulation-based learning comes with some speciﬁc requirements
for students and lecturers. From students’ perspective the learning pace is quite inﬂex-
ible and there is a big variety of different skillsets required simultaneously. From lec-
turers’ perspective the challenges from simulation-based settings arise from a long and
time-consuming introduction, demanding infrastructure requirements and an excessive
preparation time (self-study).
Nevertheless, both learning approaches are present in higher education and some
research implies that combining online and simulation-based learning is not only possi-
ble, but auspicious [5, 7]. Under the current technological, legal, and organizational
circumstances the following research questions seems relevant: To what extent can
simulation-based approaches enhance online university learning?
Starting point and research object is the development of a new module concept at
the Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts (LUASA): In 2021 the course
“Management Challenge Intensive Week” was designed as an interactive English mas-
terclass for students from LUASA as well as other internationals from MSE-partners.
The overall module’s objective is focusing on business management, especially strategic
management, and technology management.

Simulation-Based Learning in Higher Education
621
1.2
Research Goal and Structure
The research goal is to clarify and structure reasons why and how university teaching is
enhanced by a theoretical combination of online and simulation-based elements in gen-
eral in Sect. 2. Which concept-speciﬁc requirements and weaknesses of online learning
and simulation-based learnings can be compensated by making use of strengths of the
other concept? In doing so, opportunities which arise from consolidating simulation-
based, online teaching are identiﬁed and analysed. Additionally, there might be threats
from a combination in terms of increasing complexity or reinforcing weaknesses through
consolidation simulation-based with online learning arrangements.
In Sect. 3 the general ﬁndings are applied to the research object (designing the module
concept “Management Challenge Intensive Week”). The implementation, results and
students’ feedback are described in Sect. 4. In Sect. 5 the ﬁndings are summarized,
limitations are disclosed and a general as well as module concept speciﬁc outlook is
given.
2
Theoretical Background
2.1
Online Learning
Online learning (as well as blended learning) offers a higher geographical ﬂexibility. If
combined with asynchrony teaching elements like learning videos, learning nuggets or
learningassignmentsthetimeﬂexibilityoffersstudentsaself-pacedlearningopportunity.
However, studies show that off-site learning efﬁciency is limited by different reasons,
especially insufﬁcient technology tools or lecturer’ skills to make use of these, excessive
preparatory efforts compared to on-site teaching and a lack of motivating and engaging
assignments to enable self-study motivation, which is more relevant if the lecturer is not
physically present [2, 8]. The following table illustrates some strengths and weaknesses
of online learning in comparison to on-site learning (see Table 1).

2.2
Simulation-Based Learning
Simulation-based learning fosters interactivity and interaction between students, apply-
ing different gamiﬁcation elements like quick feedback cycles, different possible solu-
tion paths and competition [9]. Gamiﬁcation refers to the usage of game-based elements
like point scoring or rules of play [10]. Gamiﬁcation is strongly linked to simulation-
based learning, as a big variety of gamiﬁcation elements is utilized in simulations like a
thrilling challenge through storytelling, continuous achievement updates or competition
[11]. Challenging in simulations is the geographical and time inﬂexibility arising from
the direct inﬂuence from the single simulation-teams on each other and the simulation
environment. Complex simulations, typically used on university level, require excessive
introductions to familiarize with the user interface and options for action. Addition-
ally, there is typically a higher demand for group rooms, hardware and maybe software
compared to traditional university lectures [8]. The following table illustrates relevant
strengths and weaknesses of simulation-based learning in comparison to standardized
university lectures (see Table 2).
Table 2. Strengths and weaknesses of simulation-based learning.
Strengths of simulation-based learning
Weaknesses of simulation-based learning

2.3
Combination of Online and Simulation-Based Learning
The main challenge of online learning is securing the continues progress of the students.
This typically involves interactions with the lecturer, who structures, explains, controls
the learning environment, motivates and gives feedback. Simulations can not replace the
lecturer as anker within the learn-setting, but simulation-based, interactive learning can
reduce its signiﬁcance in different ways:
A1: Online learning requires a high intrinsic motivation of students within the semester
to work autonomously and consistently. Simulation-based learning involves
gamiﬁcation-aspects like reasonable decision pathways, motivating subtasks and
collaboration to make learning sequences more entertaining.

Simulation-Based Learning in Higher Education
623
A2: Online learning asks for outstanding clear and detailed description of tasks, ide-
ally with subtasks and time frames. This enables self-paced learning (as one big
advantage of online learning), but also compensates the online-limited options
for enquiries and feedbacks. Simulations involve game-based rules, manuals and
based on cause-effect models some more speciﬁc directives. This comes at the cost
of longer introductions but provides orientation and structure from the beginning.
Many simulations are divided into single rounds of decision-making, sometimes
involving increasing complexity and additional tasks, which transfers into speciﬁc
and timely speciﬁed work packages.
A3: Pure online learning might involve the risk for students to feel lonely without
typical university routines and social interactions with lecturers and peer students.
Simulations often involve collaborative elements like working together in groups,
competing against, or cooperating with other groups, which require discussions.
Additionally, team members or teams have different tasks simultaneously which
requires a higher level of activity instead of passive listening or taking notes in
typical classroom settings.
A4: Online learning can be tedious and fatiguing as the individual lecturers and teaching
styles appear or actually are more similar online. Simulations do not eliminate this.
But individual decision-making, different possible solution paths and dynamic
environments hold the potential and requirement for lots of individual feedback,
from the simulation itself, other team members, and the lecturer.
A5: A new online learning environment is more complex and time-consuming to estab-
lish, especially if a higher level of engagement is intended. On top of this, the design
of an on-site simulation would require additional work. However, a big variety of
simulation tools for university teaching is available, not limited to but especially
in economics, business, engineering, political and social sciences. This does not
only minimize preparation efforts for lecturers but provides an easy access to even
complex and online-available tools.
Based on this, the merger of simulation-based and online learning seems promising
from the online learning perspective to reduce its stand-alone weaknesses through a
combination with simulation- and gamiﬁcation-based approaches (see Fig. 1). Aside
from the described most obvious connections above (continuous lines), there are some
additional interactions between the listed strengths and weaknesses (dashed lines).
Weaknesses of online learning
Strengths of simulation-based learning
intrinsic students’ motivation required
motivating gamification elements

tedious and fatiguing

Fig. 1. Weaknesses of online learning and strengths of simulation-based learning (Strengths-
Weaknesses-Analysis Part 1)

624
M. Monauni and S. Götte
For simulation-based learning the most challenging factors are typically its com-
plexity and collaboration-based inﬂexibility. This requires a uniform learning speed and
simulation insight. A set of communication platforms is required, which in on-site learn-
ing requires lots of different rooms and relocations in between them. To some extent
these needs become less relevant in an online setting:
B1: The infrastructure needs for simulation-based learning is typically higher than for
traditional classroom-based learning. Teams or individuals beneﬁt from break-out
rooms to discuss and decide their strategies in private, for communication with
other teams, questions to the lecturer, coordination or debrieﬁng all students need
to switch rooms for each round, which is also time-consuming. Present online tools
like Zoom, MS Teams or Adobe Connect offer inﬁnite, easy-to-use, cost free and
quick ways to change virtual rooms.
B2: For the sake of fairness an excessive brieﬁng is necessary to enable all students
to participate in simulation-based learning. The more complex and detailed the
simulation, the longer brieﬁng time is necessary. Online settings allow virtual
asynchronous brieﬁngs in advance, which can be supported by videos, tutorials,
and self-assessments, which can be done self-paced. This reduces the introduction
to a common Q&A-session focusing only on clarifying open questions.
B3: When students work in teams or decisions inﬂuence other simulation participants,
which enables collaboration, this comes at the cost of an inﬂexible simulation
structure. Students have the obligation to attend for each decision-relevant phase,
which might be challenging within a simulation module all semester long. In an
online environment students can participate independent from their location.
B4: Additionally, simulation-based learning requires an uniform agenda and learning
speed, which can be demotivating for students who need more or less time than the
average participant. The online setting does not solve this but increases a self-paced
learning by individual break options or additional tasks. The digitally available
delivery of simulation-results enables longer and more ﬂexible decision times.
B5: Holistic simulations necessitate a broad set of different skills. In general, espe-
cially in heterogenous groups this might lead to redundancy in teaching. Learnings
nuggets, which are mostly and easier available online, provide opportunities to
increase students’ knowledge individually.
As described above, the merger of simulation-based and online learning might also
be seen as beneﬁcial from the simulation-based learning perspective to minimize its
stand-alone weaknesses through a combination with online approaches (see Fig. 2).
Other from speciﬁed above (continuous lines), additional interactions between the listed
strengths and weaknesses may be identiﬁed (dashed lines).

3
Concept and Framework
The module “Management Challenge Intensive Week” war designed as a 3-ECTS credit
class on master level in 2021. Not only students from LUASA but from the national and
international partner universities were invited to enroll, hence the module language is
English. The general module’s learning objective covers the major topics from strategic
and technology management. The module should not only cover the theoretical tech-
niques but include various business cases in order to allow the students to apply their
knowledge.
In detail, the module’s learning goals can be divided into professional, methodolog-
ical and personal skills. Professional competencies would be as follows:
– students are capable to apply the process of strategic planning and implementation
– students are able to understand the importance of an effective vision and mission
– students are able to analyze the internal and external environment of companies with
different tools and deduct business strategies from this
– students can take decisions regarding strategic initiatives and the development of
innovative products and services, pricing decisions over life cycle and manage sales
channels
– students are able to manage inventory, capacity utilization, company’s workforce and
ﬁnancial situation
Methodologicalandpersonalskillswouldfocusondecision-making(insmallteams),
ideally requiring collaboration from different nations and backgrounds. Methodological
and personal skills to be achieved are:
– students are capable to formulate and express their ideas on different decision within
the group and discuss advantages and limitations
– students are able to analyze complex problems, to decide in uncertain situations and
to present and justify their decisions
– students are willing to assume responsibility for results developed in teams
– students are able to communicate their results in oral and written form
LUASA is using a broad variety of educational simulations since more than ten
years in its different schools. Some simulations are self-developed, some are delivered

by external service providers, but most of the simulations are conducted by employees
of LUASA. In this case, the module’s target group, learning goals and online setting
required a strategic, complex and online/cloud-based simulation, which covered engi-
neering and management topics. The business simulation TOPSIM – Scale Up focuses
on the development of a traditional scooter manufacturing company to a E-scooter ser-
vice provider. Topics like digitalization, business model innovation and volatility are
covered [12].
Based on the theoretical inputs and the application of the knowledge in different
case studies during the ﬁrst two days of “Management Challenge Intensive Week”, the
students are managing a virtual company in a high-tech industry: developing appropriate
strategies, taking operations decisions, analyzing the achieved results, and reporting to
the shareholders’ assembly. Aside from knowledge transfer, showcasing best practices
and application of tactic knowledge within the business simulation, the students should
collaborate in virtual teams, make decisions under uncertainty, and reduce department-
speciﬁc silo mentality.
The relevant course material was provided in advance through LUASA’s online
learning platform ILIAS. Students were required to self-study the business simulation
manual in advance and to ask questions. The following grading scheme was used to
assess the results of the different teams:
• Share price development: 40%
• Management summary: 20%
• General assembly: 40%

627
The module’s ﬁrst implementation was set up in February 2022. LUASA has brought
Business Engineering students from the Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and
Arts, from the Zurich University of Applied Sciences and from the University of Applied
Sciences Technikum Vienna virtually together using the online platform ZOOM from
February 14 to 18 2022. The intensive week was conducted following the time schedule
shown in Fig. 3.
4
Results
The students’ evaluation as well as their performance within the three graded areas
(business simulation performance, written management report and oral team presenta-
tion) were above average. The overall evaluation of this online module was better than
the average evaluation of LUASA’s on-site modules. The students’ uniformly recorded
feedbacks give additional indications:
• Very well-structured teaching material.
• Short and crisp theory inputs.
• Current and interesting case studies.
• Very successful combination of theory and practice.
• The business simulation makes the intensive week very attractive.
• During the simulation game the teams are individually coached.
• Both lecturers were competent and motivating.
• The exchange with students from other universities is fun and helps to expand the
network.
With regards to the research question “To what extent can simulation-based
approaches enhance online university learning?”, it can be concluded that the explo-
rative and theoretically deducted advantages of combining simulation-based and online
teaching can be conﬁrmed with regards to the speciﬁcally investigated research object:
• Students’ motivation and participation during the entire intensive week was above
average. Many further questions were asked and all deadlines for handing-in tasks
were kept.
• Despitedifferentworkinggroups,complextasks,andEnglishasanon-nativelanguage
for the students, the structure and subset of tasks was clear.
• From lecturer’ perspective, the preparatory effort for designing the new module was
reasonable. However, the need for additional learning nuggets for speciﬁc topics like
‘massive production ramp-ups’ or ‘pricing decisions for ﬁrst movers’ became visible.
• The setup and management of the required online tools in ILIAS, ZOOM and TOPSIM
were less time consuming than the reservation and administration of the physical
rooms and simulations for this group size.
• The concept-speciﬁc long and time-consuming introduction to the business simulation
was successfully transferred into an online self-study.
• No physical attendance from students or lecturer was required.
• During the days, the students had team-independent, self-paced learning slots of 90
min. However, beyond that the overall agenda was ﬁxed.

628
M. Monauni and S. Götte
5
Conclusion
Within this limited research environment, the advantageousness of combining
simulation-based and online learning in higher education could be monitored. This
advantageousness is described and observed over ﬁve independent different aspects
from both online as well as simulation-based learning and illustrated in the combined
Strengths-Weaknesses-Analysis.
Limitations arise from the observation of only one single implementation, the
discipline-speciﬁc particularity, and the beneﬁcial overall setting. Although some of
the implication might be relevant for other ﬁelds of studies and learning settings, the
ﬁeld of research asks for additional investigation before a general widespread usage of
simulation-based, online learning at university level.
With regards to the research object (module “Management Challenge Intensive
Week”) some speciﬁc improvements became visible like the demand for further learn-
ing nuggets or a time schedule allowing more self-paced learnings outside the given
teamwork slots. The next implementation is planned from February 13 to 17 2023.

Development of Engineering Skills Through
Low-Cost Miniature Autonomous Guided
Vehicles
Roberto J. Mora-Salinas(B)
and David Antonio-Torres
Tecnologico de Monterrey, School of Engineering and Sciences, Ave. Eugenio Garza Sada 2501,
64849 Monterrey, NL, Mexico
{rjmora,davidant}@tec.mx
Abstract. After year and a half of not having presential activities in classrooms
and laboratories, a way was found for a new environment to generate more eas-
ily engineering outcomes on automation and autonomous driving. This learning
space is an educational innovation that allows the design and construction of low-
cost prototypes of autonomous vehicles, to carry out competitions and encourage
learning through it.
The main goal is to improve the development of skills in industrial automation
area, embedded systems, and digital manufacturing area through the implemen-
tation of a new learning space. The scope of this space is to attend different areas
of engineering majors. The necessary knowledge to develop a project that will
integrate the different prototyping technologies to improve the design, construc-
tion and start-up of a challenging project will be clariﬁed. The real impact on the
student will be found in the challenging learning experiences they will face. The
design concepts will be experimentally validated in a disruptive, innovative, and
safe space. Another impact will be the ﬂexibility in the learning process.
The purpose of this project is to be able to develop competitions in which
different areas are involved, not only engineering, and turn it into the great gateway
to electromobility projects and that when the students arrive, they already have
enough experience to experiment without fear of breaking down the team or injure
a teammate. In addition to that they are developing skills in students that are needs
of the current industry. This innovation will provide new learning spaces that will
strengthen us as leaders in educational innovation.
Keywords: Autonomous vehicles · Artiﬁcial intelligence · Educational
technology · Educational innovation · Higher education
1
Introduction
The emergence of competence-based education stems from the current needs of society
and business. Professionals not only require knowledge, but also the development of
skills, attitudes, and values. The integration of these four elements makes professionals
have the necessary tools to solve problems within their discipline. The development of
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 629–638, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_66

630
R. J. Mora-Salinas and D. Antonio-Torres
competences must be done from an integral perspective [1], so higher education schools
are changing from traditional educational models to models based on competences.
Competences can be classiﬁed into two types, transversal and disciplinary. The ﬁrst
ones refer to knowledge, skills, attitudes, and values that every professional should
have regardless of the discipline. The disciplinary competences are necessary to solve
problems in a speciﬁc area [2]. Students need to develop both during their professional
formation, so institutions must implement methodologies to ensure their development.
In 2019, Tecnologico de Monterrey launched a new educational model, Tec21, with
input from academic and education experts. Tec21 is centered on four pillars: challenge-
based learning; ﬂexibility in how, when and where students learn; inspirational faculty;
and an engaging university experience [3]. It is believed that Challenge-based learning
(CBL) is the element that most differentiates Tec21 from traditional educational models.
CBL is a pedagogical approach in which students play an active role in the solution to
a relevant problem within a real-world context. CBL implies the deﬁnition of a chal-
lenge and the implementation of a solution. Students collaborate with professors and
national/international experts to solve real-world problems to develop a deeper knowl-
edge of the subjects and topics they are studying. It is the challenge itself which prompts
the obtention of new knowledge and the necessary resources and tools. Traditional sub-
jects have now migrated to units of formation (UF). An UF is composed of contributions
from a few traditional subjects, only those topics that contribute to the completion of
the challenge are part of the UF. The topics are now organized as modules and a module
is delivered by a professor of the respective discipline, thus giving rise to a multidisci-
plinary group of professors. A module provides students with the necessary knowledge
to tackle the challenge.
Tec21 deﬁnes and groups competences according to a certain number of areas of each
academic program. Each competence is decomposed into sub-competences, which run
along three dimensions: complexity of the doing, depth of the knowing and autonomy.
Sub-competences can have one of three levels A, B and C. It is desired students start
from A-level sub-competences during the ﬁrst academic periods and reach C-level ones
by the end of the academic program.
2
Background
The cultivation of competences around real-life challenges and placing the student at
the center of all the educational activities inside and outside of the classroom are two
instrumental features of the new Tec21 educational model. The authors believe that
autonomous vehicles are an excellent means to guide the students to nurture various
disciplinary and transversal competences. Indeed, the selection of low-cost miniature
autonomous vehicles is an attractive opportunity for students to develop a great deal
of competences and skills, while they build a learning space with clear objectives and
outcomes. At the same time, the construction, programming, and tests of these vehicles
provide the professors with several elements of assessment and evaluation in line with
the new educational model. In this section, the different stages in the development
of the project are presented, highlighting the skills and competences the students are
acquiring in each and the evidence the students provide to demonstrate the level of

Development of Engineering Skills
631
accomplishment. It is also important to mention that at all stages the students receive
support and feedback from a group of professors. Before the project is started, this group
of professors is informed that students, at some point, will ask for help.
2.1
Mechanical Construction and Electrical Concepts
The assembling of the mechanical parts of the vehicle is an interesting activity the
students enjoy being immersed in. The students follow the instructions in manuals to
proceed with the construction. Despite this is a miniature prototype, the students go
away with concepts such as DC (direct current) motors, PWM (pulse-width modulation)
signals, steering direction, encoders, power consumption, tire alignment, among others.
Whereas this is an activity that is brief (going from half an hour to a couple of hours
depending on the model, the vendor, and the required mechanical adjustments) and
takes place at the beginning of the project, the students become aware of the great
many complexities in the mechanical control of a real autonomous vehicle. Also, the
students realize that the simpliﬁcations introduced by the miniature prototype are in the
spirit of reducing those complexities to make them focus on other endeavors. In case
a question related to mechanical components, power consumption or batteries arises,
students are encouraged to talk to professors of the mechanical engineering department
and/or professors of the power electronics ﬁeld.
The evidence generated by the students is photos of the completed vehicle and a
brief oral report about the use of tools during the construction.
2.2
Setup of the On-Board Computer
The current trend in miniature autonomous vehicles is that they come equipped with a
multicore single-board computer such as Jetson Nano [4], Raspberry Pi [5] and Pynq
board [6], among others. What these boards have in common is that they run an operating
system(OS)basedonaLinuxdistributionsuchasUbuntu[7],UbuntuMate[8],Raspbian
[9], etc. The use of this type of OS poses a challenge to the students, as most of them
are proﬁcient in the use of Windows-based portable computers.
In the early stages of their projects, students consult video tutorials, forums and
manuals to get acquainted with the use of a terminal, Linux commands, command-line
programming and execution of applications. As a following stage, students get familiar
with the update of the OS and the installation of a myriad of applications necessary
for the development of the project. As will be discussed in subsequent subsections, the
skills and competencies developed during these stages are valuable for the successful
completion of their project.
The evidence produced by the student are screen captures of the installation of the
OS and the required updates. If necessary, students talk to professors of the computer
engineering department to solve issues related to this stage.
2.3
Installation of Software
Once the setup and update of the OS for the on-board computer is complete, students are
then faced with the job of installing all the libraries necessary for the programming of

632
R. J. Mora-Salinas and D. Antonio-Torres
applications that will give shape to the autonomy of the vehicle. Some vendors provide
the user with a list of recommended libraries, programming languages and frameworks
that have proved to facilitate the development of applications. Other vendors offer an
image of the OS with all the applications, programming languages and libraries included.
The time the students spent during this stage depends on the competences acquired in
previous stages and the support provided by the vendor.
The evidence of this stage is once again screen captures of the installation process
of the libraries, links of the websites with the tutorials consulted to get familiar with the
libraries and frameworks and the demonstration of the execution of the code provided
by the tutorials. If necessary, students get feedback and support from professors of the
computer engineering department. Unlike previous stages, the installation of software
is continuous during the duration of the project.
2.4
Programming
This is the most important stage in the development of the project. The choice of the pro-
gramming language or languages is heavily inﬂuenced by the libraries and frameworks
supported by the on-board computer and the vendor. Python is the most popular pro-
gramming language as of the time of this writing, mostly due to the availability of many
libraries and frameworks for several programming tasks and engineering disciplines.
Among the most recurring libraries and frameworks used by the students are OpenCV
[10], Robotics Operating System (ROS) [11] and Tensorﬂow [12]. OpenCV is a collec-
tion of modules and functions for the implementation of image processing and computer
vision tasks. For these projects, the images and videos are provided by a camera or web-
cam connected to the on-board computer. Tensorﬂow is a machine learning framework
for acquiring data, training models, and producing predictions. ROS is a collection of
software libraries to build robot applications. Details of the interaction of these three
libraries and frameworks will be explained in the next sections.
This stage of the project is rich in evidence. Testing code and simulations are pro-
duced by the students to report progress in their learning and skills and the demonstration
of competence. Support and feedback from the professors at this stage is crucial to keep
the spirit of the students high. In addition, students are encouraged to exercise and rein-
force transversal competences such as long-life learning, self-motivation, teamwork, and
critical thinking to discern relevant information.
2.5
Sensors and Actuators
Autonomous vehicles rely on the operation of a group of sensors and actuators for the
correct functioning. In this project, the main component for sensing the environment
and making the correct decisions is a camera. Based on the frames provided by the
camera, a sequential processing takes place to correct for some noise on the image,
spatial operations, and ﬁltering and, ultimately, extract information necessary for the
autonomy. This information is then translated to the steering direction, under control of a
servomotor,andDCmotorsforspeed.SomemodelsalsoincludeLiDARsandultrasound
sensors for the detection of objects around the vehicle. Students are requested to gather
information for the programming and test of this collection of sensors and actuators and

Development of Engineering Skills
633
look for help among the professors to equip themselves with the best knowledge possible.
As evidence of competence, students are asked to report the sources of information they
consulted and the testing code they executed to get familiar with the operation of the
sensors and actuators.
2.6
Tests
An excellent mechanism for the students to demonstrate competence is the way they run
tests and yield results. During testing, students revisit the previous stages in search for
incomplete information or to run some more demonstrative code and examples. Little
by little, the students start to glue together all the knowledge gathered in the previous
stages and produce code and experiments of their own inspiration. At this point, students
realize that the series of activities of this project are so immersive that they can come up
with new ideas and tests and enhancements to refactor existing code.
Depending on how the different teams of students ﬁnd solutions, this stage is rich
in different tests and codes. Examining the progress of students, collaborate with them
to ﬁnd solutions and guide them to run speciﬁc tests require a very close and unique
mentoring. Availability of professors for running this mentoring plays an important role
in the formation of competences in the students.
Extracts of code, recording tests in video and live demonstrations are the usual
evidence of competence and skills provided by the students in this stage. If necessary,
examination of accomplishment of competence, during this stage, can incorporate a
round of technical questions for disciplinary competences or explanation and/or analysis
of sketches and diagrams representing the different stages of the project for transversal
competences such as collaborative work [13].
The next section provides more information about the experiments and results
obtained during the application of this project in different semesters.
3
Experiments
The experiments presented here were conducted in a course of Digital Systems and
Robotics Engineering program at Tecnologico de Monterrey. The experiment was
executed in 3 semesters: spring 2020, spring 2021, and fall 2021.
The ﬁrst group of students used a miniature vehicle called SunFounder PiCar [14].
This platform contains a small car model equipped with a PWM driver, two small DC
motors, a driver module, a Robot Hat with power and interface integrated, a camera, four
wheels and tires, and a Raspberry Pi. The kit was delivered to the students disassembled,
and they had to start assembling it from scratch (Fig. 1).
During the second semester of experimentation a group of students was asked for an
implementation of an autonomous miniature vehicle built and developed by themselves.
This vehicle should be controlled with a Raspberry pi and an Arduino. The miniature
vehicle should move autonomously and stop depending on the object that is detected
with a vehicle camera, the objects to be detected are: a stop sign, a trafﬁc light, and a
plastic puppy.

634
R. J. Mora-Salinas and D. Antonio-Torres
Fig. 1. SunFounder PiCar-V building in process
For the third experimentation group, the students used a platform for miniature
autonomous vehicles called JetRacer[15]. This platform contains a NVIDIA Jetson Nano
board developer kit which is a small computer that can deliver 472 Gﬂop and supports
AI algorithms. The JetRacer platform also contains a metal servo for steering system,
two high power motors, aluminum alloy chassis, 4 wheels and a wireless NIC. The main
goal of this miniature vehicle is to advance inside of a lane of a tiny circuit. This circuit
comes a printed canvas which is commonly used to calibrate and develop the algorithm
of self-driving. The vehicle should use a webcam attached to the chassis and should use
OpenCV algorithm to do the navigation process (Fig. 2).
Fig. 2. JetRacer assembled
4
Results
4.1
First Experiment
The ﬁrst group of students fulﬁlled the task satisfactorily but found some ﬁndings and
reﬂections during its development:
• Calibrationoftheservos,inourcasetheservo‘correspondingtothedirectionalwasnot
found mechanically adjusted at 90°, making the advance was not totally straight with

Development of Engineering Skills
635
that angle and in turns requiring more torque than can be to make a toast. Therefore,
adjustments had to be made in the code.
• Properties of the ground, among some aspects that inﬂuenced were the reﬂection of
the tape on the ground making it possible to detect nonexistent lines confusing the
functions.
• The irregularities of the ground, and the friction between the ﬂoor and the vehicle’s
tires, were uncertain. At times it was not moving properly.
• Processing speed against advance, is the highest consideration since the speed depends
proportionally on the processing load of each of the frames.
4.2
Second Experiment
The second group of students did the assigned task successfully and made improvements
to the las experiment’s group development:
• They started the tests with the camera of the PiCar-V because if the camera wasn’t
good enough, the whole project won’t be successful.
• They used the PiCar-V Chassis and mechanisms, but with another control Board.
• They decided to change for a PYNQ Z1 board. This board is more scalable to the
handling of peripherals proposed (Fig. 3).
Fig. 3. Schematic connections of the PiCar-V system with PYNQ board
4.3
Third Experiment
The third group of students built and programmed successfully an JetRacer and made it
recognize lanes inside a circuit.
They ﬁndings
• Once the tests were completed and the necessary calibration with best speeds for each
section of the track, as well as the turning angle, was completed, it was tested on the

636
R. J. Mora-Salinas and D. Antonio-Torres
track and satisfactory results were obtained, the JetRacer was able to make runs in
any direction of the track, and only rarely went off track, making an error of 1 out
of every 20 laps. In addition, thanks to the corrections now of centering, it could be
placed out of alignment and still be corrected within the track.
• More Region of Interest (RoI): Our software only uses one that detects the 2 lines of
the lane. This means that we are not using the whole resolution of the camera, because
the robot only sees the RoI. This decision was taken because the robot was taking
the laps to soon. As a result, the laps were abrupt. To solve this, another RoI may be
applied to the upper part of the camera and processing and controlling can be done
just for taking the laps and decide where the robot is going to turn and apply the right
steering and speed depending on the slope of the lane.
• Artiﬁcial Intelligence may be applied to control laps. Some control systems may not
be enough to control trajectories, this is where you can apply AI to teach the robot
and adjust speed and steering.
• We are not sure enough if the processing was done in the CPU or GPU of the Jetson,
but NVIDIA offers CUDA as a tool to use as much as possible of GPU for image
processing or AI.
• Image processing issues, the orange lanes were great to process the image, but we
cannot rely always on the color of the lanes, so a better image ﬁltering may be needed
for future applications.
• The project uses 2 scripts: one for image processing and control, and the other one just
to control motors and servo. Another program may be used for control, and processing
of as many parts of the image you may want to use. Using ROS to link everything
(Fig. 4).
Fig. 4. JetRacer on the printed canvas circuit.
4.4
Common Results in All Experiments
During all three experiments, the students shown similarities in the comments that they
share as results. Here is a short list of the main ideas.
• Change of motor controller cards, to protect from overheating and excessive motions.
• Modiﬁcation of tire structure, for better traction and balance (better wheels).
• Improved support to have a double camera and make more interesting projects (use
of a stereo camera)

Development of Engineering Skills
637
• Add current battery indicator
• Design and make your own car, considering the details already mentioned
5
Conclusions
The real impact on the student is found in the challenging learning experiences they
had. The design concepts were experimentally validated during this experimentation.
The purpose of this project was to be able to develop outcomes for the development of
skills in Robotics in which different areas are involved.
In the comments shown in the Result section, it can be seen how the students have
improved their critical judgment regarding the results obtained. They proposed improve-
ments, noted factory errors. They developed solutions to them, and in a natural way they
solved problems of greater complexity than those initially raised. The disciplinary com-
petence developed in this innovation spaced was deﬁned as: “The student implements
mechatronic/electronic systems through automatically guided vehicles that respond to
the needs of the environment”. This can be seen in the documentations that all students
present as ﬁnal deliverable papers (Fig. 5).
Fig. 5. Example of presented results by the students.
After three semesters of implementation, all the group involved in the experimenta-
tions gave verbal and written feedback about the outcomes developed during the experi-
ments. The result in general terms was a positive one. One of the main ﬁndings obtained
from the students’ reports was that these implementations of autonomous vehicle chal-
lenges help to improve the experiences of students against the traditional classroom
schemes.
This educational innovation space had an excellent response from the perspective of
the students. It had shown to be excellent model for teaching some areas of engineering.
Engineer students can implement autonomous vehicle solutions with new ideas that
come directly from them.
The new industry 4.0 requires engineers to have increasingly shorter learning cycles,
this learning space is for that. It is a disruptive environment for the construction of
miniature autonomous vehicles for the development of desirable skills in engineering
students through challenges, collaborations, and contests.
