Development of Teachers’ Judgement Skills
as a Component of Pre- and In-Service Training
Tiia Rüütmann1(B), Urve Läänemets2, Kadi Kaja2, and Kristi Kiilu2
1 Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech), Ehitajate tee 5, 19086 Tallinn, Estonia
tiia.ruutmann@taltech.ee
2 Estonian Academy of Music and Theatre, Tatari 13, 10116 Tallinn, Estonia
Abstract. This pilot study has been triggered by the need to ﬁnd a new and mean-
ingful balance between activities performed by learners and professional teachers.
The purpose of this research was to establish the foundations for development of
modelling teachers’ professional judgement skills. The focus on teachers’ pro-
fessionalism has in recent decades shifted from teaching to learning, but both are
important. Learning with achievement can be expected only in meaningful cooper-
ation between motivated learners and skillful teachers supporting students in their
activities. Teachers these days have obtained skills for both - to organize learning
web-based or traditional environments. Still they have to decide, how and when to
use remote (distant) learning, contact learning and/or hybrid learning. For that they
badly need critical thinking and judgement skills for making informed decisions
about what could make their professional work best suitable for their learners.
The pilot study is an attempt to ﬁnd out, how teachers make their judgements
concerning their different competences and opportunities for their implementa-
tion. Judgement skills require teachers’ meta-level professional thinking skills, it
is considerably more than just acquired pedagogical competencies during their
pre-service education at universities, it requires a multisided analysis of different
factors inﬂuencing both the content for learning as well as possibilities to organize
the process in supportive learning environments.
Keywords: Teachers’ professionalism · Judgmental skills · Meaningful
learning · Teacher competencies
1
Introduction
Recent pandemic and political events have considerably changed work and learning
environments available to provide education for different target groups of learners. The
question what is education for in the 21st century and what teachers/lecturers could do
more efﬁciently/differently to make all learning meaningful considering new contexts.
It requires a new in-depth analysis of teacher professionalism, especially opportunities
to specify its stages of development, leading to teachers’/lecturers’ higher-level thinking
skills.StudiesbyBiesta[1–3],andKansanen[4,5],andSepp[6]haveinitiateddiscussion
about teacher competences and their implementation in different societies and under
changing circumstances.
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 639–648, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_67

640
T. Rüütmann et al.
Decision-makers in the ﬁeld of educational policy-making have carefully studied
various descriptions of expected competences of teachers and lectures working at edu-
cational institutions providing opportunities for learners of all ages and capabilities.
Several organizations have managed to create speciﬁc lists and systems of competen-
cies relevant for their (specialist) training goals and future activities at different levels
of education. Teachers with their professional competencies are expected to meet the
demands expressed by governments and different social groups of learners in society.
Education has currently become meaningful for wider population in all countries as an
individual opportunity to use one’s potential in the best possible way for development
as a person, specialist and citizen.
2
Systems of Skills and Competencies for the 21st Century
The World Economic Forum has presented a system of skills based on research carried
out by McKinsey Institute [7]. They have characterized the future of work and speciﬁed
56 foundational skills that will help citizens thrive in their future work. These skills
are called DELTAs (distinct elements of talent) and the established system contains 13
skill groups divided into four categories (cognitive, interpersonal, self-leadership and
digital) in detail. They have also described how proﬁciency in them can inﬂuence work-
related outcomes, especially employment, income and job satisfaction. It also allows to
start deﬁning different taxonomies of skills forming desired competencies for educators
- teachers and lecturers – which they need for developing best possible and support-
ive learning environments for their learners. The recommendations for governments
and education leaders are the following: reform education systems, ensure affordability
of lifelong education and set up institutions for research and innovation in education,
speciﬁc for their cultural and social conditions.
There are also some competence systems which deserve particular attention for orga-
nizing teacher training. For example, International Society for Engineering Pedagogy
(IGIP) criteria for competencies of engineering educators and STEM teachers for general
and vocational schools [8] consist of two main groups: technical expertise and pedagog-
ical competencies. Technical expertise means in-depth knowledge and skills in one’s
specialist ﬁeld, minimally at MA level acquired during 5 years of study. Educational
competencies have been divided into six groups:
• pedagogical, social, psychological and ethical competencies (with 10 speciﬁed sub-
competencies);
• didactic skills (16 sub-competencies);
• evaluative competencies (with 5 sub-competencies);
• organizational/management competencies (6 sub-competencies);
• oral communication skills and social competencies (9 sub-competencies);
• reﬂective and developmental competencies (4 sub-competencies).
Although numerous, they have been quite precisely described and, accordingly, they
can be taken as a basis for curriculum development and organizing learning activities
both theoretical and practical. The IGIP system is covered with several corresponding

Development of Teachers’ Judgement Skills
641
handbooks and other necessary study aids, so teachers’ professional development sys-
tems can be implemented as open systems, able to accept new ideas and include them
into existing teacher training systems [9–11].
Understandably, country speciﬁc expectations concerning teachers’ professionalism
differ, and teachers working at different types of institutions and educational levels also
need somewhat different competencies. Their work environments, conditions and the
content of learning they are expected to organize have to be carefully analyzed and con-
sidered when designing curricula for teachers’ pre- and in-service training and envisag-
ing their career prospects and future professional development. All the afore-mentioned
ﬁelds should be united into a clear and meaningful system, if decision-makers wish to
have professional and experienced specialists at all schools at different educational lev-
els. Sustainability of educational staff is a serious problem for many countries, including
Estonia. There are many questions that require answers, and these, in turn, require con-
siderations of different kind, especially of the local context, which these days is more
than ever inﬂuenced by global factors.
Although appearing new competencies can be included into in-service training sys-
tems, the basic training of teachers is of utmost importance and meaning, creating foun-
dations for future professional success and ability to learn and improve lifelong. Both,
pre- and in-service training have been united in many countries into holistic professional
career systems paving different ways for individual informed decision-making and indi-
vidual paths for life-long learning. Some countries have tried to follow the Singapore
initiated speciﬁc Teacher Growth Models (TGMs) [12] aimed at motivating teachers to
be engaged in lifelong learning, take ownership of their professional life and personal
wellbeing, tailored to the values and needs of their educational cultures. They have
speciﬁed the following competence ﬁelds as ﬁve desired outcomes characterizing the
21st century teachers needed for Singapore society. Considering teachers’ multifaceted
and socially most meaningful and inﬂuential work teachers are expected to be ethical
educators, competent professionals, collaborative learners, transformational leaders and
community builders [12].
Even if the training systems, both pre-and in-service, have been smartly designed and
implemented and teachers/lecturers have been provided with relevant technical profes-
sional competences, there is a need for meta-level professional decision-making skills
about teachers’ practical agency.
Gert Biesta [1, 2] drew attention to limits of competence-based teachers’ education
already almost a decade ago by asking the following questions:
• what are the teachers’ judgement skills for informed decision-making to use particular
competences?
• what makes them decide when selecting/choosing the best and most meaningful
activities for their learners?
Even if the teachers master the required technical professional skills, they still have
to make informed decisions considering multiple factors inﬂuencing and limiting their
everyday professional activities. Biesta [2] writes: “Good teaching requires judgement
about what an educationally desirable course of action is in this concrete situation with
these concrete students at this particular stage in their educational trajectory”. Biesta

642
T. Rüütmann et al.
even presents a formula “good teaching = competences + judgement” and the problem
is, how teachers could be helped to become capable of such judgements and what could
teacher educators do to enhance development of these skills [2].
It basically means that teachers have to decide whether their intended/planned prac-
tical activities are educationally appropriate and create a meaningful synergy between
the many factors creating their particular contexts and conditions.
In short - we need judgements about the content and form of education in concrete
conditions, which requires comprehension of “a big picture” considering all its elements,
including even hidden curricula in particular societies. This makes judgement skills
about their agency particularly meaningful for development of an individual, rational
and pragmatic as well as developmentally open system for any teacher or lecturer.
Teachers may understand given instruction somewhat differently including curricula.
This is also the case with judgment skills, because not everyone knows the course/subject
they teach equally well, while others do not notice obvious inﬂuential factors in the learn-
ing environment, etc. This is usually referred to as “refraction” and it demonstrates a
different interpretation by the teacher according to his or her perceptions. These refrac-
tions are not merely multiplications of occasional opinions, but are evoked by a limited
set of largely shared and culturally conditioned ideas: even a short note can convey a
complex meaning that is based on shared ideas and stereotypes [13].
There are diverse recommendations for development and implementation of com-
petencies, which have inﬂuenced national education systems in different parts of the
world. The analysis of how European key competencies of 2006 for life-long learning
[14] have been implemented led to a new version of them in 2018. There are also recom-
mendations offered by OECD regarding competences [15], OECD Future of Education
and Skills - Transformative Competencies for 2030 [16], and the Board of Elementary
and Secondary Education (BESE) passed Professional Standards (PSTs) for teachers
in 2014 [17] from which different countries have established their own systems, with
different expected professional competencies.
Considering all different recommendations and their analyses it can be said that
some countries have followed them precisely (Estonia), some have left out particular
competencies (Italy, Portugal Spain) and some countries have adjusted them smartly
considering their local needs and educational cultures (Finland and Korea). Tero Autio
[18] offers a brilliant analysis of development of the Finnish mindset of “good enough”
which is rational, reasonable and realistic to be achieved in Finland and which has
been a success. Ji-Hye Kim [19] describes similar developments in South Korea, where
amalgamation of traditional and modern approaches to education (with particular stress
onthemeaningfulcontentofeducation)wasculturallyrelevantandanothersuccessstory.
The issue of teacher competences really requires a further step ahead - and that could
be development of teachers’ judgement skills leading to a higher-level professionalism
and efﬁcient work under diverse social and cultural conditions.
It can be summarized that professional judgement skills are meta-level and multidi-
mensional professional thinking skills, which require individual independent decision
making at the level of comprehension of teaching as a system in a particular educational
context. Biesta [2] analyses three domains in which education functions, contributing

Development of Teachers’ Judgement Skills
643
to a person’s qualiﬁcation, socialization and subjectiﬁcation and teachers need to bear
them in mind when designing their purposeful professional activities.
3
Goal of the Pilot Study
This pilot study has been triggered by the need to ﬁnd a new and meaningful balance
between activities performed by learners and professional teachers. The focus on teach-
ers’ professionalism has in recent decades shifted from teaching to learning, but both are
important. Learning with achievement can be expected only in meaningful cooperation
between motivated learners and skillful teachers supporting students in their activities.
Teachers these days have obtained skills for both - to organize learning web-based or in
traditional environments. Still, they have to decide, how and when to use remote (dis-
tant) learning, contact learning and/or hybrid learning. For that they badly need critical
thinking and judgement skills for making informed decisions about what could make
their professional work best suitable for their learners.
For designing balanced and psycho-didactically analyzed teaching that supports
meaningful learning, teachers need the following competencies for:
• Goal setting according to didactical models (who and why needs to be trained);
• Students’ entry level analysis (preliminary knowledge, entrance exams);
• Time planning (how soon the result/output can be expected);
• Curricula analysis/designing course content;
• Learning sequence analysis (subject logic - what to be taught before, what after);
• Existence of study materials corresponding to the syllabus (textbooks, web environ-
ment, laboratory equipment, etc.);
• Learning environments planning (which is more suitable for the subject);
• Learning process design (practice and other learning activities including meth-
ods/methodology of teaching and assessment);
• Relationship between the chosen teaching methods/methodology and the initial level
of the students;
• Appropriateness of assessment methods and tools (what and how can be assessed?);
• Analysis of the cost of the curriculum (educational economics);
• Analysis of external factors (e.g. current situation; labour market changes);
• Creatingtheprestigeofthespecialtyandmotivationofstudentstoacquirethespecialty
(salary, availability of jobs);
• Professional autonomy of a teacher - the right to decide on the content and organization
of studies;
• Informed decision making based on sound arguments.
The pilot study is an attempt to ﬁnd out, how teachers make their judgements concern-
ing their different competences and opportunities for their implementation. Judgement
skills require teachers’ meta-level professional thinking skills, it is considerably more
than just acquired pedagogical competencies during their pre-service education at uni-
versities, it requires a multisided analysis of different factors inﬂuencing both the content
for learning as well as possibilities to organize the process of its acquisition in supportive
learning environments.

644
T. Rüütmann et al.
4
Methodology
A mixed method approach has been used. Teachers have been asked to assess the impact
of different factors providing information for making a sound judgement for choosing
between suitable activities in one’s professional work. Data were collected web-based
and by short interviews.
The compiled questionnaire included 16 questions for assessment of above listed
competencies. For responses a Likert-type forced choice scale has been chosen as the
most widely used basis for surveys. The questions were presented as statements. A
response scale used had ﬁve choices from “High importance” up to “Not effective for
me”. Respondents had a possibility to leave a comment at the end of the analysis and
rank in order of importance their assessed competencies.
The sample of 60 teachers (N = 60) participated in the pilot survey, 38% of respon-
dents were teachers at general schools, 33% at high schools, 5% at vocational schools,
2% at hobby schools, 17% at colleges and 30% at universities (some of them working
on different educational levels at the same time).
5
Results and Discussion
The study showed anticipated differences between different target groups. Opinions
about judgement skills vary according to their work experience and also considering
their expectations regarding their professional career.
As it is presented in Fig. 1, the most preferred competencies for designing balanced
and psycho-didactically analyzed teaching are goal setting (preferred by 73% of respon-
dents), learning sequence (57%), course content (53%), and teacher autonomy (53%).
Less preferred were external factors (5%), prestige and motivation (17%), and assess-
ment methods (20%). These results show what teachers have valued and are using in
their teaching currently.
The following comments were written by participants:
• External factors are important, but not the most important. Attitudes, etc. change, and
certainly are not always positive.
• “Doubt grows with knowledge” - J. W. v. Goethe
• All of these factors have an impact on the efﬁciency of learning. A lot depends on the
contingent of students.
• I teach students and participants in in-service training at the university, the inﬂuencing
factors listed in the questionnaire have different signiﬁcance for them, because in the
case of the mentioned contingents, the competence and motivation of the students are
usually signiﬁcantly different.
• Management of engineering e-courses requires a lot of time and technical resources.
There is a lack of course-based e-support (technical management work).
• If we are able to motivate the student to use the time and available materials wisely
at the right time (from the very beginning of the course), then the rest will be easier.
This requires a good level of teaching and the ability to “read” or understand students.

All teachers develop their own systems of organizing teaching as a professional activ-
ity. Therefore, piloting of these criteria can provide elements for creating an individual
model for ascertaining foundations for making a professional judgement. Once all the
needed data are in, whether by sensing or intuition, one must decide how to process the
information and come to a decision. A teacher who prefers to be logical and analytical,
analyzing facts impersonally and objectively, demonstrates a preference for thinking
as the mode of decision making. From the other side, teachers who base decisions on
subjective, personal values and standards use feeling. Each person has a preferred mode,
and most individuals move freely between these options [9].
Judgement skills are decision-making skills and requires thinking and feeling
according to Wankat [9].
A decision-making model was developed based on [20]. Accordingly, teaching is a
subject to speciﬁc regularities and determined by a series of components throughout its
course. These 7 components – instructional objectives (why?), subject matter (what?),
psycho-structure of learners (who?), socio-structure/learning environments (where?),
educational technology and media (with what?), teaching methods (how?) and the
sequence of learning activities (when?) have a complex interdependent relationship and
need judgement skills for planning and making decisions designing effective learning
situations. Taking account of the named components an effective model of engineering
pedagogy has been designed by Melezinek [21] and Rüütmann [22]. This model can be

T. Rüütmann et al.
used as a basis for different types of analyses, if we change any of its components. If we
decrease the number of lessons/lectures/contact hours in labs, etc. we have to analyze the
inﬂuence on the volume of the selected content and/or methodology of teaching/learning
[20].
Teachers’ judgement skills remain highly individual, but must stay professional. Bal-
anced approach between cultural homogeneity and heterogeneity should lead to learning
with comprehension relevant to the logic of the subject, avoiding historical, cultural and
social refraction leading to expected achievement.

Based on the introduced pilot study a further basic study will be designed for the

6
Conclusion
It can be tentatively concluded that in addition to competences developed during
teachers/lecturers pre-service training, but also during their in-service training, there
should be activities, which would support their professional development of judgement
skills. It means comprehension of meta-level thinking skills for informed decision-
making considering options and potential of different conditions and environments the
teachers/lecturers are working in.
It is evident that state promoted systemic narratives cannot be only liberal in their
approach for organizing education. All curricula for all types of learning at different
academic levels have to provide accepted and speciﬁed information about both – the

Development of Teachers’ Judgement Skills
647
selected content for learning and guidelines for organizing the process of learning activ-
ities [23]. Accordingly, inclusion of a course for developing teachers judgement skills
could be most meaningful, as it has the potential to constitute a higher-level intellectual
system of teachers and university professors for their professional work.
Teachers’ judgement skills are meta-level integrated skills for informed decision-
making, which are based on many professional competences, starting from in-depth
subject knowledge in their respective ﬁelds, sharp observation skills and abilities to
analyze, structure and develop supportive learning environments and meaningful learn-
ing processes. Judgement skills are holistic and dynamic in character, and open for
improvement in diverse pedagogical ﬁelds throughout the teacher’s career, constitut-
ing their professional Self. They are constantly developing, meeting the requirements
of diverse changes we are facing in the 21st century. Although individual, considering
teachers’ different types of personality, their formal education, training courses and life
experience, it seems meaningful to design a speciﬁc course of judgement skills for them
in pre-service/basic teacher training already. Multifaceted judgements skills allow both,
novice and experienced teachers reach new levels of professionalism and success in their
work.

Didactic Tool for Intuitive Random Process
Visualization
András Kakucs
and Katalin Harangus(B)
Faculty of Technical and Human Sciences, Sapientia Hungarian University of Transylvania,
O.p. 9, C.p. 4, 540485 Târgu-Mure¸s, Romania

Abstract. The use of educational tools is an essential part of achieving educa-
tional goals. All practicing educators have experienced the lack of appropriate
illustrative tools. Their use helps students deepening existing or to achieve new
knowledge, applicable to other learning situations. Our goal is the development
and the presentation of a didactic visualization tool suitable in the intuitive illus-
tration of random processes. This tool visualizes the binomial distribution. It can
be used in three variants: a) based on hardware-generated true random numbers; b)
based on software-generated pseudo-random numbers; c) also based on pseudo-
random numbers, but the probability of the random process is determined by the
tilt of the stand. With data from the measurement can be used for further analysis:
e.g., using an external program the user can plot the histograms of frequencies,
he can calculate the empirical mean and standard deviation of the distribution,
he will be able to perform statistical tests etc. The scope of the demonstration is
the intuitive visualization of some real-life random processes, when the outcome
is inﬂuenced by a large number of elemental, practically unobservable random
events.
Keywords: Galton board · Didactic tool · Binomial and normal distribution
1
Introduction
Teaching via demonstration is one of the most widely used and ancient methods of
teaching. Didactic thinkers such as Comenius [1], Pestalozzi [2], Diesterweg [3] and
Usinszkij [4], give the method of demonstration signiﬁcant importance in their theory
of education.
The didactic tools used in demonstration facilitate the development of visual thinking
and help students discover the opportunities for practical applications and to systematize
what they have learned. Their use captures the attention of the students and helps to keep
them curious while helping make use of what they have learnt [5]. They also increase
the efﬁciency of the training process by making it easier for students to discover reality,
to master the knowledge related to reality, to foster the formation of the emotional
approaches to reality and to train the activities involved in transforming reality [6, 7].
Our study presents a didactic tool, which was designed to demonstrate random pro-
cesses intuitively. The tool can be used to demonstrate binomial distribution in three
ways.

2
Galton Board
In 1889, the English polymath, Francis Galton built a device designed to intuitively
demonstrate random processes, which is now known as the Galton board. This consist
of an inclined surface with nails driven into it at equal distances forming a chessboard-
pattern. The base of the board houses cells which collect discs or balls launched from
the top of the board, always from the same position. While rolling down the board, these
discs collide with the nails, which alters their paths down the slope. After bouncing off,
their path continues either to the left or to the right of the nail until it encounters another
nail. This repeats the collision and path change maneuver until the disc reaches its ﬁnal
position in one of the cells at the bottom of the board.
The outline of the disc stacks in the cells forms a bell curve, which is none other than
an approximation of probability density function of normal distribution. By increasing
the number of nails and the number of discs, we also increase the accuracy of the
approximation. For all intents and purposes, the Galton board demonstrates a kind of
binomial distribution where the probability of the disk bouncing to one side of the nail
equals p = 0.5 the probability of it bouncing to the other.
2.1
Binomial Distribution
Let us suppose that we conduct a total n number of independent experiments while
observing the occurrence of the event A. According to our experience, this event has a p
probability of occurring. Let us assume that this probability is not subject to change as
time passes.
Since our experiments serve to show whether the event A occurs or not, our sample
space can be narrowed down to A and its opposite, A. If the probability of the occurrence
of event A is p, then the probability of the opposite of A occurring is q = 1 −p.
The probability of event A occurring in both experiments on account of the indepen-
dence of the two events is p · p = p2. The probability of a failed experiment following a
successful one is p · q = p · (1 −p). The probability of a successful experiment after the
previous failed one is q · p = (1 −p) · p, which is numerically equal to the previous one.
Lastly, the probability of event A not occurring in either experiment (both experiments
fail) thus equals to q · q = q2 = (1 −p)2.
Naturally, the sum of all four probabilities have to add up to probability one, the
probability of a certain event:
p2 + 2 · p · q + q2 = p2 + 2 · p · (1 −p) + (1 −p)2 = 1.
(1)
We can see that the previous sum is equal to the square of the binomial, (p + q):
(p + q)2 = p2 + 2 · p · q + q2 = 1,
(2)
and the sum of the polynomial’s coefﬁcients is equal to the number of possible outputs.
The probability of a successful third experiment remains p, while the probability of
a failed one remains q. After the third experiment, the the repetitive variations of success
and failure is

3
The Developed Didactic Tool
3.1
Designing a Virtual Galton Board
Our virtual Galton board consists of 10 nails and the balls collect in eleven cells. After
hitting a nail, each ball has an equal p = 0.5 probability of bouncing off to the right (which
represents success) or to the left (which represents failure). Ten consecutive bounces
represent n = 10 consecutive experiments. After ten unsuccessful (left) consecutive
bounces, the ball ends up in the leftmost cell (number of successful experiments k = 0)
and after ten successful (right) consecutive bounces, the ball ends up in the rightmost
cell (k = 10). Obviously, these two events occur very rarely, the balls usually end up in
the middle cells.
The “soul” of the tool is an Arduino Mega 2560 development board which is con-
nected to a 32 × 32 RGB LED matrix. The “balls” are pixels which “fall” from the top
with a speed that can be input by the user. If it encounters a “nail” in its path, then, with
the use of a random number generator, we can decide which way it should bounce (0 for
left or 1 for right).
The user can operate the tool in three ways.
a)
based on true random numbers created via hardware. The resulting number is only
one bit, which results from sampling an unconnected analog input. The sampled
signal is a random noise, which some refer to as “atmospheric” noise, whereas
others consider it to be the thermal noise resulting from the semiconductors found
in the circuit. The Arduino Mega uses a ten bit resolution to sample the analog input
voltage which can be read as a real number using the analogRead() function. We can
only use the least signiﬁcant bit, which can be determined by using some bitwise
operations, or as the remainder after dividing by two.
b) based on software-generated pseudo-random numbers. We use the random(min,
max) function of Arduino, which uses mathematical operations to produce a real
numberbetweenthemin andmax-1values(theselimitsare0and2inourcase).These
are only pseudo-random numbers, which create a sequence of numbers in uniform
distribution and always in the same order. In order to avoid starting the sequence at
the same point (which could lead to identical results despite the random numbers),
we can alter which point to access the sequence via the randomSeed() function. We
can make this truly random by using an integer seed from an unconnected analog
reading as a parameter for the randomSeed() function.
c)
also based on software-generated pseudo-random numbers, however, we adjust the
probability of the ball’s possible paths depending on the inclination of the board.
For example, by raising the left part of the board, the balls are more likely to fall
to the right. The α inclination of the board is measured using an MMA7261QT
accelerometer sensor. The angle is that between the vertical axis of the sensor and
the direction of the gravitational acceleration (the inclination of the Galton board).

direction of the inclination.
If the Galton board has no inclination, the balls have an equal chance of bouncing
off to the left or to the right (p = 0.5). This probability changes if the board is inclined:
p = 0.5 + sin α

3.2
The Operation of the Virtual Galton Board
Pressing the second button on the operation board (see Fig. 4) allows the user to switch
between the various modes of operation. This change only takes hold once the ball
reaches its cell. The change is signaled by the red LED in the top left-hand corner of the
board. The current mode is shown bottom right-hand corner. In mode c) the inclinometer
also lights up.
The animation can be stopped by pressing the ﬁrst button, which can also be used
to resume it. The third button increases the speed of the animation while the fourth
decreases it.
The matrix has two numbers: one is showing the number of balls that have rolled
down the board, whereas the second one indicates the difference between left and right
bounces. If the board is vertical, this second number approaches zero. If the number of
right bounces is greater, this number shows up in red, else in green.
The matrix includes a 10 × 10 table which shows the consecutive right and left
bounces in green and red pixels. If the board is vertical, these have an equal probability
of occurring, therefore the resulting pattern shows no sign of regularity and presents a
fairly homogenous distribution of a close to number of green and red dots.

Each cell contains a limited number of balls, so if one cell is ﬁlled, its height needs
to be reduced to scale. We can observe how closely the resulting pattern resembles the
shape of a bell curve.
After every 100th ball, the Arduino uses the serial point to output the number of
balls in each cell, which we can copy from the “Serial Monitor” of the Arduino’s IDE
program for further use: we can use it to plot the histograms of the frequencies, we can
calculate the empirical average and deviation of the distribution and we can use it for
statistical hypotheses. When using the “Serial monitor”, the required data transmission
rate is 9600 baud. This requires connecting the device’s USB cable to a PC.
4
Summary
We have decided to present a device of our own design which was created to provide
an intuitive demonstration of random processes. The goal of the intuitive demonstration
is to explain randomly occurring events: every randomly occurring event is usually
comprised of multiple, often unobservable simple events with random outcomes, which
have a certain probability of either occurring or not. The number of possible paths for
a ball bouncing between the nails increases towards the center of the board, mirroring
how the outcomes of random processes in nature have various probabilities of occurring
despite the simple “yes-no” events they are comprised, which have an equal probability
for either outcome.
Our device uses three approaches to demonstrate binomial distribution: a) hardware-
generated random numbers; b) software-generated random numbers; c) software-
generated random number, however, the probability of the balls bouncing off to the
left or to the right was determined by the inclination of the board. In the ﬁrst two modes,
the device demonstrates the kind of binomial distribution where the probabilities of the
ball bouncing to either side of the nail both equal p = 0.5. We can observe how closely
the resulting pattern resembles the shape of a bell curve; this is due to the fact that with
a large enough sample, binomial distribution trends towards normal distribution. The
third mode shows a skewed distribution, and this skew is due to the inclination of the
board, which simulates the balls rolling down an inclined surface.

in Education Through IoT
and Gamiﬁcation
Christos Rodosthenous1(B), Efstathios Mavrotheris1, Wolfgang Greller2,

Abstract. In this paper, we present our eﬀorts and plans for creating
environmental awareness towards plants and greenery, while educating
children and their teachers in ecological learning spaces. Our approach
aims to stimulate knowledge and appreciation of plants and the eﬀects of
plants in classrooms, oﬃces, homes and open learning spaces, which have
hitherto been undervalued. By promoting plant appreciation at young
ages and the use of plants for learning, we aim to lay the foundations for
wider environmental awareness and positive attitudes towards nature. In
parallel, we enhance the learning experience with advanced sensor and
Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, stimulating interactive learning via
gamiﬁcation. Utilising this technology-enhanced approach with gamiﬁed
data sets, pupils will not only learn basic facts about plants, but also
learn about the needed care and responsibilities towards them, in order
to establish a wide-ranging plant supported school climate. Towards that
goal, we describe a number of gamiﬁcation elements in the context of
smart IoT planters and an accompanying visualisation dashboard.
Keywords: Environmental education · Gamiﬁcation · IoT
1
Introduction
In this paper, we present our eﬀorts and plans for creating environmental aware-
ness towards plants and greenery, educating young children and their teachers
in ecological learning spaces. The work presented in this paper is based on the
Erasmus+ project “Teaching Environmental Awareness with Smart Internet of
Things (IoT) Planters in Learning Spaces” (TEASPILS)1. The project’s ambi-
tion is to foster awareness of environmental issues in an educational context, e.g.,
1 https://teaspils.eu.
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 657–668, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_69

658
C. Rodosthenous et al.
the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the UN Agenda 2030. Unlike the
wider agenda of protecting natural habitats like global rainforests, our approach
aims to stimulate knowledge and appreciation of plants close to the people con-
cerned, i.e. in urban indoor environments, especially given that the eﬀects of
plants in classrooms, oﬃces, homes and open learning spaces have hitherto been
undervalued (cf. [2]).
In our work, we target young students mainly from primary and secondary
education levels, and facilitate their learning about plants in their immediate
vicinity. Typically, plants are seldomly placed in classrooms or seminar rooms,
and, even if, they usually just have a passive role as decorative items. By contrast,
it is our objective to put these plants into active use as live learning objects that
support a variety of learning activities. With this promotion of plant appreciation
at a young age, our intention is to lay the foundations of much wider protective
attitudes of natural and artiﬁcial ﬂora (and fauna) (cf. [9,20]). Furthermore, we
enhance the learning experience with live indoor plants by involving up-to-date
sensor and IoT technologies to stimulate new ways of interactive environmental
learning [17,18] and gamiﬁcation.
Utilising this technology-enhanced approach with a variety of IoT sensors
and visualisations, young students will not only learn basic facts about plants,
but also about the needed caring towards them. We use the cascading approach
via educational leaders, lecturers, primary and secondary school teachers and
support staﬀto establish a wide-ranging plant supported school climate. Towards
that goal, we apply innovative pedagogical techniques and learning scenarios,
while, at the same time, we aim to increase the learners’ engagement with a
number of gamiﬁcation elements that can be applied both in the context of
the smart IoT planters and of the accompanying online visualisation dashboard.
Furthermore, we also propose a gamiﬁcation approach for the teachers’ training,
which is realised through a Learning Management System (LMS) implemented
in Moodle.
In the sections below, we describe the current state of the project outputs
and how our pedagogical approach utilizes gamiﬁcation elements along with
digital sensor measurements, for increasing environmental awareness purposes.
Gamiﬁcation [3] is the process of applying game design elements in non-game
contexts (e.g., classroom, training, marketing, ﬁtness apps) with the purpose
to engage and motivate users towards a task, by integrating elements of fun,
challenge, and competition. The main research question we are exploring is how
we can use gamiﬁcation to promote and foster awareness of environmental issues
in an educational context and ﬁt this into the TEASPILS pedagogic model.
To facilitate plant speciﬁc insights on a number of indicators, we developed a
speciﬁc sensor instrument, called “Spike” (Smart IoT planter), which measures
continuously a number of parameters of the indoor plants and room environ-
ment. This internet connected device collects data in real time about the room
climate, such as CO2 levels, light and soil temperature. These data are stored
locally as well as in the cloud, and are available for presentation via dashboard
visualisations in real time. This IoT technology allows for interesting gamiﬁcation

Environmental Awareness in Education Through IoT and Gamiﬁcation
659
settings to be explored. In this paper, we speciﬁcally discuss how plant related
data has the potential for pupils to reﬂect on their surrounding air quality and
social climate in a learning space that is shared by plants and humans. We imple-
ment game mechanics as a motivating stimulant and scaﬀold for learning related
to environmental concerns and topics, helping to trigger wider discussions and
learning activities on the eﬀects of plants on human health and well-being, while,
at the same time, fostering digital skills and green competences.
An example of such an approach is the mapping of sensor data, like light and
temperature to plant feelings/needs, such as whether the plant is thirsty, happy
or suﬀocating. This approach will allow pupils to explore and receive feedback
from the plant directly and will lead to a number of innovative learning scenarios.
2
The TEASPILS Ecosystem
To develop environmental awareness among teachers and pupils, we focus on
three main tools which are part of the core outputs of the TEASPILS project: 1)
the design and piloting of Smart IoT planters in the classroom, 2) the creation of
a visualisation dashboard to present sensor data, and, 3) the training of educators
in the utilisation of indoor plants and sensor equipment in teaching and learning
activities, using a Small Private Online Course (SPOC). Furthermore, we are
designing a gamiﬁcation framework to enhance the use of these tools, by applying
gamiﬁcation elements to increase the engagement and interest of learners.
2.1
The Spike
A systematic design process that took into consideration a great number of ped-
agogic and usability issues, such as health and safety aspects of sensitive elec-
trical equipment, connectivity and timing of sensor measurements, reproduction
cost, error reporting, and suitability for use in primary, secondary, and tertiary
classrooms, led to the ﬁrst prototype of the Spike instrument being released for
evaluation.
This IoT system (cf. Fig. 1) includes diﬀerent sensors that measure the state
of the soil and the environment in which they are installed. The data is saved
on an SD-CARD and is also uploaded to a cloud platform. There are diﬀerent
channels to access the sensor data: 1) extracting the data from the SD-CARD
and interpreting it in a spreadsheet (e.g., csv ﬁle); 2) importing the data into a
dashboard that provides visualisation of trends; 3) using a chat to obtain instant
sensor measurements (Telegram bot for mobile or desktop). The system includes
a ring of LEDs that represents the diﬀerent variables collected by the sensors
by means of color codes. In addition, the system includes an OLED display that
numerically represents the latest measurements collected by the sensors on a
single screen.
The system design phase was accompanied by the ﬁrst implementation of
the gamiﬁcation framework that enhances the train-the-educators experience
in a TEASPILS led environmental training course (SPOC), during the winter

660
C. Rodosthenous et al.
Fig. 1. Spike’s controls and sensors on the “roof”, and the Telegram bot screen (left).
term of 2021. The next step in this process will include the creation of game-
based learning experiences and learning activities involving indoor plants and
ambient sensor technologies. This is further enhanced with IoT support to enable
interaction and dialogue between human learners and plants [19]. Subject speciﬁc
learning activities are being developed as inspirations and transferable learning
designs, suited for diﬀerent pupil ages and at diﬀerent levels of complexity. It is
anticipated that these combined strategies of real live plants, sensor technology
and gamiﬁcation in cross-disciplinary learning will foster greater interest and
awareness of environmental topics at all levels of education. The system will be
pilot tested in schools in diﬀerent European countries from the autumn 2022
onwards.
2.2
The Online Course
One of the outcomes of the TEASPILS project is a Small Private Online Course
(SPOC) which is used for training the teachers who will use the tools and meth-
ods delivered by the project in their own teaching. The SPOC was oﬀered to 30
participants between September 2021 and February 2022. The participants of
the SPOC had the chance to attend 5 synchronous sessions of approximately 2 h
each, including topics such as plant care requirements, the intrinsic relationship
between plants humans and society, pedagogic action research, the utilisation of
IoT sensors and visualisation technologies, and more.
During the SPOC, we applied a number of gamiﬁcation mechanisms such
as badges, points, levels, leaderboards and certiﬁcates to engage teachers while
attending the course. These game mechanics where connected to activities and
tasks in the elearning platform based on the Moodle LMS with the addition of
specialised plugins. The content of the SPOC and the gamiﬁcation mechanisms
applied are presented in the previous work of [14].

Environmental Awareness in Education Through IoT and Gamiﬁcation
661
The SPOC will be used as the base for developing an Open Online Course
where everyone will be welcome to join and learn about the tools developed and
how these tools can be incorporated in the educational process.
2.3
The Dashboard
The visualisation dashboard presents analytics and raw data collected by the
“smart IoT planters” to support learning activities that promote understand-
ing of environmental variables. The dashboard is a web application which is
connected with the smart IoT planters and receives data from them. These data
can then be presented in intuitive graphical formats (e.g., graphs, thermometers,
etc.).
2.4
Learning Analytics
Learning Analytics (LA) is by now an established approach to use learning traces
that users leave behind in electronic learning environments to infer knowledge
and insights into a learner’s progression along various learning paths for the pur-
pose of improving learning (cf. [4,15,23]). In our context, it oﬀers the possibility
to triangulate learning with plant data and environmental measurements (e.g.,
air quality), so as to provide a more holistic picture on the interplay between
plants and humans in a shared indoor learning space. From this approach, cer-
tain insights on pupil and teacher well-being can be obtained (cf. [6]), and more
importantly, can be used in teaching.
3
Towards a Gamiﬁcation Framework
In this section, we present our approach for providing the mechanism to increase
user engagement and make learning more interesting and fun. We present a
gamiﬁcation framework which focuses on the TEASPLIS ecosystem presented
in Sect. 2 of this work and the user type model presented by [22]. The idea is
to propose actions targeted to speciﬁc user types based on the developed tools,
i.e., the Spike, the dashboard, and the gamiﬁcation elements aiming to increase
the engagement of learners.
In particular, the gamiﬁcation framework utilises the three main outputs of
the TEASPILS ecosystem, using the collected datasets from the various ambi-
ent technologies and sensors as they oﬀer themselves for devising quantitative
gaming strategies, such as leaderboards, points, levels and other competitions
between pupils caring for their plants. The idea behind this work is to make
sensor data and the use of IoT and data visualisation technologies in plant care
interesting and engaging also to younger pupils (primary level). Gaming theory
will be used to create a framework of pedagogic models that can be used in
environmental teaching activities. The approach taken by the research team is
two-fold: At the implementation level, a virtual training course for educators
was created and hosted the materials developed in the form of a SPOC, which

662
C. Rodosthenous et al.
will eventually lead to a self-study Open Online Course. In the SPOC, a number
of gamiﬁcation elements were integrated and piloted with the participants. The
second phase aims to generate a theoretical gamiﬁcation framework for environ-
mental learning based on the analysis of the data from the IoT devices used
in the classroom. This framework will also be consolidated into the professional
development course as a sustainable pedagogic model including assessment pat-
terns to inform future adoption and application in ordinary teaching scenarios,
from primary to tertiary levels.
The User Type Model. In the work of [22], six user types are identiﬁed
based on their motivation: Socialisers are motivated by Relatedness, Free
Spirits who are motivated by Autonomy and self-expression, Achievers who
are motivated by Mastery, Philanthropists who are motivated by Purpose and
Meaning (Altruism), Players who are motivated by Rewards, and Disruptors
who are motivated by Change. These user types can be identiﬁed using a stan-
dardised questionnaire and based on the type, speciﬁc gamiﬁcation elements can
be applied which will be more beneﬁcial for that speciﬁc user type.
An this point, it is also important to clarify that gamiﬁcation does not always
bring the desired results [1,21]. There are cases where learners are discouraged
when they cannot achieve the desired targets, which could lead to demotivated
learners.
3.1
Gamiﬁcation Mechanics
Gamiﬁcation has been widely used in various domains for increasing engagement
and interest towards a non-game environment/system. In the educational context
it has been used in courses for teaching programming languages [12], medical
education [7], and in higher education [24]. The work of [10] which is relevant to
our work, explores the use of gamiﬁcation and how it aﬀects pro-environmental
behavioral change. They conclude that “. . . gamiﬁcation approaches have the
potential to educate and encourage pro-environmental behavioral change, as long
as they combine in their design extrinsic and intrinsic motivational elements,
short-term and long-term drivers, and game attributes that encourage taking
action in real life”. Our aim is to develop a gamiﬁcation framework which will
be applied on all aspects of the project, i.e., the SPOC, the Dashboard, and the
Spike, and provide a holistic approach which can be utilised by teachers.
Gamifying the Spike. A major aspect of the project is the use of the Spike in a
classroom setup where pupils will use it to take measurements and interact with
the plant(s). The gamiﬁcation framework can ﬁnd application either by directly
integrating with the Spike, the accompanying Telegram bot or in a physical
classroom modality (tech-less). As we presented in Sect. 2.1, the Spike is one of
the tools used to record sensor data and use them in a learning scenario. This
leaves the door open to a number of gamiﬁcation mechanisms, such as badges,
leaderboards, quests, certiﬁcates, gifts, etc.

mapping with the monitoring of Spike sensor values, visual observations by pupils

are free to expand and connect with other learning activities suitable for their

Gamifying Learning Analytics. Learning Analytics data can be used as a

basis can be enhanced (e.g., watering, checking, data readout). The Spike’s IoT
chatbot feature can initiate reﬂections about the well-being of pupils and plants
in the same environment. They could feel hot or cold, dry or wet, lacking fresh
air, etc. In this playful way, it is possible that learners identify more directly
with living plants in their immediate surroundings. Rather than creating a seri-
ous game simulation [16], we are using live plants as the learning object for
discovery learning.
Moreover, pupils can be given challenges and can be asked to compete against
other pupils by comparing the visualisations of the plant-related data in the
dashboard tool, which displays the graphs showing the changes and states of the
respective indoor climate and soil. Naturally, each plant species requires certain
conditions to thrive and grow. To ﬁnd the optimal settings and thresholds can
be one competitive task for pupils, and can be awarded with badges or points.
Furthermore, the consistency in delivering optimal conditions to the selected
plant over a longer period of time, can result in further incentives being handed
out. Thus, the utilisation of Learning Analytics engagement patterns paired with
gamiﬁcation is a good way to bring learners to reﬂect on their own knowledge
and competences regarding plants (their “green thumb” level) and study nat-
ural causal eﬀects (like high CO2 levels leading to fatigue). Additionally, they
are beneﬁting from enhancing their interpretation of visualisations and graphs,
structure discovery, relationship mining, and prediction [11].
Taking care of and responsibility for plants is another objective of our work.
The collected plant datasets and the interactive IoT elements of our Spike tool
lend themselves well for gamiﬁcation. This roughly follows the “Tamagotchi”
approach [8] were players willingly dedicated time, attention, and emotions to a
virtual pet - in our case a real potted plant. The higher the level of interaction
and care each pupil provides for their plant, the more this will be reﬂected in
their respective learning analytics datasets. It is our expectation that this also
leads to higher levels of appreciation of natural ﬂora in general (cf. [5,9]).
Gamifying the Dashboard. Gamiﬁcation elements can also ﬁnd application
in the dashboard. Figure 2 illustrates a suggested approach for gamifying the
dashboard with simple game elements such as a leaderboard, points, progress
bar and graphics to promote aesthetics.

666
C. Rodosthenous et al.
Fig. 2. A demo of a featured gamiﬁed version of the Dashboard where the plant status
and the leaderboard are depicted on the left, the progress bar and the current mission
are depicted in the centre and the task list is shown on the right.
Gamiﬁcation does not only need to be applied using technological means,
but it can be used successfully without any. Based on the learning activities
provided, a set of game mechanics can be used to promote engagement towards
a learning activity.
4
Conclusion
In this paper we describe our eﬀorts for delivering an innovative educational pro-
gram to increase environmental awareness through IoT and Gamiﬁcation, in the
context of the Erasmus+ Project TEASPILS. The approach followed involves
both the use of IoT technologies and a pedagogic framework which includes a
gamiﬁcation approach in order to increase the engagement and interest of learn-
ers to the program. This ﬁrst version of the gamiﬁcation framework was originally
presented in the Project’s Teachers’ Training Workshop and subsequently teach-
ers were invited to design new learning activities using gamiﬁcation mechanics.
These activities were uploaded to the ILDE+ platform2 which is accessible to
everyone interested. The platform is part of the TEASPILS ecosystem and pro-
vides a collection of short learning designs on how to use plants in teaching.
Future versions of the gamiﬁcation framework will include more actions and
activities and their corresponding game mechanics, based on the feedback we
2 https://ildeplus.upf.edu/teaspils/.

will get from the pilot period at schools. The gamiﬁcation framework presented
in this work is limited to the IoT smart planter and the dashboard and does
not refer to game mechanics that could be included in the Open Online Course
scheduled for release at the end of the project.

Sustainability Development Goals in English
for Speciﬁc Purposes
G. N. Fakhretdinova1(B)
, L. M. Zinnatullina1
, M. A. Mayakina2
,
F. T. Galeeva1
, and R. S. Valeeva1
1 Kazan National Research Technological University, Kazan, Russia
gulnaz_khamidull@mail.ru
2 Ivanovo State University, Ivanovo, Russia
Abstract. This paper discusses implementing Sustainability Development Goals
into English for Speciﬁc purpose course based on Education for Sustainable
Development (ESD) learning outcomes and the European Clothing Action Plan.
ESD develops competencies that empower people to be responsible for their own
actions,consideringcurrentandfuturesocial,cultural,economic,andenvironmen-
tal consequences on a local and global scale. This study includes textile engineer-
ing students English language curriculum and course content that is constructed in
such a way that it becomes an ideal platform for growing green movement aware-
ness. The key outcomes are connected to the learning objectives of the study
in three domains: cognitive, socio-emotional and behavioral. Cognitive learning
objectives are achieved when students learn the concept of sustainable produc-
tion in the textile industry and understand how their individual lifestyle in design
and clothing inﬂuences the environment. Socio-emotional objectives in learning
assume that students learn various ways of encouraging local industrial compa-
nies to shift toward more sustainable forms and communicate in English the need
for sustainable practices in textile production. Behavioral learning objectives can
be achieved when students identify opportunities in their local communities for
greener approaches to production.
Keywords: Sustainable development · English lesson content · Textile
engineering students
1
Introduction
1.1
Background
This study presents the experience of incorporating sustainable development principles
into a foreign language classroom. Why is it important? There are several reasons for
that. Our syllabus states that a language classroom is a place where students should
be able to discuss various topics, participate in debates and deliver presentations on
real-world problems including science, engineering, environment and economy [1–3].
Because of the rapid growth of the world population, people may face a shortage of
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 669–675, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_70

670
G. N. Fakhretdinova et al.
food, fresh water and other resources, which is a main concern for all of us, including
educators and students.
In 2015, the UN adopted the new Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for 2015–
2030 to address the complex global challenges of our time. One of the key elements in the
2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development is Education for Sustainable Development
(ESD). Another important document is the Education 2030 Framework for Action, which
is based on Sustainable Development Goal 4 that targets to ensure inclusive and equitable
quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all [4].
The ESD framework is used as a guide for hundreds of higher education institutions
to redesign curricula around sustainability principles. ESD aims at developing com-
petencies that empower individuals to reﬂect on their own actions, considering their
current and future social, cultural, economic and environmental impacts, from a local
and global perspective. In this study, these individuals are engineering students who
refer to sustainability issues in English language classrooms and this classroom content
is designed in a way that it becomes a perfect platform to grow the consciousness of the
green movement.
Since the curriculum excludes any content related to sustainability development
goals, we decided to integrate sustainability topics by developing learning materials
based on learning objectives for ESD, EU Clothing Action plan and research in this
ﬁeld.
1.2
Literature Review
The current studies show that there are numerous attempts at implementing Sustainable
Development Goals in education and developing students’ awareness on this issue [5–
7]. Some researchers have analyzed how SDGs are incorporated at the university level
and they pointed at the content of the courses based on SDGs [8–10]. Most authors
acknowledge the importance of the higher education institution’s role in implementing
SDGs [11–13].Initially, ESD was focused more on the interaction between people and
nature and environment-related issues. Nowadays, the main concern is applying SDGs
in such disciplines as history, mathematics, and foreign languages.
The representation of the SDGs in the English language syllabus and textbooks was
investigatedbydifferenteducators[14–16].Ifwelookattheforeignlanguagecontext,the
emphasis is placed on interdisciplinary curriculum design, when knowledge is provided
from different ﬁelds. The learning content in language class covers local and global
issues, nature conservation activities, biodiversity, modern economic processes, cultural
differences, intercultural communication etc. [17–22]. As research state, the learning
outcomes don’t imply only language learning, but also the skills, which students acquire
during the sustainable development education process [16, 23].
2
Methodology
The study was conducted with undergraduate students, who are getting their bachelor’s
degrees in apparel and textile design. They study English for 3 semesters, where the
third semester is English for speciﬁc purposes. It is quite challenging to cover all 17

Sustainability Development Goals in English
671
sustainability issues in one semester, so we have developed those related to their major:
green textile, environmentally-friendly materials, eco-fashion, sustainable production in
thetextileindustry,EUexperienceingreentechnologies,etc.Thesetopicsarewell-suited
to the students and focus on the language as well.
Teaching future textile engineers about the environment, green production and sus-
tainable consumption is based on Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL).
Integrating such content into the curriculum helps create interaction between students,
where teaching becomes more learner-centered rather than teacher-centered. Problem
orientation, interdisciplinary approach, and focus on a content point make it possible
to develop key competences needed for promoting sustainable development inside and
outside the classroom. We set speciﬁc learning objectives described in the cognitive,
socio-emotional and behavioral domains based on the Action plan for ESD.
3
Results and Discussion
Achieving SDGs in foreign language classroom is possible through a transdisciplinary
approach. Students’ major ﬁelds of studies should be taken into consideration when
language educators develop course outline and learning assets. Since our second-year
students major in textile engineering, we based our course curriculum and module frame-
work on learning objectives for achieving the SDGs and EU Clothing Action plan and
other research in this ﬁeld.
Education for Sustainable Development develops key competences for sustainability
and speciﬁc learning outcomes that can be integrated into the English for speciﬁc pur-
poses curriculum. Researchers [24–27] state, the following key competencies as crucial
to advance sustainable development:
• Systems thinking competency: the ability to recognize and understand relationships,
analyze complex systems;
• Anticipatory competency: the ability to understand and evaluate multiple futures –
possible, probable and desirable;
• Normative competency: the ability to understand and reﬂect on the norms and values
and negotiate sustainability values, principles and goals;
• Strategic competency: the ability to collectively develop and implement innovative
actions that further sustainability at the local level and further aﬁeld
• Collaboration competency: the ability to learn from others, understand and respect
the needs and actions of others;
• Critical thinking competency: the ability to question norms, practices and opinions,
reﬂect on own one’s values, perceptions and actions;
• Self-awareness competency: the ability to reﬂect on one’s own role in the local
community and global society, continually evaluate and further motivate one’s actions
• Integratedproblem-solvingcompetency:theabilitytoapplydifferentproblem-solving
frameworks to complex sustainability problems and develop viable, inclusive and
equitable solution options that promote sustainable development.
Speciﬁc learning objectives for all SDGs are described in the cognitive, socio-
emotional and behavioral domains.

672
G. N. Fakhretdinova et al.
• The cognitive domain comprises knowledge and thinking skills necessary to better
understand the SDGs and challenges in achieving it.
• The socio-emotional domain includes social skills that enable learners to collaborate,
negotiate and communicate to promote the SDGs as well as self-reﬂection skills,
values, attitudes and motivations that enable learners to develop them.
• The behavioral domain describes action competencies [4].
The European Clothing Action Plan is a project brining environmental and economic
beneﬁts to the clothing sector and addresses clothing sustainability. Action plan’s app-
roach encompasses sustainable design, production, consumption, recycling and has 8
action areas:
1. Inﬂuencing design practices through the Design for Longevity.
2. Implementing more sustainable ﬁbers into production
3. Making production processes focusing on reducing and reusing material waste
4. Inﬂuencing public procurement
5. Engaging European consumers to use and dispose of their garments more sustainably
6. Engaging young consumers
7. Improving textile collections
8. Integrating recycled ﬁbers [28].
The key course outcomes are connected to the learning objectives for SDGs and their
incorporation into the language environment. We consider learning objectives in three
domains: cognitive, socio-emotional and behavioral.
Cognitive learning objectives are achieved when:
• students learn the concept of sustainable production in the textile industry and under-
stand how their individual lifestyle (in design and clothing) inﬂuences the environment
and they can read and speak about it;
• students know about the concepts of sustained, inclusive and sustainable growth, full
and productive employment, and decent work in the textile industry and they can
discuss it with their peers in English;
• learners understand the local, national and global challenges in achieving sustainabil-
ity in textile infrastructure and they are familiar with the vocabulary in English to
express themselves;
• students are aware of new opportunities and markets for sustainability innovation in
textile and apparel design and they can present at least one aspect in English.
Socio-emotional objectives in learning assume that:
• students learn various ways of encouraging local industrial companies to shift toward
more sustainable forms and using appropriate vocabulary can communicate in English
the need for sustainable practices in textile production;
• learners can provide argument in English for sustainable, resilient and inclusive
infrastructure in their local area and nationwide;

Sustainability Development Goals in English
673
Behavioral learning objectives can be achieved when:
• students identify opportunities in their local communities for greener approaches to
production and can talk about them in English using the necessary words and phrases;
• learners can discuss innovation and the development of sustainable enterprises to
respond to countries’ industrial needs in the target language.
The suggested topics based on SDGs:
– environmental and social impacts of textile production and consumption;
– waste management in the textile industry: prevention, reduction, recycling, reuse;
– sustainable clothing
– green textile;
– gender inequality in the textile industry;
– design for longevity
– recycled ﬁbers
The learning approaches and methods we used were role-playing, developing busi-
ness plans for the local textile industry aimed at reducing waste, developing a project
exploring one form of either the physical or social infrastructure in the textile indus-
try, developing an enquiry-based project “Is all innovation good?”, conducting scenario
analyses for green production in textile, creating apparel portfolios that contain recycled
apparel, etc.
4
Conclusion
Sustainability is a relevant issue and applicable to engineering students. Education for
Sustainable Development can achieve the SDGs by developing key sustainability com-
petencies that are needed to deal with different sustainability challenges and to relate the
different SDGs to each other. Besides, Education for Sustainable Development can equip
learners with the speciﬁc cognitive, socio-emotional and behavioral learning outcomes
that enable them to deal with the particular challenges of each SDG. In our study we take
a step to create the curriculum having in mind these speciﬁc ESD learning outcomes
and the European Clothing Action Plan. Integrating the curriculum into the learning
process contributes to the achievement of the sustainability development goals of textile
engineering students.

Role, Audience, Format, and Topic Strategy
in the Improvement of the Writing Skill
Lorena Fernanda Parra Gavilánez(B)
, Jennifer Manzano Aguilar
,
and Ximena Alexandra Calero Sánchez
English Teaching Program, Faculty of Education, Universidad Técnica de Ambato, Ambato,
Ecuador
{lparra,jmanzano3982,xcalero}@uta.edu.ec
Abstract. Writing is considered as one of the most complicated skills that learners
present when learning English as a Foreign Language. Many learners bear in mind
a lot of ideas, but they do not know how to express them. For this reason, professors
have the need to implement engaging writing techniques to enhance students to
perform meaningful texts correctly by using their originality and creativity. Thus,
the present research work sought to study the efﬁcacy of Role, Audience, Format
and topic strategy in writing skill of university students who want to become future
English teachers. To carry out this investigation, a pre-experimental design was
performed in a single group of 36 participants who were required to take a survey to
diagnose their current writing perception. A pretest and posttest from Preliminary
English test (PET) was applied to the learners to compare their advance after
and before the implementation of the treatment. The ﬁndings demonstrated that
students improved their writing performance.
Keywords: RAFT strategy · Writing skill
1
Introduction
Communication has become of paramount importance among different cultures and
societies. To make possible communication, a language is needed as it permits indi-
viduals to convey messages and interact each other. In today’s globalizing era, most
people use and know at least one more language excluding their mother tongue owing to
their personal, academic, or professional needs, e.g. English language usage [1]. English
language has become crucial mainly in communities where it is not extensively spoken
in daily routines, and for using this language, individuals require to skill in speaking,
reading, writing, and listening [2]. Nevertheless, the majority of learners have to commu-
nicate through writing. Writing allows people to express their points of views, opinions,
feelings, etc., without the need of meeting to communicate [3]. Nonetheless, this skill is
considered as one of the most complicated to operate [4].
Writing has a differentiating setting in language instruction due to its learning system
involves plentiful comprehension and practice to master it as its spelling system differs to
its pronunciation [5]. Writing aptitude is a way to transmit ideas that is developed through

a non-natural process as individuals need to recognize some grammatical patterns and
structures that language requires to use while writing [6].
In Ecuador, writing practice as part of English as Foreign Language has been imple-
mented in teaching process to students from elementary schools to colleges [7]; in which
English purposes are aligned to the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR)
for attaining the proﬁciency [8]. Nevertheless, most of learners present difﬁculties in
writing practice on account of its complexity when using vocabulary and grammati-
cal structures of the language. The most considerable trouble students face in writing
development is ideas’ organization as they focus more in using grammar correctly [9].
For ﬁxing learners’ writing difﬁculties, there are many techniques that help both
teachers and students to facilitate their teaching- learning process when using English
language having classes more interesting and interactive. Due to their variety, each
strategy is carried out in a speciﬁc way but in general all of them play the role of
guiding students to reach their educational purposes [10]. The principal problem is that
traditional methodology is mostly used by the majority of teachers. For this reason,
writing strategies are needed to use in class in order to capitalize students’ interest for
easing their writing performance.
Accordingly, this investigation intends to analyze whether or not a writing strategy
improves the students’ writing development. The researchers applied Role, Audience,
Format and Topic strategy in a serie of sessions where key aspects were studied. The
research questions of this work were:
1. What are the student’s perceptions about writing performance?
2. How does the use of Role, Audience, Format, and Topic strategy inﬂuence in writing
skill performance?
2
Literature Review
Role, Audience, Format and Topic is a pre-writing strategy for facing some learners’
writingproblems.Thistechniqueenhancescreativitywhencreatingtextsusingorganized
steps [11]. Its purpose centers on promoting students to recognize important components
that a writing should involve like the writer role, the audience to address the text, its
format of type, and the writing topic [12]. Once identiﬁed the topic, students should think
in possible vocabulary and some other essential information to be used in their texts [13].
Moreover, a good writer encourages to the readers (audience) the topic awareness so they
are interested in continue reading the written work [14]; and depending the audience,
the learner should consider what kind of language register (formal, informal, neutral) is
the most appropriate to use [15].
RAFT strategy aids learners to follow the structure of a writing process, hence it
provides four crucial components to consider [16]:
Role (R): The author of the writing. In this part students should understand what is their
role as writers.
Audience (A): The public or readers to which the text is directed to. The audience can
alter according to the writing instructions. It is considered as the most enjoyable part as
writers in most of the cases have the chance to choose interesting characters.

678
L. F. Parra Gavilánez et al.
Format (F): Type or structure of the writing to be used. In most of the cases, the writings’
instructions already give an speciﬁc format, but there are cases that learners can choose
depending on their needs.
Topic (T): The writing matter. Students need to identify the topic in order to achieve the
writing objective and also should be able to present logical and understandable writings.
3
Methodology
3.1
Participants
ThepopulationinvolvedinthisresearchstudywerethirtysixEFLundergraduatestudents
from third semester who took English subject in Pedagogía de los Idiomas Nacionales y
Extranjeros major at Universidad Técnica de Ambato. Twenty - nine female and seven
male students were part of this sample who were from 19 to 21 years old with an
Intermediate (B1) level of proﬁciency in accordance with the results obtained in the
placement test provided by Cambridge.
3.2
Research Design
Quantitative method was needed to conduct this practical research by using a t-test
technique and a survey. A pre-test/post-test pre-experimental design was applied to
examine students’ improvement on the writing skill. This research design was needed
to determine the inﬂuence of experimenting the RAFT strategy in the writing process.
In order to know the learner’s satisfaction of the writing skill, the learners completed a
survey based on Likert scale. Then, the writing section of the Preliminary English Test
(PET) provided by Cambridge Assessment English was used as a pre-test and post-test.
The survey was applied in order to identify whether students were familiar with
writing aspects and how often they practice this skill. The questionnaire of the survey
was validated by using Cronbach’s Alpha coefﬁcient test reaching a high reliability
average of 0.88/ 1.0, which is acceptable [17]. Following the survey, the next phase
was the application of the pretest to evaluate students’ writing level to ﬁnally apply the
posttest and compare both results to analyze the inﬂuence of Role, Audience, Format and
Topic strategy (cause) in the development of writing skill (effect) which was computed
through SPSS statistical program. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to verify the
hypothesis and interpret the ﬁndings of the pre-test and post-test averages with a 5% (α
= 0.05) level of error of signiﬁcance.
The last phase of the study used a rubric to assess and score students’ writing tasks
and determine if learners found useful RAFT strategy to develop their writing works. A
total of 20 points was the score of the rubric with four criteria including organization,
communicative achievement, content and language use in which 5 points were the score
of each parameter.
3.3
Data Collection Strategies
Thisresearchworkobtainedquantitativedataintwophases.Firstly,asurveywasdirected
to students to determine their current writing situation. Percentages and frequencies

4
Results and Discussion
The survey administered to learners highlighted their perception about writing aspects
which reﬂected their familiarization with this skill when practicing English Language.
The student’s writing current situation showed in the survey are described in Table 1
through statistical data.
Based on Table 1, a huge number of respondents own up their professor always or
often guides them when producing writing tasks (M = 4.11) as well as encourages them
the correct use of spelling, grammar, and punctuation (M = 4.28) through a writing
rubric to grade their tasks (M = 4.22). In addition, there is a smaller tendency of learners
that before creating the writing they ﬁrst identify its elements (M = 3.97) or develop a
brainstorming to plan it in a better way (M = 3.89). Ultimately, considering all existing
writings types, the descriptive writing is the most developed in class (M = 4.03).
