4.1
Pretest-Posttest Contrastive Results Analysis
According to Cambridge English, the writing test leads learners to report that they can
use vocabulary and structure correctly as well as be able to write different kind of English
texts. The writing parameters are used in part two of the writing section as observed in
the pre-test and post-test which are assessed through the suggested writing rubric.
Figure 2 demonstrates the pretest-posttest comparative writing results analysis of
learners that performed their writing tests on the use of Role, Audience, Format and Topic
strategy. Students’ content writings raised from 3.8 in the pre-test (conventional strategy)
to 4.8 in the posttest (RAFT strategy) getting as difference 1 point. The communicative
achievement improved from 4 to 4.7, and the organisation to plan in a more organized
way the writings increased from 2.7 to 3.8, respectively. Finally, students’ correct use
of language in writings reported an increase from 3.3 to 3.9. It is evident that learners’
results were better in the post- test after implementing Role, Audience, Format and Topic
strategy as an alternative to enhance writing aptitude.

In this investigation, it was possible to demonstrate that Role, Audience, Format
and Topic technique improved learners’ writing performance principally in its organi-
sation matching with previous studies which indicated that RAFT strategy helps to plan
ideas before developing the writing [18]. Additionally, learners created more original
and interesting writings as they used their imagination considering some parameters to
present a high quality writing like communicative achievement, organization, language
and content [19].
5
Conclusions
The application of innovative strategies that motivate and help learners to improve their
skills is essential in the teaching and learning process. This research has demonstrated
that the application of RAFT strategy for the development of the writing skill has pro-
vided positive results. It means that the teacher and learning roles together with the type
of audience, format and topic used in the learning process can contribute with positive
results to achieve the educational goals.

The Prospect of Inclusive Pedagogy
in Efﬁciency-Centric Governance Paradigm:
Business and Entrepreneurship Teachers’
Perspectives
Tarvo Niine(B)
, Merle Küttim
, and Kristin Semm
School of Business and Governance, Tallinn University of Technology, Tallinn, Estonia
tarvo.niine@taltech.ee
Abstract. Teachingincollegeentailsmanagingsubstantialtrade-offsacrossqual-
ity dimensions – broad perspective and linkages versus in-depth focus, functional
or cross-functional approach, workplace versus conceptual emphasis, efﬁciency,
ﬂexibility, student motivation, inclusion and leveraging diversity, learning uni-
formity or individuality etc. This paper focuses on teachers’ reﬂections on their
teaching in an environment characterized by dominant expectation of standardized
output-driven education. The aim of the paper is to explore how faculty members
and visiting staff of an international undergraduate business programme lever-
age elements of inclusive pedagogy in their teaching, what is their rationale for
it and in what elements are the perceived trade-offs substantial for the teacher
to feel discouraged in further development of inclusion. Interviews were carried
out with teachers of International business administration of TalTech, Estonia – a
programme with relatively high student diversity in race, culture and educational
background. The study comments on inclusive teaching practices that are avail-
able for integration more easily (such as learning design accounting for student
learning styles, diverse groupwork facilitation, group and peer grading) as well as
practices perceived to fall outside of teacher’s reach in routine teaching (such as
personalized student motivation management, accounting for diversity in students’
capabilities, individualized feedback). In sum, teachers appear to have a moderate
amount but limited degrees of freedom in implementing elements of inclusive
pedagogy provided this is in line with their teaching philosophy regardless of the
conﬁnes of efﬁciency-centric governance paradigm.
Keywords: Inclusive pedagogy · Teaching practices · Diversity in higher
education
1
Introduction
Inclusive pedagogy broadly intends to prioritize and enable learning for all students
regardless of their race, gender, abilities, special needs, cultural and socio-economic
background [1]. From a social constructivist perspective, classroom inclusion involves
academic and social dimension, and starts with negotiating norms and expectations
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 684–694, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_72

The Prospect of Inclusive Pedagogy
685
regarding the interaction and the roles of teachers and learners [2]. The internationaliza-
tion of higher education provides an environment suitable for addressing inclusivity as
student mobility leads to varied backgrounds of students in terms of language, cultural
and learning experiences [3]. However, embracing inclusive pedagogy in the higher
education setting poses challenges and trade-offs for the learners, teaching staff and
programme design. It contradicts with the dominating view of massiﬁcation of higher
education, and the neoliberal, performative and market-driven culture of academia that
emphasizes speed and efﬁciency [4]. Furthermore, teachers strive to promote active
engagement in learning and greater dialogue through various forms of active partic-
ipation, while student participation is culturally-constructed notion and there are no
universal solutions [5]. While multicultural education views the teacher as a cultural
transmitter [6], the teacher performance is difﬁcult to evaluate to identify good teaching
practice.
The aim of the paper is to explore how faculty members and visiting staff of an inter-
national undergraduate business programme leverage elements of inclusive pedagogy in
their teaching and in what elements are the perceived trade-offs substantial for the teacher
to feel discouraged. In the latter case, the most likely approach is to rely on standardiza-
tion and apply somewhat more mechanical approach of common, intended and easily
testable learning outcomes. In reality, there are few examples of extreme positioning on
such spectrum and mostly teachers tend to ﬁnd a balance that is suitable for their own
principles and attitudes, vision of teaching and perception of the expected dimensions of
the personal development of students. Of course, all of that would be on the next layer
of rationalization to be balanced with teacher’s available skills, time and motivation, not
to mention the views of other stakeholders, be it university administration, government
or (the perception of) the needs of the economy and labour market.
If there would be nothing but clear trade-offs between the two approaches, one
could visualize teaching development as walking a tightrope. This metaphor stems from
the assumption that there is a contradiction between inclusive pedagogy and the neo-
liberal perspective of universal course and programme design [4]. This approach would
suggest that everyteachingdevelopment decisionwouldimbalancethepictureandwould
assume the teacher to rethink the entire course. However, there is still arguably some
room to design teaching to be more inclusive without major trade-offs. The tightrope
metaphor proposes a clear dichotomy, but it is also possible that it is (at least partially)
a false dichotomy and this is the research problem of this study. There appears to be
a lack of studies that address the experiences of teachers as student engagement in the
international context has been studied more from students’ perspective [5]. This study
aims to contribute new ﬁndings to this gap.
This study does so by focusing on teachers of “International business administration”
undergraduate programme in TalTech School of Business and Governance, Estonia. On
one hand, the student body is rather diverse across continents and cultures, increasing the
potential effect from designing for inclusivity. On the other hand, the local governance
paradigm appears to be rather clearly emphasizing efﬁciency and standardization –
this can be proposed from the KPIs instated to the university and from those instated
by the university to all study programmes, as well as the general notion that higher
education is locally chronically underfunded so investment of every penny needs to be

686
T. Niine et al.
as efﬁcient as possible. The resource problem cannot currently be resolved by market
forces in Estonia as the country has in broad terms been running a state-funded tuition-
free higher education model since 2013. While the international programme in question
is not tuition-free, it arguably doesn’t change the overall ﬁnancing picture signiﬁcantly.
This paper, however, is not about speculating on the causal problems of the situation,
the economics of education in general nor on the possible solutions to the local case. The
comments only illustrate the presence of a pressing resource constraint. Approaching
the challenges to inclusivity from a global view, Lawrie et al. have pointed out that a lack
of systematic integration between teacher perspectives and management perspectives to
teaching is a frequent theme across universities [7].
Certainly, at least partially, inclusive teaching is not the teaching approach of least
cost, so this asks a question if the premium elements can be achieved based on the
self-motivation and mission perception of individual teachers, or, alternatively, are there
smart ways to get more with less to reconcile elements of inclusivity with efﬁciency.
How much is it possible for a program to have “cheap inclusivity” is perhaps a blunt
way of introducing this paper.
The teaching staff of the program is, while mainly local, increasing in interna-
tional members, covers various demographics and includes a broad mix of research,
pedagogical expertise, industry experience and entrepreneurship. The qualitative study
incorporates their experiences, attitudes and practices, related to both learning output
standardization as well as diversity and inclusion in the classroom.
It needs to be emphasized that while there is a narrower notion of inclusivity sug-
gesting focus on a subset of students with “special needs”, the term can be more broadly
used to refer to experiences of connectedness and belonging of all students [8]. It ought
to be noted that this paper treats diversity and inclusivity not as synonyms but rather the
former being an element and prerequisite of latter. One can suggest that diversity is a
more objective descriptive characteristic while inclusivity builds upon it pedagogically
to achieve additional learning outcomes as well as to unlock new perceptions of learning.
Concerning structure, the subsequent chapter provides an overview of inclusive ped-
agogy, addressing characteristics of diversity and inclusion in higher education. This
is followed by research methodology, after which results are presented and discussed
and conclusions drawn to better understand teaching challenges and learning practice in
multicultural classrooms.
2
Literature Review
Inclusive pedagogy aims to consider and enable learning for all students regardless of
their diverse characteristics and not only acknowledge it, but leverage it for higher degree
of learning. Taking diversity into account is envisioned to happen within the classroom
and curriculum, rather than before or outside of the course and programme design [1].
In inclusive pedagogy, the recognition of differences is related to acknowledging indi-
viduality rather than stigmatization and all students are assumed to have both common
and unique needs [4].
Inclusive pedagogy is closely related to constructivist approach to education, where
instead of the division between the provider and receiver of knowledge, the teacher

The Prospect of Inclusive Pedagogy
687
embodies the role of knowledge co-creator together with the students [2]. Previous stud-
ies have outlined various strategies for inclusive teaching. Inclusive strategies involve
pedagogical approaches such as integrating technology, adopting culturally responsive
material and initiating collaborative learning, addressing diverse motivation and goal
strategies of students by including students’ voice, providing them with a clear ratio-
nale for studying and fostering relatedness, and creating differentiated assessment that
provide equal opportunities to participate [9].
In more detail, inclusiveness entails becoming familiar with students’ prior edu-
cational contexts, signalling conﬁdence in the potential of students, being transparent
about expectations and learners’ success strategies, acknowledging diversity in class-
room and course content, using a variety of teaching techniques and employing inclusive
assessment techniques [1].
Success in the classroom, however, is not guaranteed (at least not in short-term) as
there is inconsistency and fragmentation in perceptions of inclusive pedagogies because
inclusion itself is philosophically contested and there are no quick remedies due to the
complexity of pedagogy [4]. In an international classroom, initiating active engage-
ment and collaborative learning to address students’ differences is seen as promoting
inclusion. Student participation can be seen, however, as context-speciﬁc, culturally con-
structed phenomenon. In Western universities, students’ initiative in their own learning
is encouraged and active participation is seen as demonstrating students’ learning in the
form of attentiveness to information or ideas. In Asian cultures, students tend to view
themselves more as apprentices, guided by their teachers, and participation is less about
spontaneous verbal production and more about overall attentiveness [5]. Furthermore,
it is not only about student view to engagement, but also how the teacher sees it in rela-
tion to his/her culture. As Meyer has noted, teaching in a more confrontational culture
(compared to the one where the teacher originates) can lead the teacher to question the
balance between acceptable debate and inappropriate attack against authority [10].
A commonly used means of fostering active engagement in learning is group work,
worth to be examined in greater detail. Poort et al. have pointed out that depending on
the differences at the level of the individual, culture, language, previous knowledge and
skills, the costs and beneﬁts for learners can vary [11]. The costs of group-work in inter-
national class-room has been noted to include: time and effort (invested in the process
e.g. to coordinate or compensate for lack of skills of team members), negative psycho-
logical states (own position in the group, contribution to the group), and compromising
at the expense of personal values (end-product below own standards, lack of collabora-
tion, stereotyping). While the beneﬁts can entail: attainment value (developing oneself
as global citizen, producing high-quality end-product, correcting stereotypes), intrinsic
value (enjoying the task), and utility value (developing traits for working in multicul-
tural setting, obtaining good grade, developing ﬁeld-speciﬁc competences, expanding
international network) [11].
Gibbs et al. have counselled that it is relatively easy to hastily assume the objectives of
inclusion being achieved via applying small technical or procedural changes to facilitate
participation (such as Padlet for student co-creation or sessions of “circle of discussion”),
whereas such activities don’t necessarily encourage students to engage in the broader,
critical reﬂection on inclusion [12]. While participation, both objectively and perceived

688
T. Niine et al.
emotionally, has certainly its own value, the following critical reﬂection of students can
be seen as one of the main prerequisites of achieving most types of learning outputs.
Participation without reﬂection might not provide many of the possible dimensions of
learning. Furthermore, arguably it is more difﬁcult for a teacher to design a proper
reﬂection phase rather than direct learning event to be experienced.
For a somewhat more unorthodox approach, Livingston-Galloway & Robinson-Neal
have recently proposed a model of Inclusive Pedagogy in Practice [13]. In the view of
this model, it is not competence development that is the cornerstone of education, but
instead relationship development.
Recently it has been proposed by Hodge et al. that the covid-19 pandemic has served
as a catalyst of implementing inclusive pedagogy. Their argument revolves around higher
accessibility to coursework, more individual nature of assignments and increased stu-
dent ownership of their learning, which can lead to a deeper understanding than purely
classroom-based instruction [14].
It appears suitable to conclude this section by referencing Moriña, who has recently
presented an overview on how a broad array of faculty members have approached inclu-
sive pedagogy. Even though the approaches are much diverse themselves, a central
theme is proposed: “learning should be active and student-centred” with also noting
that “learning should be participatory, active and fun” [15]. This focus would allow for
various methods, formats and technologies. In addition, also student emotions need to
be strategically managed in order to “create a classroom climate based on respect and
elements that highlight positive over negative aspects.” On emotional front, to believe
and trust all students is seen as a deﬁning characteristic of inclusive pedagogy [15].
3
Methodology
The study employed a qualitative research design. Interviews were conducted with teach-
ing faculty and visiting teachers of the undergraduate International business administra-
tion (IBA) programme at Tallinn University of Technology, Estonia. IBA is a well-
established 3-year 180 ECTS programme launched in 2004, awarded recently with
“EFMD Accredited” certiﬁcation. 90% of students are international with larger groups
originating from Finland, Russia, Bangladesh, Azerbaijan, Ukraine, etc. The annual
intake aim is around 80–90 students (with actual intake 40–60 during recent pandemic),
and with graduation rate approx. 60%. Typically, the programme admits 50% of more
promising applicants. Key characteristics of IBA are notable amount of elective courses
and a choice between four specializations to emphasize self-conscious path-setting.
Recent top-down developments on IBA programme have been focused on reﬁning
goal formulations and ILOs to increase coherence of programme and module aims with
course-speciﬁc goals and content and initiating teaching staff cooperation to improve the
thematic sequence and avoid overlap while maintaining value-adding linkages. Another
broad initiative has been to standardize expectations for course syllabi and the quality
of e-support on LMS Moodle. Teachers are typically free to pick preferred teaching
methods and initiate changes, but cooperation with programme director is expected for
quality assurance.
In total 26 IBA teachers (5 international, 21 local; 9 male, 17 female) participated
in the interviews from the total population of around 50 (excluding guest speakers for

The Prospect of Inclusive Pedagogy
689
shorter sessions). Maximum variation sampling was used covering all modules and spe-
cializations, both compulsory (e.g. business mathematics, micro economics, manage-
ment and leadership, marketing, ﬁnance, entrepreneurship, accounting, ethics, business
research methods, etc.) and elective courses (Estonian language and culture, economic
sociology, project management, developmental trends in economy, etc.), both senior
members with 10+ years of teaching experience on IBA as well as recent recruits.
Mostinterviewswereconductedinfocusgroups,whileafewwere1:1duetoschedul-
ing difﬁculties. The focus group interviews took place in spring 2020 and lasted 1.5–2.5
h. The interviews focused on the self-evaluation of teachers, followed by speciﬁc ques-
tions on personal arsenal of teaching and grading methods, teaching innovation, blending
theory and practice, student motivation, student diversity, student interactions, the role
of feedback and personal development targets. In this paper, a selection of more topically
relevant themes are presented. The interviews were analysed by using conventional con-
tent analysis [16]. After transcribing the interviews, the data was analysed in successive
steps: coding the data, linking the codes into concepts and merging concepts into broader
themes.
It is relevant to note that the data collection took place a few weeks before the start of
the pandemic. The following turbulent two years have brought about a lot of disruption,
but among it also a lot of tech-driven teaching development as well as a push to re-
evaluate teaching and learning strategies. A post-pandemic follow-up study is targeted
for 2023 to evaluate the changes on the topics dealt in this study.
4
Findings
The interview ﬁndings were sorted into two broader themes as presented in Table 1
– the concepts and factors perceived to encourage and motivate embracing diversity
and perceived trade-off factors, suggesting that in order to allow further leveraging
of inclusivity, other aspects of teaching or learning process or output are signiﬁcantly
negatively impacted.
The teachers overwhelmingly grant student motivation the critical role in the learning
process but with partially conﬂicting views. The most widespread learning motivation
drivers are perceived skill and knowledge applicability (intrinsic motivation) and prag-
matic piece-meal grading (extrinsic motivation). While students form a diverse spectrum
of their personal motivators, it seems that teachers usually tend to emphasize either one
or the other but not the full gamut. For example, some teachers explicitly advertise their
course in the beginning to explain the value proposition in most practical terms. In other
cases, teachers build elaborate scoring schemes to award easily obtainable rewards at
start and then move to rewarding routines not dissimilar to drug-dealers handing out
ﬁrst batches for free to drive habit and addiction. The problem with both approaches,
however, is that they are assuming certain commonality across students. For diversity-
based motivation management, a teacher would need to deal with learning motivation
on a much more individual basis. This tends to be empirically feasible only in case of
small groups and in elective courses. It appears possible to boost intrinsic motivation
as secondary capacity by “providing something of interest for each student”, such as
involving a series of guests from various ﬁelds related to the course content – but as

690
T. Niine et al.
every such activity demands time, it does not come without trade-offs in seeking opti-
mal use of available time. What appeared an interesting comment, some students tend to
be at times critical about guest speakers that they perceive boring – comparatively more
than in the case of “boring main teacher”, who at least can be assumed to have academic
authority.
Table 1. Aspects encouraging and discouraging inclusive pedagogy.
Inclusivity encouragement linkages
Inclusivity trade-offs
Student research supervision
Student motivation management
Student learning styles
Diversity of learner capabilities
Cultural diversity in groupwork
Individual feedback
Group grading
The “point games” of extrinsic motivation, although popular, can be seen as opposing
individuality (“turning students into hamsters”). In the study there was no evidence of
individualized extrinsic motivation and it can be suggested it would breach the barrier
of what an average student might consider fair. As long as grades are a signiﬁcant
motivating factor, even some categorized approaches (such as separate “language group
for beginners” and another one for “accustomed speakers”) can cause friction.
The relationship between inclusivity and entrepreneurial competence development
appears curious. The modern concept of entrepreneurship education, rather valued
among faculty members, is heavily reliant on regular learner reﬂection and self-
motivation. Advancing entrepreneurial competences would certainly make a student
more aware of oneself as well as the environment and would add dynamics by mentally
welcoming change. This would logically increase the diversity across the student body
in terms of personal aims and desired development directions. While this could be lever-
aged in powerful ways in the teaching process, it seems to again rely so much on the
concept of individuality that it would ask the teacher partially to apply personal tute-
lage, which, given cohort size, could perhaps be realized only in a very limited number
of applications. It does appears that the entrepreneurial paradigm of growth mind-set
is strongly at odds with the efﬁciency paradigm – students are (luckily) not becoming
bricks in the wall.
One could suggest that the “usual suspects” of leveraging individuality are internship
and thesis research supervision. Some teachers indeed make efforts in their supervision
to direct the study towards assisting thesis author’s personal growth and career oppor-
tunities. It is possible that the supervisor even takes additional motivation-related roles
(terms psychiatrist as well as cheerleader have been used in this context). However, this
approach appeared to be rather an exception than a rule based on our sample. In the
school in question, an average of 20h of supervisor effort per student is considered a
norm, which is still rather limited to fulﬁl all the expected roles. Another option is to form
thesis writing support groups of 3–5 students, which has some potential, as students can

The Prospect of Inclusive Pedagogy
691
witness how their peers ﬁnd meaning in their study, which in turn can reﬂect back. All
in all, thesis supervision is an area where efﬁciency and diversity can partially co-exist.
In terms of diverse capabilities, ensuring the optimal development of all student
clusters, let alone each individual, presents an extra obstacle of time and effort. Again,
the study observed two approaches. In one, the teacher focuses on less-capable students
to ensure their passing. As a result, more capable students are not sufﬁciently challenged.
Evenwhenextramaterialisprovided,itisonlyutilizedbyminorityofmotivatedstudents.
Apparently “optional” translates to “allowed to skip” for most students. It would need
a lot of focus on boosting learner intrinsic motivation to turn this outcome around,
which is possible, but again, the argument started with the premise that skill-wise overly
diverse student range demands teacher to focus on the lower end just to get them past the
minimum required hurdle. As a result, this provides higher passing rates as main merit,
with other virtues debatable.
In opposite approach, other teachers dedicate their main focus to the “stars”. While
it probably boosts teacher motivation, is valued by best students and results in great
supportive feedback (making the teacher feel justiﬁed), the lower end can be left to
struggle or even fail. This is less of an issue in many management and entrepreneurship
courses, but a possible pressing issue on courses with deeper level of functional focus,
especially if mathematics is concerned. Alas it appears an everlasting conundrum that
ﬁnance cannot be resolved with teamwork discussions – someone actually needs to
crunch the numbers. In courses where facts by nature dominate over opinions and the
goal is a proof or a single correct answer, rather than the process, leveraging diversity
is seen as a challenge. In terms of programme design, while students can choose a
specialisation according to their interests and to some extent also capabilities, all still
need to pass the same core courses (consisting of economic theory, introduction to
different areas of business). For some teachers, the students’ capability spectrum is the
prime case of “negative diversity” and often it is seen that attempting to reconcile the
two camps would end up “just teaching separate courses”.
Much similar is the case with providing individual feedback, which is seen as major
obstacle even in terms of select uniform ILOs, not to mention providing relevant feedback
accounting for student’s individual characteristics. Some teachers that are accustomed
to give more extensive feedback for student tasks pointed out they are doing it mainly
for the principle (the noble goal of quality assurance), not that it would make pragmatic
sense in terms of time management.
A strong segment of teachers appeared aware of students preferring various learning
styles – e.g. while some prefer reading the manual, others prefer active practical engage-
ment and yet other students may favour reﬂecting on the practice of others. This seems to
be a dimension of diversity, which is more manageable by teachers, as various learning
methods and tasks can cater for various combinations of learning styles. In Table 1, this
dimension is listed under encouragement column, because the extra effort assumed from
teacher to set up and keep reﬁning a mix of learning styles is not seen overly taxing and
the (mostly secondary) extra effort appears to pay quick dividend.
Teachers’ views to the role of cultural diversity were found quite dissimilar. On one
side, some teachers don’t want to or struggle to leverage diversity, stating that “most
students like to stick to their cultural bubble – Finns in one corner, Asians in other”.

692
T. Niine et al.
While others see it as a missed opportunity, even such more coherent clusters can also
be seen as beneﬁcial, as they might enable stronger in-group peer-learning. Then again
in other courses, the same students are active and productive in mixed groups. Not to
rush with blaming teacher’s ignorance, not all courses need to leverage cultural diversity
due to course characteristics (or at least this was the sentiment in the interviews) and
for more single-functional courses the relevance was deemed debatable. However in
broad terms, cultural mixing was seen as a valuable tool in teaching arsenal. If utilized
carefully (including conﬂict management and, when possible, adding safety nets to guard
against at least a few groups inevitably failing to reach meaningful cooperation), this
can boost engagement and peer-learning and ensuing motivation can easily replicate
and escalate. This can and has been extended, furthermore, outside of the programme,
to link international students with local learners in joint tasks - allowing international
students an easier access to local context (e.g. companies, business environment), and
local students the possibility of more internationalisation at home.
There appears a segment of teachers, typically of more functionally outlined courses,
who feel that proper student work ought to be individual and all grading similarly. How-
ever, many interviewees explicitly valued the interactions of students in group-work
activities, boosting not only communication skills but also cultural awareness, time
management, conﬂict management and, arguably, all types of management that are the
competences expected to be developed in a proper business school. Naturally, as long
as the majority of intended learning activities on a course are group activities, group
grading follows. For the opposition, one persistent argument seems to be the “freeload-
er” problem, claimed to be present in “every other group”, and proposedly allowing for
substantial injustice. However, quite starkly, the proponents of group grading pointed
out various pedagogical methods to overcome the problem. Group grading does not nec-
essarily mean the same grade for all members regardless of their effort or contribution,
as the interviews introduced a range of ways how to differentiate grading inside groups.
For all these cases, it appears that leveraging student diversity in this regard is an efﬁ-
cient teaching approach – broader and possibly deeper results obtained with economies
of scale. Overall this allows efﬁciently to balance student personal development with
standardized ILOs.
5
Discussion and Conclusion
The study pointed out some encouraging linkages that facilitate implementing elements
of inclusive pedagogy without prohibitive trade-offs, with possibly more, given the
limitations from the sample size, chosen method of focus group interviews and interview
length. Furthermore, three major obstacles were discussed keeping teaching staff away
from embracing diversity and inclusivity in a more complete manner.
The positive aspects allow to conclude that some teachers are motivated to include
diversity elements in their teaching style in a bottom-up fashion. Top-down, the school
doesn’t have a focal strategic preference on particular teaching approach while university
administration has mostly evaluated programmes more with efﬁciency-based metrics and
with quality being evaluated through a multitude of other ways before student and alumni
feedback. However, recently a broader push for problem-based learning has emerged,

The Prospect of Inclusive Pedagogy
693
which is ﬁtting with IBA program’s present diversity and allows the program students
to possible reap more beneﬁts and synergies than students on average local programs.
A teacher wanting to apply inclusive pedagogy and collaborative learning in broader
sense and larger capacity cannot escape some of the substantial trade-offs between
standardized and inclusive pedagogy in a business school. While some teachers feel that
a small portion of diversity-driven learning can be formulated as ILOs and integrated into
the current administrative system, much of the student personal development would in
contrast seem to struggle to ﬁt the fully normative framework of assessment and grading.
Some inclusive education goals appear difﬁcult even to formulate in a concise, speciﬁc
and measurable fashion, as commonly required from ILOs. Especially when the nature
of collaborative learning and active participation is speciﬁc to a particular set of students
[5].
Perhaps one way to reconcile the two paradigms is to turn to the term ILO itself and
note that such phrasing would logically also imply the existence of unintended learning
outcomes. Leaving space for such a construct would allow students at least in principle
be evaluated both based on a common standard as well as in terms of individual growth.
However, the interviews still make it clear that the systematic regulatory obstacle is
not the main discouragement of further spread of inclusive pedagogy. Given the reality
of a publicly funded higher education, which is the case of higher education in Estonia,
one cannot ignore the resource barrier and the governance limitations that ensue. From
that perspective, we must agree with Stentiford and Koutsouris who pointed out that
inclusive education is a premium strategy, not suitable for the cases where teaching
ought to be as efﬁcient as possible [4].
There are some aspects and perspectives to inclusive pedagogy that this study did
not directly address. Some of these concepts seemed perhaps a bit too extreme (such
as putting the emphasis of the concept onto emotions primarily). Assumedly such takes
would create a more substantial rifts between the proponents of full inclusivity and what
has been called as “massiﬁcation of higher education”. However, the justiﬁcation is that
the goal was to ﬁnd examples of pragmatic common ground. Furthermore, one could
propose that historically the Estonian culture has tended to value pragmatism to idealism.
The results allow to be optimistic that the teachers interviewed are mostly innovative
and smart to discover “what works for them”. Still, there is always a potential of peer-
learning inside any faculty and this is also a strong conclusive ﬁnding from this study.
Finally, one must keep in mind that inclusivity can be developed in additive manner
in an environment not fully supporting inclusivity paradigm only to a certain extent.
Achieving any revolutionary dynamics and transformational impact is improbable to say
the least. However, over time small and sporadic qualitative changes in teaching towards
inclusivity can have an impact of proving themselves as worthwhile practices and can, in
evolutionary terms, not only survive but to thrive. Arguably, inclusive pedagogy elements
appear to have a favourable evolutionary characteristic of ﬂexibility, which at least in
some aspects the efﬁciency-centric teaching approaches tend to lack.

Introduction
The development of a country towards a balanced and sustainable prosperity must begin
with the development of the quality of its people, as shown by the cornerstones of the
12th National Economic and Social Development Plan; is people-centered development,
with the goal of being a person of integrity, discipline, curiosity, skill, and creativity;
Have a positive attitude, social responsibility, ethics and morals; in terms of science,
technology, research and innovation development strategies have set the guidelines for
the development of research personnel as an important guideline, by accelerating the
production of qualiﬁed science and technology personnel, and in accordance with the
needs; especially personnel in the ﬁeld of Science, Technology, Engineering and Math-
ematics (STEM), accelerate production and build professional researchers, as well as
developing entrepreneurs in technology [2].
The Ofﬁce of the Vocational Education Commission is an agency responsible for
supervisingvocationaleducation,hasgivenimportancetothedevelopmentofmanpower,
both vocational knowledge base, skill development, and development of competitive-
ness; to be an innovation creator as another important mechanism for driving the country
towards its goals [3]. According to the Vocational Education Act B.E. 2551 [4], the mis-
sion of the Vocational Education Institutes is to produce manpower at the skilled level,
the technician level, and the technological level, emphasizing that having a multi-Skill,
change to a knowledge-based society; Focus on producing graduates in both quantity
and quality, competent skills, accepted by the enterprise, in line with the needs of voca-
tional manpower, both at the local, national and international level. Under the current
circumstances, the skill level of skilled workers is inferior to what employers want.
STEM education refers to an educational management approach that integrates
knowledge in 4 Interdisciplinary Studies: Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math-
ematics; Emphasis is placed on applying knowledge to real-life problems, as well as
developing new processes or products that are beneﬁcial to life and work, enabling stu-
dents to make connections between 4 Interdisciplinary Studies with real life and work, is
the right choice to lead the country out of the middle-income trap [5]. There are two types
of human aptitude classiﬁcation: 1) Left-Brained, computational thinking, or in other
words, they are good at STEM skills. Most of them are doctors, engineers, scientists, and
2) Right-Brained, something that requires imagination and creativity, suitable for being
an artist; this expert educator views that many famous inventors from all over the world
are not just being a scientist but there is also an artist in itself, showing that if people
can use both hemispheres in balance, integrate STEM + artistic skills = STEAM, will
create a Holistic Way of thinking.
Gamiﬁcation is the application of basic principles of mechanical design of play
in a non-gaming context, to increase participant engagement; it is a very popular and
successful principle in the business sector. In education, the concept of Gamiﬁcation is
applied in learning management, as one of the educational methods and techniques to
motivate and engage learners, helping to improve the quality of learners well [6].
The process of organizing activities, teaching and learning in the form of Gami-
ﬁcation is the application of concepts and game mechanics, by deﬁning activities for
learners to do, Score points are presented, leaderboards or rewards are presented, and
so on. Modify the learning rules so that learners want to do more than they have to.

Digital Learning Ecosystem Based on the STEAM Gamiﬁcation Concept

For example, using experience points instead of rules, from having to attend more than
80% of the time, therefore having the right to take the exam, it is a system for collecting
experience points, for example, attending class on time, earning 100 experience points,
late entry earning 75 experience points, not enrolled earning 0 experience points; and
then summed up the experience points with other points, to be calculated as the learner’s
grades [7]. These processes aim to motivate learners to become motivated, awaken by
participating in the learning process in a fun way, creating a good learning environment,
creating enduring knowledge, able to understand complex matters more easily.
The principles of both STEAM Education focus on the development of artistic engi-
neering skills and the mechanics of Gamiﬁcation that engage students, engage in learn-
ing, and strengthen teamwork skills, in line with the process of teaching and learning in
vocational education.
Vocational learners who apply computer technology and information to all processes.
The attributes of most students are left-brained aptitudes, it is the computational thinking,

The purposes of this research are to compare academic achievement scores before
and after learning, to assess creative innovation performance, to assess creative innova-
tion skills, to evaluate the innovator attributes of students who study by using the digital
learning ecosystem, according to the STEAM Gamiﬁcation concept, to develop inno-
vator attributes of vocational students, and to study the relationship between creative
innovation achievements, innovative skills, and vocational innovator Characteristics.

Implementation
The study on the effect of using Digital Learning Ecosystem based on the STEAM
Gamiﬁcation Concept to Develop Innovator Characteristics of Vocational Learners to
use in learning development consisted of the following steps: 1) creating a Lesson Plan;
with the process of learning management according to the STEAM Education Guideline,
derived from the synthesis of STEM Education management principles, to the integration
of arts into STEAM Education, consisting of 5 steps: The process of deﬁning problems,
by researching and collecting information from various learning sources, to come up with

698
J. Kummanee et al.
the deﬁnition of a real problem. 2. The process of designing tools, using mathematics and
technology, it is the application of technology and mathematical knowledge to design
problems. 3. The process of producing instruments, for problem solving/use project for
problem solving, is to develop a tool according to the built model. 4. The process of
testing, interpreting and improving the solution, it is the application of a tool or process
that has been designed, to try to solve the problem, and then make improvements to be
effective. 5. The process of presentation/problem solving, learners present solutions to
problems that have been discovered or presented innovations created for the exchange
of learning between learners.
In conducting learning activities, Gamiﬁcation mechanics are used to stimulate inter-
est and fun in the classroom. It consists of 5 stages: 1. Goals: each game has a different
way of playing, but it is common in all games that is the objectives of the gameplay,
either to set goals for victory, by solving puzzles, or by meeting the criteria set by the
game designers, create challenges that help the player progress. 2. Rules: a game must
have a set of rules, methods of play, scoring methods, or conditions; described for players
to follow, the game designer must set the rules clear. 3. Reinforcement: consisting of
Rewards, Points, Achievements (Achievements, Challenges, Trophies, Badges), Virtual
Goods and Spaces, Levels, Leader boards, these are what the players get when they
achieve a set goal; by incentivizing the players to score points by providing a ranking of
the players’ scores. 4. Time: It is a driving force in activities or actions to make players
aware of the importance of time management, training students to know how to allocate
time management, which is an important success factor, and 5. Feedback: It is a reﬂec-
tion of the effect of thought. The wrong and correct actions of the players to guide the
proper proceedings of the activities.
The main activities of this process are used from the beginning to the end of each
learning unit, consisting of the formation of a team of participants, according to the
qualiﬁcations of each student, the goal of learning management at each step by the
learners in the team. There must be cooperation in learning and organizing activities
within the speciﬁed time, to compete with other teams; teachers will provide feedback,
rewards, and leveling to the learner’s team at the end of the course in each learning unit
and at the end of every learning unit.
Selection of tools that are qualiﬁed in accordance with the principles of learning
management, STEAM Gamiﬁcation, in order to customize the details of the system to
suit the experiment, use the learning system according to the Gamiﬁcation principle
by considering choosing a Classcraft program, which is a program that can be used on
both a web browser and applications on mobile devices such as personal computers,
Notebooks, Smartphones, and Tablets, etc.

Work-in-Progress TO2YS – Teaching
Online with Objects from Youth
to Seniors
James Wolfer(B)
Indiana University South Bend, South Bend, USA
jwolfer@iusb.edu
Abstract. The Covid-19 pandemic precipitated a major disruption in
pedagogy, especially for classes with a signiﬁcant hands-on, interactive
component. This work-in-progress describes using physical objects to
revamp a computer literacy course for non-computing students from in-
person interactive to online compatible. Since our objects span the ages
of both traditional and non-traditional students we call the individual
objects initiating classroom discussion TO2YS, Teaching Online with
Objects from Youth to Seniors.
1
Introduction
The Covid-19 pandemic precipitated a major disruption in pedagogy, especially
for classes with a signiﬁcant hands-on, interactive, or laboratory component.
Suddenly, an environment where students used all ﬁve senses was reduced to
essentially two going online, visual and audio – with visual conﬁned to 2D
imagery.
Instructors scrambled to adapt laboratories to the new reality [1]. As
described in [2], we had crafted a series of over thirty demonstrations and inter-
active experiences to support the university’s introduction to computing course
for non-computing majors. These demonstrations ranged from basic computing
objects, such as disk drives, to interactive experiences such as stereographics
and haptics which did not transition well. Inspired by [3], engaging students
through storytelling, and [4] enhancing teaching with computing history, this
work describes a revamping of demonstrations into a series of modules which
tell a computing story where each component forms an segue to a deeper dis-
cussion. We call the objects used for illustrations TO2YS (pronounced “Toys”)
since the span the ages of both traditional and non-traditional students.
1.1
The Class
The class in this case is an introduction to computing for non-computing majors.
While originally in person, the class described here assumes an online “syn-
chronous” class, where lectures are presented live using Zoom. The class covers
c

M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 707–713, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_74

J. Wolfer
(a) CPU and Memory
(b) Storage
Fig. 1. CPU, memory, and secondary storage
basic hardware and software concepts, legal, ethical, and societal impacts of com-
puting, algorithmic concepts, and a variety of computing applications and basic
coding and draws both traditional and non-traditional aged students. While most
students arrive with experience using computers, there is a weak comprehension
of computing details. Therefore, a substantial part of the class is building insight
and vocabulary. Since these students from disciplines from dental hygiene to the
arts, engaging them is a real challenge. As one component of that engagement we
are attempting to provide both a technical and a human element to our modules.
2
Sample Modules
Initially, the class begins with a discussion of early computer history, such as
Babbage and Lovelace, then continues by leveraging work done in Bletchley
Park with The National Museum of Computing to describe work there, includ-
ing Colossus [5]. We also mention work by Kathleen and Andrew Booth, Von
Neumann, Alan Turing, and others of this era [6–8]. This brings us, chrono-
logically, to the era of mainframe computers, and the later emergence of the
microprocessor. This corresponds to the memory time-frame of the older, non-
traditional, student and to a point just prior to that of the younger student.
This makes a good transition for using historic objects to anchor many of the
topics.
While there are too many to give a comprehensive picture in the context of
this paper, here we provide annotated samples of our TO2YS and their purpose.
2.1
CPU and Memory
Figure 1a shows a collection of objects that can be conveniently displayed online.
In the back-center of the photograph we have an older motherboard. Since it is
larger than many contemporary motherboards it becomes very useful to illustrate
bus interconnections from CPU to memory and peripherals.

TO2YS
709
Moving to the front-left we have an example of core memory, the mainstay
of the mainframe computers. These cores are large enough to clearly see their
construction and organization in a camera closeup, making them valuable for
showing the students what the memory really looked like “back then.”
Next, on the far right, we have a wire-wrapped, semiconductor memory from
the early microcomputer era – about the time of the early Apple and Commodore
computers.
Of course, memory is only useful when connected to a CPU. While almost
everyone knows what a CPU “is” – few have a grasp of what is actually within
the deployment package. To illustrate the CPU we acquired a silicon wafer etched
with processors, shown in the center of the photograph. This wafer, when magni-
ﬁed, illustrates that the CPU is an actual device embedded in ceramic or plastic
– making the abstract concept far more tangible.
Finally, we show a contemporary Raspberry Pi microcomputer, which con-
solidates all of these individual functions and more into a single small board,
which we then compare with the CPUs inside their cellphones.
2.2
Secondary Storage
As with the CPU and memory, secondary storage forms a story, from describing
some of Booth’s early work to more recent examples as illustrated in Fig. 1b.
Here we ﬁnd both paper-tape and punched cards, as well as an early ﬂoppy
disk. While diﬃcult to discern in the small photo, this is an eight-inch ﬂoppy
disk, which, when compared online with a sheet of paper always gets student
attention. Also shown is a 3.5 in. ﬂoppy disk that has been disassembled to show
it’s inner workings, and a hard-disk drive with the cover removed, again so we
can discuss together how these things work. We also see a CDROM in this image
as an example of optical storage. This is intentionally damaged to illustrate to
students where the data is stored and care that should be taken with them. Not
illustrated here, but included in the discussion, are ﬂash and solid-state disk
drives.
2.3
Computer Graphics and Human-Computer Interaction
When telling a story, both technical and non-technical “humanizing” objects are
used. For example, in Fig. 2a we use a collection of plush toys to illustrate the
RGB colorspace in the context of computer graphics. These can be easily placed
under a document camera and provide a “live” discussion illustration. Also,
a historically important computer graphics rendering object, the famous Utah
Teapot, is illustrated using SIGGRAPH Renderman swag – a walking teapot.
Similarly, the plush Mandril toy is representative of the famous mandril image
from the image processing community. Each of these objects tie discipline history
to the technical discussion.
Finally, the stereographic red/cyan glasses have formed the foundation for an
important illustration historically used in person. Speciﬁcally, we show the step-
by-step workﬂow taking an x-ray, CT sequence, extracting a surface mesh, and

710
J. Wolfer
(a) Computer Graphics
(b) Human-Computer Interaction
Fig. 2. Applications: computer graphics and human-computer interaction
ultimately rendering it as a 3D printed object. In addition we have extracted a
portion of the carotid artery and created a ﬂy-through illustration in anaglyphic
3D. Unfortunately, when driven online, students did not have the requisite
glasses, diminishing the eﬀectiveness of the 3D presentation. For our next term
we have made arrangements to provide a pair of glasses to each remote student
ahead of this module.
For the human-computer interactive components we have a much more diﬃ-
cult task which has not been totally resolved to date. Many of our interactions
involve senses other than sight and sound, the sensations most readily handled
online to date. For example, Fig. 2b shows some of the devices we illustrate.
The mouse is a haptically enabled mouse that has been programmed to provide
modulated vibration, used to explore imagery by touch. Likewise, the Phantom
Omni is a haptic device to give touch sensations. While they can be demon-
strated online, their true utility is not apparent in that environment – they need
to be experienced, not simply shown. Likewise, the Space Navigator is used for
Google Earth ﬂy-through navigation, but without experiencing the strain-gauge
interface in person it is diﬃcult to understand what makes it unique.
That said, the two devices that can be illustrated are the laser projected
keyboard and the Mindwave EEG interface. Even when they don’t work as
planned (the EEG interface is sensitive to mental state, which is diﬃcult to
ensure when lecturing), the students readily grasp the concept. In addition,
exploiting sound through examples of data soniﬁcation will substitute for some
of the haptic illustrations.
2.4
Artiﬁcial Intelligence and Robotics
When discussing artiﬁcial intelligence and robotics it is important to help the
student distinguish between symbolic AI and the current use of AI to mean
“Machine” or “Deep” learning; all important topics. And, as in the case of graph-
ics, we wish to connect students to the human element. Figure 3a shows some
of the objects we use to motivate the AI topics. Centered here is a plush Teddy

TO2YS
711
(a) Artiﬁcial Intelligence
(b) Robotics
Fig. 3. Applications: artiﬁcial intelligence and robotics
Bear, purchased at Bletchley Park, reminiscent of Porgy, the Teddy Bear owned
by Alan Turing. This forms a segue for discussing both Turing’s life, as well as
his contributions to computing in general, and AI speciﬁcally – including the
famous Turing Test for intelligence.
From that point we explore symbolic AI, search, and algorithms for solving
problems such as the Towers of Hanoi, introduced by the physical model in
Fig. 3a left rear. After discussing the symbolic AI we move into the realm of
Machine Learning, and Deep Learning. Since DL is modeled after biological
neural computation, we connect to the concept with a plush model neuron. This
allows us, under a camera, to point out the components modeled in artiﬁcial
neural networks. We also show an Nvidia Jetson Nano to illustrate the use of
GPUs to enable such models for inference, as well as discussing societal and
privacy issues involved.
It is a natural transition from AI to robots. Historically, we have observed
that students enjoy interacting with a set of balancing robots we deploy in-
person. Unfortunately, at 60 cm or so tall these are not deployable in a small
teaching home studio. They are more appropriate to a laboratory or hallway.
Fortunately, we were recently able to ﬁnd and build a smaller, self-balancing,
robot standing only about 15 cm tall. This robot is suitable for running on a
tabletop, as illustrated in Fig. 3b on the right, where it is posed balancing on
two wheels for the camera. In addition to the AI aspects, these robots allow
for discussions of sensors, which often transitions into discussions of ethics and
impact on society – now and in the future.
2.5
Future
As described earlier, we plan to provide stereographic glasses to students for
home use, and incorporate additional soniﬁcation, and deploy a new self-
balancing robot, into our online presentations.
As illustrated in Fig. 4, we also plan to use the sensor discussion from the
robotics module to form a transition to other sensors. For example, in conjunc-

712
J. Wolfer
(a) Chernobyl
(b) Model Supercomputer
Fig. 4. Future
tion with our senior-level operating systems course, we used a Geiger counter
to form the basis for random number generation. We also used the project to
connect with human history by visiting the Chernobyl site and sending back
radiation data to the class. During the next term we intend to use photographs
and data from that visit to tie together history and sensors [9].
We have also developed a model supercomputer, including multiple CPUs,
each with multiple cores, and three with Nvidia GPUs. This makes it capable of
running the same software development stack as “real” supercomputers, but in a
visual format so students can see evidence of the inter-computer communication
[10]. We have used this in-person classes, but plan to deploy it online in the fall.
Finally, we would like to explore ways of engaging students with learning
and perceptual challenges within the context of having only two basic sensory
modes, audio and visual, available. We have taken steps in this direction with the
soniﬁcation of both DNA sequences and elementary images, and plan to extend
this with soniﬁcation examples from other domains.
2.6
Conclusion
In an eﬀort to tell the story of computing, to bring awareness of contemporary
computing issues, and to engage non-computing majors in an online-live envi-
ronment, we have developed a series of illustrations connecting common objects,
we call TO2YS, to computing topics. We plan to deploy this online in the next
semester.
