The evaluation of the data provided an insight into the students’ previous experience
with digital learning during the pandemic which provided a ﬁrm foundation to design
the virtual collaboration.
Project Launch. The launch of the project hosted by the University of Kelaniya via
Zoom platform was conducted bilingually in English and German considering the lin-
guistic skills of the 41 participating students. This video conferencing tool was selected
because all four countries had access to it and the selected participants were more famil-
iar with it. The students from Egypt and North Macedonia were competent in English.
Several students from China spoke English although the majority was more competent
in German. The students selected from Sri Lanka were competent in both English and
German. At the launch students were given a brieﬁng about the aims and expected out-
comes as well as how the groups should work together. The project team from Alumni
University of Siegen and representatives from the host, the University of Kelaniya, were

762
N. C. Premawardhena et al.
present at the live session to witness the proceedings. Four groups were formed, each
comprising students from all four countries. The themes assigned to each group after
an initial discussion were food and beverages, fashion, cultural festival/s and place/s of
historical signiﬁcance. Each group was assigned with one or two coordinators compris-
ing staff members from the University of Kelaniya to work on the joint presentations.
Following an initial introduction round in the breakout rooms, the team members were
given two ice-breaker questions to answer to create an informal atmosphere. Firstly, each
one had to introduce one’s country with three phrases. Secondly, a common ice-breaker
question on what every participant will do if the project wins one million Euro. The ﬁrst
question led the students to introduce the country brieﬂy and the others to enhance their
knowledge about participating countries. The second question eased the tension and the
inhibition in the group caused by to the new challenge ahead of them with new faces
and backgrounds. By using their imagination, creativity and wit the participants brought
others to laugh at their dreams of spending one million Euro. The students exchanged
their contact details and decided on the ﬁrst meeting date on their own. At the end of the
event the students were requested to take part in an opinion poll on Zoom to obtain their
views and impressions. The Zoom poll comprised 6 questions on their expectations and
experience during the launch, Table 3 presents the results of the poll.

As evident by the responses the participants were eager to embark on the project
which gave them three weeks to prepare presentations on cultural aspects. These ques-
tions were also included in the ﬁnal feedback form given to the students after the com-
pletion of the project to assess whether their views changed after the experience of the
digital collaboration. Furthermore, the audience and the participating students were also

Building a Digital Bridge Across Cultures and Continents
763
given a chance to comment on their ﬁrst impressions and expectations before closing
the proceedings.
Preparation. The responsibilities of the four team leaders during the preparation of the
presentations was to coordinate with the lecturers who functioned as group coordinators.
These coordinators worked closely with assigned individual groups by arranging the
meetings and evaluating the progress. The students in each group worked together on
the assigned cultural theme to prepare the presentations. Thus, Following the launch on
29th October 2021, the students were left to work at their own pace with the assistance and
guidance of the coordinators until the ﬁnal group presentations on 19th November 2021.
Zoommeetings, WhatsAppandWeChat groups wereformedtofacilitatecommunication
among group members since a common social media facility could not be found to bring
all members of a group together owing to restrictions present in some countries. Each
group was allocated 25 min for the presentation, 5 min for feedback and comments from
the audience. The students used Google Slides and Canva to share the presentations.
However, the students from China did not have access to most applications and software
that their peers from other countries used. Thus, their slides were sent via email to be
integrated into the joint presentations. This gave an opportunity for all the participants
to iron out the shortcomings, compromise and overcome their challenges to work as a
team.
Final Presentation. The ﬁnal group presentations were shared online with a live audi-
enceofover150fromacrosstheworld.Thepresentationsonfoodandbeverages,fashion,
cultural festivals and historical places, where the students had taken maximum use of
digital tools comprised still images, audio, and video clips, mesmerized the audience
with the projection of the beauty and vividness of each culture under one single theme
and awed them with the knowledge imparted. The students from four different countries
worked as one single team in each group and the ultimate result was an excellent example
of teamwork across borders. Except for the presentation on historical places, the others
were conducted bilingually. A feedback survey was conducted online a few days after
the ﬁnal presentations to review the experience gained by the participating students. An
audio-visual summary of the entire project including the preparatory stage, launch and
the ﬁnal presentations was later compiled by the co-author from North Macedonia as a
token of remembrance. This video was presented at the Alumni Academy presentations
by the team leaders two weeks later, much to the appreciation and awe of the audience.
It was a magnanimous project which was realised through meticulous planning, sheer
hard work and commitment of all parties involved.
4
Actual Outcomes
The ﬁndings of the online survey on digital learning experience conducted prior to the
launch of the virtual mobility project showed that the students from all four countries
had similar views and experiences. Although they preferred onsite learning, they all
agreed that virtual learning was the best available option during the prevailing pandemic
situation. The students were familiar with Google Meet, Zoom and MS Teams tools

764
N. C. Premawardhena et al.
which were used at their universities. Most of the participating students had not taken
part in a virtual mobility project connecting with overseas partners. The feedback during
the opinion poll at the end of the project launch showed that the majority of the students
were highly enthusiastic and motivated to be a part of the digital cultural exchange and
looked forward to learning from each other and broaden their horizons.
The entire project from the surveys, posters, invitations to announcing and moder-
ating at the launch and ﬁnal presentations was conducted bilingually. This measure was
time and energy consuming yet rewarding since a larger audience could be reached by
using both English and German. Furthermore, time zones had to be kept in mind when
sending out invitations, preparing digital posters and selecting the appropriate time zones
for the Zoom links that were sent out.
The communication among the group members of different countries progressed
smoothly due to the presence of participants competent in both English and German.
However, one of the major challenges had been the task of arranging group meeting
due to different time zones. There was a difference of seven to eight hours between
Egypt, North Macedonia and China during winter. The weekends also differed from one
country to the other. Egypt had a Friday, Saturday weekend while the others enjoyed the
weekend on Saturday and Sunday. Furthermore, the digital applications and social media
sites that were freely available in Egypt, North Macedonia and Sri Lanka could not be
used in China. Thus, all the students downloaded WeChat to communicate with the group
members from China. The surveys conducted via Google forms had to be converted by
the team leader from China to obtain the responses of the students. Nevertheless, beating
all odds, the team spirit of the students won the challenges they faced, resulting in an
excellent outcome by way of four group presentations after three weeks from the project
launch. The ﬁnal feedback survey showed that all students gained an insight into four new
cultures, won true international friends, learned to work together virtually, and enhanced
their linguistic and well as digital skills.
4.1
Beneﬁts, Challenges and Lessons Learnt
The digital collaboration was a novel experience for all parties involved including the
four team leaders, seven group leaders and the participating students. Due to the magni-
tude of the project spanning across continents and involving multi-disciplinary students
of diverse cultural, linguistic and religious backgrounds, achieving the expected goals
successfully was a herculean task. At the completion of the project an online survey
titled ‘Survey on Cultural Exchange Experience and Digital Collaboration’ was con-
ducted to assess the success, gains, challenges faced, and lessons learnt. The ﬁrst section
of the survey included all the questions except Q2 given during the opinion poll at the
project launch (see Table 3) to ascertain whether there was a change of their views. The
responses to section 1 showed that the participants who were somewhat uncertain about
the project and the beneﬁts changed their opinion after the completion of the project.
The second section of the survey contained ﬁve open ended questions as follows:
Q1 What did you learn from the project and the teamwork?
Q2 What were the positive aspects?
Q3 What were the challenges you faced?
Q4 Any suggestions for future projects and improvements.

Building a Digital Bridge Across Cultures and Continents
765
Q5 What did you gain from working with fellow students from different countries
and continents?
Through these open-ended questions, the students were given an opportunity for
reﬂection after the successful completion of the collaboration. Comprehensive answers
were given by the students as seen in the summary below.
Q1 Lessons Learnt. How to organize the work between the members, distribution of
responsibilities, communication with the team, learning to care about others, work with
others, adapt to difﬁcult situations, be unselﬁsh and develop self-discipline, no linguistic
barriers due to motivation and interest to work together, challenge assumptions, develop
stronger communication skills, learning how to respect other cultures and how to connect
with each other across borders, exposure to different cultures and the beauty of them,
working with large groups from different countries, team work and time management.
Q2 Positive Aspects. Beating all odds group work becomes a reality with an excellent
ﬁnal outcome, participation at an international event, lasting friendships built with stu-
dents keeping in constant touch, inviting them for other virtual events, mutual respect,
broadening horizons, enhancing leadership skills and world knowledge, improving pub-
lic speaking skills, improving linguistic skills in English (for all) and German (for the
relevant students).
Q3 Challenges. Time zone differences of 6–7 h between Egypt and China, 7–8 h with
North Macedonia depending on summer and winter time, weekend on different days,
working students, bilingual and monolingual students, students not experienced in work-
ing in a team online, communication mechanism hampered by non-availability of similar
digital tools in all member countries, a few non-committal students, connectivity issues.
Q4 Suggestions. More similar projects in the future, a workshop prior to commencing
the group work, ﬁnding common digital tools that can be used in all the participating
countries.
Q5 Gains from the Intercultural Experience. Great learning experience, how to con-
nect with others from different backgrounds and work in a team, project planning
and management, stronger communication skills, enhanced creativity and innovative
thinking, unforgettable experience and memories.
5
Discussion
A collaborative project of this nature requires to be academically and socio-culturally
signiﬁcant. It was not a matter of bringing 41 students from four different continents
together to exchange aspects of their culture. According to Spitzberg and Changnon,
(2009) as cited by Bassani and Buchen [7] a minimum of ﬁve components can be
addressed during intercultural exchange as seen in Table 4. As discussed in 4.1 The
feedback obtained through the online survey conducted at the completion of the project
revealed that all these components were addressed and competency in each of them was
gained by the students.

766
N. C. Premawardhena et al.
Table 4. Intercultural competencies gained through collaboration
Component
Competencies
Motivation
Openness to others; openness to new information
Knowledge
Knowledge of more than one perspective; knowledge of alternative
interpretations);
Skills
Ability to communicate interpersonally; relationship building; cultural empathy;
interpersonal diplomacy
Context
Environmental situation, host contact conditions
Outcomes
Collaboration across borders; communication competence
The engaging of lecturers as group leaders was imperative to maximise the bene-
ﬁts of the digital cultural exchange and collaborative work. According to Cunningham
(2016) the tasks given to the students need to shift away from mere cultural exchange
and comparison to a more tangible output of developing intercultural awareness and
sensitivity through teamwork [11–15]. Hence, the active role of the group leaders was
pivotal to develop the tasks, monitor the progress and intervene, when necessary, instead
of allowing simple exchange of information among the participants [1].
The outcomes of the collaboration and the experience of the students on cultural
exchange did not deviate from the results of similar projects conducted previously i.e.,
collaborative projects between Spain, Brazil, and Germany [7] or between Spain and
Korea [8] or Morocco and Germany [9].
6
Conclusion and Recommendations
The virtual mobility project connecting three continents and four countries conﬁrmed
the positive results anticipated at the stage of developing this concept of creating a digital
bridge across borders. Despite this not being a semester long, credit bearing mobility
project, the participating students and the academic staff gained signiﬁcant insight into
other cultures and experience in executing a project of this nature. The need for a com-
mon digital platform where any country could come together and digital tools that are
accessible to all was very strongly felt while working together with participants from
different countries. By building a digital bridge across the world, this project paved way
for the next generation to work together with mutual respect, forgetting all the cultural,
linguistic and religious differences. Further, the experience gathered during the project
brought to light that such virtual collaboration is signiﬁcant in promoting intercultural
communication, understanding across borders and enhancing digital prowess. Thus, sim-
ilar collaborative projects are recommended for the future. The University of Kelaniya
was involved in several similar projects following this collaboration.
The goal of the project leaders of having students from different cultures come
together digitally and exchange ideas, learn from one another, respect each other and
work together was already achieved through this endeavour. The friendships estab-
lished across borders will be long lasting. Through digital collaboration the project

Building a Digital Bridge Across Cultures and Continents
767
team paved way for the next generation to come and work together, forgetting all the
cultural, linguistic and religious differences.
For the students of German from China and Sri Lanka this was an intercultural as
well as a rewarding linguistic experience to enhance their foreign language competence.
For all four groups of students enhancing their English language and public speaking
skill was signiﬁcant. For most of the students as well as the group leaders this was the
ﬁrst digital intercultural journey across continents. The lessons learnt and the experience
gained during the collaborative project will enhance the students’ global outlook on their
path towards becoming a global citizen.

Mathematical Model for Estimating Mother
Tongue Competencies and Learning Outcomes
Katalin Harangus(B)
, András Kakucs
, and Gabriella Kovács
Faculty of Technical and Human Sciences, Sapientia Hungarian University of Transylvania,
O.P. 9, C.P. 4, 540485 Târgu-Mure¸s, Romania
{katalin,kakucs2,kovacs_gabriella}@ms.sapientia.ro
Abstract. Education in native language should build on the existing knowledge
and use of the mother tongue at all levels of education. The development of
mother tongue literacy, which not only inﬂuences but also helps learners to study
vocational disciplines in different ﬁelds of education, begins in primary school
(preparatory – 4th grades) and continues with gradually expanding subjects in
middle school (gymnasium, 5th–8th grades) and in secondary school (lyceum,
9th–12th grade). In our research, we examine two basic areas of mother tongue
competencies, reading comprehension and writing, estimating the proportion of
students who do not possess the necessary skills to pursue their studies success-
fully. We developed a mathematical model that can be used to predict the number
of students whose poor performance in aptitude tests makes it unlikely that they
will be able to meet school expectations at the next level of education: primary
school students are unlikely to meet middle school level expectations; middle
school students are unlikely to continue their education in secondary school; and
secondary school students may not be able to meet the necessary requirements for
graduation.
Keywords: Mathematical modelling · Mother tongue proﬁciency · Learning
outcomes · Dropout
1
Introduction
Our information society increasingly requires from the education system to provide
students with training that will enable them to become cultured people with appropriate
mother tongue education, with native language skills and abilities that enable them to
communicate effectively and acquire further knowledge.
Adequate knowledge and versatile use of the mother tongue is a prerequisite for
individual and social communication. Education in the mother tongue builds on the
existing knowledge and use of the native language at all levels. Skills and competency
development is crucial to enable students to communicate orally and in writing according
to their circumstances, needs and goals.
The development of mother tongue skills, which not only inﬂuences but also helps
the learner to acquire vocational disciplines belonging to different ﬁelds of education,
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 769–776, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_80

770
K. Harangus et al.
begins in primary school and continues with gradually expanding subjects in middle
school and in secondary school.
In our study, we present a mathematical model that can be used to predict the expected
development of the level of key competence in mother tongue communication. Based
on the results of a reading comprehension and writing skills assessment, we estimate the
proportion of students who do not have the necessary skills to successfully pursue their
studies.
The results of the measurements suggest that some students are struggling with a
poor performance that hinders independent information acquisition and learning, leading
to dropout.
2
Who Can Be Considered a Dropout Student?
In everyday school life, besides the term dropout, we also use expressions such as failed
to pass, repeats the year, did not pass the exam(s), left school. Among the literature
references to dropping out, the most common interpretations are: (a) dropping out of
programs, (b) dropping out of certain program types, (c) dropping out of the full-time
school system, and (d) dropping out of the education system as a whole.
According to the Regulation on the Organization and Operation of Public Education
Institutions in Romania, students who do not attend full-time general education and/or
are two years older than the students of the relevant grade are considered to have dropped
out [1]. So, according to the regulations, students who do not attend school for their own
age group are not considered to have dropped out for two more years. During this period,
they are neither included in the education system nor registered as school leavers. The
Ministry of Education, Research and Development uses the following indicator in its
ofﬁcial reports on the state of education: the percentage difference between the number
of students enrolled at the beginning of the school year and the number of students still
registered at the end of the same school year [2]. By deﬁnition, it compares the numbers
from the beginning and the end of the school year. Although it uses a more accurate
method to identify dropouts, it is not a perfect solution, as it does not take into account
mid-year “non-dropouts” such as students going abroad, changing schools, and year
repetitions.
The European Union’s statistical ofﬁce, EUROSTAT, considers early school leavers
to be those who have not completed ISCED level 3, i.e. secondary education, until the
age of 24. This deﬁnition focuses only on acquiring a degree [3].
The Pedagogical Lexicon [4] deﬁnes the phenomenon of dropping out as “gradual
dropping out of a school-based training”. This deﬁnition does not consider anyone a
dropout if they continue their studies in the same program after repeating a year, but a
change of proﬁle or a change of program means dropping out. In the OECD’s annual
publication (Education at a Glance), the dropout rate is deﬁned as follows: [5] “Dropout
rateisdeﬁnedastheproportionofstudentswholeavethespeciﬁedlevelintheeducational
system without obtaining a ﬁrst qualiﬁcation.” According to this deﬁnition, a person who
enrolls in some form of training but does not obtain a degree at that level of training is
considered a dropout. In this sense, a program change does not mean that the student is
a dropout.

Mathematical Model for Estimating Mother Tongue Competencies
771
Although these deﬁnitions differ in content and may be contradictory, they all have
justiﬁcation. From the deﬁnitions listed, the question arises, what we mean by dropout
in this study. Based on our mathematical model, we can predict the number of students
whose poor performance in aptitude tests makes it unlikely that they will be able to
meet school expectations at a subsequent level of education. That is, elementary school
students may not be able to meet the requirements of the middle school level, middle
school students may not be able to continue their secondary education, and secondary
school students may not be able to meet the necessary requirements for graduation. The
reason of this may be that they do not have the necessary native language skills and
abilities, which are essential for the acquisition of knowledge related to different ﬁelds
of education and specializations.
3
Assessing Reading Comprehension and Writing Skills
The study samples are the results of a representative measurement in which all three
stages of school education were covered. In the assessment of reading comprehension
and writing skills, the ﬁnal grades of each stage of school education were selected: the
fourth grade of primary school (N = 792), the eighth grade of middle school (N = 812)
and the graduates of secondary school (N = 746).
The examination of the reading comprehension ability of primary school children
is justiﬁed by the fact that the elementary school develops the basic reading skills; the
knowledge and skills that are essential for middle school education are acquired during
this stage. By the end of primary education, the curriculum mentions the development
of proﬁcient reading as a requirement.
The reading comprehension level of middle school students is worth examining
because intensive and purposeful development of this skill takes place at this stage. Com-
pulsory general education ends at the end of the 8th grade, when students are expected
to be able to search for, sort, interpret and evaluate information from printed texts in
out-of-school situations as well.
The reading comprehension level of students preparing for graduation is worth exam-
ining, because reading comprehension, one of the most important elements of mother
tongue communication related to literacy, can be best assessed at this level. The quality
of this predicts intellectuals’ expected common basic communication skills within a
society.
The measuring tools consisted of different types of writing tasks and tests measuring
reading comprehension skills. In the reading comprehension test, students were given a
document and a narrative text in each grade. In examining writing skills, primary school
children had to compose a longer text in the genre of the tale. Eighth graders wrote in
four genres (writing about an experience; writing a letter; characterizing a person; giving
advice), and twelfth graders wrote in three genres (essay, report, giving advice). For each
survey, the maximum score was 100 points. The score achieved by a student was equal
to the sum of the results obtained on the tests, which was compared to 100% of the sum
of the maximum scores available for solving the tasks. Accordingly, the distribution
of performance was examined on a one-hundred-scale, on which each value interval
was merged and students were divided into ﬁve groups based on their performance:
insufﬁcient, poor, sufﬁcient, good, very good (Table 1).

4
Mathematical Modeling
By modeling, we mean the recognition of the essential properties of a real system and
their mapping in some form [6]. With its help, we can capture a part of the reality, prove
our theoretical results, and realize the prediction of various phenomena.
The most commonly used model in today’s engineering practice is the mathematical
model,whichistheformulationoftherelationshipsamongthepropertiesoftheprocessin
the system under study. This process begins with recording the purpose of the modeling,
followed by the collection of a priori knowledge that can be used to build the model,
which includes structural and parametric information about the phenomenon. Finally,
the relationships between the variables of the system to be modeled are mapped into
a mathematical structure, the knowledge of which determines the number and type of
equations in the mathematical models.
It should be noted that the more a priori information we use in modeling, the less
reasonable our model will be. In practice, the more information we use in the design
of variables and the rules of model law, the more freedom we have in the modeling
process. One consequence of this is that if we were to use the maximum, i.e. all possible
information, we do not need a model, since all the information is already available.
With a short, schematic description of modeling, we tried to illustrate not only the
complexity of mathematical modeling, but also the wide range of inherent possibilities.
4.1
The Equation that Describes the Mathematical Model
Based on the results of the native language proﬁciency test, we set up a mathematical
model that can be used to predict the development of the two skills at different levels of
education: primary, middle and secondary school.
The equation of the model was determined as follows:

where y(k) – input parameter, u(k) – output parameter, e(k) – assumed “noise” at the
output, which causes most of the model errors.
In developing the model, we sought to establish a relationship between the output and
input parameters of the system under study. Accordingly, the model was characterized
by the polynomials A and B,
A

in which the determination of the parameters was based on the least squares method, i.e.
we sought the minimum value of a squared deviation.
The purpose of our prediction was to give the future values of the characteristics of
the system in such a way that the difference between the actual and the estimated values,
i.e. the value of the error, is kept to a minimum. In the case of a perfect estimate, this
value would be zero, but in reality this is not the case, as there is always a factor whose
effect has not been taken into account. Thus, we assumed that the smaller the value of
the error, the better our prediction.

The input parameters of the model, given the order of the overlapping stages of training,
always consisted of a lower level school stage, and the output parameters consisted of a
higher level school stage. We assumed that the results measured/achieved in each grade
in the different school types are always based on the knowledge acquired at a lower stage

of education, and that the previous level always develops the skills that are essential for

the secondary school results.

5
Conclusions
The mathematical model can help to determine the expected development of the level
of native language skills. The model also allows comparison of data from current and
upcoming measurements. It has two basic roles in education, one is diagnostic and the
other is prognostic. Thanks to its diagnostic role, it provides information about the level
of knowledge at which students start a given stage of school education, whether they
meet the expectations. Its prognostic function serves as a basis for examining the trend
in the development of native language skills. Due to these roles, it can play a role in
proposing and developing remedial and support programs, in order to help the learning
process.

Cleaning Up: Interplay Between European
Standards and Veriﬁable Credentials for Higher
Education Institutions
Matthias Gottlieb1(B)
and Guido Bacharach2
1 Technical University of Munich, Arcisstr. 21, 80333 Munich, Germany
matthias.gottlieb@tum.de
2 Stiftung Für Hochschulzulassung, Sonnenstr. 171, 44137 Dortmund, Germany
guido.bacharach@freenet.de
Abstract. Student mobility is an essential topic to strengthen a fruitful discussion
in engineering education. However, required administrative exchange documents
such as transcripts of records, bachelor’s degrees, diplomas, and certiﬁcates are
analog and there is no fraud-protection. Thus, veriﬁable credentials enable sharing
for higher education institutions (HEI) because they are fully automated and fraud-
proof. To explain and create a common base, we are examining the current work
and standards. We apply a four-step approach: (1) code the descriptions of the
standards, (2) identify the standards in different layers, (3) identify interplays, and
(4) develop a coupling concept. We extend the knowledge base with a coupling
concept illustrating the interplay of global, European, and German standards in
HEI. Practitioners can apply the concept to develop an interoperable ecosystem
to exchange veriﬁable credentials. This also builds a fundamental basis to enable
the exchange of more detailed credentials such as micro-credentials on a global
level.
Keywords: European Standards · Digital Credentials · Interoperability
1
Introduction
Digitization is becoming increasingly important in almost all areas of life, which also
applies to higher education institutions (HEI). In particular, student mobility is of inter-
est in Europe and worldwide. [1, 2] Digitization through European programs such as
ERASMUS enables the transformation into a process free of media discontinuity. [5]
This means that the process allows for minimal data storage, fast retrieval of informa-
tion relevant to automated processing, improved transparency, automated record veri-
ﬁcation, simpliﬁed information and document exchange, elimination of paper ﬂoods,
location-independent and continuous access to information, and compliance with elec-
tronic record keeping in accordance with legislation. When asked how a trustworthy,
distributed, and internationally usable infrastructure standard for issuing, storing, dis-
playing, and verifying academic digital credentials must be designed, we repeatedly
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 777–788, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_81

778
M. Gottlieb and G. Bacharach
encountered various standards and services whose precise deﬁnitions of terms were
often ambiguous.
The purpose of this article is to provide an overview of the signiﬁcant international,
European, and national standards in the ﬁeld of digital credentials for HEIs, with a view
on overcoming administrative challenges [1, 2] andmaking these standards interopera-
ble. Interoperability would enable learners, subjects such as HEIs, and third parties to
exchange veriﬁed credentials based on the self-sovereign learners, who decide which of
their data can be shared. To develop an interoperable ecosystem and provide a basis for
an operational concept, it is necessary to identify the interplay of the diverse concepts
and standards in the global, Europe, and Germany. We chose Germany as an example
for this interplay due to its speciﬁc federal system to get an idea of how standards can
be transferred from state to country and respectively from country to a global level. This
overview of the ecosystems creates order and provides a basis for practitioners to build
a common denominator of key variables for seamless data and information exchange.
Inanexplorativestepinsolvingthepuzzleofinfrastructurecomponentsforalearning
ecosystem, we answer the research question: What is the interplay of global, European,
and German Standards for Digital Credentials in HEIs?
2
Related Work
To clean up the different standards, we provide state-of-the-art veriﬁable credentials on
Global, European, and German standards.
The complex process of standardization requires a strategy with clear goals. [3]
presented the ﬁrst help to identify such a strategy for the development of digital IDs for
HEIs—one step of it is an integrative process. E-government can be applied to digital
higher education processes [4]. This ﬁnding can address signiﬁcant previous work and
knowledge in this research area.
[5] presented the ﬁrst overview of processes and standards in Europe. Developing
a common standard for digital credentials seems complex due to the different projects,
initiatives, positions, interests, and established products. Developers of student infor-
mation systems have already overcome the ﬁrst barriers towards holistic processes [5].
A signiﬁcant amount of work and time seems to be necessary for the development and
establishment of integrated processes, [5]. Addressing the issue requires a more abstract
level and has to draw on existing knowledge. Thus, one solution for creating veriﬁable
digital credentials is the concept of an envelope. This envelope contains international
standards such as US-Letter or DIN-A4 (German standard paper format) [6].
One of the critical issues in European countries, compared to others, is the General
Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Several contributions still raise digital credentials’
privacy and data integrity issues [7, 8]. Technical standards and frameworks such as the
Common Criteria can increase trust in the system. In addition, digital competencies are
needed to create awareness about data handling.
Issuing digital credentials requires the establishment of identities. Digital identities
for automated credential veriﬁcation are still an open ﬁeld of research [9]. The establish-
ment of identity is a process that ensures that only the authorized person receives their
credential in advance of its issuance. The enrollment ofﬁce performs veriﬁcation during

Cleaning Up: Interplay Between European Standards and Veriﬁable
779
the enrollment process in HEIs currently analog. However, there is still an unresolved
challenge in performing veriﬁcation using electronic IDs. For example, international
students do not receive an electronic residence permit until they are enrolled, which
would be necessary for the digital process.
This paper focuses on European standards and services and their interaction with
international standards to explore a base for global standards. To ﬁnd an answer
to the research question, we focus on conceptionalizing standards in models and
services: European Learning Model (ELM), ELMO, European Digital Credentials
Infrastructure (EDCI), Erasmus Without Paper (EWP), Europass, EMREX, European
Blockchain Services Infrastructure (EBSI), European Self-Sovereign Identity Frame-
work (ESSIF), XHochschule (XHEIE), XSchule, DigiZ, Single Digital Gateway (SDG)
and the international Veriﬁable Credentials (VC).
3
Method
To clean up and create a common base, we looked at state of the art current applications
and standards. We focused on available open-source standards to provide transparency
and we applied a four-step approach.
First, we coded the descriptions of the standards and looked for technical guidelines
to identify the elements of the ecosystem.
Second, we grouped the identiﬁed standards into Service, Infrastructure, and Model
on a metalevel to highlight the distinct stages.
Third, we identiﬁed the links between the standards to clean up and disclose their
interrelationships.
Forth, we explored a way for a possible coupling concept, which is the missing key
element to enable interoperability for operators.

4.1
European Learning Model
The European Commission developed the European Learning Model (ELM) to describe
learning opportunities, qualiﬁcations, credentials, and accreditations. ELM also uses
the EDCI technical infrastructure. ELM also provides a standardized, single format to
describe different learning certiﬁcates (such as degrees and diplomas or examination
results) within the European Union and the European Economic Area[8]. It is oriented
on the ELMO/EMREX Standard [8] described below. In addition, ELM can be applied
as the subject in the W3C Standard for veriﬁable credentials. In the latest release, version
2.0 (version 3.0 in draft), ELM provides [7]:
• Learning processes (learning speciﬁcations, learning qualiﬁcations, and learning
achievements, learning outcome, learning activity and learning activity speciﬁcation,
assessment and assessment speciﬁcation)
• Description of issuer and credential subject
• Concepts for describing learning opportunities and accreditation
• Price details
• Concepts for veriﬁable presentation and Europass presentation
• Deﬁnition of the Europass extension of a Europass Veriﬁable Credential
• Deﬁnition of the Europass extension of a Europass Veriﬁable Presentation
• Deﬁnition of a Europass learning opportunity
The issuer uses ELM when aiming to use a standardized format for issuing a digital
credential. After issuing, the relying party (RP) uses this standardized format to verify
the credential.
4.2
ELMO
ELMO is an XML format that supports assessment information included in diplomas,
transcripts of records, and diploma supplements. Moreover, it describes these assessment
qualiﬁcations, programs, and courses [9]. EMREX [10], EWP [11], and ELM are based
on ELMO as data format [8].
4.3
European Digital Credentials Infrastructure
The European Commission developed the European Digital Credentials Infrastructure
(EDCI) with the European Digital Credential data model. EDCI consists of standards,
services, and software enabling institutions to issue digital, tamper-proof qualiﬁcations
and other learning credentials within the European Education Area, i.e., European Digital
Credentials for Learning - EDCL [8]. EDCI is an evolution of ELM and consists of three
numbered pillars [12].
The implementation enables organizations to efﬁciently issue qualiﬁcations such
as a degree or certiﬁcates of attendance via a secure, trusted, and tamper-proof digital
infrastructure.

Cleaning Up: Interplay Between European Standards and Veriﬁable
781
4.4
European Student Service Infrastructure (EDSSI), European Student Card
Initiative (ESC), and Erasmus Without Paper (EWP)
The EU has been a driving force for developments in higher education. The European
Student Service Infrastructure (EDSSI) is at the core of digitalization measures within
the EU higher education landscape, forming the architectural and technological basis
for an EU service landscape regulating: identity, signature, and transport.
Analyzing EDSSI in detail:
• It merges varying technological approaches within a decentralized infrastructure
• Individual standards, such as EMREX, are bundled into an overall package
• eIDAS creates a uniform legal basis for trust services; interestingly, since 1997, EU
regulation
• Samsung & others cover the commercial context
The European Student Card Initiative (ESCI) is on the one hand a passport and,
on the other hand is part of the EDSSI to enable a more ﬂuent exchange process. [13]
While the EWP is part of the ESCI, EWP is designed to replace paper-based Erasmus
workﬂows with digital workﬂows. This procedure enables HEIs to exchange student
mobility information quickly and securely. EWP consists of two components a network
and Erasmus Dashboard [14]:
• EWP network: interconnects a multitude of student information systems (whether
individual universities or third-party providers that represent multiple institutions)
using APIs (i.e., connectors between the network and users)
• Erasmus Dashboard: A web solution for exchanging student data electronically
Furthermore, EWP is also involved in the ELMO educational data standard [15].
HEIs use EWP, i.e., issuer, to exchange and manage student data.
4.5
Europass
Europass is a set of online tools and information. It allows students to store and exchange
secure, digital and veriﬁable credentials [16]. As a European Union project, it uses EDCI,
such as the EDCI wallet, to obtain veriﬁable credentials [8].
4.6
Emrex
EMREX is a secure electronic data exchange format for digital credentials [9, 10]. It
is one of the few formats and it already enables cross-border data transfer. Students
can use EMREX directly to submit their transcripts digitally. Institutions can also use it
for transcripts provided by students [5]. EMREX is part of the EDSSI. In addition, the
Eramus + program can use EMREX for student mobility exchanges.

782
M. Gottlieb and G. Bacharach
4.7
European Blockchain Services Infrastructure
The European Commission and the European Blockchain Partnership (EBP) created
EBSI. It is the ﬁrst EU-wide blockchain infrastructure based on open standards and a
transparent governance model [17]. The goal is to use blockchain to create cross-border
services used in public administrations and ecosystems [18, 19]. The EBSI architecture
consists of the following layers [17–19]:
• Infrastructure layer: providing generic capabilities and connectivity to blockchain
networks, i.e., validating, authorizing, and storing the proposed transaction(s) on the
chain of blocks
• Chain and storage layer: It controls and enables the execution of trusted transactions
for blockchain protocols. Furthermore, it is also used to manage trusted registries for
off-chain protocols
• Core services are a set of standardized interfaces (APIs) that provide third parties with
the capabilities to develop applications and ensure compliance with guiding principles
deﬁned and approved by the EBP.
EBSI underlies seven use cases while we focus on Diploma Management.
4.8
European Self-soveraign Identity Framework
Self-Sovereign Identity Framework (ESSIF) is one EBSI use case. It implements a
self-sovereign identity and allows users to create and control their own identity across
borders [7, 20]. ESSIF coordinates veriﬁable data and status registry between issuer,
holder/subject, and veriﬁer/service provider [20].
4.9
DigiZ
DigiZ stands for “Digitales Zeugnis” (Digital Certiﬁcate) [21]. It refers to a solution for
digitizing German certiﬁcates based on the Online Access Act (German: Onlinezugangs-
gesetz, OZG), which came into force in Germany in 2017. It obliges the federal, state,
and local governments to make their administrative services available electronically by
2022 [5].
DigiZ is based on signed PDF ﬁles secured via a blockchain. Attached to the PDF
ﬁle is machine-processed education data in ELMO format using XML schemas. The
EMREX service processes this ﬁle.
4.10
Veriﬁable Credentials
A veriﬁable credential is a tamper-evident credential with authorship that can be cryp-
tographically veriﬁed [14]. A veriﬁable credential consists of three roles. The learner
holds a veriﬁable credential; the issuer provides it, and the RP processes and veriﬁes it.
Therefore, all three levels are handling veriﬁable credentials.

Cleaning Up: Interplay Between European Standards and Veriﬁable
783
4.11
SDG
In 2018, the European Parliament and the European Council decided to create uniform
digital access to the administration in the EU with the Single Digital Gateway (SDG)
regulation [22].
The EU regulation on the SDG pursues the goal that the digital offering of the admin-
istration should be citizen-oriented and user-friendly. In addition, all public administra-
tion services are to be found via a single portal. At the European level, the existing Your
Europe information portal [23] is to be expanded, modernized, and developed into a
central point of contact for the offerings and information of the public administrations
of all European member states. To this end, the “Your Europe” portal will be linked with
the portals of the member states. Synergies with digitization projects of the respective
member states will be used - in Germany, for example, the implementation of the SDG
regulation is part of the OZG implementation and part of the “Overall management of
register modernization” project [24].
By December 2023, 21 of the most important bundles of procedures (Annex II
of the SDG Regulation) and services from four directives (2005/36/EC, 2006/123/EC,
2014/24/EU, and 2014/25/EU) are to be made fully available digitally and across borders
in all member states and connected to the Europe-wide Once-Only-Technical-System
(OOTS). With the help of the OOTS, evidence is to be exchanged across borders and
automatically between authorities throughout Europe. This will eliminate the need for
citizens and companies to provide evidence more than once, provided they agree to the
respective evidence being transmitted.
In these 21 administrative procedures, the following procedures are involved in the
ﬁeld of (higher) education:
• Applications for student funding for higher education studies, e.g., student grants or
loans, from a public agency or institution
• Submissions of an initial application for admission to a public HEI
• Application for recognition of academic diplomas, certiﬁcates, or other evidence of
study or coursework
Unfortunately, the related Commission Implementing Regulation of the SDG is only
available in a draft. However, it already indicates that in order to reduce the costs of and
the time necessary for establishing the OOTS, the architecture of the OOTS should, to the
greatest possible extent, rely on reusable solutions, be implemented technology-neutral
and accommodate different national solutions. For example, the OOTS should be able to
use the existing national, including central, regional and local levels, procedure portals,
data services, or intermediary platforms that have been created for national use. This also
applies to the EMREX service by name. That would mean that the ELMO data model
could be used as the data model to exchange educational data. Other existing services
and systems could also be used.
It can be expected that the SDG will come with some requirements to be SDG
compliant. In other words, an existing system can be used. However, this system must
fulﬁll at least a certain level of criteria. However, all this is currently (May 2022) still
under discussion.

784
M. Gottlieb and G. Bacharach
4.12
XHochschule and XSchule
XHEIE (XHochschule) is a standardization project based on the OZG [25]. The project
aims to standardize the exchange of student data in the national higher education system.
This is to ensure interoperability between the student administration systems of the uni-
versities for media-independent processing of existing and future digital administrative
services.
This will consider domestic and international efforts to improve connectivity to
international systems. In addition, XHEIE provides information about its work in the
context of standardization and coordinates similar projects.
XSchule has a similar orientation; it is based on German schools [26]. It creates a
uniform speciﬁcation for data exchange in school administrations across all countries.
It enables data exchange between the players in the school environment without media
discontinuity. Thus, it ensures that school administration services are digitized in an
interoperable manner following the OZG and the Single Digital Gateway (SDG).
4.13
Coupling Concept
To develop a coupling concept, we derived the interplay of standards. Therefore, we
explained the standards by grouping them into buckets. We distinguished the buckets
between the Models stages containing the actual data structures or data models carry-
ing the educational data, Interface structures connecting the Model with Services, and
Services containing applications used to transport data. Thus, this article groups the
identiﬁed standards into Models, Infrastructures and Services to highlight the distinct
stages.
Model contains the schemas of the data. The schemas contain, for example, iden-
tifying data such as decentralized identiﬁers, personal data such as ﬁrst and last name
and further credential data such as payload. The identiﬁed European and international
applied standards include ELMO, ELM v3, and Veriﬁable Credentials. XHochschule
(XHEIE) and XSchule arrange themselves nationally in Germany. Both are based on
German variables to the best of our knowledge. Therefore, we consideres them as a
stand-alone scheme. We focused on the big three ELMO, ELM v3 and Veriﬁable Cre-
dentials because they are the basis for the ecosystem. Within the group model, we see
increasing information density. Veriﬁable Credentials can be seen as an envelope that
holds more data in an agnostic way. For example, this envelope may contain data in the
structure of ELMO or ELM. While ELMO deﬁnes explicit variables for the user data
and is also designed explicitly for credentials such as the high school diploma as well
as upper secondary diploma, the ELM v3 contains variables from ELMO but has more
details about the variables. The complicated relationship between the ELM and ELMO
structures is still subject to further investigation.
Interface is part of a technical system for communication. In this speciﬁc case, EDCI
stores data as the model does. However, it seems to appear similar to an interface as an
infrastructure. The SDG project is currently working on solutions that, according to
available information, still require tuning to existing services and data models. It envi-
sions the development of an interface called the Once-Only-Transport-System (OOTS),
whose data model covers a variety of life situations (not only educational data). The

Cleaning Up: Interplay Between European Standards and Veriﬁable
785
SDG is not our focus because we are unaware of conﬁrmed associations with the Euro-
pean standards. The SDG has the same goal as the OZG: “The digital offering of the
administration should be citizen-oriented and user-friendly. In addition, all services are
to be found via a single portal.” [27].
Service includes serving performance to generate a product such as Europass with a
CV or infrastructures to store, manage, or provide information, credentials, or certiﬁcates
such as EWP, EMREX, EBSI, ESSIF, or DigiZ. EWP is part of the European Student
Card Initiative (ESCI) and the EWP service has been using ELMO in productive use
since 2022. In comparison, the EMREX service has been established across Europe for
years. The German solution for digitizing certiﬁcates, DigiZ, is also based on ELMO.
The Europass service uses ELM via the EDCI interface to develop the EDC data model
further. The EBSI infrastructure also applies ELM as its data model. ESSIF uses EBSI
as a use case and thus has no direct application of a model or interface.

5
Discussion
A coupling concept extends the knowledge base on different levels. At the level of data
models, two major European data standards are emerging. One is the ELMO, and the
other is the ELM. In fact, from the authors’ point of view, there are currently only
two initiatives in Europe in the ecosystem that we have presented that do not support
the ELMO or ELM data models. These are the initiatives XHEIE and XSchule, which
have announced that they will ﬁrst design a German national data model and use it for
German services. However, converting the national model for existing services such as
DigiZ to the ELMO model seems possible. Furthermore, data models such as ELM are
not mutually exclusive for the operators of these initiatives in the future.
Translating the variables to German in the XSchule and XHEIE initiative adds com-
plexity. Due to the international nature, each HEI would have to provide a transformer

786
M. Gottlieb and G. Bacharach
from English to German as a service, which would lead to costs and staff requirements
at each HEI. Therefore, such a solution appears to be an additional expense. At present,
it does not make sense to present these standards in the coupling concept.
ELM, in turn, supports Veriﬁable Credentials technology, so systems that use ELM
can process them. Considering that the ELM data model is based initially on the ELMO
data model, understands ELMO as a subset of its structure, and is intended to be fully
aligned with ELMO in version 3, a solution to the interoperability of these two models
and the services that use them is obvious. However, the agnostic standard of veriﬁable
credentials allows the addition of a payload structure as a subject. There is a shift to
JSON as data format, which is also recommended for veriﬁable credentials. Thereby,
we see veriﬁable credentials as a fundament for the coupling concept.
At the interface level, the services of the EBSI infrastructure are also planning to use
ELM as a data model connected via the EDCI. The use of ELM or ELMO for individual
services and infrastructures is still under discussion. EDCI seems to be the gate for
further services.
The SDG and OOTS connection and location of the interfaces to the coupling concept
are still unclear. So far, we have classiﬁed SDG more as an infrastructure. However, it
could develop into a platform that provides access, so it would be considered a service.
Thus, we recommend adopting current standards to the coupling concept for an efﬁcient
international standard.
The coupling concept needs a common denominator to connect data models and
infrastructures with the surrounding services. Thus, the coupling concepts work as a clear
and speciﬁc interplay between the ﬁxed standards as core components of the ecosystem
and the ﬂexible services of the ecosystem. This concept means that more and more
services can be developed and set up on the coupling concept in the future.
As mentioned, GDPR is a signiﬁcant topic in the European Union. Thus, it requires a
deeper discussion of common criteria and IT security standards for the interplay between
digital credentials.
6
Conclusion and Future Work
This paper extends the knowledge base with an overview of global, European, and
German standards for digital credentials in HEI and their interplay with veriﬁable cre-
dentials. In addition, we highlight how and in what way the application architecture
interacts explicitly with currently existing European standards for digital credentials in
the HEI environment. Moreover, we illustrate that interoperability can be achieved easily
by creating a coupling concept in the current mainstream of this ecosystem. On the one
hand, this interoperability concept is the smallest common denominator. To a semantic
level, on the other hand, getting the best coverage is the biggest common denominator.
We extend theory with a coupling concept that can combine European standards
with veriﬁable credentials (W3C Standard). Practitioners can apply the structure to
implement a solution for several ongoing approaches in Europe and to be internationally
interoperable with the veriﬁable credential standard. This concept enables a process free
of media discontinuity with all its beneﬁts to lifelong learning. A learner can easily share
theircredentials,whilethirdpartiesdirectlybeneﬁtfromfraud-freecredentials.Everyone

Cleaning Up: Interplay Between European Standards and Veriﬁable

can trust the system and is independent from a single institution. The community can
discuss the coupling concept in more detail to validate it and strengthen its validity.

The Intersection Between the CS
Students’ Perceived Ideal Workspace
and the Actual One
Hamna Aslam1,2(B), Eleonora Ilina1, Joseph Alexander Brown3,
and Jean-Michel Bruel2
1 Innopolis University, 420500 Tatarstan, Russian Federation
{h.aslam,e.ilina}@innopolis.ru
2 Universit´e de Toulouse IRIT-CNRS 31000, Toulouse, France
bruel@irit.fr
3 Brock University, St. Catharine, Canada
Abstract. The concept of ideal workspace for software developers is
being researched widely through individual and grouped studies. Such
studies rely on the information provided by the participants. However,
an individual’s perception of an ideal space might not align with the
space in which they are actually productive. Therefore, it is necessary
to further investigate by considering the individual’s actual workspace
settings when they believed themselves to be productive. This research
work examines the perception of an ideal workspace (for study and com-
puter science education related tasks) of computer science students and
the intersection between their perceived ideal settings and the actual set-
tings when they felt satisﬁed with their work results.
We interviewed nineteen computer science students using the focused
conversation method. All participants are students of the bachelor’s pro-
gram in computer science. The participants provided the visual descrip-
tion of their ideal work environment through drawings, and they also
drew the workspace of the scenario, when they believed themselves to
be productive. We examined both drawings to identify the intersecting
features between them. Both workspace settings (desirable and real),
identify the features (of the desirable working environment) that are an
integral attribute of the student’s productive work.
Keywords: Student’s workspace · Developer’s workspace · Focused
conversation method · Ideal workspace · Workspaces
1
Introduction
The notion of an ideal workspace is a subjective question, and therefore, a single
space cannot be ideal for all individuals. The questionnaires-based investigation
is the most common approach applied while investigating the workers’ satis-
faction with their work environment [6]. Considering the software domain, the
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 789–801, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_82

790
H. Aslam et al.
developers diﬀer in their perceptions of productivity [9] and consequently might
require diﬀerent workspace conﬁgurations. Diversity in the workspace conﬁgu-
ration is indispensable to acknowledge to promote productivity among work-
ers. Studies conducted years or even decades ago demonstrate the impact of
human factors [7] and diﬀerent work environments on the worker’s productivity
[3,4,13,15]. Lean evaluation methodologies for workstations’ design is a common
approach to better ergonomics [2], and 5s pillars provide a solid base for initi-
ating an eﬀective workspace design [8]. Recent research suggests that workers
in STEM prefer private workspace [14], and even in shared spaces, there is a
need for adaptation possibilities [12]. Furthermore, giving the workers freedom
to organize their workspace promotes the productivity rate as well [1]. Therefore,
we examine the compute science (CS) students’ workspace settings and identify
which features are integral to their productivity. The participants are students
of the computer science program and are actively involved in programming and
software engineering (SE) assignments and projects.
Although we asked students to explain what productivity means to them,
this research work does not examine productivity perceptions. The perceptions
of productivity slightly diﬀered among some participants; however, this does not
impact our research question as we do not compare participants.
Our research contribution lies in identifying the intersection and the diﬀer-
ences between a CS student’s perceived ideal workspace or study space and their
actual workspace in which they self-identiﬁed themselves to be productive.
When this paper uses the term ‘workspace’, the participants are referring
to the space where they study and perform SE-related tasks. The participants
drew their perceived ideal workspace and the space in which they worked pro-
ductively in reality. Both drawings of participants were compared and analyzed,
and the results suggest that certain features in the participant’s perceived ideal
settings do not relate to their study related work. These features are desirable to
make the workspace pleasant. In drawing of their actual workspace, the students
illustrate the features that are critical and speciﬁcally linked to their work and
productivity.
The research outcomes identify the intersection between the CS students’
perceived ideal workspace and their actual workspace. Furthermore, we observed
that certain features are shared among participants in their ideal and real space
drawings. Therefore, we provide a general checklist (not exhaustive), for the uni-
versities and employers to conﬁgure settings that are integral to the CS students
and developers’ work directly and those features that accentuate the desirability
of the workspace, see Table 1.
2
Focused Conversation Method and Aﬀordance
Examination
This research applies the focused conversation method to examine the partici-
pants’ preferences and aﬀordances concerning their workspace. The word aﬀor-
dance has been coined by the ecological psychologist James Jerome Gibson.

The Intersection Between the CS Students’ Perceived Ideal Workspace
791
Aﬀordance implies action possibilities [5]. All the actions that students take
within their workspace are the aﬀordances of that workspace. For example, a
chair aﬀords the action of sitting, a pen aﬀords the action of writing, and so on.
An object can be used for purposes other than the ones for which it was
designed. A chair, for example, may be used to place books and other items.
While Gibson’s aﬀordances refer to all action possibilities (i.e., any usability),
Norman (in the ﬁeld of human computer interaction) refers to correct usability
while discussing aﬀordances [10]. Norman’s view on aﬀordances of a pen would
only allow writing as this is the correct usability. Gibsonian aﬀordances include
the pen being used as a hair clip, a tool for poking and pointing, and any
other possible use. As a result, it is critical that we question participants about
the aﬀordances they associate with workspace features. This indicates whether
the workspace has all of the requisite items and features to create a productive
environment. On the other hand, how do student developers achieve the required
functionality by tinkering with items.
To examine participants’ aﬀordances inside their workspace, we used the
focused conversation method (FCM) for the interview. United States Army
Chaplain and Art Professor, Joseph Mathews developed the focused conversa-
tion method as an art appreciation, and reﬂection methodology [11]. The focused
conversation method include four categories of questions, Objective, Reﬂective,
Interpretive, and Decisional. Hence, it is sometimes also referred to as the ORID
set of questions or framework. The ORID method allows questions to be asked
in a series that replicates a normal human thought process. Initially, the partic-
ipants are given objective questions that provide data and facts on the scenario
under discussion. Based on the facts collected, the reﬂective questions assess the
participant’s emotional state. The interpretive questions, which follow the objec-
tive and reﬂective questions, ascertain the implications and meaning of informed
events. The last set of questions is for making a decision. Hence, the conclusion,
next steps, and plans are all understood through the decisional questions.
The ORID set of questions are signiﬁcant in understanding the Gibsonian
and Normans’ aﬀordances. The participants could reﬂect systematically on their
workspace settings. Furthermore, the participants were not given any instruc-
tions about their ideal workspace settings. They were free to describe anything
they ﬁnd desirable in their ideal work settings; hence no rule books or guidelines
were imposed. This informs us of their Gibsonian aﬀordances, such as how they
would like to design and interact with their environment without any constraints
(i.e., all action possibilities). Further, when participants drew the settings of their
actual workspace, their Norman’s aﬀordances became visible, such as the fea-
tures in their environment that actually helped them get their job done (through
correct aﬀordances of the workspace features) productively.
3
Study Design
The research consists of an interview with the participants who are computer
science program students with an average age of twenty years approximately.

792
H. Aslam et al.
The participants are asked questions regarding how important it is for them
to be productive. Further, the interview questions are geared toward gaining a
better understanding of their ideal and actual workspace.
The interview started with a light conversation with the participants about
their day or anything they wanted to share. As part of the interview, the partici-
pants were then asked to draw their ideal workspace. Participants also described
and drew the workspace in which they felt eﬀective when working in a real-
life task scenario (software engineering related work). Through ORID set of
questions, we could understand the Gibsonian and Normans’ aﬀordances of par-
ticipants within their drawn ideal and actual workspace. Finally, participants
discussed their preferences after seeing the visual representation of their ideal
and actual workspaces.
The interview starts with the question
1. What do you think, is it essential for you to be productive during your work?
Did you think about your productivity? Rate your productivity according to
the ten-point scale (this question sets the context for further questions).
The ORID set of questions are detailed as follows.
2. What is your ideal workspace? (furniture, atmosphere, location, anything).
Describe it. Could you draw it? (objective question)
– Where are you in this space? (reﬂective question)
– Why do you need all these things? (interpretive question)
– How could all these details help you to work? (decisional question)
3. Now, could you please remember the situation when you were the most pro-
ductive (maybe it is one of your projects where you managed to achieve the
outstanding results).
– How was your workspace in that situation? Describe it. Could you draw
it? (objective question)
– Where are you in this space? (reﬂective question)
– What helped you to be the most productive? (interpretive question)
4. Do these workspaces (ideal and actual) coincide/intersect? Which features
coincide? Which do not? Why?
– What could be the combination of these spaces? (interpretive question)
– Imagine the third space that includes the important things of both spaces
(ideal and actual). Describe it. (decisional question)
5. Is there anything you would like to share in regards to your workspace pref-
erences and philosophy?
4
Analysis of the Responses

The ﬁrst question concerns the participants’ understanding of the value of being
productive and what productivity entails. Even if participants have diﬀerent
ideas about being productive, the purpose is to understand their productivity

notions. The participants solve programming-related tasks frequently as their
