they were referring to software-related tasks.
We asked them to provide a number (on a scale from one to ten) that
describes their productivity level when satisﬁed with the outcomes. Participants
gave diﬀerent numbers, and we asked them what does this number means in
terms of productivity. All participants stated that this number of productivity
in a day means that they did all the work planned and skipped only non-urgent
tasks, such as ﬁnished prioritized tasks in their to-do list. Some also stated that
productive time is a state for them when they work and do not feel the time
passing. One participant also mentioned that in addition to ﬁnishing tasks, they
feel that their time was productively organized when they could ﬁnd time to eat
well and do some personal activity or learn something new.
4.2
Ideal Workspace
The second question required participants to describe their ideal workspace. Fur-
thermore, the interviewer asked them to draw to provide visualization. Table 1

794
H. Aslam et al.
shows the things participants mentioned in their ideal space. The drawings sug-
gest that all participants have drawn ideal space in much more detail than their
actual space. Considering the pictures’ quality, it is noticeable that the drawings
describing ideal working conditions are much more complicated and even more
extensive than the ones about the actual surroundings. Sixty-three percent of
them (12 participants) utilized more space on the sheet, or the whole sheet, draw-
ing ideal working conditions than in the pictures about the real environment, as
shown in Fig. 1. Moreover, these pictures have more details and descriptions.
Fig. 1. Left to right: ideal and real workspace
The most common things that participants drew in their ideal workspace
include a table and a chair. All participants mentioned that they would like their
chairs to be very comfortable and adjustable. The same comment was given for
the table also, as they stated that they would like to alter the height of the table
according to their comfort. The other frequently mentioned items include a hot
beverage, window, and stationery boxes. Some participants provided and drew
details of the sensory features of the environment. They wrote the temperature
reading they would prefer in their room, drew air-conditioner and heater, and
described the light intensity.
The uncommon things include a lamp and a candle. The participant who
drew the lamp stated that they do not like the sunlight and prefer a bit dark
atmosphere, and they would like to have a lamp that gives lights of diﬀerent
colors. Another participant drew the candle and stated that the candle gives the
perception of comfort to them. Participants drew food, fridge, water cooler, and
coﬀee machine, saying that they would like to have such things in access in their
ideal space as they prefer having drinks and snacks while working. Having more
descriptions in exemplary drawings (compared to actual workspace drawings) is
unexpected because participants should know the real workspace much better
(they had the experience of being there). It is much easier to reproduce what

The Intersection Between the CS Students’ Perceived Ideal Workspace
795
we already know than creating an absolutely new situation. However, during the
work with ideal pictures, participants are much more eﬀective. This is possible
because dreaming and using imagination helped them increase their activity (i.e.,
drawings) productivity at once. This condition seems to be a crucial integral
attribute of the students’ productive work.
4.3
Window, the Most Idealized Commodity
The window has been the most desirable object in the ideal workspace. Fifteen
out of nineteen participants drew the window in the ideal workspace, and nine
participants drew the window in their actual space. However, the windows drawn
in the ideal space are elaborated in detail.
In the ideal drawings, windows showed nature. Trees were drawn as well as
some description was provided to emphasize the desire to see nature. A partici-
pant wrote beside the window picture,
“Beautiful view [such as] landscapes on the Sviyaga river.”
Some participants drew the sun and wrote the words, warm, and sunny. Another
participant wrote (describing what should window lead to),
“Some sort of garden with a fountain in the middle probably.”
Another wrote, always sunny, as shown in Fig. 2. Furthermore, some participants
also drew the balcony and stated that they would like to have the opportunity
to see nature. Even those participants who informed that ideally, they would like
to have maximum sensory deprivation such as no distracting visuals or audio,
drew window. The participant stated,
“Window can be a distraction but gives relaxation. So, I would like to have a
window as relaxation can induce focus.”
One of the participants drew a simple space consisting of only a table, chair,
a cup of tea, and books on their table. They placed themselves in nature out-
side. They informed us that if the weather is perfectly warm, this is the ideal
workspace for them. The following are the phrases used by some of the partici-
pants while discussing the window in their diagrams.
– I can take inspiration from nature.
– I would like to be in a colorful place, a mountainous area. There’s a room in
this hilly area, and when I go outside, I see nature.
– Plants relieve stress.
– I need a window so that I do not entirely feel isolated.
– I need a good view to outside so that I can take short breaks from work and
feel fresh again.
The window’s signiﬁcance in the perceived ideal workspace of our partici-
pants is evident through their drawings and statements. However, how integral
it is to make them productive is another question. The illustrations of their
real workspace are analyzed to identify what role the window played in their
productivity. The discussion continues in the following sections.

796
H. Aslam et al.
Fig. 2. Window to the nature and sun as idealized by the participant
4.4
Real Workspace
The third question required participants to consider the scenario when they
felt themselves to be productive. The participants referred to their projects
when they gave an example of when they felt satisﬁed with their productiv-
ity level. Examining the drawings of the student’s actual surroundings, as we see
in Table 1, participants have mentioned things that they primarily interacted
with during the work. All participants drew a table and a chair. They also drew
teacups, snacks, stationery, paper pile, and monitor displays (details in Table 1).
Those participants who drew the window (in the real workspace) did not specify
the scenery (outside the window) or the weather. This shows that they were
so immersed in their work(at the time they were working in that space) that
they overlooked the details outside the window. However, in ideal settings, they
idealize a window to a beautiful view.
The participants worked either in their dormitory room, reading hall, or
small meeting rooms in the university, as shown in Fig. 1 right-side image. The
description in the original workspace drawings is much less as compared to the
ideal workspace. Furthermore, the participants drew the real workspace very
fast and did not think much while drawing. It was visible that they enjoyed the
drawing of their ideal space and gave it much thought. Participants also draw
their colleagues if they were present in their real workspace.
4.5
Combination of the Ideal and Real Workspace
We observe some diﬀerences between the ideal and real space. However, these
diﬀerences are not signiﬁcant (for the majority) other than those cases when
they would like to have a beautiful view outside their window.
When participants were asked to combine the ideal and the real space, some
commented that they would add two monitor displays in their actual workspace
as this is more convenient for them. They would also add a comfortable chair
and table, a fridge, and a coﬀee machine to have eatables in access, and would
like to have better lights in their surrounding.
The majority of the participants (14 out of 19) stated that their real
workspace is very close to their ideal space. The signiﬁcant diﬀerence was in

The Intersection Between the CS Students’ Perceived Ideal Workspace
797
the drawing in Fig. 1, where the participant created a studio apartment space
in their perfect illustration (left-side image), and their real workspace was the
meeting room in the university. Another signiﬁcant diﬀerence is observed in the
picture (ideal) when the participant has placed themselves in nature outside,
and they were working in the university reading hall when they were actually
productive (actual workspace).
5
Research Outcomes and Discussion
This research provides insight into two fundamental constituents of the CS stu-
dents’ workspace. These include,
1. A checklist that ensures that all the vital features exist in the workspace that
is an integral part of the productive work.
2. A checklist to improve the working environment, but it is not connected with
the work directly. The things in this list aﬀect the mood of the student and
can aﬀect their productivity.
While we examined the ideal workspace drawn by all the students, we also
concretely analyzed these students’ actual workspace. This workspace is chosen
explicitly by the students themselves as they were asked to provide an example
of the scenario when they felt themselves to be productive and were satisﬁed
with the results they achieved in this scenario. Both drawings were instrumental
in recognizing both integral features of the workspace to ensure productivity and
those features that the university would integrate into the workspace to provide
pleasurable surroundings for the students.
We are sure about the integral elements that we have identiﬁed as they were
illustrated signiﬁcantly by the students, and they provided comments on the
usefulness of these features. However, we had an exception, in which a partici-
pant represented the real scenario and informed that they were very productive
in this surrounding, but they would never like to work in this place. In that
example, they were sitting in the kitchen and had a chair and table as the only
furniture. They did not want to disturb their roommates and preferred to work
separately. The motivation for ﬁnishing the work made them productive, and
this was the only reason. They did not consider this environment suitable for
them. Apart from this case, all other participants were generally satisﬁed with
the surroundings of their actual workspace.
The analysis was done individually on each participant’s ideal and real set-
tings. We compared both settings for each participant to ﬁnd the intersection
between them and understand which features are actually part of the productive
work. However, the individual analysis outcomes of all participants have com-
mon patterns. Therefore, these standard features provide us with the checklist
of the majority of the integral elements of the students’ space. These features
include
– A comfortable chair
– Height adjustable table

798
H. Aslam et al.
– Window in the room
– Two monitor screens
– Stationary and papers
– Whiteboard
– Beverage and water
The other features that are good for the universities to consider (to enhance the
workspace) include,
– A window to a good view outside
– Plants in the workspace
– Possibility to block the sensory distractions
– Eatables
– Lamp
– Space where students can shift to do some other activity as a short break
– Good internet connection
– Relevant books
These lists are not exhaustive to be applied to all students. However, the nineteen
participants of our study helped us determine those features that are desirable
for them and integral to their productivity.
5.1
Gibsonian and Norman Aﬀordances
As previously stated, Gibsonian aﬀordances are all action possibilities, and Nor-
man’s aﬀordances are the optimal and correct usability actions. The participants’
responses do not always refer to Norman’s aﬀordances, and they associate Gibso-
nian aﬀordances with some features. As an example, the window has a function
of ventilation. However, participants prefer it to elevate their mood. The window
is aﬀording calmness and a desirable mood for the participants. This aﬀects a
person’s productivity, but the window is not essentially required as a tool for
project completion. A window can also be regarded as providing an emotional
component of Norman’s aﬀordance of windows. Ventilation is eventually leading
to calmness. However, it is more on the side of Gibsonian aﬀordances as windows
are not required for the work itself. It is only creating a pleasant atmosphere for
work.
In another case, a participant drew creativity space (i.e., embroidery tools)
in their ideal settings. However, while discussing their productive time, they
informed that their concentration is entirely on the project with a plan written
to proceed. This creative space which is being idealized within the workspace,
provides a Gibsonian aﬀordance of relaxation through art. It is not directly
related to the work but still desirable to elevate the overall work atmosphere.
The responses suggest that CS students prefer certain features in their
workspace that are not directly connected to their work. Besides, they use cer-
tain items for the purpose they are not intended for. Therefore, it is signiﬁcant
to know what an item aﬀords for the participant. It can be the items’ intended

The Intersection Between the CS Students’ Perceived Ideal Workspace
799
usability (i.e., Norman’s aﬀordances), or they might explore and utilize it for
other purposes to suit the needs (i.e., Gibsonian aﬀordances). Furthermore, the
examination using the aﬀordance concept from both Gibson and Normans’ app-
roach allows workspace designers to understand the rationale behind installing
any feature. This makes it clear to the relevant workspace designers what settings
the students could use.
6
Reﬂections
Another signiﬁcant outcome of this research is the realization that participants
had after visualizing their drawings. The interview’s last question was if they
would like to share their thoughts about this whole process and discussion. Par-
ticipants informed that this study helped them to rethink their perception of
an ideal space to be productive. One of the participants who placed themselves
alone in their ideal workspace informed that after thinking about their most
productive scenario, they have realized that the presence of people is vital for
them and is a crucial factor in making them productive. They were working with
their friends in the actual workspace.
Another participant informed that looking at their drawings clariﬁes what
actually helps them the most to be productive and what they would like to
change. One participant stated that both pictures made them realize that they
need more comfort in everything, such as a comfortable chair and a room where
they can adjust the lights and the temperature as they are aging.
Similarly, one participant informed that they realized that desirable sensory
features contribute much more to their productivity than the environment’s
physical characteristics. A general comment given by the majority of the par-
ticipants was that upon visualizing both drawings, they feel that their actual
workspace is quite close to their ideal space.
7
Conclusion
This research examines the intersection between the student’s perception of
their ideal workspace and their actual workspace (producing productive out-
comes). The students concentrated on their software projects while discussing
their workspace and productivity scenario. The study also aims to identify how
accurate the participants are in assuming what they idealize as their workspace
would actually help them to be productive. The responses demonstrate that
certain features the students drew in their ideal workspace are not related to
their work. Other features in their ideal space that also existed in their actual
workspace are integral to be productive. The analysis is done individually, and
each student’s ideal and actual workspace drawings are compared. This study did
not compare all students’ drawings with each other, as productivity deﬁnition
might vary from one student to the other. However, once the analysis was done
for each student separately, we observed shared interests between them. The
students being in the same age group and solving similar tasks, plus being close

800
H. Aslam et al.
to each other in their productivity perceptions, allow us to introduce a general
checklist for the students’ workspace conﬁguration. One list is the essentials and
features related to the work, and the other list describes features (not directly
related to the work) that enhance the workspace and, consequently, introduce
positivity and increase the work environment’s desirability. This study provides a
strong base for further developments in understanding optimal workspace in any
organization. The ORID questions stated above are applicable for examining stu-
dent’s perceptions of their study space and hence the research setup is extendable
to any university students and employees of software industry. We also refer to
the concept of aﬀordance while understanding how the participants interact with
their work items. The primary source of information for this study is students.
It is signiﬁcant for them to understand what improves their work environment.
However, their perceived improvements, might actually do not aﬀect their work
and productivity. Such subtle details are capturable through drawings and visu-
alization. Furthermore, imagining their ideal work environment and discussing
their real productivity scenario and workspace helped students also realize the
integral features of their workspace.

Strategic Viewpoints for the Awareness
of Educational Competition in Response to New
World Order (NWO)
Case Study: The Fraction Project as an Example for Higher
Education (HE) Partnerships Between Asia and Europe
Adisorn Ode-sri1(B)
, Thomas Köhler2
, Peeratham Techapalokul1
,
Pisit Wimonthanasit1
, and Panom Kaewphadee1
1 Rajamangala University of Technology Lanna, Chiang Mai 50300, Thailand
adisorn.odesri@gmail.com, {peeratham,pk}@rmutl.ac.th
2 Technische Universität Dresden, 01069 Dresden, Germany
thomas.koehler@tu-dresden.de
Abstract. This research is conducted at the time when the term “New World
Order” is causing a stir. The world has reached a pivotal point in human history
where to-day’s pressing issues can no longer be tackled by any individual coun-
try alone, but with some concerted effort through international collaborations.
The pressing issues of today’s world—the changing global balance of power,
geopolitical changes, the emergence of alternative ﬁnancial infrastructure, etc.—
are inescapably impacting all lives. Several sectors have been harshly hit and the
education sector especially HE is no exception. It is more vital than ever that HE
needs to quickly transform to increase its capability to compete as negligence in the
“next normal” era—the dramatic restructuring changes following the “new nor-
mal” era—may lead to its downfall. This work takes a critical look at the possible
causes of the collapse of HE and recommendations to address them. These recom-
mendations comprise a set of strategies and a model developed that can help guide
HEIs to increase their capability to compete. The proposed guideline is based on a
case study of the FRACTION project, an academic collaboration between Asian
and European countries that help the member institutions to increase their capa-
bility to compete and achieve their goals. Speciﬁcally, our study is driven by the
following research question: From a strategic aspect of international collaboration
as a way to increase capability to compete and build institutional excellence, how
can HEIs proactively prepare and respond to changes in the NWO era?
Keywords: Higher Education · Educational Competition · New World Order
1
Introduction
“The New World Order (NWO) is a conspiracy theory that hypothesizes a hidden tyran-
nical world government.” [1] This is a deﬁnition from an extreme viewpoint through a
lens of conspiracy theory. Speciﬁcally, the deﬁnition describes the changes caused by

the NWO as the ultimate historical moment of the progress toward a single totalitarian
world government. From a political point of view, “The term “New World Order” has
been used throughout time to refer to any period of history evidencing a new dramatic
change in world political thought and the balance of power.” [2] Regardless of any eco-
nomic point of view, “the business world witnesses the change from “Globalization”
to “The Great Decoupling”, a state in which the global economy is divided into two
supply chains, through the inﬂuence of superpowers like China and the United States.”
[3] This great divide will have an impact on the existing interconnected global economic
structure. This movement to dismantle the old economic engine in combination with
the current global situations (e.g., wars, global pandemic, political instability, uncon-
ventional ﬁnancial systems, natural disasters, etc.) cause a great wound to the world,
resulting in a negative impact on the global economy at both macro and micro levels. It
is regarded as an era in which traditional trust in traditional science is declining rapidly
and coming to an end. Today, geopolitical and economic changes caused by the “New
World Order” have hit all countries across the world. To some extent, these changes are
the catalyst that forces nations to adapt, reform, and transform to survive. These actions
are vital to ensuring the nations’ capability to sustainably compete in a global stage
and avoid becoming “the victim of changes”, a state characterized by stagnated growth
and isolation. The impact of changes has already become exacerbated as the COVID-19
situation lingers for more than two years. In times of crisis, every nation falls into one
of the three groups. First, the “Winner countries” are the countries that can recover
from the crisis and grow quickly. On the opposite end, the “Loser countries” are the
ones most hard hit by the crisis and are on the brink of collapse. [4] Although these
countries can survive in the end, their growth is well below an acceptable level, often
resulting in a declining growth rate. To recover, these nations may need to build back up
from zero or even negative growth levels. The last group are those that “neither won nor
lost”, as they are able to withstand the impact due to their stable political and economic
foundation, as well as their ability to maintain a competitive advantage for growth and
recovery. A classic example is the period after the Cold War around 1985–1991 in which
the once-mighty world superpower, the Soviet Union became one of the losers and “the
fall of the Soviet Union nearly a quarter of a century ago forced geographers and policy
makers to rip up their maps.” [5].
The collapse of the Soviet Union led to the United States’ dominance as the world-
most powerful nation, “the Winner” in the Coming World Order at the time. The U.S.’s
world superpower status continued for almost three decades up until the Beijing 2008
Olympic Games. It was the ﬁrst time the Olympic Games were held in China, marking an
important moment in which China started to demonstrate its potential as world leaders
while the U.S. started to lose its grip on bargaining power. Today, it becomes clear about
the bipolar world in which the U.S. and China are competing for their position as the
global superpower. In this age of rapidly changing world, Higher Education institutions
(HEIs) need to strategically transform to connect to the “new world”. To address this
urgent need, we conduct an interview with experts in the higher education domain to
gather their views on the challenges of today’s HE and their recommendations. This
study places a speciﬁc focus on the strategic aspects of increasing HEIs’ capability to
compete and building institutional excellence by means of international collaboration.

804
A. Ode-sri et al.
To ensure the practicality of our results, we use a case study of the operational frame-
work employed in the FRACTION project, whose important objective is to develop
successful collaborations and partnerships between Asian and European countries. How
the FRACTION project thrived during the pandemic crisis makes it a worthwhile subject
to investigate and analyze to gain insights. Speciﬁcally, our study is guided by the
following research question: From a strategic aspect of international collaboration as a
way to increase capability to compete and build institutional excellence, how can HEIs
proactively prepare and respond to changes in the NWO era?
2

2.1 To study and analyze strategic aspects by education experts who have author-
itative knowledge on both the impact of the “NWO” on education at international
levels and the challenges that HEIs must address to survive.
2.2Tostudyandpresentamodelandasetofstrategiesforestablishinginternational
academic cooperation through research collaboration.
2.3 To study, analyze, and provide scenarios of how the HE partnerships between
Asia and Europe could attain the status of excellence under the circumstances of
NWO, a supporting international framework, and various restrictions surrounding
their future ongoing collaboration.

Perspectives and Strategies from 5 Education Experts Through

4.1
Higher Education Institution: Three Generations in the Normal, New
Normal and Next Normal
If one were to compare an academic institution and a human being, the administration
would function as if it were the brain. Similar to what the brain does by controlling
other body parts to work together, the institution’s administration provides direction for
its institutional operations with its ideal academic goal of beneﬁting the society and
the students, as well as managing its human resources. To take this analogy further,
according to a Buddhist belief, these institutions can be seen as being under Samsara,
the cycle of birth, aging, ailing and death that can happen at any time.
Table 2. Identify characteristics of 3 main stages of human life.as compared to higher educational
institutions.
Life Stage
Summary of key characteristics
Childhood
Eager to learn and imitate. New experiences often lead to a fruitless,
short-term excitement
Adolescence
Desire to ﬁnd a role model, develop its unique character to reach its potential
Adulthood
Long for stability and strong foundation. Better decision making. Know
when to make compromises to achieve goals
End of Life
Mostly remain indifferent with no desire to adapt. Hold on to past success,
attitudes, and systems. On a path to shutdown
Asst. Prof. Dr. Sethakul, P. and Dr. Lekapat, S. (Interview, July 9, 2022) shared their
views on the behavioral characteristics of today’s academic institutions by comparing
them to the three stages of human life (see Table 2). Some academic institutions are still

806
A. Ode-sri et al.
in their “childhood” stage, characterized by the desire to learn new things and emulate
other institutions. At this stage, they also tend to become excited for a brief period when
trying new ideas without being fully com-mitted, making it hard for them to achieve their
goals, resulting in wasted efforts. Some academic institutions are in their “adolescence”
stage. With some experience, these institutions start to seek a role model to develop their
character as an academic institution. If it was before the 21st century, this could mean
building the institutions’ identity. However, in the 21st century academic institutions as
well as world leading organizations place their focus on identifying the niche, relying
on the agility and power at this stage to reach their full potential. For matured academic
institutions (reaching their “adulthood” stage), they often set goals toward maintain
stability by laying a strong foundation for their organization. They are aware of the
need to make a trade-off. In other words, their maturity guides their design choices and
decision making based on situations. To achieve their various goals, they understand that
it often means a decrease in quantity, quality or some other success criteria to compensate
for the other goals. Simply put, with limited resources, when one thing goes up, some
other things must go down. When excluding emerging HE institutions (formed during or
after the NWO), all older HE institutions can be characterized by one of the three stages
or exhibits a combination of attributes. In other words, some institutions possess a set of
attributes from different stages. These deﬁning characteristics are developed in a distant
past or through ongoing development. These institutions would be seen as “HEIs that
still see the future of existence”. Their existential future depends on the adjustment or
strategic change in the management of HE institutions regarding the ability to keep their
institutions in operation and produce graduates, as well as other institutional capabilities
such as the ability to innovate, conduct research and serve community and industry.
These considerations need to match with the contexts and needs of stakeholders and job
markets on a global level. Those institutions refusing to adjust or change are “near the
end of life”. They are not only falling, but also heading towards a collapse.
Academic institutions are currently in the midst of transitioning to a new era inﬂu-
enced by three main factors: political concept, economic, and international relations. In
this new era, the thriving academic institutions are the ones that can adapt to changes
and are able to build on their strengths developed in different stages to gain competitive
advantages. However, several academic institutions can be seen as “asking and waiting
for” the return of “Normal”. This observation reminds the authors about an insightful
remark by Davis, I., McKinsey and Company (2009) at the time of a global ﬁnancial
crisis known as “Hamburger Crisis” 13 years ago: “For some organizations, near term
survival is the only agenda item. Others are peering through the fog of uncertainty,
thinking about how to position themselves once the crisis has passed and things return
to normal. The question is ‘what will normal look like?’ While no one can say how
long the crisis will last, what we ﬁnd on the other side will not look like the normal of
recent years.” [7] At the moment, what we refer to as “Normal” in recent years may
no longer be the challenge for the new era. This is evident by how Sneader, K. and
Singhal, S. from the same organization as Davis, I. insisted on the same stance their
colleagues took 11 years ago and took it further by introducing the idea of the “Next
Normal”, which comes after the “New Normal”: “It is increasingly clear our era will
be deﬁned by a fundamental schism: the period before COVID-19 and the new normal

Strategic Viewpoints for the Awareness of Educational Competition
807
that will emerge in the post-viral era: the “next normal.” In this unprecedented new
reality, we will witness a dramatic restructuring of the economic and social order in
which business and society have traditionally operated. And in the near future, we will
see the beginning of discussion and debate about what the next normal could entail and
how sharply its contours will diverge from those that previously shaped our lives.” [8]
Academic institutions might cling to what once nurtured them (e.g., outdated characters
or contexts). These institutions may operate without the leadership and decision making
that respond to the “New Normal” and “Next Normal” environments. As an analogy
to the human body, a failing institution administration can be compared to a brain that
focuses only on short-term outcomes, neglecting body wellness, becoming too big and
clumsy, unable to compete with others in the new era.
4.2
The Academic Institutions’ Challenges: Escaping the Collapse Caused
by the NWO
Experts’ views on the challenges of academic institutions to escape “the collapse” caused
by the NWO.
1. Building institutions’ excellence and international standards to gain back trust–As
the COVID-19 situation gets better, the return to “normal” might mean the return of a
normalwayoflivingwithoutexcessiverulesforprotectingpublichealthsafety.However,
higher-education institutions at the top of the education system hierarchy, have been
impacted by the pandemic, becoming “the sick man of the education system” as a result.
Many colleges and universities are failing at delivering online and hybrid classrooms,
facing countless problems. The institutions’ capability to produce quality graduates
has also been degraded. Consequently, the trust gained from the outside also becomes
weakened. Rebuilding trust quickly is needed to prepare for future changes that come in
different forms. Institutional excellence and international standards through international
collaborations is one of the key drivers to help institutions rebuild trust successfully. Dey,
S. R. (Interview, July 8, 2022).
2. Expectation of Stakeholders on increasing dimensions–the four main groups of
stakeholders are as follows:
2.1 Students and Parents – the ﬁrst group of stakeholders has the need to receive quality
education amidst the rapidly evolving body of knowledge. Therefore, the challenge is
how to best prepare academic instructors in both knowledge and skills that match the
needs of the future graduates to ensure their success when they enter the workforce.
Köhler, M. (Interview, July 8, 2022).
2.2 Companies, Labor Market, and the Industry – Currently, several companies have
developed specialized courses that train their workers to meet the speciﬁc knowledge
and skill set of various job responsibilities. This increasingly common trend of in-house
course development sends the signal to academic institutions about the urgent need to
change. Speciﬁcally, the institutions need to meet the demand of the labor market in
a collaborative or mutually beneﬁcial approach. These efforts can help the academic

808
A. Ode-sri et al.
institutions keep pace with the industry’s advances regarding job training (e.g., knowl-
edge, skills, instructional methods) that are often many steps ahead of their academic
counterparts. Sethakul, P. & Lekapat, S. (Interview, July 9, 2022).
2.3 Competitors–At the moment, the competitors of academic institutions are not limited
to only peer institutions. The ﬁrst group is non-traditional competitors known as edu-
cation technology (Ed-tech) companies. Previously focusing on products and service,
many ed tech companies have evolved to become full-ﬂedged education providers. This
trend is in direct response to the failure of traditional academic institutions to produce
graduates that meet the demand of the labor market. Another group is the Inﬂuences, who
provide an alternative venue for learning. This type of competitor has a lot of potential
and ﬂexibility to attract a large group of learners that was previously considered the main
audience of academic institutions. These inﬂuencers can motivate and inspire learners
more convincingly than traditional instructors when discussing practical topics (e.g.,
knowledge and skills development, job responsibilities, career goals, etc.). Sethakul,
P. & Lekapat, S. (Interview, July 9, 2022) There are 2 basic viewpoints when it comes
to qualifying professionals as follow: 1) The demand of companies to qualify personnel
exactly for their needs. This would lead to an enormous dependence of the personnel on
this company. 2) The demand of universities and other academic institutions to qualify
skilled personnel in such a way that they are not only employable in 1 company. This
will strengthen the ﬂexibility of the personnel. Even though it may mean that personnel
turnover is high for a speciﬁc company, this approach creates high importance for the
labor market. Skilled workers can be relatively easily upskilled and redeployed to other
areas where they are needed. Köhler, M. (Interview, July 8, 2022).
2.4 Domestic and Foreign Partnerships – This group of stakeholders plays an impor-
tant role in the advances and development of academic research. These stakeholders
include peer institutions and other organizations (both for-proﬁt and nonproﬁt). From
an investor’s point of view, partners seek genuine interest from each other to collaborate
to achieve a mutual goal. Equally important are the clarity, continuity, and fairness of
policies as they are deciding factors when assessing risks, costs and beneﬁts. Köhler, M.
(Interview, July 8, 2022).
3. Incorporate Dynamism in the Design of Academic Administration–The academic
administration of educational institutions needs to embrace dynamism to drive institu-
tional development, focusing on the beneﬁts for the organization, students, faculty and
the society. The dynamism is important especially when it comes to meeting the demand
of the labor market, and various international standards. The operation of government-
funded academic institutions in particular often requires complex procedures. Therefore,
adopting a more lightweight approach employed in fast-paced companies to its institu-
tional operation can give a competitive edge before more agile Ed-Tech companies get
too far ahead in the game. Trinh, N. T. T. (Interview, July 8, 2022).
4. Maintaining the balance between administrative power and academic freedom–Aca-
demic institutions have the obligation to provide a safe space for academic freedom
(e.g., freedom of conducting research, freedom of teaching, freedom of expression).

Strategic Viewpoints for the Awareness of Educational Competition
809
However, academic institutions’ underlying organizational structures often makes “pol-
itics” an inevitable part of institutional governance, resulting in the imbalance of the
two. The imbalance can be problematic when administrative positions inﬂuence aca-
demic research, causing academic freedom to become weakened. To further exacerbate
the problem, some institutions’ traditions lend themselves to a biased selection process
of governing positions despite its democratic process. To address this issue, it is of utmost
importance to maintain the balance so that “administrative power” has boundaries and
does not cause undue inﬂuence that limits academic freedom. Trinh, N. T. T. (Interview,
July 8, 2022).
5. Recruitment and Selection Process–Jobs in government-funded agencies and orga-
nizations used to be highly attractive options and account for a large portion of total
employment in many countries. It was common to have a competitive recruitment and
selection process to hire talented, high-quality applicants. However, in this new era, the
labor market in the “next normal” has become more open and global. This new labor
market is a vast pool that can attract talents from every corner of the world. The types of
jobs available in this global labor market are also more challenging and offer unprece-
dented freedom when it comes to work styles and how workers receive compensation
with respect to the quality and quantity of work being done. Most academic institutions
are nowhere near this view of open and globally competitive recruitment and selection
process. In the future, it could become increasingly more difﬁcult to recruit and retain
quality employees to the point that the need to set lower expectations on the quality of
employees can negatively impact the academic institutions. Sethakul, P. & Lekapat, S.
(Interview, July 9, 2022).
5
Fraction Project - An Example for HE Partnerships
In response to changing situations and environmental factors both in the middle and
after a turning point, a pivotal moment in history that led to the formation of a NWO.
The role that HEIs must play is to formulate effective strategic policies that will lead
to actual implementation for their existence. One of those strategies being unavoidable
is to have national and international partners who will be a key factor in maximizing
limits of competitiveness on the path of excellence. These are still the efforts of “Col-
leges and universities worldwide—of all types and serving the full spectrum of student
populations—are grappling with how best to equip their graduates with the knowledge
and skills needed to succeed in the globalized world of the twenty-ﬁrst century, and
ensure their own relevance and standing in the global higher education community.
When done carefully, in accordance with overall institutional mission and goals, build-
ing relationships with counterparts abroad can be a key aspect of strategies to address
these issues. Increasingly, the question is not whether to engage globally, but how?” [9]
For answering the question in the dimension of “How to?”, the researchers propose a
strategy for applying the research working model through the ﬁve main phases of the
workﬂow, as shown in Fig. 2, as a way of pursuing cooperation between countries on the
view of seeking cooperation partners for the establishment of centers of excellence, by
having HEIs in Asia and Europe as a case study, in which this manner of the implemen-
tation of a research process-led strategy is different from that of other strategies such

810
A. Ode-sri et al.
as scholarships awarding, exchange of learners or teachers. This is because common
goals and needs can be sought from the beginning of the process, resulting in a picture
of possibility or termination without much time wastage compared to other strategies
implementation manners. The ﬁve-phase process can be brieﬂy classiﬁed as follows:
1) The selection of partners who are of interest and have the potential.
2) Coordination to achieve agreement for the establishment of pilot centers both within
the country and abroad.
3) Academic Embedment prior to proceeding the pilot project in actual practice.
4) Study additional case studies from a Center of excellence in Asia – Europe.
5) Academic research, writing and compile research content related to the theoretical
basics and principles.

6
Conclusion and Recommendations
This section provides a summary of key points to highlight important ideas of this
study. Speciﬁcally, we restate our classiﬁcation of the “winners” and “losers” in the
Changing World Order arenas, and discuss them in relation to the points presented in the
Introduction section. This discussion interprets and builds on the ideas of Dr. Tungnirun,
A., who attended the keynote speech at the SEC Capital Market Symposium titled “World
Order new” [3], in combination with our ﬁve experts’ perspectives. If comparing to be
economically clear the “winner countries group” and the “loser countries group” may
see the past circumstance, present situations, and future status, in a nutshell,
1) The winner countries group are those that keep pace with technology. The losers are
countries that have fall behind on technology, seriously injured.

Strategic Viewpoints for the Awareness of Educational Competition
813
2) The winner countries group are those countries that previously have focused on
constructing of foundations and sustainable growth. The losers are those that do
not focus on an inverted pyramid of economy, do not adhere to the principle of
self-reliance until fallen from the framework of sustainable development.
3) The winner countries group are the countries that will connect the future world. The
losers are those that may have to close down itself and restore. (adapted from [3]).
From the summary above, the HE sector should try to keep pace with the rapid
changes to survive. In our context, “The Winners are the Connectors of the Future World”
means building connections and networks at international level is the key factor to put
academic institutions in a place to compete. These connections and networks are not only
limited to peer institutions but also include industrial sectors and various labor markets at
an international level. Fostering good relationships among academic institutions abroad
could help with starting new relationships and collaborations with other non-academic
institutions and organizations. This international cooperation is an important contribut-
ing factor for building institutional excellence, increasing the institutions’ capacity to
compete in a sustainable way. This idea is well aligned with the interview data collected
from the ﬁve experts when asked the following question: “If your organization would like
to abruptly change to gain excellence in HE, what are the importance of the following
factors or procedures?” All experts’ choices include the concept of “international” as its
core, for example, “Received quality and standard certiﬁcation from international orga-
nizations”, “Received awards and honors from international organizations”, “Received
cooperation from international organizations”.
The winner is the one who connects the world. These winning groups are in the
position to provide a helping hand for others, thereby creating a condition for gaining
bargaining power. As a result, building international collaboration and promoting insti-
tutional excellence while adapting institutions’ identity to the rapidly changing contexts
or environmental factors will be key to survival of HE institutions.

Integrating Code Reviews into Online
Lessons to Support Software Engineering
Education
Juan Carlos Farah1(B), Basile Spaenlehauer1, Mar´ıa Jes´us Rodr´ıguez-Triana2,
Sandy Ingram3, and Denis Gillet1
1 ´Ecole Polytechnique F´ed´erale de Lausanne, Lausanne, Switzerland
{juancarlos.farah,basile.spaenlehauer,denis.gillet}@epfl.ch
2 Tallinn University, Tallinn, Estonia
mjrt@tlu.ee
3 University of Applied Sciences (HES-SO), Fribourg, Switzerland
sandy.ingram@hefr.ch
Abstract. The use of peer code review exercises is well established in
software engineering education. Nevertheless, challenges involving stu-
dents’ ability to perform code reviews have been identiﬁed as barriers
to successfully integrating code reviews in educational settings. We have
previously proposed code review notebooks as a way to address this issue.
Code review notebooks resemble computational notebooks but focus on
reviewing rather than executing code and can serve to introduce stu-
dents to the code review process. In this study, we evaluated the eﬀects
of using a code review notebook via a case study whereby 25 university
students were taught how to identify code style issues in JavaScript. Our
mixed-method analysis suggests that the code review notebook format
encourages students to reﬂect on their learning process and can result in
short-term learning gains. These ﬁndings could serve instructors looking
to incorporate code review exercises into their practice.
Keywords: Code review · Software engineering education · Online
lesson
1
Introduction
Code reviews—the process whereby code written by one programmer is cross-
checked by another programmer for potential bugs or issues—are standard prac-
tice in software engineering. Most studies addressing the use of code reviews
in education focus on peer code reviews, in which students complete a pro-
gramming assignment and review each other’s submissions [12]. Peer review has
been championed as a way to teach students to provide and receive constructive
criticism [2], as well as to build collaboration skills [24]. Furthermore, the ris-
ing popularity of social coding platforms (e.g., GitHub, GitLab) as pedagogical
tools has resulted in students being exposed to professional code review tools
c
⃝The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 815–826, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_84

816
J. C. Farah et al.
and processes as part of their education [10]. Nevertheless, one of the challenges
of using peer code review in education is the fact that students often lack the
ability to perform code reviews [12]. In this paper, we present the evaluation of
an online lesson format aimed at teaching students how to perform code reviews.
We refer to lessons following this format as code review notebooks, as they resem-
ble computational notebooks, but focus on performing code reviews and not on
executing code. By completing lessons featuring code review notebooks, students
could both learn about the code review process through example code snippets
and get practical experience through interactive exercises.
In a previous study [8], we assessed the usability of the code review notebook
format, achieving positive results. In this study, we focus on the format’s eﬀec-
tiveness in achieving short-term learning gains, encouraging students to reﬂect
on their learning process, and providing a satisfactory learning experience. We
conducted a case study comprising a within-subjects experiment with 25 univer-
sity students. The ﬁndings from our mixed-method analysis suggest that code
review notebooks could serve as a way to introduce students to software engi-
neering concepts such as programming best practices, as well as to illustrate how
the code review process works. Students would therefore be better equipped to
participate in peer code review exercises. Through this evaluation, we aim to
consolidate the design of online lessons aimed at preparing students for the code
review process as a part of their software engineering education.
2
Background and Related Work
In a recent systematic literature review, Indriasari et al. reported that the ﬁrst
“use of peer code review in a programming course was published in 2003”, with
187 studies published as of April 2019 [12]. Indriasari et al. also emphasize that
the most common approach to incorporating code reviews into educational con-
texts is to include them as a peer review exercise. To provide the technological
context for these peer code review exercises, instructors often integrate social
coding platforms or bespoke tools (e.g., CaptainTeach [18], EduPCR [26], Cae-
sar [23]), speciﬁcally designed for peer code review. These peer code review
tools provide functionalities that are particularly useful to instructors, such as
code partitioning and automatic review assignment [23]. Indeed, Indriasari et
al. underline that “[one] of the main beneﬁts of peer code review, particularly
in large classes, is to assist the instructor in providing timely feedback to stu-
dents” [12]. Nevertheless, properly motivating and training students to provide
feedback is a challenge that these same authors identify as a barrier to the suc-
cessful adoption of peer code review exercises in the classroom. If students are
expected to review code submitted by their peers, they should be able to do so
satisfactorily, as otherwise the exercise is neither useful for the student conduct-
ing the review nor for the student receiving the feedback. To address this chal-
lenge, a few studies have proposed focusing on teaching the code review process
to individual students, namely, work by Ardı¸c et al. [3], Ribeiro Guimar˜aes [19],
and Song et al. [21]. Our work is most aligned with this line of research.

Integrating Code Reviews into Online Lessons
817
In a previous study [8], we presented a code review application that could be
used to scaﬀold code review notebooks. Our evaluation using standard instru-
ments for measuring user experience (System Usability Scale [5] and the short
version of the User Experience Questionnaire [20]) suggested that students rated
the usability of the code review notebook and the underlying code review appli-
cation positively. The current study builds on these results, this time addressing
the potential code review notebooks have to support learning experiences for
software engineering students.
3
Methodology
The purpose of our evaluation was to address one main research question:
What are the eﬀects of using a code review notebook on students’ experi-
ences learning to identify code quality issues in JavaScript?
To frame our evaluation, we focused on three aspects of the learning expe-
rience: (i) learning gains achieved, (ii) self-reﬂection on the learning experience,
and (iii) feedback regarding the lesson. We evaluated our code review notebook
through a case study focusing on these three aspects. Our study consisted of a
within-subjects experiment that took place in an online learning environment.
In this section, we present the methodology used for our evaluation.
3.1
Context
To perform our evaluation within an educational setting, the context for our case
study was an asynchronous online lesson1 on code linting. The process of linting
code dates back to the 1970s and involves the use of static analysis tools designed
to detect issues in software [13]. Linting tools are often used in industry to enforce
code quality standards and help automate code reviews. It is therefore pertinent
to teach the concept of code linting using a code review notebook, especially
since the code review process has also been proposed as a pedagogical tool for
introducing students to code quality standards [15]. In our case, we speciﬁcally
introduced students to ESLint [25], a linting tool designed for JavaScript, as well
as the Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide [1], a popular conﬁguration for ESLint. In
the following sections, we highlight the technological and pedagogical contexts
used to carry out our study in an educational setting.
Technological Context. Our code review notebook was implemented on the
Graasp digital education platform [9]. Graasp allows instructors to create online
learning experiences featuring a varied set of web-compatible resources. Instruc-
tors can therefore prepare an online lesson comprising textual explanations
alongside multimedia content and interactive applications. To prevent over-
whelming students with content, instructors can divide the lesson into phases,
1 The online lesson is available here: https://graasp.eu/s/sm12t9.

818
J. C. Farah et al.
Fig. 1. Code quality issues were explained using text accompanied by a code snippet
containing the issue and another snippet illustrating a possible solution.
which the students can explore using a vertical navigation bar. For our imple-
mentation, we followed the code review notebook format. Textual explanations
regarding the code review process and code linting were intercalated with images
and code snippets. Code snippets were presented using the code review applica-
tion [8], which allowed students to annotate each line of code with comments.
Furthermore, a text input application was used to allow students to answer
open-ended questions. This online lesson—depicted in Fig. 1—was shared with
students via a link, which they could access anonymously.
Pedagogical Context. Our online lesson was structured following the Fixer
Upper pedagogical pattern, whereby students are presented with code “that is
generally sound but [contains] carefully introduced ﬂaws [that] can both intro-
duce a complex topic early and serve as a way to introduce error analysis and
correction” [4]. The lesson was structured into seven phases that students were
meant to navigate in order. The ﬁrst phase (Getting Started) introduced the
ﬁrst code snippet that would serve to highlight the code style issues that would
be addressed in the lesson. Students were presented with an exercise comprising
a code snippet and were asked to annotate it with any potential issues they
could identify. This initial exercise served as a pre-test to gauge the student’s

Integrating Code Reviews into Online Lessons
819
initial knowledge of code reviews, linting, and JavaScript best practices. In the
second phase (Introduction), we formally introduced the lesson with a short tex-
tual introduction to linting. The third phase (ESLint) presented ESLint and the
Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide. The fourth (Styling) and ﬁfth (Best Practices)
phases made up the core of the lesson. In these phases, we used the code qual-
ity issues seeded into the pre-test as examples and walked the student through
them using (i) an explanation based on the ESLint documentation and Airbnb
JavaScript Style Guide, (ii) a code snippet highlighting the issue, and (iii) a code
snippet illustrating a possible solution. Figure 1 depicts the fourth phase, high-
lighting an explanation block featuring the code review application. In a sixth
phase (Exercise), we presented an exercise that served as a post-test to gauge
students’ short-term learning gains. A seventh phase (Conclusion) served as a
wrap-up, presenting the answers to the post-test and asking students to provide
(i) a short reﬂection on their performance and (ii) feedback regarding the lesson.
3.2
Participants
We recruited 27 students pursuing degrees in technical subjects via our inter-
nal networks at the ´Ecole Polytechnique F´ed´erale de Lausanne and the School of
Engineering and Architecture of Fribourg in Switzerland. Students were informed
that this was an optional, ungraded exercise. Two students did not complete the
post-test and were therefore excluded from our analysis. A total of 22 students—
9 female and 13 male—completed an optional demographics questionnaire. Of
these students, 17 were currently completing a master’s degree, while 5 were
enrolled in a bachelor’s program. Students were also asked to report on a scale
of 1 to 5—with 1 being Beginner and 5 being Expert—their programming expe-
rience both overall and speciﬁcally using JavaScript. Results show that while
students’ programming experience was above average (¯x = 3.18, Mode = 4),
they were mostly uninitiated in JavaScript (¯x = 1.95, Mode = 1).
3.3
Procedure
Our study took place in January 2022 and was conducted remotely. Students
were sent a link to the code review notebook described in Sect. 3.1 and were
instructed to take a total of 30 min to complete the evaluation. Students accessed
the online lesson anonymously and completed an initial exercise that served as
a pre-test before going through the code review notebook and then taking a
post-test. Upon completion of the online lesson, students were directed to an
online questionnaire that included an optional demographics section.
3.4
Instruments
To address our research question, we operationalized the ﬁrst aspect—learning
gains—using a bespoke instrument based on data from the pre- and post-tests.
Learning gains were calculated as the diﬀerence between a student’s post- and
pre-test scores, with a possible range from −100% to 100%, inclusive. The second

820
J. C. Farah et al.
aspect—self-reﬂection—was addressed via a question2 asking students to provide
feedback on their performance in short answer form. Finally, the third aspect—
feedback—comprised an open-ended question3 asking students to provide their
thoughts on the lessons as well as any comments or suggestions.
3.5
Data Analysis
The dataset used for our analysis was extracted from the Graasp platform using
its learning analytics pipeline [7]. To analyze our data, we followed a mixed-
method approach. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and infer-
ential statistics. Speciﬁcally, we report the sample mean (¯x), median (˜x), and
standard deviation (s), and use a dependent t-test for paired samples to compare
the distributions of pre-test and post-test scores. Qualitative data were analyzed
using line-by-line data coding [6]. We also performed sentiment analysis on the
self-reﬂection and feedback comments. For this analysis, we used VADER [11]—
a sentiment analysis model trained on social media data—to assign a sentiment
score ranging from −1 to +1 to each comment.
4
Results
In this section, we outline our results following the three aspects of our study.
4.1
Learning Gains
In the pre-test, students detected 14.5% of issues on average (¯x = 14.5%, ˜x =
9.09%, s = 13.1%), while in the post-test, the mean increased to ¯x = 48.6% (˜x =
50.0%, s = 23.1%). The diﬀerences between the pre- and post-test resulted in a
mean learning gain of ¯x = 34.0% (˜x = 35.7%, s = 20.0%, xmin = −1.95%, xmax =
71.4%), with all students except one achieving positive learning gains. To assess
the distribution of learning gains (and therefore the distribution of the diﬀerences
between the pre- and post-test) we performed a Shapiro-Wilk test, which did not
show evidence of non-normality (W = 0.967, p = 0.578). Indeed, Fig. 3 depicts
a histogram of the learning gains, visually suggesting a normal distribution. A
dependent t-test for paired samples showed that there is a signiﬁcant diﬀerence
in the distribution of the pre- and post-test scores (t(24) = 8.51, p < 0.001).
Figure 2 illustrates the diﬀerences between both distributions.
4.2
Self-reﬂection
A total of 23 students provided a short open-ended answer to a question asking
them to reﬂect on their performance in the post-test. Comments ranged from

you ﬁnd any of them particularly tricky/helpful?”.

Feedback

(R2 = 0.165, F(1, 19) = 3.767, p = 0.0673). Finally, using line-by-line coding,

hand, 15 students highlighted the positive aspects of the lesson, describing it as

5
Discussion
The results of our study suggest that using a code review notebook to support
an online lesson on software engineering education leads to tangible short-term
learning gains. The fact that—on average—students detected 34% more code
quality issues in the post-test than in the pre-test indicates that the lesson
had a considerable impact on students’ understanding of what constitutes good
quality JavaScript code and on their ability to detect and annotate issues present
in the code snippet. These results suggest that our online lesson format could
serve to address one of the issues identiﬁed by Indriasari et al. [12], namely, that
students often lack the skills necessary to perform code reviews [24]. Speciﬁcally,
our lesson format could be used to address issues similar to the one experienced
by Stalhane et al., who reported that almost all students found only 2–3 out of
20–30 defects (10%), even though they were expected to ﬁnd around 60% [22].

French by the authors.).

According to the authors, one of the possible explanations for this gap could be
that the “process was unfamiliar and hence daunting” [22] for students. Thus, a
code review notebook similar to the one used in this study could be exploited to
guide students through the code review process before exposing them to more
complicated code review exercises. Our work also sheds light on how to help
address some of the concerns teachers have with the peer code review process. In
a study of two computer science university-level courses, Kubincov´a et al. noted
that teachers perceived the feedback provided by students (to other students)
as focusing mostly on minor coding issues [14]. By harnessing a code review
notebook similar to the one used in our experiment, teachers could provide
speciﬁc examples of both the type of issues that they want students to look out
for, as well as the way they want students to highlight these issues when they
encounter them while reviewing their peers’ code.
Our analysis of the self-reﬂection comments provides evidence that students
took the time to reﬂect on the learning experience. Exercises promoting self-
reﬂection have been shown to be positively correlated with student success
in software engineering courses [17] and students have reported ﬁnding self-
reﬂection helpful [16]. Instructors could harness answers from these exercises in
conjunction with the performance on code reviews to identify learning gaps, and
thus personalize teaching strategies targeting students struggling with the con-
cepts at hand. Furthermore, while the sentiment analysis of these self-reﬂection
comments yielded a negative score on average, this result could be due to the
way the question was posed to students. More concretely, the fact that we specif-
ically asked students to reﬂect on the issues they had not been able to identify
could have negatively biased the sentiment scores of their responses.

824
J. C. Farah et al.
Conversely, the feedback provided was overall positive, indicating that the
lesson content and the code review notebook format were predominantly well-
received by students. Speciﬁc themes and comments that emerged from our
qualitative analysis highlight the potential that code review notebooks have to
serve as an introduction to complicated or broad topics that students can then
go on to explore on their own. As there are a vast number of issues that can be
encountered when performing an open-ended code review exercise, using a code
review notebook to motivate the most common ones could be useful for instruc-
tors looking to prepare students for open-ended peer code review exercises.
Finally, the regression analysis performed shows that learning gains were not
a good predictor of either the sentiment score of students’ self-reﬂection com-
ments or students’ feedback on the lesson. While this study’s sample size is
limited, the results of our regression analysis could suggest that actual perfor-
mance on the code review exercises was independent of motivation to reﬂect on
the learning experience and of the perception of the lesson itself. This makes
these types of lessons more adequate as a ﬁrst exposure to the code review pro-
cess for novice programmers, who should not feel discouraged if they do not
perform as well as expected.
6
Limitations and Future Work
Our study has some limitations worth highlighting. First, as previously men-
tioned, while the sample size achieved in this study is suitable for an initial
within-subjects short-term learning gains analysis, data from more subjects
could allow us to consolidate our ﬁndings and draw clearer conclusions with
respect to how learning gains are related to self-reﬂection and feedback. Second,
our learning activity took place outside the formal classroom, as an optional exer-
cise. This might have resulted in sample bias, as those students who responded
to our request for participation might have been students already motivated
enough to take part in an ungraded exercise. To address this, the experiment
should be reproduced in the context of a formal software engineering course,
possibly as a mandatory—albeit ungraded—exercise, which would provide us
with a possibly less-biased cohort of students. Third, this study focuses on one
particular use of code review notebooks, which concerns introducing code linting
concepts for JavaScript programming. In order to generalize our conclusions, it
is necessary to replicate our methodology with code review notebooks tackling
other subjects—such as introducing basic programming concepts (e.g., loops,
conditional statements, functions)—that could also be applicable to software
engineering education. Finally, while feedback on the lesson was mostly positive,
some negative comments regarding the usability of the interface emerged during
our analysis. In future work, we aim to address these limitations and explore the
potential to expand the code review notebook to more use cases.

Integrating Code Reviews into Online Lessons
825
7
Conclusion
In this paper, we presented results from a case study aimed at assessing the
impact of code review notebooks on students’ learning experiences in the context
of an online lesson on detecting code quality issues in JavaScript. Results from
our mixed-method analysis provide insight into the potential for code review
notebooks to help students learn how to perform code reviews. Our ﬁndings
are particularly pertinent to practitioners who use or are looking to incorporate
code reviews into their courses. By introducing the code review process using
an online lesson following the code review notebook format, instructors could
prepare students to conduct reviews that are both useful for themselves and for
the student receiving the feedback. As more instructors adopt such approaches,
research into how best to scaﬀold these online lessons for diﬀerent audiences (e.g.,
age groups, ﬁelds of study) could shed more light on the impact our approach
could have in domains outside of software engineering education.

The Application of Academic Article Writing
Techniques for Content Creation
for the Promotion of Buddhist-Based Learning
Communities and the Conservation
of Buddhism via Online Communities
Case Study: A Fund-Raising Project to Establish the Meditation
Center at Mahavana Ashram, Nepal Using Facebook Page
Adisorn Ode-sri1(B)
, Thomas Köhler2
, Panom Kaewphadee1
,
Pisit Wimonthanasit1

Abstract. This research paper explains the characteristics of academic and con-
tent writing for online platforms. At the same time, it aims at presenting guidelines
for the implementation of some academic writing techniques on content writing
for online learning communities and social services. The researchers used the
Fund-raising Project to Establish the Meditation Center at Mahavana Ashram,
Nepal and a Facebook Page: Super Richy as a case study for this research. The
project and data collection were carried out from October 7, 2021 to March 3,
2022, dividing the execution into 4 time periods to collect 4 statistical data sets
before and after the project execution. Prior to the implementation of the project on
Facebook Page: Super Richy, data collected from October 7 to November 4, 2021,
the Facebook Page reach was -64.2%, Facebook Page visits was -47.2% and New
Facebook Page likes was -69.4%. After the implementation, there was a signiﬁcant
increase on all sections of the page; Facebook Page reach increased at + 319.6%,
Facebook Page visits at 353.1% and New Facebook Page likes at 285.7%. These
results address the question, “how are academic article writing techniques applied
to content creation for the promotion of Buddhist-based learning communities on
social network?” This research transforms the tacit knowledge of writers into an
explicit form by using the art and skill of conducting academic work to identify
the guidelines that ensure ﬁtting content creation.
Keywords: Article writing technique · Content creation · Learning community
1
Introduction
1.1
Background: From Academic to Social Services
In regard to communication, publicity, and human’s theories of learning, no matter how
advanced the technology the world has, how great the economy is, whether we are in

times of waging wars, suffering from natural disasters, or facing the deadly pandemic, the
role of writing is as important as that of speaking, in terms of being the medium or channel
of communication, “which has nowadays important social and educational function and
its status has a high social prestige. It has its speciﬁc norm, which is a structure of its
kind.” [1] this research, being both qualitative and quantitative in its method, attempts
to explain and show the difference between academic writing in general and content
writing for online platforms. This is achieved through observation of the process of
writing, data collection, writing style, components of articles or writing pieces. The
comparison between the two types of writing can show distinct differences, concrete
and abstract, and thereby leads to guidelines or suggestions on the implementation of
the process of academic writing, which can be applied in improving and developing
content writing for online learning communities. Online communities are becoming
inﬂuential on the global population in their lifelong pursuit of knowledge. These seekers
of knowledge include people of different age groups, looking for information online
that would beneﬁt them, as well as to participate in various activities available. One of
these activities, being the case study used in this research, is the Fund-raising Project
to Establish the Meditation Center at Mahavana Ashram, Nepal. In spite of the fact that
the ashram is located in nepal, the project was initiated in thailand where most of the
population are buddhists. Thailand is one of the countries that has the most numbers
of Buddhists in the world. The researchers were invited by the sariputra foundation to
be part of the project and help in writing contents for publicity and promotion of the
project in Thailand. In this sense, this research can be used to answer the question, “how
are academic article writing techniques applied to content creation for the promotion of
Buddhist-based learning communities on social network?” This is intended to make the
content writing as applicable and academic as possible, or at least to make the audience
form unbiased opinion when they read the contents. As a result, the audience would be
able to analyze and understand what they read based on their knowledge, experience,
and the information presented to them.
1.2
The Relevance and Background of Mahavana Ashram, Nepal
Nepal is said to be the land of the Buddha’s birthplace, and other important places asso-
ciated with the life of the Buddha are in Nepal as well, such as the place where he taught
his dhamma, the Mahasamaya Sutra, or other places where he spent an important por-
tion of his life. These places appear in texts in the names of forests, villages, towns, or
cities, such as Mahavana forest, Lumbini, Kapilavastu, and Devdaha. (adapted from [2])
Nepal has a fascinating history of Buddhism for over 2,600 years. The decline of Bud-
dhism in Nepal came about after the time of the Buddha, especially with the emergence
of “Tantrism” on the Indian subcontinent. Rituals, the worship of images, talismans,
beliefs in miracles are based on the principles of Brahmanism-Hinduism or Tantrism.
All these factors were playing their role to make the aforementioned religions hold sway
over Buddhism and in time people ceased to practice the teachings of the Middle Path.
“At the end of the 13th century, the Nepalese social revolution started to manifest, which
gradually brought Buddhism in Nepal to decline. As a result, the practices of Buddhism
were banned and many Nepalese priests had to seek refuge in foreign countries. Later,
when the Rana Dynasty came to power in 1951, the people gained freedom to follow

The Application of Academic Article Writing Techniques
829
Buddhism, either Mahayana or Theravada sects, and Buddhism ﬂourished again in
Nepal.” [3] These historical changes signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the number of Buddhists in
Nepal. According to reports by the Central Bureau of Statistics, “Buddhists comprise
only 9% (2,396,099) of Nepal’s population which makes Buddhism the religion with the
second highest number of adherents in the country, while more than 80% (21,551,492)
are Hindus.” (adapted from [4]) However, devoted Buddhist adherents in Thailand show
their devotion towards the religion the same way other religious adherents around the
world do. The adherents want to preserve the places associated with the leaders of their
religions. Hence, in the many projects and activities that aim at reviving Buddhism in
Nepal, Buddhists from Thailand play a very important role. There have been Thai monks
and novice monks who come to Nepal to study Theravada Buddhism in Buddhist schools
or colleges, and events organized by the Thai government in the places afﬁliated with
the Buddha, building a platform where adherents can donate to build monasteries or
Buddhist memorials, and to maintain these places in good condition. The establishment
of the Meditation Center at Mahavana Ashram, Nepal has been successful owing to
the efforts of Thai Buddhists who wanted to revive and promote Buddhism in Nepal,
with the initiative from the current president of Sariputra Foundation, Lumbini, Nepal.
During the ﬁrst onslaught of Covid-19 pandemic, the residents of Mahavana village
who were Buddhist adherents took the president to Mahavana forest. The forest was
located around 50 km away from Royal Thai Monastery Lumbini, the birthplace of
the Buddha, and 20 km to Kapilavastu, the ancient capital of the state of Sakka in the
time of the Buddha, where he was born and raised as a prince. These places are now
in Nepal, near the northern border of India. At Mahavana forest, foundations were laid
and construction work already began to build Mahavana Ashram in commemoration to
the Lord Buddha’s preaching of Mahasamaya Sutra, an important sutra appeared in the
Digha Nikaya scripture of the Sutta Pitaka. The Sutra says,“The Lord Buddha preached
to the 500 monks who were of royal lineage, all of whom were the Arhats. The devas
were also present in countless numbers to hear his sermons. It was the most auspicious
of all occasions when all the gods from heavens came to listen to the Buddha’s sermons.
It was said that a trillion gods attained enlightenment from hearing this great Sutra.”
[5] Sariputra Foundation was granted 40,000 square meters of land by the government
of Nepal to rent in that particular area for any development projects. There are 2 rivers
cutting through the area from which the villagers can use the water for farming. The
Rohini river is 200 m away from the Mahavana forest. It is a suitable place to build
an ashram on, having all the characteristics recommended in the Seven Sappaya: “1)
suitable abode 2) suitable travel 3) suitable speech 4) suitable person 5) suitable food
6) suitable climate 7) suitable posture” (adapted from [6]) Currently, there has been an
increasing interest from people around the world who want to practice Dhamma at the
place.

Research Purposes
The research attempts to answer the question, “how are academic article writing tech-
niques applied to content creation for the promotion of Buddhist-based learning commu-
nities on social networks?” Therefore, the research’s sub-objectives have been deﬁned
as follows:

3
Methodology
This research used some elements of qualitative and quantitative research. That is to say,
it attempted to compare and highlight signiﬁcant characteristics of academic writing
and content writing on social networks, to see what are the differences in writing style,
format, process, rules, distinct features, as well as the norms practiced in writing.
Fig. 1. Theoretical framework
Following that was the analysis of the collected data, the results of which would be
collected after the application of the academic writing techniques on content writing for
a social network platform, which in this case was the Facebook Page: Super Richy. The
results would include relevant rules and characteristics of academic writing. The appli-
cation of academic writing techniques was intended to make online content writing more
systematic in format, contain sources of information, and not lacking writing ethics. In
creating contents, one should keep in mind that the contents one creates will conse-
quently have inﬂuences over a select group of audiences, and might lead the audiences
to develop a sense of belief or attachment toward any identity or ﬁgure. Therefore, the
researchers had adopted the Fund-raising Project to Establish the Meditation Center at
Mahavana Ashram, Nepal and a Facebook Page as a case study and tool. Moreover, since
there were information and examples from history and religion used in this research,
it was best to conduct the research following the principles of descriptive qualitative

research. In the last section of the research there would be the analysis of statistical data.
The results of the analysis were used to determine the success of the case study, that is
to say whether the relevant principles of academic writing could be applied to content
writing for online social networks in real life.

The Application of Techniques of Academic Writing for Content
