4.1
Review of Previous Application of the Techniques
After Sariputra Foundation’s invitation to the research group to participate in the Ashram
project in Nepal, it was imperative that the researchers reviewed the potentials of the
writings completed prior to the invitation, so that the group could determine the possi-
bility of its involvement in the project. The researchers looked at the success of projects
previously done with similar scope and framework to the case study. This was crucial
because if the research group did not have experiences with this type of project, it would
deﬁnitely affect the project as a whole.
So, the research group had reviewed the previous projects which involved academic
writing techniques being applied in content writing for online social networks of which
mainly aimed at social services, and those that encouraged understanding and promotion
of the preservation of Buddhism, Hinduism, or social responsiveness through online
community. Five such projects were listed in Table 1. They are the examples to show
that academic writing techniques had been applied in content writing for these projects.
The contents were distributed in learning communities and used as a tool to contribute
to public welfare numerous times in the span of 15 years.
4.2
The Differences Between Academic Writing and Content Writing
The authors of the research view writing for academic purposes as encompassing in
nature, in the sense that it can be used in any kind of writing. It has distinct features and
forms, presenting ideas in a very formal and scientiﬁc way.
Academic writing needs to have sources of information. The information offered
are relevant and crucial to target audience. It has a formulaic way of presenting and
reconstructing ideas, referencing sources, analysis of results as well as formal usage of
language. The followings are characteristics of academic writing and content writing.
In contrast with academic writing, content writing often contains elements that aim for
marketing purposes. This kind of writing focuses on emotions and engagement from
the audience. It has a variety of content subjects with the use of language that is free
of forms. It can be said that content writing tries to achieve premeditated results from
its audience. Thus, the writing can have restricted formats or no ﬁxed formats at all.
The writing can be formal or informal in tone, and aim to achieve publicity than facts.
Helixdigital has deﬁned both writing types very interestingly as summarized in Table 2.

4.3
The Selection of Platform for the Project and Case Study
For the Fund-raising Project to Establish the Meditation Center at Mahavana Ashram,
Nepal, the researchers had chosen to use various platforms to promote and publicize the
project, e.t, Facebook Page: Mind and Divination, Facebook Page: Vision and Divination,
Facebook: George Hyde, and Application Line. However, the channel used for the case
study for this research was the Facebook Page: Super Richy which had the Like numbers
over 6,138 accounts. The Page had a unique identity and the Page’s followers met
the criteria, which were:1) the Facebook Page discussed the subjects on Buddhism,
2) its followers had interests in Buddhism, the preservation of Buddhism, and social
responsiveness.

4.5
Choice and Design of Media
It can be said that this part is essential for the success of any writing presentation. It
is important to use suitable media for any particular contents. They can be images of
buildings, places, or activities in action. They can be in the forms of video or 3D images.
It is crucial to use the media that make the writing interesting and pique the interest of
the intended audience.

Results and Conclusion
5.1
Engagement and PAge’s Post Reach
When the Fund-raising Project to Establish the Meditation Center at Mahavana Ashram,
Nepal was chosen to be used as a case study for the research, the researchers also chose
Facebook Page: Super Richy as an online platform for the execution of the project. The
researchers decided to use the sample data during the period of December 5, 2021 to
January 5, 2022. The data sets are shown in statistics in Fig. 2.
(a) Pre-Application Period (1)
7.11. 2021 – 5.1.2022
(b) Application Period
7.12.2021 – 4.1.2022
(c) Pre-Application Period (2)
7.10 – 4.11.2021
(d) Post-Application Period
7.2 - 3.3.2022
Fig. 2. Statistical data showing the Application results [8]
The discussions of results were done by comparing and analyzing statistical data on
3 different time periods: 1) Pre-Application period 2) Application period and 3) post-
Application. The Facebook Page: Super Richy had 6,138 likes of which 65.6% were
female and 34.4% were male. Most of the followers were residents of Bangkok, which

836
A. Ode-sri et al.
accounted for over 30.5% of the followers, it was followed by that of Chiang Mai at
20.9%, and Nonthaburi at 2.4%. The ﬁndings showed satisfactory results. Prior to the
implementation of the research on Facebook Page: Super Richy, October 7 - November
4, 2021, the Facebook Page reach was shown to be at -64.2%, Facebook Page visits was
at -47.2% and New Facebook Page likes was at -69.4%. After the implementation, there
was a signiﬁcant increase on all sections of the Page. The Facebook Page reach was
found to have increased by + 319.6%, Facebook Page visits increased by 353.1% and
New Facebook Page likes increased by 285.7%. It should be noted that, according to
2(a), December 5, 2021 was the ﬁrst time that a content written with some elements and
techniques of academic writing was posted. In comparison to that, on December 1, 2021,
the Page had a Facebook Page reach lower than 500 but the number went up to over
1.5k on the ﬁrst day, and it was able to maintain a 500 to 2k reach until January 4, 2022,
a period of 1 month. After this period, the contents created with the academic writing
techniques were not posted on the page, it was evidently shown that the Facebook Page
reach decreased by -67.7%, and Facebook Page visits by -48.2%.
5.2
Phase 1 of the Promotion of the Project
As this was a long-term project, it was necessary to set the execution of the project
in intervals. Phase 1 of the project was carried out during the period of December
5, – January 5, 2022. Initially, the donation transactions coming in via the account of
Facebook Page: Super Richy was 929 times. The overall donation amount of Phase 1,
at the time, was 11,333.33 USD. However, after the implementation of the academic
writing techniques on content writing, the Ashram project, along with other 6 sub-
projects, was promoted and publicised to wider audiences through online platforms, the
donation amount from the Ashram project on its Phase 1, as of February 19, 2022, was
75,278.30 USD.
5.3
Answering the Research Questions and Academic to Social Services
The researchers answered the research questions by demonstrating in Sect. 4 the exam-
plesoftheprocessandapproachtoapplyacademicwritingtechniquesoncontentcreation
for online Buddhist-based learning communities, especially in Sect. 4.4 and on Table 3.
This can be seen as an archetype of a simple approach to working for the community.
In breaking the writing process of any article into sections and topics, it is similar to the
way a human body is dressed and decorated in different parts with different garments.
Improving on or adding new features on different parts can create something spectacular
as a whole. This process is called “Application of Academic Writing Techniques in Con-
tent Creation”, which makes content writing interesting without taking away its nature.
Contents become not only a source of information and entertainment, but also credible
learning materials. The audience can differentiate what is fact, conjecture, belief, or only
just a story.
The researchers were made aware from the outset that participating in the current
research was to be socially engaged, what is called in the academic circle as socially-
engaged scholarship and University-Community engagement. It means that academic
institutions should play bigger roles in social services. Although these are not new

The Application of Academic Article Writing Techniques
837
in academic circles, it is crucial that education institutions involve more with social
services, making social services a commitment of the institutions. “Society is calling for
scholars and university to participate and contribute more to the community, to help solve
problems,andcreateapathtoastablesociety.Scholarsandhighereducationinstitutions
have more opportunity and favorable conditions at present than in the past owing to the
fact that there are examples of social service-committed scholars all over the country.
There are universities that make social services their missions to encourage scholars
and students alike to work closely with the community to solve local problems, through
research and academic services based on the need of the community. As a result, these
efforts put forth by all parties involved will lead to the development and sustainability
of the society.” [9] It cannot be denied that working for the greater good of society can
only come true when there is a “collaboration” among all parties: the parties are divided
into “upstream”, “middle stream”, and “downstream”, to use logistics’ terms. Looking
through the lens of humanities and social sciences, it can be said that there are various
units to make up a society. If the members of any society want change or development,
they have to work together. In light of this statement, “the following are the 4 principles
of collaboration: 1) partnership 2) mutual beneﬁt 3) scholarship, and 4) measurable
social impact.” (adapted from [10]) In the case of this research, there is a collaboration
of the researchers, online Buddhist communities, and Sariputra Foundation. The three
partners have a common goal in the preservation and conservation of Buddhism. In this
project, the researchers have been entrusted with 2 tasks:
1) Providing academic services for the community through the application of knowl-
edge and to meet the objectives of the project, and
2) Using research skills to offer services to the community, developing knowledge in
order to meet the need of the community.
In the regulation of the Civil Service Commission in Higher Education institutions,
titled Criteria and Procedure for Academic Ranking, issue 9th (2013), it states that, “
being part of the Civil Service, one should contribute to the development of the com-
munity, making use of the knowledge one has for the beneﬁt of the nation. By working
closely with the community, identifying possible solutions to various problems, one can
grow and gain experience in one’s ﬁeld of expertise, not just in the education institutions
but in the real world as well.” [12] So, one’s growth process in the research ﬁeld can be
seen as illustrated in Fig. 3, which is the ultimate goal of doing research, that is to say
to meet the need of the society. By establishing online learning communities, education
institutions can bring about change and sustainability that beneﬁts all parties.

Expanding Access to Computer Science
Education–The FDU CS Hub
Laila Khreisat(B), Kiron Sharma, and Neelu Sinha
Fairleigh Dickinson University, Madison, NJ 07940, USA
khreisat@fdu.edu
Abstract. In this paper we share our experience in expanding access to Computer
Science (CS) education in Kindergarten through grade 5 (K-5) in the state of New
Jersey (NJ) in the USA. Fairleigh Dickinson University (FDU) with funding from
the NJ Department of Education (NJDOE) created the FDU CS Hub to expand
access to CS education by building a framework for sustained, evidence based
Professional Learning (PL) and outreach activities in CS for K-12 educators and
students. The major goal of the Hub is to increase the number of well-prepared
educators by providing grade-level, active learning, content and implementation
focused PL workshops for teachers from all subject areas over a 13-month period.
This plan directly impacted forty-one K-5 teachers and over 4000 students. This
impact will be even greater as we maintain a Web-repository of resources including
tools, and lesson plans for all to access. Our PL was aimed at alleviating teacher
anxiety of content knowledge including hands-on technology with a focus on
equitable access and Computer Science for all. Structured support for teachers as
well as the involvement of CS under-graduate and graduate students as mentors
encouraged students from diverse backgrounds to be engaged in CS activities.
Our project increased the number of K-5 educators prepared to teach CS and
expandedequitableaccesstoCSeducationforstudents.Wecollecteddatafromour
program and analysis of data suggests that teachers who attended the workshops
are prepared to begin teaching and incorporating CS in their classrooms.
Keywords: Computer Science · Teacher training · K-12 · Expanding access
1
Introduction
Computing, in the context of K–12 education, ﬁrst emerged with Seymour Papert’s
MIT pioneering work in the 1980s of children developing procedural thinking through
LOGO programming [9, 10]. Then came Computational Thinking (CT), envisioned
by Jeanette [13] to become a fundamental skill to be used by everyone in the world
by the middle of the 21st Century, just like reading, writing, and arithmetic. Deﬁned as
“involving solving problems, designing systems and understanding human behavior that
draws on concepts fundamental to computing” CT is often described as a key motivator
for bringing computer science (CS) back into schools. CT complements and combines
mathematical and engineering thinking which we use to approach living and not just the
software and hardware that touch our day to day lives. It is the thought processes involved

in formulating a problem and expressing its solution in a way that a computer—human
or machine—can effectively carry out. Following this, CT as a concept and associated
research agenda witnessed increasing attention not only from a growing community of
researchers, but also educators and policymakers. In 2010, the issue of CS Education
in K–12 came to the forefront following a troubling report by [12] which revealed
dismal numbers for women in computing along with very few schools that offered CS.
Grover and [5] reviewed the current state of discourse on CT in K–12 education by
examining mostly recently published academic literature that uses Wing’s article [13] as
a springboard, identiﬁes gaps in research, and articulates priorities for future inquiries,
noting that it was “an idea whose time had come.”
Fast forward to 2021, the number of students taking AP courses and participating
in these exams has signiﬁcantly increased, various teacher certiﬁcation standards and
programs are being established, and many school districts now count CS courses in their
graduation requirements. CS and CT are no longer just subjects for a single special-
ized or interested teacher, teachers of various grades and disciplines are being asked to
use CS as a tool to help students become the problem solvers our world needs for our
future. Some education systems have introduced teacher qualiﬁcation and preparation
programs and made efforts to increase student interest and engagement in CS. Addition-
ally, many education systems are investing in research and development of new methods
of instruction for CS education. Signiﬁcant progress has been made even though much
work remains to be done in making CS an integral part of the K–12 education system
(e.g. [4]).
Fairleigh Dickinson University (FDU) with funding from the NJ Department of
Education (NJDOE) in the USA created the FDU CS Hub to expand access to CS
education by building a framework for sustained, evidence based Professional Learning
(PL) and outreach activities in CS for K-12 educators and students. In this paper we
address our efforts for educators in grades K-5. Our project was designed to answer a
two-part question about CS education for all: What kind of Professional Learning (PL)
do teachers need to support all students? and How can we support and sustain evidence-
based CS programs in and beyond the classroom? With a broad experience in teacher
preparation and PL activities through the STEM Institute of Education (SIE) & School of
Education at FDU, we were well positioned to prepare teachers with skills & pedagogical
expertise to deliver superior CS education for all students. The goals of the CS Hub are
to: 1. Increase the number of well-prepared educators to teach CS in K-12; 2. Expand
equitable access to superior CS education for all students by creating evidenced based
models rooted in research; 3. Collaborate and provide resources to school districts for
expanding CS education; 4. Infuse CS PL into the teacher preparation program for pre-
service teachers. We partnered with 6 school districts (LEAs), Jersey City, Florham Park,
HanoverPark,Morris,HackettstownandBoonton,andincludedotherdistrictstobroaden
impact. Two of the larger partners have minority, underserved populations of 86% and
50%. During the 13- month project we trained 73 grade K-12 (41 K-5) teachers from 34
different school districts in NJ directly impacting over 7000 K-12 students exceeding
our set of goal of impacting 3200 students. We set out to increase teachers’ content
knowledge and skills in CS, and introduce and practice strategies to ensure persistence
and success of all students by promoting hands-on, active learning strategies. Senior

administrators from our LEAs were fully committed to implementing novel CS tools, and
proven strategies i.e. augmented and virtual reality and IoT, with new ways to visualize
data and employ inquiry-based learning. The main purpose on imparting professional
development for teacher learning is to enable these teachers to impart improved learning
to their students and prepare them to become effective thinkers, problem solvers and
communicators, and have the skills needed for high-skilled, high-demand jobs. Teacher
professional development, with appropriate pedagogical techniques for different grade

student learning and improve the quality of CS education in U.S. schools. To implement
the 2020 New Jersey Student Learning Computer Science Standards (2020 NJSLS-CS),
we need to prepare the teachers for our youngest students, i.e., K-5 teachers, by offering
teacher learning opportunities so that improved instruction can follow, and students will
receive 22nd century education, with practical applications in the critical computational
thinking skills that are so relevant in our daily lives.
2
Standards and Framework
We are at a crucial point in our temporal and spatial landscape as our nation’s education
systems are adapting to a 21st century vision of our students who will not just be com-
puter users but will also become computationally literate creators with proﬁcient skills
both in the concepts and practices of CS. Also, crucial is the collaboration between our
community (higher ed faculty, researchers, K-12 teachers), technology companies, and
several other states and large school districts to steer a process to develop conceptual
guidelines for states and districts to create a K-12 CS pathway. The New Jersey Depart-
ment of Education (NJDOE) supports schools, educators, and districts to ensure all of
New Jersey’s more than 1.5 million students have equitable access to high-quality edu-
cation and achieve academic excellence and have released the 2020 New Jersey Student
Learning Standards (NJSLS)–CS and Design Thinking in June 2020 [11]. CS and design
thinking education prepares students to succeed in today’s knowledge-based economy
by providing equitable and expanded access to high-quality, standards-based CS and
technological design education. New approaches necessary for solving the critical chal-
lenges (we face as a society) require harnessing the power of technology and computing.
Rapidly changing technologies and the proliferation of digital information have perme-
ated and radically transformed learning, working, and everyday life. To be well-educated,
global-minded individuals in a computing-intensive world, students must have a clear
understanding of the concepts and practices of CS. Elementary and middle schools are
the ideal places to ensure that every student has access to high quality foundational CS
instruction. Elementary schools need to identify CS instruction and practice that can
be integrated into core classes. By September 2022, all NJ students in K-8 must learn
CS, and all NJ high schools must offer CS. To be prepared for postsecondary success,
students must become effective thinkers, problem solvers, and communicators, and have
the necessary skills for high-skilled, high-demand jobs. Computer programming will be
included in all grade bands K-12, ensuring all students receive a 22nd century education
in the critical computational thinking skills that are the underpinning of so much of our
work and so many of our transactions. As education systems adapt to a vision of stu-
dents who are not just computer users but also computationally literate creators who are

842
L. Khreisat et al.
proﬁcient in the concepts and practices of CS and design thinking, engaging students in
computational thinking and human-centered approaches to design through the study of
CS and technology serve to prepare students to ethically produce and critically consume
technology.
The 2020 NJSLS–CS and Design Thinking, based on the structure of a house, include
10 disciplinary concepts and core ideas and 7 practices, are broadly divided into: the
Vision and Mission; The Performance Expectations; The Disciplinary Concepts and
Core Ideas; The Practices.
The Vision and Mission serve as the foundation for each content areas’ standards.
They describe the important role of the discipline in the world and reﬂect the various
statutes, regulations, and policy. The Performance Expectations are the studs and serve
as the framework for what students should know (concepts) and be able to do (practices).
They incorporate the knowledge and skills that are most important for students to know
to be prepared for post-secondary success. The Disciplinary Concepts and Core Ideas
are the joists and play an integral role in the framing by making connections among
the performance expectations. Core ideas help to prioritize the important ideas and core
processes that are central to a discipline and have lasting value beyond the classroom.
They provide clear guidance as to what should be the focus of learning by the end of
each grade band (i.e., end of grades 2, 5, 8, and 12). The Practices are the roof and
represent two key ideas. Positioned as the top of the house, they represent the apex of
learning. The goal is for students to internalize the practices (habits of mind) and be
able to apply them to new situations outside the school environment. The practices span
across all aspects of the standards and are an integral part of K-12 students’ learning of
the disciplines.
There are other standards and frameworks as well - the K-12 CS Framework (2016)
[8], the CS Teachers Association (CSTA) K-12 CS Standards (2017) [2], and the Inter-
national Society for Technology in Education (ISTE) Standards (2016) [6]. The K-12
CS Framework includes 5 core concepts and 7 core practices. The CSTA K-12 CS Stan-
dards include 5 concepts, 16 sub-concepts, and 7 practices. The ISTE Standards provide
the competencies for learning, teaching, and leading in the digital age, providing a
comprehensive roadmap for the effective use of technology in schools worldwide.
Additionally, there are standards for advanced topics as well. CYBER.ORG has
developed the K-12 Cybersecurity Learning Standards [3] which have been designed
with usability in mind. CYBER.ORG has designed the standards to be comprehensive,
easy to use, and easy to ﬁnd. States, districts, and all educators will be able to use the
standards. They are available for wholesale adoption and are available for districts and
educators to incorporate into existing curricula opportunities or course standards. The
Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) for K-12 initiative (AI4K12) is jointly sponsored by AAAI
and CSTA [1]. The initiative is developing national guidelines for AI education for K-
12, an online, curated resource directory to facilitate AI instruction, and a community
of practitioners, researchers, resources, and tool developers focused on AI for K-12
audience.

Curriculum Resources
Over a period of 9 months, FDU CS Hub conducted a series of Professional Develop-
ment (PD) sessions for two groups K-5 and 6–12 teachers. All the sessions were based
on the various standards and frameworks we discussed in Sect. 2 above. The topics we
covered based on the State of New Jersey Department of Education’s 2020 NJ Student
Learning Standards (and other standards and frameworks) for K-5 teachers included:
Computing Systems–hardware, software, devices; Networks and the Internet; Engineer-
ing Design - systematic approach to creating solutions to technological problems, lim-
itations; Data and Analysis–data collection, data storage, visualization of data, making
inference from data; Algorithms and Programming–instructions for computing devices,
sequence of steps, break down complex tasks, control structures, variables, develop
programs; Interaction of Technology and Humans–tools to improve tasks; Impacts of
Computing; Nature of Technology–using technology to solve problems in our natural
world; Effects of Technology on the Natural World; Ethics and Culture.
Short lecture sessions were followed by hands-on, active learning, and practical
sessions, which were conducted individually and in teams, where participants got a
chance to implement applications related to the topics introduced in the lectures. Before
our participants created their apps or programs, we discussed how to foster an inclusive
computing culture, how to collaborate, how to recognize a problem, and how to use
abstractions. We also showed them how to use debugging skills, and test reﬁne their
creations. After each creation, participants shared and communicated their computing
and design solutions. The various curriculum resources are listed below (with appropriate
links):
• MIT App Inventor; Scratch and ScratchJr; Code.org–Blockly visual programming
language; Micro:bit Educational Foundation - BBC micro:bit
• CS4NJ–promotes and advances K-12 CS education in NJ; CSTA–a voice for teach-
ers and driven by teachers offers teachers a community to connect, grow, and share;
Harvard Creative Computing Lab; BootUp PD Teacher Resources; Google for Edu-
cation - CS First; Open Educational Resources (OER) Commons - Android Apps with
AppInventor; CS is Elementary (Pathﬁnders Online Institute) Programming Essen-
tials in Scratch (Pathﬁnders Online Institute); Computing for ANyONe (CANON
Lab); Computer Science for All in SF; Common Sense Org - helping all kids thrive
in a world of media and technology; Coding and Craft with the micro:bit; Google’s
Blockly Games; PBS Kids–ScratchJr K-2; MakerEd Cyber Arcade: Programming
and Making with micro:bit; HelloRuby–whimsical way to learn about computers.
Advanced topics covered included Machine Learning, Data Science, AI, and
Cybersecurity. Curriculum resources are listed below:
• Cybersecurity for Everyone–creating a culture of cybersecurity for everyone;

Lesson Plans and Activities
Activities for all the PD sessions for K-5 teachers were hands-on and based on active
learning. Each participant worked at their own pace, and we had several lab assistants
guiding them.
Our ﬁrst hands-on activity revolved around using MIT’s AppInventor. Using this
visual, block-based programming language, our participants were able to create their
very ﬁrst app in just a few minutes. We walked them through the process of creating,
debugging, and testing their app. We also introduced them to advanced features such
as text-to-speech, animation, sound components, and sensors such as the accelerome-
ter which detects changes in acceleration. Next, we introduced them to drawing and
animation and they created a Digital Doodle App.
ScratchJr (for K-2 teachers) and Scratch (For K-2 & 3–5 teachers) block-based
programming was used to work on several projects. We introduced the language and
then walked them through the installation process. We showed them the interface and
discussed all the blocks and what they did to enable them to create their own interactive
stories, games, and animations.
All the above three platforms enabled us to teach basic programming concepts of
conditional statements - selection, looping, variables, and more. Each hands-on lesson
incorporated a CS topic along with debugging skills. We encouraged our participants
to make errors, explore, and use debugging techniques to ﬁx them as they developed
advanced skills. Code.org has excellent videos and hands-on programming to drive
home many of the CS topics. Code.org’s CS Fundamentals course supports a number
of different languages thus making it easy to offer CS skills even to students who do
not use English as their main language. We demonstrated how to create lesson plans for
ScratchJr and Scratch using fun animations and games, based on the 2020 NJSLS-CS.
Then, our participants created their own lesson plans for their individual classrooms,
and many presented these on the last day of our PD session.
Along with learning the programming language it is also important to expose our
K-5 teachers to the hardware. Thus, in our later PD sessions, we introduced partici-
pants to various curriculum, some of which also used hardware - Micro:bit Educational
Foundation curriculum, MakerEd Elementary and Middle grade curriculum, Curricu-
lum resources from other K-5 teachers, CS for All in SF curriculum, Harvard Creative

Computing curriculum, Google for Education - CS First curriculum, Apple Teaching
Code resources, etc. For the CS Ed Week in December, we encouraged all our partici-
pants to host an hour of code or a similar activity. In fact, our Lab Assistants (our FDU
CS students) also visited a few schools in our area to conduct such activities in the
K-12 classrooms. This beneﬁted both the K-12 teachers and students and involved the
community and helped form partnerships with K-12 schools and FDU. We had invited
expert speakers to present on various topics – including the 2020 NJSLS CS standards.
It is important for our K-2 participants to hear from such experts and learn about the
importance of teaching CS to all K-12 students.
Our last PD session introduced some advanced topics such as Cybersecurity, Arti-
ﬁcial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Data Science & Data Visualization, Internet of
Things, Cloud Computing, and hardware.

Culturally Responsive and Inclusive Pedagogies
Culturally responsive and inclusive pedagogies connect students’ cultures, languages,
and life experiences with what they learn in school. Such connections not only help
the students but also help the teachers. These connection help students access rigorous
curriculum and develop higher-level academic skills, and make them feel included, val-
ued, validated, and safe. These connections help teachers draw on culture to shape their
curriculum and instruction, communicate in culturally responsive ways, expand their
global thinking, bring real-world issues into their classroom, recognize bias and form
strategies to mitigate them, model high expectations for all students, and promote respect
for student differences. A lot of research has already been done for higher education [7]
and many of the same tools can be applied to K-12 education as well.
6
Strategies for Achieving Systemic Change
One of our goals in this project is to expand equitable access to CS education for all K–12
students. This was achieved by expanding awareness, in communities of participating
school districts for all stakeholders, about the importance of CS and the urgent need
for access and positive experiences for all students. We collaborated with participating
districts for organizing events and outreach activities and we created a repository of
open source tools and techniques that provide early positive experiences for students.
We developed and supported extracurricular activities in schools and in the community
supported by school districts, and we involved accomplished students from minority
groups such as Hispanic students and women to participate as role models. Schools
and school districts were provided with resources to assist in expanding CS education
across grades K-12 in the classroom or through extra-curricular activities. CS tools
were developed and shared with K-12 students for inquiry-based learning. These efforts
created avenues for all students to enhance their CS skills, thus supporting all students
including ones with special needs, Hispanic students with language hurdles and very
young students. We built a network/community of teachers that connected during PD
workshops and collaborated in breakout rooms on activities and developing lesson plans.
We developed replicable process models for implementation in local communities of

846
L. Khreisat et al.
LEAs to involve all stake holders including parents, parent-teacher organizations, school
administrators and community leaders. The processes enabled open conversations and
developed awareness via community events focused on expanding knowledge about the
signiﬁcance of CS, methodologies to expand access and the changing workforce skillset.
This included communicating about computing and helping build collaborations with
LEAs and industry to demystify the ﬁeld of CS while stimulating systemic change for
expanding opportunities for all students to learn about CS.

Outreach Efforts
We partnered with 6 school districts (LEAs) in the state of New Jersey and offered
PD workshops to teachers from 21 no-partnering LEAs serving a total of 73 teachers,
impacting over 7000 K-12 students, exceeding our set of goal of impacting 3200 students.
Forty one K-5 teachers were trained which will result in over 4000 students learning
cutting edge topics in CS with hands-on experiences within the ﬁrst year alone. We built
a network/community of teachers that connected during PD workshops and collaborated
in breakout rooms on activities and developing lesson plans. The FDU CS Hub (fduc-
shub.com) webpage lists all events and activities and the link to the site was shared will
all partnering LEAs. Registration for our PD workshops was handled through Eventbrite
and the link was shared on the FDU CS Hub website and was also emailed to all part-
nering LEAs and all participating teachers. Prior to each event, reminder emails were
sent out as well (3 emails on average before each event). Our events were also posted on
CS4NJ. All our PD workshops were recorded and the recordings were shared with teach-
ers. All instructors sent follow-up emails to teachers after each PD session/workshop
and continued to provide teachers with support and help.
We created avenues for all students to enhance their CS skills and utilized outreach,
extra-curricular programs and social media to support all students including ones with
special needs, Hispanic students with language hurdles and very young students and
beginners. We created a repository of, and shared easy to access tools and games for
students with different abilities, age groups, and language barriers. FDU CS majors
from diverse backgrounds were trained and engaged as mentors for school students to
enhance interest in CS. Acting as role models these mentors encouraged and motivated
K-5 students to pursue education in CS. They also served as lab assistants acting as role
models during PD workshops and outreach activities and event.
Several outreach and support activities took place during the project period includ-
ing during CSEdWeek, including: Code.org’s Chief Academic Ofﬁcer Pat Yongpradit
was invited to kickoff CSEdWeek and inspire our participants; CodeHS account exec-
utive Ms. Haley Cwiakala conducted an hour-long training session where she intro-
duced teachers to the CodeHS environment and its capabilities in creating lesson plans;
our TAs made presentations about cybersecurity, visited classrooms in our partner-
ing LEAs and conducted CS activities including: block coding, coding with scratch,
Blockly, code.org/minecraft tutorial where the children were able to learn and create
small programs using Minecraft.
The FDU CS Hub team provided continuous mentorship for administrators and
teachers to increase their knowledge about early exposure to and integration of CS and

Discussion of Our Survey Results
We surveyed the teachers after each PD session. Our survey was aimed to determine
whethertheteachersfoundthecurricula,paceofthesessionsandtheeducationalmaterial
provided appropriate for their grade levels and for their ability to learn new concepts in
CS that they can implement in their respective classrooms. We deployed a survey that
consisted of questions consisting of a ﬁve-level Likert type scale and a set of open ended
question. Roughly 80% of the participants responded to the survey in each session. For
the ﬁrst session that lasted for six hours each for four days, the survey results were
collected and an analysis was performed for Days 1, 2 and 3. All participants were
encouraged to share their thoughts. There was a technical error that related to survey
deployment for day 4. Upon analysis of the results the following observations stood out.
The workshops were designed to offer a variety of skills and introduce a wide variety
of topics. All respondents reported that they learned new skills in CS. Regarding the
pace of the ﬁrst session, roughly 30% respondents felt that the pace of the instruction
was fast for them. A qualitative analysis of the open-ended questions revealed that not
all participants were able to keep up with the pace as they got overwhelmed with the
setup process. So, going forward, we decided to offer help sessions–staffed by our student
TA’s to enable the participants to perform the setup tasks during these help sessions–thus
alleviating some of the issues. The instructors also adjusted the pace for the upcoming
sessions. In subsequent surveys, such issues did not surface. Overall more than 80% of
the respondents in the next session were either very comfortable or comfortable with
the pace of the sessions. The participants came to our workshops with mixed skills.
While some had exposure to CS, others were new to the subject matter. Breakout rooms
were created to provide individualized instruction. Each session included strategies for
inclusive pedagogies and 92% of the responses from the survey result indicate that
teachers were made aware of and were receptive to ideas on inclusive learning in CS for
all students.
During the ﬁrst PD session, 77% percent of respondents reported that the material
they learned was either very appropriate or appropriate for their students. More than
80% agreed that active and inclusive learning was used in PD sessions. The teachers
shared some of their concerns regarding CS topics and the faculty incorporated their
ideas in future sessions. As a result 93% of respondents in session 2 indicated that
the material they learned was either very appropriate or appropriate for their students.
Throughout all the sessions the faculty were receptive to comments and suggestions
provided by teachers and that helped greatly enhance experiences for all participants.

848
L. Khreisat et al.
All respondents either agreed or strongly agreed that the faculty in the program as well
as the TAs were helpful and supportive. For the third session that lasted for three days
with four hours each day we had some new teachers and 72% of the teachers were
returning from the ﬁrst set of sessions. This time 93% of the respondents reported that
they were completely satisﬁed with the pace of the PD sessions and materials covered.
All of respondents either agreed or strongly agreed that the faculty as well as the lab and
teaching assistants were helpful and supportive. For the last session that was held after
the winter break, few teachers completed the survey but all indicated that they learned
new features; all but one of the teachers were returning participants and therefore it
seems they did not all complete the survey at this session.
9
Conclusions
It is quite apparent that 21st century students will have all aspects of their life embed-
ded in technology which will continue to expand at an accelerating speed. The students
will not just be computer users but will also be required to be computationally literate
creators with proﬁcient skills both in the concepts and practices of CS. A collabora-
tion between higher education faculty, researchers, and grade school teachers, is a time
tested technique to help develop the mind set for teachers to learn new material and to
develop new skills. It is imperative to expose students early on to CS skills for them
to become proﬁcient, succeed and thrive in the digital age. Well qualiﬁed teachers are
key to students’ success. The New Jersey Department of Education (NJDOE) supports
schools, educators, and districts to ensure all of New Jersey’s students have equitable
access to high-quality education and achieve academic excellence. With that aim, the
State Board of Education released the 2020 NJSLS–CS and Design Thinking Standards
and has it mandatory for all schools in NJ to offer appropriate opportunities for students
in CS. This requires extensive investment in teacher preparation with focus on skills
development for teachers and for providing a cutting edge and dynamic set of tools that
can be used by teachers in their classrooms to teach their students at all grade levels.
In addition, there is a need for a support structure for teachers to address ‘just in time‘
issues for implementing CS topics in grade school so as not to overwhelm the teachers
or the students. The creation of the FDU CS Hub lead to such a system where all the
teachers who participated from grades K-5, from a wide network of districts, received
skills training, appropriate equipment for use in classrooms, in addition to timely sup-
port from faculty and from graduate and under-graduate CS students from FDU as TAs
who could visit the classrooms to help implement the curricula. Teachers worked col-
laboratively to develop and share grade-appropriate lesson plans based on the skills they
learned, and the teachers were encouraged to align their lesson plans with the NJSLS
for CS. Our program was a success with every measure and the teachers already have
begun teaching CS topics to their students and using the expansive Web-repository of
curricula materials made available to them. The FDU CS Hub received positive com-
ments from the teachers who attended the PD sessions and from the NJDOE. The Hub
has now received additional funding to expand the program to more school teachers and
to develop a systematic set of curricula materials for all teachers in NJ.

Abstract. The academic registration process takes place at the beginning of each
academic period, and it is very relevant because it deﬁnes the modules students
will enroll into. Thus, students must recognize and evaluate several factors during
their registration process, including identifying critical paths. A critical path is
a sequence of courses that minimizes the graduation time. However, choosing a
critical path is not an easy task as it implies a complex analysis of the requirements
and restrictions imposed by the career master plan. This article presents a deci-
sion support system to help students deﬁne critical paths during their academic
registration process. The system considers semestral academic terms and has been
applied at the Computer Science career at the Universidad de Talca (Chile). Pre-
liminary results from polls show that over 90% of participant students consider
that the system is both useful and usable and would utilize it as support for their
academic registration process.
Keywords: Support system · Academic registration process · e-learning
1
Introduction
An educational master plan is the curricular structure in which university careers are
framed, encompassing a graduate proﬁle that deﬁnes the curriculum, competencies,
and skills that students should possess at the culmination of their studies [1]. The cur-
riculum deﬁnes a list of courses, requirements (e.g., enroll in at least two courses per
semester) and restrictions (e.g. a course is a prerequisite of another). A curriculum-path
is a sequence of courses that leads to graduation, satisfying the corresponding require-
ments and restrictions. A curriculum-path is optimal when the sequence of courses can
be completed in the minimum possible time.
Ideally, every student should follow an optimal curriculum-path, however it is usually
not possible, in particular when the student fails a course. In this case, a new curriculum-
path must be chosen, implying a delay in the graduation process. Thus, selecting a new
curriculum-path is critical to minimize the graduation time.
The Computer Science Career (Ingeniería Civil en Computación) at the Universidad
de Talca [2, 3] (ICC-UTAL) has a curriculum that encompasses 5.5 years’ worth of
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 850–857, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_87

851
courses, but the real graduation time is 6.5 years on average. One of the main reasons
for such a negative difference in graduation time (one year more) is a wrong selection
of curriculum-paths.
After reviewing related work, we conclude that the management of curriculum plan-
ning is applied to speciﬁc contexts under different priorities. STOPS is a tool of the
undergraduate program of the School of Engineering at Aalto University, Finland, that
allows students to create personal study plans by organizing resources to maintain and
develop course content [4]. Sakon Nakhon Rajabhat University, Thailand, uses Machine
Learning techniques [5] to improve students’ personal study plans by analyzing their
learning achievements before their graduation.
This article presents iPlanner, a software system created to support ICC-UTAL stu-
dents in choosing (right) curriculum-paths. iPlanner allows students to simulate differ-
ent feasible registration scenarios, considering a set of enrollment constraints. During
preliminary testing, iPlanner has proven to be useful for students.
2
Background
This section describes the academic master plan and the registration process used in
ICC-UTAL.
2.1
ICC-UTAL Academic Master Planning
ICC-UTAL implements a competency-based methodology [6], an educational approach
that focuses on the demonstration of desired learning outcomes as the center of the
student’s learning process. Fundamental concepts related to the ICC-UTAL academic
master plan are deﬁned below.
A curriculum is a set of courses or modules in sequential order, each valued in SCT-
Chile credits [3]. The current ICC-UTAL curriculum is called Plan 16. A section of
the curriculum is shown in Fig. 1. Each rectangle represents a course (or module), with
its corresponding credits amount shown in its upper right corner. A course is a work-
learning unit related to a speciﬁc competence or set of skills declared in the graduate
proﬁle [7, 8]. The curriculum details prerequisites that must be satisﬁed when registering
for particular modules. These prerequisites are as follows:
• Completed module prerequisite: Deﬁnes that certain modules from the curriculum
must be completed prior to registering another. A completed module is one enrolled
in previous academic periods, that may or may not have been passed.
• Passed module prerequisite: Deﬁnes that certain modules from the curriculum must
be passed prior to registering another. Unlike the previous prerequisite, the student
must have passed the required modules.
• Approved credits prerequisite: Deﬁnes the number of credits that must have been
approved by a student to register a speciﬁc module. Approved credits are obtained by
adding each passed module’s credits, based on the curriculum.

852
L. Silvestre et al.
Fig. 1. A fragment of the ICC-UTAL Curriculum (Plan 16).
A sequence of modules that depend on one or more prerequisites, and that leads to
the student’s graduation. This aspect is quite relevant, because it determines the delay
in graduation time a student incurs by failing a module (or modules). In general, these
paths cover courses from the ﬁrst two and last three semesters, since most of these are
mandatory and have prerequisites.
At the beginning of each semester, students carry out their module registration pro-
cess, which is divided in two parts. First, automated preregistration forcefully enrolls
students inlower-level modules (i.e., fromprevious semesters) that havebeencoursedbut
not passed. After that, students register modules of their choice among those authorized
for a given period, until their maximum allowed credits is reached. Courses registered
automatically count against this maximum.
3
iPlanner ICC-UTAL
Two relevant aspects have been deﬁned for the implementation of iPlanner. The ﬁrst is
the design of an academic registration simulation algorithm; the second is a user frontend
system to access the algorithm. Both are described below.
3.1
Simulation Registration Algorithm
The proposed dynamic algorithm [9, 10] must satisfy the following objectives:
• Determine the minimum number of semesters required by a student to graduate.
• Estimate one or more module registration plans for each remaining semester, that help
the student graduate within the previously obtained minimum of semesters.

Work-in-Progress: Decision Support System
853
In addition, the following restrictions must be considered by the algorithm:
• Mandatory enrollment. Before a student can register their chosen courses, some
modules are pre-registered automatically (failed courses from previous semesters).
• Maximum number of credits per semester. Literally, the maximum number of credits
a student can spend to register courses on a given semester.
• Maximum number of modules per semester. Some students register a limited number
of courses instead of their potential maximum (i.e., leave credits unused).
• Curriculum prerequisites. Some modules require previous courses to be passed or
completed, or a number of approved credits to be reached, to allow registration.
• Semester availability of modules. Some modules are available only during the ﬁrst
semester, some during the second, and others during both.
• Leave no remaining credits. The number of credits must be taken in such a way that
no module that could have been registered is left out of a speciﬁc registration.
These objectives and restrictions help generate an algorithm capable of delivering
correct and concise information to students. However, the algorithm works under the
assumption that there always are openings in every module. Likewise, a ﬁxed maximum
number of credits per semester, deﬁned via parameters, is also required.
The algorithm applies dynamic programming [10] to generate all possible statuses
that meet thedeﬁnedconstraints, offeringfeasibleregistrationscenarios, andtheir critical
paths. Accordingly, a set of statuses is provided as a registration suggestion, along with
a plan for the remaining semesters’ registration.
• ICC-UTAL iPlanner System. A support system that implements the proposed algo-
rithm. IPlanner implements several functionalities, including user management, appli-
cation of restrictions, declaring academic status, and carrying out simulations. These
functionalities, as well as the implemented vistas are described below.
• Restriction management. Allows students to adjust parameters for a simulation,
speciﬁcally the curriculum, maximum number of credits, maximum number of
modules, and current semester. Some are declared by default but can be changed.
• Academic status management. Allows students to state their advancement on the
career’s curriculum (i.e., modules that they have passed or failed).
• Simulation execution. After conﬁguring and inputting progress, the simulation
can be performed. Data is sent to the server and fed to the algorithm, and when
recommendations are obtained (shown in Fig. 2), they are sent back to the user.
The use of iPlanner is entirely voluntary. The system is available for free to students
with enabled accounts, with new students being incorporated into the system every
semester. IPlanner is available at http://dcc.utalca.cl/iplanner/estudiante.

4
Preliminary Exploratory Case of Study
Several authors suggest the use of exploratory cases when the phenomenon of interest is
not fully discovered and understood [11]. To design our study we followed the method
proposed by Yin [12], deﬁning a research question to guide the research:
RQ: How does the academic registration support system works for student use?
With this in mind, we designed and conducted an exploratory case of study to collect
and analyze student registration data. Two student classes were selected for the study,
both from ICC-UTAL. The study subjects, the evaluated features, and the data collection
and analysis process, are all described below [11].
4.1
Subject Selection
This study considers the participation of 28 volunteer students from the Software
Requirements and Software Construction modules of the ICC-UTAL program, all sub-
scribed to the Plan 16 curriculum. These modules belong to the 5th and 7th semesters of
the curriculum, respectively. This allows for a greater variation in terms of the academic
status these students possess (i.e., their curriculum progress).
4.2
Evaluation Feature Description
Instructions were given to test subjects to analyze the functionality and usability of the
system: Access the system, request a password, conﬁgure parameters for a simulation,
declare academic status, apply the simulations, and complete the survey.

Work-in-Progress: Decision Support System
855
The functionality and usability aspects were based on some loose deﬁnitions and
metrics from ISO-9216 [13]. A system is functional if it provides functions that satisfy
the explicit and implicit needs of the user. A system is usable if it has the capacity to be
understood and utilized.
4.3
Data Collection
The method used to collect data for the study is software engineering experimentation
[14]. Since utilization was voluntary, several students did not enable their accounts.
Thus, the data collection considers a total of 28 students who used the system and then
answered the system evaluation survey.
The students’ declaration of academic progress was required to be true and coherent,
to provide consistent and feasible information to the system. Simulations could be run as
many times as needed, testing different parameters based on their assumptions of feasible
paths for their graduation. This means all 28 users executed at least one simulation,
although several more were executed with different parameters and potentially different
results.
On the other hand, the system evaluation survey has 3 sections:
• General opinion of the system: Five questions with short qualitative and quantitative
responses, including the following:
– How much can the system help in making better registration decisions?
– Would you rely on the system to help decide your academic module registration?
• System functionalities: Nine questions with short qualitative and quantitative
responses, including the following:
– Are the provided functionalities sufﬁcient for the system to be useful?
– Are the results delivered by the system reliable?
• System usability: Nine statements recorded using a Likert scale [15], including the
process of running the simulation and choosing a graduation plan
4.4
Analysis of Results
To understand the conclusions of the analysis, we will summarize the results of the study
from the general points of view of the system, functionality, and usability.
General Opinion of the System. 90% of surveyed students afﬁrm they would rely on
the system to decide their module registration. Results indicate the system has from
moderate to great impact on decisions made by the students, regarding enrollment.

856
L. Silvestre et al.
System Functionalities. 85% of surveyed students afﬁrm that the functionalities are
sufﬁcient for the system to be useful. In addition, no more than three bugs (on average)
were reported while performing the tests, all of them subsequently resolved.
System Usability. 85% of surveyed students state that the system is easy to use and does
not require additional instruction, and they agree with the layout of most of the elements
on the screen. 90% afﬁrm that the controls to select the approved and failed modules
and the display of simulated results are adequate and easy to understand.
Evidence suggests that iPlanner has adequate operation and usability rates to be used
massively at ICC-UTAL. Simulations and results from student scenarios have proven to
be reliable and coherent with the current enrollment system. In addition, iPlanner has
demonstrated to improve decision making during academic enrollment.
However, although results are promising, a larger number of experiments, long-term
follow-up, and a more detailed analysis of the execution of the simulations are required
to compare it to the current academic enrollment process. Finally, the threats to the
validity of this exploratory case of study are as follows:
• Construction validation. We have worked for two years in the construction and consol-
idation of iPlanner. However, exploration of different simulation strategies is required
to improve results.
• Repeatable experimentation. We have deployed iPlanner in a public domain, and are
working on improving its usability and extending its use to other organizations.
• Internal validation. We have followed the protocol of an exploratory case of study
suggested by Yin [12]. Although the implementation of the study was conducted
methodologically and formally, a questionnaire evaluation is not detailed and explicit
enough to gather more detailed and useful feedback. Our next challenge is to carry
out a conﬁrmatory case of study, focused on different aspects of evaluation.
• Externalvalidation.Althoughourresultsshowpromise,wecannotafﬁrmthatiPlanner
will generate simulations compatible with other careers at the University of Talca,
and/or other universities. This is mainly due to the particularities that each university
or department might enforce on their curriculum or registration processes.
5
Conclusions and Future Work
The proposed system can be used when planning semester modules, helping determine
tendencies on student enrollment in each period. This could allow predicting student
quotas for modules, supporting making decisions such as creating additional classes for
a given module, or planning a module on a different semester to allow more students to
enroll.
For ICC as a career, implementing the system offers the student community a useful
and effective tool to plan their professional development based on their academic perfor-
mance on a semestral basis. In addition, the system provides students with projections
of the time they have left on the career, letting them know their graduation time for a
given plan.
The current version of iPlanner is fully functional, but we have several ideas and
improvements that we want to develop for future versions of the system. Some of the

Work-in-Progress: Decision Support System
857
proposed functionalities and suggestions include exploring new simulation possibilities
through artiﬁcial intelligence techniques, modify the algorithm to support annual and
quarterly periods, extend the algorithm or design a new one that works in conjunction
with module scheduling, and applying a long-term case of study to understand the true
impact of the system on student decisions and outcomes.

Abstract. The ERASMUS + project “Development of practically-oriented
student-centered education in the ﬁeld of modeling of Cyber-Physical Systems”
(CybPhys) focuses on curricula modernizations in close cooperation with poten-
tial employers. Since the CybPhys project pursues to develop practically-oriented
student-centered curricula, we involved industry representatives in the creation
of new courses from the very beginning of the project. In the paper, we describe
the curriculum development stages and obtain feedback from the main stake-
holders. As part of the practically-oriented education, European partners in Riga
Technical University, KU Leuven, and the University of Cyprus should arrange
three schools for Ukrainian students. In this research, we focus on implement-
ing practically-oriented and student-centered training methods at the school for
Ukrainian students arranged at the RTU in January 2022. We describe novel meth-
ods and approaches applied in the students’ school, such as transversal skills,
Design Thinking, involvement of industry representatives in the teacher team, etc.
The survey of Ukrainian students and teachers revealed the presence or absence
of correlations between students’ general perception of the school and teaching/
learning methods, e.g. developments of creative thinking, practical application of
theory, etc.
Keyword: Cyber-physical systems · Practically-oriented curricular · Design
thinking methodology · Survey

1
Introduction
The ERASMUS + project “Development of practically-oriented student-centered edu-
cation in the ﬁeld of modeling of Cyber-Physical Systems” CybPhys focuses on curricula
modernizations in Ukrainian universities in close cooperation with potential employers
[1, 2]. The CybPhys project started its activities in November 2019 for three years.
It was planned that three Belarusian and three Ukrainian universities would take part
in the project, however, the Belarusian government refused to register the project.
Thus, the project moved from a regional to national status with the participation of
only Ukrainian partners: Chernihiv Polytechnic National University (CPNU), Kharkiv
National Automobile and Highway University (KhNAHU), and Kryvyi Rih National
University (KNU). EU universities are presented by the Riga Technical University (RTU)
from Latvia, which is the coordinator, the University of Leuven (KU Leuven) from
Belgium, and the University of Cyprus (UCY).
In the beginning stage of the project, a research study aiming to deﬁne industry needs
and perceptions about education on the modeling of CPS was conducted [3]. As a part of
the student-oriented education, three schools for Ukrainian students should be arranged
by the European partners in RTU, KU Leuven, and UCY.
In this research, we focus on implementing practically-oriented and student-centered
training principles in the school for Ukrainian students arranged at the RTU in January
2022. In this paper, we describe novel methods of teaching and learning applied in the
students’ school, such as transversal skills, Design Thinking, involvement of industry
representatives in the teacher team, etc. In this school:
1. The students obtained a perception of the importance to be involved in research
activities.
2. The students were acquainted with state-of-art technologies and had the opportunity
to watch presentations and discuss with industry representatives.
3. The students accumulated a combination of theory and practical work in laboratories.
4. The students had the opportunity to apply “in real life” engineering knowledge in
combination with transferable skills like working in a team. More precisely, they
had the task to develop a prototype of a novel product.
5. All students broadened their cultural awareness about RTU, as a European university,
and Latvia in general.
Finally, the CybPhys project team was eager to get feedback concerning methods
and approaches applied for the development of the programs and courses for students
training during the project and to know, whether corrective actions might be needed.
The remaining part of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 describes the
related works. The authors summarize the materials and methods applied in this research
in Sect. 2. Section 3 demonstrates the methods applied in the CybPhys project including
gap analysis, an ex-ante survey of the Ukrainian stakeholders, and a novel approach
to developing the new industry-oriented curricular. Section 4 describes the methodical
approach to students’ school arrangement, provides an analysis of results, and offers dis-
cussions. Finally, Sect. 5 presents the conclusions, limitations of research, and directions
for future works.

Implementing the Practically-Oriented Curricular
863
2
Review of Literature
The Conceive, Design, Implement, and Operate (CDIO) framework [4] includes ambi-
tions to make engineering education more efﬁcient and provides a systematic methodol-
ogy for educational design and innovation in curricula [5]. The paper [6] argues that the
basic principles of Design Thinking (DT) have the potential to promote entrepreneurial
competencies in European school curricula. Examples in the literature of DT being used
in the development of new curricula and curriculum reform include the use of DT in
entrepreneurship education, language courses, and industrial engineering [6, 7].
Project-based learning (PjBL) refers to an inquiry-based instructional method that
engages learners in knowledge construction by having them accomplish meaningful
projects and develop real-world products [8]. The authors [9] discuss several studies,
which examined the process of problem-based learning (PBL) and how its components
impact students’ learning.
Graham [10] summarized the outcomes of a study, which focused on case studies
of four universities considered the “emerging leaders” in engineering education. In this
sense, the CybPhys project utilizes a variety of pedagogical aspects revealed in [10],
such as engaging students with the university’s research activities, a wide range of
technology-based activities, experiential learning throughout the curriculum, etc.
However, for a teacher team in the students’ school in Riga, it was a challenge to
apply effectively different novel teaching methods in a very restricted two-week time
and to get reliable feedback from students who participated in the school.
3
Methods Applied in the CybPhys Project
The CybPhys project team strives to combine the DT methodology in engineering cur-
ricula design with the needs of industrial partners from the automotive, transportation,
electronics, IT and software, and general manufacturing sectors.
• Students’ research activities have been involved in the newly developed curriculum.
• Online ﬂexible and relevant learning has been embedded. For this purpose, an eLearn-
ing platform has been created in the CybPhys project. A Sharing Modelling and Sim-
ulation Environment (SMSE) platform for common learning, teaching, and research
will be developed by the end of the project.
• PjBL, PBL, and self-directed-learning approaches are applied and tested in the agenda
of the student schools arranged in RTU and KU Leuven universities.
• Three state-of-the-art laboratory classes were equipped in Ukrainian partner’ uni-
versities, which are used for experiential learning across the curriculum. These lab-
oratory classes, Moodle-based eLearning platform, and SMSE platform enable the
development and replication of remote labs and experiments.
• The consortium partners enhance relationships with the industries involved in the
project by creating new partnership agreements addressing long-term relationships
beyond the project.

864
A. Zabasta et al.
Fig. 1. Development of the curriculum with the feedback from stakeholders
The CybPhys project approach involves the main stakeholders (students, teachers,
researchers, employers, the national accreditation institution, and the Ministry of Edu-
cation of Ukraine) in the entire project life cycle. The education curricula have been
developed and adjusted considering stakeholders’ feedback in six stages (see Fig. 1).
• Gap analysis includes existing curricular analyses, elaboration of the best practices
of EU partners, and input from the industry representatives.
• Development of new curricula: learning, teaching, didactic materials, and develop-
ment of learning tools.
• Accreditation of the courses and education programs.
• Obtaining feedback from teachers and students during the course’s development
process. This stage is ongoing during the publication of the present paper.
• Testing of new and modernized courses and obtaining feedback from stakeholders.
• Post-ante evaluation and feedback from potential employers, other stakeholders, and
external quality assurance experts. Post-project enhancement of the curricula will be
continued beyond the CybPhys project in cooperation with the industrial partners and
other potential employers.
3.1
Gap Analysis and Ex-ante Survey of the Employers
At the beginning of the project, existing courses and training programs in Ukrainian
partners’ universities were evaluated against the best practice of EU universities. Then,
at the beginning of 2020, the partners surveyed industry representatives.
A total of 81 experts who represented a broad range of industrial and research orga-
nizations, familiar with the CPS-related curricula and programs were interviewed [11].

The respondents represented managerial and high-tech personnel from transportation
systems, robotics, car industry, building automation, computer engineering, Smart City,
production processes, energy production, etc. The ﬁndings of the survey served as inputs
for the new industry-oriented cross-domain study programs in CPS. Furthermore, the
partner’s universities acquired a good perception of the requirements of research insti-
tutes, enterprises, and other employers regarding the qualiﬁcations of undergraduate and
master-level students.
3.2
Approach to Developing New Industry-Oriented Curricular
Aiming to increase the synergy of the partners, we suggested developing a system of
interconnected didactic tools to teach students. As a result, nine-course e-books for
students and teachers have been elaborated and among them are “Bringing innovations
to the market”, “Mathematical modeling of mechatronic systems”, and “Model-oriented
control in intelligent manufacturing systems”.
Transdisciplinary and CDIO framework-related approaches have been introduced in
all training and teaching materials, e.g. engineering reasoning, problem-solving (includ-
ing modeling and qualitative analysis), studying the interaction of the CPS systems, etc.
were applied in the course e-books. For example, the e-book “Bringing innovations to the
market” provides the students with the necessary expertise, such as project management,
e-commerce, product prototyping, inventing commercialization, etc.
By the end of the project, 20 new and modernized courses and 3 education pro-
grams for bachelor’s and master’s level students will be developed and accredited at the
Ukrainian universities. Table 1 gives a perception of the type of courses developed in
the CybPhys project. Due to lack of space, we only publish the names of courses of the
CPNU university.

A Case Study of Students’ School at Riga Technical University
4.1
The Methodical Approach to Students’ School Arrangement
A group of twelve Ukrainian engineering students from three universities: KNU,
KhNAHU, and CPNU, plus three Ukrainian professors participated in a two-week train-
ing program at the Riga Technical University in January 2022. Motivated students with
sufﬁcient English language knowledge were selected from the course groups, which just
had acquired newly developed courses in the autumn semester of 2021.
The team of teachers was represented by several RTU professors and Ph.D. students,
engineering staff of two energy sector companies (simultaneously as Ph.D. students of
RTU), and one professor of Kaunas University of Technology (KTU) (she had a teaching
mobility visit under Nordplus program) and three Ukrainian professors, the members of
CybPhys team.
Cultural awareness was included by a general introduction at the beginning of the
school, followed by an excursion to the Ethnographic Open-air Museum, a tour at the
Scientiﬁc Library of RTU, and a touristic tour in the old city center of Riga.
The mainly research-based training focused on a broad range of topics including
renewable energy (solar and hydrogen energy), security of Cyber-Physical Systems,
energy storage systems, application of Cyber-Physical Systems, etc.
The school arrangement included different forms of teaching, e.g. a short campus tour
including laboratory demonstrations: solar energy, wind energy, fuel cells, and robotics.
Since on-site visits to industrial partners were prohibited, a virtual tour to a Smart City i.e.
Jelgava Municipal Operational Information Centre (MOIC) was arranged. The courses
were conducted as a combination of practical and seminar discussion, e.g. security of
CPS. The students were taught practical work in a 3D laboratory for modeling and
printing. By the end of the school, the students applied their new knowledge to printing
parts of the product prototypes. Additionally, a course in the virtual laboratory has been
included: the theory and practice introduced the students to the modeling of CPS.
The school program was arranged around the main task: during the course, the
students had to create a prototype of any new product of their own choice. They had to
apply engineering knowledge and transversal skills working in creative teams.

Implementing the Practically-Oriented Curricular
867
Aiming to introduce the students to new product development an online introduc-
tion session was conducted by the RTU team one week before the students arrived in
Riga. The students were introduced to the school agenda, targets, and methods of study.
Additionally, the students received a home task: to generate an idea for a new innovative
product to be created at the school in Riga.
At the ﬁrst session in Riga, the students were divided into three creative teams, and
each of them was responsible for a product prototype creation. The Belbin test for the
self-evaluation of students was applied to share the students among the creative teams.
The purpose was to make the teams, which might include the students with different
roles, e.g. creative individuals, leaders, implementers, etc. However, at the end of this
session, the professor let the students create the teams based on their home universities
aiming to save the time needed for team building.
During two weeks, the students navigated through all phases of the development
of a new product. Starting from a problem deﬁnition followed by an identiﬁcation of
customer needs, the students ﬁnished with the plan for further development (see Fig. 2). It
is worth noting, that the prototype development was mostly implemented as independent
teamwork in the dedicated student laboratory after the main lectures and practicums.
Attheendoftheschool,thestudentsdemonstratedtheirprototypestothecommission
consisting of RTU, KhNAHU, KNU, CPNU, and KTU professors. They discussed with
their peers and teachers the technical solutions and economic beneﬁts.
Fig. 2. Phases of development of a new product taught at the School for the students
4.2
Analysis of Results of the School in RTU
A survey of Ukrainian students and teachers has been arranged at the end of the school
after issuing certiﬁcates of participation in the school of students. The survey was imple-
mented in the form of an anonymous questionnaire and answered by the participants.
The survey included a set of questions, where participants were asked to rate, according
to their perception, the relevance of each of the following evaluation criteria. A Likert
scale from 1 (not relevant) to 5 (very relevant) has been used. The distance between each
scale point is assumed to be equal, and 3 represents the neutral value in this scale.
The purpose of the survey was to get feedback on the results of the school of students.
Additionally, the project team evaluated some elements of the newly developed courses

868
A. Zabasta et al.
after teaching in the autumn semester. We needed to check, how design thinking method-
ology, transversal skills, and problem-based learning have been comprehended by the
students. We also desired to encourage students on providing comments and suggestions
about the training methods that might be used for further improvements. Furthermore,
it might be useful to ﬁnd how the level of knowledge of the English language impacts
the success of the training.
We asked the respondents to answer eleven questions. Ten of them were devoted to
the content and quality of the organization of the course. Additionally, one question about
English language skills, which could help to evaluate the ability of students to acquire
learning material, was included in the questionnaire. In Fig. 3 a histogram of students’
and teachers’ answers is depicted. All sixteen respondents ﬁlled in the questionnaire.
Furthermore, eight of them added comments and suggestions about how to improve the
arrangement of such a school in the future. Some of the comments were broader than
the school arrangement topic, e.g. one of the students expressed satisfaction with RTU
laboratory equipment, and the other one was delighted with the conditions in the library.

We applied the t distribution (Student’s t-distribution) to evaluate the survey results
because it is suitable for estimating population parameters if the sample size is small
and the population variance is unknown. We calculated a conﬁdence interval for the t
distribution in Excel using CONFIDENCE.T(α, s, n) = k, when (¯x – k, ¯x + k) is the
conﬁdence interval of the sample mean, and “n” is the sample size. For example, the
CONFIDENCE.T for “The logical structure of the lecture was maintained” (topic 3,
Table 3), the 95% conﬁdence interval of the sample mean is equal (4.8043, 5.0707).
According to opinions expressed by the respondents, the topics “The lec-
turer/professor’s attitude to the students was positive and helpful”, “The course was
well-structured and the themes were explained in a comprehensible manner” and “The
logical structure of the lecture was maintained” have been evaluated with the highest
mark (mean 4.9375) (see Table 2). Furthermore, the respondents were conﬁdent in their
evaluation, since the standard deviation was very low: 0.2500. Also, a rather high rating
was given to the question “The information about the classes organization was clear and
easily available”: 4.8125. The lowest rating was entitled to the statement “The time for
the completing of the practical tasks was enough” (mean value of 4.0625). This result is
not surprising bearing in mind that only ﬁve of sixteen respondents strongly agreed with
this statement. Three respondents wrote comments in their questionnaires that it would
be useful to devote more time to the student’s group projects.
