4.3
Discussions
We have noticed that English language knowledge differs among the students of three
universities (see Table 3, row 11). Respecting our previous experiences, we expected
to ﬁnd a correlation between the overall evaluation of the school by the students and
their English language proﬁciency. We compared evaluation marks put by students and
teachers to the topic “My knowledge of the English language was sufﬁcient to understand
all learning materials presented by a teacher” with the general opinion about the school.
We applied Excel as calculated by the formula CORREL. The correlation coefﬁcient of
0.1423 revealed a weak positive correlation between English language proﬁciency and
the general evaluation of the School. Probably, the lack of English language proﬁciency
among the students was tempered, and students’ stress was reduced by the fact that
additionally to English, Ukrainian and Russian languages were used by the teachers.

Since we applied different forms and modes for the student’s training, it was impor-
tant to evaluate a correlation between the topic “During the class, the amount of theoret-

5
Conclusions and Recommendations
Transversal skills, Design Thinking, and other innovative methodologies integrated
into the courses of the students’ school in Riga helped to build the curriculum frame-
work around competencies identiﬁed by both industry and academia while ensuring
the students engage in a signiﬁcant learning experience through practical-oriented and
student-oriented learning using the latest immersive technologies.
The high level of motivation demonstrated in the survey was supported by the results
of the IEEE ENRGYCON 2022 conference when student teams of Ukrainian universities
received three prizes for the best student research works, which were presented at the
student section of the conference. At the conference, the students demonstrated new
product prototypes created in the students’ school: “Desktop Lighting Control System”,
“Remote Monitoring of Indoor Station” and “Automatic plant watering system using a
built-in reservoir”.

872
A. Zabasta et al.
We are aware of the restrictions of the research since the survey cannot guarantee
the exhausted perception of students about the newly developed courses and teaching/
learning methods because we have tested a rather small group of students.
For future research, improvements should be made in the form of an assessment
of the student’s feedback. It looks reasonable to supplement the questionnaire with
additional open-ended questions. This approach should engage students to make more
comments, concerning possible improvements in the content of the courses, and the
teaching methods. We also are interested to evaluate, to which extent the involvement of
industry representatives in the teachers’ team increases the motivation of the students.
We planned to arrange a survey of students, who should participate in student school
at the University of Cyprus in March 2022. A comparison of the results of both surveys
would be useful for reviewing the delivery methods and the content of the courses.
Unfortunately, the warship in Ukraine prevented students travel abroad, furthermore, all
training activities were shifted online, but the school in UCY has been postponed.

Perception of the Internationalization
Process by the University Employees:
The Case Study of Innopolis University
Hamna Aslam1,2(B), Maria Naumcheva1, Petr Zhdanov1, Iouri Kotorov2,3,
Manuel Mazzara1, Elmira Akhmetgaraeva1, Radik Valiev1,
and Yuliya Krasylnykova3
1 Innopolis University, 420500 Tatarstan, Russian Federation
{h.aslam,pe.zhdanov,m.mazzara,e.akhmetgaraeva,r.valiev}@innopolis.ru,
m.naumcheva@innopolis.university
2 Institut de Recherche en Informatique de Toulouse (IRIT), Universit´e de Toulouse,

Abstract. The COVID-19 pandemic has been a game changer for many
aspects of the educational environment worldwide. Together with pos-
itive aspects of digital acceleration, there have also been obstacles in
keeping internationalization processes on track. In this paper, we con-
sider a case study of an educational institution: Innopolis University. We
analyze the perception of teaching and research staﬀfor what concerns
internationalization. We organized a survey involving Innopolis staﬀand
survey questions aimed at revealing their attitude and understanding of
the process and its relevance. The outcome is twofold: on one hand the
understanding of the perception will be instrumental for the Interna-
tional Relation Oﬃce to better involve the faculty in the process; on the
other hand, sharing the result with the scientiﬁc community will help
other organizations to reﬂect on their own progress and to better involve
their staﬀ.
Keywords: Internationalization · Faculty support · Education
globalization · Internationalization policies
1
Introduction
The successful internationalization of an educational institution can only be
achieved via the operational support of their front-line workers, meaning research
and teaching staﬀ[11]. A good performance in the major university rankings
such as THE and QS is worldwide considered a good indicator of an healthy
internationalization process [15]. It is therefore of instrumental importance that
faculty and research students of a university are informed about the detailed
c

operations of their International Oﬃce and how the ranking agencies measure
their activities [7].
In this paper we consider a case study of an IT Russian educational institu-
tion. Innopolis University (IU) is an IT University founded in Tatarstan, Russia,
in year 2012. The focus is on education, and scientiﬁc research in the ﬁeld of
IT and robotics [10]. The campus is located in the newly created Innopolis City
(near the capital city Kazan) which also comprises ICT companies and the Innop-
olis Special Economic Zone. Innopolis aims to be the major Russian IT hub [35].
In its development the University was trying to follow the main trends of IT edu-
cation borrowed from the world’s leading higher education institutions [3]. One
of these trends was and still is internationalization. Since the very foundation,
the university tried to hunt international faculty members as well as attracting
international students. Additional, the university has been developing various
international initiatives including summer schools, exchange programs, confer-
ences etc. [12]. Existing for ﬁve years, the university succeeded in creating an
international environment on campus.
From the ﬁrst step, IU showed its internationalization invitations. In Decem-
ber 2012, just few days after its creation, the University concluded an agreement
with the Carnegie Mellon University (CMU). Under the agreement, the sides
agreed to transfer a master’s degree program on Software Engineering from CMU
to IU. In spite of the fact, that IU transferred its ﬁrst educational program from
CMU, IU always took as a role model a slightly diﬀerent type of a higher educa-
tion institute, i.e.young technical universities. The best examples worldwide are
KAIST (South Korea), IT University of Copenhagen (Denmark), and the Hong
Kong University of Science and Technology (Hong Kong).
Innopolis University is now in its eight year and reached a students popu-
lation of about 800 with more than 300 employees of which about 30 faculty
members and teaching and research stuﬀ, including industrial research units, up
to 200 people. It has an extensively developed network of international institu-
tions collaborating under diﬀerent forms: students exchange, Erasmus +, visit-
ing professors, joint PhD supervision and joint projects. One of the collaborative
projects as seen partners such as CERN and Newcastle university [1,4] and col-
laborative PhD supervisions involve several universities including University of
Toulouse, Nice, University of Southern Denmark and University of Messina. All
these activities dramatically supported the internationalization of the project.
In turn, the internationalization of the university also helped the development
of the city itself.
Research questions addressed in this paper are as follows:
1. To what extent is IU staﬀaware of internationalization processes?
2. To what extent they are aware of impact of the process in the achievements
of IU objectives?
3. How staﬀsee their contribution to the process?
4. Is there any diﬀerences of perceptions among groups (admin, faculty...)?
5. In case, how to overcome these diﬀerences for a common strategy?

Faculty Perception of Internationalization
875
We analyze the perception of teaching and research staﬀfor what concerns
the internationalization process via a survey involving Innopolis staﬀand we
ask questions aimed at revealing their attitude and understanding of the process
and its relevance. The outcome is twofold: on one hand the understanding of the
perception will be instrumental for the International Relation Oﬃce to better
involve the faculty in the process; on the other hand, sharing the result with
the scientiﬁc community will help other organizations to reﬂect on their own
progress and to better involve their staﬀ. The research is organized via a survey.
The theoretical background is presented in Sect. 2, while the study design in
Sect. 3. Results are presented in Sect. 4 and discussed in Sect. 5. Finally, Sect. 6
will summarize the outcome of the study.
2
Background and Related Work
Internationalization of the faculty policies and practices as well as the recogni-
tion of the faculty members’ key role in the overall internationalization process
of a university are becoming increasingly important in today’s globalized world
[12,29]. Universities are starting to not only consider international experience as
one of the preferred backgrounds while hiring faculty members and thus formal-
ize it in their policies and practices but also encourage and reward the current
faculty members for their international engagement, especially in research [8].
Understanding its own role and potential in the institutional internationaliza-
tion, the faculty members might though be able to contribute even greater as in
the quality and the quantity of international initiatives [13,30].
In higher education, the international relations oﬃces often represent the
enforcers that compel the faculty members, students and administrative staﬀto
follow the institutional international strategy [9]. However, in the universities
where the faculty is internationalized to a signiﬁcant degree and is also aware
of its roles, capabilities, and opportunities, the international relations oﬃces are
likely to take the role of a matchmaker that balances the strategic goals with
the current activities of the faculty and facilitates connections between the ‘top
down’ and ‘bottom up’ initiatives [8].
Greater engagement of the faculty can, ﬁrst of all, allow the university to
join the global community building vast international strategic partnerships and
networks upon the existing activities such as joint research or other collabora-
tions and maintain the partnerships and networks purposefully introducing and
involving active faculty members [2,26,32].
One of the primary beneﬁts from the internationalized faculty for the univer-
sity as an institution is its growing international reputation that, especially in
the age of the immense popularity of the world university rankings, often serves
as the backbone of university’s success [7,33]. Depending on the ranking, the
reputation of a university can have a weighting accounting for up to 70% of the
ﬁnal score.
Many educational organizations in recent years had to readjust their teach-
ing, research and internationalization proﬁle due to the consequences of the

876
H. Aslam et al.
COVID-19 pandemic [19]. However, despite of changes in the current practises,
we believe the commitment to internationalization of such institutions did not
fundamentally change [20]. This is certainly true for Innopolis University.
3
Study Design
The study is centered on a survey designed for Innopolis staﬀ. Employees par-
ticipated from administrative, research and teaching units. The questions are
centered around the idea of exploring the attitude towards the processes related
to the internationalization and global visibility of the organization. Employees
who understand the university’s internationalization objectives will be able to
better support them. This would lead to improved teaching practices and better
branding for the organization. In this section, we state the questions presented
to the survey participants.
The survey was based on the questions presented below (please note that
questions Q4 to Q7 have the same set of options provided).

4
Analysis of Survey Responses
The survey had been conducted with the employees of the university. After
receiving the responses the employees were categorized according to their
areas of work. There are three categories of respondents, Professors, Junior
Researchers, and Administration. Participants self-identify their work areas
in the survey, which is used to categorize them. As a result we have thirteen
professors, seven researchers, and six administrative staﬀ.
The survey questions as listed in Sect. 3 allowed participants to select multiple
options as their answers. We ran Marascuillo test to examine if any diﬀerence
exists among the three groups (Professors, Researchers, Administration).
4.1
Professor-Administration
The marascuillo test [16] shows diﬀerence between professors and administration
groups in the options of faculty exchange, student exchange, internships, men-
toring, guest lectures, citations, publications, cotutelle, mentoring and raising
grants. The diﬀerence occurred in almost the same options for all questions. The
outcomes are more noticeable as most of the time no one from administration
group selected these options. The diﬀerence supports intuition as administration

878
H. Aslam et al.
employees are not involved in research publications directly and do not attend
conferences. However, they provide organizational support for conference reg-
istrations, guest lectures, internships, student and faculty exchange and travel
etc.
As the data suggests, administrative staﬀdo not consider their work as
a signiﬁcant support in promoting the university’s international visualization,
employer and academic reputation, and increasing the bibliometric rankings.
They are not primary actors in producing publications. Therefore, they do not
perceive themselves to be a part of bibliometric ranking process.
The question about academic reputation of the university shows similar per-
ception of the administration group. The important point is the mentoring
aspect. The academic reputation of any institution is impacted by the qual-
ity of organizational processes [14]. In this regard, the administrative staﬀdo
impact the academic reputation as they are involved in the administration of
exchange programs, correspondence with international students and staﬀ, and
relevant organizational details. Administrative staﬀmentors and support their
academic colleagues but they do not perceive it as mentoring. This contribution
needs to be highlighted among signiﬁcant services provided by administration.
4.2
Junior Researcher - Administration
The diﬀerence between junior researchers and administration group occurred in
the options of student exchange, joint research, and internships. The no signiﬁ-
cant diﬀerence in other options is due to the low number of participants selecting
the options. In all these diﬀerences, none of the participants from the adminis-
tration group has selected that particular option. Therefore, the diﬀerence has
occurred because at least four participants have selected these options from the
researchers group.
In the diﬀerences, the perception of administration regarding the impact of
their work appears to be undermining. The student exchange programs and
internships are largely supported by staﬀin administrative positions. Further-
more, the lacking of the diﬀerence among groups shows that administration and
junior researchers are on the same page about the perceived impact of their work
outcomes for the university. The administration are closer to junior researchers
as compared to the professors in their perception of impact.
4.3
Professor - Junior Researcher
The diﬀerence between professors and junior researchers group occurred in the
question about the bibliometeric aspect of the ranking (Q5) where none of the
researchers believe that their mentoring activity impacts the bibliometric rank-
ing and ﬁve professors believe that their mentoring activity has bibliometric
impact. In questions 4, 6, 7, one participant from researchers group selected the
mentoring option with marascuillo test showing no diﬀerence.
The other point of diﬀerences are the options conference visits (in question
6) and guest lectures (in Q7). The point about conference visits is important to

Faculty Perception of Internationalization
879
understand the perception about the impact of these visits. In question 5, three
out of seven researchers believe that conference visits can boost visualization of
the university but only one researcher believe that these visits impact bibliomet-
ric ranking. Furthermore, none of the researchers believe that conference visits
impact the academic reputation (Q6) of the university and one believe that it
impacts the employer reputation (Q7) of the university. In other questions, no
signiﬁcant diﬀerence is detected between the researchers and professors group.
5
Discussion
Overall joint research is perceived as the most important activity: it was men-
tioned by 93% of professors and 86% of researches as their activity that can
support the university towards its worldwide visualization. This activity is also
considered the most important for bibliometric aspects of the ranking (mentioned
by 86% of professors and 57% of researches) and for academic reputation of the
university (mentioned by 86% of professors and 71% of researches). Another
important activities include guest lectures, conference visits, and internships
Administration staﬀmentioned only a few activities that they believe can
contribute to the university internationalization process: guest lectures, organiz-
ing external events, and student recruitment. None of the activities was men-
tioned by more than 33% of the administrative employees.
Answers related to teaching:
Among the answers suggested in the questionnaire, faculty and student
exchange, guest lectures, internships, and cotutelle were supported by more
than 40% respondents. In addition, survey participants suggested introducing
joint curriculum and course teaching exchange1
As a result of student exchange a number of highly motivated students join
the existing student cohort. The outcome of the faculty exchange is twofold.
On one hand, the experienced faculty members from another universities can
share their teaching practices and teach the courses that are not present in the
curriculum. On the other hand, the outgoing faculty members learn from their
experience of teaching abroad. This is the opportunity to exchange the expertise
and teaching practices.
In general, internationalization of a higher education institution can support
teaching in various diﬀerent ways, including incorporation of internationalized
content into the curriculum and its subjects, incorporation of appreciation of
other cultures and worldviews, incorporation of universal teaching practices, as
well as development of common understanding of international environment of
academic discipline [28].

H. Aslam et al.
6
Conclusions
The COVID-19 pandemic has been a game changer for many aspects of the
educational environment worldwide. Together with positive aspects of digital
acceleration, there has been obstacles also in keeping internationalization pro-
cesses on track [24]. Despite of this, and acknowledging the eﬀorts made by
universities to adjust the educational methods [19], the internationalization race
seems to have just slowed down. It is hard to foresee a close future where univer-
sities will become isolated entities, independent from each other [14]. Students
and faculty exchanges, internships, dual study programs, joint research and all
related activities will still continue in some form, however probably using new
instruments and exploiting more remote communication formats [25]. The insti-
tutional attitude should not change in the incoming years: contracts, agreements,
Memorandum Of Understanding and all the legally-bounding papers of the old
world will still exist in the new world, while people are slowly getting use to the
new formats of life [25]. In our study, we exploited the window of opportunity
given by the slowing down of the internationalization process, to explore the
understanding of these activities by the very same people that could help them
and, at the same time, beneﬁt from them. We asked the employees of Innopolis
University how they perceive the work of international aﬀairs.
We have seen that, when compared to professors, administrative staﬀdo
not consider their work as a signiﬁcant support in promoting the university’s
international placing. The fact that they are not directly involved in research
may be the cause of this perception. The conclusion is, however, misleading
since administration has a pivotal role in the achievement of the global brand-
ing [5]. Internalization processes are no exception. In the study, we have also
observed diﬀerences when it comes to senior versus junior researchers. Profes-
sors, for example, fully understand the bibliometeric aspect of the rankings and
the impact of their work on them [21], while the junior researchers are not able
to see the impact of their mentoring and of participating to conferences [21].
All these diﬀerences clearly underlie a partial failure of the communication
patterns within the university [6]. On one hand, professors have not been able
to communicate the importance of rankings, how they work and how junior
researchers can impact them. On the other hand, a well-known problem of com-
munication between administration and research staﬀ(which goes way beyond
Innopolis) points to the fact that administrative staﬀcannot see how their work
is of crucial importance.
It is probably time to suggest solutions, after pointing the ﬁnger to problems.
The role of supervision by senior academics should be enriched with aspects of
training the juniors not only in terms of scientiﬁc and technical content, but also
for what concerns matters related to the “academic business” as a whole [23].
The same “academic business” is sometime alien to some layers of the university
administration too [22]. This demands to the mid and top managers a diﬀerent
attitude so to involve into the communication gears also those employees that
are not in the ﬁrst line of action when it comes to impacting the ranking as a
result of teaching and research activities.

Faculty Perception of Internationalization
881
Innopolis University, as an IT university, has the potential to impact also
from the technological viewpoint. Some of the authors have long experience of
research in the Software Engineering [17] and business processes areas [34]. Our
research in Software Engineering and Artiﬁcial Intelligence in particular [18],
can be applied (and it is currently applied) with the goal of producing tools to
support the internationalization process, such as analytic tools for participation
in international rankings, tools to monitor faculty and students’ performance
and to build academic digital blueprint. We are on the ﬁrst line in term of
digitalization processes and our objectives are to strongly contribute in this
direction in the short and long term. Innopolis itself is moving into the direction
to become a fully digital smart city [27] involving autonomous vehicles and M2M
micropayments [31]. For future work, the study should be extended, in theory,
to the full set of Innopolis employees and repeated in other organizations to
compare the results.

Learning Vehicular Wireless Connectivity
in Steps: From Theory to Vehicle Protocol
Julia Maria Engelbrecht1(B), Sven Grunwald1, Oliver Michler1, Koteshwara Raju2,
and Wilson Lee2
1 Chair of Transport Systems Information Technology, Technische Universität Dresden,
Dresden, Germany
julia_maria.engelbrecht@tu-dresden.de

Abstract. In the context of the education of engineers, it has always been a
special challenge to convey the balancing act between necessary theory and result-
oriented and structured or practically relevant working methods. The ﬁeld of trafﬁc
engineering forms a special role in the context of education. The range of possible
disciplines is very wide, which inevitably requires a strong application orientation
to convey specialized knowledge in a targeted manner. Trafﬁc telematics is a
special discipline with a close connection to electrical engineering and information
technology. The subareas cover everything from simple analog sensors to very
complex planning and design of smart mobility systems. Nevertheless, it is an
essential part of the latter to be able to understand, classify and use individual
subcomponents holistically. This paper presents a practice-oriented approach that
bridges the gap between theory and practice without losing focus on engineering
education using V2X (Vehicle-to-Everything) technology as an example.
Keywords: Hybrid teaching · Engineering training · Industrial partnership
1
Introduction/Motivation/Background
In times of increasing hybrid work, historical teaching methods with abstract examples
and to specialized special cases must also be reconsidered and reinterpreted in the con-
text of student education. Pure online eLearning concepts are difﬁcult to implement in
engineering with a practical reference regarding later working life. To give students eas-
ier access to complex measurement technology, an edutainment approach can be used [1,
2]. By making the operation of a measuring device easier and allowing users to integrate
or use it like an interactive game, greater learning success can be achieved. Students
can thus learn how to use otherwise expensive measurement technology in a playful and
sustainable way [3].
Therefore, it is necessary to divide the content into educational packages with the
aim to guide the students step by step towards trafﬁc telematic applications. Starting with
the basics and generating aha-effects based on already existing knowledge and extend
them up throughout the whole topic. In Fig. 1 the course plan “Road to trafﬁc telematics”
and the didactic outcome is shown.

2
Connected Technology in the Context of Teaching
In the ﬁeld of trafﬁc sensors and especially in trafﬁc telematics, new technologies have
been introduced over the course of time. Due to the digitalization and the demand for
greater safety in the transport sector modern sensors and communication technologies,
which are already established in the industrial and consumer sector, are adopted form. For
example: wireless communication systems and optical sensors can be found in modern
vehicles as well as in the smart city infrastructure. Therefore, the number of Advanced
Driver Assistance System (ADAS) and V2X technologies increased. In Fig. 2 a smart
city environment with intelligent infrastructure plus vehicle communication is shown.
Radio-based technologies such as IEEE 802.11p or V2X-LTE are already an integral
part of the overall system and must be understood holistically and considered in terms
of system integration.
Fig. 2. Smart city environment with intelligent communication.
2.1
Technical Change vs. Educational Demands
It is already apparent that this technological leap also poses enormous challenges for uni-
versity education, especially regarding the engineers of tomorrow [4, 5]. After successful

886
J. M. Engelbrecht et al.
completion of their studies, they should be able to understand, program and ultimately
further develop these systems and to transfer them into applications. In the area of teach-
ing, it is necessary to reﬂect the technological change and at the same time to convey the
necessary basics. In this context, it is advantageous to manage the transfer from industry
to academic education through cooperation. Beneﬁts can be shown on different levels,
which results in a higher quality of teaching and transfer of knowledge. This is justiﬁed
on the one hand by the proximity of industrial partners to actual commercial use cases,
but also by the technological availability of the individual components and innovations
in the enterprise.
The ﬁeld of trafﬁc engineering plays a special role in the context of education [6]. The
range of possible disciplines is very high, which inevitably requires a strong application
reference to convey specialized knowledge in a targeted manner. Trafﬁc telematics is
a special discipline with a close connection to electrical engineering and information
technology. The sub-areas cover everything from simple analog sensors to very complex
planning and design of smart mobility systems. The goal is to enable this bridge even
under difﬁcult conditions, such as a global pandemic. Students should not and must not
experience any disadvantage within their education due to these rare but possible global
scenarios.
2.2
Teaching V2X-Technology Wirelessly and if So Remotely
In times of increasing hybrid work, even historical teaching methods with abstract exam-
ples and to specialized special cases must be reconsidered and reinterpreted in the context
of student education. In this context, the experiences of the last two years of the still
ongoing global pandemic show that this ﬂexibility as well as the remote way of work-
ing is demanded by students. This is comprehensible change, because complex topics
and teaching content sometimes cannot be transferred at a ﬁxed prescribed time in a
sustainable way. Each participant has a different rhythm regarding the absorption of
teaching material. Nevertheless, a pure remote teaching in the ﬁeld of trafﬁc telematics
cannot work, just because of the proximity to the practical realization or the necessity
and familiarity of and with measurement equipment.
Pure online eLearning concepts are therefore difﬁcult to implement in engineering
with a practical reference to later working life, since the understanding of technical
contexts is usually not created purely virtually and is also not close to reality in relation to
later working life. As a core competence, measurement devices with online functionality
are used to check and validate expectations with the help of state-of-the-art hardware.
As a useful side effect, inhibitions about very expensive, but at the same time necessary
measurement technology are also reduced.
Thecoreobjectiveoftheapproachisthusthemediationofcausalitychainsinaddition
to the necessary basic knowledge, e.g., in the high-frequency range, and the subsequent
independent working method from theory to ﬁnal implementation and the knowledge of
how speciﬁed expectations can be validated and veriﬁed. Thereby the experience was
made that a deep dive into very specialized sub-areas is not necessary to guarantee the
possibility of the evaluation and treatment of trafﬁc telematic questions. The following
focal points are to be didactically addressed and expanded:

Learning Vehicular Wireless Connectivity in Steps
887
• Self-conﬁdence in dealing with complex engineering problems and tasks
• Independent and goal-oriented action with a view to the holistic issues in the ﬁeld of
trafﬁc telematics
• Building up an expectation towards a technical challenge with partly pronounced prior
knowledge
• Getting to know and using measurement tools with the aim of validating expectations
The goals were rated as very important in the context of university education and a
deﬁcit in the independence of students or persistence in solving problems in the technical
sense was identiﬁed, especially at the beginning of the global pandemic. In the context of
teaching learning content, a dual system has been established in trafﬁc telematics, which
is being successively expanded and extended to include technical innovations from the
respective market segments with a focus on trafﬁc telematics.
In the age of networked technology and cloud, this teaching content must be sup-
plemented with mobile radio technologies, communication protocols and, ﬁnally, end-
to-end security. In doing so, the proven ISO/OSI layer model is used to convey the core
content or points that are important for the specialist area of telematics. The advan-
tage, also for the ﬁeld of education, is that these technologies are increasingly designed
for remote and cloud connectivity (e.g. MQTT, CoAP, LWM2M). On the one hand,
theoretical basics and correlations are explained or conveyed on the blackboard or on
slides. In the second part, which is usually also underpinned by practical training dur-
ing the semester, the theoretically acquired knowledge is expanded and deepened in an
application-oriented manner.
3
Didactic Methodology in the Age of Remote Working
3.1
Learning Goals
Radio-based telematics systems are the standard in vehicle connectivity. For this rea-
son, it is important to teach students of trafﬁc telematics the basic concepts of radio-
based communication and radio frequency technology, cmp. Fig. 3. The learning goals
especially for the subject of trafﬁc telematics are listed below:
• use technical terms correctly,
• interpret data sheets,
• make technological decisions,
• evaluate and classify real measured values,
• and if necessary, plan and develop ITS systems themselves.
The approach of experience-based learning is central. It refers to the pedagogy of
pragmatism, shaped by John Dewey, and states that learning should always be based on
active, reﬂective engagement with concrete experiences [7]. Through personal experi-
ence and working through the contents and principles, these can be consolidated. The
Hattie study [8] demonstrated in the context of a large meta-analysis of learning studies
that structured and cognitive analysis and decision-making processes can be reproduced

J. M. Engelbrecht et al.

sation of Trafﬁc Telematics
verywellthroughthegamiﬁcationlearningmethod.Therearemanyapproachestoimple-
ment interactive learning in engineering education using digital games, as described for
example in [9]. These approaches facilitate access to technology and reduce barriers.
In the case of transport telematics, the high degree of application demonstrates that the
inﬂuence of the environment, e.g. transport route or transport mode, must also be taken
into account. Consequently, the creation of a virtual test ﬁeld has many advantages and
should be used in the long term as part of the training [10]. The handling of technical
equipment, which is also applicable in the industry, is also a pillar of the training. The
focus here is also on learning how to apply what has been learned to the subject, i.e. the
application-speciﬁc transfer of knowledge.

A central component of the most-important RF terms is the power level p. It describes
the measured power PX of a RF signal always in comparison to another value P0 and
is given in logarithmic dimension and uses the unit decibel (dB), cmp. Eq. 1. For V2X
signals, this is usually set in relation to 1mW and thus receives the unit dBm, shown in
Eq. 2.

A ﬁrst basic understanding of RF signals can be achieved through the difference
between the signal representations in the time domain and in the frequency domain.
The time domain is used, for example, to analyze data over a period of time. A V2X
communication signal from an RF transceiver can be viewed with a voltage-time diagram
or a current-time diagram on an oscilloscope, among others. Here, the “1” s and “0” s
of the transmitted signal are used to analyze transmitted information.
In the frequency domain, signals are analyzed in relation to their frequency. To
examine time domain functions in the frequency domain, a transformation is neces-
sary, the most used transformation is the Fourier transformation. A possible measuring
instrument is a spectrum analyzer, with which RF signals can be examined over a deﬁned
frequency range.
The link budget describes the received power at the receiver PRx in dBm, in relation
to the transmitted power PTX sent by the transmitter. Attenuation inﬂuences describing
the radio transmission are subtracted. Figure 4 shows an example of vehicle-to-vehicle
(V2V) communication, and Eq. 3 shows this mathematically.
Fig. 4. V2V communication: without obstacles (left) and with a truck as an obstacle (right).
The following parameters describe the transmitter: PTX (transmit power), GTX (gain
of the transmit antenna) and LTX (losses when feeding the antenna). On the receiving
side, antenna gain GRX and feed line losses LRX are also taken into account. Radio
propagation can be deﬁned by the path loss, it summarizes all losses that occur during
propagation. It is composed of the free space path loss (FSPL) and additional losses.
The FSPL describes the dependency of a radio communication signal on the transmission
frequency and the distance r between the transmitter and the receiver. Equation shows
the simpliﬁed form of the FSPL in dB. Additional losses summarized in LM can be
caused by diffraction or shadowing of the signal by obstacles, for example.
PRX = PTX + GTX −LTX −LFS −LM + GRX −LRX

3.3
Toolset and Educational Questions
Following the experience-based learning approach, the basics presented above, can best
be consolidated through practical exercises. The use of good RF measuring devices for
evaluating the V2X communication parameters is planned. The following requirements
for measuring devices are evident:
• simple operation,
• large range of functions,
• additional evaluation software and
• the possibility of working remotely.
On company among others at the market focusing on the educational sector is Tek-
tronix. Tektronix offer with a range of USB-powered real-time spectrum analyzer and
the analysis software SignalVu PC a good opportunity to evaluate communication sig-
nals. Engineers and students have so the change to analyze RF and vector signals easily
from their PC without charging thousands of dollars.
In the following, three questions of one practical training by using the spectrum
analyzer to evaluate V2X communication quality are presented:
Question 1: In the scenario 1, see Fig. 4 on the left, one vehicle is transmitting a content
awareness message (CAM). In terms of trafﬁc safety (real application) it is important to
know the possible distance this message can travel throughout the air. A rough calculation
could be performed with the use of formula 3 but this needs additional information out
of the air (received power).
Question 2: Let us extend scenario 1, cmp. Fig. 4 on the right. What happens if obstacles
occur within the line of sight and near the cars? Is the signal increased or decreased? What
does this mean to signal robustness and availability of trafﬁc information throughout this
scenario.
Question 3: What happens if interferer e.g. multiple pedestrians with smart devices
nearby transmitting near or at the same frequency?
In general, easy tasks on paper but without appropriate tools impossible to decline
in a sustainable way. Tooling enabling easy out of the box experience can be used to
help simplify even the most complex RF measurements and achieve a learning effect.
The SignalVu PC has multiple displays (or measurement options) where each display
performs a respective analysis and provides measurement results. To verify the channel
losses and distance between the transmitter and receiver we need the total channel power

Learning Vehicular Wireless Connectivity in Steps
891
instead of peak power (where total channel power is the integrated power within the
3 dB bandwidth.) The following display (Fig. 5) shows how the power markers can
be conﬁgured. Now, the integrated power is around –8.5 dBm, whereas the calculated
power level using free space path loss formula is –6.5 dBm.
Fig. 5. SignalVu PC spectrum display and the power display.
Do You Know the Difference? (Answer: it is –8.5 dBm because of the losses in the
cables between the antennas) The placement of markers is important for integrated
power measurements, where markers have to include 3 dB bandwidth of the waveform.
To avoid all manual errors, one more display which ﬁnd the integrated channel power
automatically.
Tools where which one can analyze signal parameters with bare minimum settings
which reduces the learning curve are becoming more and more educational state of the
art. Going a step further, hands-on measurements and recorded sessions can be made
remotely as part of lectures and laboratory exercises. This remote capability speaks to
industry practices post COVID, but also speaks to the growing trend that students learn
asynchronously with the proper remote access to industry proven equipment.
4
V2X-Technology in the Lab
For the area of training in hybrid or remote operation, it is important to convey the core or
thecorrectclassiﬁcationofthetechnologicalinnovationsaroundupcomingtechnologies.
In this context, V2X communication from vehicle to vehicle is to serve as an example,
followed by the transmission of vehicle-side data in the direction of the cloud. To carry
out this project didactically, a semester story is offered. The simple representation of a
connected car functionality including infrastructure will be used for this purpose. The

892
J. M. Engelbrecht et al.
story is linked to Fig. 2 with the goal to equip a trafﬁc light with connectivity functionality
and maximize transmit distance. Furthermore, students need to ﬁnd the nearby interferer
by analyzing the pre-recorded signals as shown in Fig. 6. The following ﬁgure shows
the signal capture of a V2X-communication on physical level, which was recorded in
the context of a research project suitable and usable for the lectures.
The learning objective is now the correct assignment of the sub-areas used, technolo-
gies and an understanding of the causality chains within this application. The focus is
not on specialized detailed solutions of the mentioned sub-disciplines, but rather on the
interlocking of areas. The main topics, which are broken down into work packages, are
to be analyzed and processed in a process like the V-model, thus sharpening the focus for
the essentials and arousing the curiosity of the prospective engineers regarding problem
solving in trafﬁc telematics.
Furthermore, possible problem areas and potential sources of error are to be analyzed
and communicated. For example, the connection and placement of an antenna to the
vehicle and possible results in terms of system performance. The focus is less on the
speciﬁc design of an antenna system or the ﬁeld-theoretical, mathematical principles,
but rather on the interaction in the network and the possible technical consequences and
results regarding performance.
Fig. 6. V2X message evaluation (logical vs. physical)
At the beginning, an expectation is created based on the taught content, participants
are to be enabled to derive an application-related expectation based on the taught content
in the physical area. The expected range of a wireless system based on IEEE 802.11p is
mentioned here. With the help of measurement technology such as a spectrum analyzer,
the handling of common measurement equipment in these areas is to be trained. Fur-
thermore, this approach creates a systematic approach to engineering issues and reduces
inhibitions towards expensive but established measurement technology. With the help
of the software provided by the industrial partner, it is possible, for example, to record
signals and signal characteristics from the real radio environment and to read them in
later and analyze them or carry out investigations.
Thus, no constructed examples are taught in the context of teaching, but rather
real existing challenges are analyzed. Solution approaches plus the hand tools for the

Learning Vehicular Wireless Connectivity in Steps
893
development of the solution are shifted to the respective classrooms (on site or virtually).
Figure 7 gives an insight to one lecture with the focus on V2X communication and
analyzingradiofrequencyspectrumwiththequestionsmentionedabove:receivedpower,
noise level, existence of interferer and the inﬂuence of them to the V2X signal. Thus, it is
not necessary to teach directly on the real object, which may not always be possible for
reasons of time and efﬁciency, and in some cases may result in overly contrived examples.
In addition, the software is also accessible to students and can be used without incurring
costs. As a side effect it can be stated that as soon as laboratory activities are scheduled
in the context of an internship, the necessary measurement technology or hardware is
attached and the operating concept is identical to the purely virtual variant.
From the point of view of the person carrying out the work, there is no difference in
terms of operation. The measurement technology is therefore only to be seen as a kind of
dongle or interface to the environment. The V2X-communication is used for the empty
contents and the mediation of a speciﬁc application-speciﬁc problem and can be made
available to the students as an assignment.

Conclusion
The technological change as well as the increasing complexity of networked systems in
the trafﬁc telematic sense are leading to increasing challenges within the education due to
thehighbandwidthoftopics.Finally,frameworkconditionssuchasapan-demicsituation
shape the transfer of knowledge and the interactive design of courses. In cooperation
with industry partners, the tools of the trade can be used and conveyed early in the path
of future engineers, which can also be applied in practical everyday life. It can therefore
be stated that a change towards more ﬂexible models is taking place to shape the learning
experience in a sustainable and individually tailored way. It has been found that hybrid
constructs are more motivating and provide a more sustainable learning experience for
the individual. The feedback of the participants from the year 2021 was very positive in

presence.Furthermore,deﬁcitsinthedidacticapproachcouldbeidentiﬁedandoptimized

Abstract. This research is subject to the nature of qualitative research by using
technique of descriptive study to analyze and synthesize data and scenario of the
necessity of integrated curriculum development through collaboration between
two major agencies in Thailand: WIT and CSTC. The collaboration has led to
actual implementation of jointly creating the B. Tech. Program in Welding Tech-
nology to provide education based on the characteristics of Hands-on Education.
This is to serve as a channel for a group of qualiﬁed graduates with High Vocational
Certiﬁcate in TVET to continue studying to strengthen competencies and enhance
qualiﬁcations through further expanding the knowledge, expertise and practical
skills to qualify for the demand of manpower reﬂected by the industrial sector.
Upon passing the educational assessments, graduates will be conferred 1 degree,
namely B. Tech. And 1 diploma from IIW at the level of IWS. The research team
focused on studying and presenting the rationale-level content, necessity, process,
events and phenomenal outcomes that have emerged in line with the policies of
the Thai government. Ultimately, this integrated model of B. Tech. And the Inter-
national Welding Specialist course through the collaboration of CSTC and WIT
will inevitably serve as a prototype, a guideline leading to actual implementa-
tion of other integrated learning courses in preparation for further development
and production of manpower in harmony with the demands of the target industry
sector.

are an essential proportion of the success of any operations, but not every organization
wantstohirea“human”whowalksinempty,whattheywantfromthe“person”tobecome

skill, which will be a mechanism driving the organization to achieve its goals in various
ﬁelds. Looking at the requirement of an employee having to possess greatly desired
“skills” by the employer, it can be counted as a competitive advantage in advancement
in the labour market. “Skills are vital for competitiveness and employability, as structural

But nowadays, both Thailand and many countries around the world are facing the
same problem: a persistent gap between the skills needed in the labor market and those
offered by the workforce [4], the cause of which must be looked for upstream. The
developer of the main feeder (Input), hereby referred to as “institutions”, especially
educational institutions in the Vocational education and training (VET) systems, needs
to deliver the right mix of skills both to meet student needs and to match the requirements
of the labor market [5]. However, what gained as the outcome is that these educational
institutions are unable to produce skilled manpower in accordance with the needs of
the industry, for example, once people are recruited, companies or organizations still
need to send them for training, to learn about the job, technology and various working
standards. This came about due to the fact that relevant “skills” needed for the job are
not available, or in a worst-case scenario, there is the inability to perform the work at
all. According to the interview with Asst. Prof. Dr. Panarit Sethakul, Acting CEO of

matching of training and jobs, which is of paramount importance for every country
in the world. In recent years, better understanding of labour market needs and skills
matching have featured high on the policy agenda of many countries, driven by both
rapid technological advances and global competition.” [1] Looking at the success in
driving the integration of the IIW curriculum developed according to the feedbacks of
the welding international professional community, Dr. Sethakul further expressed his
views on the curriculum development and the need to meet the demand of the industry:
“the method to develop or produce manpower to have skills and expertise in welding
technology to most efﬁciently meet the needs of the industrial sector; it is imperative that
educational institutions and professional standards regulators must participate in the
curriculum development that adheres to the principles of industry-recognized standards
at the scale as close as possible to internationalization. Such proceeding, therefore,
will enable education for development and production of manpower on the basis of
excellence to appear and continue to be sustainable.” Sethakul, P. (Interview, July 8,

5.1
Deﬁnition of Integration and Compatibility
Before entering the comparative content at the organizational level, it is essential to create
exact understanding of the deﬁnitions of the 2 terms: Integration and Compatibility. This
is because two terms represent a factor and a precursor to a more complete answering to
the research questions. Additionally, it is important to understand the abstract, tangible
and natural aspects of the two words that tend to have example of phenomena; therefore,
the researcher would like to raise the deﬁnition that can be said to be the most tangible by
referring to the document of the international engineering organization, namely, IEEE
standard glossary of software engineering terminology, together with images of the
semantic structure for better understanding, as shown in Table 1.
Table 1. Deﬁnitions of Integration and Compatibility (applied from [7] and [8])
Integration - The process of combining
software components, hardware components,
or both into an overall system
Compatibility - The ability of two or more
systems or components to exchange
information
In the context of “The Testing Standards Working Party, a volunteer group devoted
to the development of new software testing standards” [8], it can describe the ﬁgure
in Table 1 on the “Integration” side, along with an additional example that “shows two
components interacting to form an integrated system. Integration testing is concerned
with whether the two components when combined (integrated) to form an integrated sys-
tem behaves as the system as a whole is expected to behave. An example of integration
testing would be where the aperture control component and the shutter control compo-
nent were integrated and tested to ensure that together they performed correctly as part
of the camera control system.” [8]; and on the “Compatibility” side, in company with
an additional instance that “shows two components in the same environment. They are
compatible with each other as long as both can run (or simply reside) on the environment
without adversely affecting the behavior of the other. An example of compatibility test-
ing would be to test whether word processor and calculator applications (two separate
functions) could both works correctly on a PC at the same time.”[8].

5.2
An Overview on the Comparison Role of WIT and CSTC
5.2.1
WIT - International Welding Course Representative
“The Welding Institute of Thailand (WIT) was founded by TFII Executive Board since
2001 under cooperation between Institut de Soudure (IS) and Thai-French Innovation
Institute Project, KMUTNB.” [9] “It is a member of International Institute of Welding
(IIW). In 2004, the Institute was approved by IIW to be the sole Authorised Nominated
Body (ANB) of Thailand.” [10] The IIW mentioned is an organization with more than
70 years of growth and operation and represents 59 Member countries. They “developed
standards, best practice documents and educational programmes representing an inter-
national stamp of scientiﬁc and technical excellence for enhancing human safety and
responsible growth via safe and appropriate use of materials joining technology.” [11] It
is therefore considered a leading institution with a global network connecting industry,
education, training and research sectors together ﬁrmly, securely, and clearly in a posi-
tion of sustainability. For WIT, it is currently an organization unit within the Ofﬁce of the
President, KMUTNB. Besides the International Welding Specialist-IWS course stated
in this research, WIT also offers different certiﬁcation categories and levels, including:
International Welding Engineer-IWE, International Welding Practitioner-IWP, Interna-
tional Welder-IW and International Welding Inspection Personnel- IWIP, [10] and so
on. “These courses are developed by expert representatives from the member networks
industry sectors, and will be updated and developed to be up-to-date in accordance with
the needs of the relevant industry sectors; hence, they are relatively dynamic, at least
2 years/time to be offered through the Annual Assembly. Therefore, the WIT has to
conduct the process of quality management system employing ISO 17024 to ensure
that any person, anywhere in the world, has unrestricted access to education, training
and certiﬁcation in welding and related technologies, in accordance with international
standards” Lekapat, S. (Interview, July 8, 2022).

offers 9 Industrial Technician courses on 2 levels: Vocational Certiﬁcate, High Vocational
Certiﬁcate and 2 Bachelor’s degree programs, 1 of which is Welding Technology. CSTC
has been selected by OVEC to be 1 of the Center of Vocational Manpower Networking
Management (CVM) in the area of mechanical techniques from a total of 25 branches
across Thailand. Secretary-General of OVEC (2021) stated that, “One of the missions

all sectors; and the purpose of today’s event is to present the concept of mobilizing the

in accordance with the needs of the country, as well as to follow to the policy from

5.3
Mission and Curriculum Compatibility Analysis – An Integration Model
Towards “Integrity”
If a process of benchmarking called Identify the best performers for comparison is
drawn on to assist in the consideration for comparing the mission statements between
WIT and CSTC, it will be found that the mission compatibility of WIT and CSTC, at
least if not including internationalization, both institutions have 1 mission and 1 goal
that are compatible with each other. To elaborate the statement, both institutions have a
mission on producing and developing manpower through TVET education and Hands-
on graduates by providing education and training to meet the needs of the industry.
Additionally, they have a goal that aims for excellence and distinction from others; and
both institutions also have to achieve a unique distinctiveness within the organization.
When the mission is consistent only in the educational management dimension, the
integration of the curricula is then a further step of the proceeding. Through taking the
courses of both parties into consideration and analyzing them to look for compatibility, it
can lead to the integration of the curriculum. Table 2 shows the operating characteristics
in brief. Methods for ﬁnding compatibility can be performed in a variety of ways, but
in this paper, a simple framework raised relies on the matching of two primary datasets,
but each pair of data must have inherent compatibility characteristics of each dataset,
that is:
1) Match WIT’s Module & Topics dataset against CSTC’s Subject dataset;
2) Match the WIT Teaching Hours dataset against the CSTC Semester dataset.
This is because when comparing and analysing WIT’s Module & Topics dataset with
CSTC’s Subject dataset to look for compatibility; naturally, the result of differences,
similarities, and compatibility will appear easily owing to the datasets having innate
compatibility characteristics. Similarly, when pairing WIT’s teaching hours with the
CSTC’s semester dataset, they are both in the category of time. In addition, the WIT
course dataset is considered as a base because the number of subjects requirements of
all courses are less and they are all mandatory subjects. While the CSTC course offers
not only speciﬁc professional subjects but also other subject groups such as those in the
General Education Courses or Free Elective Courses, etc. Therefore, adhering to a lesser
course and a compulsory learning will result in time saving while also encouraging a
clear focus on the issue of the pursuit of compatibility.
In this case, the result showed that “a compatibility between courses can be clearly
sought”. This indicates that the curriculum has “concordance between educational qual-
iﬁcation originating from the course of CSTC and Professional qualiﬁcation formed by
the course of WIT with internationally recognized certiﬁcate. Then it enters into clas-
siﬁcation, ﬁnding a relationship, appending the content, combining learning materials
between courses, time management, determining methods of measurement, assessment,
methods of graduating and passing of course accreditation criteria for obtaining one

CSTC. The full analysis set focuses on 6 important topics namely institutional admin-
istrator, budget, curriculum, lecturer, student, and collaboration but in this paper points
on administrator, curriculum, lecturer, and student which are very important topics as

7
Recommendations and Conclusions
Since the B.Tech. Program was created from an integration of the two courses under the
collaboration of WIT and CSTC, it can be assured by the curriculum itself that it will
be able to meet the demands of the industry, because the core of the course is adopting
learning, training standards of International Welding Specialist designed and built by
the representatives from the international industrial sector to fully incorporate under the
supervision of a world-class organization like International Institute of Welding.
For the discussion on the collaboration between “Accreditation organization of the
International Professional Certiﬁcate” and “General Educational Institutions”, the group
of experts and those involved from the WIT and CSTC have made recommendations in
a similar direction to the research team. It can be summarized as follows:
1) “Preparing instructors to match with the standards of the cooperation partners” –
In the case of Thailand, focusing on TVET educational institutions, at present, it is
found that “teachers, instructors or those who act as educators, “mostly, they obtained
only a degree or qualiﬁcation but were not accredited any professional qualiﬁcations
or standards emerging from industry sector recognition. If a TVET educational insti-
tution will integrate its curriculum with another international professional standard
curriculum, at least there must be a plan for personnel development, that is, “in-
structor groups”, to have qualiﬁcation, skills, and to be certiﬁed according to those
standards in order to avoid delays in the implementation. This problem certainly
does not occur only within Thailand.
2) In the case of other institutions where a course in the ﬁeld of Welding Technology
is provided, they should learn and take an example from CSTC to implement, such
as, sharing curricula to mutually create an internationally recognized standard of
education for speciﬁc ﬁelds. Similar to other disciplines, educational institutions
or the government should also expedite the implementation of the development or
integration of curricula to have features that response to the demands resonated by
the industry as much as possible.
In the real world, industries have been facing skills mismatch problems for a long
time. Even the use of employment service providers, it still has not yielded the expected
outcomes. Thus, the assembling of the industries, both to form a group and to join the IIW
membership, plays a role going beyond the mere expressing of demand, but mutually
creating the course, establishing the professional standards, as well as organizing train-
ing, building and developing manpower to respond to their own demands. This becomes
signiﬁcant to reﬂect to the education sector, such as TVET group or Hands-on group,
of how critical the labor market is in terms of skills mismatch, and of the necessity that
the industry and the education sectors must seriously collaborate, both in the prepara-
tion of the courses, the development of teaching personnel, the collective management
of learning and teaching, the cooperation on practical skills training, joint measure-
ment, assessment and certiﬁcation of professional qualiﬁcations. When this concept was
spread and implemented in a wide area, only then, the problem of skills mismatch will
be solved. The need for employment service providers may diminish. “According to

906
A. Ode-sri et al.
neo-classical economic theory, in a labor market with perfect information, skills match-
ing would require no intervention from employment service providers” [13], because the
labor market or employers already know “where their future colleagues who have the
skills that match the needs are.” In the past, Thai industrial companies even set up tables
at educational institutions they trusted in the quality of education, waiting to recruit
students to work, and many students were promised to be recruited, even though they
had yet to complete their education. It is the hope of the research team to see this kind
of scenario today.

Contributing to the Green Transition
with Interdisciplinary Learning Approaches
Judit Klein-Wiele(B), Yannik Knau, Marc Kuhn, Harald Mandel, and Daniel Beigel
DHBW Stuttgart, Rotebühlstraße 133, 70197 Stuttgart, Germany
indis@dhbw.de
Abstract. “Green Transition” and sustainability are facing increasing focus in
industryandsocietycontexts.Integratingrelatedaspectsinhighereducationseems
crucial to prepare students for their future work and to show them how innovations
can be created in this area. In this regard, it is at interest if and how stakehold-
ers from various disciplines might enrich the education process. In the article,
the following question is to be answered based on the above-mentioned topic:
How can innovation emerge at the interface between business and science through
interdisciplinary collaboration? For this purpose, three types of academia-industry
partnerships within teaching will ﬁrst be presented in general. Afterwards, exem-
plary solutions of the Duale Hochschule Baden-Württemberg will be presented,
in which solutions for the challenges of the “Green Transition” and the sustain-
ability of students have been developed. In addition, a possibility for a curricular
anchoring is described to perpetuate interdisciplinary cooperation between stu-
dents. Overall, it is shown that exciting innovations can arise in different scenarios
of interdisciplinary collaboration at the interface between companies/institutions
and students.
Keywords: Green Transition · Sustainability · Interdisciplinary
1
Context
The “Green Transition” is closely linked to the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals
(SDGs), which aim to create globally sustainable structures with their three dimen-
sions of social, economic and environmental. In addition to the comprehensive SDGs,
communities of states and countries agreed on climate protection targets, which were
broken down to the level of cities, municipalities and institutions [1, 2]. These were set
out in international agreements and commitments to reduce greenhouse gases and limit
the increase in average temperature to 1.5 °C [3] to reduce the risks and consequences
of climate change. The EU aims to be carbon-neutral by 2050 and has committed to
reducing its emissions by at least 55% compared to 1990 by 2030 [3]. Advancing the
SDGs and the “Green Transition” requires people with the competencies to tackle the
complex challenges and develop innovations for implementation. For this purpose, these
people need an appropriate education, which addresses the many complex issues in the
classroom and in the ﬁeld. However, this also means that problems must be considered
from different perspectives and disciplines, and universities must create offerings that
introduce students to interdisciplinary collaboration.

M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 907–912, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_92

908
J. Klein-Wiele et al.
2
Purpose and Goal
To accompany students on this path, various partners must jointly develop studies and
concepts. In this example, these are the Baden-Württemberg Cooperative State Uni-
versity (DHBW), its dual partners (cooperating companies and institutions), and the
students themselves. As a practice-integrated university, the DHBW enables students to
build up a theoretical background as well as gain practical work experience with dual
partners [4]. With the theory-practice transfer, students can put academic competencies
into practice as well as bring practical experience into the courses and projects.
The switch between theory and practical phases also offers the advantage of acquiring
important skills for the future working world and being in direct contact with a dual
partner that is already attractive as a potential employer during the studies at DHBW.
Basedonthisspecialrelationshipbetweentheactorsintheeducationofdualstudents,
this paper addresses the question: How can innovation emerge at the interface between
business and science through interdisciplinary collaboration?
3
Approach
The Academia-Industry partnerships arise from three types of cooperation on current
problems and challenges for education in social, economic and environmental areas.
The ﬁrst possibility is project cooperation between companies or institutions and
teaching/learning formats with teaching-integrated research [5]. For this purpose, com-
panies or institutions support student projects and studies, which are carried out within
a deﬁned course.
In the second case, companies or institutions pose a problem or challenge. This topic
is worked on directly by the students. Students are given the opportunity to develop
approaches, recommendations, and innovative solutions to the company’s or institutions’
problems The students are in close contact with the company and have a direct contact
person for their work. This gives the students an insight into explicit challenges of the
working world which are solved in the context of the university and reﬂected in an
environment of learning.
The third option is a partnership of the students with a company or institution. In this
case, the challenge either identiﬁed by the students themselves or deﬁned in advance by
the educators. After the selection of the challenge and the ﬁnalization of the problem to
be solved, the teams either directly look for a partner from the real world (companies or
institutions) or ﬁnd one during the project. In most cases, it is only during the student
project that the need arises to exchange ideas with experts in the ﬁeld and to ﬁnd support
for certain phases. These can be, for example, interview partners for market and demand
analyses or companies to the implementation of a prototype. The experts support the
students with their idea as well as solution development and help to implement the
practical solution. The solutions are also reﬂected in the university context.
All three possibilities describe Academia-Industry partnerships, in which Problem-
Based Learning can be implemented as a practice-oriented method. Real and application-
oriented problems and challenges are used as a basis for an action-oriented implemen-
tation of student projects. Figure 1 shows how problem-based learning works.

Contributing to the Green Transition
909
Fig. 1. The process of Problem-Based Learning, which is used for real and application-oriented
problems and challenges to ﬁnd innovative solutions (adjusted after [6]).
If then still the interdisciplinary cooperation between the students among themselves
in addition, with the enterprises and/or mechanisms is added, the problem deﬁnitions
and challenges can be regarded from different perspectives and solved with the ways of
thinking and methods of the different disciplines comprehensively.
4
Actual and Expected Results
In the following, examples of the DHBW’s implementation of Academic-Industry part-
nerships in the context of education are described. These are student projects that address
both problem-based learning and interdisciplinary collaboration. The “Green Transition”
and the SDGs were used here as learning content.
4.1
Project Cooperation Between (Dual) Partners and Educational Scenarios
In the interdisciplinary student project E-Hunter 2018/19, students from the departments
of engineering and business investigated the charging infrastructure of electric vehicles.
In addition to economic (reliability, payment and service), the teams also collected and
evaluated technical research data (charging process, range and thermal comfort). A total
of 450 charging points were recorded within Germany and on the way to Venice and
the Austrian Reschenpass (see Fig. 2). The study was supported by the energy supply
company EnBW AG [7]. In this case, current and relevant problems are analysed, data
is collected and a public-impact evaluation is presented in a report and at an event.

910
J. Klein-Wiele et al.
Fig. 2. An electric vehicle in the snow at a charging station on the way to skiing [8]
4.2
Challenges from (Dual) Partners
The Center for Interdisciplinary Teaching and Research (INDIS) is: “a location and
faculty-wide center and stands for interdisciplinary cooperation in teaching, research
and transfer” [9]. Students at INDIS work on sustainability challenges over a period of
6 or 12 months. The topics of the challenges are based on the chosen annual theme of
the INDIS.
One of these challenges is: “Sustainable Social Space Development” was set by the
Diakonische Hausgemeinschaften Heidelberg e.V., which is about: “promoting inter-
generational exchange, intercultural exchange, ensuring opportunities for participation
and civic engagement that counteracts marginalization” [10]. This task was worked on
by the students by founding the “Mosaik Wiesloch”. The Mosaik is about people: “of
different population groups meeting and getting to know each other through joint actions
and mutual support” [11]. The offer is open to all and should be affordable for all on
a cost-effective basis. The Diakonische Hausgemeinschaften e.V. supports the student
team in the implementation of the project and provides a contact person for questions
and problems.
4.3
Challenges from Students and Educators
Another INDIS challenge was set by the center team educators. It deals with exoskeletons
in the real estate industry. In their market and needs analysis, the interdisciplinary student
team conducted expert interviews with manufacturers and users, as well as with medical
staff and facility managers [10]. In a later phase, they were able to get in touch with a
manufacturer of passive exoskeletons (Ottobock) during a ﬁeld trip, who subsequently
continued to provide feedback on their idea for a modular exoskeleton [12].
In the previous project “Urban Mobitlity Lab” (2019–2021), students independently
deﬁned the problem of too little distance to bicycles in road trafﬁc in an interdisciplinary
team. For this purpose, the students built the “Kesselbox”, a bicycle distance measuring
device consisting of a circuit board with sensors, a small computer, a memory card and
a power supply. After programming the Kesselbox, it was given a 3D-printed housing
[13]. In this case, a newspaper (Stuttgarter Zeitung) became aware of the project and
distributed Kesselbox to testers in a high-proﬁle campaign together with the student
team [14]. This made it possible to record and evaluate a lot of data on bicycle distances
to other road users, so that the problem became visible (Fig. 3).

Contributing to the Green Transition
911
Fig. 3. The inside of the bicycle distance measuring device (left) [15] and in the 3D-printed
housing on the bicycle (right) [16].
4.4
Possibility of Inclusion in the Curriculum
So far, participation in interdisciplinary student projects with Academic-Industry part-
nerships is limited to only two possibilities: One is voluntary participation without credit
points for the project, and the other is that participation can be rewarded with credit points
based on other modules of the curricula [9]. This means that students have very different
study achievements depending on the course of study, which is difﬁcult to compare. Due
to different times for the theory phases at the university, the deadlines for the examination
achievements are also not synchronous.
The aim is to create a third possibility to counteract these difﬁculties and to make
it easier for students to participate in such projects. The solution sought is the approval
of an interdisciplinary module with uniform credit points [9]. This should be able to be
studied either as an elective or as an additional module and should be integrated into all
curricula of the degree programs. This will enable a uniform approach for both students
and teachers and improve equal opportunities for students.
5
Conclusions and Recommendations
Outcomes are expected to be, on the one hand, developed solutions and innovations to
successfully promote green change both within the university and in companies. On the
other hand, the DHBW and the INDIS aims to anchor topics such as “Green Transition”
and sustainability in the curriculum and to further develop the interdisciplinary com-
petencies of students together with DHBW’s dual partners. Due to the increasing com-
plexity of individual subject areas, it is difﬁcult for isolated specialist areas to develop
innovations in the ﬁeld of “Green Transition”. Through interdisciplinary cooperation
between universities, students, and partners from industry, different or new perspectives
on problems can emerge, and innovative solutions can be developed. With interdisci-
plinary learning approaches, both students and universities are expected to contribute to
the topics of “Green Transition” and SDGs in cooperation with practice partners.

J. Klein-Wiele et al.
