Development of KALCEA Novel Collaborative
Platform for Sustainable Development
of Western Balkan Countries
Anatolijs Zabasta1(B), Aleksandra Petrovic2, Aphrodite Ktena3, Nadezda Kunicina1,
Nebojsa Arsic2, and Amela Ajanovic4
1 Institute of Industrial Electronics and Electrical Engineering, Riga Technical University,
Riga 1048, Latvia
Anatolijs.zabasta@rtu.lv
2 University of Pristina in Kosovska Mitrovica, 38220 Kosovska Mitrovica, Kosovo
3 National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, 157 72 Athens, Greece
4 Technische Universitaet Wien, 1040 Vienna, Austria
Abstract. The global challenges of the transition towards low-carbon energy,
with energy security as well as accessibility and affordability, cannot be success-
fully addressed without the contribution of knowledge-based innovations draw-
ing on education and research in the energy ﬁeld. New innovative solutions are
requested along the entire value chain of the energy sector in Western Balkan
Countries. The ERASMUS + project “Knowledge triangle for a low carbon
economy (KALCEA)” is aiming to introduce KT mechanisms and structures
through improving technical capacities at Higher Education Institutions, building
strategic partnerships with the industry sector and research centers, establishing
Knowledge-Innovation Centers, and developing open innovation platforms with
virtual learning environments. Our research is focusing on the following aspects
of KALCEA: Clariﬁcation of the needs, topics, and problem issues of collabora-
tion between the academy, research, and business institutions; Practical aspects
of the creation of the novel Collaborative Platform, including the establishment
of KICs, development of collaboration model and ensuring sustainability beyond
the project. A preliminary survey has provided interesting results concerning the
facilitators and barriers to cooperation between HEIs and the industry. The results
revealed that, with respect to research and innovation, the perception of industrial
partners differs slightly from that of the academic partners.
Keywords: Knowledge triangle · Knowledge-based innovation · Sustainable
development
1
Introduction
Education for sustainable development (ESD) plays a signiﬁcant role in achieving
the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and simultaneously tackling the current
global ecological challenges. Integration of ESD in Vocational Education and Train-
ing (VET) offers opportunities for private sector actors to contribute to reaching these
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 913–920, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_93

914
A. Zabasta et al.
global goals [1]. ESD further required a rapid shift from teacher-centered to learner-
centered approaches with task-based instruction, problem orientation, interdisciplinar-
ity, and transdisciplinarity [2], and also the use of digital tools and approaches in the
development of required competencies for promoting sustainable development [3]. The
need for a labor force with skill sets that made it possible to establish and sustain
new environmental industries, services, and practices is proposed by the global urgency
for sustainable development [4]. It should be emphasized that the development of new
innovative solutions would not be possible without the support of academic and research
centers [5]. Such centers have to ensure the necessary intellectual and technical resources
essential to create innovation [6, 7].
The global challenges of the transition towards low-carbon energy, with energy secu-
rity as well as accessibility and affordability, cannot be successfully addressed without
the contribution of knowledge-based innovations drawing on education and research in
the energy ﬁeld. New innovative solutions are requested along the entire value chain
of the energy sector in Western Balkan Countries (WBCs). The Knowledge Triangle
initiative (KT) highlights the importance of jointly fostering research, education, and
innovation and plays a signiﬁcant role in the sustainable development of WBCs. How-
ever, cooperation with the industry sector in WBCs is weak and mostly ad hoc, based
on individual contacts, while a systematic approach does not exist.
2
ERASMUS + KALCEA Project
The ERASMUS + project “Knowledge triangle for a low carbon economy (KALCEA)”
is aiming to introduce KT mechanisms and structures through improving technical
capacities at Higher Education Institutions (HEIs), building strategic partnerships with
the industry sector and research centers, establishing Knowledge Innovation Centers
(KICs) and developing open innovation platforms with virtual learning environments
[8]. The needs for establishing strong cooperation with the industry sector and increas-
ing the capacities for research and innovation are deﬁned in the development strategy
of all WBC partners, namely the University of East Sarajevo – UES (BIH), Interna-
tional Burch University – IBU (BiH), University of Dzemal Bijedic Mostar – UNMO
(BiH), European University of Tirana – EUT (ALB), Polytechnic University of Tirana –
PUT (ALB), Aleksander Moisiu University Durres – UAMD (ALB), the University of
Pristina in Kosovska Mitrovica – UPKM and Universum College – UC (Kosovo). EU
partners – National and Kapodistrian University of Athens (NKUA), Technical Univer-
sity of Vienna (TUV), and Riga Technical University (RTU) provide their knowledge
and experience through workshops, training, studies, lectures, exchange of students, etc.
The innovative approach is implemented by the following activities:
1. Introduction of KT principles is a novelty for all institutions involved in the project.
2. Establishing a structured cooperation framework between the HEIs, industry sector,
and research institutions, through the proposed network is innovative for all WBC
HEIs, since cooperation between the HEIs and industry sector currently relies mostly
on personal contacts.

Development of KALCEA Novel Collaborative Platform
915
3. Launching the novel Collaborative Platform is an innovative way of establishing
and implementing the collaborative activities between the HEIs, industry sector, and
research institutions in KT.
4. Introducing Living Labs & Learning Factories are a novelty for all WBC HEIs.
5. Establishing Knowledge Innovation Centers (KICs) that will serve as hubs for all
KT activities (education, research, innovation) will enable the sustainability of KT
activities.
6. Professional courses on Sustainable energy technologies, as a KIC activity, will
contribute to capacity building in the WBC as well as to addressing SDG-related
challenges at the local and global levels.
In this paper, we focus on two main topics of the KALCEA project: a) Clariﬁcation
of the needs, topics, and problem issues of collaboration between the academy, research,
and business institutions; b) Practical aspects of developing the novel Collaborative
Platform, including the establishment of KICs, development of collaboration model and
ensuring sustainability beyond the project.
3
Survey on Current Cooperation Between HEIs and the Business
Sector in Kosovo UPKM
At the beginning of the project, the clariﬁcation of the needs, topics, and problem issues
of collaboration between the academy, research, and the industry in the energy sector
was carried out. A survey with industry partners was conducted by each WBC HEI. The
survey conducted by the University of Pristina in Kosovska Mitrovica (UPKM) could
serve as an example of the methodology applied by KALCEA HEIs.
Twenty-one respondents participated in a survey arranged by the UPKM in the ﬁrst
part of 2021, out of which 52.4% were from the industrial and business sectors (Energy,
ICT, economics, technical control, and other engineering ﬁelds), while 47.6% were from
UPKM (academic staff, university authorities, researchers, students in all three cycles).
Representatives of the Faculty of Technical Sciences (70%), Faculty of Science and
Mathematics (20%), and Faculty of Philosophy (10%) were involved in the survey.
To the question “What is the purpose of collaboration between Universities and
Companies, Research centers and Companies, Universities and Research Centers?” the
majority (60%) of academy respondents answered “Curriculum co-delivery (e.g., guest
lectures)”. In turn, “Mobility of students”, “Dual education programmers” and “Indus-
try support” were selected as the purpose of collaboration by 40% of the academic
respondents (Fig. 1).
To the same question, the majority of respondents from the industry answered: “Mo-
bility of students (i.e., student internships/placements)” (63.6% of respondents). “Col-
laboration in R&D (incl. Joint funded research)” was selected by 54.5%, but “Dual
education programs” was selected by 45.5% of the industrial respondents (Fig. 2.).
Amongthemainsuccessfactors(facilitators)foreffectivecollaboration,theacademy
representatives selected the “Commercial orientation of the university” (70%), “A better
integration of researchers in business activities” (50%), “Mutual understanding between
partners” (50%), etc.

916
A. Zabasta et al.
Fig. 1. What is the purpose of collaboration between Universities and Companies, Research

Fig. 2. What is the purpose of collaboration between Universities and Companies, Research

The perception of the industry respondents concerning the top 5 success factors
differed from academic participants, since 63.6% of them, as the main success factors,
selected “Ability of staff to work across institutional boundaries”, “Willingness to devote
time and resources from both parties”, “A better knowledge of the opportunities to
collaborate”, “Shared vision, goals, and objectives deﬁned, with clear expectations”.
The “Lack of private sector funding” was recognized as the main barrier to effec-
tive collaboration by the academic respondents. Additionally, “Cumbersome and com-
plex procedures (too much bureaucracy)”, “Lack of awareness of opportunities arising
from collaboration”, “Motivations by universities and motivations by the business are
not well understood by both parties” and “Lack of interface structures or appropriate
contact persons to establish communication” were identiﬁed as barriers for effective
collaboration.

Development of KALCEA Novel Collaborative Platform
917
On the other side, the industry respondents, as top barriers to effective collaboration,
identiﬁed “Motivations by universities and motivations by businesses are not well under-
stood by both parties”, and “Lack of employees from universities – research centers with
an adequate level of business knowledge and understanding the business situation and
trends in the country and worldwide”.
The perception of academic and industry respondents, concerning the reasons which
could motivate collaboration, is also rather different. For example, academic representa-
tives consider that improvement of the knowledge transfer process and the possibility to
create spin-offs are the main motivation factors. However, industry representatives think
that access to better-qualiﬁed graduates, access to new technologies and knowledge, and
the opportunity to improve the skills of current employees through training are the main
motivation factors for collaboration with universities.
Due to the lack of space, we do not publish all charts in this paper.
4
Implementation of Collaborative Platform for Sustainable
Development
Since one of the main goals of the KALCEA project is to establish systematic networks
for cooperation between the three pillars of KT for each institution separately, and
ﬁnally to merge them into one regional network with a tendency to expand, the interna-
tional experience to be taken into consideration. A framework proposed in [9], describes
the tools supporting the development of KT cooperation in the raw materials sector.
This framework includes a dedicated platform devoted to three areas of collaboration:
information, promotion, and dissemination. A regional collaborative innovation sym-
biotic system, which is characterized by knowledge, with the components of producer,
consumer, decomposer, and catalyzer is described in [10].
From an organizational perspective, the KALCEA project develops the innovative
Collaborative Platform as a process, which manages and integrates innovative resources
in order to establish a seamless circle of talents, knowledge, and capital, and to improve
and optimize constantly the synergy of each subject in this process. The collaborative
innovation process manages three core ﬂows: talent ﬂow, knowledge ﬂow, and fund
ﬂow. The architecture diagram of the Collaborative Platform is shown in Fig. 3. The
Collaborative Platform supports knowledge transferring among the partners involved in
the innovation process, where ﬁve KICs of eight WBCs universities arrange this process
as intermediaries between academics, research institutions, and industry.
In our research, we deﬁned the main components of the collaborative innovation
process as follows. An Online Platform will be used for easier networking and informa-
tion transfer. The aim of this mechanism is to enable easier access to data from various
participants in the knowledge triangle and to promote opportunities for joint projects.
For example, companies will be able to post job listings, to which students can apply.
Students will be assigned to Faculties and able to post and update their proﬁles, in its turn,
registered companies will be able to search and contact students, etc. From a technical
perspective, the online platform includes a web interface and a PostgreSQL powerful
open-source object-relational database system that will enable CRUD operations. IBU
university has started developing the platform on its own infrastructure, however, the

918
A. Zabasta et al.
Amazon RDS (Managed Relational Database) service will be subsequently considered
and tested, as an alternative.
Fig. 3. The architecture of the innovative Collaborative Platform
Life-Long Learning Platform. The development of the courses for professionals
opens opportunities for lifelong learning, where in addition to students, industry pro-
fessionals should directly beneﬁt from attending these courses to gain additional, up-
to-date, knowledge and skills that they could apply in their work. In this project, each
WBC higher education institution will develop a minimum of 2 courses, while a total
of approximately 15 courses per country are expected to be completed. Existing LLL
Centers will be linked to KICs. A blended learning system is established as a part of the
Collaborative Platform.
Uniﬁed cooperation agreements between HEI and industry will serve as a mechanism
toward a more structured cooperation process, where areas and rules of cooperation can
be clearly deﬁned.
Joint Commercial Projects. Participation in joint commercial projects with industry,
such as the development of new products and services by University accredited labo-
ratories, is one of the effective ways for HEIs to attract the funding necessary to cover
operational costs, such as recruiting young researchers and teaching staff as well as
ﬁnancing the modernization of educational laboratory.
Joint Research Projects. Participation in various research projects is an effective way
to establish systematic cooperation between different pillars of the knowledge triangle. In
addition, most companies located in the Western Balkans do not have sufﬁcient capacity
and need to fund research projects, because they are small and medium enterprises.
Participation in international research, educational and science & technology networking
projects such as Eureka, Horizon, COST action, Erasmus+, etc. will help knowledge

Development of KALCEA Novel Collaborative Platform
919
transfer and collaboration with other countries. Living Labs are a tool for knowledge
transfer and capacity building, as well as testing novel products in actual operating
conditions.
Exchange of Scientiﬁc, Student, and Professional Staff Between Industry and HEIs.
The exchange of both scientiﬁc and professional staff and students between industry
and higher education offers various advantages such as constant monitoring of market
needs, access to new technologies, insight into the real industrial environment, etc.
The advantages primarily for universities are reﬂected in the strengthening of industrial
practicesforstudents,improvingthecurriculumaccordingtotherealneedsofthemarket,
and creating a more dynamic atmosphere for lectures, where part of the teaching process
could take place in real industry conditions. In this way, companies could use both new
human and intellectual potential for their expansion.
Master and Doctoral Thesis Driven by Industry. As one of the mechanisms for KT,
master’s and doctoral theses based on speciﬁc problems in the industry are deﬁned.
This enables young professionals as well as researchers to work on concrete industrial
problems as well on applied research, which may enhance their employment prospects.
On the other hand, companies proﬁt from low R&D costs, new innovative products,
and the pool of potential highly specialized employees familiarized with the challenges
of their production process. This also opens opportunities for companies to ﬁnd new
employees, who meet their criteria, as well as to solve the problems, they have in their
production process.
Participation of Industry Experts in the Education Process. Introducing a part of the
teaching process held by experts from the real industrial environment enables students
to have an insight into the real processes taking place in the market. Learning Factories
is a promising methodology toward this end. Such an approach makes teaching a more
dynamic and interesting process for students, while it facilitates the identiﬁcation of
possibilitiesforothermechanisms,suchasjointprojectswithstudentsandHEIs,master’s
and PhD industry-driven theses, etc.
Intellectual Property Management. An innovation may be protected through a com-
bination of IPRs, (e.g. patents, designs, copyrights, trademarks, etc.) Furthermore, the
IP strategy must be in coherence with the commercialization strategy.
The ﬁrst practical steps towards the creation of KICs have been implemented, e.g.
creation of organizational charts, allocation of responsibilities and tasks of employees,
etc. However, important challenges should be overcome by WBC HEIs with the support
of EU partners, e.g., how to facilitate communication between university and industry,
how to organize technology transfer between universities and companies, etc.
5
Discussions and Conclusions
All HEIs, which participate in the KALCEA, have established networks with the busi-
ness stakeholders. The survey of stakeholders has revealed useful results concerning
the facilitators and barriers to cooperation between HEIs and the industry. The results
demonstrated that, with respect to research and innovation, the perception of industrial
partners differs slightly from that of academic partners. For example, representatives
of HEIs recognized the following as one of the main success factors (facilitators) for

920
A. Zabasta et al.
effective collaboration: “Commercial orientation of the university” and “A better inte-
gration of researchers in business activities”. In turn, business representatives consid-
ered that “Shared vision, goal, and objectives” is the determining factor for successful
collaboration.
As far as barriers to effective collaboration are concerned, university representatives
pointed out: “Lack of private sector funding” and “Cumbersome and complex procedures
(too much bureaucracy)”. On the other hand, business representatives recognized “Lack
of understanding business logic and business trends in the country and worldwide by
HEIs” as one of the main hurdles for successful cooperation.
The creation of the novel Collaborative Platform will support systematic cooperation
with the industrial sector and promote the transition towards a low carbon economy,
which is the focus of the project, and which can be extended to other spheres related to
Sustainable Development in WBC.

A Practical Approach
to an Undergraduate Computer Science
Senior Design Project Experience:
Partnering with Industry to Create
an Eﬀective Transition from Academia
to the Next Chapter
Margaret R. Scaturro Heil(B) and Ignacio X. Dom´ınguez
North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA
{heil,ignacioxd}@ncsu.edu
Abstract. The North Carolina State University Computer Science
Department’s Senior Design Center began in 1994 to foster a relation-
ship between local tech industries and academia. The teaching team and
industrial sponsors collaborate to create and emulate an industrial set-
ting to expose students to the expectations of a professional environment
beyond graduation. Sponsoring companies provide problem statements
for small teams of undergraduate seniors who solve these problems by
creating software. Students are expected to meet with industrial sponsors
weekly and provide meeting agendas and minutes. Student teams work
closely with sponsors and academic advisors to explore system require-
ments and discuss trade-oﬀs of various approaches to software design.
Student teams create software using an organized development process
as well as formally write and speak about this process. In the most recent
semester, 39 student teams working on 39 unique projects were formed.
The discussion serves as a guide to help other academic institutions to
create a similar experience. Tips for ﬁnding and maintaining industrial
sponsors are outlined. The history of the multidisciplinary approach is
described and details related to identifying and preparing projects, as
well as intellectual property/conﬁdentiality and funding considerations
are explored. The collaboration of students, industrial mentors and aca-
demic advisors is also described.
Keywords: Academic-industrial partnerships · Small team
communication · Capstone project experiences

1
Introduction
The North Carolina State University (NCSU), USA, Computer Science Senior
Design Center (the Center) was established in 1994 to facilitate interaction
between the Computer Science Department (the department) and North Car-
olina industry for the purpose of providing computer science seniors realistic
project experiences. The Center’s mission is to help undergraduate students to
integrate their technical expertise, teaming experience, professional communica-
tion skills (project management, writing and speaking), and their knowledge of
software development methodology while creating software to solve problems.
The intent of this senior design capstone course is to emphasize software
development process, professional communication, and teaming. The experience
emulates an industrial setting so that students experience what it may be like
to work and thrive in a corporate setting.
1.1
Approach
The Center’s approach has evolved from 28 years experience in oﬀering a 15-
week capstone senior design project course, CSC 492, taught by instructors with
diﬀerent backgrounds. CSC 492 is team-taught by the Director of the Center,
a Technical Communicator and Team Specialist; the Assistant Director of the
Center, an Assistant Teaching Professor of Computer Science; as well as other
Computer Science faculty who serve as technical advisors to the student teams.
Approximately 20–40 individual teams (3–5 students/team) are formed each
semester. Industrial sponsors provide monetary donations, project statements
and contact engineer(s) who mentors the students throughout the semester.
At this time, the Center has hosted over 200 sponsoring companies, and
approximately 3000+ students have been mentored and placed on more than
700 teams. Virtual experiences were also completed during the pandemic. The
pedagogical approach used in the Center has been previously described [1,3,6].
1.2
Where We Are Now
During Spring 2022, 39 student project teams were formed, and 39 projects and
194 students were accommodated. During that time, the Center teaching team
included the Director, 6 technical advisors, and 4 teaching assistants.
2
History
2.1
The Idea
NCSU is located in Raleigh, North Carolina and surrounded by the Research
Triangle Park (RTP), a 7000-acre area that includes hundreds of science and
technology companies, and was founded in 1959 [5].
In 1994, the head of the NCSU Computer Science Department wanted to
develop a dynamic relationship with the department and industrial neighbors in

Industrially-Sponsored CSC Senior Design Experience
923
RTP. He reached out to a faculty colleague to brainstorm ideas about how to
forge this relationship and how it could potentially beneﬁt undergraduates. Since
the department head and faculty colleague had been involved with the depart-
ment since the 1960 s they had many contacts in the area including alumni of the
department. They reached out to former students and industrial acquaintances
to brainstorm ideas about what would help undergraduates to best transition to
the next chapter after graduating, that is, working as a professional computer
scientist in a corporate environment.
2.2
The Senior Design Center Is Formed
Industrial partners were extremely willing to participate in such an experiment.
The department head’s faculty colleague was named the ﬁrst Director of the
Center; the Director worked with industrial partners to establish the Senior
Design Center, a lab-type experience that became an elective project course.
Industrial mentors (sponsors) provided short problem descriptions for student
teams to solve by creating software in one semester.
Students met with sponsors weekly to explore and determine system require-
ments, to determine software design and an approach to implementation, and
to create test plans. The Center Director served as technical advisor to 3- to
4-person student teams.
2.3
Challenges
The Director asked students to not only create software per a development
methodology, but students were also expected to organize meetings with spon-
sors, work eﬀectively as a team, manage their projects, write formal documenta-
tion, and deliver formal oral presentations. These activities became challenging
for just one instructor to handle, so the Director reached out to colleagues for
assistance in these areas.
Other faculty in the department were reluctant to manage the teaming and
communication components of these projects; in 1996, the Center Director there-
fore decided to consult with a technical communicator/team specialist to develop
a teaching paradigm for this senior design experience.
2.4
The Center Evolves: Multidisciplinary Pedagogy
The ﬁrst Director of the Center and the newly hired Team Coordinator (currently
the Director of the Center and author) created a multidisciplinary pedagogy that
included skills development in the areas of teaming, writing, speaking and project
management. Student teams were coached and monitored in these areas [1,3,6].
Industrial sponsors wholeheartedly supported these activities, as this meant
that undergraduates would be better prepared for professional life as they entered
industry. Through their sponsorship of a project, sponsors were easily able to

924
M. R. Scaturro Heil and I. X. Dom´ınguez
recruit top-notch computer science students. The Center’s unique multidisci-
plinary approach caught the attention of local industry and students appreci-
ated the contact with sponsors - this proved to be an advantageous experience
for all parties. The Center grew at a fast rate and in the early 2000 s s became
a required course for all undergraduate Computer Science majors at NCSU.
3
Securing Industrial Partners and Projects:
Collection, Intellectual Property Rights and Donation
Considerations
3.1
External Relations
As the Center grew, the department created a Director of External Relations
position. This person’s primary responsibility is to establish relationships with
industrial contacts and promote activities that beneﬁt the department, the stu-
dents, and the companies. These activities include career fairs, guest speaker
series, and project involvement. At the NCSU Computer Science Department,
a well-established ePartnership program is in place [4]. Because of this position
and program, the Director of the Center has assistance with ﬁnding and retaining
sponsors for the Center.
3.2
Collecting Projects
The Center has created a Call for Projects link to our Course Website [2].
This webpage includes important deadlines and dates, guidelines for success-
ful projects and a Project Proposal Template. At NCSU, this link is sent to
prospective sponsors by both the Director of the Center and the Director of
External Relations 3 months before the start of the semester.
It is important to collect draft, short (1–2 page) project descriptions from
sponsors at least 1 month in advance of the start of a semester. This allows plenty
of time for interaction between technical advisors/faculty and sponsors to ask
questions and clarify project details (see Sect. 4 for additional guidance).
Determining project feasibility with industrial sponsors is essential during
this initial stage of the project preparation process. For example, in the case
of the Center at NCSU, we expect that the problems presented to students
require extensive planning, design and implementation, and that the need for
data analysis is minimal and peripheral to the main problem solution. Sponsors
understand that the semester goal for the students is to work toward creating a
proof-of-concept or prototype solution.
3.3
Intellectual Property
Our undergraduate students own the Intellectual Property (IP) rights of their
Senior Design projects unless the sponsoring company draws up an agreement

Industrially-Sponsored CSC Senior Design Experience
925
between them and each individual student on the team. If the sponsoring com-
pany requires that students turn over their IP rights to them, the agreement
should be given to students at the initial meeting with sponsors for each student
to sign. Before students choose projects, we include a statement that says stu-
dents will be required to sign over their IP rights. It is best to check with one’s
University legal counsel when determining these guidelines.
3.4
Donations
Since educating our students is the main mission of the Center, there are no con-
tractual agreements between industrial partners and student teams. The teaching
team must properly represent this concept to industrial sponsors before these
partners become oﬃcially involved with the Center; this helps to prevent spon-
sors from exploiting the students for their work done during the semester. We
ask for a $5000 donation/project from sponsoring companies; these funds are
placed in an Excellence for Undergraduate Education account and are used for
expenses related to the Center (e.g., hardware/software resources, classroom
renovations/equipment, extra staﬀas needed).
4
Project Preparation
4.1
A Short Description
The ﬁrst task for the industrial sponsor(s) is to provide a 1-page project descrip-
tion that summarizes a problem and presents the beginning of a potential solu-
tion (that is, some preliminary requirements of the system to be developed) that
will evolve as a result of the work of a student project team. On the ﬁrst day
of classes, project descriptions are presented to the class and technical advisors
provide oral summaries of projects to their respective section of senior design
students. Each student is allowed to choose their 1st, 2nd, and 3rd choice of
projects from the list of projects available to their section.
These project descriptions work best when they are attractive to the students
and when they easily answer questions that students may have when bidding for
projects. Sponsors should include preliminary or sample system requirements
and use cases - this helps students to picture how the end-product will be used.
Students also like to know what technologies sponsors are expecting them to use
during development; students often choose projects based on their familiarity
with the expected technologies or because of technologies that they are interested
in exploring. Students also respond well when project descriptions indicate that
the sponsoring mentors will provide assistance with unknown domains, software,
and design approaches.
4.2
Additional Information and Data
Sponsors should also have additional information available to students once
teams are formed. This can include any related preexisting code, user inter-

926
M. R. Scaturro Heil and I. X. Dom´ınguez
face ideas, additional use case examples, a description of proprietary interfaces,
and cleansed dummy data.
If sponsors are concerned about conﬁdentiality, they should prepare a docu-
ment that covers conﬁdentiality and students should only have access to sanitized
data while working on project. As a part of our course requirements, students
must create formal presentations and documentation describing their project -
the audience for these artifacts are classmates, instructors and in the case of
presentations, other sponsors. We also host an end-of-semester exposition that
is open to the public. In our case, industrial sponsors work with their student
team to ensure that conﬁdentiality is preserved. Over the years, our sponsors
have willingly worked within these guidelines.
4.3
Project Types
Since project ideas come from industrial sponsors, the types of projects oﬀered
by the Center each semester are driven by industry trends. This approach oﬀers
several advantages. First, it ensures projects oﬀered in a given semester expose
students to technologies and challenges they are more likely to encounter at the
time they enter the workforce. Second, it enables engaged sponsor mentorship
by allowing sponsors to advise students in their area of expertise and in domains
that are relevant to the sponsors’ business needs. As a side eﬀect, the Center’s
staﬀcan focus less on what types of projects are being oﬀered in a semester to
focus instead on ensuring that projects have an appropriate scope to be com-
pleted by a student team in a single semester.
The list of projects hosted by the Center by semester since Spring 2001,
including sponsors and project descriptions, is available at the Center’s website1.
5
Sponsor Meetings - Prepping Students and Industrial
Mentors
5.1
KickoﬀMeetings
Students submit project bids on the evening of the ﬁrst day of class and teams
are formed by the ﬁrst Friday of the semester. Once a project team is formed, the
industrial sponsoring mentor(s) will be invited to participate in an initial sponsor
kick-oﬀmeeting that usually takes place within the ﬁrst 2 weeks of class. This
meeting is held on the NCSU campus (or virtually) and typically lasts for ∼1 h.
Sponsors, student team and Center advisors attend these meetings.
To prepare for these kickoﬀmeetings, the Center staﬀprovides students
with lectures that cover the proper way to conduct a meeting, meeting agenda
construction, and protocols related to creating and maintaining meeting minutes.
Students send draft agendas (for initial kick-oﬀmeeting only) to the Director
for review and approval before sending to other invitees.
1 https://sdc.csc.ncsu.edu/projects.

Industrially-Sponsored CSC Senior Design Experience
927
The Center Director works with sponsors before the beginning of the semester
to schedule kick-oﬀmeetings during class time. Remaining meetings are sched-
uled outside of class time. Gathering common times for Center advisors, sponsors
and students, especially with a large number of project teams, is tedious. Advi-
sor times are announced using a Google Calendar, students choose times that
intersect with those posted times, and then students oﬀer to sponsors to try to
ﬁnalize meeting time.
5.2
Weekly Meetings
Over the remainder of the 15-week semester, the sponsoring mentor usually
meets with the student team once/week (in-person or virtually) for approxi-
mately 1 h to discuss progress and potential issues. Students are expected to
create agendas prior to meetings and minutes after meetings are conducted. The
Center staﬀreserves conference room space for these weekly meetings. Sponsors
often comment on the eﬀectiveness of this protocol and appreciate the prepared-
ness of the students.
During these weekly meetings, industrial mentors familiarize the student
teams with the project domain and the current state of any software in use.
Mentors will also help to solve problems that students may have with existing
software or development tools. Students often rely on the sponsors for assistance
with design trade-oﬀdecisions and product usability. The Center advisors also
work with students on design decisions and to troubleshoot technical obstacles.
In the early years of the Center when fewer project teams participated in this
Senior Design experience, the Center instructors were able to attend all weekly
meetings with every team. As the number of teams has grown, however, students
and sponsors usually meet without Center instructors; the Director and technical
advisors do attend weekly meetings when needed and randomly to evaluate how
sessions are conducted.
6
Additional Interactions with Industrial Mentors
6.1
Communication Beyond Weekly Status Meetings
Asking Questions. Oftentimes, students will send questions to sponsoring
mentors via email in-between meetings. Since the pandemic, the Center has
created Slack channels for all teams and their sponsors; Center advisors are
also included in the channel to monitor the interaction between sponsors and
students.
Formal Writing and Speaking. Students may also ask industrial mentors
to review documents written by the student team that are related to project
development; this review helps to facilitate clariﬁcation of project details. Spon-
soring mentors are also invited to monthly presentations made by the student
teams; knowing that sponsors may be in attendance usually inspires students

928
M. R. Scaturro Heil and I. X. Dom´ınguez
to be better prepared for these presentations. A ﬁnal 1-h presentation, demo
and question/answer session by each student team is held either at the sponsor
site or on the NCSU campus during exam week at the end of the semester. The
Center staﬀelectronically sends ﬁnal code and documentation to sponsors after
the ﬁnal week of the semester.
6.2
End-of-Semester Exposition
Students participate in Posters & Pies, an end-of-semester exposition that
includes short presentations from each team followed by tradeshow-style posters
and demos. Industrial sponsors look forward to this event and will often invite
colleagues from their company so that others are aware of the program; sponsors
appreciate the opportunity to talk with students at Posters & Pies and these
discussions often lead to recruiting students for software developer positions.
7
Conclusion - A Win-Win for Industrial Partners
and Students
Industrial mentors are crucial to a successful senior design project experience
Mentors collaborate with Center staﬀto create meaningful and feasible software
development problems for student teams to solve. Throughout the semester,
these mentors (along with Center instructors) work with student teams on a
weekly basis to monitor progress, troubleshoot issues with software requirements
or design, and help with project domain or technology issues. Sponsors also
review documentation and presentations created by students. At the completion
of the semester, the Center staﬀwill confer with industrial sponsors to reﬂect on
the semester’s experience. Anecdotally, we understand that many of our sponsors
make use of the proof-of-concepts and prototypes created by our students; we
are currently exploring ways to formally collect data related to this usage.
Industrial sponsors continue to participate in our Senior Design project
course - it is a major recruitment eﬀort for them and an opportunity for outreach.
They appreciate partnering with the University to form a well-versed community
of novice computer scientists. Our industrial partners value the multidisciplinary
teaching perspective and have reported that such exposure improves the com-
munication skills of our students (and hence their recruits). Students learn to
integrate their technical expertise with their teaming, project management, and
communication skills. Toward the end of the most recent semester, students were
asked to rate the overall excellence of the course - they responded with an aver-
age of 4.5/5 (with 5 being the highest rating). Over the last 28 years, students
have commented consistently that this senior design model provides a robust
experience that better prepares them for the professional world.

Integrating Higher Education, Science
and Industry: Towards a Partnership
for Training Competitive Financial Managers
Petr Osipov
, Elena Girfanova
, Julia Ziyatdinova(B)
,
and Natalia V. Kraysman
Kazan National Research Technological University, Karl Marx Str. 68, 420015 Kazan,
Russian Federation
uliziat@yandex.ru
Abstract. Long-term growth of industrial companies largely depends on their
integration with higher education and science to satisfy the advanced demands of
the global economy. Therefore, collaboration between higher education and indus-
try is at the forefront of academic programs, including those focusing on ﬁnancial
managers. The ‘higher education – science – industry’ triangle, however, often
lacks joint efforts to develop degree programs aimed at solving real life problems.
The paper aims at analyzing the integrative model of collaboration in this triangle
and eliminating the existing gaps by developing guidelines for an effective train-
ing of professional ﬁnancial managers under the university degree programs. The
paper gives recommendations on efﬁcient collaboration for training professional
ﬁnancial managers through university degree programs based on literature review,
observation, case studies and a survey of over 400 ﬁnancial managers working in
administrative positions in real industry. All these efforts aim at preparing compet-
itive professionals for the global labor market. The paper lists a set of guidelines
for a practical implementation of these recommendations based on experience of
Kazan National Research Technological University, Russia. Further research and
practice of collaboration will show its beneﬁts and drawbacks.
Keywords: Training ﬁnancial managers · Hard and soft skills · Teaching and
learning methods · Student research · Industrial practice
1
Introduction
Long-term growth of industrial companies largely depends on their integration with
higher education and science to anticipate and satisfy the advanced demands of the global
economy. Therefore, increasing collaboration between higher education and industry
is at the forefront of many academic programs, including those focusing on ﬁnancial
managers. The ‘higher education – science – industry’ triangle, however, often lacks
joint efforts to develop degree programs aimed at solving real life problems.
Real life problems are becoming globalized, therefore, approaches to solving them
are also becoming generalized for university education in different parts of the world.
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 930–937, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_95

Integrating Higher Education, Science and Industry
931
Higher education aims at sustainable development of the society as a whole thus focus-
ing on these issues under different courses [1, 2]. Universities in different countries
are developing similar approaches for integrating the educational systems [3, 4], and
various courses to make the university education interdisciplinary with elements of
entrepreneurship [5, 6] and practice-oriented with experimental research techniques [7],
online courses [8], VR [9, 10], and special software [11]. Business games are introduced
into other areas of education, including engineering education [12], and project-based
learning is becoming a key approach to teaching students [13, 14]. At the same time,
ﬁnancial education is focusing on social issues [15].
Moreover, there are new issues for ﬁnancial managers at the workplace, where they
are expected to demonstrate their soft skills [16] and get adjusted to the changing envi-
ronment [17]. Therefore, it is important to distinguish factors and barriers in training
ﬁnancial managers [18] and to introduce educational innovations to satisfy the main
demands from industry [19].
In the research literature, special attention is paid to the interaction of the labor
market and universities in terms of the competitiveness of graduates, demand for them
in the labor market, and the level of education received. Modern society is interested
not only in the training of young highly qualiﬁed personnel, but also in the continuous
improvement of the qualiﬁcations of those who already have certain knowledge and
skills in this area.
Practice shows that university professors who actively conduct scientiﬁc research
show deep knowledge of the courses that they teach. Professors of this level are in
demand in the modern education system. The interaction between the professor and
students is based on a high degree of trust, high scientiﬁc expertise of the professor
creates the basis for the future expertise of ﬁnancial managers. Only in this case, a special
atmosphere of scientiﬁc creativity and research approach is created. These professors
can deal with students from different cultural backgrounds [20] showing a high level of
intercultural competence [21] and a foreign language proﬁciency [22]. Thus they can
contribute to personal development of students and their possible academic and non-
academic mobility [23]. As a rule, such professors enjoy popularity and respect among
students.
The paper aims at analyzing the integrative model of collaboration in the ‘higher
education – science – industry’ triangle and eliminating the existing gaps by devel-
oping guidelines for an effective training of professional ﬁnancial managers under the
university degree programs. Thus, the objectives of the study are: 1) to deﬁne the role
of prospective employers in formulating the hard skills and soft skills ratio in the cur-
riculum; 2) to demonstrate the importance of research in solving real life problems of
ﬁnancial management in industry; 3) to rationalize the interactive collaborative teaching
and learning methods in training professional ﬁnancial managers; 4) to develop guide-
lines for applying the existing integrative ‘higher education – science – industry’ model
for training professional ﬁnancial managers.
2
Materials and Methods
The authors use qualitative and quantitative approaches to research focusing on the labor
market demands for ﬁnancial managers, comparing them to the university practices,

932
P. Osipov et al.
ﬁnding the gaps and developing guidelines for ﬁlling these gaps. Thus, we explore the
nature of hard and soft skills, their ratio in degree programs for ﬁnancial managers based
on interviewing prospective employers.
The research is multidisciplinary as it implies design of different courses focusing
on hard or on soft skills in the curriculum. Through observation of real life problems
in work of ﬁnancial managers and through discussing case studies, we demonstrate the
signiﬁcance of science and research in developing effective solutions for the practi-
cal problems. Using student-centered approach, we rationalize interactive collaborative
teaching and learning methods giving students the feeling of real-life experience of
working in an enterprise. We use statistical analysis methods to interpret the data from
the survey of over 400 people from industry who once received degrees in Financial
Management, and are now in high or senior administrative positions. The survey aimed
at evaluating the quality of degree programs and ﬁnding the gaps between the graduation
requirements and industry demands.
In order to determine the most effective forms of collaboration between universities
and employers, we planned and conducted a survey. Its purpose was to ﬁnd the level
of compliance of the competencies of future ﬁnancial managers with their future pro-
fessional activities. Designed in accordance with the purpose of the study, the survey
questions were tested for validity and reliability and proved to be effective. The sur-
vey was conducted among employers who are able to assess the quality of professional
training of graduates from the “Financial Management” degree program.
In total, about 400 people took part in the study. These are graduates of Moscow
University of Economics, Tashkent State University of Economics, Ulyanovsk State
Technical University, Kazan (Volga Region) Federal University, etc.
Most of the employers participating in the survey hold a managerial position (head of
the highest category −51.72%, middle staff −48.28%). More than half of the managers
have about 20 years of experience in a managerial position. The age of the respondents
ranged from 24 to 56. By gender and age, women ﬁnancial managers make up 51.72;
men make up 48.28.
The survey revealed the following results: employers highlight that the problem of the
quality of ﬁnancial management graduates is due to insufﬁcient or complete absence of
interaction between universities and ﬁnancial enterprises. In this regard, it is obvious that
employers need to take part in the educational process and make their own adjustments
to the formulation and implementation of professional competencies that meet both
individual employers and the labor market as a whole.
When hiring ﬁnancial managers, much attention is paid to a document about higher
education (68.97%), personal characteristics (51.72%), recommendations from a previ-
ous job (48.28%), documents on additional education in accordance with ofﬁcial duties
(48.28%). At the same time, only half of the surveyed employers (51.72%) were inter-
ested in the need for specialized education in the ﬁeld of ﬁnancial management 89.66%
of respondents gave a positive answer to the following questions “Are ﬁnancial managers
in your organization being interviewed or tested for compliance with their future posi-
tion?”and“Doesyourorganizationhavejobdescriptionsinaccordancewithprofessional
standards?”.

Integrating Higher Education, Science and Industry
933
To improve the quality of training of ﬁnancial managers in universities, it is nec-
essary to provide more time for practice-oriented classes and possibility of internships
at enterprises and organizations in the ﬁnancial sector. The industrial partners, in their
turn, should implement the research work of students, focused on solving real life prob-
lems. Universities and employers should sign agreements for the internship of students,
which provide for the obligations of each of the parties. Unfortunately, according to the
results of the study, only 48.28% of employers are interested in providing internship for
students.
The motivation for cooperation with a university in training ﬁnancial managers was
mainly the awareness of the need to train specialists for a particular organization or indus-
try (68.97% of respondents), as well as increasing the reputation and competitiveness of
an organization in the industry through connection with a university (48.28%).
One of the survey questions was: “Which of the following competencies should be
mandatory included in the curriculum for training ﬁnancial managers?”. Employers gave
preference to the three most signiﬁcant competencies:
– theabilitytoanalyze,evaluateanddesignriskmanagementsystemfortheorganization
(86.21% of respondents);
– legal knowledge in the ﬁeld of ﬁnancial management (62.07% of respondents);
– digital competence, work in the Internet (41.38% of respondents).
Based on survey results, we developed guidelines for effective collaboration of all
stakeholders in the ‘higher education – science – industry’ triangle.
3
Results
Literature review and interviews with prospective employers showed that people from
industryareopenforadialogandreadytoinvesttheirtimeandeffortindevelopingdegree
programs together with universities to focus on real-life hard and soft skills. Moreover,
research ﬁndings can be directly applied for solving real life problems that ﬁnancial
managers face. The most appropriate interactive methods to be used are student-led
discussions, gamiﬁcation, simulated events, and real-life practices including internships.
These methods contribute to developing both job-speciﬁc and soft skills of the future
ﬁnancial managers.
The survey of ﬁnancial managers in administrative positions in industry gave a
number of guidelines for developing effective collaboration in the ‘higher education –
science – industry’ triangle. These guidelines include:
– employers need to take part in the educational process and make their own adjustments
to the formulation and implementation of professional competencies that meet both
individual employers and the labor market as a whole;
– in universities, most of the time should be devoted to conducting practice-oriented
classes and organizing certain types of practices provided for by the curriculum, with
the possibility of internships at enterprises and organizations in the ﬁnancial sector;

934
P. Osipov et al.
– universities and employers should sign agreements for students to have internships
and involve people from industry in conducting practice-oriented classes, in the form
of business games;
– it is necessary to develop social partnerships between industrial enterprises and
universities based on agreements;
– universities should monitor the satisfaction of employers with the quality of training
of university graduates, in order to improve the quality of training ﬁnancial managers.
– It is necessary to develop a system of practical training of ﬁnancial managers, to
intensify and introduce new forms of cooperation with employers into the learning
process at all levels so as:
– to develop an integrative ‘higher education – science – industry’ triangle model for
training of professionals in the ﬁeld of ﬁnancial management;
– to include research and real life problems into the practical part of ﬁnancial
management degree program;
– to integrate professional and soft skills competencies that will contribute to the high
competitiveness of specialists in the labor market;
– to introduce innovative forms of education into the process of training professionals
including master classes and interactive forms of education.
Thus, the main forms of university teaching should include industrial practice of
students in the workplace, invited lectures and master classes from the industry people,
gamiﬁcation of teaching and learning with participation of practicing ﬁnancial managers,
and applied research.
4
Discussion and Conclusions
The integrative ‘higher education – science – industry’ triangle model in the training of
ﬁnancial managers is based on the class system of the most important competencies of
specialists:
1) competence in deﬁning their goals and forming mental models;
2) professional and special competencies;
3) the ability to independently apply knowledge in practice;
4) managerial competencies;
5) competence in information management;
6) leadership qualities and ability to innovate.
While the system of education in our country in the ﬁeld of ﬁnancial management
includes general professional and specialized competencies, the developed integrative
‘higher education – science – industry’ triangle model allows the above-mentioned
competencies to be formed in the conditions of a manufacturing enterprise as part of
research.
Such a competency-based training model for ﬁnancial managers allows the graduate
to work effectively in ﬁnancial management organizations. In the creation of an integra-
tive ‘higher education – science – industry’ triangle model, all stakeholders including

Integrating Higher Education, Science and Industry
935
colleges and universities, and employers as links of one chain are involved. Employers,
as representatives of the labor market and the professional sphere, are included in the
process of forming a set of competencies necessary for professional activity.
They determine the quantitative and qualitative requirements for the training of
professionals. The main criterion for the functioning of the integrative model is the
correspondence of the professional competence of graduates to the real conditions of
the economic environment.
Thus, the paper gives recommendations on efﬁcient collaboration in the ‘higher
education – science – industry’ triangle for training professional ﬁnancial managers
through university degree programs based on literature review, observation, case studies
and a survey of over 400 ﬁnancial managers working in administrative positions in real
industry. All these efforts aim at preparing competitive professionals for the global labor
market.
The paper lists a set of guidelines for a practical implementation of these recom-
mendations based on experience of __ University. Further research and practice of
collaboration will show its beneﬁts and drawbacks.

Work-in-Progress: Framework
for Academia-Industry Partnership in Ukraine
Galyna Tabunshchyk1
, Anzhelika Parkhomenko1(B)
, Sergey Subbotin1

Ukraine
parhom@zntu.edu.ua

Kyiv 02152, Ukraine
3 Infocom LTD, T. Shevchenko Blvd., 56, Zaporizhzhia 69001, Ukraine
Abstract. The paper presents problems and solutions for organizing effective
Academia-Industry partnerships within a new kind of communities of practice
that develop training modules for universities and businesses based on a modern
organizational template and innovative forms of ensuring the competencies of
participants in the educational process. Today, there is a traditional for Ukrainian
universities the process of forming an individual trajectory of student learning
based on a combination of compulsory and alternative (at the student’s choice)
academic disciplines. In this case, the structure of the material of a discipline is
ﬁxed at a certain point in time. The approach proposed in this work provides more
ﬂexible organization of each discipline based on a core and a set of alternative
modules. This will make it possible to take into account the requirements of the
market more fully and form the students‘ competencies necessary for stakeholders.
Keywords: Academia-industry partnerships · Open community of practice ·
Modules for business · Organizational model
1
Introduction
The modern world is rapidly changing and moving to the next level of digitalization, as
well as to a new technological and economic reality [1]. Digital transformation is the
deﬁning trend of the future world of Work. This should be reﬂected in higher education,
especially if it focuses on the needs of the labor market [2]. Therefore, European uni-
versities need to adapt their curricula to prepare future professionals for careers in the
digital, globalized and connected world [3].
The search for organizational patterns of the educational space, which are built on
the basis of new didactic concepts and methods for developing educational content and
can be used by various universities, even in different countries, remains an urgent task.
Combining the efforts of universities will create a new digital educational ecosystem,
which is accompanied by a special learning experience - interdisciplinary, intercultural
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 938–945, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_96

and international [4, 5]. A complete digital transformation of content should change the
way universities provide and graduates acquire competencies [6].
The issues of creating safe working space of the future based on the Competence
Model for Work 4.0 and the Digital Transformation Maturity Model are the priority in the
implementation of the international educational project “Interdisciplinary Competences
for Healthy and Safe Work in the 21st Century” (619034-EPP-1-202 -EPPKA2-CBHE
-JP [WORK4CE]). The project consortium unites partner universities from Ukraine,
Germany, Belgium, Spain and Azerbaijan. The grant holder of the project is National
University “Zaporizhzhia Polytechnic” [7].
One of the goals of the WORK4CE project is to improve cooperation with the
regional and local industry by means of Open Communities of Practice (OpenCoP),
which should make this cooperation more effective.
2
Open Communities of Practice Organization and Functioning
The main feature of the project implementation is the organization of OpenCoP, bringing
together European, Ukrainian and Azerbaijani academic and professional experts for the
joint development of open educational resources according to the Competence Model
for Work 4.0. In the project, OpenCoPs are aimed to develop 9 components of Master’s
programs: Data Analytics for Work, Digital Technologies, Industry 4.0, Distributed
Teams, Work 4.0, Safe Workplaces, Managing Digital Change, Life Cycle Thinking and
Sustainable Management, Developing Digital Business Ecosystems (see Fig. 1) [5].
Fig. 1. ELearning modules on Master‘s level
For efﬁcient organization, the partners from European universities have developed
the strategy, goals, structure, concept and ecosystem for support of the OpenCoPs [5].
The example of roles distribution in OpenCoP is shown in Fig. 2 [2].
The innovative component of the project is the usage of Agile approach to organizing
project activities [1]. The created common project environment OpenCoPs provides

940
G. Tabunshchyk et al.
organizational and methodological support to communities of experts and practitioners
for the development of modules for the formation of new competencies for Work in the
21st century. The developed methods and modules are regularly tested in the framework
of summer/winter schools and trainings for trainers.
Fig. 2. Example of roles distribution in OpenCoP
The analysis has shown that the deﬁning feature of the project implementation is
a ﬂexible approach to organizing the structure of the developed educational compo-
nents. Each of them is based on a key component that is mandatory for study, aimed
at acquiring basic knowledge, as well as several additional components that are chosen
by the participant in the educational process independently [5]. For example, for “In-
dustry 4.0” module (8 ECTS (European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System)),
two components are required: “Introduction to Industry 4.0” (2 ECTS) and “Conse-
quences and pathways to Industry 4.0 project management” (2 ECTS). In addition, a set
of additional components is proposed each of them has a volume of 2 ECTS and can be
selected for study: “Digital Twins” [8], “Internet of Things” [9, 10], “Additive manu-
facturing”, “Building Information Modelling”, “Quality of industrial systems/predictive
maintenance/condition monitoring”, “Data analysis for Industry 4.0/Use of Big Data”.
Thus, the proposed approach makes it possible to ensure the formation of the required
set of competencies not only through the traditional for Ukrainian universities arrange-
ment of compulsory and alternative (at the student’s choice) academic disciplines, but
also through the formation of the structure of certain disciplines of the curriculum
depending on the needs of the region, the requirements of employers, etc.
This organizational model for developing the structure of academic disciplines can
be recommended for improving curricula at the Ukrainian universities, especially in the
caseofdistancelearning.Thisisgoingtomakeitpossibletobuildamoreﬂexiblelearning
pathforstudentsbasedonacompetency-basedinnovativeapproachtocurriculumdesign,
as well as to organize student-centered educational environment to ensure the quality of
education and result-oriented learning.

3
Academia-Industry Cooperation Within the OpenCoPs
Framework
The developed framework of Academia-Industry cooperation is based on the analysis
of the needs of stakeholders conducted by all partner universities, and it includes the
following activities: Creation of the new knowledge based on international experience
and national requirements; Open access to the developed modules; Upskilling and re-
skilling of the companies, based on the developed module material; preparation of the
case-studies from the business; Quality analysis of the curricula.
Zaporizhzhia cluster “Engineering-Automation-Machinery” and stakeholders, in
particular Infocom LTD company, are the part of the OpenCoP. They demonstrate sig-
niﬁcant interest in project effective implementation, the desire to join the discussion, the
development of educational modules and further pilot training for business.
The involvement of representatives of Zaporizhzhia cluster “Engineering-
Automation-Machinery” in the framework of the WORK4CE project ensured the expan-
sion of the knowledge and project’s outcomes not only at the regional and national level,
but also abroad. In particular, the WORK4CE project was presented in the process of
discussing the potential of Zaporizhzhia cluster “Engineering-Automation-Machinery”,
negotiating and signing memorandums of cooperation with foreign clusters from the
Czech Republic (Industry cluster 4.0) and Lithuania (Authorization Automation). Today,
the cluster community has expanded signiﬁcantly, and the Ukrainian cluster alliance was
created in the spring, 2022. The preliminary agreement of cooperation on the WORK4CE
project receives new prospects for additional expertise and as signiﬁcant audience of
consumers.
In Ukraine project facilitate cooperation between Ukrainian business, education and
government in a dialogue on the adaptation of Ukrainian youth to challenges of Industry
4.0 in order to agree on key joint actions for the nearest future.

(Fig. 3) the modules for business were developed. Table 1 shows the correspondence of
project modules and proposed modules for business.

to get acquainted with the basics of cluster analysis as a section of data analysis and
machine learning, to understand how to use cluster analysis methods in applied prob-

Digital Twins” introduces the basics of digital transformations in Industry 4.0, allows
to understand how to overcome the challenges of digital transformation projects and the
consequences of the process of implementing Industry 4.0 in the organization.
It shows that change management and impact on project management are key pro-
cesses, and also provides basic knowledge on the creation and implementation of Digital
Twins to understand the technological challenges of the digital transformation of Indus-
try 4.0. Module “Internet of Things for Industry 4.0” provides the understanding why
the Internet of Things (IoT) technology is the driving force behind Industry 4.0 and

5
Peculiarities of Module Data Analytics for Work Implementation
Data Analytics technologies are one of the key tools for ensuring the competitiveness of
a modern enterprise. Both at the level of the economy and at the level of production, large
amounts of data are generated and stored. The analysis of available data allows to extract
patterns and models from the data that form deeper representations and knowledge about
the ongoing process. This allows to use such knowledge for more efﬁcient management
of the enterprise and production processes, also to improve the quality of products.
Revealing dependencies allows enterprises to gain value from their data as modern data
analytics methods can uncover hidden data models through predictive, self-learning, and
adaptive capabilities.
As a part of ERASMUS + WOR4CE project in the module M01 “Data Analytics
for Work” students will be familiarized with methods of data analytics, will receive both
theoretical and practical knowledge to use the methods and to develop software for data
analytics for various problem speciﬁc domain. The module intends to give students a set
of theoretical methods and practical tools making possible to automate data analytics in
various domain speciﬁc problems.
The module deals with such target groups as students of MSc programs in Com-
puter Science, practical specialists in programming (needs: data analytics to develop
decision making and analytic software), practical specialists and students in various
applied domains (needs: to identify and predict states of multidimensional objects and
processes). The module provides: knowledge (highly specialized knowledge in methods

944
G. Tabunshchyk et al.
and tools of data analytics, which is at the forefront of knowledge in a ﬁeld of work and
study, as the basis for original thinking and/or research, the critical awareness of knowl-
edge issues in the ﬁeld and at the interface between different ﬁelds), skills (specialized
problem-solving skills on data analytics application required in research and/or inno-
vation in order to develop new knowledge and procedures and to integrate knowledge
from different ﬁelds), also as responsibility and autonomy (manage and transform work
or study contexts that are complex, unpredictable and require new strategic approaches;
take responsibility for contributing to professional knowledge and practice). Students
will consider different practical cases for which they will use data analysis tools and
methods. Students will encourage that for the solution of real problems for companies
or other stakeholders.
The module contains palette of elements, which the course instructor can use to
form a problem or user speciﬁc course. The elective block “Exploratory Data Analy-
sis and Data Visualization” contains such topics as: Introduction to R Programming,
Exploratory Data Analysis with Dplyr package and Applied Plotting [11, 12]. The core
block “Unsupervised learning. Cluster Analysis” contains such topics as: Basics of unsu-
pervised machine learning, Methods of centroid-based cluster analysis, and Methods of
connectivity-based cluster analysis [13, 14]. The core block “Supervised machine learn-
ing. Support Vector Machines and Decision Trees for Data Analysis” contains such
topics as: Basics of Supervised machine learning, Support Vector Machines, and Deci-
sion Trees [15–18]. The elective block “Prediction and Decision Making, and Results
Visualization” familiarizes students with Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visual-
ization using R programming. It provides concepts and skills that can help students
tackle real-world data analysis challenges. It also helps students develop skills such as R
programming, data wrangling and visualization, and reproducible document preparation
[11, 12].
6
Conclusion
The results of the pilot training of students at the National University “Zaporizhzhia
Polytechnic” in the Spring semester of the 2021/2022 academic year, as well as the
discussion of the conceptual framework with representatives of Ukrainian companies
and industrial enterprises, conﬁrmed its appropriateness and feasibility, as well as the
effectiveness and usefulness of performed research and development.
So, new training modules designed to provide modern Industry 4.0 skills and com-
petencies will be useful not only for universities, but also for businesses. Accordingly,
the WORK4CE project encourages the community of practitioners and educators to the
broad dialogue, exchange of experiences, as its results can be of great interest for many
companies and manufacturing enterprises, other Ukrainian and European universities.

Work in Progress: Importance of Industry

Abstract. The paper provides insight of holistic education system which is origi-
nated in India which used to impart embedded lifelong learning skills with hands-
on sessions in that context of era. It describes the indicative foresights of world
economic forum from education perspective. The section two of paper details
overview of constituents of interaction avenues of institutes with industries. This
third section of papers describes the importance of involvement of industries in
terms of parameters of assessment criteria of National Board of Accreditation
(ABET –Washington Accord). In the fourth section, author has put forward the
impact of weightage on industry involvement in NBA process and has put for-
ward its suggestive rearrangement with urge to establish separate criteria as far
as assessing the industry involvement in engineering education is concerned. The
author has put forward conclusions in last section which states anticipated impact
of modiﬁcations suggested in fourth section of the paper.
Keywords: NBA · National Board of Accreditation · ABET · Accreditation
Board for Engineering and Technology · NAAC · National Assessment and
Accreditation Council · NEP · National education policy
1
Introduction
Indian education system has rich history. The concept of imparting holistic education
has been originated in India and eventually was the backbone of ancient Indian educa-
tion system which was very much focused not for only fostering knowledge and making
individual job ready but also making product of education system with social respon-
siveness showcasing ethical and professional character. The ancient Gurukul education
system used to prepare the individual for not only as job seeker but also being good
human being to be able to contribute towards society and in turn towards country in
nation building process.
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 946–954, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_97

Work in Progress
947
The Gurukul education system evolved in ancient India was very much perfect in
to today’s context of education system which is expected to cater diversiﬁed need of
industries i.e. employers. During last decades and in forthcoming decades to come, the
modern technical and professional education to be governed through national education
policy (NEP-2020) is marching towards imparting skills and hands-on based education.
As per the report of world economic forum, imparting skill based and hands-on based
education is need of the hour. The world economic forum report has categorically listed
of the challenges before technical and professional education which can be categorized
but not limited to as.
1.1
Increasing Need for Life-Long Learning in a Non-linear World
Lifelong learning is not a new concept. In the recent past and days to come, due to
nonlinear nature of world the concept of lifelong learning has become very challenging.
Building and implementation of education models are required to be created to coun-
terattack the requirements of nonlinear nature of world. The nonlinear nature of world
demands extensive interaction of academia with industries.
1.2
Evolving Needs and Expectations of the “Student-Consumer”
The education sector is by and large getting driven by changing demand of its stakeholder
consumer i. e. students and society. Expectations of stakeholders is becoming seamlessly
multidimensional that ﬁt different lifestyle circumstances and preferences of individual.
This is leading to learner driven and learner centric.
1.3
Emerging Technologies and Business Models
The pace of change in the education sector is slower than that of in industries. The
education landscape is bound to change signiﬁcantly in the next decades. Now univer-
sities are experimenting with changes to their traditional business models to counterat-
tack disruptive new entrants in the education sector competing and collaborating with
the traditional actors. With concepts like semester internships, pre-board training and
internships, live industry projects, earn and learn systems the collaboration between
professional/technical education sector and industries in various process of imparting
education is very vital.

948
M. M. Khanapurkar
2
Towards a “Skills over Degrees” Model
There can be different opinions about whether the traditional higher education is still
the best way to provide the skills needed within individual to compete in unpredictable
competitive job markets. The degrees which ruled job market over last century are
now becoming obsolete and getting replaced by acquisition of skills. Stakeholders have
started posing question over value of degree in job market over skills. Focus of measuring
employability is shifting from degrees to new ways of skill acquisition as a consequence
of the changing nature of work.
By above challenges it is predicted that in coming three to four years of time emerg-
ing job market areas will be Data Analytics and Scientists, Artiﬁcial Intelligence and
Machine learning Specialists, Software and Application Developers, Sales and Market-
ing Professionals, Big Data and Digital Transformations specialists and Professionals,
IT Services etc. on the other side, the current job market areas are predicted to be on
declining trend for example Assembly and Factory Workers, Data Entry Operators and
Specialists, Accountants and Auditors, Material Recording etc.
This complete scenario is on the horizon and is indicating lot many messages to tra-
ditional and professional education systems. Looking it to all above, quality education
ensuring accrediting agencies have started taking measures for counterattacking these
challenges. Regulatory authorities and accrediting agencies have initiated many mea-
sures towards the foresighted scenario of technical and professorial education system.
One of measure is enhancement of industry institution interaction and collaboration at
all levels of education system.
3
Involvement of Industry in Professional Education
The sole objective of involving the industry expertise and infrastructure in the profes-
sional education is to make the product (student) more job ready. The other objective
amongst many is to have better understanding amongst education administrators, faculty
and students about the latest technological advancement in industries along with industry
culture and processes. This leads to impact the challenges foresighted by world economic
forum as listed above. The involvement of industries was very much limited to few activ-
ities like organizing industrial tours/visits, guest lectures of industry experts, industry
based projects, consultancy projects etc. which experienced progressive involvement
and its respective growth. Amongst these activities few have played vital role in shift of
focus from traditional classroom teaching to industry based teaching learning process.
Over the period the involvement of industry in professional education got widened and
can be broadly mentioned at various levels. Few of the levels are mentioned in Table 1.
