4
Importance of Industry Involvement in Assessment Criteria
of National Board of Accreditation
As put forward in section two and section three above it is clear that involvement of
industry/experts in education system at different levels is gaining momentum and edu-
cation system is ﬁnding new avenues for interaction with industries for making their
products more employable and adapting lifelong learning experience to student stake-
holders. The National Board of Accreditation agency in its evaluation mechanism under
tier-I and tier-II has given special importance and weightage to initiatives taken by
program/Department/institute undergoing accreditation on industry involvement and its
outcomes.
National Board of Accreditation under tier-I and tier-II has total one thousand marks
spread over ten criteria. Various parameters leading to ensure quality of education and
continuous improvement of program undergoing accreditation are given due weightage
in the evaluation process. As described above industry involvement has also been given

952
M. M. Khanapurkar
due weightage. Out of one thousand evaluation marks, weightage of sub-criteria dealing
with ensuring industry involvement, its impact and outcomes is to the tune of forty marks
on higher side. In addition to this few sub-criteria also reﬂects the weightage to industry
involvement and its outcomes in indirect way in teaching learning process imparting
by program undergoing accreditation to the tune of thirty marks. This total of around
seventy marks (on higher side) weightage out of one thousand marks is not more than
ten percent (on the higher side).
Industry involvement at various levels and in various forms in education system is
highlighted in section three i.e. Table 1. By going through it is very clear that weightage
of below ten percent for involvement of industry in education system and its impact and
outcome to ensure quality education and continuous improvement is very insufﬁcient.
Programs undergoing accreditation are ﬁnding easy escape for this weightage because
even though program doesn’t have sufﬁcient industry involvement for ensuring quality
education, gets few of marks for doing some or the other activities involving indus-
tries. Due to insufﬁcient weightage, program has way to qualify even though not having
sufﬁcient industry interaction and involvement. With this ﬁnding, author is proposing
following suggestions for enhancement of weightage of industry interaction and involve-
ment in the program towards accomplishment of outcome based education to make the
product students more employable and raise satisfaction levels of its stakeholders.
5
Suggestions for Enhancement of Weightage of Industry
Interaction and Involvement
With reference to details provided in section two and section three of the paper, author
is putting forward following suggestions for enhancing the weightage for industry inter-
action involvement in teaching learning and evaluation process imparting by program
undergoing accreditation to ensure quality education and also leading for continuous
improvement.
5.1
Merging of Common Oriented Sub-criteria of Criteria 2 and Criteria 3
Criteria II has one hundred marks and criteria III has one hundred and seventy ﬁve marks.
Total weightage is to the tune of two hundred and seventy ﬁve marks. Sub criteria of
criteria II dealing with program curriculum and teaching learning process can be clubbed
with criteria III to form new criteria as criteria II having total marks to the tune of one
hundred and ﬁfty. The thus formed criteria II will have program curriculum, teaching
learning process and computation of course outcomes and program outcomes/program
speciﬁc outcomes along with gap analysis for further actions to be initiated.
5.2
Formation of Separate Criteria for Industry Interaction and Involvement
Separate criteria as criteria III having full ﬂedge scope of accessing industry interaction
and involvement should be created carrying around approximately one hundred and
ﬁfty marks. The sub criteria of other criteria which has indirect reﬂection weightage of
industry interaction can be shifted to newly proposed separate criteria III as above or
can be kept as it is. This will have weightage to industry interaction and involvement to
the tune of one hundred and ﬁfty marks (amounting to tune of ﬁfteen percent).

Work in Progress
953
5.3
Mandatory Qualiﬁcation of Criteria Dealing with Industry Involvement
As minimum scoring is required for few of criteria to get qualiﬁed for award of three/ﬁve
year accreditation. The above suggested new criteria dealing with industry interaction
and involvement should also be treated as mandatory qualifying marks for awarding
of accreditation. The threshold values of scores can be decided for three/ﬁve years
award of accreditation. This will thus avoid the possible chances of escapes for the
institutes/programs undergoing accreditation process.
5.4
Weightage to Incubation/Entrepreneurship Development Initiatives
Government has initiated many schemes and is providing funding to the incuba-
tion/entrepreneurship development related activities in institutes. In thus formed new
criteria for evaluation of industry involvement in academic processes, facilities and ini-
tiatives taken by institute to encourage and undertake incubation/entrepreneurship devel-
opment related activities should also be given sufﬁcient weightage. The enhancement of
weightage to these parameters will be in tune with support to the policies of government
of India for promoting and encouraging incubation/entrepreneurship development and
will lead to some contribution towards making the country a self-reliant i.e. nationwide
call given by honorable prime minister of country as Atmanirbhar or Make in India.
6
Conclusions
Putting forward the details of existing system of evaluation and assessment of profes-
sional institutions by NBA, ﬁndings thereof and suggestions in the subsequent sections,
The author has chalked down few of the conclusions as below.
• With above modiﬁcations, the industry interaction and involvement will become
mandatory part of evaluation and assessment process of National Board of Accredi-
tation with moderate weightage and institutes will be accountable and responsible for
having involvement of industry in academic process as serious affair.
• With implementation of National Education Policy - 2020, the academic systems
and processes are expected to become more open ended. Thus more involvement
of industry in academic processes with more types of avenues of involvement of
industries/industry experts in the academic processes are expected in days to come.
The forthcoming expected changes as far as industry involvement in academics is
concerned needs to be reﬂected in the evaluation criteria’s of accreditation agencies
to have its true impact.
• If separate criteria for industry involvement is kept with minimum scoring for award
of grant of accreditation (with minimum number of ‘Y/‘C”) then it will have its impact
leading to outcome based education & its beneﬁts to stakeholders.
• With NEP-20 in force and under implementation, enhancement in networking and
associative activities amongst professional societies, Consortiums like CII is going
to play vital role in professional education and thus should be part of evaluation and
assessment with sufﬁcient weightage.

Trends in Master and Doctoral Research

New Challenges for Remote Experiment Design
in the Digitalization Era (Industry 4.0)
Cornel Samoil˘a1,2(B), Doru Ursut,iu1,3, Horia Alexandru Modran1,
and Tinashe Chamunorwa1
1 Transylvania University of Brasov, Brasov, Romania
{csam,udoru,chamunorwa.tinashe}@unitbv.ro
2 Technical Science Academy of Romania, Bucharest, Romania
3 Academy of Scientists of Romania, Bucharest, Romania
Abstract. CONTEXT. A very careful analysis shows that many of the current
digital technologies and current trends in digitalization are not found in remote
experiments already created. So, it is necessary to rethink their design principles.
PURPOSE OR GOAL. Digitization is related to computer science and its
tools. Digitalization is related to the improvement of processes through digital
technologies. Digitization transfers information from the analog to the digital
environment, which allows faster access to information and reduced access and
archiving costs. Digitalization allows the improvement of the monitoring and
control of industrial, economic, and/or social processes, another decision-making
system, and a better consideration of the clients regarding the accessibility of the
ﬁnal products of the processes.
APPROACH. Remote experiment (RE) is a technology that has gone through
almost necessary stages through digitization and digitalization and can be one of
the important poles of digital transformation in education. A global understand-
ing of this process implies that emerging technologies in the ﬁeld of IT allow the
construction of another system of knowledge transfer and evaluation. It is obvi-
ous, from this stage of setting the transformation goals, that the road to digital
transformation is not linear (as it was and still is the road to digitization). The
non-linear character is given by the need to change the organizational culture in
education and, as always when the change of people is included in a process, a
non-linear component is added immediately. The process of digital transforma-
tion must include the relationship of education with industry. It does not have a
separate phase, one in education and one in industry. These phases must be inter-
twined so that graduates can be prepared for their future careers and the industry
can use them from the faculty benches. As a result of this principle, the remote
experiment must have the same characteristics regardless of the ﬁeld to which it
applies, education or industry.
ACTUAL OR ANTICIPATED OUTCOMES. Because the remote experiment
is geared toward the application side of learning, it requires a pragmatic approach
to the phases it must go through to align with the demands of digitalization and
digital transformation. These phases are Monitoring which involves learning at a
medium level the measurement, transfer processing, and storage of data, Warning,
Remote Control, Optimization, Prediction, and Intelligent Response.
CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS/SUMMARY. Many researchers
say that the hard part of the digital transformation in Industry 4.0 is not the digi-
tal part but the conceptual and adaptive transformation of people. The effects on

Apparently, all remote experiments are subject to digitalization because they cannot be
created outside of information technology. This was apparently because a very careful
analysis shows that many of today’s digital technologies as well as current trends in
digitalization are not found in remote experiments already created. So a rethinking of
their design principles is needed [1]. Emerging as an inexpensive solution for imple-
menting e-learning labs, remote experiment technology has recently become a pole of
development. The transition from a learning exercise status to a development pole status
was the result of a revolution called Industry 4.0 (Cyber-Physical Systems). How to get
to this stage, what are the steps you went through, are illustrated in Fig. 1.

2
Digitization and Digitalization
It is important to reserve a small passage from this material to clarify the mistake that
is made quite often, through confusion, related to the two notions. For the proposed
discussion we start from unanimously recognized deﬁnitions. “Digitization is the process
of changing from analog to digital form, also known as digital enablement. Said another
way, digitization takes an analog process and changes it to a digital form, without
any difference in kind changes to the process itself ”- said Gartner. Also, Gartner said:
“Digitalization is the use of digital technologies to change a business model and provide
new revenue and value-producing opportunities. It is the process of moving to a digital
business” [2].
From these two deﬁnitions, it can be concluded that:
• Digitization is related to computer science and its tools.
• Digitalization is related to the improvement of processes through digital technologies.
Digitization transfers information from the analog to the digital environment, which
allows faster access to information and reduces access and archiving costs. Digitaliza-
tion allows the improvement of the monitoring and control of the industrial, economic,
and/or social processes, another decision-making system, and a better understanding of
the clients regarding access to their ﬁnal products. The best example of digital tech-
nology that serves to change the way we approach processes is cloud computing. It
has introduced data storage without the need to purchase servers and offers very good
data security without investing in specialized software, allowing good networking and
Artiﬁcial Intelligence programs.
The use of cloud computing technology for remote experiments is a recommendation
because it introduces in the learning process an element that students will use more and
more in practice and which adds to the transmitted knowledge:
– Trust: - all data transferred to the cloud are always available, and secure.
– Flexibility:-becauseonecanthinkfromsimplelevelstocomplexlevelswithouthaving
as a brake (limitation) the computing power, because it allows access regardless of
geographical area and also allows the addition of servers and storage networks actions
that, in outside of cloud computing technology, they were limited by the hardware
available.
– News: - the latest version is always offered for databases, platforms, and software
applications as well as the advantage of using emerging technologies such as ML
(Machine learning), AI (Artiﬁcial Intelligence) and IoT (Internet of Things).
Both digitization and digitalization were used in the ﬁeld of the remote experiment.
Digitization was used when laboratory experiments, written in analog format, were trans-
ferred into digital form without intervening with the content. The stage was dominated

960
C. Samoil˘a et al.
by simulations and the desire to provide students with online access to laboratory work
so that e-learning is possible for disciplines that require not only theoretical training but
also experimental training.
As industry demands exceeded the demands of simulation-based lab work, remote
experiments based on virtual instrumentation were introduced, in which the computer
became a measuring instrument thanks to expert software (such as LabVIEW and a
DAQ data acquisition system) that allowed the leap from simulation to monitoring and
control.
The next stage of development was the one in which, due to the development of
sensors and wireless technologies, real experiments can be monitored and controlled
remotely, approaching, in a proportion of 90%, the requirements of the industry. This
stage led to the completion of IoT technology and its application in social life (smart
cars, smart homes, etc.). It is expected that remote experiments will penetrate even more
in the practical training of students because cloud computing technology has diversiﬁed
being not only the platform for storing and accessing data but also:
• SaaS -Software as a Service. Remote experiment users will also have other software
to use for other applications, derived from those learned in the classic framework. The
offer of software is complex and allows, for derived experiments, many applications
with running time available, with access to user networks, data storage and security
assurance.
• PaaS – Platform as a Service. Users of remote experiments have at their disposal a
development platform so that, starting from a remote experiment considered pivot,
they can create branched applications on different domains than the starting domain
(pivot);
• IaaS – Infrastructure as a Service. Remote experiment users can rent computing
resources (operating systems, hard drives, networks, storage systems, etc.) to be able
to cover with resources all the developments they are thinking about, without investing
in additional hardware.

almost necessarily gone through the stages of digitization and digitalization and that it
can be one of the important poles of digital transformation in education (see the decisive
inﬂuence it has had RE in the deﬁnition of IoT). The global understanding of this process

another system of knowledge transfer and evaluation.
It is obvious, from this stage of setting the transformation goals, that the road to digital
transformation is not linear (as it was and still is the road to digitization). The non-linear
character is given by the need to change the organizational culture in education and, as
always when the change of people is included in a process, a non-linear component is
immediately added.

industry. It does not cover distinct phases, one in education and one in industry. These
phases must be intertwined so that the graduates are ready for their future careers, and
the industry can use them from the faculty benches. As a result of this principle, the
remote experiment must have the same characteristics regardless of the ﬁeld to which it
applies, education or industry (Fig. 4) [6].

4
Possible Solutions for Remote Experiments
Because the remote experiment is geared toward the application side of learning, it
requires a pragmatic approach to the phases it must go through to align with the demands
of digitalization and digital transformation. These phases are:
1.- Monitoring: Learning the digital actions needed to monitor experiments involves
learning at an intermediate level of:
• Measurement actions. Any experiment aims to measure some parameters so that
the experimenter can follow in real-time the evolution of the studied process. Dig-
italization means learning virtual instrumentation software (LabVIEW, VEE-Pro,
etc.).
• Data transfer actions. The measured values must be transferred to a database.
The transfer can be analog (with subsequent digitization), digital, with or without
support (wireless). At this stage, databases are the central element of learning.
• Data processing actions. Not all data collected in an experiment are directly usable.
Inordertobringthemtothisstage,preconditioning,ﬁtting,compensation,lineariza-
tion, mediation, etc. operations are necessary. The course of experimental data
processing is necessary to be generalized, regardless of the branch of engineering.
• Data storage actions. An experiment can be completely described by the data it
generates and which must be able to be tracked both online and after registration.
Different storage media should be used such as those of the measurement setup
(low capacity), of local servers (higher capacity), with SCADA systems, and more
recently in the cloud (highest capacity).
2.- Warnings. Any monitoring must have some limits of variation, recommended values,
dangerous areas, or of type minimum threshold, maximum threshold, etc. These limits
can be dedicated to stopping processing, mitigating the process, notifying deviations
from the recommended areas, etc. There are digital systems that fulﬁll these functions,
and that the designer of remote experiments must learn.
3.-Remotecontrol.Theshiftfrommonitoringtocontrolisamajorleapforwardinthedig-
italization of remote experiments. The simplest control is the start/stop. More advanced
control is to change the reference point and reset the experiment. A pretentious solution
is to change the ﬁrmware. The most modern controls are “hardware reconﬁgurable soft-
ware” which is dependent on the special design of the hardware. And also evolved is the
control that allows changing the sub-algorithms that decide the type of control.
4.- Optimization. It is a very advanced stage of remote experiments that requires either
the creation of virtual models or the creation of algorithms that simulate the experiment.

New Challenges for Remote Experiment Design in the Digitalization Era
963
Artiﬁcial intelligence is the most advanced solution to be able to change the process
parameters after an imposed legit.
5.- Forecasting. It is a more advanced stage than optimization. The prediction of the
reliability and, implicitly, therefore, of the failure of the systems, is an important stage
of the remote evolved experiments. To achieve this, it is necessary to process a large
amount of reference data, experiment modeling algorithms, and advanced knowledge
about the mechanisms of failure, all in digital form in order to be included in an artiﬁcial
intelligence software.
6- The smart answer. It is the one that allows the remote experiment to automatically
activate protection measures-based prediction. This reduces maintenance times and thus
reduces the costs caused by accidental interruptions.
Apparently, the six solutions presented are things known before the emergence of
the concepts of digitalization and digital transformation. But their approach is different
from the classic one after the appearance of some “restless children” of these two new
concepts. Reference is made to:
• IoT – Internet of Things – with an exponential technological spread in the last
period, due to the involvement of the producers of goods and services in the process.
This is how all types of connectivity come to be compatible with IoT requirements,
namely Ethernet, Bus, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Li-Fi. This has made the digitalization
of objects strongly supported by connectivity to be available to as many customers
as possible.
• IoP – Internet of People – which connects not only people with each other but
also people with equipment (the best example of fast spread and digital progress is
phones).
• IIoT – Industrial Internet of Things – which illustrates the need to use all the
connections mentioned above, but for industrial use. The tendency to differentiate
from customers is required by the need for standardization in the digitalization of
the industry. It has been found that cloud data storage, equipment connectivity, and
smart device interfaces do not mean digitalization but only the existence of practical
tools. And the Industry 4.0 revolution means standardizing these practical tools
so that implementation operations are compatible with each other and no longer
consume human intelligence on local variants that nullify much of the large-scale
viability of solutions and the possibility of interconnection.
5
Human Resources in Digital Transformation
An analysis of the labor market shows that without immediate measures applied in
education, the inertia of the education system (high) will become a stagnant factor
for the reforms in Industry 4.0. Due to the acute lack of specialists. Areas of reference
would be CS (Cloud Systems), BD (Big Data), AI (Artiﬁcial Intelligence), ML (Machine
Learning),andIoT(InternetofThings).Inadditiontotheimmediatemeasuresmentioned
above, a global system of values in education adapted to the industry 4.0 revolution must
be created, which should change the balances of top education and dozen education, a
system of values that will succeed in establishing the average curve of those two trends
as high as possible.

in the Cyber-Physical System area requires the creation of a new model of them (Richter
and Naidu-2016) [3]. The pivots of this model are shown in Table 1. It has been found that
when the pivots shown in Table 1 are put into practice by classical methods of knowledge

and offers two knowledge transfer technologies, namely: - VR (Virtual Reality) and AR
(Augmented Reality). Adding to them intelligently: virtual classes, dynamic information
(smartphone, books, articles) collaborative spaces, and MOOC / MOOL, an environment
is created that shortens or even cancels delays in obtaining positive effects.

Comments and Conclusions
Many researchers say that the hard part of the digital transformation in Industry 4.0
is not the digital part but the conceptual and adaptive transformation of people. The
effects on mentality and culture are not obtained by buying technologies, and software
or accumulating data. There is a need for retraining based on the new skills created by
digitalization and digital transformation. The increasing application of digitalization in
education also contains important risks that must be known to cancel out their negative
effects. So:
1. “Face to face” education tends to move from the real world to the virtual world.
2. Combining Cyber-Physical Systems with AI (Artiﬁcial Intelligence) and BDA (Big
Data Analytics) will create huge digital campuses that will be increasingly sought
after by students at the expense of geographically limited campuses, which will
nullify many of the gains in mentality and culture have given by socialization.

New Challenges for Remote Experiment Design in the Digitalization Era
965
3. Students will have, gradually positioned, learning resources in a global system that,
without executive leadership, can negatively change the management principles and
hierarchies that the students will later encounter in their economic and social activity.
4. The expansion of intelligent robots, through advanced digitalization and digital
transformation, will create the social problem of jobs. Digitalization must offer
occupational alternatives.
5. The education of young people is endangered by the invasion of the virtual environ-
ment with unrealistic data or manipulative data. That is why digitalization must also
deal with the creation of selection ﬁlters of the true/false type. And people should
authenticate themselves through digital biometric techniques so that we don’t end
up with fake students/pupils or diplomas and fake titles.
In universitati, digital transformation poate aduce beneﬁcii. Astfel:
In universities, digital transformation can bring beneﬁts. So:
• For students
– learning is improved by increasing the area of accessibility.
– beneﬁcial navigation is created between school and life.
– the evaluation is improved.
– collaboration is improved.
• For teachers
– the balance between school and life is improved.
– the school’s orientation toward social needs is improved.
– several learning styles are created to which students adapt according to their own
personalities.
– giving up the penalty of mistakes and moving on to learning through mistakes.
– a complex environment of collaboration between teacher-student, student-student,
student industry, and teachers-industry is created.
• For institutions
– the level of competitiveness between institutions is raised.
– the poles for the recruitment of students and teachers are extended.
– students’ access to school is improved
– the evaluation in which the industry is also involved is improved.
– management is improved.

tools developed in the Creativity Laboratory (CL) of the Center for Valorization
and Transfer of Competencies (CVTC) for the training of Ph.D. students and to
facilitate their “University-Industry” cooperation. Students and teachers develop
software and testing tools using NI LabVIEW (National Instruments – Laboratory
Virtual Instrumentation Engineering Workbench) and speciﬁc educational hard-
ware (myDAQ, NI-ELVIS, USB SMU, etc.) from NI and Keysight Technologies.
Step-by-stepdevelopmentandeasygraphicalProgramminginLabVIEWfacilitate
development and comparatively test Energy Harvesting devices to power IoT sys-
tems in CVTC collaboration with STEINEL company. In this way, Ph.D. students
develop their capacity to use Virtual Instrumentation in their research tasks and
develop intelligent testing systems sound in selecting of necessary components
for in-room power of IoT devices by Energy Harvesting systems.

Introduction to Energy Harvesting for IoT
Energy Harvesting (EH) is the process by which energy is derived from external sources
(in our case the ﬁrst attempt was to use solar panels for indoor use) and usually provides a
small amount of power for low-energy electronics (for example in our case IoT sensors).
Piezoelectric, thermoelectric, electromagnetic, and photovoltaic techniques are some
examples of energy harvesting technologies that can be used to collect energy from the
ambient environment to generate electricity nowadays.
The simplest general structure of one Energy Harvesting system can be like the block
schema presented in Fig. 1.
Looking for the actual research stage in the ﬁeld of EH some of the publications try
to improve EH sources, to increase the efﬁciency of the conversion module, the better
solution to store the energy (rechargeable batteries, supercapacitors, or hybrid systems),
and ﬁnally, optimize the consumption of powered devices.
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 967–978, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_99

968
D. Ursut,iu et al.
Fig. 1. General structure of one energy harvesting system
The same model (Fig. 1) can be applied for both situations – indoor and/or out-
door – applications with speciﬁc changes. For example, speciﬁc photovoltaic sources
for indoor or outdoor use and some supplementary sources (other sources). Solar energy
is one of the most favorable energy sources because it provides a higher power density
than other sources, such as the piezoelectric, thermoelectric, or radiofrequency (elec-
tromagnetic one) [1–3]. Generally speaking, the evolution of solar cell efﬁciency is a
dynamic research ﬁeld and there is need to carefully select the speciﬁc solar cell for
both indoor/outdoor applications. For example, recently a German research team has
developed a tandem solar cell that reaches 24% efﬁciency - measured according to the
fraction of photons converted into electricity. This sets a new world record as the high-
est efﬁciency achieved so far with this combination of organic and perovskite-based
absorbers [4].
In some cases, with “dimensional restriction” one must select the maximum efﬁ-
ciency cells, but it can also be considered if other sources can be added. For educational
reasons, students need to understand the solar cells’ functional model and evaluate many
types/dimensions [5–8].
In [9] a power harvesting technology is presented, which reduces the need for batter-
ies by using super capacitors. [10] discuses that employing energy harvesting techniques
depends on whether the IoT device is ﬁxed or mobile, the parameters to be measured,
and and on whether it is indoors or outdoors.
The second and most important part of the EH system must be the conversion module,
that can contain many important parts like: MPPT subsystems, DC-DC converter, charg-
ing/protection circuits, etc. All these components must be optimized for indoor/outdoor
applications with a maximum conversion factor. On the market can be ﬁnd many semi-
conductors design with a huge variability – but there is a need to carefully select some
of them to respond to our desire to train students well and offer them the necessary
speciﬁcity understanding.

Digital Tools and Energy Harvesting in IoT Education
969
To summarize some of the conversion module parameters:
• DC basic parameters (presence of MPPT, input voltage range, maximum out-
put current, input-output isolation, output voltage accuracy, output voltage range,
over-current protection, soft-start operation, etc.)
• Performances/Features (Efﬁciency, output voltage ripples, temperature coefﬁcient,
DC line/load regulation, output noise, 50/60 Hz power supply rejection, line/load
regulation, shutdown current, etc.)
• Optional features (Input voltage protection, interface protocols, over temperature
protection, miniaturization, soft-stop operations, etc.).

Some Similar Outdoor Tests
For the outdoor applications, one 20W panel was selected (it has a good dimension/power
ratio) that was ﬁxed outside and used for live tests. For special tests, the American Optics
Instruments OAI solar A + AA Solar simulator [15] can be used (uniform illumination
1.2 SUN on high area 21 cm × 21 cm, Peltier temperature thermostat, and temperature
regulator and with a calibrated power meter, etc.).
Figure 12 (A) shows a LabVIEW monitoring interface for power injected by the
20 W solar panel in Brasov for a normal day. There was need to understand the power
distribution in one day and then repeated monitoring for more days. After analyzing
this power distribution, it the necessity to increase the injected current in the conversion
module was noticed. In Fig. 12(B) a LabVIEW application is presented, which monitors
one combination of the outside 20 W panel with LM 5118 [16] a Texas Instruments wide
voltage range Buck-Boost switching regulator controller integrating all of the functions
necessary to implement a high performance, cost-efﬁcient Buck-Boost regulator using a
minimum of external components when to inject the generated power in a constant load
4 V/0.64 A.
Fig. 12. (A) One day power injected by 20W panel/(B) LM 5118 LabVIEW application

with intelligent LED solar illumination systems, the LiFePO4 batteries, supercapacitors,
and hybrid batteries have been also studied. Figure 13 Illustrated the test of the capacity
of hybrid batteries (was one 3200 F GTCAP) that was charged and discharged in the
range of 2.5 V to 4.1 V at a temperature of −23 °C (maintained for more days).
For low temperature applications, these new hybrid batteries were selected, because
they put together some of the superior quality from supercapacitors together with the
best qualities of lithium rechargeable batteries.

6
Conclusions
This study promotes and sustains with clear examples the idea of UNIVERSITY –
INDUSTRY collaboration as the only solution for universities to prepare the new range
of future demanding engineers, able to solve the new challenges and problems-imposed
day to day by industry development.
For the selected ﬁeld connected with “Digital Tools and Energy Harvesting in IoT
Education” hardware and software used for many years in Creativity Laboratory were
put together, and it was proved:
• The solar panels for indoors must have small dimensions and high efﬁciency
• Measured and compared for different situations
• In the same applications, some light concentrators are needed to improve the
dimension/power ratio of the solar panels
• How can the research system be developed using LabVIEW software and necessary
hardware
• How the researchers must select the EH component function of indoor or outdoor
applications
• Use Hybrid Batteries (better at low temperatures)
• High current capability of charging sources must be used for outdoor applications.
In the future, it is intended to add Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) to adapt charg-
ing/discharging cycles at local variability and improve entire systems.
Also, applying easy reconﬁgurability from software using special hardware and
envisioning that the combination of Artiﬁcial Intelligence with Reconﬁgurable Hardware
and Virtual Instrumentation will be dominant in modern instrumentation.

Embedded Student Board for Digitalization
of Engineering Education
Tinashe Chamunorwa1, Horia Alexandru Modran1(B), Doru Ursut,iu1,2,

Abstract. Hands-on practice laboratory experience is an essential component for
effective engineering education. Thanks to the recent technological advancement,
remote and virtual laboratories are becoming more and more popular.
The study presented in the current paper is focused on developing a student
board that can be used by both teachers and students in the education process. For
this board, several PSoC™6 applications have been developed, to provide stu-
dents hands-on experience with various electronic basic concepts, which they can
later practice by developing their own applications. Although many applications
can be demonstrated using this board, in this paper the design and development of
two practical applications is presented - LabVIEW Control of RGB Led Intensity
and Signal Generation and Acquisition with LabVIEW Display. Those two appli-
cations are both using the PSoC 6 microcontroller and were prototyped on the NI
ELVIS II device.
The developed board has the main advantage of being an inexpensive mixed
signal platform to teach important concepts in electronics embedded system
laboratories, and it will suit well the educational needs of the post-COVID era.
Keywords: PSoC 6 · Bluetooth BLE · IoT · LabVIEW · Embedded · PCB ·
Digitalization

It is generally accepted that a hands-on or “practice-by-doing” laboratory experience
is valuable in engineering education. The students can overcome the major dispar-
ity between theoretical know-how and experimental practice. In the current times of
COVID-19 pandemic crisis, remote and virtual laboratories are growing into fundamen-
taleducationalresources[1].Toincreasethestudentparticipationinelectroniclaboratory
practical lessons, access of laboratory equipment at home is an essential consideration
for universities. The access can be done online or without internet connection, by pro-
viding kits to students. The take-home kit can have discrete components, and in this
study a PCB based structured kit is described as a possible solution. The development of

the student board will be done on a reconﬁgurable chip-based student board. Example
applications will be illustrated as a learning tool for students before they can develop
their own applications.
ThispaperillustratesthedevelopmentofastudentboardbasedonaCYBLE-416045–
02 module with various peripherals connected. The student board presents a robust hard-
ware design platform built around the scalable and reconﬁgurable PSoC (Programmable
System on a Chip) CYBLE-416045–02 EZ-BLE Creator Module [2], which combines
an Arm® Cortex®-M4 CPU and Cortex-M0 + CPU with programmable analog and
digital blocks. The module also contains high-performance analog-to-digital conversion
(ADC), low-power comparators, and standard communication and timing peripherals
[2]. The student board is Arduino Uno compatible and has double prototyping area. It
also contains Pmod connectors for a variety of sensors.
The following hardware is provided on the board:
• PSoC CYBLE-416045–02 EZ-BLE Creator Module – this is the core controller of
the student board.
• Micro B USB 2.0 Receptacle Connector 5 -CONN RCPT USB2.0 MICRO B SMD
R/A and USB Bridge-IC USB TO I2C BRIDGE DEVICE 14SO - provides USB-
UART interface and connection
• The PMOD connector – this allows connection to Digilent’s PMOD peripheral
modules.
• Programming Header – For Programming CYBLE Module.
• Prototyping area – provides additional resources usable for other complex experiments
and applications
• One Arduino expansion header (Uno R3 compatibility), can relate to Arduino shields
Several take home laboratory units have been evaluated and analyzed in a review
paper [3]. The systems analyzed use open-source software and Arduino and myDAQ
platform with cost ranging from $20 to $130. One the major challenges observed was
the use of high-level language which had an effect of steep learning curve on students.
The PSoC 6-based solution has the main advantage of being reconﬁgurable by using
graphical programming, which is intuitive. An educational board is also presented in
[10] which uses a PSoC1 chip and PSoC creator software. The PSoC1 is replaced with
the CYBLE module the which provides for more function like Bluetooth and much more
inputs and outputs.
2
Design Process
The CYBLE-416045–02 EZ-BLE™Creator module is the choice for the design of the
student’s take-home board because:
• It can handle mixed signals and is inexpensive compared to options like FPGAs (the
price of it is about $15).
• Offers ﬂexibility through hardware and software reconﬁgurability.
• module chip is BLE capable, thus conforming to current IoT trends.

LabVIEW Control of RGB Led
In this application, the RGB LED’s intensity is controlled from the LabVIEW environ-
ment. The connection between the board and the PC hosting the LabVIEW program is
enabled by serial communication [4, 5] through a USB cable. Figure 4 and 5 shows the
PSoC 6 Top Design Schema and C programs for controlling the LED intensity.
The individual LEDs in the RGB chip unit are controlled separately. In the PSoC
Schema, three Pulse Width Modulation components were supplied with the same clock
frequency of 1 MHz and conﬁgured with same period (Fig. 5). Furthermore, a UART
component was added to communicate with the LabVIEW Program via the Serial Port
of the computer.
Pulse width modulation (PWM) is a digital technology that generates varying width
pulses representing an analog input signal magnitude. It is broadly used in applications
to control the speed of a DC output or speciﬁcally the brightness of a light source like
LEDs [6].

4
Signal Generation and Acquisition with LabVIEW Display
The signal generation and acquisition system was developed using the affordable and
accessible PSoC 6 BLE chip.
The PSoC 6 microcontroller was programmed in PSoC Creator, using the C pro-
gramming language, to be able to generate sine wave signal on an external pin and then
to measure any signal from another pin. The developed application has the role of gen-
erating and acquiring data, as well as sending the measured data through the serial port
to the computer via the UART component.

986
T. Chamunorwa et al.
Fig. 9. PSoC application top design
In the main diagram of the application (Fig. 9), a 12-bit Voltage Digital-to-Analog
Convertor (abbreviated VDAC) and an Analog-Digital converter (abbreviated ADC)
were added. A universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART) component was
also used, for printing data through the serial port and. A clock with a frequency of
10 kHz was connected to the VDAC Component. The ADC component has 2 connected
pins – V_plus, on which it will receive the signal to be measured, and V_minus, for
ground. Thanks to the built-in security, the developed application is, therefore, protected
and secured [9].
By using the Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter (UART) component, the
PSoC will be able to print voltage data through the serial port. The UART Block Pins
(Tx and Rx) have been associated with ports P5.1 and P5.0 on the PSoC 6.
A Virtual Instrument (VI) that uses the VISA function to obtain a connection to the
computer’s serial port and to read the signal values was developed using the LabVIEW
Environment (Fig. 10).
In this VI, the parameters used to conﬁgure the UART were stored in a Cluster; the
bytes sent from PSoC 6 via the serial port are read using the Visa Read function and
then converted to double-precision numbers. The numeric values are stored in an array
and displayed in a Waveform Chart.
The oscilloscope from the NI ELVIS II device was used for measuring the sine wave
signal generated by the PSoC 6. Then the sinewave from the LabVIEW Waveform Chart
was compared with the sine wave signal illustrated by the oscilloscope on NI ELVIS
(Fig. 11). As it can be observed in Fig. 11, the two sinewave signals look very similar,
with just very low variations.

The student board can also function as the following:
• CYBLE-416045–02 module based development board.
• Stand-alone take-home kit for electronic applications.
• Arduino expansion expansion platform.
• Motherboard for Digilent’s PMOD modules
• Development platform for MiniSmartGPU test and application.
• Design small digital and analog electronic circuits.
• Sensing and measuring environmental Signals (IoT adaptable)
• Bluetooth PWM in RGBW LED lighting applications.
• Generate, process, measure and analyze analog signals
• Prototype a small device using touch-screen capabilities
• Reconﬁgure the processing unit.
5
Conclusions
Learning by experience is a crucial component for a modern engineering education. In
the recent years, due to the rapid technological developments, virtual and remote and
virtual laboratories are used on a large scale.

988
T. Chamunorwa et al.
The current paper presents the design and development of a student board that can
be used by both teachers and students for educational purposes. The board is an inex-
pensive mixed signal platform to teach various concepts in electronics embedded system
laboratories, such as:
1. Communication protocols (UART, SPI, I2C)
2. Analog Electronics (ampliﬁcation, ADC, DAC)
3. Digital Electronics (Logic, PWM, FSMs)
Several practical applications were developed, two of which are presented in this
paper - LabVIEW Control of RGB Led Intensity and Signal Generation and Acqui-
sition with LabVIEW Display. Both those applications are both using the PSoC 6
microcontroller and were prototyped on the NI ELVIS II device.
In conclusion, the board and applications that were developed are innovative because
they are reconﬁgurable and easy to use. Furthermore, as it provides students with a very
good hands-on experience, we strongly believe it will be suitable for the post-COVID
era as well.

Uploading Files to a Course Through
the Command Line Run from Outside
the Moodle e-Learning Platform
Vasile Banes,(B) and Cristian Ravariu
Polytechnic University of Bucharest, Bucharest, Romania
vasile.banes@stud.etti.upb.ro, cristian.ravariu@upb.ro
Abstract. This paper describes the development of a new Moodle plugin for
uploading course ﬁles to the Moodle e-learning platform using command lines.
The ﬁles will be uploaded to the course sections, which must then be available
for viewing and downloading. The proposed goal is to develop a command line
utility that will have three arguments: comma-separated course ids, the username
of the person who will perform this operation, and the absolute location of the
folder where the ﬁles needed to upload to desired courses. The utility will add all
available ﬁles in that folder to past courses as an argument. The created Moodle
plugin will be conﬁgured from the site administration according to the standard
plugin installation procedure and the command lines will be executed from the
command prompt. Simplify the process of transmitting ﬁles to the platform by
using a computer level command. It eliminates the steps that were previously taken
to authenticate and authorize access to the document transmission functionality.
While actual Moodle platform spends up to 470 s for uploading of 5 ﬁles of 20 MB,
our proposed method offers a time spending of only 5 s for these ﬁles.
Keywords: Moodle · E-learning · Command line
1
Introduction
Digital transformation in higher education requests new organizational models [1],
based on digital learning tools [2]. They must connect updated business models, like
e-commerce, hybrid meetings, swift payments, with the institution’s operational per-
formance [3]. Moodle is an e-learning platform designed to provide educators, admin-
istrators and learners a single robust, secure and integrated system. The Moodle Trust
oversees the platform’s core development, but the software is designed to be modular,
and numerous developers and organizations have created plug-ins and other add-ons to
increase functionality over the years. In addition to the standard methods, the implemen-
tation of another way of uploading ﬁles using command lines interface was considered.
CLI is the acronym used for Command Line Interface, which are conventional interfaces
extensively used in 1980’s. A command-line interface (CLI) allows users to write com-
mands in a terminal or console window to communicate with an operating system. It is
a medium where users respond to a visual prompt by writing a command and receive
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 990–997, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_101

a response back from the system. Users have to type command or string of command
to perform a task. CLI’s are more accurate than GUI’s, but it requires mastery over the
commands and syntax. CLI is required for the computing technology where input pre-
cision is the priority. Within the Moodle (Modular Object Oriented Dynamic Learning
Environment) platform [4], there are several types of resources such as books, folders,
pages, labels or ﬁles. Steps to upload ﬁles to a course. The platform is accessed from
the browser based on a link after which the username and password are entered. From
menu select site home, after that select available courses, from courses turn editing on,
from topic add an activity or resources and select from resources ﬁle, from ﬁle select
add and after that write name and description, select ﬁle from computer location, upload
ﬁles and ﬁnish with save and display. After that, the document appear in topic with
the name document. The presented new method simpliﬁes the process of transferring
ﬁles to the platform using a computer level command. In addition to the low execution
time, compared to other platforms related to the Moodle environment, the steps required
to upload ﬁles in order to enter new documents or modify existing ones, as shown in
Table 1, are simpliﬁed. This eliminates the steps that were taken for authentication and
authorization in order to access the functionality of sending documents. No additional
or speciﬁc technical knowledge is required for the use of this functionality, it is enough
to launch a script, which leads to ease of use. The information regarding the conﬁgu-
ration of the paths where the server, the course and the location of the related ﬁles are
located is set once, after which they remain conﬁgured without the need for any further
modiﬁcation and conﬁguration.
2
Advantages of Using the Command Line Interface
The operating system offers a CLI vs GUI user interface to interact with an electronic
device. Some operating systems provide CLI and GUI, while others offer only CLI. GUI
means a Graphical user interface while CLI means the command line interface. As the
name suggests, one has to write commands to perform a certain CLI system task. On
the other hand, GUI offers graphics that consist of icons and images that enable users
to do a task directly. CLI requires expertise in commands for performing a certain task,
while a beginner can operate GUI. The Department of Computer Science & Engineering
at Blekinge, Sweden, Institute of Technology in partial fulﬁllment of the requirements
for the degree of Bachelors of Science in Computer Science conducted a study showing
the representation of the interface that indicates the users they use based on experience.
This study was conducted in 2015 [5] and some results are picked in Fig. 1. Another
study was based on what type of operating system matters when using CLI or GUI or
both. In Windows, about 32% use a graphical interface, while in Mac the number drops
to 15.5% and in Linux 1.5%. From our point of view, we believe that those ﬁgures show
a correlation between how dependent the GUI is on an operating system and what type
of user interface users use. In this case, it would mean that there is a strong negative
correlation. The same could be said for CLI where about 49% of Windows users, 61.9%
of Mac users and 82% of Linux users use a CLI, which in turn would suggest a strong
positive correlation. There are several beneﬁts of CLI [6]. Ease of understanding - due
to the memory remaining in the commands.

992
V. Banes, and C. Ravariu
Fig. 1. The users experience for a digital learning interface, adapted from [5].
Low-resolution monitor - As CLI is a text-based interface, so that it can also run
well on a low-resolution screen [7, 8]. Requires memory - requires little memory. Speed
- because the keyboard is used to execute the command. Appearance - no customization
required. The interface is consistent for all time. Complex tasks - the command line
interface is best for managing complex tasks [9]. You can manage the complex task by
typing a few commands. AutoComplete - when writing commands in the CLI, then most
commands are completed automatically by clicking the TAB button on the keyboard [10].

Actual Outcomes
The originality of this functionality is given by the fact that it provides users and system
administrators with a simple, fast, efﬁcient, easy to use, independent of the operating
system interface, through which ﬁles can be transmitted on the Moodle platform without
using steps, login for authentication, authorization, and without navigating the platform
until you reach the screen for the document transmission service. This provided an easy,
useful and fast tool for transmitting documents within the Moodle platform, without
having to authenticate and authorize using the web interface of the site. This new working
method was achieved by developing a plugin, where the parameters and arguments were
written, which the role of making the command line has run functional. Advantages
of the new working method: independence from the operating system is ensured, the
script can be run on any platform, and uploading ﬁles can run from outside the platform
without connecting to the server and the Moodle platform, simplifying the process of
transmitting ﬁles through the platform, by simply using a command at the computer

5
Conclusions
Moodle provides a way for a teacher or administrator to present materials to students,
which can take the form of ﬁles. These ﬁles can only be uploaded and accessed through
Moodle if editing is active. In Moodle you can upload several ﬁles at once only archived
in zip format and for viewing you can only see the content after unzipping and if you
want to display documents as a list you must upload one and repeat the steps for each ﬁle
or by the drag and drop method. Most of the time the content changes or the improvement
of the functions cannot be done because most of the e-learning platforms are embedded
or require costs for access, unlike Moodle, which is open source platform, and free. This
new working method was achieved by developing a plugin, where the parameters and
arguments were written, which the role of making the command lines has run functional.
With this method, a new way of uploading ﬁles to courses has been created within the
Moodle platform. Traditional upload methods have been based on accessing the platform
with the user and password and have the main disadvantage of taking at least 10 steps to
complete the process, while our proposed new method is superior in that you no longer
need to log in to the platform as well as by simplifying, speeding and managing the
process. While actual Moodle platform spends up to 470 s for uploading of 5 ﬁles of
20 MB, our proposed method offers a time spending of only 5 s for these ﬁles.

The Development of an IoT Standard Package
for Carinthian Municipalities
Julia Kositz1, Andreas Probst2(B), and Maximilian Lackner1
1 UAS Technikum Wien, Höchstädtplatz 6, 1200 Vienna, Austria
2 HTL Wels, Fischergasse 30, 4600 Wels, Austria
Andreas.Probst@eduhi.at
Abstract. While urban digitalization is constantly progressing as part of smart
city initiatives, digitalization projects on a municipal level are being imple-
mented only sporadically. At the same time, new technologies, such as the Inter-
net of Things (IoT), offer possibilities to improve the efﬁciency of communal
infrastructure management.
This paper explicitly focuses on IoT needs within municipalities in the Aus-
trian state of Carinthia, elaborated in the master thesis: “The development of an
IoT standard package for Carinthian municipalities”. Based on the legally deﬁned
responsibilities of communes, current IoT needs have been assessed empirically
in the form of an online survey. In addition, a problem-centered interview with a
Carinthian municipal pioneer for digitalization provides empirical values gained
from implemented IoT pilot projects. An expert interview with the digitalization
ofﬁcer of all 132 Carinthian municipalities provides an overarching perspective
of the current state and future development potential.
Based on the research outcome, a standard IoT package has been developed
consisting of IoT use cases that can signiﬁcantly support the most expensive and
management-intensive tasks identiﬁed. Market research shows that two network
technologies are currently emerging for municipal framework conditions. Further-
more, key challenges arising at the forefront of digitalization projects have been
determined.
Keywords: IoT · Municipalities · Carinthia · Austria · Digitalization · LPWAN ·
Internet of Things
1
Introduction
Technological progress is a crucial driver of a society’s economic growth and prosperity.
The invention of the World Wide Web in the 1990s marked one of the decisive milestones
in the history of digitalization. Its basic idea was to make data accessible to users globally.
However, there was one decisive compromise at this early stage of development: User
access was tied to a speciﬁc locality [1].
With the subsequent mobile revolution, this limitation soon became a thing of the
past.Theintroductionofmobiledevicessuchassmartphones,tablets,andlaptopsopened
the possibility of location-independent communication [2].
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 998–1009, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_102

The Development of an IoT Standard Package
999
Today, science has reached the beginning of the next technological advancement,
known as the Internet of Things. This technology allows the interconnection and com-
munication of smart devices within a network [3]. Thereby, numerous new business
ﬁelds and application opportunities emerge [4].
The progressive development of new and the advancement of existing measurement
technology steadily constitutes new IoT application possibilities [5]. One area with
considerable future potential is the use of IoT in cities and municipalities. With smart
city initiatives, densely populated cities successfully strive for a more sustainable and
effective operating approach. This development has been pursued only sporadically at a
municipal level due to the restricted scope for action [6].
This paper presents a standardized package consisting of commune-speciﬁc IoT use
cases to facilitate municipalities’ strategic entry into IoT-enabled governance. Although
the communal sphere of action is deﬁned by law, priorities in infrastructure management
vary depending on individual municipalities. Accordingly, the IoT standard package is
based on an empirical survey in the state of Carinthia. Only in this way can a selection
of IoT use cases be created that cover the needs of the deﬁned target group.
Municipalities tend to cover large distances and landforms such as agricultural land,
forests, or mountains. Network technologies need to function appropriately in given
framework conditions for IoT applications to be implemented in communes [7]. Based
on the IoT standard package, suitable network technologies for municipal framework
conditions are compared.
However, before IoT solutions can be implemented in the administrative apparatus of
a commune, various obstacles can arise. Therefore, a compendium of current challenges
that slow down the progress of digitalization at the municipal level is compiled.
In Sect. 2, different components of an IoT system are elucidated using related lit-
erature. A subsequent research overview in Sect. 3 highlights the objectives and non-
objectives of thestudyandpresents theresearchquestions. Section 4outlines themethod-
ological research approach and the conducted research evaluation. Section 5 presents
the research results. A conclusion and outlook on the future of IoT in municipalities
conclude this paper in Sect. 6.
2
Internet of Things
Internet of Things refers to the connection and interaction of uniquely identiﬁable phys-
ical objects via the Internet’s telecommunications infrastructure. The aim is to connect
all physical “things” and processes that can be handled via the Internet. “Things” are
understood as sensors, machines, people, animals, or plants, among other objects [8].
Reliable and efﬁcient data transmission forms the foundation of any IoT system.
Particularly in widespread network structures, however, this creates a complex challenge.
Communicating information between different networks requires a means of translation
or transmission. Network protocols carry out this task by converting information into
the correct format, transmitting the data and its meaning, and ensuring the correct order
of information ﬂow [9].
Two reference models for IoT system architectures that logically structure the dif-
ferent network protocols are the Open Systems Interconnection model (OSI model) and

1000
J. Kositz et al.
the Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP model). The OSI model
concept enables the interoperability of different communication systems by standard
protocols. This ensures that users on the same layer speak the same "protocol language".
The TCP/IP reference model is named after its primary protocols and forms the basis of
today’s Internet. Due to different network complexities in IoT ecosystems, there is no
uniform system architecture. However, all architecture models have expandability and
scalability in common [10, 11].
Figure 1 illustrates the structure of a service-oriented architecture (SOA) consisting
of individual subsystems and is considered the mainstream architecture at present:
Fig. 1. Service-oriented IoT system architecture [10]
The four-layer stack ensures interoperability between IoT devices through its dif-
ferent key functions and network protocols [11]. At the bottom layer of any IoT system
architecture, two functions are essential: acquisition and addressing.
While sensors are used for data acquisition, actuators are responsible for controlling
and repairing “things”. Both ﬁeld devices can be built into or attached to an IoT device
[10].
Telecommunication networks are required to transmit data via the Internet, which
forms the second layer of the SOA. Depending on the area of application, suitable tech-
nology needs to be selected. Fundamentally, two types of telecommunication networks
are distinguished: wired and wireless [12]. For IoT systems, long-distance wireless
telecommunication networks and their speciﬁc communication technologies are par-
ticularly relevant. These are referred to as low power wide area networks (LPWAN)
[13].
The service and platform layer is where the creation and management of services
occur, which users subsequently request [11]. In this context, IT services are used to
provide storage and computing resources and application software via the Internet,
regardless of physical location [14].
As the top layer in the service-oriented architecture, the application layer enables
user interaction [11].
The use of cloud computing services optimizes the user’s work process. Nevertheless,
there needs to be awareness of security-related issues, limitations, and potential risks
associated with sensitive information. Since IoT is a new ﬁeld of business, the legal
framework needs to be adapted accordingly. Above all, this applies to aspects of data
protection and necessary transparency [15].

The Development of an IoT Standard Package
1001
3
Research Questions and Goals
This research aims to provide municipalities with a more accessible entry point to the
wide range of IoT applications in the form of a standardized IoT package. To ensure
this, the following three research questions are formulated:
RQ1: Which IoT use cases provide the highest added value for Carinthian municipalities
in a standardized IoT package?
RQ2: According to the developed commune-speciﬁc IoT standard package, which
network technologies suit communal framework conditions?
RQ3: What challenges need to be considered before implementing IoT solutions in a
municipality’s administrative apparatus?
The goal of this study is not to develop new IoT solutions. Instead, currently tested
IoT use cases or pilot projects are being explored.
The explanation of the standard package does not focus on technical solutions.
Instead, it highlights the most costly and management-intensive activities and illustrates
the concepts of the IoT use cases.
The development of the IoT standard package does not consider commune-speciﬁc
impact areas, which are merely administrative management activities. Emphasis is
placed on IoT use cases providing more efﬁcient activities in managing communal
infrastructure.
4
Methodology and Design of the Empirical Study
In this study, both qualitative and quantitative research methods are applied. On the
one hand, a problem-centered guided interview was used to document the experience
of a municipal pioneer for digitalization, the commune Neuhaus [16]. On the other
hand, a guided expert interview was used to obtain an overarching perspective of the
digitalization ofﬁcer of all 132 Carinthian municipalities.
Based on the collected information, a quantitative survey was created. Thereby,
research questions RQ1 and RQ3 can be answered. Research question RQ2 is answered
by market research conducted to develop the standard package.
While Sect. 4.1 addresses the design of the online survey, Sect. 4.2 describes the
deﬁned target group and the approach to conducting the survey. Section 4.3 focuses on
data preparation carried out before evaluating the results.
4.1
Design of the Online Survey
The online survey consists of 13 questions, including eight closed and ﬁve open ques-
tions. While speciﬁc questions were used to gain an average impression of the current
digitalization status in Carinthian municipalities, four of them served as key questions.
Table 1 presents each of the four key questions:

Key Question
KQ1:
What are the main challenges of digitalization in your commune respectively which
obstacles are in the way of the digitalization of your commune?
KQ2:
Which managing activities of your communal infrastructure are particularly cost and
management-intensive?
KQ3:
Does your commune already have digital solutions for managing communal
infrastructure? If so, which ones?
KQ4:
In your perspective, what would be needed to drive communal digitalization forward?
4.2
Target Group and Conduction of the Online Survey
The target group of this research consists of all 130 Carinthian municipalities (except
for the statutory cities of Klagenfurt-Stadt and Villach-Stadt). Before the online survey
was sent out via email, the draft question was presented to ﬁve pretesters to be checked
for comprehensibility. The survey was addressed to the leading administrative ofﬁcials
to gain the broadest possible insight. Since the target group consists of public service
employees, relevant contact details could be obtained via municipal websites. Within
14 days, participants could take part in the online survey.

Out of 130 potential municipalities, the online survey was completed by 43 munic-

communal survey was processed with a duration of 08:54 min.

research was conducted to identify already proven IoT use cases.

Results
Based on the ﬁndings derived from the empirical research, the three deﬁned research
questions can be answered. Furthermore, this section provides an economic overview of
the current ﬁnancial situation in Austrian municipalities.
6.1
Q1: IoT Standard Package
Out of the 12 identiﬁed most management- and cost-intensive activities in the infras-
tructure management of Carinthian municipalities, a standard package consisting of 13
IoT use cases was developed. Depending on the ﬁeld of action, these can be categorized
into ﬁve modules. Implementing the individual IoT use cases into a commune’s admin-
istrative apparatus can signiﬁcantly support municipal operations. Figure 3 contrasts the
left-hand side municipal activities with the right-hand side IoT use cases of the standard
package:
6.2
Q2: Network Technologies Suitable for the IoT Standard Package
Urban sprawl, low building and population density, and community areas covering long
distances are features of municipal frameworks [23].
When implementing IoT projects, it is essential to consider these factors. Based
on the developed standard package, two network technologies could be identiﬁed for
deployment in communes. This applies to the leading LPWAN technologies LoRa (Long
Range) and NB-IoT (Narrowband IoT). Market research has shown that of the 13 IoT use
cases included in the standard package, 12 have already been implemented with NB-IoT
and 13 with LoRa. For wireless transmission of measurement data, radio technologies are
used to provide necessary device connectivity. LPWAN technologies are characterized
by high ranges, low energy consumption, and low data rates [13].

1006
J. Kositz et al.
Fig. 3. IoT standard package
6.3
Q3: Challenges in the Forefront of IoT Project Implementation
Overall, six different challenges were identiﬁed to slow down the progress of municipal
digitalization.
According to the online survey, the biggest challenge lies in the ﬁnancing of IoT
projects. 28% of the 43 participating Carinthian municipalities rated this obstacle with
the highest evaluation level. Although the state of Carinthia supports communes with
subsidies of up to 75% of the initial IoT investment costs, communes still face consider-
able costs. Digitalization projects often play a subordinate role in the communal agenda
in municipalities that do not generate a persistent surplus [24, 25].
The lack of human resources proves to be an organizational obstacle. Incorporating
new digital solutions takes up additional time alongside the main business of a commune.
From a technical perspective, there is a need for greater communication of best
practice examples. The added value of IoT solutions for communes is often hidden
behind a seemingly complex system.
The use of new digital solutions also creates a legal challenge. It is necessary to
adapt the legal framework for communes regarding liability and damage issues to the
progress of digitalization.
Another challenge for Carinthian municipalities lies in political approval. Imple-
menting IoT projects requires a long-term political focus on digitalization and support
in the form of appropriate ﬁnancial resources.

The Development of an IoT Standard Package
1007
In the social context, mainly due to the advanced age structure in many Carinthian
municipalities, the population has limited acceptance. Furthermore, the chance man-
agement process triggered by the implementation of IoT projects requires learning new
ways of working.
6.4
Financing of Digitalization Projects - Economic Consideration
Due to the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, the ﬁnancial situation in Austrian com-
munes is very strained. In 2020 and 2021, these municipalities lacked about 2.5 billion
euros to cover necessary current expenditures and system-relevant investments [26]. The
lack of ﬁnancial resources to cover current expenditures pushes the investment sector
into the background. In 2020, resources in this regard were reduced by 40% [25].
To realize IoT pilot projects, extensive initial investments are necessary. These are
ﬁnanced through need-based allocations by the state of Carinthia. According to the
2020 ﬁnancial statements, the need-based allocations of the pilot municipality Neuhaus
consist of severance payment and a municipal ﬁnancial equalization payment [27].
Severance payments are granted to communes unable to cover current expenditures
from their resources. A drop in revenue due to the COVID-19 pandemic resulted in no
severance payments to Carinthian municipalities in 2021. This additionally inhibits the
progress of municipal digitalization. Given the current state of development, a quan-
tiﬁable cost breakdown of the IoT standard package is not carried out in this study. In
Carinthian municipalities, subsidies of up to 75% of the initial IoT investment funds are
available [24]. Field reports from initial pilot projects have shown that IoT solutions can
signiﬁcantly support infrastructure management. This contrasts with the current ﬁnancial
situation faced by communes due to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
7
Conclusion and Outlook
Research results have shown that Carinthian municipalities are still in the early stages
of transitioning to smart communes. The scale and diverse applications opened up by
the Internet of Things are unforeseeable for municipalities and other economic sectors.
From today’s municipal perspective, the focus needs to lie on informing municipalities
about the possibilities and added value to facilitate their entry into IoT.
This study provides a starting point for implementing IoT solutions in the adminis-
trative apparatus of a commune. The standard package includes the most cost-intensive
activities in infrastructure management identiﬁed by at least three of the 43 participants.
Covering all eight districts (excluding statutory cities), this response rate represents one-
third of Carinthian municipalities. It is expected that all 132 communes will have taken
the ﬁrst step towards IoT within ﬁve to ten years [24].
The state of Carinthia is striving to standardize IoT systems in the long term. By
analyzing pilot projects, necessary adjustments and improvements can be carried out.
Subsequently, these pilot applications will be available to other Carinthian municipali-
ties. For example, network technologies such as LoRa or NB-IoT can be used to deploy
wireless water meters. Live images from a trafﬁc surveillance camera, on the other hand,

1008
J. Kositz et al.
require technologies capable of transmitting higher amounts of data. Standardization on
the IoT platform level will enable any network technology to be exploited in the future.
The COVID-19 pandemic has signiﬁcantly limited municipal investment opportu-
nities in the medium term. Accordingly, communes are heavily dependent on provinces
and federal government support [25].
Funding for the progress of municipal digitalization differs across states. Conse-
quently, results derived from this study can only be directly applied to Carinthian munic-
ipalities. This opens up the possibility of further investigating how much IoT needs are
similar or different across the states. After all, to support communes with the use of IoT,
it is ﬁrst necessary to determine where digitalization can create added value.

Experts’ View on AR/VR in Engineering
Education at Universities
Juliane Maria Probst(B)
and Horst Orsolits
FH Technikum Wien, Höchstädtplatz 6, 1200 Wien, Austria
juju3018@gmail.com, horst.orsolits@technikum-wien.at
Abstract. Innovative teaching methods focus more on student engagement and
start to become more common in the university landscape supported by digital
technologies. These technologies include Augmented Reality (AR), Mixed Reality
(MR) and Virtual Reality (VR). The research of this paper focuses on the use of
AR/MR in education, with particular attention to engineering education at the
university level. Therefore, a structured literature review is carried out to form the
basis for conducting interviews with international professors from universities that
are already using Extended Reality (XR) in their classroom settings. The research
method used to gather data are qualitative interviews with selected experts from
Europe and US followed by a structured qualitative content analysis with focus on
reasons why respective XR experiences are used in class, beneﬁts that have been
identiﬁed after the experts evaluated their use cases and ﬁnally which challenges
had to be overcome.
Keywords: Mixed Reality (MR) · Augmented Reality (AR) · Virtual Reality
(VR) · Extended Reality (XR) · Higher education (HE) · Engineering education
1
Introduction
Humans think, act and experience their environment in three dimensions, but two-
dimensional information is often used to convey knowledge. In order to create a real
three-dimensional image in the mind from this digital information, cognitive load is
caused. This reduces the cognitive capacity for other tasks, as the brain is busy trans-
ferring the digital information into physical space. Virtual technologies offer enormous
potential for increasing positive learning effects while costs for hardware and software
solutions continue to decrease. Augmented and Mixed Reality are mature technologies
that are applied in various ﬁelds [1]. While the technology itself is not an emerging
technology anymore, it is still an emerging trend in education. Education is an area that
can beneﬁt from the utilisation of AR/MR [2, 3]. However, while there are occasional
occurrences of AR/MR in lectures [4], this technology has yet to reach a broad level of
usage in education, especially in higher education. Therefore, this paper is an attempt
to shine some light on the usage of AR/MR at universities in 2021/2022 in engineering
education. It is going to determine where AR/MR is used and how it is applied in lectures
as well as identify challenges educators face before and during the usage of AR/MR in
