their lectures. Industrial engineering education has a strong focus on and afﬁnity toward
technology. While Extended Reality (XR) hardware and applications advance and learn-
ing behaviour changes, it is particularly interesting to determine what role immersive
technologies play in current university classroom settings.
1.1
Terminology
Talking about AR and VR seldomly goes without mentioning Mixed Reality. Milgrams
Reality-Virtuality (RV) Continuum [5] is often used to distinguish and explain these
terms. A different term used quite often to describe AR, VR and MR in literature is
Extended Reality (XR). XR is an umbrella term for all real-and-virtual combined envi-
ronments and therefore refers to AR, VR and MR in equal measure [6, 7]. Whereas
these previous descriptions are deﬁnitions of AR, MR and VR, they are not the only
deﬁnitions found in the literature. It often depends on the context, hence it is essential
to communicate the deﬁnition used in research to avoid confusion [8]. Rauschnabel
et al. [9] conducted a literature review and found four existing AR/MR/VR frameworks.
Those frameworks are: the MR-dominant view, VR-dominant view, MR-centered view
and the Extended Reality view. Additionally, they created a new xReality framework.
The different frameworks are visualised in Fig. 1.
Fig. 1. Schematics of AR/MR/VR relations [9]
This paper works with the MR-dominant view, see Fig. 1, which is based on the
Reality-Virtuality (RV) Continuum [5, 9].
1.2
State of the Art
Thevirtualisationofteachingandlearningaspartofblendedlearningisrapidlybecoming
the norm at universities. Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality take this development
one step further. They transfer not only the methods of learning but also its content
to a partially or fully artiﬁcial reality. Students assemble virtual engines at the RWTH
Aachen, work with virtual aircraft systems at the TU Hamburg or practice handling
difﬁcult situations in the virtual classroom at the University of Würzburg. VR/AR in
teaching achieves better adaptation to heterogeneous student groups (with a special focus
on gender and diversity strategies) through didactic reduction, making content clearer
and easier to design, achieving better comprehensibility, and simplifying learning in the
trial and error principle [10].

1012
J. M. Probst and H. Orsolits
Garzon [11] performed a literature search with the search term “augmented reality
in education” on 13 July 2020 on the Web of Science (WoS) Website see Fig. 2. The
graphic pictures a steady increase of publications per year. The found studies show that
AR has been successfully implemented in many ﬁelds of education. The most popular
areas are natural sciences, mathematics and statistics, followed by arts, humanities and
health.
Mystakidis et al. [12] conducted a systematic mapping review of AR applications
to support STEM learning in higher education. The authors identiﬁed and analysed 45
papers, published between 2010 and 2020, for this review. The study shows augmentation
techniques,instructionalstrategiesandinstructionaltechniquesforARinSTEMsubjects
in higher education.
Fig. 2. Number of studies of AR in education per year in the WoS [11]
Various beneﬁts of using AR/MR in education are mentioned throughout the litera-
ture. Following key beneﬁts have been identiﬁed by Alzahrani in conducted systematic
literature reviews [13, 14]:
• Allows more efﬁcient visualisation
• Allows distance & remote learning due to portability and convenience
• Allows student-centred learning
• Boosts students’ motivation and engagement
• Enhances collaborative learning
• Enhances knowledge retention and spatial abilities
• Increases student’s physical interactions and concentration
• Increases learning satisfaction
• Increases interactivity and information accessibility
• Supports kinesthetic learning
• Supports creative learning
• students can gather ﬁrst-hand-experience in subjects which would not be possible
otherwise

• self-paced learning for students
Similar beneﬁts and advantages for using AR speciﬁcally in STEM education have
been identiﬁed by Sırakaya & Sırakaya [15] in a conducted literature review study. In
this paper, the authors additionally created categories for the beneﬁts. The categories are
a contribution to the learner, educational outcome, interaction, and other advantages.
2
Problem Statement
Althoughproofofbeneﬁcialusageofvirtualtechnologiesineducationispresentinscien-
tiﬁc literature, XR is typically introduced in classroom settings by respective technology
afﬁne educators. This paper aims to create a snapshot of how and why AR/MR is applied
in an educational setting, speciﬁcally in engineering university lectures. The goal is to
highlight different application areas and ways of applying AR and MR. Furthermore, the
reasons why or why not AR/MR is used in education should be determined. Therefore,
selected experts, who already have introduced AR/MR/VR into their classroom settings
and evaluated their scenarios, are interviewed.
3
Methodology and Empirical Research
The research method used to gather data are qualitative interviews. The qualitative
research follows the seven-stage model for an interview inquiry after Kvale [16].
The seven stages are: Thematizing, Designing, Interviewing, Transcribing, Analysing,
Verifying and Reporting. Except for the stage Verifying, all stages are carried out.
The qualitative interview is a guided interview, which means it follows a pre-deﬁned
interview guideline and has the form of an expert interview, according to Misoch [17].
3.1
Interview Questions/Guideline
The interview questions (IQ) are formulated according to the method of Kaiser [18].
Based on the research questions, dimensions of analysis were established and in further
steps, the interview questions were created.
The Interview guideline is structured according to Misoch [17] in four phases: infor-
mation phase, warm-up, main phase and end note. The information phase is the intro-
ductory talk of the interview, where the participants are informed about the study and the
data handling. The other three phases contain the interview questions and are visualised
in Table 1.

1014
J. M. Probst and H. Orsolits

Section
Interview questions
Warm-up
IQ1: To start this off, could you please explain how you ﬁrst got the idea of
incorporating AR/MR into your lectures and your reasons for using AR/MR in
your classes?
Main phase
IQ2: In which of your lectures do you apply AR/MR?
IQ3: In which ways do you apply AR/MR in your classes? (passive/interactive,
quiz,..)
IQ4: For what kind of content do you use AR/MR? (Content self created)
IQ5: What beneﬁts do you see when applying AR/MR in your lectures?
IQ6: Do you have a particular approach/method for creating AR/MR
experiences?
IQ7: What challenges have you encountered when applying AR/MR in your
lessons?
End note
IQ8: To conclude this interview, do you want to add a topic that’s important
from your point of view, which we haven’t touched on yet?

primary ﬁeld and they use AR/VR in some sort of way in their teaching.

the interviewees were confronted with the questions for the ﬁrst time during the actual
interview. The interviews took place in March and April 2022.

3.3
Interview Analysis
The method used to analyse the interviews is the structured qualitative content analysis
according to Kuckartz [19].
The structured qualitative content analysis has seven steps. Phase 1 consists of the
initial text work, where memos are noted down, and case summaries are created. In
Phase 2, the main categories are developed. It is often the case that the main categories
can be derived from the research questions or the method of data collection itself. Hence
this is often called deductive categorising. Phase 3 covers the ﬁrst coding process. The
text is analysed, and individual sections are assigned to the previously created main
categories. Phases 4 and 5 are closely linked together. In Phase 4, all text passages
with the same coding are compiled. In Phase 5, subcategories are developed for selected
main categories. Main categories are more general than subcategories. The subcategories
are derived from the text itself. Therefore, this method is called inductive categorising.
The transcript gets analysed and coded again in Phase 6. In Phase 7, the coded text
is evaluated, and a suitable visualisation is chosen. The software used to support the
structured qualitative content analysis is MAXQDA 2022 [20].
4
Results
All interviewed experts create their experiences themselves in some way. No one uses
pre-existing apps. The preferred technology used is AR and in some cases VR is used. No
educator stated the use of MR explicitly. Furthermore, hardly any of the interviewed pro-
fessors had a set method for creating AR/MR/VR experiences. Most of the experiences
are created through trial and error and based on know-how on the creators’ side.
Characteristics, that are tied to the use cases, mentioned by the experts during the
interviews, are: What XR was used for the experience, the level of interactivity, how the
XR is applied in class if the XR is graded and if the XR is self-created and by whom.
The use cases have been numbered alphabetically, see Fig. 3.
Fig. 3. Overview of the characteristics of the use cases mentioned in the interviews

1016
J. M. Probst and H. Orsolits
The characteristics of the different use cases each expert mentioned during the inter-
views are summarised to better understand their implementation of XR in education.
Five use cases have been used to visualise assemblies/structures, four for explaining
technical equipment and to learn to create XR experiences. Three experiences are used
for design review processes and two use cases are determined for giving instructions.
For the Level of Interactivity, three subcategories could be established. The use cases
include passive models (virtual model, able to zoom and turn), information/instruction
models (additional information of a model can be viewed or step wise instructions are
given) and interactive models (students can explore the model feely and the experience
reacts to inputs students make).
The XR experiences can be mandatory, optional or an integral part of the class. The
difference between a mandatory experience and an experience that is part of the class
is that the compulsory experience is required for the course, like reading pre-readings,
and the part of the class experience is an integral part of the class, like creating a 3D
model in a designing class. The interviewed educators mostly apply the experiences as
an integral part of the class.
All interviewed educators are working with self-created content. In some cases, the
students themselves create the XR experience and even the 3D models, instead of the
educators.
Except for particular points tied to core features of the respective technologies
(AR: contextualised information, VR illness), there are no indications of distinctions
for reasons, beneﬁts and challenges between AR and VR.
4.1
Reasons
After the content analysis, it was possible to identify the three most mentioned reasons
for using AR which are listed below, further signiﬁcant reasons are shown in Table 3:
1. students get a better understanding of the object
2. to get students familiar with the technology
3. give the students direct experience
Access: On account of using AR/MR/VR students can explore objects independent of
location. This remote access can also be used to share the content with students via
online classes, making the experience accessible for more students. Even people who
are not experts in the operation of CAD programs can access the XR.
Interactive/Guide: It is possible to give hints to the students currently exploring the
model. Hence an instructor does not have to be present to guide the student to essential
aspects of the model.
Sense of Scale/Spatial Relations: It is hard to get a feel for the physical scale of things
with only pictures. People tend to grasp general dimensions and spatial relations between
parts better when viewing models in AR/VR compared to computer screens.

Understanding: Viewing the model in XR lets people understand functionalities and
how parts could be assembled when designing a product.
Direct Experience: Using XR, students who do not have access to a physical model
can directly experience the product. The dynamic aspect of conducting the task, like
disassembling the model, facilitates understanding the product details.
Student Motivation: Only one educator mentioned student motivation as an initial
reason, far more educators mentioned that aspect of using XR as a beneﬁt.
Reviews/Showcase: People review and evaluate a 3D model differently if the design
review is conducted in VR.
Familiar with the Technology: The students should be familiar with these technolo-
gies and aware that these trends are coming. Students don’t have to be computer scientists
anymore to be able to use AR/VR.
4.2
Beneﬁts
In the previous section, the reasons for applying AR/VR given by the interviewed edu-
cators are summarized. Apart from the initial reason for using AR/VR other beneﬁts can
also arise. The beneﬁts mentioned during the interviews are summed up in this section
and can present reasons for further educators to use the technology in class. The three
most mentioned beneﬁts are (Table 4):
1. motivation, excitement and curiosity
2. contextualised information
3. interactive/ﬁrst-hand experience
Access: The AR/VR experience can be shared with hundreds or thousands of students
outside the university and can be accessed by many students simultaneously.

Guidance: For remote AR exercises, where the lecturer is not present, some guidance
can be given through the AR experience if the students require it, e.g., in the form of hints.
This lets the students explore the model of the product on their own without missing
important points.
Uniformity: An AR experience won’t vary from teacher to teacher. All students can
have the same kind of experience.
Contextualised Information: AR situates the information in the physical world. This
is helpful because it puts the information right in front of the user, the access to the
information is more agile, and information can be given at the right time and place
where it is needed for the current step.
Motivation/Excitement/Curiosity: The most signiﬁcant beneﬁt is the excitement of
the students. The students experience a kind of wow-effect and are more enthusiastic
and motivated. The exercises are interactive, and this is interesting for students because
they can explore something and having this curiosity triggered is something that can
give an educator a real advantage in education.
Visualisation: With an AR experience, things can be made visible that otherwise would
be obscured. Additionally, things can get visualised dynamically, and simulations can be
added to the experience. Compared to books, PowerPoint presentations or engineering
drawings, things are better visualised.
Interactive/First-Hand Experience: By using an interactive AR/VR experience, stu-
dents have to do something on their own. It is learning based on activities, and they can
experience it ﬁrst-hand.
Spatial Thinking/Physical Scale: To see the objects/products in scale lets the user
understand dimensions better and grasp spatial relations.

4.3
Challenges
The most mentioned challenge are technical issues with the hardware and software
(Table 5).
Table 5. Challenges for Educators when applying AR/VR in class
Challenges
Experts

Technical (Software/Hardware): One technical challenge is accessibility. Students
often just use tablets or smartphones to view the XR Experience. Additionally, the
user interface is not necessarily optimised for both smartphones and tablets, resulting
in difﬁculties to navigate the app. In collaborative VR sessions, one software issue that
arises is that sometimes people suddenly lose the connection and are thrown out of the
session. Educational software bundles available for universities often do not include XR
software licences. The devices like VR headsets are very diverse in terms of control-
ling them, causing troubles regarding operation when switching between devices. Not
only software and hardware can be challenging. The network capability is an additional
factor.
Technology Acceptance: It can be challenging to help other instructors understand the
capabilities of AR/VR and get them to be comfortable with the technology. Introducing
this kind of technology into some more traditional disciplines can be a kind of culture
shock for some educators. Not only do other instructors have to be on board with imple-
menting the technology but also the students who are supposed to use it. Some students,
especially those who do not have any issues with traditional forms of learning, might
have an inner barrier.
Cost/Funds: There is always a challenge when trying to implement something extraor-
dinary or some innovative learning scenario because of the need to ﬁnance it some-
how. The implementation requires a certain amount of money invested in hardware and
software.

1020
J. M. Probst and H. Orsolits
Knowledgeable About AR/VR: The ﬁrst challenge that keeps people away from the
technology is the question of which hardware and software to use and what to do with
it. Much knowledge about the implementation is needed, which restricts most people.
Furthermore, knowledge about the process ﬂows from one tool to another. Currently, it
is a trial and error method to ﬁgure out which combinations of programmes and formats
work. Moreover, choosing the right tool is essential. Sometimes a simple 3D web viewer
could solve the problem where the initial thought was to use VR. There is a lot to be
done in regard to methods.
Effort for the Educator: Someone needs to prepare the models/environment/technical
setup. To incorporate AR/VR in a course, the educator must invest much effort. It is
not like plug and play. Moreover, device management takes a lot of time and effort,
providing/storing/lending the headsets. It is up to the educator to become familiar with
the software because even software representatives are not that familiar with their tool
besides the usual use cases.
Availability of 3D Model: For VR experiences and full overlay AR experiences, 3D
models are essential. Sometimes there are no 3D models available because, in the dis-
cipline, it is common to work with 2D drawings or the company where the machine is
from does not hand over the CAD data of the machine. It is often too time-consuming
to ﬁrst create the exact 3D model and then the experience.
VR Illness: There is an issue with VR illness. After an extended period of time using
the VR headset, some participants did not feel comfortable. After using a VR headset,
some people get dizzy and even fall.
5
Discussion
While the usage of mixed reality in education has evolved greatly in the last decades,
there are still many possible ways to further use XR in education. Overall, the employ-
ment of alternative teaching methods like XR experiences is not common yet. The expert
interviews showed in which cases XR experiences are used in higher education in dif-
ferent engineering topics for several different reasons. Reasons and beneﬁts have been
measured and described reasonably in different classroom settings as well as challenges
educators are facing when XR is used for teaching. It is interesting to see that all experts
share the same emphasis on virtual technologies which might explain that they have
been willing to overcome the challenges as all of them are convinced by the beneﬁts of
XR in education. Therefore, it can be summarized that currently XR is used in higher
education through pioneer work mostly by educators already having a background in
XR. All described use cases have been developed by the expert or their students, so all
of them started at the same point and went through the same process which can be sum-
marized as the current state for the use of XR for teaching. There seems to be a lack of
standardized frameworks or platforms for teaching experiences where educators might
have access to easy to use XR experiences. As the beneﬁcial usage of XR is evident in
literature and also acknowledged by the conducted interviews of experts in this study it is

Experts’ View on AR/VR in Engineering Education at Universities
1021
crucial for future research to work on standardized guidelines and tools for creating XR
experiences as well as elaborate platforms for sharing and exchanging XR experiences
throughout the university landscape.

Wildﬁres Detection System for Low-Income
Economies
Mirella Elias(B), James Sora, Ronald Musona, and Tinashe Chamunorwa
Transilvania University of Brasov, Brasov, Romania
{mirella.elias,ronald.musona,chamunorwa.tinashe}@unitbv.ro,
james.sora@student.unitbv.ro
Abstract. This paper discusses a technological but low-priced intervention for
one of the major challenges faced in the management of forests, which is wildﬁres.
The paper suggests an affordable solution to mitigate wildﬁres for developing
nations. Numerous advanced technologies have already been developed but in
developing nations it is unaffordable and unsustainable.Systems that are usually
used to mitigate forest ﬁres include NASA satellites, optical cameras, and wireless
sensor networks. In this paper, a system based on low priced but effective IQRF
(technology for wireless packet-oriented communication via radio frequency (RF)
in sub-GHz ISM bands) based wireless sensor nodes is suggested. This paper is
a work in progress to develop a relatively low-cost WSN-based system with low
power consumption and energy harvesting capabilities. A Solar or piezoelectric
energy system can be used for purposes of harnessing ambient energy. A typical
systembasicallywouldcomprisesensornodesthatcollectsenvironmentaldataand
a base node that connects to the internet. The system is envisioned to have a long
ﬁeld life since IQRF is easily programmable and is suited for further adjustments
to suit changing requirements. This paper is a synergy between silviculture and
electronic engineering.
Keywords: Ambient energy · IQRF · Wildﬁres · WSN
1
Introduction
When the term "forest," is mentioned many people immediately envision lush foliage
and trees bursting with ﬂowers and fruits. A forest is an ecosystem consisting of trees
alongside myriad forms of biological diversity. Forests cover around 30% of the global
land area [1] and they provide fresh air, shelter, construction, industrial inputs and many
other vital resources. They actively contribute to climate change by controlling the water
cycle mechanism. When forests are destroyed by natural or human-made disasters, the
natural ecosystem will be disturbed [2]. Forest ﬁres are one of the most prevalent threats
in a forested landscape [3]. Many sophisticated methods do exist for controlling forest
ﬁres, but there are not affordable and sustainable for developing countries. This paper
presents ongoing work to design and develop an affordable alternative.

The importance of forests includes [3]:
• Productivity - It provides a variety of foods, fruits, and medicines. Apart from that, it
provides lumber, which is the main raw material for other businesses’ input.
• Protection - It is home to around 80% of all terrestrial creatures. The forest ﬂoor
comprises a lot of decomposers.
• Social and Recreational - It is a place for going out and also provides a pure atmosphere
for health recovery.
• The forest can reduce the sound pollution from automobiles by absorbing it.
• Forests prevent soil erosion because their roots aid in the appropriate binding of the
earth’s surface layer, therefore aiding in soil richness.
• Forests manage the climate by actively assisting the water cycle process. It also
controls the temperature.
• Forests control runoff, recharge the water aquifers and reduce water in ﬂoods period.
• Forests act as natural cleansers by absorbing CO2 and CO. After the seas, forests are
the biggest CO2 storehouse. As a result, they are playing a signiﬁcant role in reducing
the stages of universal warming impacts.
Forest ﬁres are a worldwide phenomenon with major implications for the environ-
ment, population, and property, and the increased frequency and intensity of wildﬁres
in recent years has been linked to climate change. Forest ﬁres are a serious problem
that affects a wide range of environmental, ecological, and climatic processes and struc-
tures [4]. They are one of the most important variables inﬂuencing global vegetation
succession, composition, and carbon budgets. The huge amount of smoke emissions
emitted by forest ﬁres are of particular concern on a worldwide scale because it alters
the atmospheric composition, degrades air worth, and contributes to universal warming
and climate variation. Africa contributes forty percent of worldwide yearly carbon emis-
sions, yet also has the world’s greatest incidence of grass ﬁres. Because of the frequent
and extensive incidence of wildﬁres, Africa is frequently mentioned as the "ﬁre conti-
nent". This deﬁnition applies equally to all the parts of Africa including the Savannah
which is a signiﬁcant plant society. Africa is vulnerable to thunderbolt storms and has
a ﬁre environment with wet and dry seasons. Even though the thunderbolts were the
direct ﬂaming source of ﬁres in the Africa Savannah in the past, today human factors
have become a threat to forest more than lightning as a source of ﬁres causes. A pre-
vious research report by NASA presented that about (130 million ha) of Savannah and
grasslands burn yearly in Africa (for comparison, the country of South Africa covers an
area of 122 million ha). The heaviest burning is centralized mostly in the subtropical
belt which comprises parts of Mozambique, Congo, Zambia, Angola and Tanzania [5].
The eastern Mediterranean Sea basin had mass-destructive wildﬁres in 2020, which
are becoming an annual occurrence owing to climate change. Syria was one of the
most impacted countries, with ﬂames killing four people and injuring 45 others with
respiratory problems and skin burns. Wildﬁres were recorded in 265 localities in the
governorates of Lattakia, Tartous, and Homs in eastern Syria, with between 50 and 60
main ﬁre spots. These ﬂames caused material and environmental devastation, destroying
individuals’ houses, agricultural crops, and extensive areas of ﬂora, woods, and nature
reserves. Furthermore, it is estimated that wildﬁres burnt more than 30,000 hectares

households via the destruction and damage to houses and livelihood assets, as well as

The target of this research is to create a system to monitor forests to do early detection
of ﬁre in the forest by using sensors of the smoke, especially in developing countries.
2
Related Systems
Some of the systems that has been suggested includes ﬁre detection algorithms for
accurate ﬁre detection [7]. The algorithms like Faster R-CNN are used to reduce false
detection and enhance early ﬁre detection ability. In [8] aerial videos were used to detect
forest ﬁres. By using motion and color characteristics of ﬁre, they were able to extract
ﬁre pixels.
Wireless sensor networks were used in [9] to determine the forest ﬁre types in the
early ﬁre detection. Analysis of the noise power spectrum of the forest ﬁre determined
the magnitude of the ﬁre. A number of related systems that uses wireless sensor networks

1026
M. Elias et al.
and machine learning techniques were developed in [10–12]. In [10], the authors discuss
the utilization of a wireless sensor network in the mitigation of natural disaster effects
in the Himalayas mountains region. In [11], machine learning techniques is used for
prediction of forest ﬁres. Data mining techniques is integrated into sensor nodes for early
detection of forest ﬁre in [12]. A ZigBee-WSN- based forest ﬁre detection system was
implemented in [13]. The system consisted of sensor nodes, cluster heads, coordinators,
routers and remote decision servers. Apart from ﬁre detection, this system also offers
protection management. The general structure of the proposed system is shown in Fig. 2.
Fig. 2. A typical wireless sensor network [13].
The network topology structure for the system is a cluster tree. This topology was
implemented because it offers reduced energy loss and data packages during transfer.
ZigBee technology was used since it is appropriate for low-rate wireless PAN and low
power sensors applicable in multi frequencies. Other beneﬁts of using the ZigBee tech-
nology are that it offers a system that is small in size, long battery life, is highly reliable
and is low cost.
Different types of hardware with WSN nodes are found in the market today for
ﬁre detection and monitoring. The actual sensor that was fabricated is shown in Fig. 3.
This sensor comprises carbon, smoke, humidity and temperature sensing on one module
to detect all the parameters which are highly associated with forest ﬁres. Several nodes
wouldbedeployedintheforesttobemonitoredandprotected.Eachnodewasresponsible
for sending information to the WSN coordinator that has the duty of gathering all the
data from the scattered nodes.

3
Proposed System
The proposed system intents to use IQRF technology to provide a cost-effective solution.
The IQRF technology consists of transceivers, protocols, development tools, gateways
and supporting services. The routing protocol is called IQMESH and it is very robust
with high throughput. The ﬁre detecting sensors will be connected to the sensor node.
Figure 4 shows the wireless network architecture it makes use of the sub GHz ISM
bands (916 MHz,868 MHz, 433 MHz) to provide reliable, low-power, low-data wireless
connectivity. Coverage can extend up to several hundreds of meters. Mesh topology is
chosen in wireless sensor networks because it is more reliable as there is no single point
of failure. In addition, scalability is easy and offers consistent data transmission since
each node is connected to all other nodes. The IQRF module oriented approach offers
low cost (60USD) and low power solution to mitigate the effects of wild ﬁres. The overall
architecture is composed of the following components.
3.1
Transceiver Module
It is a small electronic board with circuitry for realizing wireless RF connectivity. This
module has low power consumption making it suitable for battery-powered applica-
tions. The transceiver contains a built-in microcontroller with an operating system for
supporting MESH networking. In addition to general I/Os, other protocols such as SPI,
I2C and UART can be used. The small compact module in the SIM card format (25 ×

1028
M. Elias et al.
14,9 mm) requires no external components. It offers bidirectional RF communication,
wireless monitoring, control and regulation, remote data acquisition, point-to-point or
network wireless connectivity and the internet of things.
3.2
IQRF Mesh Network
Thebasecomponent of theMeshnetworkis theIQRFtransceiver withaneight-bit micro-
controller unit and an operating system for organizing the operations of the transceiver.
The Mesh network is superior to the star topology with regard to robustness, reliabil-
ity and range. The hardware proﬁle (HWP) plug-in application software implements a
device peripheral access (DPA) byte-oriented protocol, therefore programming is not a
requirement. One coordinator manages the Mesh network with devices up to 239 nodes
and data packets are accessed for the node that is addressed.
3.3
Gateway
The gateway provides an interface between the IQRF network and the internet. The IQRF
Alliance has developed the GSM, Wi-Fi and Ethernet gateways. It includes a sensor node
that can be programmed by the user. The gateway can communicate via HTTPS through
its internal web server and in addition IQRF’s proprietary UDP protocol can be used to
communicate via the UDP transport layer. The IQRF gateway can also be created using
an open-source package, IQRF gateway daemon.
3.4
Cloud
The data is uploaded to the server as soon as the data is logged in the gateway. The
server cloud provides a plug-and-play service between the IQRF network and the users.
The application program interface (API) can be used to access the data on the cloud.
This can be used for monitoring tools such as PHP or java script but however, but a web
interface can be used for simple monitoring and conﬁguration.
3.5
Sensors
The sensors continuously measure carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and methane gases
which are commonly present in the combustion process. In addition, the temperature
and humidity data will also be provided. MG-811 sensor module will be used to sense
the carbon dioxide present in the air. For carbon monoxide sensing, the MQ-7 module
will be used due to its fast response and good sensitivity. The MQ-2 sensor module will
be used for general smoke detection.
3.6
Power
The power unit is composed of a photovoltaic module and a battery. Electrical energy
is required to power the sensor nodes. During the day, excess energy from the PV is
used to charge lithium-ion batteries so that during the night when there is no production,
they will still be powering the sensor nodes. Lithium-ion batteries are the suggested
energy storage devices because of the advantages of long life, high efﬁciency and low
self-discharge.

3.7
Transceiver Components
The transceiver is highly integrated and it contains the RF circuitry, the microcontroller
unit, serial EEPROM and an onboard antenna. The microcontroller is built-in with an
operating system which reduces the development time of the application. As shown from
the manufacturer datasheet, TR-75D transceiver provides serial EEPROM of 256Kb,
three channels A/D converter, analog comparator, 10mW RF output power and PWM
output. Figure 5 and Fig. 6 show the transceiver module and block diagram respectively.
Fig. 5. IQRF module [14].
The IQRF technology has been chosen as it offers a user-friendly interface GUI and
an easy-to-follow procedure for conﬁguring. The system will be tested in the lab prior
to test deployment. A typical interface is shown in Fig. 7.

4
Conclusion
This paper presented a cost-effective solution to mitigate the effects of wildﬁres in
forestry. The solution involves the use of a wireless sensor network of IQRF sensor

Wildﬁres Detection System for Low-Income Economies
1031
nodes that collects data from the sensors and transmits the data through the gateway to
the server. Forests safeguard the earth’s natural equilibrium unfortunately; forest ﬁres are
frequently only discovered after they have spread over a broad region, making control
and containment difﬁcult, if not impossible, at times. As a result, there is a terrible loss
and permanent harm to the environment and climate (30% of (CO2) in the atmosphere is
caused by forest ﬁres), as well as irreparable damage to the ecosystem (large volumes of
smoke and (CO2) in the atmosphere). Long-term devastating repercussions of forest ﬁres
include inﬂuence on local weather patterns, global warming, and the loss of endangered
species of ﬂora and wildlife. Forest ﬁres are a major issue in many nations, and global
warming may exacerbate the situation. The system is envisioned to be an early detection
and warning system which can be saved with timeous response.

Creating Mobile VR Visualisations of 3D
Objects from the Area of the Silk Road
Jerzy Montusiewicz1
, Stanisław Skulimowski1
, Marcin Barszcz1(B)
,
and Rahim Kayumov2
1 Lublin University of Technology, Nadbystrzycka 36B, 20-618 Lublin, Poland
m.barszcz@pollub.pl
2 Scientiﬁc-Experimental Museum-Laboratory, 703004 Samarkand, Uzbekistan
Abstract. The paper presents a process of creating, optimising and testing a
virtual reality application for displaying the “Hujra”, a room for students of the
17th century madrassa in the area of the Silk Road, together with interactive
objects. Introduction of manual 3D modelling could allow the cooperating teams
to work at a distance, aggregating their qualiﬁcations in the area of IT and cultural
heritage. By applying the procedure of optimisation, the designed 3D objects had
sufﬁciently small ﬁle sizes to be introduced into virtual reality, and the fully mobile
application worked effectively using smartphones within the price group available
to the average user. The combination of the complexity of the project and its high
availability via smartphones was considered a successful solution.
Keywords: Mobile VR application · Cultural heritage · Generation Z · Virtual
museum · Immersion
1
Introduction
The development of 3D and 2D computer technologies (hardware and software), as well
as mobile technologies, makes it possible to put into practice the process of digitisation
of cultural heritage objects and use them in many different way.
Firstly – it allows for digital archiving of historic buildings threatened with destruc-
tion due to their age, condition or the conditions in which they are located. For example,
as a result of the ﬁre of the National Museum of Brazil in Rio de Janeiro in 2018, 90%
of the local resources were irretrievably lost [1].
Secondly – the use of 3D technology makes it possible to reach young people.
Representatives of generation Z (according to various sources, the generation born after
1990 and before 2010), the so-called “Digital natives” appreciate the possibility of not
only consuming digital content, but also using the interaction layer. This situation also
applies to cultural heritage objects that can be transferred as 3D models to the VR world.
Thirdly – the popularisation of digital 3D technologies allows for the democratisation
ofaccesstoculturalgoodsofpeoplewithdifferentsocialstatus,economicstatus,political
status. Digital worlds of cultural goods also make it possible to counteract the exclusion
of people with various degrees of physical and mental disabilities.
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023
M. E. Auer et al. (Eds.): ICL 2022, LNNS 634, pp. 1032–1043, 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26190-9_105

Creating Mobile VR Visualisations of 3D Objects
1033
Fourthly – digital objects presented with the use of various available technologies
allow for continuous access to educational and cultural content (independence from the
opening time or the capacity and number of visitors).
Therefore, the process of reconceptualisation [2] of museology requires the creation
of attractive and interesting visualizations of museum artefacts and historic architectural
objects. The term of museology reconceptualisation is understood as supplementing
the traditional exhibition by introducing additional exhibitions, which, for example,
allow to get to know the copies of museum artefacts by touching them (not only for
the blind), to simulate the time of events by the use of inter-active touch monitors, to
get immersed in digital space through the use of VR technology. Employees of the
Department of Computer Science of the Lublin University of Technology (Poland) have
been cooperating with Samarkand State University (Uzbekistan) for several years in
the area of using 3D computer technologies in the area of broadly understood cultural
heritage, museology, protection of architectural objects [3], as well as the reconstruction
of damaged museum objects [4].
The present article pursues the following goals:
• Presentation of the remote cooperation procedure for teams with different professional
competences that will be able to create a joint interdisciplinary project using VR
technology.
• Building digital 3D visualisations of various historic objects which are faithful copies
of originals from a students’ room (hujra) from a typically equipped 17th century
madrassa and transferring the whole to the world of virtual reality.
• Selection of computer technologies, software, tools and optimisation methods and
devices for the proper low-cost, fully autonomous and mobile interactive application
that works properly in the VR environment – the “Hujra” application.
By the term low-cost solution the authors mean that to display the VR world a
smartphone belonging to the mid-price segment will be used, and the phrase completely
autonomous solution means that to render scenes in VR the smartphone will not be
connected to a computer station, will not use cloud resources via internet communication
or be connected to an external source of water.
The created application “Hujra” introduces the user to the pupils’ room, where there
are 7 objects of equipment characteristic of Islamic culture (lauch, book, table, turban,
carpet, two kilims) and 2 objects from outside of this culture (sculpture and painting).
2
Literature Review
Virtual models in the context of creating digital museum exhibitions were introduced
in 1991 by Tsichritzis and Gibbs in a speech presented at the Pittsburgh conference
[5]. In [6], the authors describe their own approach to designing and constructing a VR
museum, but this is an era of solutions that do not use glasses and the experience of
these activities is not fully transferable to modern times. Among the methods of creating
digital 3D objects, they recommend manual modelling when the object consisted mainly
of geometric forms. Strategies for designing VR applications related to cultural heritage,

1034
J. Montusiewicz et al.
describing the guidelines for the development of VR systems and presenting their own
stereoscopic MNEME system (which does not correspond to VR systems in the modern
sense of the term) are presented in [7]. The use of VR in the area of cultural heritage
and museology was presented in works [8–10].
In [11] the authors describe the classiﬁcation of application-oriented VR installa-
tions that can be used in the area of cultural heritage, and practical comments on the
creation of VR exposures in the form of a procedure consisting of 6 steps are found
in [12]. In [13], the authors indicate that the use of modern computer technologies
enables the acceleration of the creation of a network of museum units that represent a
common geographical and cultural area, as well as various centres with collections on
the same subject. Examples of VR applications for mobile platforms can be found in
[14] – studying the possibilities of teaching music to a group of children aged 10–11
with a multi-platform mobile application called VR4EDU, [15] – description of a low-
cost mobile platform (based on Samsung Gear VR Innovator Edition and a Sam-sung
smartphone) intended for research on the impact of the immersive environment on the
efﬁciency of the teaching process (research results not included).
Researchers are more and more willing to implement VR in the ﬁeld of museology.
In [16] the proprietary MARAT (Mobile Augmented Reality Authoring Tool) device
was proposed, which allows mobile creation of complex interactive content in AR in
WYSIWYG mode. Also in [17], a proposal of the VIRTUE system for creating 2D and
3D static and dynamic museum exhibitions was included.
The high quality of VR applications for mobile devices affects the user experience.
Therefore, in [18] the performance analysis of VR application rendered locally on the
phone and remotely – thanks to the server and wireless network (802.11ac standard)
was carried out. Based on the results of the analyses, FURION was proposed – a VR
framework to support high-quality VR applications over a wireless network (Wi-Fi) with
a delay of less than 14ms with a performance of 60 frames per second. The issues of
high quality, low latency in the wireless network (for 4K resolution) and rendering were
also analysed in [19]. Another approach to scene rendering is found in [20], describing
the FlashBack project for weaker HMD VR mobile devices. A very interesting approach
to high-quality sensory immersion is presented by researchers in [21], i.e. CloudVR.
The system provides improved throughput, lower latency and good graphics quality
(multiresolution rendering).
Researchers appreciate VR, AR and MR more and more, anticipating future appli-
cation directions in the ﬁeld of cultural heritage [22] – not only for the visualisation of
museums, but also old cities, monuments, excavations or the reconstruction of damaged
cultural objects.
The literature research shows that the subject of creating mobile applications for
smartphones, commonly available to users, for sharing digital museum resources in VR
technology, is not overly described and implemented. This is mainly due to technical
challenges including, among others: striving for high-quality visualisation on a mobile
device, minimising image generation delays, ensuring good data streaming as well as
correct rendering with its optimisation to relieve the entire process of creating virtual
space. The previously presented works of researchers [18–21] largely focus on technical
problems, the omission and unresolved status of which will not allow for quick and

Creating Mobile VR Visualisations of 3D Objects
1035
easy implementation of mobile VR applications in museology, where graphic details
and accurate mapping are important, e.g. objects, pictures. It can be seen that the subject
matter is developing at the fastest rate possible, despite the dominance of desktop VR
applications in the area of cultural heritage.
However, the available works on the implementation of VR technologies in the
area of broadly understood cultural heritage do not pay attention to the geographical
context. What is a technological standard, e.g. for most European countries (devices
used, wireless network availability, data transfer speed, data processing availability in
cloud computing, low costs in relation to the average income of residents) is not a rule in
other regions or countries. Such a situation occurs, inter alia, in many places in the area
of the Silk Road in the countries of Central Asia [23, 24]. Therefore, the solutions used
to create applications intended for VR technology should be designed and prepared
to be completely autonomous and cheap. The authors of this work exclude solutions
intended for installation on specialised VR devices and systems, recognising mobile
VR as technologies more conducive to the democratisation of access to educational and
cultural content. In addition, it was assumed that the devices used, such as a smartphone,
will not have to use a connection to a computer or a cloud-based system to parallelise
and accelerate the calculations.
3
Method and Materials
3.1
Substantive Competences of Cooperating Teams
Creating digital 3D exhibitions of historic objects for the purposes of VR, regardless of
whether they are obtained by 3D scanning or based on documentation (photos, descrip-
tions, dimensions), requires cooperation between people from the IT and museology
industry. IT specialists are knowledgeable about the available technologies and tools
that can be used to transfer objects to the digital world. They can choose the right tools
for speciﬁc needs. They also have the skill to operate them, which allows them to cre-
ate digital displays. On the other hand, museologists are specialists with the necessary
knowledge in the ﬁeld of the humanities: history of art, general history and religion,
monument conservation, didactics and cultural studies.
The development of digital expositions at a distance requires the cooperation of both
teams, where one of them has access to real historical objects and is at their place of
occurrence (a team gathering museum professionals and art historians), and the other
will perform a digital exhibition (a team of computer vision specialists). For the pur-
poses of this article, the authors developed procedures that divide the activities between
the two teams according to their substantive competences. Figure 1a shows the areas
of competence of both teams. On the Polish side, there are employees of the Depart-
ment of Computer Science at the Lublin University of Technology (LUT) – specialists
in computer graphics, 3D computer modelling, virtual reality and reverse engineering
(representing the Laboratory of Intelligent Systems Programming and 3D Technologies –
Lab 3D). On the Uzbek side, these are people working in the Scientiﬁc and Experimental
Laboratory of the Museum of the Samarkand State University (SamSU) – specialists in
the ﬁeld of art history and museology.

1036
J. Montusiewicz et al.
According to work [25], competences can be considered a combination of three
main components, which include knowledge, skills and responsibility, Fig. 1b. One of
the components of theoretical knowledge was taken into account when developing the
algorithm for creating digital exposures at a distance (in cooperation with teams), since
an important aspect is that each team should have basic theoretical knowledge about
the competences of the other team, Fig. 1c. This approach allows for efﬁcient work
and correct performance of the agreed activities by employees representing LUT and
SamSU. It also helps for terms, deﬁnitions and concepts to be understood correctly
and reduced the risk of errors. SamSU employees were provided with basic theoretical
knowledge in the ﬁeld of 3D computer modelling, so that the employees could correctly
prepare appropriate documentation: photos, sketches, dimensions. On the other hand,
LUT employees were provided with knowledge in the area of cultural heritage in order
to consciously apply methods of optimising 3D models that reduce their size.
Fig. 1. Diagram of cooperation between Poland and Uzbekistan teams: a) areas of substantive
competences of the LUT and SamSU teams; b) the components of the overall competency model;
c) areas of competence and their scope for both teams.
Before starting the project, a detailed algorithm for creating a museum exhibition in
the VR environment was prepared, Fig. 2. There were three main phases in it: planning,
prototyping and testing. There are appropriate activities in each phase. Both phases and
activities are closely related and must be carried out in the order represented by the
arrows. If it turns out that the data are incomplete at the stage of the 3D modelling and
texturing process, there is a feedback with the relevant information for the planning
phase – data acquisition. Generally, most activities are performed by employees repre-
senting IT skills, but the beginning and end of activities are carried out by employees
representing the museology sector.

3.2
Selection of the Target Platform and Devices for Building Applications
in the VR Environment
From among the available platforms offering VR projection, i.e. Oculus Rift, Oculus
Quest and HTC Vive, the authors have chosen a low-cost solution proposed by Google.
Unlike a stationary VR set, which divides the process of generating a virtual scene and
projection, between a workstation and dedicated VR glasses, respectively, the Google
VR platform uses only an Android mobile device. Moreover, Google VR is an additional
function that does not disturb the work of other processes on the mobile device and does
not prevent further use of the device in the usual way. On the other hand, standalone
VR, which, like Google VR, is based on a device that integrates the computing and
projection layers, cannot be used for anything other than the consumption of VR content.
Nevertheless, the authors are aware of the limitations and risks associated with basing
the project on Google VR technology.
Hovewer in addition to limitations, there are also facts that clearly support the need
to use Google VR. First of all, mobile devices that are able to generate and display VR
projections (mobile devices with Android, a display with a minimum resolution of full
HD and at least equipped with a magnetometer) are much more widespread in relation
to workstations dedicated to VR and standalone VR devices.

1038
J. Montusiewicz et al.
To run the mobile VR application, you need a device with Android version at least
6.1, with a screen diagonal no smaller than 5 in., with a resolution of no less than 1920 ×
1080. The device must be equipped with a magnetometer.
In addition, an investment in a new smartphone is much lower compared to one in
a dedicated workstation meeting the requirements for projection using stationary VR
headsets, or to standalone VR devices.
In summary, a solution using mobile devices signiﬁcantly reduces costs for the user –
apart from the phone that meets the minimum requirements, which he most likely already
has. Usually it is enough for the user to obtain relatively cheaply and easily a VR frame
and Bluetooth controller (Fig. 3).
Fig. 3. (A) Example of devices used for the presentation of mobile exhibition in the VR environ-
ment, (B) Initial version of the application running on the test device, (C) example of VR frame
to put Android smartphone into, (D) additional movement controller).
In addition, the entry barrier for new users is much smaller when they can use devices
they already have and with which they are familiar, as opposed to a group that would have
to buy a new workstation or a dedicated mobile VR headset. It should be remembered
that the group of potential users of the application proposed by the authors may not be
interested in investing in computer equipment.
3.3
Selection of Interactive Virtual Scene Creation and Programming Software
To prepare the project of an IVS, the authors decided to use the editor used mainly to
create games – Unity. There were three reasons behind this. First, high convergence of
the project assumptions with the project of a typical computer game (virtual space, user
interaction with the virtual environment through a virtual avatar, triggering visual effects,
etc.). Secondly integration of many tools helpful in creating a IVS in one program (e.g.
module for assigning behavioural patterns to objects on the scene, creating and managing
collisions, proﬁler taking into account the level of complexity of the scene, number and
complexity of visual effects, etc.). Thirdly, the ability to port prepared projects to multiple
target platforms, including Google VR mobile platform.
To create scripts describing the application’s main logic, rules of interaction
and changing the characteristics of IVS objects over time, the Visual Studio 2017
development environment was used.

3.4
Selection of Tools for Creating 3D Models and Textures
That is Autodesk software was selected to prepare the 3D models. AutoCAD 2020 was
useful for the design of the entire room due to its parametric programming capabilities.
3dsMax 2020, a mesh modelling program, was used to design individual pieces of
equipment.
Furthermore for the preparation of photorealistic textures, which are mapped to the
surfaces of 3D models in a timely manner, a free program for creating and editing raster
graphics, i.e. Gimp version 2020 was chosen.
4
Project Implementation
4.1
Creating Photorealistic Models of the Hujra and Its Equipment
The 3D model of the hujra, along with its furnishings, was made by the employees of
the LUT Department of Computer Science on the basis of documentation in the form
of photos and sketches with dimensions provided by a team from Uzbekistan. There are
7 different objects in the students’ room, which are typical equipment of such a room.
Particularly noteworthy is the lauch – a folding book stand cut from one board (the
ﬁnal structure is created without gluing or using other techniques for joining wooden
elements). The lauch is a unique woodcarving product characteristic of the Islamic art
of Uzbekistan.
The modelling process was divided into two stages. The ﬁrst is the creation of 3D
models, and the second – the preparation of textures to generate photorealistic objects.
The models prepared were saved in the .fbx format (which allows to store all infor-
mation about models, textures and settings) and ﬁles were imported into the Unity
environment. Figure 4 shows the photorealistic 3D models rendered with optimal
settings.
Fig. 4. 3D models: (A) kilims and turban, (B) hexagonal table, (C, D) lauch in two animation
example states.
Additionally digital models of objects that do not belong to Muslim culture were
made: a 3D model of a porcelain ﬁgurine representing a woman of European features
and a portrait of the “Lady with an Ermine”. Of course, the authors of the article knew
that the culture of Islam did not allow the creation of works depicting persons. Placing
such artefacts was to make it possible to check whether application users were able
to focus on what they observed despite the perceived immersion into the VR world.

1040
J. Montusiewicz et al.
The 3D model of the porcelain ﬁgurine, located in the Zamoyski Museum in Kozłówka
(Poland), was created using the 3D scanning technique using the Artec Eva scanner. The
data obtained in the form of a cloud of x, y, z coordinates was processed using the Artec
Studio Professional 15 program, which ultimately resulted in obtaining a mesh model
with the applied texture. From Artec Studio, the model was exported to an.obj ﬁle, the
total size of which was over 4.9 MB. Two ﬁles were obtained: in one the mesh model
of a 3D object was saved, and in the other – a texture. The image of the “Lady with an
Ermine”, a famous painting by Leonardo da Vinci located at the Czartoryski Museum
in Kraków (Poland) were made by means of classic modelling in the 3ds max program.
On the surface of the model there is a texture of 800 × 1046 resolution with an image
of a woman with an ermine. Ultimately, the size of the object in the 3ds max format was
close to 590 kB, and after transfer to the .fbx format, it was 22.8 kB.
The obtained 3D model of the porcelain ﬁgurine, due to too many edges (vertices:
37041, walls: 73914), was not suitable for use in the VR application, because it would
load it too much. Converting the .obj ﬁle to .fbx format using 3ds Max reduced its size
to approximately 2.76 MB (56% of the original ﬁle). In order to further reduce its size,
optimisation of the mesh was performed. The optimal solution was the mesh model of
15,100 vertices and 30,031 faces, the ﬁle size of which is approximately 1.26 MB. For
a mesh with fewer vertices and faces, there were too many distortions especially visible
on the model face.
4.2
Transfer of Models to VR Environments
Based on the adopted design assumptions and prepared assets, it was possible to prepare a
proof of concept for the VR application in Unity software. The prepared sketch included:
the implementation of the stereoscopic image rendering function (Google VR SDK
integration) along with the basic interaction control mechanisms, calibration of light
sources on the stage and the method of shading objects.
Further work on the “Hujra” application required, above all, to deﬁne the scope of the
participant’s freedom in contact with the virtual scene, expressed by the way the user’s
avatar moves within the scene, ways of interacting with elements of the environment,
and determining the results of the interaction. For this purpose, a set of functions was
developed, which were assigned to the scene objects using the Unity script mechanism.
These were, among others:
• the function recognising the user’s state of concentration (the object at which the user
was staring could be highlighted),
• interaction management function (based on: the avatar’s distance from the object,
directing the participant’s gaze to the object, willingness to interact by pressing a
button),
• function delegating interaction actions (each object was assigned a unique function
that deﬁnes how the object behaves when the interaction is to be performed, e.g. for
the hapan it was only displaying the text, while for the book and lauch it was triggering
the page turning animation).

4.3
Application Testint and Optimisation Process
During the initial tests, most of the errors related to the rendering (Single Pass Stereo
rendering on which Google VR SDK is based) of the scene were eliminated. Similarly,
overall optimisations resulted in ensuring the stability of the application and extending
the operation of the device due to the reduction of energy consumption. Optimisations
were mandatory since the image refresh rate and the application’s response to user
interactions are crucial as in the case of VR applications they are a decisive factor for
the willingness to continue participation. In an extreme case, the low performance of
the application may lead to VR sickness (dizziness, labyrinth disorders, nausea, etc.)
and effectively break the participant out of the experience. A detailed description of the
optimisation mechanisms used (like baked lighting and shadows resolution reduction,
the level of details technique, or occlusion culling), as well as problems related to the
conﬁguration and testing of the application, are described in [26]. The interior view of
the hujra presented in the VR environment is shown in Fig. 5. Figure 5b presents example
photo reference.
Fig. 5. View of the interior of the hujra: (A) in the VR environment, (B) reference photo.
5
Conclusions and Future Work
Collaboration between Lab 3D – Lublin University of Technology (Poland) and
Samarkand State University (Uzbekistan), based to a large extent on remote work, was
successful both in terms of preparing all materials for the application and its testing.
This conﬁrms the authors in the belief that this type of international cooperation projects
do not differ so much from other local IT projects, which, due to the ongoing COVID19
pandemic, are also implemented remotely. The difference, however, is the ability to build
an international network of contacts and the ability to reach a wider audience.
The authors intend to continue working on the application in four areas:
1. Adding more advanced interactions with digital objects on stage and creating group
VR sessions.
2. Adding analytical tools for automatic collecting of data about VR sessions, for the
content better adjustment and to conduct more complex research.

1042
J. Montusiewicz et al.
3. Expanding the database of the Interactive Virtual Scene and 3D artefacts.
4. Preparing several language versions of descriptions of exhibits.
In addition, the authors plan to test additional optimisation methods (such as the use
of asynchronous reprojection offered for devices compatible with the Daydream speciﬁ-
cation, and others and check whether they will be able to provide a higher quality image
or content richer in additional interactions, without negative effects on the performance
of the device used.

Laurent,iu Beldean and Fulvia Anca Constantin(B)

Abstract. Now-a-days musicians including composers are tempted to encom-
pass in their strategy of composing not only the solid features implied by the
traditional emergent formulas (of writing gestural sequences on sheets of paper)
showing the need of recurring the patriarchal patterns. They aim to stop the imi-
tative, sedimented expression (depicting a canonical crescendo), being prepared
to meet ideas from outside the ‘western ear’. With an agnostic attitude most of
composers who live in an authentical present are insisting to start thinking on the
“zero degree” occurence, that factor of atypical, ex-musical (non-fundamental)
processes from whose speciﬁc vacuum arises an immersive media, the display of
new art-work possibilities. Considering important the mission of interacting with
art (let it be musical, visual etc.) by means of intellectual channels capable to com-
municate technological innovations, or a (super)praxis with computer as the main
ambassador within the globalized culture, the composers call dominantly for a
interruption of the rustic paradigm of ‚canonical crescendo(s)’ bringing closer the
dialog with the digital world. Our paper respondes to questions with regard to the
need of translating −just this complex part −into performative composing strate-
gies. Then emphasizes the function of media heterogenity absorbtion which inte-
grates a cross-modal perception as generative setting for digital communication
environment.

Lateral thinking
1
Introduction
Digitalization and technological developments reveal ﬁelds of exploration conditioning
the criteria of locating ourselves and accepting our solitude in the proximity of the com-
puter’s intelligence as Platonic companion. Appearing for the composer as precocious,
the voice of the digital intuitions remains – in this regard – present, and has an evident
effectiveness upon thinking about music, about the interregnum concerning its meaning
around the traditional logo. The digital pulse and the sonic tools in composition or per-
formance are entirely recognized −coming into contact with the non-arbitrary physical

interface [1] −by devoting their telos on the (post)modern features and characteristic
coherence.
In the last decades, the “computer revolution” has brought new, signiﬁcant capa-
bilities for musicians. Therefore, the educational system changed its historically con-
formed “optical point of view” exhibiting some rethought cognitive maps, attempting
to emphasize the frame of human computer interaction’s seductiveness. It bears thus a
new promise, articulating the larger world surrounding the means of creative composing.
The aim of this paper is to locate- and enter- the cutting edge room for new researching-
ﬁelds built as multi-sensory input (revealed by a cross-modal perception[2]) as reference
space, and then to point out ways which enable “the composer/performer to interact with
the computer […] by understanding the program and by making sounds to communicate
with it.” [1].
The unifying ﬁeld associated with cross-modal perception can be understood as a
preexisting transmission of a cognitive motion “from visibility to invisibility, presence
to absence”.[3] The key-distinction between the lineary, ﬂat delivered stimulus (a some-
where else effected one), and the distinguishable, well separated faculties of discerning
senzorialities signalizing the articulation of a “surprising kind of musical coordination,
but often also […] a number of unforeseen timing complexities that contribute to the
musical ﬂow” [1] deﬁnes a co-existence of a control productivity alongside with data
which have to be detailed in structures and particular speciﬁcations. The multipresent
interaction between man and the artiﬁcial concern of the computer which actually avoids
the rectlinear matching, led composers like Iannis Xenakis or John Cage to imagine the
departure and returning of the sound-events in a dinamic ﬁeld of resources, groups of
events available in a mobile cosmos of parameters which work due to the distant obser-
vation (remote control), being “open to chance operations” [1]. Xenakis was among the
pioneers who introduced computational calculus and algorithmic practice by respond-
ing to his internal needs of formalization in composition. Even if now his ideas are
viewed as mainstream for the composers who sprang up in the electroacoustic paradigm
Xenakis intuition became evident since the 1960s, when he produced specialized com-
puter programs generated in IBM environment. Remaining their strong background and
the terrain for a philosophy of composition the radically thought of Xenakis, his art of
“unmusicality” was able to deﬁne a new system of reference: through features of ugliness
and Antihumanism. Through his signature he clariﬁed to the musicians’ community that
the mark of raw material must govern (as a generative engine) the informal subjection
of sound. The design of the technological means was constantly called upon to enable
a creative role, where the man and the dynamic system of computer’s software become
coauthors in the compositional process through calculation and stochastic distributions;
that this process is based on a maxi-science [4]. At risk – so to say −Xenakis achieved
the understanding of his role, of his integrity as composer examining the invasive [2]
behavior of the sound, insisting to reconsider its use its all physical force not only that
in a small portion devoted to the traditional syntax.
The re-territorialization of the music composing episteme in the last decades of XXth
century and in our time due to the new expanded hegemony of a wider social narrative
broadens the horizon of composer’s identity letting him become richer in approach and
in a powerful contact with the ‘visual polyphony’ of the digital world.

2
Digitalization as a Cultural, Technical and Psychological
Phenomena
The development in technology and the narrative informatics illustrate the complete
power and control by means of the software systems, and is close to the moment which
makes free the involvement in creation of the “virtual musicians” [5] which are breathing
nearby humans, nearby the real composers. Without substituting the humans, computers
become the necessary tools for processing electroacoustic musical art. They achieved
the features of both subjects and objects, explaining the process of visibility as central
point in a multimedia communication. Whilst they play a role of an image and projec-
tion, they are also acknowledged as real messengers in the networking Internet-chain, as
members of a new cultural-distribution medium. Composers learn technical knowledge
connected to computers’ programming by self-studying decoding manuals about soft-
ware and making research in Internet for information [6]. The software programs created
by IRCAM-Paris technologies offer the possibility of experimenting and evaluate digital
musical instruments. Thus, synthetic sounds −units of manipulation of sound objects
−transform perceptual data, are associated with emotional reactions and “can even be
organized around an emotional node.” (Idem).
The disciple (graduate student or master’s degree achiever) animated by the idea of
electroacoustic composition must immerse himself in a different world, to understand
the relationship with phenomenally of the sound spectrum, that it is necessary to know
the “three pillars of Sound Design” and that “psychoacoustics will be needed to help us
understand how we perceive physical sounds.” [2].
2.1
From Written Scores to Digitalization
Digitization (digitalization) as a phenomenon of engagement in a culture of post-
humanism has been absorbed into the ﬁeld of contemporary music as a form of de-
petriﬁcation of a worn-out compositional episteme in which the relationship between
written score (notes) and sound in the deterministic sense dominates. Music transmitted
through written culture has endured for centuries through collections of signs (semiotics
(e.g. a “semiological excess” (Roland Barthes)) in the traditional or contemporary sense).
Sounds were transported by the composer into the cosmos of signs trying to display his
internal voice. And from that clarity, from his language (story’s arsenal) expressing the
exigency of the notated and edited page(s), the reverse route was taken co-opting the
interest of the receiving subject.
Taking this stage into account, we can realize that the need to go beyond the elemen-
tary, this solidiﬁed way of communicating the work had to be partly rethought, since
the construction of music involved another semantic pressure, the discourse of a new
stability. The digital world entered the realm concerned by the stable architecture of
structures (having lived in the frozen mind of the earlier composer for a very long time)
and emptied the toolbox mechanisms which have built the old roots of their story using
a new force of growth, up to exhaustiveness; is to be the digitalization in composing
offensive? Or cathartic? It is difﬁcult to argue about. The binary meta-motif constrained
to be made of bits and conformed fundamentally on the causal scheme of <0>, <1> is
the element of action which changes the modality of producing imagery of sounds.

Modes of Interaction with the Digital Environment
1047
Parceling out the data of computer software by means of preservation, this meta-
motif allows – by making use of mathematical (trivial) operations as that additive or
multiplicative −the condition of conveying messages. Pedagogical speaking, it can
identify these messages by distinguishing an input, an output and −in between −a
chainofinternalprocesses.The<0>,<1>meta-motif fortiﬁestheoverlappedprocesses
activating in a large amount the computer technology.
An elastic psychology is therefore born. By decentering the steps of the lonely,
homogenous composer (accustomed to work in the écriture-paradigm), a more ﬂuid
attention will bring him close to the non-homogeneity manifested through interaction
with the computer, in terms of programming its duties. Part of the new syntax works
with samples-technologies; his adherence to the web of megabytes letting apart the
cliché of thinking in keys and notes-system (tonalities, modes, and series (using the
Row-technique for example)) establishes a reformulation of his artistic identity, and,
in the long run, an audio-visually conﬁgured experience. Confronting the frozen envi-
ronment of composing with written notes and ‘already being said’ sounds (nowadays
understood mainly as a Xerox-machine reﬂex,) the ‘atypical’ composer activates a much
lively relationship with his artistic product bringing into question understandings of
new, possible cultural patterns of interaction with media and digital art in his social life
communicational experience.
The psychology behind the interaction with the phenomenon of digitalization
remains linked to the need of freeing the composer from the prejudice of respecting
a system of codes, of hierarchies bound to the thematical rhetoric −as music history
has continually been taught that the score’s conventionality works −, and to answer
the question whether the art nowadays should be more inclined to digitalization, or to
ornamentation [7].
Digitalization articulates a new way of processing information by letting the humans
sensory world’s experience to encounter and accept the presence of binarity and the
new semantic equipping played by a computer and technology; the composer is to
be confronted with categories of ‘non-ornamental’ data being oriented to rely on a
ﬁxed compositional archetype; it is that archetype based on the mentioned cross-modal
perception which proposes the engagement of the computer in sharing experience with
the composer and to switch the abilities of the latter to those of the ﬁrst. Human Computer
Interaction (HCI) paradigm which deﬁnes a gravitational contact between the two, adds
meanings and a larger dispositive of work in conceiving a musical ópus.
Thus, the implementation of compositional laws in which the synthesizer’s sound, the
reaction of a machine, e.g., the computer can disclose and validate its “artistic latency” by
working side by side with the programmer who is also the composer (performer) implies
the vision of a combination of qualities on both sides. The ﬁeld of re-presentation of
human-machine, interchangeable skills, imply lateral, creative thinking. This thinking,
different from critical / vertical (traditional) thinking, involves a practice that approaches
the light of consciousness differently, using inter-sensory knowledge tools.
The discipline of projecting a speciﬁc program able to connect the functions of the
dialogue composer – computer articulates its ground when the live-performer exposes
a sound texture to a MIDI piano (for example), requiring to the computer expression
consistency for being able to react sonically to the human input; this duet-performing
